title: Chat to strangers and let your kids be bored: how to embrace a ‘slow September’ – and enjoy life more | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: The pressure to self-optimise at the start of the new school year can lead to disappointment and burnout. Instead, here are seven ways to slow things down and reap the benefits
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The pressure to self-optimise at the start of the new school year can lead to disappointment and burnout. Instead, here are seven ways to slow things down and reap the benefits
Content: Illustration: Lisa Sheehan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Lisa Sheehan/The GuardianHealth & wellbeingChat to strangers and let your kids be bored: how to embrace a ‘slow September’ – and enjoy life moreThe pressure to self-optimise at the start of the new school year can lead to disappointment and burnout. Instead, here are seven ways to slow things down and reap the benefitsRebecca CopeFri 4 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is a hangover from our school days that September can feel like a time for getting back to the grind. As in January, there is a sense that we should return as better workers, partners, friends and parents. This sense is even stronger now a culture of optimisation – has taken over – evidenced by the fad for adding “maxx” to everything. Yet that can lead to disappointment and burnout, which Mental Health UK reports up to91% of adults were at risk fromover a recent 12-month period.One antidote to this drive is to embrace a slower way of living. Rather than always rushing from one activity to the next, we could be enjoying life.“In the age of digitisation, from work to socialising, we are seeing everything intensify,” says Heejung Chung, aprofessor of work and employment at King’s College London. “But by doing everything, we’re also creating a culture where it’s seen as normal. So you are not only creating a standard for yourself, but for everyone else as well. There is a creeping set of collective expectations that we can do everything, especially women, and we need to change it.”So say “no” to self-optimisation this September, and instead embrace these practical ways to slow everything down – from work to parenting.Make time for micro-connectionsMore often than not, we feel as though we don’t have enough time to converse with strangers in our daily lives, whether that be the woman next to you at the bus stop or the barista making your coffee. Yet taking the time to mindfully have a conversation with someone we don’t know has tangible benefits.double quotation markWhen we’re busy, we feel like we can’t spare time for other people, but if we never take that time, we’ll never stop feeling busyInOnce Upon a Stranger: The Science of How Small Talk Can Add Up to a Big Life, Dr Gillian Sandstrom argues just this. “Research shows that even tiny conversations with strangers improve our mood,” she explains. “They naturally slow you down, so you start paying more attention to the people around you and your surroundings. They also help you learn new things – I’ve met someone who rescues bats at Durham Cathedral, and a publican who taught me that asparagus squeaks.”Sandstrom points to a 2012 study,Giving Time Gives You Time, which shows that when you spend time on other people, you end up feeling as though you have more time yourself. “When we’re busy, we feel like we can’t spare time for other people, but if we never take that time, we’ll never stop feeling busy,” she adds. “It’s counterintuitive but it works.”Walk at someone else’s paceOne literal way to slow down is to start walking at someone else’s pace. “If you’re with a child, an older adult, or even your dog, let them set the pace instead of pulling them along,” says Sarah Hodges, therapy network manager at the mental health and meditation app Headspace. “When we stop rushing to keep our own schedules, we often notice things we would have missed, like the small moments, conversations and connections that make life meaningful. Research on mindfulness and attention shows that when we slow down and intentionally notice what is happening around us, we can reduce stress.”Prof Mark Williams, founding director of the Oxford Mindfulness Foundation, also suggests walking with an upright posture. “Most of us walk leaning into the future, mentally rushing towards whatever comes next,” he says. “Research shows that simply standing or walking a little more upright can positively influence how you feel.”View image in fullscreenIllustration: Lisa Sheehan/The GuardianLet your children be boredIf you are a parent who is preoccupied with ensuring your child is always busy, you might be doing them a disservice. “Being bored is part of the human experience,” says Stephanie O’Dea, author of Slow Living: Cultivating a Life of Purpose in a Hustle-Driven World.“This is how creativity, imagination and independence begin. A child saying they are bored isn’t an indictment of your parenting.”Nine life lessons from the happiest man in the world: from embracing tiny changes to not overthinking meditationRead moreAllow them the space for imaginative play. “A child is more likely to play independently if you spend time with them beforehand,” says Dr Maral Amani, a paediatric physical therapist and child development expert. “A helpful response the next time your child says, ‘I’m bored,’ is to resist immediately solving the problem. Instead, try offering confidence. You might say: ‘Hmm, I wonder what you’ll come up with.’ This communicates that you believe they are capable of finding something to do on their own.”Another suggestion is to invite your child to help you with whatever you’re doing. “If you’re folding laundry, cooking dinner or putting dishes away, you could say: ‘Do you want to keep me company and tell me a story while I do this?’” says Amani. “Sometimes children aren’t looking for entertainment, they’re looking for connection. Inviting them into your everyday activities shows them that ordinary moments can be meaningful.”Do a ‘no outcome’ activityMany of us feel we always need to be productive, even during our downtime. Yet there is much joy to be had in actual leisure time, whether that is doodling, kicking a ball around the garden with your child or listening to music. “Do something with no goal beyond enjoyment,” advises Hodges. “Research on rest and recovery highlights the importance of activities that allow us to step away from constant achievement and performance. Doing something simply because we enjoy it helps restore our energy and reminds us that our value is not only tied to what we accomplish.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRosie Nixon, the author ofThe Pro Method: Pause, Reflect, Organise – Three Simple Steps to Reinvent Your Life, a new book about how to overcome burnout, also recommends doing a “joy audit” of what you actually like doing, and sticking to those activities. “Take a minute to pause and reflect on what genuinely fills your cup, and enables you to cope with the more demanding aspects of your life,” she says. “Then deprioritise anything that isn’t serving you any more – whether that’s friendships, or social media accounts you are following.” And if there’s a TV series or book you’re just not getting into, don’t feel you have to complete it.Schedule pauses at workOur always-on work culture means many of us feel as though we can’t take a break during the working day. But as Chung has discovered through her research, having sufficient time away from work makes you a better worker the next day. “For athletes, resting their body isn’t optional; it’s how they are able to perform so well,” she says. “The brain works in much the same way. If your job involves creative thinking, problem-solving or knowledge work, rest isn’t wasted time. It’s what enables you to perform at your best.” For this reason, she argues that working long hours into the night will affect the quality of your work not only at the time, but the next day too.double quotation markMicro-breaks – where you stare out the window, doodle or lean your head back and shut your eyes – are great for mood, productivity and concentrationYet finding time to pause during the day can feel impossible. “Finishing one task simply acts as the trigger to begin the next,” says Williams. “So one particularly useful moment to pause is immediately after completing something.” He recommends taking a “mindfulness minute” , whether that be 10 slow breaths, or walking to refill your water bottle.Claudia Hammond, author of Overwhelmed: Ways to Take the Pressure Off, suggests scheduling your meetings for five past the hour, so that you always have five minutes to catch a breath between hour-long calls. “Arecent studyfound that micro-breaks of just two minutes each hour – where you stare out the window, or doodle, or lean your head back in your chair and shut your eyes – are great for mood and therefore productivity and concentration,” she says.Simplify your social lifeMany believe that in order to have a meaningful experience with our friends, we must be dining at a restaurant, going to an exhibition or attending a party, but some of the most meaningful interactions happen when we’re doing very little at all. “Organising seeing friends can start to feel like a job in itself,” says Hammond. “Especially if there are conflicting priorities, or somewhere requires a deposit, or is fully booked. So it’s a question of remembering that you don’t need to do something massive: it can be as simple as going for a walk.”The same can be said of hosting. Remove the pressure to cook a gourmet meal and design a tablescape. Instead, focus on the joy of sharing a meal together – whether that’s something homemade or a takeaway.“September is about fortifying yourself for the winter, and delving into the pleasures of home and slowness after the freneticism of summer,” says cook and food writer Jago Rackham. “Eat slow-roasted meats and poached fruit, do as little as possible to the excellent seasonal ingredients, and plan long lunches and early dinners to catch the last of the light.”Habit-stack your mindfulnessIf you think you don’t have time for mindfulness, try to incorporate it into what you are already doing. “You can build these small moments of awareness into everyday life without adding anything else to your schedule,” says Williams. “If you’re eating lunch, really pay attention to the experience of eating. When you’re walking, ask yourself: ‘What else is here, apart from all the thoughts in my head?’ You might notice an interesting roofline, a bird perched on a fence, or the way the light falls on a building. Appreciation is incredibly valuable. It brings a little more positivity into the day, and we know that being in a positive mood increases creativity too.”Explore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingWork-life balanceMental healthParents and parentingFamilyHealthWork & careersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at all | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: Such is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for voters, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: Such is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for voters, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Donald Trump at a rally and campaign event at Coastal Carolina University, South Carolina, 10 February 2024.Photograph: Randall Hill/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at a rally and campaign event at Coastal Carolina University, South Carolina, 10 February 2024.Photograph: Randall Hill/EPAOpinionDonald TrumpHow much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at allJonathan FreedlandSuch is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for votersFri 4 Sep 2026 12.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.08 EDTShareWhat is Donald Trump playing at? If it’s true that the best way of understanding the behaviour of an organisation is to assume it’scontrolled by a secret cabalof its enemies, perhaps that same logic extends to the current conduct of the president of the United States. Maybe he secretly wants Republicans to lose the looming midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in the US for the next two years and for whichthe first postal ballotswere sent out today.That’s not as mad a theory as it sounds. Indeed, there are at least two reasons why Trump might either be unbothered by Republican defeat in November or even covertly desire it. We’ll come to those, but let’s start with a pattern of behaviour that is hard to explain as anything other than calculated self-sabotage.At the centre of it is the single act that is already defining Trump’s second term: his reckless, failed war of choice against Iran. No matter how many times he declares mission accomplished or claims to have destroyed the Iranian military or to have reopened the strait of Hormuz, the facts keep telling a different story. In the past week, the two sides shifted from an economic standoffback to a shooting war, with the US firing on Iranian targets that included a wedding party, killing four, and Tehran striking out all over the neighbourhood, hitting Iraq, Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain.The impact on US voters is severe, felt most directly through rising petrol prices and grocery bills. But look atthe graphmeasuring the cost the US government must pay to borrow money: it’s been a steep upward climb since 28 February, the day the war began,hitting a fresh high on Tuesday. For consumers, that rise translates into an expected jump in interest rates. It means that many of those casting ballots are likely to be doing so just as they start paying more on their credit card bills and mortgages. Given that Trump was elected in November 2024 on a promise to bring down inflation, it’s hard to think of a worse environment for a governing party about to face the voters’ verdict. And that’s before you consider the disenchantment of the Maga faithful, who thought the whole point of Trump was an end to forever wars in the Middle East.And yet, Iran may not even be the most electorally damaging of Trump’s foreign adventures. He is, and it would once have been absurd to write this sentence, leading his country into a state of war with … Canada. It’s easy to laugh at the petty gestures, such as Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America, a move shamefully followed, and therefore endorsed, byApple and Googlein their map apps. But the economic confrontation is serious – and seriously damaging to Republicans’ electoral prospects.For which US states are hit hardest by Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” response to Trump’s tariffs? Why, it’sMichigan, Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Texas, all of which just happen to have key senate contests this year. Republican candidates in those states now have to explain why a crucial and previously friendly export market – Canada takes nearly a third of Iowa’s exports, for example – has suddenly turned icy.What’s odd is that Trump’s trade wars are also wars of choice, and they are hurting especially badly what should be a reliable Republican constituency: farmers. Take Iowa: Democrats have not won a senate seat in that farming state for nearly 20 years, yet now, thanks to Trump’s tariffs, they have a genuine shot.Still, perhaps the most egregious illustration of Trump’s apparent determination to ruin Republican chances in the midterms is his support for datacentres. Few issues have seen their salience rise so quickly and in such a clear direction: almost overnight, they have become objects of fear and loathing across the country and across the political spectrum, withseven in 10 Americanssaying they would not want one anywhere near where they live. Even among Republicans,there is deep concernover their environmental impact, energy consumption and water use. For others, datacentres have become a lightning rod for a broader anxiety over AI and what it may do to our jobs and our lives. Either way, they are kryptonite to voters.So where does Trump stand? “The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want data centres is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,”the president postedon Monday. In that remark, he not only put himself at odds with most US voters, he insulted them too.It’s almost a talent, this ability of Trump’s to land on the wrong side of so-called 80/20 issues, siding with one-fifth of the electorate against the rest. Likewise, strong majorities oppose his vanity projects, whetherdemolishing the East Wingof the White House to build a ballroom or putting his signature on the dollar bill, yet he persists not only in doing them but in talking about them constantly.And all the while, he has hobbled his party by endorsing radioactively unpopular candidates. Few politicians in the US are more tainted than Ken Paxton, who as attorney general of Texas wasimpeached by his fellow Republicanson a long list of charges that included bribery and abuse of public trust. Yet who did Trump back as the Republicans’ senate choice in Texas? As a result, now even thatred-state stronghold is shaky.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higher | Sina ToossiRead morePut it all together, and these look like the actions of a man who has no fear of the blue wave that seems to be coming and who could not care less if it sweeps away the Republicans’ current majorities in Congress. That’s curious, given how useful it has been for Trump to have Capitol Hill serve as a rubber stamp that, combined with a largely pliant supreme court, has allowed him to rule with the scarcely fettered power of a would-be autocrat. What could explain the insouciance?One answer is that Congress’s most potent weapon – the power of subpoena and investigation – holds no terror for Trump because he knows that the House and Senate have no means to enforce their will. They have no police or troops at their command. They can issue their writs and summonses, and he will simply ignore them – comforted by the near-blanket immunity he has already been granted by the supreme court. If Congress goes after his aides and advisers, he will instruct them to follow his lead, on the promise of a comprehensive presidential pardon protecting them from any and all legal consequences. The only real weapon Congress has – impeachment and removal from office – he knows they will never use. If senate Republicans could acquit him after the 6 January insurrection, as they did, he knows they will never vote to convict him of anything, no matter how great the crime.But that only goes so far. It explains why Trump does not fear Republican defeat in November, but not why he would actively seek it. For that, one has to look into the abyss that passes for the president’s soul. The bestselling new bookRegime Change, by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, spells it out: “If Republicans were wiped out in the 2026 midterm elections, or in 2028, he could simply boast that they couldn’t win without him” on the ballot paper. Such is Trump’s narcissism, he will take an epic Republican defeat in two months’ time not as a repudiation, but as a compliment. And, it seems, he is doing all he can to earn it.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS midterm elections 2026US politicsUS economycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m used to doing the impossible’: George Lucas unveils new LA museum – what’s its story? | Museums | The Guardian
description: Spaceship-shaped gallery, featuring works from Banksy, Norman Rockwell and Frida Kahlo, is devoted to ‘visual storytelling’ – and is finally ready to open
Author: Matthew Cantor
Headline: Spaceship-shaped gallery, featuring works from Banksy, Norman Rockwell and Frida Kahlo, is devoted to ‘visual storytelling’ – and is finally ready to open
Content: The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art aims to be a testament to visual storytelling across all kinds of media – paintings, comics, murals, photography, sculpture.Photograph: Courtesy Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtView image in fullscreenThe Lucas Museum of Narrative Art aims to be a testament to visual storytelling across all kinds of media – paintings, comics, murals, photography, sculpture.Photograph: Courtesy Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtMuseums‘I’m used to doing the impossible’: George Lucas unveils new LA museum – what’s its story?Spaceship-shaped gallery, featuring works from Banksy, Norman Rockwell and Frida Kahlo, is devoted to ‘visual storytelling’ – and is finally ready to openMatthew Cantorin Los AngelesFri 4 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m used to doing the impossible,”George Lucassaid on Wednesday. But “this one almost broke my will”.The film-maker was describing the decades of work that went into his latest project, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, as it was unveiled to the press inLos Angeleseight years after breaking ground, following attempts to build it in two other cities. Shaped like a spaceship and towering over the nearby University of Southern California – Lucas’s alma mater – the long-awaited institution finally opens on 22 September. It aims to be a testament to visual storytelling across all kinds of media – paintings, comics, murals, photography, sculpture.The result is 100,000 sq ft of gallery space featuring a striking variety of pieces, ranging from works by Judy Baca,Norman Rockwell, Diego Rivera and Banksy to the Wizard of Oz’s Cowardly Lion costume to drawings of Asterix and Garfield. What unites the seemingly disparate works is their function: to tell a story, often in a single frame, as Lucas’s co-founder and wife, Mellody Hobson, told members of the press on Wednesday.Visual storytelling “is the art that surrounds us”, said Ryan Linkof, the museum’s senior curator. “It is the art in the visual history that we assume every day, often without even realizing it. Newspaper photographs, advertisements, book covers, comic books, posters, street art, movies.”View image in fullscreenGeorge Lucas and Mellody Hobson, the founders of the Lucas museum.Photograph: Deanna Templeton/Courtesy of Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtThe couple sees this storytelling as fundamental to the human experience. Narrative art “depicts the myths that anchor us, the stories that we believe in”, Hobson said; pictures, Lucas added, make those myths feel real. All that “creates a group of people with a common belief system, and that common belief system allows them to work together and not kill each other”.The Lucas museum is divided into two sections, one containing most of the galleries and a pair of cinemas, and the other housing its mural collection as well as a research library. With its sleek, flying-saucer-like design, it’s impossible not to think ofStar Wars, though the museum’s architect, Ma Yansong, says he was inspired more by tree canopies and clouds. A plaza between the sections offers shade as well as an oculus: a round opening that allows visitors to “see the sky and the universe”, Yansong told the media.The museum’s construction is a saga of its own. Lucas began collecting art in the 1970s and over the years combined his collection with Hobson’s, Bates said. About 20 years ago, according to Bates, Lucas began working toward the museum’s creation. Plans for it to be built in San Francisco or Chicago fell through. Finally, the project broke ground in Los Angeles in 2018, and eight years later, it is ready to open. LA, Hobson told the media, is “where we believe we were always meant to be”. Bates agreed: “The largest, most popular form of narrative art is cinema. So what better space for it to be than the home of storytelling?”View image in fullscreenThe Robert Flaherty theater in the Lucas museum in Los Angeles.Photograph: Lou Caltabiano/Courtesy Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtThe ground floor features a brief tour through thousands of years of visual storytelling, beginning with an immersive reproduction of cave paintings before moving to paintings, mosaics and sculptures – some original, some reproduced – depicting stories from ancient civilizations and the Bible. The exhibition sets the historical context for the museum’s core collection, mostly from the 20th and 21st centuries, reached via round glass elevators that do nothing to dispel the Star Wars aura.The galleries here are sorted into an odd mix of categories. There are rooms that focus on medium – the comics room contains strips from Krazy Kat, Little Orphan Annie, The Adventures of Tintin and Superman; the children’s stories room contains art from Where the Wild Things Are and fairytale illustrations; the manga room features Astro Boy and a portrait of Pikachu.Other rooms are divided by theme: the “community” area contains neighborhood scenes by Ernie Barnes and aFrida Kahloself-portrait; the “childhood” area hosts a Margaret Keane painting, Children of Paris, and a Picasso drawing titled Little Girl; “civic life” features photography of a 1968 sanitation workers’ strike and a painting by Shepard Fairey and Ernesto Yerena Montejano opposing immigration raids.View image in fullscreenThe Critic’s Corner by renowned African American artist Ernie Barnes.Photograph: Matt Kroening/Courtesy Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtStill other galleries are organized by single artists – NC Wyeth, Jessie Willcox Smith, Maxfield Parrish – and others by genre: science fiction, fantasy, adventure. And while this is very much not a Star Wars museum, it has plenty to offer fans, including an exhibit that focuses on modes of transportation in the films and contains vehicle models, production artwork and costumes. (There are other surprise nods to the films around the museum.)Finally, there is the mural room, with some of the museum’s most memorable pieces. A video traces the length of Judith Baca’s mural of the region’s history along the Los Angeles River; nearby are several Banksy works on walls that have been extracted and hung in the space. There’s also a huge image of the French artist JR’sKikito, an installation that shows a child looking over the US-Mexico border wall.Each work has a small plaque giving its title and year, the artist’s name and the materials used. But there isn’t much else on the walls to tell visitors what they’re viewing – no blurbs or lengthy descriptions. That was deliberate, Linkof said. Lucas and the curators didn’t want a “heavily mediated” experience, telling people “where to look, how to look, what to think, how to understand and interpret something”, he said. “We’re encouraging people to have their own individual encounters with works of art and take away what they feel like speaks to them.” That said, those who are curious about a work’s origins or context can scan the images with their phone to get a brief description of who made the work and why.View image in fullscreenRafael Navarro’s Sonámbulo: Mexican Stand-Off.Photograph: Courtesy Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtMany of the artists here are well-known, but as the museum’s leadership emphasizes, they often don’t receive the same institutional respect their peers do. John Romita Jr’s Spider-Man panels don’t tend to appear in museums that also feature the Sistine Chapel ceiling, re-created here with backlit photography. “Rockwell in his day was not considered an artist, more an advertising illustrator, but actually, the process, the level of depth in those images – he is one of our greatest storytellers,” said Tracey Bates, the museum’s CEO, in an interview. With the museum, Lucas and Hobson – who call the Sistine Chapel “God’s first comic book”, Bates says – hope to elevate the standing of these visual storytellers.“How many of us here in this room have learned to face our fears because of the work of Maurice Sendak, or learn moral lessons while studying EH. Shepard’s drawings of the 100 Acre Wood?” Bates asked. “George calls it the People’sArt, and this museum is its home.”Explore more on these topicsMuseumsLos AngelesArtGeorge LucasStar WarsCaliforniaBanksyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Farage meeting a ‘shadowy foreign donor’? It can only be another establishment stitch-up | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: The only thing more dodgy than Reform’s financial dealings is the egregious lunchtime combination of oysters, Guinness and champagne, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: The only thing more dodgy than Reform’s financial dealings is the egregious lunchtime combination of oysters, Guinness and champagne, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Nigel Farage with his adviser Dan Jukes, who has just ‘stepped down, pending an investigation’, Clacton-on-Sea, 2 July 2024.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenNigel Farage with his adviser Dan Jukes, who has just ‘stepped down, pending an investigation’, Clacton-on-Sea, 2 July 2024.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersOpinionNigel FarageNigel Farage meeting a ‘shadowy foreign donor’? It can only be another establishment stitch-upMarina HydeThe only thing more dodgy than Reform’s financial dealings is the egregious lunchtime combination of oysters, Guinness and champagneFri 4 Sep 2026 09.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.10 EDTShareHow many sarcastic air quotes is too many for quotingNigel Farage’s suggestionthat Reform have been ““““““““hoaxed”””””””” by some undercover investigators into appearing to seek to get round electoral law to bag a £500k donation from a foreigner, as well as commissioning off-the-books polling and failing to identify it to newspapers? I don’t feel eight was too many. I could run to nine. Amazing, really, that it’s been as long as a few weeks since Farage had a crash-out and forced a byelection. All any of us wants is for Nigel to once again resign after a staged shitfit and ask a few thousand members of the public to judge him.For whatever reason, though, the law of our country does not amount to an “ONLY THE PEOPLE OF CLACTON CAN JUDGE ME” tattoo, and so it is that as Reform’s conference gets under way today, the party has been reported to the police for allegedly using foreign money to fund its activities. It’s all based ona covert stingcarried out by Verbatim – an investigative group founded by journalists from the non-profit Centre for Climate Reporting – and broadcast last night on Channel 4 News.Though Farage has some very significant walk-on parts in this secretly filmed footage, the chief protagonists in the hokey cokey are James Orr, the party’s director of policy, and Nigel’s right-hand man Dan Jukes. Jukes is one of the many Farage aides to physically resemble an Apprentice candidate who crashes out in week four after miscalculating quantities in the sweetshop task. Still, he’d make a lovely Rolf in a regional production of The Sound of Music. And, happily, would now have the time to really commit to the role.“If Nigel makes it to No 10,” he honks at one point during filming carried out by an undercover “donor”, “you’re having a pint with who’s effectively going to be his chief of staff in No 10. If that isn’t a business interest, I don’t know what is.” As it turns out, the guy is effectively having a pint with someone the party chair, Lee Anderson, this morning said was “gone” with “no chance of them coming back”. Slightly less definitively, the official party statement said that Jukes and Orr had stepped down pending an internal investigation. Can’t imagine what form that will take. I always picture Reform’s internal affairs department as a toy phone ringing out in an abandoned wendy house.But perhaps this sort of thing is the job of flailing enforcer/terminal shitposter Zia Yusuf, who this week could be found branding a possible Labour byelection candidate for Keir Starmer’s vacated Holborn and St Pancras seat as something other than the tireless community servant her career has thus far marked her out as. Or as Zia put it: “The front runner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former Prime Minister Keir Starmer in our Parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what is happening?” If not, certainly one to discuss with that much-vaunted recent defector to Reform, the Iraq-born Nadhim Zahawi. Still, the episode does at least confirm Yusuf as the biggest Pick-Me in British politics. He’s really not like the other children of immigrants, you see – he actually enjoys being racist for approval.Back to the undercover investigation, though, whicha highly defensive Reform statement whingeswas “perpetuated by foreign-funded climate-change activists posing as would-be party donors”. Foreign-funded! That’s a bit rich in the circumstances. But the real standout bit of footage for many will be the moment when Orr laments: “We just don’t have British resident donors, British entities, that would support us. That’s the grim reality.” From the horse’s mouth, then, comes apparent confirmation that Reform is funded by foreign-based money for reasons on which we can only speculate.It’s often the incidental details that seem most weirdly illuminating. Take the scene when the fake American donor finally journeys to some sort of Clacton beer garden, where he and Farage and co seem to have settled themselves in one of a row of cursed teak gazebos. Here, Nigel chortles about “Guinness with a champagne top”, confirming his undying addiction to an even more annoying brand of alcohol-based identity politics than a Gin O’Clock poster.He’ll no doubt be butching it out with a drink at the Reform conference this weekend. The rest of the country might do well to once again ponder the 64,000-of-indeterminately-sourced-dollars question: why does this sort of thing keep happening to Farage and his party? Is it because of a byzantine conspiracy involving climate activists, “the establishment”, the deep state and Big Gazebo? Or is it because they are just endlessly, repeatedly and ineptly dodgy? Watching the footage, it’s fairly difficult to conclude anything other than that we are dealing with a bunch of preposterously self-regarding amateurs.We’ll have to see if this latest exposure further fans the anger that has been radiating off Farage all summer, ever since hisundeclared £5m giftfrom a Thai-based crypto billionaire was revealed. As discussed here before, I am ever-more convinced that Farage is too mentally fragile for the highest office – indeed, leading anything other than an insurgent party seems to be either spinning him out or finding him out. Today’s attempt to shift focus saw him promise to declare a “national emergency” in the event he becomes prime minister. On the basis of all we keep discovering about him, you can’t argue with that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarina Hyde is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
