title: ‘Like a tired boxer, battered by applause’: as Andrew Scott’s biopic premieres, Richard Eyre remembers Ian Charleson’s superb, near-death Hamlet | Telluride film festival | The Guardian
description: In 1989, the Chariots of Fire actor took on the incredible task of playing Shakespeare’s prince while terminally ill from Aids. This weekend sees the world premiere of Elsinore, a new film about the episode, itself heavily-tipped for awards
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: In 1989, the Chariots of Fire actor took on the incredible task of playing Shakespeare’s prince while terminally ill from Aids. This weekend sees the world premiere of Elsinore, a new film about the episode, itself heavily-tipped for awards
Content: One of the finest Hamlets seen on stage … Ian Charleson in an earlier version of the play, on tour with the Cambridge Theatre Company in 1974.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyView image in fullscreenOne of the finest Hamlets seen on stage … Ian Charleson in an earlier version of the play, on tour with the Cambridge Theatre Company in 1974.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyTelluride film festival‘Like a tired boxer, battered by applause’: as Andrew Scott’s biopic premieres, Richard Eyre remembers Ian Charleson’s superb, near-death HamletIn 1989, the Chariots of Fire actor took on the incredible task of playing Shakespeare’s prince while terminally ill from Aids. This weekend sees the world premiere of Elsinore, a new film about the episode, itself heavily-tipped for awardsNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentFri 4 Sep 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIan Charleson was one of the finest actors of his generation and an important figure in the fight for gay rights. Yet the extraordinary circumstances of his final performance as Hamlet, just months before his death, are less familiar.Now, a new film is bringing that haunting production back to life. Elsinore, directed by Simon Stone and starring Andrew Scott as the Scottish actor, will premiere at Telluride this weekend beforeopening the London film festival in October.Charleson was 40 and terminally ill with Aids when he was cast as Hamlet in Richard Eyre’s 1989 production at the National Theatre, after Daniel Day-Lewis abruptly left the role. Charleson had first played Hamlet 15 years earlier and persuaded Eyre to let him reprise it, despite the director’s misgivings about his health.“Ian was very bright, very witty, mischievous,” Eyre told the Guardian. “He was beyond good-looking. He was beautiful, and he had a beautiful singing voice.”Eyre remembered sitting with Charleson in the National’s canteen a year earlier, when the actor was starring in Cat on a Hot Tin Roof. “He said, ‘I’m hungry for the big Shakespeare roles’. So when Dan had his breakdown” – Day-Lewis believed he saw the ghost of his father onstage – “I thought, I will approach Ian. We met, and then I realised Ian was was very ill. But I thought I will go with him anyway.”View image in fullscreen‘I realised he was very ill’ … with Lindsay Duncan in Cat on a Hot Tin Roof.Photograph: Alastair Muir/Rex FeaturesThe cast, crew, and audience were told that Charleson’s face was swollen after a sinus operation. In reality, he was suffering from septicaemia, enduring painful acupuncture during rehearsals and, later, chemotherapy.“Ian’s beautiful face was actually deformed by the disease,” Eyre said. “But I just thought, he is determined, and I felt determined, and it was sort of an act of love for a friend. Most people told me I was absolutely insane. The press were characteristically loathsome in their probing. I just stubbornly stuck to my decision. In retrospect, it was the right one. He was heroic, and utterly brilliant in the part.”View image in fullscreen‘He was beyond good-looking’ … Charleson at the Chariots of Fire opening.Photograph: Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty ImagesThe production ran for six weeks and was widely regarded as one of the finest Hamlets seen on stage. The day after Charleson’s last show, Ian McKellen refused the Evening Standard award for best actor and gave his statuette to Charleson instead.Charleson died on 6 January 1990, eight weeks later, having asked that Aids be recorded as the cause – an unusually public act at a time when the disease was feared and stigmatised.Eyre has written of how fitting it was for Charleson to play Hamlet in the last months of his life. “Do you think I can go on as Hamlet looking like this?” Charleson asked him. “You’ll get better,” Eyre replied. “We have to be positive,” Charleson said.“Hamlet is a poem of death,” Eyre wrote. “It charts one of the great human rites of passage – from immaturity to accommodation with death. Hamlet grows up, in effect, to grow dead.”Born in Edinburgh in 1949, Charleson trained at the Bristol Old Vic. He played Eric Liddell in Chariots of Fire, which won four Oscars including best picture, and also appeared in the following year’s best picture winner, Richard Attenborough’s Gandhi.Charleson seemed to have all the ingredients of a major film career: he was handsome, charismatic and intelligent, with a formidable technical ability. Yet his film career never took off as expected. Instead, he repeatedly returned to the stage, performing Shakespeare, Tennessee Williams, Chekhov, Sam Shepard.Michael Billington, the Guardian’s former chief theatre critic, remembers Charleson as Eddie in Shepard’s Fool for Love at the Cottesloe in 1984. Initially unconvinced by his interpretation, Billington later came to remember the performance for its “mixture of masculinity and sensitivity”. Charleson performed Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, he said, with “the same blend of supposedly contradictory qualities: athleticism and delicacy”.View image in fullscreenBest-known role … as Eric Liddell in Chariots of FirePhotograph: Moviestore/REX/ShutterstockCharleson was gay at a time when being openly so could damage an actor’s career. Diagnosed with HIV in 1986, he took part in Before the Act, McKellen’s 1988 anti-Section 28 gala, alongside Judi Dench, Vanessa Redgrave and Stephen Fry.Scott,who played Hamlet150 times in London in 2017, has found himself returning to the role while portraying the actor who performed it at the end of his life.“The idea that Ian was doing this when he was so sick is still, to my mind, just completely mind-blowing,” Scott told People. “And his decision to do it was just incredibly courageous.”Scott said he was moved by “the opportunity to play a part that Ian and his contemporaries would not have gotten while they were working actors.”He added: “I wanted people to be able to understand that he was trying to live – it’s not about fetishising his death. He was so full of life and fun, and he did this extraordinary thing.”View image in fullscreen‘He looks like Ian, and he touches the heart like Ian’ … Andrew Scott in Elsinore.Photograph: Photo by Anthony Dickenson - © 2026 - Focus FeaturesCritics and industry insiders are heavily tipping Scott for a best actor Oscar nomination following early praise for his performance. Eyre called it “brilliant”. “He looks like Ian, and he touches the heart like Ian,” he said.Charleson’s most celebrated performance was never preserved on film. What remains are recollections, photographs and accounts of an actor performing with extraordinary intensity while his body failed him.Eyre recalled that Charleson had flu and missed two nights, but felt guilty: “If they pay you, you should turn up.” His final, Monday night performance, Eyre wrote, was “like watching a man who had been rehearsing for playing Hamlet all his life. He wasn’t playing the part, he became it.”At the curtain call, Charleson stood “like a tired boxer, battered by applause”.A few weeks before he died, just before Christmas, he wrote to Eyre: “One day when I’m better I’d love to attempt Hamlet again, and all the rest; and together we can revitalise Shakespeare. Anyway I hope this is not a dream and I can’t tell you how much of a kick I got out of doing the part, if only for the short time I could …”Explore more on these topicsTelluride film festivalRichard EyreAndrew ScottnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t know if I’d ever have sex again’: inside Sharon Horgan’s excruciating post-divorce comedy | Television | The Guardian
description: Horgan’s hilarious new show probes the perils of ageing and the horror of being single again – and it has sex scenes so wild you’ll be laughing for weeks. The creator and her co-stars open up about Youth
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Horgan’s hilarious new show probes the perils of ageing and the horror of being single again – and it has sex scenes so wild you’ll be laughing for weeks. The creator and her co-stars open up about Youth
Content: It’s complicated … Rupert Friend as Patrick and Sharon Horgan as Alex in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBOView image in fullscreenIt’s complicated … Rupert Friend as Patrick and Sharon Horgan as Alex in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBOTelevisionInterview‘I didn’t know if I’d ever have sex again’: inside Sharon Horgan’s excruciating post-divorce comedyZoe WilliamsHorgan’s hilarious new show probes the perils of ageing and the horror of being single again – and it has sex scenes so wild you’ll be laughing for weeks. The creator and her co-stars open up about YouthFri 4 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 09.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenSharon Horganwalked into HBO to pitch her new series, Youth, she basically just said “sandwich generation” to them. Alex, the protagonist, is squished between a teenage son and two elderly parents. That’s the classic; the rest of it – the recent divorce, the dating hell, the busy, creative professional life full of pricks – is the icing on the sandwich (if you like). Horgan had been incubating some of the characters for five years, but “honestly”, she tells me, “I said about three sentences and a week later, they said yes. I’ve never had that experience before.”You might think you can imagine it, but Youth is unlike any portrait you’ve ever seen in the gallery of (for brevity) menopausal women doing everything for everyone. There’s an urgency and valour to it that is very much drawn from Horgan’s own experience. “Everything just changed for me when I hit my 50s,” she says. “I was very bamboozled but I really had a hunger to make time count.” Not every situation is lifted directly from her own life, post-divorce – she’s also borrowing from her friends, she emphasises – but in general terms, the pressures, the worries, the outrages, the surprise and the delight are all so exquisitely drawn that even if it’s not Horgan herself, you hope someone, somewhere, is living this in real life.View image in fullscreen‘She could have chemistry with a toaster’ … Sharon Horgan.I caught some of the shooting on a blowy day in April this year, in east London. Horgan and her co-starRupert Friendwere filming a crux scene. Friend plays Patrick, slightly younger than Horgan’s Alex, a little indecisive and shambling. “He’s not a Prince Charming character. I don’t think I’m the answer to all her ills,” he says, walking around a little park in between takes. Patrick wants to be with Alex, but he also thinks he wants children and there’s no way she’s going back there again, even if she could. “Sharon flips the proverbial biological clock on its head,” he says. “Men think it doesn’t apply to them because they ostensibly can make children all the way through. He’s never considered that it’s not his clock.”Nothing passes between Alex and Patrick that’s overstated or even out of the ordinary, unless you count the fact that she gets hit by a cyclist as she walks away. But when it slots into the finished show, it is, like every other scene, hilarious. I just do not know how Horgan does what she does – which is what every one of her co-stars says about her. “She could have chemistry with a toaster,” saysAran Murphy(yes, son of Cillian), who plays her son. “She’s so fizzing with energy.” Rupert Friend puts the emphasis on her agility: “Sharon’s just brilliant at writing. She’s able to do that dance between jokes and pathos in a way that I don’t know anyone else can do.” But it’s Horgan herself who, in an absolutely unboastful way, explains it best: “I’m allergic to sentimentality. I can’t abide anything that is sweet or schmaltzy. But I love genuine emotion. I love to make people feel things. As much as I love the laughs, I’d feel like I’d failed in some way if I wasn’t giving people pain.”Murphy’s Ruari is a gift of a part, the most believably wrecking-ball 18-year-old son you’ve ever seen. Some things he wrecks on purpose (the last day of secondary school), some he wrecks by accident (his first week at university; his life), but the stakes are agonisingly high and the actions all plausible. Horgan has a lot to say about parenting kids this age, “even though I do not have a son, I have daughters” (Sadhbh, 22, and Amer, 18). “Gen Z have that awful feeling of being the last generation. They’re here at a point in time where they’re being told that everything’s fucked and AI’s going to take your jobs. I sometimes don’t know how to get out of bed in the morning, but they’re the ones who care the most and feel things the most.”View image in fullscreen‘Everything just changed when I hit my 50s’ … Sharon Horgan in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBOMurphy is pretty reserved in real life (he speaks to me by Zoom from Italy, where he is on holiday), and the performance he turns in is one of the most thrillingly angry teenagers ever. “We really got lucky with Aran,” says Horgan. “There’s nothing about him that isn’t real. It made life so much easier to be working with someone who you literally can’t see acting.” She wanted Ruari to be “complex but not in a Dawson’s Creek way – a real boy who’s a little bit broken. All Alex wants is for him to normalise. But what’s normal?”Besides, Ruari is probably saying the same about his mother, who he is furious to discover still has gentleman callers. Patrick isn’t Alex’s only love interest; there’s also a sex scene withTim McInnerny(Percy from Blackadder) that I am still laughing at weeks later. None of the relationships, fleeting or otherwise, are at all a classic love story – Rupert Friend says ruefully, “I’m really the best of a bad bunch, which I am happy to take as the quote for my gravestone” – but the men are drawn so truthfully that you can’t help but love them all slightly (apart from the ex-husband, and even he’s not abadguy, more of an emotional no-mark).“When I found myself divorced,” Horgan says, “I genuinely thought I’d be alone for ever. I didn’t even know if I’d ever have sex again. There’s that extreme fear of being alone and being lonely. But at the same time, you think you have a freedom as well. You do suddenly think: ‘My kids have finished school, I’ve got some time to try and get this right.’” Alex’s love life is anything but over, yet this isn’t a “you go, girl” tale where every woman remains perpetually 35 through Botox and force of will. “You put yourself out there in a slightly different way,” says Horgan. “It’s still incredibly difficult, as a woman of that age, to find someone – the men who are left are either institutionally single or they’re divorced or they’re looking for someone much younger.”View image in fullscreenWrecking-ball … Aran Murphy as Ruari in Youth.Photograph: Colin HuttonThe subplot of Alex’s ageing parents, meanwhile, is so honest it’s exhilarating. Dramedy tends to be respectfully saccharine about the elderly, and skate over the inconvenient bits: the stubbornness, the denial, the endless hospital appointments. But (I’m allowed to say this, being an orphan – Horgan’s mother is still alive, her dad died in 2023), those bits are almost the whole of the experience. “There is a huge amount of non-cooperation there,” she says, “and why shouldn’t there be? Ageing is hard. It’s harder when it begins to affect you mentally. When you’ve always been sharp as a tack, or when you begin to lose your mobility and you’ve always been a fucking go-getter. Losing those basic functions is brutal.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut from Alex’s point of view, “all the planning, all the phone calls, it becomes such a huge part of your life. As it goes on, you’ll see how it affects her sibling relationship as well. I wanted to explore that all so much but you run out of time and space. That could have been a whole show.”Alex works in publishing, and there are some fabulous performances by her authors – Anne Reid, as a grande dame of airport fiction, turning her hand to erotica, alongside Harriet Walter as her ice-cold daughter. “I could talk to you about Anne Reid for the entirety of the interview,” Horgan says. “It’s hard to even mention her and not just wax lyrical about being aged 91 and still delivering work on that level and still caring so much.” Damian Lewis, within 30 seconds of arriving on screen, has distilled everything that is bad about publishing, celebrity, London, private members’ clubs and the world. “Everyone who came on to do their bits was influencing the show,” says Horgan. “I was writing it at the same time as making it, which was hell.” On the upside, it meant she was building relationships with her co-stars as she wrote, and incorporating those connections. Friend remembers deep conversations about what love actuallyis. “We talked about how heartbreaking it is to think about things in terms of if they fail. You know, if you meet and immediately think: ‘We could date, but if we date we might break up.’ Why do anything? Everything has a pessimistic possibility, and Alex is always considering it, but it’s no way to live.”Pulling, Sharon Horgan’s 00s comedy, andMotherland, a decade ago, did the same thing – which is to say, if you’d asked: “Do you want to see a show about three single women? How about a school-gate show about neurotic middle-class people and Chardonnay and mini Babybels?” I’d have said: “No, not at all, sounds drab and also too close to home.” But then when they landed, they were all I wanted to watch. Youth is technically about the grinding sandwich years, when everything gets harder at once, and then your joints stop working. But it’s really about the sheer bliss of being alive when so much happens that is funny, stitched together by a fearsomely long to-do list.Youth is on HBO Max from 21 September.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionSharon HorganDramainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conference | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Splits emerge within party after resignation of officials reported to police for apparent plot to evade donations law
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Splits emerge within party after resignation of officials reported to police for apparent plot to evade donations law
Content: 1:21'Reform broke no law': Nigel Farage responds to latest donation revelations – videoNigel FarageFarage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conferenceSplits emerge within party after resignation of officials reported to police for apparent plot to evade donations lawRowena Mason,Ben QuinnandPippa CrerarFri 4 Sep 2026 14.16 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage sought to shore up his damaged leadership on Friday as he attempted to distance himself from two of his most senior officials reported to the police for apparently plotting to evade the law on foreign donations.As the scandal engulfed Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham, Farage was forced to suspend close aides Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr after anundercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim.He later acknowledged Jukes and Orr had made “human error” and were “not authorised” to act in the way they did when trying to orchestrate donations to benefit the party from a fake US businessman, who was not permitted to give money.View image in fullscreenDan Jukes, left, speaks to Nigel Farage before an interview in Clacton-on-Sea in July 2024.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersThe Met police are now assessing the evidence after a complaint thatFarage, Orr and Jukes may have broken political funding laws, with sources suggesting a full investigation is highly likely to be launched. They all deny wrongdoing.One possibility would be for the police to extend an existing Met investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.Orr is an associate professor of divinity at the University of Cambridge who had been working for Reform, reporting directly to Farage, since February. In relation to the undercover footage of Orr, a spokesperson for the university said Cambridge was “looking into these matters”. Jukes is Farage’s closest aide, and has been at his side for more than a decade working on communications and strategy.Farage had been introduced by Jukes to the would-be donor from the US promising to give £500,000 despite not being eligible, who was really an undercover reporter. The Reform leader then appeared to endorse the scheme for the impermissible US donor to give money through his son, a UK intermediary, by saying “thank you, both” and “all above board”.11:20Reform donations scandal: is this the final blow for Farage? - The LatestAfter dismissing the sting as a “hoax”, Reform began an organised campaign to limit the damage to Farage personally before his main conference speech, after a summer of scandals over his finances, including anundeclared gift of £5m.Addressing the allegations, the Reform leader responded by reading out a legal statement in which he dismissed the allegations as “a little local difficulty” and described the reports as “an exercise in entrapment”.Farage claimed Orr and Jukes had merely been “contractors” who engaged in “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true”. One party figure,Nadine Dorries, claimed Jukes had merely booked transport and carried bags, despite being a senior adviser integral to Reform’s operations and success for many years.View image in fullscreenA man in chainmail and a crown attends the Reform UK conference.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianWhen it was put to Farage that he had thanked the bogus donors and understood what was going on, he said: “It was the middle of the byelection. I was told I had to go and meet these people. I didn’t have to, but I did. I was told they had a global family trust headquartered in London. I asked the question: is this all above board?”The Reform leader also insisted that the party’s internal processes would have stopped any impermissible donors and said neither Jukes nor Orr should have been carrying out fundraising. He said a suggestion by Jukes in the footage that other foreign donations had been channelled through UK intermediaries was not true and the donors did not exist.The pair were caught out after being filmed by undercover reporters from the group Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, and broadcast by Channel 4 News on the eve of Reform’s party conference.View image in fullscreenFarage’s speech was interrupted by protesters.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianIn the footage, Orr and Jukes appeared to help orchestrate an impermissible donation of £30,000 from the fake US donor, which was used to pay for polling that would benefit Reform and made front pages of national newspapers. The money from an American company was transferred to the polling company JL Partners after being organised at the behest of Reform to boost its policies and political narrative. It was not declared to the Electoral Commission.Jukes went on to discuss whether the US businessman could give £500,000 through a UK intermediary, who was an undercover reporter, and introduced the would-be donors to Farage at a lunch in Clacton over oysters and champagne.Jukes issued a statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals using selective editing who had their own agenda to discreditReform UK.”Orr said: “I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party’s internal investigation into the conduct of the program, with which I will cooperate fully.”The Lib Dems have asked the standards commissioner to investigate Farage’s conduct.The row comprehensively overshadowed the first full day of the party’s conference with every Reform politician repeatedly questioned over the scandal.It also exposed splits at the top of the party, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, strongly distancing himself from Jukes and Orr. He told reporters “anyone who supports Reform is disappointed”, and added of the investigation: “It’s just not something I am personally involved in.”He also launched a personal video about his backstory, leading to speculation he could attempt to run for the leadership as a rival toRobert Jenrickor Richard Tice if Farage were to be forced out over his financial scandals.Reform UK exposé comes just as Farage was hoping to change the narrativeRead moreHowever, some Reform insiders are convinced Farage will part company with Yusuf before long, partly over his ambition and combative style on social media, including one post on X that saw him accused of racism towards a Somalia-born Labour councillor. Farage is understood to have used a rude term about Yusuf recently in relation to his troublemaking on social media.One senior Reform figure said they believed Yusuf would have to go as a precondition for some sort of reconciliation withRupert Lowe, whose party, Restore Britain, has eaten into the party’s voters on the hard right. Farage has recently condemned Lowe as vindictive, but some of their friends believe a rapprochement could be possible if Yusuf were no longer in the party.Reform had wanted the main event to be Farage announcing a deal with the hard-right French National Rally president, Jordan Bardella, to return small boats crossing the Channel if both parties achieve power. However, a press conference was dominated by questions about the foreign donations scandal.View image in fullscreenThe National Rally ​party’s chief, Jordan Bardella, attends a joint press conference with Farage on Friday.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianFarage’s main speech was later delayed by security concerns after climate protesters disrupted Tice’s stage appearance. More activists later repeatedly interrupted his address. While waiting to go on stage, the Reform leader danced and sung with the crowd.He began his speech by calling for Andy Burnham to hold a general election and accusing Labour of planning to put up taxes.The speech was light on policy but Farage at one point hinted he could look at the way judges are appointed in future – suggesting the party could look at a system of political appointments as is the case in the US.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKRupert LoweRichard TiceRobert JenrickNadine DorriesMetropolitan policenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday review | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Nazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his death
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Nazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his death
Content: Nazir Afzal, who was head of the CPS in the north-west of England from 2011 to 2015, is now chancellor of the University of Manchester.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNazir Afzal, who was head of the CPS in the north-west of England from 2011 to 2015, is now chancellor of the University of Manchester.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianJason ArdayCambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday reviewNazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his deathRichard AdamsEducation editorFri 4 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUniversity of Cambridgehas asked Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, to lead the first part of its review into the death of the scholar Jason Arday.Arday died at his home in south London on 14 August, nine days after his resignation as a Cambridge professor amid swirling allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said the time since Arday’s death had been “a period of profound sadness and reflection” for the university, and she sought to defend her institution from criticism.“We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus but given the devastating outcome, we are all asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more. This review will answer that question,” Prentice said.“We are committed to ensuring that any recommendations arising from the review are addressed and adopted with clear accountability for delivering necessary changes.”View image in fullscreenJason Arday was found dead at home in south London on 14 August.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianArday was named professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, with the university highlighting his appointment as the university’s youngest ever black professor at the age of 37.Arday denied accusations of plagiarism levelled against him but on 5 August the university said it would hold an investigation into his academic qualifications.Arday resignedhours after the investigation was announced.Prentice said the review would be in two parts, with the first, led by Afzal, to focus on the support given to Arday in the immediate period before his death.Afzal said: “I am honoured to have been asked to lead part one of this important independent review. At its heart is a person, a family and a community who have been profoundly affected by Professor Arday’s death. It is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity.“My responsibility will be to listen carefully, examine the evidence thoroughly and understand what support, interventions and protections were available to Professor Arday in the period before his death. We must be willing to ask difficult questions, including whether more could and should have been done. This work will be conducted independently and with urgency.”Afzal, a University of Birmingham graduate, is the chancellor of the University of Manchester, having been head of the CPS in the north-west of England during which he prosecuted child exploitation rings in Rochdale. In 2022 he led anindependent review into London fire brigadethat exposed a culture of misogyny, racism and bullying.Prentice said: “I am very grateful to Nazir for agreeing to lead this part of the review. He is a highly respected legal professional who will ask challenging questions about the support that was offered to Professor Arday during his time at Cambridge.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue researchRead moreThe university said the review’s second stage would consider “the wider context of Professor Arday’s time at the university”, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, the university’s response to allegations of research misconduct, and the support it gave to academics “subject to extraordinary public and media scrutiny”.Cambridge said it would appoint an independent external chair for the second part and an expert panel “including individuals with lived experience” to advise the review.It said part one of the review was expected to report within three months, and the second part within six months of establishing the expert panel.Earlier this week, Jacqui Smith, the minister responsible for higher education, told parliament that she was “more than just keeping an eye” on Cambridge’s response to Arday’s death. Smith said England’s higher education regulator, the Office for Students, had the powers to investigate further if necessary.Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayUniversity of CambridgeHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia strikes Ukraine intelligence HQ in ‘major escalation’ | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has told SBU to deliver ‘appropriate, tangible response’ to Kyiv strike
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has told SBU to deliver ‘appropriate, tangible response’ to Kyiv strike
Content: The Russian drone attack struck near St Sophia's Cathedral, a world heritage site.Photograph: Mark Edward Harris/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Russian drone attack struck near St Sophia's Cathedral, a world heritage site.Photograph: Mark Edward Harris/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockUkraineRussia strikes Ukraine intelligence HQ in ‘major escalation’Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has told SBU to deliver ‘appropriate, tangible response’ to Kyiv strikeAmy Hawkinsin KyivFri 4 Sep 2026 11.37 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head office of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency has been hit in a Russian drone attack, sending plumes of black smoke rising into the air in the heart of Kyiv.Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he had instructed the SBU to deliver an “appropriate, tangible response” to the strike, while the foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, described it as a “major escalation”.The streets around the SBU headquarters were cordoned off shortly after Friday’s attack, with armed officers patrolling the area.Numerous ambulances and emergency services vehicles were stationed around the site, which is close to St Sophia Cathedral, a Unesco world heritage site.“Unfortunately, a Russian drone hit the central building of the SBU on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv, opposite the St Sophia Cathedral,” Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram. “The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building.”Kyiv has been undera barrage of daily drone and missile attacksfrom Russia for over a week. Zelenskyy on Friday called for Russia to halt its attacks during a visit of US negotiators, Steve Witkoff ‌and Jared Kushner, to the city on Sunday and said Ukraine would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace while they were in Moscow.Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors which can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-modeljet-powered droneswhich can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept.It is rare for government buildings in central Kyiv to be reached by Russian strikes, especially in broad daylight. The explosion from the hit on the SBU building could be heard from several blocks away.The incident is likely to intensify theescalating attacksthat Moscow and Kyiv have been launching at each other in recent weeks in efforts to destroy each other’s resilience and morale. It will also raise questions about Kyiv’s ability to defend its key infrastructure against Russia.Sybiha said the attack was “a major escalation that demands resolute responses” and called on international partners to “unequivocally condemn these actions and step up pressure on the Putin regime”.At least nine people were injured in Friday’s strike, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.Stanislav Zavertailo, the co-owner of the nearby Zavertailo cafe, said one of his customers was injured in the strike, which sent shockwaves through his premises, shattering all the windows.“It’s a normal cafe,” he said. The customer was “eating one of our famous poppy seed rolls” when the attack occurred, he added.Staff and customers rushed into an underground shelter after the strike, fearing a double-tap attack, a tactic which Russia has employed, in which a second drone is sent in soon after the first, hitting emergency service workers.An hour later, there had been no second strike, but Zavertailo said he did not feel at ease. “We are all waiting for another attack,” he said.The SBU is responsible for coordinating complex operations against Russia, including last year’sOperation Spiderwebwhich destroyed aircraft worth billions of pounds inside Russia.Friday’s hit was “awful” said a Zavertailo cafe employee who had recently emerged from the underground shelter. As “a person who lives in Ukraine for all this time, it’s just hard”.The strike came two days before Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were expected to visit Kyiv for the first time.US-led diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s four-and-a-half-year invasion have stalled in recent months as the US has shifted its focus towards the war with Iran.Additional reporting by Illia DyadikExplore more on these topicsUkraineEuropeRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case after jury deadlocked again | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Defense lawyer had asked for time to request emergency stay after jury was split 11 to one
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Defense lawyer had asked for time to request emergency stay after jury was split 11 to one
Content: 2:25Judge declares mistrial amid hung jury in Lindsay Clancy murder trial - videoMassachusettsJudge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case after jury deadlocked againDefense lawyer had asked for time to request emergency stay after jury was split 11 to oneEdward HelmoreandMaya YangFri 4 Sep 2026 14.41 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe judge in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, theMassachusettsmother accused of killing her three young children, has declared a mistrial after the jury could not reach a unanimous verdict and remained deadlocked aftera week of deliberations.Jurors in Plymouth state court spent more than 38 hours in deliberations over the charges against the 36-year-old mom, which came on the heels of a weeks-long trial that directed national attention to maternal mental health issues that can occur postpartum.The 12-person jury was made up of nine women and three men and, according to the notes given to the court, was split 11 to one.Lindsay Clancy judge declares mistrial – what happens next?Read moreAfter the jury returned without a verdict for the third time, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial but was interrupted by a last-minute request from Clancy’s lead defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, who requested one hour to petition for an emergency stay to seek relief from a superior court judge.That emergency filing with theMassachusettssupreme judicial court asked a single justice to order Sullivan to further question the juror arguing the juror was “biased” and, per jury notes, unwilling to follow the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt.“Intervention is necessary in this case to avoid an avoidable mistrial of a case that is so time and labor intensive and that has captured so much public attention,” the filing reads, which also claimed that the court had “abdicated its responsibility to ensure the integrity of the jury”.The filing also asked that the juror be barred from further deliberations if Sullivan determined that they could not follow the instructions issued by the court.“A mistrial at this point is entirely avoidable, but only if the court does its job,” the filing says.Additionally, the filing claimed the court “reflects a bias against those who suffer from debilitating mental illness”, arguing that mental illness is a “protected category” under the fifth and 14th amendments of the US constitution.The filing was discussed with the Massachusetts supreme court justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt during a Zoom hearing that was open to the public for viewing. Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague summarized what happened with the jury and their repeated notes indicating a deadlock before defense attorney Dana Goldblatt argued that the supreme judicial court had the discretion to order the trial court to make the inquiry of the juror. Wendlandt then said she would take the matter under advisement.The petition was subsequently denied.Clancy, a former neonatal and delivery nurse, had been accused of strangling her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, in the family’s Duxbury home in January 2023.Prosecutors argued in opening statements that Clancy had “coldly and efficiently executed” her children, doing so with “no hesitation, with deliberate premeditation and extreme atrocity and cruelty” after she “drew her husband out of the house, their father, so that she had the opportunity and the time to carry out these murders”.But Clancy’s defense team argued she was “suffering from psychosis” when she killed her children and allegedly attempted suicide by jumping from an upper window in her home, which left her partly paralyzed. Reddington told jurors that Clancysuffered from postpartum depressionafter giving birth to her third child, Callan, and been prescribed a cocktail of medications.“This is a young woman who, with her husband, tried very hard to get the help she needed,” he said.Clancy has not denied that she had killed her children but her not guilty plea was predicated on a lack of criminal responsibility because, as her defense team said, she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, which included auditory hallucinations that commanded her to harm her children, and undiagnosed bipolar disorder.Under Massachusetts law, the defendant must have “retained the substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness or criminality of their conduct and to conform their conduct to the requirements of the law” in order to be found guilty.Throughout the trial, jurors heard from Clancy’s former husbandPatrick Clancy, her mother and aunt, and anarray of psychologistsand treating physicians. The court heard that Clancy had been prescribed 13 different medications for anxiety and sleep, which the defense said may have exacerbated her symptoms of depression.Clancy had checked herself into psychiatric clinic in the weeks before the killings. Later, on 24 January 2023, she had sent her then husband out for food and to collect pharmacy medications. In that time, police say she strangled their children with exercise bands. Her ability to orchestrate a window of time to carry out the killings, prosecutors argued, was evidence of premeditation.Before resting his case last week, Reddington called forensic psychiatrist Dr Phillip Resnick to testify that Clancy had “severe depression” and a history of anxiety, which increased after the birth of her children to the point that she “felt she couldn’t function”.“At the time of the crime on Jan 24, 2023, Ms Clancy was frankly psychotic,” Resnick said. “She was clearly psychotic on that day.”After the declaration of Clancy’s mistrial, prosecutors have the option of trying her again. The court has set a status conference for 9am ET on 29 September.Clancy’s criminal trial will be followed by a civil claim brought by both Lindsay and Patrick Clancy against her medical and mental healthcare providers. The former couple claim the providers committed medical malpractice by failing to properly diagnose, treat and monitor her severe postpartum psychiatric condition.After formally declaring the mistrial, the judge thanked the jury for their time and consideration.“Each one of you knew how long the case was going to go. You knew how difficult the case was going to be to listen to facts-wise, but still, you braced for that duty,” Sullivan said before dismissing them.He also indicated that should there be a re-trial, he would want it to happen “sometime in the fall”.Plymouth county district attorney Tim Cruz told reporters that Clancy’s had been “an emotional trial for everybody”.“This was and has always been about getting justice for those three little babies,” Cruz said. “We’re here at this courthouse today because those children are not. Our priority has always been to fight for Cora, for Dawson and for Callan.”Cruz also praised assistant district attorneys Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham, who he said “are both mothers themselves – and went home to their families after each long day in court”.Reddington addressed reporters outside the courthouse, too, saying that Cruz “knows he was crushed”.“I’m representing a woman who is a fantastic, wonderful individual,” Reddington said. “This woman is so brave, so awesome. She sat there through seven weeks of the trial, where nobody had anything bad to say about her except the two prosecutors.”Reddington also thanked the jury, “minus one” – referring to the holdout juror who he says he “hope[s] they can sleep at night”.In response to how Clancy’s parents are doing after the mistrial, Reddington said: “Not good.”“They know that they were robbed by one [juror] for whatever [their] agenda was,” Reddington remarked. “And I got a funny feeling that [the jury] would have gone on for another week if they had to. So I hope that [juror] can sleep well at night.”“If we didn’t have that one individual, we would’ve had a verdict and we would be out of here,” he continued. He added that Clancy is “like a a daughter to me”.It was not immediately known for what outcome the 11 decided jurors had voted.Reddington also said that if Clancy is retried, he will “request” that the jury be sequestered.After Friday’s mistrial declaration, Patrick Clancy’s lawyer, David Meier, issued a statement saying his client was “grateful to the court and to the jurors for their hard work, their commitment and their perseverance”.“The loss of Patrick’s children is something from which he will never recover and from which there will never be closure,”saidthe statement, obtained by a CBS Boston reporter. “The prospect of reliving this tragedy through another trial is extraordinarily painful – for Patrick, for his family and for all us.”Donald Trump also weighed in on the trial, telling reporters at the White House that the case was a “horrible tragedy” and a “terrible situation”.“I assume there’s going to be another trial,” the president said. “She did a horrible, horrible thing. Can’t be worse.“There’ll be a price. It’s going to be a mental institution or jail or something ... It’s too bad.”In the US, thenational maternal mental health hotlineis 1-833-852-6262. In the UK, thePandas foundationoffers support via Whatsapp on 07903 508334. In Australia, thenational maternal and perinatal mental health hotlineis 1300 726 306Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Jackdaw gasfield set to be approved by ministers this month, sources say | Environment policy | The Guardian
description: Energy secretary could recommend new North Sea drilling next week, as ministers also consider approval for Rosebank oilfield
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Energy secretary could recommend new North Sea drilling next week, as ministers also consider approval for Rosebank oilfield
Content: Climate activists protesting against the new fields. Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank closed last month.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenClimate activists protesting against the new fields. Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank closed last month.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEnvironment policyJackdaw gasfield set to be approved by ministers this month, sources sayEnergy secretary could recommend new North Sea drilling next week, as ministers also consider approval for Rosebank oilfieldKiran StaceyPolicy editorFri 4 Sep 2026 03.55 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 03.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters are poised to approve a controversial new gasfield in the North Sea this month, according to government sources, and are considering approving a major oilfield later this year.Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, will give her recommendation to approve the Jackdaw field off the coast of Aberdeen as soon as next week, according to people close to the decision, and the formal approval could follow a week after.Meanwhile, officials are looking for ways to make sure any proceeds from the separate Rosebank project – if it is approved – go towards clean energy projects, as happens in Norway.Officials have not yet finished their analysis of Rosebank’s environmental impact, but some close to the process believe they will soon decide the project should be approved.Both projects have become emblematic of the government’s commitment to the North Sea, with green campaigners calling for them to be abandoned while the US president, Donald Trump,urges the prime ministerto open them up.A spokesperson for the energy department said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security. We are clear that oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come, alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.”Consultations on both Jackdaw and Rosebank, which the industry says will provide 10% of the UK’s oil and gas output at their peak, closed last month, since when Fahnbulleh has been considering her response.Campaigners say the fieldswould produceas much as £336bn worth of damage to the economy as a result of the carbon pollution from the oil and gas that are produced.Both fields have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled the companies running them – Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor – needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be produced by burning the oil and gas they produce.The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. Granting those environmental permits would not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment not to issue new oil or gas licences, but many of the party’s MPs are opposed to the projects entirely.Since he entered Downing Street, Andy Burnham has signalled he has concerns about the way in which the move to green energy has affected workers in the north east of Scotland, telling MPs this week: “I know that people have struggled with the impact of transition.”Officials stress final decisions have not been made for either Jackdaw or Rosebank, but those close to the process say Fahnbulleh is likely to signal her approval for Jackdaw as soon as Monday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe will give her recommendation to the North Sea Transition Authority, which officials hope will issue the formal approval as soon as a week afterwards. Some in government think the NSTA process could take several weeks, however.A decision on the £8.7bn Rosebank field, which is the biggest undeveloped field in UK waters and is estimated to contain as much as 500m barrels of oil or oil equivalent, is likely to come later in the year.Fahnbulleh is likely approve that project if the environmental impact assessment allows it, according to sources, but is looking at ways to redirect the proceeds from it to clean energy projects in the UK. One option would be to put the tax revenues from the project into thenational wealth fund, which has been set up to fund green energy schemes and other infrastructure projects.Some in government warn this will be difficult, though, because the consenting process is already advanced and it could prove legally complex to change the terms on which the project is approved. The money has also already been accounted for in the Treasury’s forecasts, given the projects have their licences, meaning the chancellor, John Healey, would have to redirect it from other parts of government spending.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsEnvironment policyGas (Environment)Oil (Environment)Oil (Business)Gas (Business)CommoditiesEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Howard announces ‘devastating’ death of baby son | Culture | The Guardian
description: Comedian and his wife, Cerys Morgan, set up charitable foundation in memory of Felix, who died shortly after birth
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Comedian and his wife, Cerys Morgan, set up charitable foundation in memory of Felix, who died shortly after birth
Content: To help launch the foundation, Howard will host a special charity gala at the O2 in London on 8 February.Photograph: /David VenniView image in fullscreenTo help launch the foundation, Howard will host a special charity gala at the O2 in London on 8 February.Photograph: /David VenniCultureRussell Howard announces ‘devastating’ death of baby sonComedian and his wife, Cerys Morgan, set up charitable foundation in memory of Felix, who died shortly after birthSammy GecsoylerFri 4 Sep 2026 08.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 14.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Howard has announced the death of his baby son, in what he described as the “most devastating time of our lives”.The 46-year-old comedian said his family had been “changed for ever” after their “beautiful baby boy”, Felix, died shortly after birth.In a statement on his Instagram account, Howard said: “During the most devastating time of our lives, the hospital staff who cared for us showed extraordinary compassion, kindness and humanity. They helped us navigate an unimaginable heartache and gave us support when we needed it most.”Howard praised the support he and his wife, Cerys Morgan, had received from a bereavement midwife named Lauren, who he said had experienced a similar tragedy.“Her care meant more to us than we can ever put to words,” he added. “During our time in hospital, Felix was placed in a cool cot, which meant that my wife and I were able to spend precious hours with our beautiful boy.“Those hours are among the most precious memories we have of Felix.”Howard and Morgan, who is an NHS doctor, have set up the Felix Foundation, in memory of their son, to help other families facing the same “devastating circumstances”.To help launch the foundation, Howard will host a special charity gala at the O2 in London on 8 February featuring a lineup of friends and colleagues made up of Michael McIntyre, Jimmy Carr, Aisling Bea, Guz Khan, Greg Davies, Mo Gilligan, Michelle Wolf and John Bishop.He said of Felix: “We miss him dearly, every single day but we take some comfort in knowing that his name will stand for kindness, compassion and laughter and that his legacy may help other families through the darkest moments of their lives.”The foundation will aim to relieve the needs of parents, siblings and other close family members affected by miscarriage, premature birth, stillbirth, neonatal death or related bereavements, including by providing funding for specialist facilities, training or other forms of support.Explore more on these topicsCultureInfant and child mortalityBereavementParents and parentingFamilyComedy (Culture)TV comedynewsShareReuse this content

title: Man jumps out of first-floor window to escape kidnappers in Lincoln | Lincolnshire | The Guardian
description: Five jailed after targeting victim and subjecting him to ordeal linked to past relationship breakdown
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Five jailed after targeting victim and subjecting him to ordeal linked to past relationship breakdown
Content: 0:56Man dives out of first-floor window to escape kidnappers in Lincolnshire - videoLincolnshireMan jumps out of first-floor window to escape kidnappers in LincolnFive jailed after targeting victim and subjecting him to ordeal linked to past relationship breakdownMark BrownNorth of England correspondentFri 4 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDramatic footage shows a kidnapped man jumping from a first-floor window into a tree before running into the street and, by chance, coming across a police car.Lincolnshire police said the ordeal of the unnamed man had been “horrifying” and the presence of a marked police vehicle “may have saved his life”.DC Liam Henderson said the CCTV footage captured a desperate moment in which the victim “quite literally risked everything to get away from those holding him captive”.Lincoln crown court heard that the victim had been targeted and subjected to a terrifying ordeal linked to a past relationship breakdown. On 4 July 2025, he was lured to an address in Market Rasen where it soon became clear he would be unable to leave.Inside the address were Brad’Lee Ranyard, Nathan Gladwell, Jackson Nicholson, Craig Ranyard and Danielle Thompson. For hours the victim endured violence and intimidation, police said. He was “repeatedly assaulted, threatened, humiliated and tormented” by his captors, who filmed the abuse on their mobile phones and laughed.The next day the man was forced into the back of a Isuzu pickup truck and driven along back roads to a property in Lincoln. He arrived at 7.30am and was again held against his will.At 11.23am the man seized his opportunity. He can be seen diving from the window into the tree, before getting to the ground and running into the street. Footage from a police car, which had turned into the street, shows the man running towards it saying: “Let me in, let me in”.Police said the officer immediately recognised the man’s distress, realised he was fleeing a dangerous situation and took him to safety.Henderson, who led the investigation, said: “This was a sustained and deeply distressing ordeal in which a man was subjected to violence, threats and humiliation at the hands of people who appeared to find amusement in his suffering.“The victim showed remarkable courage in seizing the opportunity to escape.”Henderson said it was sheer chance that a police car had entered the street. “That moment changed the course of events and allowed officers to get him to safety when he needed help most,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We often hear concerns that victims may feel alone or that help will not arrive when it is needed. This case is a powerful reminder that when someone reaches out for help, we will do everything we can to protect them and bring those responsible to justice.”Police said the victim had given permission for the footage, which also shows the arrests, to be shared.A judge at Lincoln crown court gave nine-year jail terms to Brad’Lee Ranyard, 20, and Nicholson, 25, for kidnap and false imprisonment. Craig Ranyard, 42, was jailed for five years and three months after being convicted of false imprisonment.Thompson, 38, was jailed for four years and nine months after being convicted of false imprisonment. Gladwell, 36, was jailed for three years and seven months after being convicted of false imprisonment.Explore more on these topicsLincolnshireCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale | Africa | The Guardian
description: Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland
Content: Africa on the traditional world map based on the Mercator projection, left, and on the 2018 Equal Earth map, right.Composite: equal-earth.com, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAfrica on the traditional world map based on the Mercator projection, left, and on the 2018 Equal Earth map, right.Composite: equal-earth.com, Getty ImagesAfricaUN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scaleTogo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to GreenlandEromo Egbejulein AbidjanFri 4 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 22.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUnited Nationshas voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design.At the session, 164 countries voted in favour of the resolution. Only the US voted no, with its representative saying the resolution was “superfluous”. There were six abstentions.UN resolutions are non-enforceable, so countries and institutions will not be mandated to use only the new projection or forbidden from using the old one. However, the outcome is expected to result in an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.View image in fullscreenThe 1569 map by Gerardus Mercator (1512-1594) has remained the global standard.Photograph: Stock Montage/Getty ImagesTogo, which spearheaded a campaign for the resolution on behalf of theAfrican Union, said the resolution “recognises and affirms that disproportionate cartographic representations, particularly those resulting from the Mercator projection, have had lasting cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic effects, contributing to a drastic reduction in the perceived size of Africa and other regions of the world in the global collective imagination”.Speaking before the resolution passed, Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality.”The Mercator layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later, it remains the global standard.Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map showsAfricaas being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says apetitionon Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.On Friday, before the vote, France’s foreign minister spoke in support of the resolution. “[We] will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists,” Jean-Noël Barrot said during a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris, in a move seen as part of France’s push to increase goodwill among its former colonies.France will now use the Eckert IV projection, which is close to the Equal Earth projection recommended in the resolution.View image in fullscreenA comparison of the Mercator and the Eckert IV mapsIllustration: French foreign ministryHistorians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.View image in fullscreenThe 1973 Gall-Peters world map has been used as an alternative to the Mercator.Photograph: Michael Schmeling/AlamySome argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This is said to have reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.View image in fullscreenThe 2018 Equal Earth Map.Photograph: equal-earth.comTogo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign promoted the use of the 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.Some analysts agree. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.He said: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”View image in fullscreenA map of Africa from Mercator’s atlas dating from between 1595 and 1602.Photograph: Royal Geographical Society/Getty ImagesTogo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.Speaking before the vote, Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say: why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”Explore more on these topicsAfricaUnited NationsTogoAfrican UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s ‘retribution’ could now include Falklands as favor to Milei – and revenge on the UK | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: US president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands
Content: The Falkland Islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, on 16 March 2026.Photograph: Ricardo Mazalán/APView image in fullscreenThe Falkland Islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, on 16 March 2026.Photograph: Ricardo Mazalán/APDonald TrumpAnalysisTrump’s ‘retribution’ could now include Falklands as favor to Milei – and revenge on the UKRobert Taitin WashingtonUS president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islandsFri 4 Sep 2026 16.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 21.01 EDTShareDonald Trumphas long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” hedeclaredto an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House.It is unlikelyArgentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time.But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president.Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas.Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland IslandsRead moreThe centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory.Britain reclaimed them after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender.An uneasy peace has reigned in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their fewer than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British.This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over theFalkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now?Milei jumped onTrump’s commentthat he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control.Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’sdeep-rooted suspicions of Britainand its imperial past.The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked.And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf.In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday.“Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said, ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets.It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump.Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China.Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran.He has repeatedlythreatened to bombor “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping.The White House also announcedthe withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germanyafter the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict.Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally.Turbulence under TrumpBut Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side.Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did.Javier Milei: ‘winds of change’ support Argentina’s claim to Falkland IslandsRead moreThis time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him.But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of afamous speechin 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa.“The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.”In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced.He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor which may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses.Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes.But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpArgentinaFalkland IslandsTrump administrationUS foreign policyUS politicsAmericasanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘There’s no plan’: as instability in global bond markets rises, what are the knock-on effects? | Bonds | The Guardian
description: From mortgages to inflation, concerns about the public finances of major economies have wide-reaching consequences
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: From mortgages to inflation, concerns about the public finances of major economies have wide-reaching consequences
Content: Yields on US Treasury bonds and UK gilts recently hit their highest levels for decades.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenYields on US Treasury bonds and UK gilts recently hit their highest levels for decades.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPABonds‘There’s no plan’: as instability in global bond markets rises, what are the knock-on effects?From mortgages to inflation, concerns about the public finances of major economies have wide-reaching consequencesHeather StewartandPatrick ComminsFri 4 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Donald Trump was asked recently about the threat of rising interest rates on US government debt, he told baffled reporters: “The ultimate intervention is our military. And if we have to use that, we will.”Perhaps not surprisingly, his bellicose words did not soothe fractious bond markets, and his resumption of the bombing campaign against Iran only made matters worse.The past fortnight has seen a wave of instability sweeping through government bond markets in major economies – with knock-on effects for millions of borrowers. The interest rate, or yield, on 10-year US government borrowing hit 4.8% on Friday, up from 4.64% 10 days ago. At one point midweek, the 30-year yield touched its highest level since 2008.Neil Shearing, the chief economist at the consultancy CapitalEconomics, said one impetus for the current wobble had been markets taking a fresh look at the state of US public finances. “There’s been a recalibration,” he said.Graph showing government borrowing costs are increasing in many countriesTotal US government debt hassurged past $40tn(£29.5tn), and annual deficits are forecast to be an eye-watering 6% of GDP for the foreseeable future.Such figures were long deemed barely to matter given the status of US government bonds, or treasuries, as the ultimate safe-haven investment. But as the events that led up to the 2008 financial crisis revealed, things don’t matter in the markets until they do.“I think we are starting to see a more realistic reassessment of the fiscal pressure in the US,” Shearing said. “What marks the US out is that there’s not really an acknowledgment of the fact that there might be a problem. There’s no plan.”Graph showing US government debt is projected to rise sharplyRussell Jones, a veteran bond market analyst at Llewellyn Consulting, said: “The thing about economics is that often markets delay the judgment and, you know, you can’t really time when they suddenly decide that that’s enough.”The US treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s recentfumbled attempts to intervenein financial markets – to help Tokyo prop up the yen and then to calm bond yields – have only added to the sense that policymakers are panicking.Layered on top of these concerns is a more immediate worry about inflation taking off again as a result of renewed hostilities in the Middle East. Oil prices have risen back above $90 a barrel since the US and Iran resumed tit-for-tat attacks.That has increased expectations that central banks will have to raise interest rates – another factor that puts upward pressure on yields.Graph showing oil prices have risen since the start of the US-Iran warEvery pronouncement by policymakers is being closely scrutinised for clues, including a key speech by the new Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, last Friday that was read by markets as signalling a willingness to act.The European Central Bank is expected to lead the charge with a rate rise next week, but markets are telegraphing higher borrowing costs across major economies.That includes the UK, where investors are now pencilling in three quarter-point rate rises over the next 12 months, and Japan, where the decades-long period of deflation and rock-bottom rates is finally coming to an end.A dramatic expansion of borrowing by AI “hyperscalers” in the US, to help fund the
