massive planned expansion of datacentres, has offered investors an alternative home for their cash – and raised questions about the market’s ability to absorb so much debt simultaneously.Recent calculations by the investment group Vanguard put the value of debt issued by five major tech companies at $135bn (£100bn) this year, up from an average of $35bn between 2020 and 2024.Graph showing rising spending by tech giants including Alphabet, Amazon and MetaThere is potentially an even more fundamental explanation for an upward shift in borrowing costs, too – based on the growing prevalence of inflationary shocks not just as a result of geopolitical chaos but because of the climate emergency.Some economists, including the Bank of England policymaker Swati Dhingra, have argued these increasingly regular shocks, as a result of extreme weather events and resulting economic upheaval, could lead to structurally higher interest rates.Whatever the causes of rising bond yields, the impact is already rippling out worldwide. Public borrowing has increased dramatically in recent years as policymakers have stepped in to cushion consumers against Covid shutdowns, wrestled with sharply higher energy prices since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and stepped up defence spending. That means small changes in global interest rates can have an outsized impact on government budgets.In the UK, where £1 in every £12 of public spending already goes on debt interest, Andy Burnham, the prime minister, was pressed this week by the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, about the rising cost of government borrowing.Higher yields on gilts, as UK government bonds are known, will feed through into predictions of higher interest rate costs for the Treasury ahead of the new chancellor John Healey’s autumn budget.David Aikman, the director of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, urged the government to take the opportunity to implement spending cuts and/or tax increases to help insulate the UK from higher borrowing costs.“There will be a lot of talk about the fiscal rules. I think that’s slightly missing the point,” he said. “The big point here is we’ve just got a lot of debt, whether you’re missing the rules or not. And it means we’re really vulnerable.”On the other side of the world, Australian policymakers have been wrestling with similar challenges. Bond yields have breached 15-year highs just days after the country passed A$1tn in government debt.The timing of the two milestones comes at a difficult time for a Labor government that is under pressure to rein in historically high levels of spending.Falling house prices in a property-obsessed nation are adding to a mood of discontent. Bets have firmed that the Reserve Bank of Australia could deliver another interest rate hike later this month to tame stubbornly high inflation.Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, has been at pains to highlight Australia’s relatively strong budget position internationally. Australia’s debt is equivalent to about half the size of the economy, which pales against other advanced nations. Similarly, the commonwealth is running deficits, but of less than 1% of GDP.Chris Richardson, an independent budget expert, said Australia’s government indebtedness wasn’t “bad by world standards”. “But it’s still a lot of debt. And the higher cost of money means the difficult choices that were there already are that much harder.”For developing countries, these issues are all the more urgent. The International Monetary Fund warned earlier this year that these economies hadbecome more exposedto the risk of higher interest rates, because of the growing importance of lending from short-term investors such as hedge funds, which tend to be more flighty during periods of market volatility.Matthew Martin, of the advocacy group Development Finance International, said: “A lot of these countries are very near the edge, and if they have to go back to the markets and refinance another bond at 1% or 2% higher than it was before, that will mean even less money to spend on climate action, health and education.”If higher yields are sustained, the effects will be felt far beyond the world’s treasuries, muddying the maths for corporate investments and putting upward pressure on mortgage rates, which in the UK have already started to rise.Aikman argued corporate balance sheets worldwide looked less shaky than before the global financial crisis. “We’re not in the place we were in the run-up to 2008,” he said. But he pointed to “pockets” of concern, including the huge scale of debt-fuelled private equity projects that could prove vulnerable in a world of higher rates.By the end of the week, the sell-off sweeping global bond markets appeared to have eased, for now. But it left yields at levels significantly higher than three months ago – and delivered a painful reminder to policymakers, including Burnham, that in globalised financial markets their plans can be buffeted by forces far beyond their control.Explore more on these topicsBondsGiltsGovernment borrowingUS Government borrowingInflationGlobal economyEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sex symbol in a 70s tank top: how Richard O’Sullivan blazed a trail for funny, frisky, cheeky chappies  | Television | The Guardian
description: The star of Man About the House scored an unprecedented run of hit series during the 70s and 80s, bringing a youthful vitality that audiences – and tabloids – loved
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: The star of Man About the House scored an unprecedented run of hit series during the 70s and 80s, bringing a youthful vitality that audiences – and tabloids – loved
Content: Liberated times … O’Sullivan at the time of Man About the House.Photograph: Fremantle Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLiberated times … O’Sullivan at the time of Man About the House.Photograph: Fremantle Media/ShutterstockTelevisionSex symbol in a 70s tank top: how Richard O’Sullivan blazed a trail for funny, frisky, cheeky chappiesThe star of Man About the House scored an unprecedented run of hit series during the 70s and 80s, bringing a youthful vitality that audiences – and tabloids – lovedRichard O’Sullivan, star of 70s sitcom Man About the House, dies aged 82Dandies, docs and robbers: a life in picturesMark LawsonFri 4 Sep 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHaving started as a child actor – first appearing on screen aged seven – Richard O’Sullivan, who has died aged 82, went on to a major TV career playing still relatively youthful characters, representative of the social and sexual freedoms that grew from the liberations of the 1960s.Between 1972 and 81, he appeared in more than 100 episodes of peak-time ITV comedies as funny, frisky men in their 20s and 30s. The first of these was Dr Lawrence Bingham in the hospital sitcom Doctor in Charge, radiating a cheeky charm that led to his career-defining casting as Robin Tripp in Man About the House, in the mid-70s and its spin-off, Robin’s Nest, a few years later.double quotation markMan About the House spawned a formidable franchise, from Robin’s Nest to George and MildredIn the first, Robin shared a flat with two young single women: Chrissy (Paula Wilcox) and Jo (Sally Thomsett). The living arrangements were platonic, partly to appease the TV regulator – from whom formal approval had been sought to show a “mixed” house – but also to establish a sexual tension unusual in mid-evening shows. In the sequel, Robin had qualified as a chef and, again daringly for the TV times, was living with a woman to whom he was not married.View image in fullscreenDandy highwayman … O’Sullivan in Dick Turpin.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockThe attractiveness of screen actors has become a contentious question amid valid concerns about performers being objectified for looks rather than talent. But O’Sullivan had both – with a role in the Richard Burton-Elizabeth Taylor movie Cleopatra, a Hollywood career at one point seemed possible. But, as remained the case from Poldark in the last millennium to the Poldark remake in this one, casting has often been calculated to make viewers fantasise. In Man About the House, O’Sullivan, Wilcox and Thomsett offered something for every viewer, as long as they were heterosexual.Indeed, a running gag in Man About the House was that Robin was gay, a ruse designed to neutralise the living arrangements in the eyes of their landlords (Brian Murphy and Yootha Joyce as George and Mildred), although the humour depended on Robin projecting randy straightness.View image in fullscreenSexy persona … in Doctor in Charge.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockThe sexiness of O’Sullivan’s onscreen persona – that even the period male fashion for knitted tank tops did little to dampen – was helped by reports of relationships with female co-stars and front page red-top newspaper coverage when Tessa Wyatt, O’Sullivan’s onscreen girlfriend in Robin’s Nest, left her then husband, DJ Tony Blackburn, to replicate the role off-screen.Man About the House spawned probably the most formidable franchise in British TV, with Robin’s Nest running alongside Murphy’s and Joyce’s own spin-off, George and Mildred. Core audiences of tens of millions for O’Sullivan’s two instalments gave him an audience-drawing power on which ITV was keen to continue to capitalise, casting him as another telegenic rebel, a legendary highwayman, in Dick Turpin, which ran from 1979 to 82.Approaching his 40s as that series ended, O’Sullivan faced the challenge of moving on from representing the fun of the young. Although the title of Me and My Girl in the 1980s flirted with offering more of the sitcom same, his character in this was a grey-haired widower and the female lead his teenage daughter, played by Joanne Ridley. The impact of this programme was helped by unusually short gaps between series due to fears that Ridley would age faster than the teenager she was playing.When Me and My Girl ended, O’Sullivan had starred in five successive hit series, with the recognition and wealth that such exposure brings. Sadly, there was to be little more of either. Due to declining health, O’Sullivan’s final screen credit was in 1996 and, after a stroke in 2002, he was cared for at the admirable Brinsworth House entertainers’ retirement home in London.A career ended by ill-health would be a misfortune for any performer but a small consolation in O’Sullivan’s case is that an actor who specialised in projecting youthful vitality and energy remains forever so on rerun channels.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV comedyComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Katseye review – petulant hyperpop bops from a girl group in crisis | Music | The Guardian
description: Fans scream ‘eat zucchini’ as if their lives depend on it as the six-piece’s remaining members strut their way through chest-rattling hits, ludicrous bangers and flaccid flops
Author: Michael Cragg
Headline: Fans scream ‘eat zucchini’ as if their lives depend on it as the six-piece’s remaining members strut their way through chest-rattling hits, ludicrous bangers and flaccid flops
Content: Just the right side of goofy … Katseye at the O2 ArenaView image in fullscreenJust the right side of goofy … Katseye at the O2 ArenaMusicReviewKatseye review – petulant hyperpop bops from a girl group in crisisO2 Arena, LondonFans scream ‘eat zucchini’ as if their lives depend on it as the six-piece’s remaining members strut their way through chest-rattling hits, ludicrous bangers and flaccid flopsMichael CraggFri 4 Sep 2026 07.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 07.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt takes a certain amount of resilience to be a Katseye fan. Since debuting three years ago via the boot camp meets reality TV show The Debut: Dream Academy, the multinational K-pop hybrid girl band have put their so-called Eyekonsthrough the wringer. Last month alone they lost their second member to a “personal health and wellness” related hiatus, with Sophia joining Manon (who stepped away in more mysterious circumstances back in February) on the sidelines. Weeks later, they landed their first US No 1 album with Wild, a collection led by the carbonated dance-pop rocketPinky Up– a song referred toby the band’s many online detractors as “skibidi toilet music”(ie slop).Even as this debut arena tour arrived in the UK, there were fears the newly reshaped quartet might be reduced to a trio after Megan sprained her ankle. But if the fans are worried, they don’t show it, their ear-piercing screams drowning out the openingHootie Frutti, a sonic melange that somehow makes Brazilian funk sound leaden. By the time petulant hyperpop bopInternet Girlkicks in they’re screaming lines like “eat zucchini, eat zucchini” as if their lives depend on it.View image in fullscreenEar-piercing screams … Katseye at the O2 ArenaA now healed Megan, Lara, Daniela and Yoonchae do their best to reward the enthusiasm. They lock into the featherlight early singleTouch, which recalls their K-pop peersNewJeans, while last year’s breakthrough single,Gabriela, is given a delicious flamenco makeover. The choreography is frenetic throughout, aided by 10 dancers, but the minimalist staging – just a raised platform and a short runway – means the focus is very much on the songs themselves. That causes problems when the best they can muster isAnimal, a flaccid Ed Sheeran co-write, orMy Way, a song so dated it’s essentially a refried X Factor winner’s single.How Katseye became the world’s biggest girl group – while falling apartRead moreThings pick up when the band are allowed to unshackle themselves from the rigid choreography. The strutting new-wave ofBel Air– a resuscitated Charli xcx demo from 2013 – offers up flashes of their individual personalities, while a chest-rattlingGnarly, complete with its “I’m the shit” hook, shows how well they can sell ludicrous bangers as long as they stay just the right side of goofy. Not that the fans care a jot; to them, Katseye can do no wrong and the skibidi toilet music is simply part of the charm.At theO2 Arena, London, 4 September, thenCo-op Live, Manchester, 6 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockK-popreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wide-legged trousers for men are having a moment. Just ask Gary Neville | Men's fashion | The Guardian
description: Neville may have been mocked for wearing them on Monday Night Football, but he is actually bang on trend
Author: Priya Elan
Headline: Neville may have been mocked for wearing them on Monday Night Football, but he is actually bang on trend
Content: Jamie Carragher pokes fun at Gary Neville over his baggy trousers during Monday Night Football.Photograph: Sky SportsView image in fullscreenJamie Carragher pokes fun at Gary Neville over his baggy trousers during Monday Night Football.Photograph: Sky SportsGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Men's fashionWide-legged trousers for men are having a moment. Just ask Gary NevilleNeville may have been mocked for wearing them on Monday Night Football, but he is actually bang on trendPriya ElanFri 4 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom Kylian Mbappé’s World Cup style to Erling Haaland’s hair tie, football has had many viral fashion moments in 2026.Perhaps the one that speaks to the fashion crowd, and a larger debate happening in menswear right now, isGary Nevillebeing mercilessly teased on Sky Sports’ Monday Night Football for sporting wide-legged trousers.As a producer played Baggy Trousers, by Madness, Neville’s chino-style, wider-legged black slackswere mockedby fellow pundit Jamie Carragher, who compared Neville to Frank Worthington, the forward from West Yorkshire whose dandyish off-pitch style raised eyebrows in the 1970s.View image in fullscreenFrank Worthington pictured in 1974.Photograph: Brian Bould/ANL/Rex/Shutterstock“I went shopping in London,” Neville explained as Carragher jogged along to the Nutty Boys’ hit. “This guy styled me. I think they’re pretty cool, you know.” He predicted that Carragher would be wearing a pair soon.Neville seems to be on to something. Because as far as the cut of your trousers goes, girthisgreater.Nick Pope, the site director at Esquire, said: “In terms of what people are actually wearing on the street, it is the wider silhouette.” Retailers from Cos to Next andMarks and Spencerare going great guns selling wider-fitting trousers in the menswear aisle.The width currently in style can’t quite be described as “baggy trousers”, however. Pope said what Neville wore was a relaxed 90s fit for today, like the trousers seen onA$AP Rockyat the Tribeca festival in New York City in June.The silhouette dominated men’s fashion week for autumn/winter 2026-27 among designers including Dior, Prada and Saint Laurent. On the red carpet, the style has been seen on fashion magnets such asConnor Storrie(at the Golden Globes) andJoe Alwyn(at the Baftas).View image in fullscreenConnor Storrie at the Golden Globes, Joe Alwyn at the Baftas, and A$AP Rocky at the Tribeca festival.Composite: JC Olivera/Getty Images; Neil Mockford/FilmMagic/Getty; Noam Galai/GettyThe classic football pundit dress code grew out of newsreader style: a suit and tie. It was a safe option for the footballer turned television presenter who could not show up wearing their home kit. But Neville and fellow presenter Jamie Redknapp donning a wider leg on Sky Sports speaks to a moment where TV dress codes are morphing.James Andrew, the editor of FourFourTwo, a football magazine, said: “It’s more relaxed now.”Pope added: “I think punditry is becoming more fashion forward in the sense that they’re wearing knitted polos and chinos. But it’s still very tonal and sensible.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe style was seen at the Dior men’s fall/winter 2026 fashion show at Paris men’s fashion week in January.Photograph: WWD/Getty ImagesPaul Monks, who dresses the pundits for Sky Sports, including Monday Night Football, said he believed the clothes should echo the easygoing feel of the show and its audience.“We want what we do on screen to feel relevant to the viewer,” he said. “The way people dress generally has become more relaxed. You see far fewer men wearing suits day to day now, so it wouldn’t make sense for television to become more stiff or overly formal.”The wardrobes of pundits, as well as the England star Jude Bellingham and managers such asPep Guardiola, have started to have an impact on everyday style.Pope said: “They’ve become these unlikely style influencers for middle-aged men. Someone like Gary Neville is probably quite aware of that.”The viral incident illustrated Neville’s growing interest in fashion: he has a clothing collection withHawes & Curtis.Corina Gaffey, a stylist, said: “Gary seems receptive to switching up his on screen style, trying different brands, silhouettes and cuts. He’s obviously in tune with fashion and interested in it.”Pope predicted there would be more collaborations between footballing and fashion. “I think we’re going to see more pundits with their own lines,” he said.One-nil to wider leg trousers, then.Explore more on these topicsMen's fashionMenGary NevilleMen's trousersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Isak’s rapid double sinks Ipswich to give Andoni Iraola first Liverpool win | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Two early goals from Alexander Isak gave Liverpool a 2-0 win at Ipswich, Andoni Iraola’s first as head coach
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Two early goals from Alexander Isak gave Liverpool a 2-0 win at Ipswich, Andoni Iraola’s first as head coach
Content: Alexander Isak jumps for after scoring his second goal.Photograph: Dave Shopland/APView image in fullscreenAlexander Isak jumps for after scoring his second goal.Photograph: Dave Shopland/APPremier LeagueIsak’s rapid double sinks Ipswich to give Andoni Iraola first Liverpool winJohn Brewinat Portman RoadFri 4 Sep 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA first win for Andoni Iraola’sLiverpool, the introduction of the latest star signing in Bradley Barcola making for a successful Friday night. Better yet, continuing signs that Alexander Isak, last year’s model, is coming back to life, his two, well-taken early goals securing the three points. That Cody Gakpo, Isak’s supplier, might have been at Manchester City or Tottenham had the transfer runes been right, added further to a sense of renewal. Liverpool’s attackers were full of the speed and invention sorely lacking for much of last season.Once Barcola arrived in the second half, those velocity levels increased yet further, Liverpool playing the attacking style, high on risk and entertainment, the appointment of Iraola promised. “We are starting to get to the way we want to play,” said Isak afterwards.Ipswich Town v Liverpool: Premier League – liveRead moreTravelling Liverpool fans were made to wait for their first glimpse of £123m Barcola, his being on the bench adding further suspense to a deal that took an entire summer to complete.If Ipswich looked to show the “emotional discipline” their manager, Gary O’Neil, said they lacked in losing 5-2 at Old Trafford, little was in evidence in a ruinous opening spell that betrayed the decent performance they went on to put in.How long will Iraola’s doctrines take to embed? Perhaps not as long as feared. Isak, the most expensive player signed under the outgoing sporting director Richard Hughes, looks – at last – to be flowering. To follow his strike against Nottingham Forest, he had scored twice by the 10th minute. “If Alex is fit and is available, he will produce the numbers,” said Iraola.Assisted for both by Gakpo, the finishes were of the gold standard Liverpool invested so heavily in. “Cody was outstanding,” said Virgil van Dijk, sharing the credit. “I said it before the transfer window had closed, he’s important for us, and he will be important this season.” Iraola joined the appreciation society: “I had no doubt with Cody … he knows how much we value him.”“The level is ruthless,” said O’Neil, otherwise exalted by his team’s response to adversity beyond those opening nine minutes. “If you make mistakes against players like Gakpo, Wirtz and Barcola, there’s a chance you will get punished.”Just as at Old Trafford, two Ipswich goals were conceded in quick, damaging succession, the defence far too open and chaotic. After Víctor Muñoz had set off on a long run stopped only by Issa Diop’s last-man tackle, Julio Enciso controlled the ball, taking a beat by standing on the ball, as if calling for calm.Isak, who had a third first-half goal disallowed for offside, made the runs into scoring positions that made his reputation, nothing like the sorry figure of his debut, lost season. Meanwhile, a no-look pass from Ipswich’s captain, Dara O’Shea, straight to Gakpo, betrayed a collective cognitive dissonance.View image in fullscreenBradley Barcola beats Dara O’Shea on his Liverpool debut.Photograph: Dave Shopland/APFlorian Wirtz becoming involved with the tricks and flicks offered another pointer that last summer’s huge Liverpool outlay may not be so wasteful as it appeared in Arne Slot’s dog days. Iraola’s appointment came with a reputation for improving players. Should the Basque get the best from the German, in a similar price bracket to Barcola and Isak, then this week’s pronouncement he is happy with his squad will ring truer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAn obvious gap in the Liverpool squad left by Hughes is a commanding defensive midfielder. Enciso often located space, though suffered for a lack of quality around him. Beyond the break, with O’Neil in full flow, barking at players and officials alike, Ipswich were more confrontational, less admiring of their opponent’s higher skill levels. “I hate having to talk about good performances when you don’t get points because you need to maximise them,” said O’Neil, painting a picture that will not match many other summations of the match.Muñoz, stocky and adventurous, might well prove the answer to the right-wing vacancy left by Mohamed Salah, showing off a ready work ethic before departing in the double substitution that brought Barcola on. Isak also departed, returning after full time to an ovation from fans finally seeing something close to his potential.With Gakpo pushed to centre-forward, Barcola’s first touches came off the left flank, one drop of the shoulder and sprint beyond O’Shea lifting the volume among the away supporters. “He hadn’t played a single minute since the World Cup so we had to be careful,” said Iraola. “He was always a threat.”That burst of Barcola preceded another loss of Ipswich faculties as Leif Davis first pulled Dominik Szoboszlai, and then knocked him over for what appeared a clear penalty. Only an offside ruled by the video assistant protected the Ipswich defender’s modesty. The announcement of that decision brought the loudest cheer of the night from the home contingent.Barcola, even amid the warp speed of thePremier League, showed lightning acceleration when creating a late chance for Gakpo. An impressive cameo and the expectation of far more to come from the player and his new team.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueIpswich TownLiverpoolmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka halts US Open match due to cannabis smell  | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Aryna Sabalenka briefly stopped her US Open match, complaining about the strong smell of cannabis on court
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Aryna Sabalenka briefly stopped her US Open match, complaining about the strong smell of cannabis on court
Content: Aryna Sabalenka needs to win the US Open to retain her No 1 ranking.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersView image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka needs to win the US Open to retain her No 1 ranking.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersUS Open Tennis 2026‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka halts US Open match due to cannabis smell‘It’s tricky to handle when you’re trying to compete’Alcaraz into fourth round after straight sets victoryTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsFri 4 Sep 2026 17.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAryna Sabalenka briefly stopped her match at the US Open to complain about the strong smell of cannabis on her court as she comfortably reached the fourth round in New York.Sabalenka, the two-time defending champion, continued her attempts to rebuild her form as she overcame a challenging test from Kamilla Rakhimova before winning 6-3, 6-4.Early in the match, a smiling Sabalenka approached the chair umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore while leading 3-0, stating “Someone is smoking weed, do you mind … because it’s so strong,” Afterwards, Sabalenka laughed as she described her interaction with the umpire: “I was, like, Guys, you can do whatever, you can smoke whatever, you can relax as much as you can, but please, do not do it around the tennis courts. It’s a bit tricky to handle that smell while you’re trying to compete at your best.”US Open tennis: Alcaraz beats Wu, Sabalenka, Pegula and Medvedev advance on day six – liveRead moreCannabis is legal in New York and weed can be smelled around tournament grounds, as is the case all around the city. This has become a common talking point at the US Open in recent years. Although Sabalenka initially seemed to believe that the smoke may have been coming from a spectator in or right by the crowd, she later said she was unclear about its origins but the smell of cannabis was stronger than she had ever smelt it during her years of competing in New York: “That strong, yeah. Also, because it was a bit windy. I don’t know if it was, like, coming from the crowd or was from the outside because the wind blows it into the stadium. I don’t know. I just hope they’re going to be a bit more aware of that stuff,” she said.Most importantly for Sabalenka, she has returned to the round of 16 without dropping a set and she appears to be finding some rhythm on the court. This victory was spearheaded by a stellar serving performance, with the Belarusian serving 10 aces and facing zero break points. She had arrived in New York in some of her most difficult form for years, having failed to reach a final since spectacularly winning Indian Wells and Miami back-to-back in March. Sabalenka will lose her No 1 ranking, which she has held for 97 weeks, unless she wins her third US Open title in a row and Elena Rybakina, the world No 2, loses before the semi-finals.Although Sabalenka has put together a series of encouraging performances on-court, the added pressure on her shoulders has perhaps been revealed elsewhere. After her dominant second round win over Polina Iatcenko, Sabalenka clashed with a reporter in her post-match press conference when the reporter described her week before the US Open as “parties and fun”.View image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz enjoyed a straightforward win over Yibing Wu.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAThis was the second time during the tournament that a reporter had referenced pre-tournament obligations leading up to the US Open, prompting a forceful response from Sabalenka: “You guys are, like, a joke,” she said. “‘Parties, fun …’ like, why would you even say that? Why would you even think about that? What kind of question is that? Just because I posted, like, some activities with brands, and you think that I’ve been partying, not training?”Sabalenka eventually ended the lengthy, heated exchange by imploring the reporter to: “Think before you say stuff.”A tougher test awaits Sabalenka in the fourth round as she faces the home favourite Taylor Townsend, who followed up her great run to the fourth round last year with another excellent tournament in New York. Townsend defeated the 15th seed Diana Shnaider 6-2, 6-7 (3), 6-3 to return to the fourth round.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDaniil Medvedev, the 2021 men’s singles champion, also continued to find his feet in New York as he reached the fourth round with a 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 victory over the 29th seed Arthur Rinderknetch.Carlos Alcaraz, the men’s defending champion, continues to grow in confidence on his return to tennis from a four-and-a-half month injury layoff and he moved into the fourth round with a 6-3, 6-4, 6-1 win over Wu Yibing of China. Alcaraz, who until the tournament had not competed since injuring his right wrist at the beginning of April, had to hold his nerve and problem solve during some tight moments in the first two sets. However, he elevated his game in those decisive moments and he continues to show that he will be difficult to defeat despite how early it is in his comeback.Alcaraz will next face the 20th seed Tommy Paul, an American player, who overcame the 15th seed Alexander Bublik 6-4, 3-6, 6-7(4), 6-1, 6-3: “To be honest, I’m better than I thought,” Alcaraz said. “Physically, I thought I was going to be bad after the first match but I’m recovering really well, I’m doing great things off the court out be in a good shape and right now I think my level is good. I’ve got the rhythm of the competition. Every time I step on to the court, I give it my all.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Aryna SabalenkaTennisUS Open tennisUS sportsCarlos AlcaraznewsShareReuse this content

title: Kimi Antonelli: ‘The F1 environment is great but at times it can be very brutal’ | Kimi Antonelli | The Guardian
description: Before his home grand prix, the Mercedes driver tells Giles Richards about his rocky debut and quest to become the first Italian world champion since 1953
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Before his home grand prix, the Mercedes driver tells Giles Richards about his rocky debut and quest to become the first Italian world champion since 1953
Content: Kimi Antonelli has a 59-point lead at the top of the F1 drivers’ championship standings.Photograph: DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli has a 59-point lead at the top of the F1 drivers’ championship standings.Photograph: DPPI/ShutterstockKimi AntonelliInterviewKimi Antonelli: ‘The F1 environment is great but at times it can be very brutal’Giles Richardsin MonzaBefore his home grand prix, the Mercedes driver opens up on his rocky debut season and quest to become the first Italian world champion since 1953Fri 4 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIfKimi Antonellifeels any pressure as the favourite to take the Formula One world championship at just 20 years old and in his second year in the sport, it is imperceptible. He admits F1 can be brutal but a thing of beauty too, a labour of love for the Italian who has been a revelation this season.Compelling and brilliant, that he is also endearing and likable marks Antonelli out as more than just a potential champion. Sitting in the Mercedes motorhome it is impossible not to be struck by how young he looks, the tousled hair, engaging smile and eyes gleaming with youthful enthusiasm. He speaks with an open candour, the air of a kid in a sweetshop who still can’t quite believe all those sherbet lemons are there for the taking.Lewis Hamilton ready to rock Monza with ‘phenomenal’ Italian GP win for FerrariRead moreIt is striking precisely because so many F1 drivers lose this sense of exhilaration all too soon in their careers, and it is almost infectious. Yet for all that his F1 career has been brief after making his debut for Mercedes last season, it has been quite the ride since he climbed into a kart as a five-year-old.“I do what I love to do, it’s something that I’ve dreamt of for such a long time and I want to enjoy it fully,” he says with the smile that it is very much the Antonelli default expression.“But it’s different, because growing up you just see the races, the drivers driving, you don’t see what’s behind all of that. Last year I probably would have said different things compared to this year, especially because I think the F1 environment is very brutal. It’s great, but at times it can be very, very brutal.“I feel like last year I suffered a bit from that when there was a lot of speculation about my future, it was difficult for me, but thanks to the team and to my family and all the support I had, I was able to overcome that, but that was a thing that as a kid I didn’t see it coming until I actually experienced it.”A rocky debut season and public debate over his future in F1 – for all that it was never entertained at Mercedes – was borne with great fortitude and he has come out the other side a stronger character and delivered emphatically on his great promise. Antonelli leads the drivers’ championship, ahead of his Mercedes teammate, George Russell, and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton by a whopping 59 points.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli’s victory in the Chinese Grand Prix kicked off a run of five consecutive race wins.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersThe youngster has learned hard and he has learned fast. When he made a mistake on the penultimate lapat last season’s Qatar Grand Prix, with Lando Norris passing him, he was subjected to a torrent of abuse and absurd accusations that he had moved over for the British driver, who went on to take the title.“After Qatar all the, let’s say, the hate … what was hard for me in Qatar was getting blamed for something that I would never do,” he says. “To get really criticised publicly, openly about something that I would never do on purpose, it was tough.”Antonelli is admirable because he does not shy away from addressing these questions. He is self-aware to an extent that belies his years. If he must still be considered the kid in F1, he wears a personable maturity more comfortably than many of his contemporaries in the sport.On track his driving has spoken for itself this season, not least in the five consecutive wins he delivered from the Chinese to Monaco grands prix, which has put him in such a dominant championship position. His team, from Toto Wolff down, recognise they have not only a special talent but also a special person, for whom being in F1 is a very simple and very human equation.“I always try to be myself,” he says. “This is the way I am, I feel like it’s good with the mechanics, with the team, to joke around a little bit when it’s the right time. Just to create an even better environment and I think if you’re able also to connect in that way with the team all of us are able to enjoy even more the weekend together, working together.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli is the home hero as he targets success at Monza … but he will start from the back of the grid.Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP“Of course there are certain situations where I might be a bit more serious than usual but at the end of the day myself is being positive, smiling, having fun, joking with the mechanics, with the team in general and then just driving the car as fast as I can.”At which he excels. The competitive verve of his driving style is enthralling, even as the bravura approach might obscure what is clearly an immaculate touch in a controlled, intuitive balancing of a car at its very limit. It has put him in unprecedented territory.The last Italian to win the world championship was Alberto Ascari in 1953 and the country has embraced their wunderkind in the German marque wholeheartedly. For all that Ferrari is a religion in Italy, in Monza Antonelli has brought Mercedes into the faith.Yet the young man remains so grounded. That his father, Marco, a former driver, has played such a huge part in his career has been key and for which he deserves much credit as Antonelli acknowledges what is clearly a fundamental bond.“My dad always comes to most of the races, we have a really strong relationship, he’s kind of my rock,” Antonelli says. “I feel like my dad knows me inside out. I always like to discuss with him because it’s what we’ve been used to since I was in karting.“He’s going to give me advice and then if I decide to listen, good, but if I don’t decide to listen, it’s OK as well. He always tells me that I need to be also free to take my own decisions about things, that I don’t need to be stuck by what he says.”Lewis Hamilton ready to rock Monza with ‘phenomenal’ Italian GP win for FerrariRead moreThis weekend Antonelli and Mercedes have already made one decision which is to put the title tilt first. The Italian is taking a raft of new engine components for which he will receive a penalty that means he will start from the back of the grid. He recognises that the overtaking opportunities at Monza made this the right choice, even as he deals with the weight on his shoulders as the home hero.“Being Italian I know how we can think, how we can react and I know as an Italian when we get excited about something we create expectations – very high expectations,” he says. “But then when something bad happens then we’re like completely the opposite, we tend to exaggerate things. So I’m aware of the expectations, but I’m also happy about the support that I received.”The bigger picture is the plan for this engaging young man, who only turned 20 late last month. Should it work out, and few would bet against Antonelli at this point, he hopes the Mercedes team will be singing from his songsheet of the Italian national anthem when he is world champion.“I mean, they’ve got to learn it,” he says, eyes gleaming. “If I achieve the goal by the end of the year then I’m going to print the lyrics so then they can.”Explore more on these topicsKimi AntonelliFormula OneFormula One 2026Mercedes GPMotor sportinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Amy Hunt left trailing by Julien Alfred in women’s 200m Diamond League final | Athletics | The Guardian
description: The British sprinter finished third behind the Olympic 100m champion, on a night where the pole vault superstar Mondo Duplantis pulled out with an injury
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The British sprinter finished third behind the Olympic 100m champion, on a night where the pole vault superstar Mondo Duplantis pulled out with an injury
Content: A season’s best for Amy Hunt (right) was not enough to win the Diamond League women’s 200m against the pace set by Julien Alfred (centre).Photograph: Omar Havana/APView image in fullscreenA season’s best for Amy Hunt (right) was not enough to win the Diamond League women’s 200m against the pace set by Julien Alfred (centre).Photograph: Omar Havana/APAthleticsAmy Hunt left trailing by Julien Alfred in women’s 200m Diamond League finalBritish sprinter finishes third behind Olympic 100m championPole vault superstar Mondo Duplantis pulls out with injurySean Ingleat King Baudouin StadiumFri 4 Sep 2026 17.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 21.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s Amy Hunt was given a jolting reminder of the gap between her and the world’s very best female sprinters as she finished nearly half a second behind Julien Alfred in the Diamond League 200m final.But afterwards Hunt insisted that coming third in a season’s best time of 22.16sec, on tired legs on a dank Brussels night, amounted to one of the better races of her career.Cameron Myers shines in star-studded field to win 1500m at Diamond League finalRead more“I’ve shown the last few 200s, I’m getting a lot stronger, and I think I was probably one of the closest athletes up to my personal best tonight,” said Hunt, who won four European gold medals last month in Birmingham. “So on a very freezing cold night in northern Europe, in September, at 10pm – I think that’s probably one of the best 200s I’ve ever done.”Certainly there were plenty of signs for optimism as Hunt made a fast start and was in touch with Alfred around the bend. But then the St Lucian, who won 100m gold in the Paris Olympics, applied the afterburners to take victory in 21.79, with Kyla White of the US second in 22.00 as Hunt faded.“That was the closest I’ve ever been to Julien on the bend, and I thought: ‘Oh my gosh, if I had completely fresh legs, I could really take you on right now,’” said Hunt. “And that’s such an exciting thing to me because she’s such an incredible athlete. She’s so fierce, but also kind. And to know that that was probably the best first half of the race I’ve ever put together makes it really, really exciting for next season.”The race of the night came in the men’s 1500m as the AustralianCameron Myers found his way out of a boxon the home straight, swerved between Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Phanuel Koech, and then got his nose in front to win in 3:30.14.It was vindication of sorts for Myers, who was a little disappointing in taking Commonwealth Games silver in the milebehind Josh Kerrin Glasgow last month. But there was also encouragement for Ingebrigtsen, even though he ran out of steam in the final 30 metres, as his time of 3:30.52 was the quickest since his comeback after missing 11 months due to an achilles injury.View image in fullscreenEmmanouil Karalis broke Mondo Duplantis’s Diamond League pole vault record.Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/ReutersThis Diamond League final also doubled as the 50th memorial meeting to be staged in memory of Ivo Van Damme, the brilliant Belgian athlete who won silver medals over 800m and 1500m at the 1976 Olympics before dying in a car accident later that year, aged just 22.After a lengthy tribute to Van Damme, several of the famous athletes to grace this track – including the nine-time Olympic champion Carl Lewis – were paraded in front of the crowd and Philippe, King of the Belgians.Lewis had taken his place next to the king in time to see the Jamaican world champion Oblique Seville take the men’s 100m in 9.90sec, recovering from a poor start to beat the Commonwealth champion Emmanuel Eseme by three-hundredths of a second.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSoon afterwards another world champion, Emmanuel Wanyonyi, had the crowd standing to applaud as he destroyed a strong field to set a meeting record of 1:41.80 in the men’s 800m.“Today was all about winning and I knew that I would have to run 1:41 to win and I did,” said Wanyonyi, who finished nearly a second ahead of the Algerian Djamel Sedjati, with Britain’s Ben Pattison fifth in 1:44.29. “The conditions weren’t ideal tonight. The wind didn’t bother me that much, I was happy it stopped raining.”Elsewhere Busang Collen Kebinatshipi won the men’s 400m in 43.40, breaking his own Diamond League record, while Emmanouil Karalis broke Mondo Duplantis’s meeting record by clearing 6.12m in the pole vault. But there was disappointment as Duplantis pulled out beforehand with tightness in his leg and admitted that his chances of making the new $10m Ultimate Championships in Budapest next week were in question.“The worst possible thing to do is having to pull out of a competition,” said Duplantis. “My head is everywhere right now. It’s super difficult but that’s the life of an athlete. I try to stay calm and positive. We will see if I can make it to the Ultimate Championships. I don’t have the answer right now.”The two-day meeting will conclude on Saturday, with Audrey Werro’s attempt on the women’s 800m world record topping the bill. There should be British success too, with Georgia Hunter Bell favourite to win the women’s 1500m – and a first prize of $60,000.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alexia Putellas begins WSL ride as London City outclass Manchester United  | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Alexia Putellas made her Women’s Super League bow as London City Lionesses brushed aside Manchester United in the season opener
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Alexia Putellas made her Women’s Super League bow as London City Lionesses brushed aside Manchester United in the season opener
Content: The talk was all about London City’s new players, but it was one of last season’s big-name signings Daniëlle van de Donk who made the game safe.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe talk was all about London City’s new players, but it was one of last season’s big-name signings Daniëlle van de Donk who made the game safe.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianWomen's Super LeagueAlexia Putellas begins WSL ride as London City outclass Manchester UnitedSuzanne Wrackat Copperjax Community StadiumFri 4 Sep 2026 16.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are few scenarios since Millwall Lionesses broke away from Millwall and became London City Lionesses that would have felt more surreal than the idea ofAlexia Putellas captaining the sideto a statement win in a WSL season-opener in Bromley just seven years later.Here we are though: referees have to get used to the formerly talismanic Barcelona captain stooping to pick up the coin after the toss, as is her custom; players must get used to eyes and cameras looking past them to focus in on the influential No 11; and the two-time Ballon d’Or winnerhas to get used to playing with teammatesnot drilled in a very specific style of play from such an early age that it becomes an inherent part of them.London City claim sponsor deal is record and bigger than some in Premier LeagueRead moreOf course it is a step down to go from the three-time European champions to a team embarking on their second season in the WSL, but off the pitch, with the owner, Michele Kang, committed to giving female athletes the best of everything, the difference will be more negligible, even before the approved new world-class training facility is built.Regardless of what you think of her movements in women’s football,or about private finance investment in it, Kang, who walked the perimeter of the stadium prior to kick-off taking photos with fans in her ‘Kang 27’ emblazoned home shirt, is the antithesis of the owner of last night’s opposition, Jim Ratcliffe,and his dismal references to his women’s teams.View image in fullscreenMichele Kang did the rounds at a sold-out stadium, the first time London City Lionesses have done that since starting to play at Bromley.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianPutellas led the team out to a ­raucous welcome at the sold-out home of Bromley FC, her steely stare only broken to crack a quick smile and share some words with the mascot gripping her hand.In this corner of London’s outskirts, the midfielder experienced her first proper taste of her new reality. At 32 and with her very best years likely behind her, it was a solid rather than showstopper performance. She was outshone by teammates such as Rosa Kafaji and Lucía Corrales, who unfortunately went off on a stretcher late on after overstretching for the ball.“Everybody knows what [Putellas] can create and bring to us,” said the London City manager, Eder Maestre. “It’s not just the things she’s capable of doing, it’s the things she facilitates for other players too.“Having this kind of player in the squad is very important because she represents the highest standards and having her involved in it is not only because of her performance, but also because of the leadership she can bring in terms of helping us to reach that standard. But it is not only about Alexia, she is only one player, and I think the most impactful thing was the way everybody connected, the chemistry that we are building around the players.”View image in fullscreenAlexia Putellas was solid rather than spectacular on her WSL debut.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianMaestre has been tasked with gelling a squad stacked with new players, includingthe former England goalkeeper Mary Earps, who was on the bench with Elene Lete starting.Maestre explained: “Mary had some issues in pre-season so that was why there was inconsistency in game involvement. We have two strong goalkeepers. Today, Elene deserved to be in the lineup. She was very strong in her actions.”Maestre has said the identity he wants to create for the side is “related to all those things we felt when we were playing football as children”.That ethos was evident in their play, with London City on the front foot from the off. Despite not always being pretty, they looked like they were having fun as they pressed and attacked aggressively, and when they broke the deadlock nine minutes in it was not surprising.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlanna Kennedy provided the pressure, rising above a hunkered-down Julia Zigiotti Olme who could only turn the ball into her own net.View image in fullscreenDelphine Cascarino (left), who set up London City Lionesses’ second goal, was named player of the match.Photograph: John Walton/PAIt was a cruel introduction to life in the WSL, and its spotlight, forthe new Manchester United manager, Eva Olid, particularly with Chelsea and Arsenal up next, but on this showing andafter a lacklustre summer transfer window, few games would have offered a kind introduction. United were outclassed in Bromley, conceding 60% possession.They did at least manage three shots, but by the time they did any hopes of a leveller were crushed by the home side, when Mapi León’s corner was worked towards Delphine Cascarino and the French forward’s cross was delightfully flicked into the far corner by Daniëlle van de Donk.“It’s a process,” said Olid. “I think it was something more mental in the first half, we could feel like the players were not believing.“At half-time I say that this is not us, we need the ball to be ourselves … in the second half, we were building through the middle, finding the free player, playing between the lines. That is us, and I can feel my team in the second half. It’s my job to help them to believe that we can always be the team of the second half.”There was a late consolation for Olid’s humbled charges deep into added time, when Simi Awujo powered in the loose ball after a free-kick was cleared into empty space, but it could not dampen the enthusiasm of an emphatic performance from Maestre’s side – a performance that is a very solid foundation to build on.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueLondon City LionessesManchester United WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: José Mourinho sick as a Parrott as Real Madrid sunk by Real Betis and Irish supersub | European club football | The Guardian
description: Mbappé sees late penalty saved by Valles while PSG were beaten by league leaders Monaco
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mbappé sees late penalty saved by Valles while PSG were beaten by league leaders Monaco
Content: Troy Parrott celebrates after scoring the winner against Real Madrid.Photograph: Raúl Caro Cadenas/EPAView image in fullscreenTroy Parrott celebrates after scoring the winner against Real Madrid.Photograph: Raúl Caro Cadenas/EPAEuropean club footballJosé Mourinho sick as a Parrott as Real Madrid sunk by Real Betis and Irish supersubMbappé sees late penalty saved by VallesPSG are beaten by league leaders MonacoAgenciesFri 4 Sep 2026 18.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReal Madrid’s perfect start in La Liga ⁠ended on Friday when Real Betis beat them 1-0, with the ⁠substitute Troy Parrott ⁠scoring ​nine minutes from time and goalkeeper Álvaro Valles saving a stoppage-time ⁠penalty from Kylian Mbappé.The clash began at a high tempo but the pace ⁠dropped after the interval in the heat in ​Seville. The Republic of Ireland star Parrott, introduced ‌in the 68th ‌minute, broke the deadlock in the 81st when ‌he reacted quickly after Thibaut Courtois parried a header into his path.Mbappé struck the crossbar four minutes later before the substitute Carlos Espí met a cross from Vinícius Júnior with a spectacular bicycle kick, only for the equaliser to be ruled ​out for offside following a VAR review.Tough start for PSG but Luis Enrique has faith in burst of ‘new energy’ from signingsRead moreNelson Deossa then nearly sealed the victory for hosts Betis with a long-range effort after spotting Courtois ⁠off his line, but the goalkeeper recovered to ​make ​the save.José Mourinho’s Madrid got one ​final opportunity when Natan brought down ​Vinícius inside ‌the area, ​deep ​into stoppage time, but Valles saved Mbappé’s spot-kick to preserve Betis’s lead and secure the three points.“My team played a great game, and sometimes you lose and you don’t know why,” Mourinho said. “We dominated, controlling everything, lots of attacks, lots of chances. If we had drawn we would have been left frustrated, so imagine how we feel after losing.“I don’t know how we lost because we played very well collectively. I cannot fault the attitude of any of my players. We deserved to win but deserving to win does not ⁠give you points. I’m very happy with ​my players, all ​of them. I cannot fault ​any of them individually. As for the penalty, when ​one of us ‌steps up to ​take it, ​we all stand together.“The Betis players are more streetwise than the Madrid players, who are very honest. With the backing of a fantastic crowd, they manage to gain these kinds of advantages.”Paris Saint-Germainlooked to be on their way to their first Ligue 1 win of the season when Marquinhos put the hosts ahead in the 31st minute, butMonacorallied with goals from Flavio Nazinho in the 58th minute and Stanis Idumbo in the 72nd. Monaco lead the table as the only team to win their opening three games.“We clearly deserved to win. That is my opinion,” said Luis Enrique.“I saw the game and it was the typical game in which we were better than the opposition and created a lot more chances, but the opposition goalkeeper was the best player on the pitch.”The US striker Folarin Balogun was left out of Monaco’s squad after the collapse of his proposed transfer to Everton this week, while Lamine Camara played after his move to Chelsea was called off at the last minute.View image in fullscreenPSG’s Fabián Ruiz (left) challenges for the ball with Monaco’s in-demand Lamine Camara.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/APPSG had already drawn 2-2 with Rennes and Lille in their first two games and also lost the French Super Cup to Lens 1-0 last month.The first league defeat came hours after PSG announced contract extensions for coach Luis Enrique and several players. João Neves, Lucas Beraldo, Senny Mayulu and Willian Pacho all signed new deals through to 2031, while Fabián Ruiz had his contract extended until 2028.LyonbeatAuxerre3-1 earlier on Friday and are second in the league, two points behind Monaco and level on points withLille, who won 1-0 atToulouseon Thursday thanks to an Ayase Ueda goal.Assane Diao bagged a brace asComorolled to a 4-1 win atGenoainSerie A. Nico Paz and Martin Baturina also added goals. Cesc Fabregas’ side lead the Italian standings by one point ahead of a pack of six teams who have yet to play this weekend.Como will make their Champions League debut against Leipzig on 10 September, with Manchester United to visit in October and PSG in January.In Germany,Stuttgartromped to a 4-1 win overKölnin theBundesliga.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballReal BetisReal MadridLa LigaParis Saint-GermainLigue 1MonaconewsShareReuse this content

title: St Helens miss out on playoffs after Charnley news caps Leigh’s perfect night | Super League | The Guardian
description: St Helens miss out on the playoffs for the first time in over 60 years after a 48-10 defeat at Leigh
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: St Helens miss out on the playoffs for the first time in over 60 years after a 48-10 defeat at Leigh
Content: Josh Charnley touches down for the first try in the thrashing of St Helens which secures Leigh’s place in the Super League playoffs.Photograph: Ed Sykes/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJosh Charnley touches down for the first try in the thrashing of St Helens which secures Leigh’s place in the Super League playoffs.Photograph: Ed Sykes/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueSt Helens miss out on playoffs after Charnley news caps Leigh’s perfect nightLeigh 48-10 St HelensCharnley scores and agrees contract extensionAaron Bowerat Progress With Unity StadiumFri 4 Sep 2026 17.26 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt ended not so much with a bang, but with a whimper. One of rugby league’s most extraordinary streaks has felt as though it was coming to an inevitable end for quite some time but as it transpired, St Helens’ 64-year run of making the playoffs ultimately concluded in a manner that summarises their fall from grace.You have to go back to 1962 to find an end-of-season playoff series that did not include one of rugby league’s true heavyweight clubs. In theSuper Leagueera, they have won 10 titles and were champions of the world as recently as 2023. But this, sadly, is a shadow of that side – and indeed that club.St Helens’ 60-year playoff record hangs by a thread after thrashing by LeedsRead moreThey have been outsiders all season long for the playoffs, and their hopes were emphatically ended here against a team who themselves have genuine Old Trafford aspirations. Without over a dozen first-team players, Saints’ defensive frailties that have plagued them all season were exposed brutally yet again to ensure they will finish seventh. History for all the wrong reasons.But this was just as significant a night for Leigh as it was for St Helens. These two teams have been on contrasting journeys in recent years with Saints slowly slipping away from being the best team in the world, and the Leopards rising year-on-year to become a genuine Super League threat in 2026. They scored eight tries, four in each half, to blow Saints away in crucial moments and book their playoff spot. They could yet finish fourth and get home advantage in the opening week should they beat Wakefield next Friday. After a slow start, Leigh look genuine contenders.“We’ve got to rely on other teams winning over the weekend and then it’s still mathematically a chance,” their coach, Adrian Lam, said. “But we would have taken this a third of the way through the season so I’ve got to appreciate that.” His side were far too good when it mattered here, with their attack in devastating form all evening.Super League’s all-time top try-scorer, Josh Charnley, opened the scoring with his 281st career try – and celebrated by signing a fake contract extension which was officially announced in the stadium moments later. David Armstrong doubled the lead soon after. There was a brief flurry of resistance from Saints but tries for Jacob Douglas and Tristan Sailor proved a false dawn. They collapsed again as half-time approached, with two more Leigh tries making it 24-10.From there, it always felt unlikely at best that Saints could keep their season alive going into next weekend. “The group are very disappointed but they should be proud,” their interim coach, Eamon O’Carroll said. “The scoreline blew out but there were some St Helens traits in there. But there needs to be changes now.”Those changes will be headlined by the arrival of the Australia coach, Kevin Walters, in 2027 – and he has plenty to work on based on this display. Leigh put the result beyond doubt as the hour mark approached when the outstanding Umyla Hanley scoring his second after Edwin Ipape barged over from close range.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBy then, it was merely a case of how many Leigh would win by. The answer was a resounding 38, as Jacob Alick-Wiencke exposed more timid St Helens defending before Robbie Mulhern strode through to score late on with the kind of ease that has been too common a sight in Saints’ play this season.Sport is cyclical, and history suggests St Helens will be a force again. But there is a major rebuild ahead that suggests that return to the top table is some way off. For the first time in over a generation, the Saints will watch the playoffs with the rest of us as spectators.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueLeigh LeopardsSt HelensRugby leaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Vuelta a España: Wout van Aert battles scorching heat to claim stage 13 victory  | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Belgian star edges out Valentin Paret-Peintre in breakaway while Enric Mas keeps red jersey with 1m 45sec lead
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Belgian star edges out Valentin Paret-Peintre in breakaway while Enric Mas keeps red jersey with 1m 45sec lead
Content: Wout van Aert celebrates after landing his first stage win of this year’s Vuelta a España.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPAView image in fullscreenWout van Aert celebrates after landing his first stage win of this year’s Vuelta a España.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPAVuelta a EspañaVuelta a España: Wout van Aert battles scorching heat to claim stage 13 victoryMas keeps hold of red jersey with 1min 45sec leadKooij claims stage win at Tour of BritainAssociated PressFri 4 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 12.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWout van Aert won his fourth career stage at theVuelta a Españaamid scorching heat on Friday, while Enric Mas kept the red jersey.On a hot and sunny day in southern Spain, Van Aert beat fellow breakaway rider Valentin Paret-Peintre to claim the hilly 192km jaunt from Almuñécar to Loja.The elite Belgian rider stopped the clock after four and a half hours of racing. It was Van Aert’s first win of this edition after he won three stages in 2024. It added to his long list of triumphs, which includes 10 stages of the Tour de France and several one-day classics. It was also the fourth team win for Team Visma Lease a Bike at this edition.Mas, the Movistar leader,kept his leadof one minute 45 seconds over the four-time winner Primoz Roglic. They crossed in a group around three minutes after Van Aert.Riders had to handle more heat as thermometers recorded 36C (97 F) in Loja, where the stage finished. One rider compared the heat to having a “hairdryer blowing in your face”. Another said he spent the day pouring water over himself at every opportunity.View image in fullscreenThe Spanish Movistar cyclist Enric Mas celebrates on the podium wearing the red overall leader’s jersey following stage 13.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPA“It was a very tough stage because of the heat and the hard pace,” the American rider Sepp Kuss, of Visma Lease a Bike, told broadcaster RTVE in fluent Spanish. “If you tried to attack, you just cracked. But we all had to compete in the same conditions. I must also thank the organisers for adding extra spots where we could grab water. If not, it would have been impossible.”Mas has led the race since the Tour de France champion, Tadej Pogacar, withdrew following a crash last Saturday. Mas has finished the Vuelta as runner-up on three occasions, in 2018, 2021 and 2022. He is trying to become the first Spanish rider to win the home race since Alberto Contador in 2014. The key to Mas finally coming out on top will likely rest on him having a big enough lead to withstand Roglič during a time trial on stage 18.Friday’s stage 13 was just south of Granada, where the three-week race will finish on 13 September. On Saturday, riders face a 154km (95m) stage from Jaén to Sierra de la Pandera. “Our goal tomorrow is just keeping the red shirt for the next day,” Mas said.This year’s Vuelta is entirely in southern Spain and without any of its classic mountain finishes in the country’s greener north.Kooij claims stage win at Tour of BritainOlav Kooij edged out Tim Merlier in a chaotic sprint to win stage three of the Tour of Britain in Beverley. Kooij began his charge well down in the pack but, with Thursday’s stage winner Merlier finding himself boxed in, the Dutchman spotted his opportunity down the left and, by the time he belatedly found some room, Merlier could not respond.View image in fullscreenOlav Kooij wins stage three of the Tour of Britain in Beverley.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAIt was an eighth career stage win for Kooij at this race, putting him second in the Tour of Britain’s record books alongside Edvald Boasson Hagen, two behind the all-time record held by Sir Mark Cavendish.After a second consecutive sprint finish to end the 181km stage from Hull, the stage one winner Lewis Askey continues to lead overall. Askey leads by 12 seconds from Tim Wellens, with Matteo Trentin a further seven seconds back in third.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Carse left out in cold again and told to ‘work through issues’ after Derby bar incident | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Brydon Carse has been left out of England’s white-ball squads to face Sri Lanka and told to ‘work through the issues’ that led to him being handcuffed by police outside a bar in Derby
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Brydon Carse has been left out of England’s white-ball squads to face Sri Lanka and told to ‘work through the issues’ that led to him being handcuffed by police outside a bar in Derby
Content: Brydon Carse pictured this week at Chester-le-Street.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenBrydon Carse pictured this week at Chester-le-Street.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PACricketCarse left out in cold again and told to ‘work through issues’ after Derby bar incidentFast bowler left out of England squads to face Sri LankaPlayer being investigated regarding late-night episodeAli MartinFri 4 Sep 2026 10.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrydon Carse has been left out of England’s white-ball squads to face Sri Lanka at the end of the season and told to “work through the issues” that led to him being handcuffed by police outside a bar in Derby last month.Carse, 31, is being investigated by the Cricket Regulator regarding thelate night incident in Augustthat prompted his removal from England’s plans for the ongoing Test series against Pakistan. Derbyshire police are also looking into an alleged assault that night, albeit Carse’s involvement is not currently known.Test cricket ponders end times again, but this decline feels both real and symbolic | Emma JohnRead moreIn the meantime, Carse is technically available for England selection but has been left out of the Twenty20s and one-day internationals against Sri Lanka that start in Southampton on 15 September. Henry Crocombe, the uncapped seamer who has claimed back-to-back hat-tricks for Sussex in the past week, has taken Carse’s place in the ODI squad.An England spokesperson said: “Given recent events, we feel it is important for [Carse] to work through the issues that led to the Derby incident and take time for a proper reset. This decision does not prejudge the outcome of any investigation.”Though a close friend of the white-ball captain, Harry Brook, and centrally contracted, it would appear Carse has fallen foul of the England management at large as they attempt to change the image and culture of the men’s national teams. Joe Root, the Test captain, had previously asked his players to be “role models”.Jacob Bethell will also miss the white-ball fixtures against Sri Lanka after recently undergoing surgery on the knee problem that has kept him out since mid-July. Bethell is not expected to be fit until the limited overs tour of Australia in November, with Derbyshire’s Aneurin Donald now earning a maiden T20 call up.If selected, Donald would become the first Glamorgan product to play for England since Simon Jones during the 2005 Ashes, even if he has moved counties since. The 29-year-old struck 489 runs in this year’s T20 Blast at a remarkable strike-rate of 230 and went on to shine in the Hundred for the runners-up, Trent Rockets.There is a third Test against Pakistan to complete first, however, with the tourists having now begun life under their new interim head coach, Mike Hesson. Sarfaraz Ahmed wasstood down from the roleafter going 2-0 down at Lord’s last Sunday, while seven members of Pakistan’s touring party were also dropped.As Pakistan’s white-ball coach, Hesson had only flown to the UK to attend the PakistanCricketBoard’s official reception with King Charles at Clarence House on Wednesday. “It’s been pretty challenging,” said the New Zealander. “I was heading over to see the King and be part of a nice occasion. That got expedited.”View image in fullscreenKing Charles shakes Sajid Khan’s hand during the Pakistan team’s visit to Clarence House in London.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/Pool PA/APAfter holding one-on-one talks with the remaining squad members this week, and then drilling them at Edgbaston’s indoor school due to rain, Hesson believes a fresh start has occurred. Of the seven players being flown in, three were still due to arrive in the UK on Friday.As for the departed, Hesson tried his best to explain.In essence, three of the seven dropped – Imam-ul-Haq, Mohammed Rizwan and Salman Ali Agha – were told their tour was over immediately after the defeat at Lord’s. Hesson claims he was not privy to this decision by the high performance director, Aaqib Javed, nor was he able to share the precise reasons why.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter
