London, 10.30am startWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.But once asked to take over as Test coach, for Hesson it was then a case of assessing the team’s remaining shortcomings and the blend needed in Birmingham, resulting in four further members of the tour party being swapped out. Ali Usman, for example, was sent home as a spinner is unlikely to be needed.Hesson said: “I don’t think anyone wants this to happen in the middle of a series, clearly not. From my perspective, it’s about putting a balanced squad together so we actually have some variety in our attack. Pakistan is known for pace, unusual actions, mystery spin – we haven’t really been able to present any of that.Quick GuidePakistan squad for third TestShowBabar Azam* (c), Abdullah Fazal*, Abdullah Shafique, Arafat Minhas*, Azan Awais, Mohammad Abbas, Mohammad Ali, Muhammad Imran*, Mohammad Imran Jnr*, Muhammad Ghazi Ghori (wk), Razaullah*, Saad Baig (wk)*, Saim Ayub*, Sajid Khan, Saud Shakeel, Shan Masood, Ubaid Shah*New additions to the squadWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“There’s been talk about having an identity as a Test team, and that does come from stability. But it also comes from being authentic to the way your team plays. We have to get back to that.”Hesson did not commit to the Pakistan Test role beyond next week’s Third Test and, despite hitting out at what he claims were some erroneous news reports this past week, has looked to inject some calm into proceedings overall. “The guys are probably more used to a little bit of chaos than I am,” he said.Explore more on these topicsCricketEngland cricket teamEngland v Pakistan 2026Pakistan cricket teamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham presents his new government as more leftwing than Keir Starmer’s. In reality, it’s barely moved at all | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: The prime minister talks the talk about reversing decades of privatisation and austerity, but we’re yet to see any policies to this end, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: The prime minister talks the talk about reversing decades of privatisation and austerity, but we’re yet to see any policies to this end, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Keir Starmer and Andy Burnham in Manchester, 12 May 2024.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKeir Starmer and Andy Burnham in Manchester, 12 May 2024.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham presents his new government as more leftwing than Keir Starmer’s. In reality, it’s barely moved at allOwen JonesThe prime minister talks the talk about reversing decades of privatisation and austerity, but we’re yet to see any policies to this endFri 4 Sep 2026 07.57 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.21 EDTShareIf Starmerism sought to present theLabourgovernment as more rightwing than it is, Burnhamism seeks to do the opposite.The change in rhetoric is certainly stark. Unlike his sulking predecessor, the new prime minister offers both an analysis and a vision. British stagnation and decline,Andy Burnhamcorrectly told the House of Commons, can be explained by a series of “wrong turns” taken from the 1980s onwards: the privatisation of economic power, the deindustrialisation of the country and the ruinous austerity that followed the 2008 crash.The solution, Burnham suggests, is public control of the essentials, the devolution of power and the rebirth of industry – to rebuild living standards and the economy and give long-abandoned communities a future. Keir Starmer, by contrast, had no vision, relying instead on a technocratic image of competence that was swiftly shattered by one fiasco after another. That left him defined by his opponents, and the electorate baffled as to where his government was headed.The Starmer project foregrounded all of the government’s reactionary elements and buried its social-democratic features. Stringent fiscal rules, the assault on the winter fuel allowance, the attack on disability benefits, the construction of one of Europe’s most punitive asylum regimes, the arrest of pensioners who opposed Israel’s genocide: all became headline policies by design.Now consider what they shouted least about: the semi-nationalisation of the railways, the creation of the publicly run Great British Energy, modest improvements to workers’ and renters’ rights, and some progressive taxation measures, such as hiking capital gains tax.That was for a reason: defining itself against the left was the core strategy of Starmerism. When, in opposition, Starmer committed to retaining the Tories’ two-child benefit cap – even though it plunged hundreds of thousands of children into poverty – his advisers believed, as the journalist Andrew Marrput it, that “the public will notice him standing up to the left”.Starmer junked the radical policy commitments he made to become leader and claimed Labour had gone “from a party of dogma to a party of patriotism” and “from a party of protest to a party of public service”. Labour voters defected en masse to Zack Polanski’s Greens, first in the Gorton and Denton byelection and then in June’s local elections. Starmer’s strategy of insulting progressive voters and their values succeeded in plunging Labour into an existential crisis.Burnham, then, takes the opposite tack, having understood that, in the Britain of the 2020s, the left is a significant political constituency that Labour must appeal to, rather than wilfully alienate.He bemoansthe Starmerite purge of leftwingers, such as economist Faiza Shaheen and former Labour mayor Jamie Driscoll. He sells himself not as a factionalist but as “a Labour politician that’s about unifying people”. Notably, when Jeremy Corbyn asked the prime minister a question about rent controls in the House of Commons, Burnham called the expelled former leader “my right honourable friend”: by parliamentary convention, “friend” is reserved for members of one’s own party.The presentation has certainly changed. But what about the substance? When he stood in the Makerfield byelection in June, Burnhamsaidthat public ownership “is what should be done” in the case of Thames Water. Last week, he backtracked:“I’ve deliberately talked about public control rather than necessarily nationalisation.”It is certainly true that “public control” has been his preferred formula. It allows voters – whooverwhelmingly supportnationalisation – to believe it means public ownership. But as he told Newsnightthis year, it could mean anything from “much tougher regulation” to “public ownership”. That simply allows the existing approach to be rebranded.During his byelection campaign, Burnham demanded that the government’s £39bn Affordable Housing Programme be entirely reserved for council and social housing.In office, his government allocated 40% of the first £10bn tranche to other types of housing – continuity with his predecessor’s approach.Before his victorious return to parliament, Burnham had backed a £500,000 cap on donations to political parties.In power, he has U-turned.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile just a few months ago, Burnham had said he had “long been persuaded” by the case for a land value tax, andproposedit as a replacement for the “iniquitous” council tax, as prime minister he declared: “That won’t be happening.” He has already embraced fiscal rules that block the investment needed for resource-starved public services and infrastructure.Burnham apologised for Labour’s positioning on Gaza, but notably only for its record in opposition. He avoided stating that Israel had committed war crimes, with all the legal obligations that would impose on the government. His new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, now touts sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank, but these are small, piecemeal measures that avoid imposing tough measures on Israel itself.If vibes are your thing, then Burnhamism is a political sensation. Alas, what should matter is the substance. Our prime minister is correct that Britain took a series of wrong turns from the 1980s onwards. The logical conclusion arising from that is that the country needs a new economic model. Burnham has traced the path that led Britain here with admirable clarity. What remains unclear is whether he is prepared to leave it.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I can’t be bought,’ Nige tells Reform’s faithful – however different it may look | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Just as the party leader had hoped to change the narrative, along came Channel 4 News to spoil his conference fun
Author: John Crace
Headline: Just as the party leader had hoped to change the narrative, along came Channel 4 News to spoil his conference fun
Content: After some tacky smoke and pyrotechnic effects to introduce him, the rest of his speech was standard Nige.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersView image in fullscreenAfter some tacky smoke and pyrotechnic effects to introduce him, the rest of his speech was standard Nige.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersThe politics sketchNigel Farage‘I can’t be bought,’ Nige tells Reform’s faithful – however different it may lookJohn CraceJust as the party leader had hoped to change the narrative, along came Channel 4 News to spoil his conference funFri 4 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 18.51 EDTShareWhy, oh why, oh why? You could almost feel Nigel Farage’s frustration. Why was it always him? Surely it was about time someone gave him a break. There he was trying to earn some money from a Thai crypto billionaire and a gold bullion dealer, and yet still Reform kept getting linked to dodgy cash.It was almost as if a pattern was emerging. First there was the £5m gift, then the Posh George donations via Dicky Tice, and now Channel 4 News had done a sting on him andtwo of his most trusted aidesin which it looked as if they were happy to break the law on political donations. Life can be so damned unfair at times. Always kicking you when you are down.Farage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conferenceRead moreThe headlines from Reform’s party conference in Birmingham weremeant to be all about Nige declaring a national emergencythe moment he got in to No 10. Instead he was dealing with a rather more pressing crisis. Every time he tries to persuade the country he’s running a serious party and that it isn’t a one-man band, something seems to happen to make it look like a dodgy, third-rate clown show.Operation Failed Clean-up was initially left in the hands of Richard Tice and Lee Anderson. Imagine how bad it has to be for these two to be left in charge. Dicky is one of the least plausible politicians you can hope to find, so he didn’t even appreciate the irony of claiming it was all an establishment plot run by leftwing eco activists.As for Lee, he was adamant that the two Reform members involved – James Orr, a Cambridge associate professor and supposed brains behind the party, and Dan Jukes, Nige’s trusted right-hand gofer for more than a decade – had been out of line and suspended from the party. More than that, they weren’t coming back. More than that he couldn’t say as an investigation had been started. So who was leading the investigation, he was asked. “I don’t know because the investigation hasn’t started,” Lee replied. Sometimes he runs Dicky a close second.Others were equally as confused. Danny Kruger was in a more forgiving mood and thought there might be some way back for Orr and Jukes once the Reform investigation had exonerated them. Nadine Dorries speculated that maybe they hadn’t known they would be breaking the law. Though the undercover footage rather indicated they had known exactly what they were doing. That accepting money from foreign donors was not an alien concept.Nige was just baffled. Fed up. Couldn’t believe how this had happened. Orr and Jukes were just contractors. Freelance labourers who had been brought in to paint the kitchen and had overstayed their welcome. He didn’t even know them, had barely met them. Even though both had been the closest of mates with him. Nige is never slow to throw comrades under the bus. It’s the narcissist’s first line of defence. Self-protection at all costs.11:20Reform donations scandal: is this the final blow for Farage? - The LatestAt a lunchtime press conference, he had more to say. First he announced he had a spontaneous statement to make that sounded as if it had been carefully worded by his lawyers. It’s probably been an expensive day for Nige. It was a hoax. No laws had been broken. No money had been taken. Except Reform had allegedly taken £35,000 to pay for the opinion poll, and the film suggested they would have been more than happy to take the £500,000 if it had been genuine. Details, details.It was all a misunderstanding. James and Dan had just misspoken. And he couldn’t believe he had been caught on film having a “man of the people” champagne and oysters lunch with them and the undercover journalists in Clacton. Because he had only ever been in Clacton once in his life. What were the odds? “It was just some jack-the-laddery,” he said. “Pub talk.” Quite right. Which one of us hasn’t spent a long time chatting about crimes we were going to do and their exact modus operandi every time we have a couple of drinks?Still, at least some things about the Reform conference were business as usual. The queues. Who would have guessed that 8,000 people might turn up at once when you had already sold 8,000 tickets? This came as a surprise to the organisers. And to the member who had turned up dressed as Richard I. Where better to find support for a crusade against Muslims than at the Reform conference. First we take Birmingham, then we take Baghdad.Nigel Farage meeting a ‘shadowy foreign donor’? It can only be another establishment stitch-up | Marina HydeRead moreWith the conference already running an hour late before it had even started, it was left to Jeremy Kyle to fill in. He interviewed one punter who told him that all woke people should be hung. This was a little extreme even for Jezza. And there are plenty of people he would like to hang. Finally, though, we were up and running. First a tribute to Ann Widdecombe, then Anderson being given licence to try out his standup routine. Suella Braverman was a proper man, he insisted. Don’t call us, Lee. We’ll call you.Then came Zia, the self-appointed shadow home secretary who is too unpopular in his own party to be allowed to stand for election. All he really wanted to talk about was small boat crossings. The audience whooped regardless.The guest speaker was Jordan Bardella, the president of the far-right National Rally party in France. Not the sharpest pencil. He started by congratulating Nige on his brilliant win against the establishment bin in Clacton. It’s possible he doesn’t understand English humour. He then praised the Brits for standing up to Hitler in the war. A bit rich from a man whose party was founded by Nazi collaborators. The session closed with a handshake for Nige as they signed a new version of the entente cordiale.Much of the afternoon was a write-off. Matt Goodwin, Sarah Pochin, Dicky. I mean, who really cares? They are all lightweights. That just left Nige to round things off. Eventually, after yet another unscheduled delay and some 80s wedding filler songs. Cue some tacky smoke and pyrotechnic effects and the appearance of the Messiah. “I can’t be bought,” he declared on the video above him. Except it rather looks as if he can.The rest of the speech – with a few interruptions from protesters – was standard Nige. He would change the world in 100 days and sack any ministers who failed. There’s going to be a lot of ministerial vacancies. There was the invention of a reality where he was the Divine. It was all just lazy. Boring. Just one reference to the ongoing crisis. “The party has done nothing wrong,” he said. Mmm. With respect, that’s not something he gets to judge.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageThe politics sketchReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: As AI madness encroaches, we need human connection more than ever. But we’ll have to fight for it | Van Badham | The Guardian
description: We don’t want the isolating, automated outputs tech lords are selling us. We’re yearning for a shared frame of reference
Author: Van Badham
Headline: We don’t want the isolating, automated outputs tech lords are selling us. We’re yearning for a shared frame of reference
Content: Elon Musk, the trillionaire owner of social media platform X, has mooted making an ‘AI Odyssey’. Van Badham writes that as AI regulation is debated, we should ‘take a wild, political stand for authentic preference over forced consumption’.Photograph: Anton Dos Ventos/AlamyView image in fullscreenElon Musk, the trillionaire owner of social media platform X, has mooted making an ‘AI Odyssey’. Van Badham writes that as AI regulation is debated, we should ‘take a wild, political stand for authentic preference over forced consumption’.Photograph: Anton Dos Ventos/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)As AI madness encroaches, we need human connection more than ever. But we’ll have to fight for itVan BadhamWe don’t want the isolating, automated outputs tech lords are selling us. We’re yearning for a shared frame of referenceFri 4 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 20.16 EDTShareIhave a cherished memory of a family trip to the movies. In the Australian tradition, we bought choc-top ice-creams, chattered through pre-show trailers and a hush fell on the full house as the movie started.It wasChristopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, on film, only a couple of weeks ago, months after its release.In an AI-supercharged world of algorithmic recommendations and atomised cultural space, I’ve come to suspect The Odyssey’s ongoingpopular appealis no longer its Greeks with gifts, or superstar director.It’s the increasingly rare opportunity to share even a single cultural reference with other people. Despite our human instinct for interaction, we live in a global moment wherehealth authoritiesbelieve social isolation is an epidemic.Yet in the same city of my fun night at the cinema, this week it wasnewsthat Australia’s Macquarie University has introduced an AI chatbot into the weekly teaching of two mandatory psychology subjects.Lost jobs, inequality, rogue agents: why are we accepting oligarchs’ AI agenda? | Robert ReichRead moreDisplacing human beings from what should be stable jobs isn’t the only outrage here.As someone whose dainty, addled, depressive brain obliges tender care from trained professionals, Macquarie, please record this data in your feedback corpus: I cannot trust or validate the insight of a supposed expert whose contact with adult realities has been compromised by being taught by a machine.If I want a chatbot to talk me out of a panic spiral, I’ll consult it within my already-paid-for subscription service whenI’m freaking out at midnightlike a normal person, thank you.Far more positive social impacts can be measured from Australia’s academics’ union, this week takingstrike actionat the University of Sydney against the encroach of AI madness.“We want enforceable protections against AI being used to cut jobs, intensify workloads, undermine academic and professional judgement, or replace work and human interaction that are fundamental to a university,” said the NTEU’s Vince Caughley.Solidarity, brother. My gratitude extends to Australia’s writers’ union, theAWG, as well as itsentertainment and communications union, theUS actors’ unionandWriters Guild of America,Canada’s performance union,Germany’s service workers union and actors’ union, an alliance ofItaly’s dubbing unions and all industrial organisations striking AI-use agreements not merely to protect their members’ workplace rights, but to remain on the side of public opinion.Because studies repeatedly suggest consumers don’t want the isolating, automated outputs being sold to them.double quotation markWe missed the boat on regulating social media. Nazis, radicalisation and deadly misinformation sailed inIn the world of commercial literature,one study found“consumers perceived human-written books more positively in all investigated dimensions than ones written by AI”. While other researchers have found the intrusion of AI titles to Amazon is now as many as 20% of its ebook catalogue,the same studyshows they only made up 12% of sales and 10% of bestsellers in their genre. A considerable underperformance.In music, global consultancy Bain learned that62% of consumerswould not engage with music generated by AI.French streaming service Deezer revealed fully AI-generated music constituted as much as 18% of its daily uploads but amounted only to about 0.5% of listening – whilethe Guardian reportedthat up to 70% of those streams appeared fraudulent.Bain found the only majority tolerance for AI content was in video games: 71%did not want AI in their books, and 65% did not want it in their news and magazines.Similarly, in sales, studies show that telling customers beforehand they are engaging with chatbots in outbound callsreduces purchase rates by 79.7%. In 2025,Deloittelearned 74% of customers preferred human interaction even for routine banking questions. In anotherinternational 2025 study, chatbots were the least popular form of customer service engagement: a mere 8% of respondents chose them voluntarily.Consumer sentiment backlash is registering faster than the slow pace of democratic governance. Governments have struggled with the speed of tech encroach, with regulation lagging in the face of relentless economic and political pressure from the world’s mostaggressively overcapitalised, cashed-updipshits who own all this stuff. Australia is considering its approaches to AI regulation, butit does not have it yet.‘If you build something vastly smarter than you, it better be on your side’: can we stop AI from deceiving us?Read moreFriends, we missed the boat on regulating social media. Nazis, radicalisation, deadly health misinformation andaddictive and dangerous productssailed in.As more comprehensive AI regulation is debated, the Australian government is mooting community calls for defaultopt-in obligationson platform algorithms, to stop the use of apps being conditional on what preferred form of slop its tech lord wants to shove into your consciousness.We should all support it, if just to take a wild, political stand for authentic preference over forced consumption. Elon Musk has mooted making an “AI Odyssey”, and if you think the algorithm he paid $44bn for will let you escape that horror show, there are some relevant scenes fromA Clockwork OrangeI suggest you try to catch at a midnight screening.Cinema, writing, education, psychology and, yes, even shopping and banking facilitate human interactions.Unless the clients of AI’s robots are also robots, I have to ask: just who are y’all making products for?Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionSocial mediaChatbotscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade | Games | The Guardian
description: A string of distractions on the US government’s own website invite you to catch pixelated migrants – showing gaming’s potential to be nastily weaponised
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: A string of distractions on the US government’s own website invite you to catch pixelated migrants – showing gaming’s potential to be nastily weaponised
Content: Fascist fun … A screenshot from one of the White House Arcade games, Build The Wall.Photograph: The White HouseView image in fullscreenFascist fun … A screenshot from one of the White House Arcade games, Build The Wall.Photograph: The White HouseGamesThe Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcadeKeza MacDonaldA string of distractions on the US government’s own website invite you to catch pixelated migrants – showing gaming’s potential to be nastily weaponisedFri 4 Sep 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.41 EDTShareThe Trump White House on Thursday released ahorrible little propaganda arcadevia its website, a collection of nasty riffs on popular games. Wrapped in the cutesy, nostalgic aesthetic of early-90s pixel art, these mindless fascist diversions are harmless-looking, but their intent is stomach-turning: this is the appropriation of play in service of propaganda. It’s just the latest in a series of attempts from Trump’s administration to usevideo game memes and imageryto further its messaging.Having riffed on Halo and Pokémon in social media ads last year, inviting potential ICE recruits to “stop the flood” and “catch ’em all”, this time the administration has ripped off a series of recognisable games. Flappy Bill, perhaps the least gross, is a version of the old mobile hit Flappy Bird, except here you’re an eagle with a scroll in its claws. Supply Line could almost be an educational game about healthy food in schools, where you sort junk food off a conveyor belt destined for school lunches, except for some reason you play as a boxer who becomes more bloodied with every seed-oil containing, ultra-processed food item that you fail to punch into the garbage chute.Then come the really nasty ones: Build the Wall, which warps Tetris into a game where you must fortify the southern border to keep out “the coming horde”, and an evil little take on Snake where you patrol the Rio Grande, collecting brown people who then follow you around in orange jumpsuits. The final game is Trump Savings Tycoon, where you “fill your kids’Trump accounts” by catching bills and gold coins in a net. (The algae-beset Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is depicted in the foreground, inaccurately coloured in blue.)I have played all of them, so that you don’t have to. Build the Wall and Rio Run are actively disgusting, built around the naked dehumanisation of migrants, but mostly these games are just embarrassing. Like most things that come from the Trump White House communications team, they are mean-spirited, unimaginative and lazy. I have a strong suspicion that they are vibe-coded using AI, and I almost hope that they are, because the idea of humans spending their precious time on Earth making these horrid, half-arsed games makes me even sadder than playing them did.Anyone involved in the creation of the original games that the White House Arcade is ripping off is surely cringeing. Members of the original Halo team were moved to speak out on social media after the White House posted a picture ofTrump as Master Chieflast year; I wonder if Sega will have anything to say about this trailer, which opens with a digital chorus singing “Magaaaa”, soundtracking the sorry collection with music that sounds alotlike Sonic’s Green Hill Zone.The leveraging of video games and their imagery for political influence has been under way for some time, beginning perhaps with 2014’sGamergate, an online harassment movement that was stoked by Steve Bannon and far-right website Breitbart. Trump, alongside other rightwing regimes, has had an enormous head start on this front. “The use of video game content, culture and aesthetics for communication is a feature of Trump’s White House, rather than a bug, because much of the modern political right emerged from toxic game communities,” says George Osborn, author of Power Play: Video Games, Politics and the Battle for Global Influence.“Activists who shaped the Gamergate movement have become an established part of the political right … Until now, it seemed to be restricted to social media posting.I estimated that video game-coded posts had approximately twice the reach of a regular White House Instagram post, suggesting it was able to simultaneously rile up audiences offended by its post and delight supporters. But the deployment of an arcade on its website marks a change of course … Now, it appears that Trump’s White House is ready to use games to begin to try to win over audiences – escalating from appropriating video game culture to ensnaring the medium itself for its own ends.”Artists and activists have been using video games to put across political messages for a very long time. I have played games about escaping war-torn countries; about examining the paperwork of desperate people at the border of a fictional eastern bloc country; about running a dictatorship or taking one down. Governments, however, are new players in this space.These games, in line with the Trump administration’s wider social media and communications strategy, are culture-war shitposting. They are almost entirely valueless, and exist more to rile us up than to actually persuade anyone of anything. If we attach too much outrage to them, we are being drawn into someone else’s game; it is deeply unlikely that a round of Rio Run is about to radicalise anyone who isn’t already fully on board with Trump’s whole schtick. But at a time when the Saudi Arabian wealth fund now co-ownsone of the world’s biggest game publishersalongside an investment firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, gaming’s propagandist potential should not be a blind spot.Explore more on these topicsGamescommentShareReuse this content

title: When does rage help us, and when does it harm us? Ukraine has taught me the answers | Charlotte Higgins | The Guardian
description: Fury at Russia’s death and destruction has fuelled art, action and resistance. But eventually, rage’s fire is all-consuming, says the Guardian’s chief culture writer, Charlotte Higgins
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: Fury at Russia’s death and destruction has fuelled art, action and resistance. But eventually, rage’s fire is all-consuming, says the Guardian’s chief culture writer, Charlotte Higgins
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionCultureWhen does rage help us, and when does it harm us? Ukraine has taught me the answersCharlotte HigginsFury at Russia’s death and destruction has fuelled art, action and resistance. But eventually, rage’s fire is all-consumingFri 4 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.49 EDTShareTwice, I have heard Ukrainians perform Verdi’s Requiem. Oncein Lviv, last Maundy Thursday, and once last month, under the great dome of St Paul’s Cathedral in London. InSt Paul’s, performed by the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra with the Philharmonia Chorus, the greatDies irae– “day of anger” – unfurled in an operatic gale of fury, reverberating so powerfully around Wren’s lofty spaces that the music felt like thunder echoing between mountain peaks.In Lviv, where it was performed by a Ukrainian chorus and orchestra, the evening began with a call to remember the war dead. Lviv’s lay a mile up the road: 153 graves when I first visited in autumn 2022, and by this year more than 1,000. Ranks and ranks of soldiers killed in their 20s, 30s and 40s, each grave planted with flowers and plants, flags flying above. On that occasion,Dies irae– in the more sober acoustic of the Lviv Philharmonic Hall – seemed to contain the furious ache of grief. Certainly I have never heard a more wrathful day of anger.I have thought a lot about Ukrainian rage. This was a rage againstRussiaand Russians, and it burned with a fury that was at times hard to step close to. Ukrainians, too, have sometimes been taken aback by the depth of their anger. Oleksandr Mykhed, an author now in the armed forces, has written a wartime alphabet book for children in which L stands forlyut, rage. He defines it as a “special mixture of feelings when the desire to defend what is yours, hatred for the enemy and enduring love for your own people are mixed in equal proportions”. This complicated, extreme cocktail of feelings is not a peacetime emotion, nor an easy one.View image in fullscreenUkrainian Freedom Orchestra founder and conductor Keri-Lynn Wilson at the St Paul’s concert in London on 18 August.Photograph: Frances MarshallI found myself making sense of it through literature, specifically Homer’s epic poems. Epics need fuel to motor them on their poetic journey. They also need delay, so that they become long poems, not short ones. Inthe Odyssey, the fuel of the poem is desire – the desire to get home – and the delay is the divine malevolence that brings many obstacles in Odysseus’s path. But in the Iliad, set during the Trojan war, Achilles’ rage is the fuel of the poem: first his outrage as a subordinate insulted by his commander, later the raging grief of a man who has lost his dearest friend in battle. Grief and rage are cousins; that is also clear to me in Ukraine.It would be wrong to suggest that Ukrainian rage is like Achilles’. His veers beyond the human, into the supersize, mythical emotional zone inhabited by the children of the gods. But I found myself thinking about the vastness of this Homeric rage when encountering the fury of Ukrainians at civilians killed, cities bombed, people raped and tortured. The poet Iryna Shuvalova, in an interview with the writer Kateryna Iakovlenko for Suspilne, the Ukrainian national broadcaster, said rage was “pouring out of us as a reaction to the incredible trauma, the blow, the provocation, the terrible losses”.View image in fullscreenIryna Shuvalova’s poem February deals with to the month of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Photograph: Olga ZakrevskaShuvalova’s poemFebruary– referring to the month of the full-scale invasion in 2022 – begins gently, wryly, by pointing out that “we planned to get through February / like any other month— / only shorter”. But then the invasion begins, and “instead, the river roars and grabs us by the legs / this red slippery foaming / February-fury”. The translators, Amelia Glaser and Yuliya Ilchuk, used the phrase “February-fury” to mimic the echo in Ukrainian betweenlyutyy, the word for February, andlyuta, raging. For me, the immediate resonance of Shuvalova’s blood-soaked river is Homer’s Scamander River, choked in blood and the corpses of the war dead.And what is the “day of anger” that powers Verdi’s Requiem? The words, no longer often used as part of a requiem mass, are from a medieval Latin poem that summons up the chaos and terror of the Earth’s final dissolution. The intensity of its expression – the visceral, gut-felt outpouring – that I heard in those Ukrainian performances of the work reminded me of Homeric wrath, although it is a rage that has a different force. The anger of theDies iraeis a kind of world-fury produced when everything is disrupted, put out of order by human actions. A world locked into war, perhaps.I am not a Christian, and the values of Homer’s Iliad are alien to me. But I think perhaps there are different orders of rage. Some rage is trivial and petty; the everyday rage of frustration and aggression. But Mykhed told me of a generative rage: a rage that produces action, that fuels resistance. His rage provided him with the impetus and energy to write his bookThe Language of War. He told me that he wanted his rage-filled book about the first year of the full-scale invasion of his country to be “a time capsule for myself so that I know where I’ve been, when in five years or 10 years, my rage won’t be so sharp”.The feeling, he said, is specifically “not hatred, it is rage, because hatred doesn’t give you power, it’s more chaotic. But rage gives you words.” In 1981, Audre Lordewrote urgentlyof the fury provoked into flame by racism – a fury that could alienate and be resented by white people. Black women, she wrote, “tremble their rage under harness”. But pulled into service, channelled towards action and words, anger “is loaded with information and energy”. So it has been for Ukrainians: rage turned into action fuelled resistance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenOleksandr Mykhed has written a wartime alphabet book for children in which L stands forlyut(rage).Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianBut now, in 2026, Ukrainian rage burns low, at least among my friends. The fire cannot be sustained; it would consume you in its overwhelming heat. What is left? Fatigue, emptiness, an alertness to the dreadful idea that however bad things are now, they could get worse. “I feel like anything is possible – nuclear war, anything,” Iakovlenko told me. “Everything that was written in books and in films is actually happening to us.”Sasha Dovzhyk, the director of Index, Ukraine’s Institute for Documentation and Exchange, told me that she felt “pure spite and grit and grim determination and a memory of what it felt like to have feelings and a loyalty to that past version of the self who felt rage”. She missed rage, she told me. Rage and grief gave her the power to write her forthcoming book,Apocalypse Baroque: Tales from Ukraine at War, which mixes genres – documentary and fairytales – with rageous energy. Maybe rage sometimes brings one too close to the perilous realm of myth, to the destructiveness of an Achilles. But if you can tame the wild horse of rage, it can be ridden, for a while.Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writer and the author ofUkrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War, published by Jonathan Cape. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.comOn Wednesday 30 September,join Charlotte Higginsand our panel of acclaimed Ukrainian writers to reflect on the profound connections between war, art and life. With Olia Hercules, Sasha Dovzhyk and Olesya Khromeychuk. Book ticketshereExplore more on these topicsCultureOpinionUkraineGiuseppe VerdiPoetryHomerRussiaEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Drones, teargas, riot squads: why has the UK gone to war against asylum seekers already fleeing conflict? | Diane Taylor | The Guardian
description: Burnham and Macron have committed to going further in the crackdown on French beaches. But little is being done to offer refugees  safe alternative routes, says human rights writer Diane Taylor
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Burnham and Macron have committed to going further in the crackdown on French beaches. But little is being done to offer refugees safe alternative routes, says human rights writer Diane Taylor
Content: French police try to stop migrants from boarding small boats on 13 June 2025, in Gravelines, France.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFrench police try to stop migrants from boarding small boats on 13 June 2025, in Gravelines, France.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionImmigration and asylumDrones, teargas, riot squads: why has the UK gone to war against asylum seekers already fleeing conflict?Diane TaylorBurnham and Macron have committed to going further in the crackdown on French beaches. But little is being done to offer refugees safe alternative routesFri 4 Sep 2026 06.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 06.25 EDTShareGarang*, 18, is one of thousands of refugees recentlycaught in the crossfireof French riot police, who threw teargas and beat them with batons when they boarded dinghies to travel to the UK. He is a victim of a war in his home of South Sudan – and one being fought on France’s northern shores.He borrows a phone from anyone with credit who will let him try to call home, where his family is displaced. Garang doesn’t have enough money on the£10-a-week allowancefrom the Home Office to make a long-distance call. All he wants is to speak to his mum, to hear her voice, and let her know he is alive and safe in the UK despite the violence he has faced.On Thursday, stopping more people like Garang from reaching the UK in small boats topped the “to do” list of the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron,when they held talks. The leaders agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.How much further can the war on refugees go? Along with the use of teargas and beatings, there are now surveillance drones and more French officers to tackle dinghy launches from other parts of the coast. The UK government is increasingly using military terms such as “surge” and “neutralise” in relation to small-boat crossings. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has vowed to continueto be “relentless”in this battle. Burnham said the government wanted to “prevent smugglers exploiting vulnerable migrants”, but was silent on alternatives to offer to these vulnerable people.‘I would rather die than return to France’: the brutal reality of the UK’s one in, one out schemeRead moreWhen the government tried to seal off the lorry route for people crossing from France into the UKa decade ago, ministers did not foresee its replacement with small boats. The maritime option required greater reliance on smuggling networks, which have vastly increased in size, complexity and profits. Worst of all are the optics, which have been seized upon by the right – shots of overcrowded dinghies carrying people in orange lifejackets bobbing up and down against the blue horizon.These images have fuelled anger, with some Britons believing that most refugees are shunning other countries to beat a path to our door. In fact, the number of irregular arrivals to Europe in the last year has dropped significantly, and the UKranks 16thin Europe per head of population for asylum claims. According tothis newly released data, a majority of asylum seekers do not arrive in small boats – 41% were already in the UK and held a visa or other leave prior to claiming and 20% arrived by other routes, many likely to be clandestine means, such as lorries.Channel crossings so far this year from France to the UK have dropped bymore than 40%compared with the same period last year. Countries such asTurkey and Irantower over us in terms of the number of refugees they take in.But the UK government continues to pursue its war against refugees on the beaches of northern France. Home Office data shows that those in small boats overwhelminglycome from war and conflict zones: Eritreans fleeing indefinite military conscription; Afghans escaping the Taliban; Iranians who have opposed the regime or converted from Islam to Christianity, trying to dodge execution; and Sudanese crossing the desert to escape a brutal civil war. Nobody steps into an overcrowded dinghy that might end their life if it capsizes unless they are desperate.Nigel Farage and Reform UK have poisoned the public discourse on people fleeing war, people who run because they don’t want to be killed or to kill others. The UK government can shift the dial. Instead of boasting about the paraphernalia of war deployed against refugees who have experienced unimaginable horrors, ministers can restore the humanity of those seeking refuge. Along with promoting safe routes, it can remind people of how few refugees in absolute terms are arriving here seeking safety – and of what they have been through.As for Garang, he is still desperately trying to get through to his mum on the phone, relying on South Sudan’s hopelessly overwhelmed phone network. A few days ago, he managed to reach his brother, but by the time he had run to find their mum, the call disconnected. Just as Garang wants to tell her he’s OK, he wants to know the same of her. “Now I know she’s alive I will not give up trying to call whenever anyone lets me use their phone,” he says. “All I want is to speak to my mum.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion* Name has been changedDiane Taylor writes on human rights, racism and civil libertiesDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Reform’s funding scandal: Nigel Farage has questions to answer | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: An undercover investigation raises issues around foreign money, political transparency and the rightwing populist party’s fitness for power
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: An undercover investigation raises issues around foreign money, political transparency and the rightwing populist party’s fitness for power
Content: Nigel Farage and Dan Jukes arrive at a polling station for the Clacton byelection.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenNigel Farage and Dan Jukes arrive at a polling station for the Clacton byelection.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersOpinionReform UKThe Guardian view on Reform’s funding scandal: Nigel Farage has questions to answerEditorialAn undercover investigation raises issues around foreign money, political transparency and the rightwing populist party’s fitness for powerFri 4 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.09 EDTShareReform UK’s conference was to open showcasing a party ready for government. It did so with two top aides removed after an investigation aired onChannel 4, its finances underpolice scrutinyand seven in 10 voters, polls suggest, regarding its leader, Nigel Farage, assleazy– double the number who thought the same of Andy Burnham. Reform, a rightwing populist party, says it will take power back from a corrupt establishment. The latest scandal raises a question: does Reform oppose the influence of big money – or just who benefits from it?Undercover reporters fromVerbatim Investigations, founded by journalists from the US Center for Climate Reporting, pretended to be a wealthy American father and his UK-based son who wanted to donate to Reform. In the UK, foreign donations are banned from politics. But that allegedly was ignored. Verbatim’s team filmed their meetings with James Orr, aCambridge academicspecialising in ethics, and Reform’s head of policy, as well as with Dan Jukes, Mr Farage’s close aide. Both have been “removed” from their posts.View image in fullscreenJames Orr.Photograph: Zuma Press, Inc/AlamyReform officials allegedly commissioned£32,500of polling, arranged for what they believed was a US company to pay the bill, hid the party’s role and used the results to generate favourable newspaper headlines. Verbatim wired the money from a US firm to pollsters JL Partners, whose boss wasfilmedsaying that he should have disclosed that his client was Reform. JL Partners admits procedural “weaknesses”. When the supposed American benefactor later explained the arrangement to Mr Farage over lunch, the Reform leader’s filmed response was not alarm but celebration: “It worked. Boom.”The second main allegation is that the American father was willing to provideReform with £500,000through a “permissible” British intermediary – his son. This, if true, would be unlawful. At the lunch Mr Farage does not say that the father cannot be the cash’s source or that the son can legally only donate his own money. Rather, he is filmed saying “thank you both” when it was explained.Gavin Millar KC, a noted media lawyer, toldreportersthat “there is enough being said, in the presence of Mr Farage and to Mr Farage, for it to be a red flag – for it to be understood as the reality that this money is coming from an American in a disguised form. And he should be questioning that … On the contrary, he seems to be quite happy to receive the money.”In response, Reform says that it has “broken no laws”. Mr Farage told LBC that while his party had done “nothing wrong”, the footage looked bad and hence party aides were suspended. Reform has not offered much of an explanation, preferring toclaimthat it has “been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate change activists”. Political opponents havereportedReform to the police and the Electoral Commission.Reform’s problem is not that two aides forgot about the rules. It is that senior figures appear to have understood them, discussed how to circumvent them and assumed that nobody able to stop them would find out. A party accused of plotting how to get around the law is now promising to impose a “national emergency” so that judges and officials will not get in its way. That is a telling and ominous reveal about how Reform understands power.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on music and drama education: reversing elitism starts at school | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The number of students taking creative subjects at A-level and GCSE is at a record low. The arts must not become the preserve of the most privileged
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The number of students taking creative subjects at A-level and GCSE is at a record low. The arts must not become the preserve of the most privileged
Content: ‘Learning an instrument … is now a luxury not every child can afford,’ Ed Sheeran wrote in an open letter last year.Photograph: Keith Morris/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Learning an instrument … is now a luxury not every child can afford,’ Ed Sheeran wrote in an open letter last year.Photograph: Keith Morris/AlamyOpinionMusicThe Guardian view on music and drama education: reversing elitism starts at schoolEditorialThe number of students taking creative subjects at A-level and GCSE is at a record low. The arts must not become the preserve of the most privilegedFri 4 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.09 EDTShareHow many of the young people who attended Reading and Leeds festival or a Prom this summer will be picking up a guitar or clarinet when they return to school? New figures suggest not many. The number of students taking A-level music is ata record low: under 5,000, a drop of nearly half from 15 years ago. “We are facing the worst-case scenario prospect of A-level music disappearing from English state schools entirely,” warned Deborah Annetts, the chief executive of the Independent Society of Musicians. Music GCSE entries have alsofallen. It has thewidest attainment gapfor disadvantaged students of any subject. Private violin lessons are beyond the purse strings of most parents.The statistics for drama are similarly bleak. A-level drama entries have almosthalvedin 10 years, with by far the biggest drop in state schools.Forty per cent of state schoolsno longer even offer music or drama GCSEs. Leading universities have been forced toclose music departmentsand arts courses. The number of teachers training in creative subjects has alsodeclinedsharply over the past 15 years. It is no coincidence that the Ebacc, which prioritised core academic subjects at the expense of the arts, was introduced by the Conservatives in 2010. No wonder the worlds of music, theatre and television have become so privileged.View image in fullscreenFemi Koleoso of Ezra Collective.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“How did British singers get so posh?” asked a recent piece in theNew Statesman. Exceptions such as Adele, Raye and Olivia Dean are all alumni of the Brit school, the only state-funded vocational school for the performing arts in the UK. “Learning an instrument and getting up on stage … is now a luxury not every child can afford,” Ed Sheeran wrote in anopen letterlast year, asking the government to commit £250m of funding for music education. Its 600 signatories included Elton John, Harry Styles and Stormzy. Alison Balsom, the world-class classical trumpeter, hassaidthat her career would not be possible for a state-school pupil now.Julie WaltersandMichael Sheenhave spoken out about the challenges facing children from working-class backgrounds hoping to become actors.Sir Keir Starmer was hailed as the mostmusically accomplished prime ministersince Ted Heath, playing four instruments as a child and becoming a junior exhibitioner at the Guildhall School of Music. “To everyone who makes music happen – this government is on your side,” the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, haspromised.Scrapping the Ebacclast year was a welcome start. Other plans include theNational Centre for Arts and Music Education, finally launching this autumn. Andy Burnham, an English graduate and music fan, has already putvocational educationon the agenda. Now he must take up the baton for the arts. Mood music is not enough.Every child should have the right to discover their gifts and fulfil their potential. Music and drama help develop discipline, confidence and social skills, and enhance wellbeing. The creative industries – a source of great economic value and soft power on the world stage – must be accessible to all. Reversing elitism in our recording studios, concert halls and theatres starts at school.As Femi Koleoso of the jazz quintet Ezra Collective put it in theiracceptance speechat last year’s Brit awards, giving a young person a trumpet or a saxophone might be the solution to many of society’s problems: “Because when you do that, you give them a dream, an aspiration and a goal.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Could this radical idea transform social care in the UK? | Social care | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Paul Sagar’s article suggesting a ‘Care First’ year for students in exchange for 50% off university fees
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Paul Sagar’s article suggesting a ‘Care First’ year for students in exchange for 50% off university fees
Content: ‘Care work is too often unfairly maligned as unskilled work and kept on low wages by an economy that favours profit over worker wellbeing.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Care work is too often unfairly maligned as unskilled work and kept on low wages by an economy that favours profit over worker wellbeing.’Photograph: AlamySocial careLettersCould this radical idea transform social care in the UK?Readers respond to Paul Sagar’s article suggesting a ‘Care First’ year for students in exchange for 50% off university feesFri 4 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTShareI am sorry that Dr Paul Sagar experienced his injury, but grateful for his moment of enlightenment (The big idea: Could this policy fix the care system and slash student debt at the same time?, 30 August). It is the sort of suggestion that family carers such as myself have been making for years, having been failed by the statutory services for decades.It needs backing up with some infrastructure: more special schools, more special colleges, better provision in mainstream schools for children with special needs via smaller class sizes, and through more care villages/intentional communities with accommodation, not only for those needing care and support but also for the staff and volunteers on the same site, and housing for family carers.For our family, enlightenment came more than 60 years ago when my younger brother was born deafblind with additional complex multiple disabilities. When my parents asked the authorities which special school he could attend, the reply was devastating: there was nowhere in the north of England that could cope with the severity and complexity of his disabilities. My parents were left in despair.Thankfully, we embarked on a tour of the UK as a family with our car and caravan in search of a special school that could help. By some form of divine intervention, we came across the Camphill Rudolf Steiner school in Aberdeen.My brother started there at the age of five and a half, and within a few weeks was toilet-trained and feeding himself – something that the officials at South Shields town hall had said was impossible.The houseparents at the school were supported by a team of unwaged voluntary workers, many of whom were from other European countries and doing their “civil service” – an alternative to military service in their own country.Our family was saved by the conscription policies of other countries and the civilian alternative provided by Camphill. The young voluntary co-workers gained a lifetime of experience and expertise, a confidence in working with and supporting vulnerable children and adults, and training in social care, communication and life skills, as well as learning English with an Aberdonian twang.Simon BurdisMorpeth, NorthumberlandPaul Sagar is right to think that radical solutions are needed to transform social care in the UK, but social care deserves more consideration than an amped-up Duke of Edinburgh award. Care work is too often unfairly maligned as unskilled work and kept on low wages by an economy that favours profit over worker wellbeing.These proposals to incentivise participation in social care work through student debt forgiveness and voluntary service won’t change that without engaging with the poor working conditions and pay in the sector. Rather, we need to consider what an economy that centres care in all its decisions looks like.Moving away from extractive capitalist models of care provision is an essential part of this, and one that Andy Burnham has acknowledged. So too is a new narrative about care as being valuable, alongside meaningful support for the 6 million unpaid carers and an investment in care work and conditions. Our welfare state, public services and communities all have a role to play in a more caring economy, and we shouldn’t have to twist anyone’s arm to know that.Hannah WebsterCo-founder,Care Full,and former unpaid carerPaul Sagar’s “Care First” proposal assumes that almost any school leaver can become a suitable carer after training. But caring is not easy or interchangeable work. It requires patience, judgment, emotional maturity, safeguarding awareness and the ability to preserve someone’s dignity during intimate or distressing situations.What evidence suggests that school leavers motivated principally by reduced university fees would remain in demanding social care roles for a full year?Social care already has a retention crisis. More than one in five domiciliary care staff leave their roles annually. Turnover rises to 38% among workers under 25 and 43.5% among those with less than a year’s experience. Recruiting a rotating supply of school leavers would do nothing to address the low pay, insecure hours, exhausting travel and working conditions driving experienced carers away.Most importantly, people needing care have a right to choose who supports them and to expect competence, continuity and genuine commitment.The proposed reward is also remarkably unequal. At current fee levels, one year in social care could earn a student up to £14,685 in tuition-fee reductions. A family carer providing at least 35 hours of care a week receives only £4,495.40 a year through carer’s allowance – and many receive nothing.After more than 30 years as an NHS midwife, I left my career to care full-time for my mother, who has dementia. I lost earnings, pension growth and the freedom to work normally. If care is worth thousands when performed temporarily by a prospective student, why is sustained care provided by relatives valued so little?Jacqueline HyltonLeedsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: In the picture and missing out | Smartphones | The Guardian
description: A camera can interfere with fully experiencing the moment, writes Greg Lewis, while Alan Payling recalls the privacy of the photo booth
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A camera can interfere with fully experiencing the moment, writes Greg Lewis, while Alan Payling recalls the privacy of the photo booth
Content: ‘I was the only one who saw the whale. Everyone else was looking at their mobile phones.’Photograph: robertharding/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘I was the only one who saw the whale. Everyone else was looking at their mobile phones.’Photograph: robertharding/AlamySmartphonesLettersIn the picture and missing outA camera can interfere with fully experiencing the moment, writesGreg Lewis, whileAlan Paylingrecalls the privacy of the photo boothFri 4 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTSharePhoebe Greenwood is right (Sunsets, disasters, dinners: we now record them all with our phones. But what is that doing to our souls?, 29 August). Having been a photojournalist, I find that the camera can interfere with fully experiencing the moment.Many years ago, my wife discovered previously unknown relatives in Denmark. When we visited, they took us to a cemetery where one of her ancestors was buried.She stood there quietly for a few minutes and began to cry. I started photographing and suddenly realised that I had shifted into work mode, both physically and mentally. I put the camera down and gave her a hug.After deciding that I wasn’t going to take photos when not working, we were on a whale-watching trip. I was the only one who saw the whale. Everyone else was looking at their mobile phones.Greg LewisClovis, California, USIn the absence of a personal camera, in the late 1960s, the commonly used alternative for young lovers to record their undying devotion to each other was the photo booth.Apparently they were used by some to provide passport photos, but I recall that on Friday and Saturday evenings in Birmingham city centre, they were an essential part of a good night out. Not only would you get four photos to share; the curtain also provided a few moments of privacy, although only from the waist upwards!Alan PaylingTorquay, DevonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? description: Letters: Sundays in the 1950s are remembered by Bob Waring and Martin Cooper
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Sundays in the 1950s are remembered by Bob Waring and Martin Cooper
Content: Tony Hancock puts his feet up.Photograph: Daily Mail/REXView image in fullscreenTony Hancock puts his feet up.Photograph: Daily Mail/REXLife and styleLettersGood riddance to those dull Sundays that Tony Hancock and I loathedSundays in the 1950s are remembered byBob WaringandMartin CooperFri 4 Sep 2026 12.55 EDTShareIn 1958 Tony Hancock had a very different take on the British Sunday from Sian Dudley’s bucolic vision (Letters, 30 August), as outlined in theHancock’s Half HourepisodeSunday Afternoon at Home: “I might just as well be in bed: there’s nothing else to do. [Sigh] I wish I hadn’t got up now … I hate Sundays. It’s not like this on the continent: it’s their big day over there. All the cafes open and football matches and race meetings – everybody’s gay. Aahh! Not over ’ere though! Everything’s shut up.”My memory accords with the bard of East Cheam. What we have now, and didn’t then, is choice.Bob WaringSouthport, MerseysideSian Dudley was lucky having such a relaxed Sunday as a child. My 1950s Sundays were rather different. My brothers and I had to go to church in the morning and Sunday school in the afternoon, we didn’t have a telly and I hated board games. I like my 2026 Sundays.Martin CooperBromley, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
