title: ‘‘Never Forget’ is not a slogan’: Mamdani designates 9/11 as a Day of Remembrance and Service | New York | The Guardian
description: The New York City mayor will sign two executive orders honoring those impacted by the attacks, as he faces campaign to exclude him from the 25th anniversary commemoration
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: The New York City mayor will sign two executive orders honoring those impacted by the attacks, as he faces campaign to exclude him from the 25th anniversary commemoration
Content: People mourn at the 9/11 Memorial on the 20th anniversary of the September 11 attacks in Manhattan, New York on September 11, 2021.Photograph: Mike Segar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople mourn at the 9/11 Memorial on the 20th anniversary of the September 11 attacks in Manhattan, New York on September 11, 2021.Photograph: Mike Segar/AFP/Getty ImagesNew York‘‘Never Forget’ is not a slogan’: Mamdani designates 9/11 as a Day of Remembrance and ServiceThe New York City mayor will sign two executive orders honoring those impacted by the attacks, as he faces campaign to exclude him from the 25th anniversary commemorationMaya Yangin New YorkFri 4 Sep 2026 14.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 14.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew York City mayorZohran Mamdaniis set to designate September 11 as a Day of Remembrance and Service ahead of the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks.Mamdani’s officeannouncedon Friday morning that the mayor will sign two executive orders honoring victims, first responders, survivors, city workers and families affected by the attacks. The orders will also strengthen the city’s ability to protect New Yorkers and maintain essential services during emergencies.The first executive order is expected to designate time on September 11 for a moment of silence honoring those killed in the attacks, as well as those who have suffered health consequences in the years since. It will also encourage city agencies to hold memorial ceremonies, educational programming and other remembrance activities.The designation would mark the first city-level action of its kind by aNew YorkCity mayor, Mamdani’s office said.The second executive order will overhaul the city’s emergency continuity plans for the first time since 2007. It will also create a new interagency team to coordinate the city’s response and continuity planning.In a statement on Friday, Mamdani said: “I am honored to establish the City’s first Day of Remembrance and Service on September 11th to remember those we lost on that horrific day and the first responders, families and city workers whose lives were irrevocably changed in the aftermath. Through this executive order, we are calling on New Yorkers to honor their memory through service and deep reflection.“We must also recognize that remembrance carries a responsibility to strengthen our city, protect New Yorkers and ensure that government is prepared to deliver for people no matter the circumstances. ‘Never Forget’ is not a slogan. It is a commitment that we must carry forward through action. And that is precisely what these two executive orders demonstrate,” he added.The city’s fire department commissioner Lillian Bonsignore echoed similar sentiments, saying: “Service was the legacy of those who answered the call on September 11, 2001, and those who have died since. The greatest tribute we can pay them is to continue serving one another with compassion, courage and a shared commitment to building a stronger New York.”Mamdani’s announcement comes amid a wave of attacks, some Islamophobic, targeting the 34-year-old democratic socialist, who is the city’s first Muslim mayor.A recent petition with more than 98,000 signatures, including from family members who lost relatives in the attacks, calls for Mamdani to be excluded from September 11 commemorative events marking the 25th anniversary.Among other claims, the petition accuses the mayor of supporting individuals whose public statements or records are viewed as “dismissive of American institutions or insufficiently critical of extremist ideologies”.Former New York governor George Pataki, a Republican, has alsosaidMamdani should skip the 9/11 memorial.But other families and local lawmakers have pushed back. Elizabeth Miller, whose father was killed in the attacks,toldCBS earlier this month: “The focus should be on where are we in this world, 25 years later?”“Mayor Mamdani has assured 9/11 families that he wants to be there to honor our loved ones, and I think he should be allowed to do that,” added Miller, the project director of September 11th Families for Peaceful Tomorrows, a remembrance organization.In a separate statement, the organizationsaid: “We strongly condemn the anti-American accusations and Islamophobic sentiment underlying the effort seeking to prevent him from being at Ground Zero.“For decades, we have firmly maintained that Ground Zero is sacred space and should never be used as a platform for political speech or partisan politics. Ground Zero remains a burial ground.”Meanwhile, city council speaker Julie Menincalledthe push to exclude Mamdani “absolutely inappropriate”, adding: “I think mayor [Mike] Bloomberg made a terrific decision in making sure that there were not political speeches because, again, it shouldn’t be politicized … So, those that are trying to politicize this, what is happening on the 25th anniversary, I think that that is unfortunate.”Responding toa question about how he felt about the petition a few weeks ago, Mamdani told reporters: “I will proudly honor the families, the survivors, the first responders, forever impacted by that horrific terror attack, by standing alongside them at this year’s 9/11 commemoration, reaffirming that we will never forget the solemn day felt by all of us who call this city home, and frankly, by all of us who call this country home.”Even before taking office, Mamdani facedIslamophobic attackson the campaign trail, including from hispolitical opponents, former governorAndrew Cuomo,House Republicanswho have called for his deportation, as well asDonald Trump.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkSeptember 11 2001Zohran MamdaniIslamophobiaUS politicsShareReuse this content

title: Woman, 45, killed in Florence in seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August | Italy | The Guardian
description: Lorena Isceri was thrown off a motorway bridge, allegedly by ex-boyfriend Federico Vella
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Lorena Isceri was thrown off a motorway bridge, allegedly by ex-boyfriend Federico Vella
Content: Lorena Isceri still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted.Photograph: FacebookView image in fullscreenLorena Isceri still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted.Photograph: FacebookItalyWoman, 45, killed in Florence in seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-AugustLorena Isceri was thrown off a motorway bridge, allegedly by ex-boyfriend Federico VellaAngela Giuffridain RomeFri 4 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 45-year-old woman abducted and thrown off a motorway bridge near Florence has become the seventh alleged femicide inItalysince mid-August.Lorena Isceri was abducted on Thursday afternoon, allegedly by her ex-boyfriend, Federico Vella, in the Rifredi area of Florence, before being forced into the boot of his car and driven towards a bridge on the A1 motorway.Isceri, who worked in the veterinary sector, still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted.Vella, 38, stopped the car, snatched the phone and allegedly threw her off the bridge, before jumping off himself.After Isceri’s call to the helpline, police traced her phone signal but arrived too late to prevent her murder. Officers are establishing whether Isceri was killed before she was thrown off the bridge.Isceri’s mother toldSkyTg24that she had last heard from her daughter on Thursday morning, and said she sounded fine. When asked about the relationship with Vella, she said Isceri had spoken to her about it and was “very afraid”.Italian interior ministry data had indicated a downward trend in femicides during the first six months of 2026.Figures compiled by the feminist allianceNon Una di Menoshowed that as of 8 August, 40 women had been killed so far this year.But numbers have risen since 15 August, Italy’s Ferragosto national holiday, with seven women, including Isceri, killed by a current or former partner.Giorgia Meloni’s ruling coalition, which on Friday celebrated becoming the longest-serving government in the history of the Italian republic, had pledged to crack down on gender-based violence after the strong public reaction to the killing ofGiulia Cecchetin, a 22-year-old medical student, by her former boyfriend, in November 2023.Two years later, the government approved a law that for the first time introduced a legal definition of femicide in criminal law, punishing it with life in prison, while increasing sentences for crimes including stalking, sexual violence and the sharing of intimate images without consent.However, a campaign to educate schoolboys about healthy relationships was thwarted after the government made it conditional on parental approval.Luisa Rizzitelli, the Italy coordinator of One Billion Rising, which campaigns to end violence against women, said: “Perhaps Meloni is right to celebrate her government’s longevity, because there is precious little to celebrate in terms of concrete results.“The approach to the tragic issue of male violence against women has been based on security policies while completely lacking strategic, structural programmes for training and prevention. The stubborn refusal to implement sex and relationship education in schools is a major factor fuelling the epidemic of femicides in Italy.”In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123 and thedomestic abuse helplineis 0808 2000 247. In the US, thesuicide prevention lifelineis 988 and thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis on 13 11 14 and the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines can be found viawww.befrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsItalyFemicideViolence against women and girlsEuropeWomennewsShareReuse this content

title: UK hits back at Argentinian Falklands claim and insists islands remain British | Falkland Islands | The Guardian
description: Ed Miliband says Britain’s position remains ‘unwavering’ in response to remarks by Argentina’s president
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Ed Miliband says Britain’s position remains ‘unwavering’ in response to remarks by Argentina’s president
Content: Javier Milei making a television address on Thursday in which he said the ‘winds of change’ favoured his country’s claim to the Falklands.Photograph: Argentina's presidency press office/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJavier Milei making a television address on Thursday in which he said the ‘winds of change’ favoured his country’s claim to the Falklands.Photograph: Argentina's presidency press office/AFP/Getty ImagesFalkland IslandsUK hits back at Argentinian Falklands claim and insists islands remain BritishEd Miliband says Britain’s position remains ‘unwavering’ in response to remarks by Argentina’s presidentUK politics live – latest updatesKiran StaceyPolicy editorFri 4 Sep 2026 05.24 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish ministers have hit back after theArgentinian president said“winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the Falklands were “blowing around the world”.The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the UK would “resolutely uphold” the self-determination of the islands after the Argentinian president,Javier Milei, said his country needed to take them back.Miliband said in a post on X: “The UK’s position on theFalkland Islandsis unwavering. The islands are British and will remain so because that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders.“Their right of self-determination is paramount, grounded in international law and we will resolutely uphold it.”Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said Milei’s statement “tells us more about domestic politics inArgentinathan it does about the Falkland Islands”.Headded on X: “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British. Our commitment to the Falklands is absolute and unshakeable.”Lucy Powell, the education secretary, also insisted the islands were British, adding: “We will defend the right of those who live in the Falkland Islands to determine their own future.”The latest diplomatic spat over the south Atlantic archipelago came after comments by the US president, Donald Trump, who has cast doubt on American support for British control of the islands.View image in fullscreenMount Tumbledown behind Stanley on the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls Malvinas.Photograph: Ricardo Mazalán/APThe US has traditionally remained neutral on the Falklands’ sovereignty, while recognising Britain’s de facto control over them.Britain and Argentina fought a war over the islands in 1982, when British forces defeated Argentinian troops, who had landed there to stake a territorial claim.In more recent years, the British oil company Rockhopper and the Israeli company Navitas have been developing the Sea Lion oilfield, 140 miles to the north of the islands.Asked on Monday whether he could review British sovereignty over the islands as a way to push the UK to spend more on defence,Trump said: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”On Thursday, when questioned about whether the US would back the UK in the event of an Argentinian invasion, he referred to the government’s refusal to let him use British bases in his initial attack on Iran earlier this year.“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”He added: “The Falklands is very interesting because your country is not the same country it was 20 years ago, 25 years ago. That was a long time [ago], you went there and you just took it back very quickly. There was no games, so I don’t know if you’re prepared to do that.”On Thursday night, Milei highlighted Trump’s comments, saying: “President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas [the Argentinian name for the Falklands].”He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.Rockhopper’s shares dropped 7% in early trading on Friday.Explore more on these topicsFalkland IslandsJavier MileiArgentinaForeign policyDefence policyTrump administrationEd MilibandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Richard O’Sullivan, star of 70s sitcom Man About the House, dies aged 82 | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: Actor, who also played title roles in Robin’s Nest and Dick Turpin, dies peacefully at Royal Variety Charity care home
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Actor, who also played title roles in Robin’s Nest and Dick Turpin, dies peacefully at Royal Variety Charity care home
Content: Richard O'Sullivan, who was described by his son as a ‘doting grandfather and a wonderful dad’.Photograph: AllstarView image in fullscreenRichard O'Sullivan, who was described by his son as a ‘doting grandfather and a wonderful dad’.Photograph: AllstarTV comedyRichard O’Sullivan, star of 70s sitcom Man About the House, dies aged 82Actor, who also played title roles in Robin’s Nest and Dick Turpin, dies peacefully at Royal Variety Charity care homeRichard O’Sullivan obituarySex symbol in a 70s tank top: how Richard O’Sullivan blazed a trail for funny, frisky, cheeky chappiesKevin Rawlinsonand agencyFri 4 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRichard O’Sullivan, known for his role as Robin Tripp in the 1970s TV sitcomsMan About the Houseand Robin’s Nest, has died aged 82.The actor, who was also famous for playing the title character in the TV series Dick Turpin, died peacefully with his family at his side at the Royal Variety Charity’s care home on Friday, the organisation said.Dandies, docs and robbers: Richard O’Sullivan – a life in picturesRead moreHis son James O’Sullivan paid tribute to him, saying: “My dad was as funny and charming in real life as he appeared on our TV screens over the years. Always kind-spirited, good-humoured, a doting grandfather and a wonderful dad – I will miss him dearly.“Although much of his career happened before I was born, I was fortunate enough to be able to enjoy and witness his incredible talents on the countless reruns of his shows that made him the respected and loved actor that he was.”View image in fullscreenO’Sullivan in the garden of Brinsworth House care home in 2021.Photograph: Andy Newbold/Royal Variety Charity/PAO’Sullivan had lived at the Royal Variety Charity’s Brinsworth House in Twickenham for 23 years. His son thanked the “incredible team” there for their “love, kindness and care”. He said: “They have been truly amazing and will always hold a special place in my heart.”O’Sullivan’s career began when he appeared in The Yellow Balloon as an eight-year-old in 1953. He later appeared in Peter Hall’s production of Love’s Labour’s Lost at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1956.He appeared in two films with Cliff Richard in the 1960s: The Young Ones in 1961 and Wonderful Life in 1964. In 1963, he starred opposite Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton in Cleopatra in the role of Pharaoh Ptolemy XIII.View image in fullscreenRichard O’Sullivan as Pharaoh Ptolemy XIII in Cleopatra (1963).Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarMan About the House ran for six series from 1973, following the trials and tribulations of a man sharing a London flat with two single women, Chrissy, played by Paula Wilcox, and Sally Thomsett as Jo.Giles Cooper, the life president of the Royal Variety Charity, said: “Richard O’Sullivan was a master of effortless charm and impeccable comic timing, bringing pure warmth, wit, and unforgettable joy to millions of living rooms as a true giant of British television. He will be sorely missed by us all at the Royal Variety Charity.”Explore more on these topicsTV comedyComedyTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK has not done enough to prepare for shocks to food supplies, says watchdog | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: National Audit Office urges government to act as climate crisis, disease and cyberattacks pose growing risks
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: National Audit Office urges government to act as climate crisis, disease and cyberattacks pose growing risks
Content: The climate crisis poses a growing risk to the UK’s food supplies, the National Audit Office has warned.Photograph: Matías Basualdo/EPAView image in fullscreenThe climate crisis poses a growing risk to the UK’s food supplies, the National Audit Office has warned.Photograph: Matías Basualdo/EPAFood & drink industryUK has not done enough to prepare for shocks to food supplies, says watchdogNational Audit Office urges government to act as climate crisis, disease and cyberattacks pose growing risksJoanna PartridgeFri 4 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe climate crisis, disease and cyber-attacks pose growing risks to the UK’s food supplies and the government needs to act to make the system more resilient, according to the public spending watchdog.The National Audit Office (NAO) is urging the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) to work more closely with households, communities and businesses to ensure the flow of crucial food into the country can withstand supply shocks that are becoming increasingly common and severe.Its latest report found Defra – the department responsible for security of food supply – had taken some steps to better prepare for future shocks, but said it had not done enough in recent years to get citizens and industry to plan for possible emergencies.Britainrelies on overseas importsfor more than a third of its food, most of it entering through four ports – Dover, Felixstowe, Southampton and London Gateway – making supplies particularly vulnerable to potential disruption.The NAO’s report comes after months of warnings about the resilience of the UK’s food supply chain from experts who havetold households to build up a stockpileof long-life items they could rely on in an emergency. Britonsare less preparedfor potential future catastrophic events than citizens of several other European countries, according to government research.The supply chain has already come under pressure during the Covid-19 pandemic and after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, although businesses including the nation’s largest supermarkets managed to keep goods flowing, in most cases without the need for significant government assistance.However, Defra is less confident about the private sector’s ability to withstand future shocks, such as extreme weather events, without greater government intervention.Food industry businesses praised Defra’s engagement with them during the pandemic, but told the NAO it had communicated with them less frequently since. The report said the companies had limited input into the government’s plans for reacting to supply disruption, which could mean officials created proposals that would not work in practice.Gareth Davies, the NAO’s head, said: “Recent disruptions have shown the resilience of the UK’s food supply chain, but risks are increasing in likelihood and severity.“Defra should learn from approaches taken in other countries, and strengthen preparedness for emergencies by testing plans with local government and industry.”The government has designated food as one of 13 critical national infrastructure sectors it considers essential for the proper functioning of the country.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, food industry representatives have said that does not go far enough and have called on ministers to add the UK’s cold stores and food transport hubs to the critical list, which would ensure their power supplies would be maintained in the event of widespread outages.The NAO report comes just a few months after the trade body for cold storage and logistics, the Cold Chain Federation,accused the government of “complacency” over national food storage and urged ministers to make potential disruption to the UK’s food system an “immediate national priority”.The last national exercise testing Defra’s preparedness for catastrophic events that would severely disrupt the availability of food took place in 2023, but did not include most supply chain businesses, the NAO found.In addition, local resilience forums indicated they lacked clarity from Defra on what would be expected from them in the event of disruption.Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryDefence policynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Astronomical’ fuel price surge hits farmers in UK and US | Oil | The Guardian
description: Intensification of Middle East conflict and ongoing Russian export ban leads to diesel prices rising 10% in less than a week
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Intensification of Middle East conflict and ongoing Russian export ban leads to diesel prices rising 10% in less than a week
Content: Red diesel for agricultural vehicles and machinery is taxed at a lower rate than standard diesel fuel in the UK.Photograph: Geography Photos/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRed diesel for agricultural vehicles and machinery is taxed at a lower rate than standard diesel fuel in the UK.Photograph: Geography Photos/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesOil‘Astronomical’ fuel price surge hits farmers in UK and USIntensification of Middle East conflict and ongoing Russian export ban leads to diesel prices rising 10% in less than a weekJoanna PartridgeandAlex DanielFri 4 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFarmers are facing an “astronomical” jump in the price of fuel needed to operate their vehicles and machinery after a surge in diesel costs in the UK and the US.Renewed fighting between the US and Iran has driven up the price of crude oil, while last weekRussiaextended a ban on diesel exports, further pushing up market prices.Anintensification of Middle East hostilities over the weekendpushed fuel costs even higher for farmers, said Alex Harrison, a fuel buyer at Fram Farmers, a not-for-profit farmer-owned co-operative. The price of all fuels had gone up by “an astronomical amount in just a few days”, she said, rising by between 10p and 14p a litre since Monday.This represents about a 10% increase in the cost of red diesel – fuel used for agricultural vehicles and machinery that is taxed at a lower rate to standard diesel – which currently costs about £1.10 a litre.The average price of diesel for UK motorists had climbed to 183.5p a litre on Thursday, according togovernment data, up from 164.5p in mid-July.On Friday, US diesel prices at the pump reached an all-time high of $5.85 a gallon compared with an average of $3.71 a year ago, according to the American Automobile Association. The figure outstripped the previous high that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.The volatility in oil wholesale markets has left farmers struggling to decide how much fuel to buy and when, with many calling for advice from Fram Farmers, which represents more than 1,400 farm businesses across the UK.While the harvest peak demand for red diesel and other fuels has passed, many growers traditionally buy more fuel at this time of year as they begin to prepare their land for winter.“This latest spike has really caught everybody by surprise and hit them quite hard because it’s been such a large spike and because of the time of year,” Harrison said. Farmers are “trying to decide what’s best to do, how to order for [managing their] cashflow”.The co-operative’s members have changed their buying patterns since the outbreak of war in Iran sent oil prices soaring. Harrison said: “A lot of people have ordered in much smaller increments and more often, as they are trying to hedge their bets a little.”View image in fullscreenCo-operative members had been ordering fuel ‘in much smaller increments and more often’, said Alex Harrison of Fram Farmers.Photograph: Henry Arden/Getty Images/Image SourceThe rise in diesel prices comes amid a squeeze on global refining capacity. Russia, which normally supplies about 10% of the world’s diesel despite western sanctions, has been hit by Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries in August, prompting the export ban extension.That has been compounded by a wider increase in the price of crude oil. The international benchmark Brent crude was trading at close to $97 a barrel on Thursday, its highest point in about six weeks.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere was amajor flare-up in attacksin the Middle East last weekend, the first US strikes since July. Two Saudi supertankers were hit in the strait of Hormuz late on Monday, fuelling concerns of a longer-term return to hostilities.Tehran warned ⁠that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf despite athreat by Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard”in response to the Iranian strikes.Small businesses and larger companies that rely on vehicle fleets, such as delivery firms and construction companies, will also face higher running costs as a result.Back in the UK,the price of paraffin, or heating oil– widely used on farms to heat buildings including farmhouses and barns – is also higher, at a time of year when many households, mostly in rural communities that are not connected to the gas network, would usually be starting to think about filling their tanks ahead of the winter.The current price for paraffin is close to £1 a litre compared with prices of about 60p a litre just before the Iran war.Explore more on these topicsOilFarmingUS-Israel war on IranRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: how companies ‘secretly’ use billions of litres of public water in drought-hit England | Water | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: As millions of people face hosepipe bans, many companies are not required to report, let alone cut, use of public supply
Author: Rachel Salvidge
Headline: Exclusive: As millions of people face hosepipe bans, many companies are not required to report, let alone cut, use of public supply
Content: The site of the Fawley oil refinery in Southampton was shown to be the largest industrial user of the public water supply.Photograph: Daniel Leal/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe site of the Fawley oil refinery in Southampton was shown to be the largest industrial user of the public water supply.Photograph: Daniel Leal/AFP/Getty ImagesWaterRevealed: how companies ‘secretly’ use billions of litres of public water in drought-hit EnglandExclusive: As millions of people face hosepipe bans, many companies are not required to report, let alone cut, use of public supplyRachel SalvidgeFri 4 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLess than 1% of businesses inEnglanduse more water than the daily needs of 10 million people, as millions of households face hosepipe bans and three-quarters of the country is in drought.Businesses across England use 2.6bn litres a day from the public water supply, which includes potable and non-potable water provided by water companies.In total, businesses account for about 30% of public supply use, with two-thirds of their consumption in water-stressed areas, according to Mosl, the organisation that operates England’s business water market.Tracking industrial water use appears difficult. Regulators say they are frustrated by a lack of data and “commercial secrecy”, and the water sector says it is prevented from planning effectively for growth industries.The biggest users of the public water supply include oil refineries, chemical plants and paper mills, and some face no requirement to cut their consumption.Mosl’s map of business water supply points, ranked by volume used, showed the site of ExxonMobil’s Esso refinery at Fawley, Southampton, as the largest user of public water supply. However, the site includes a number of other operators that also use the water, including waste, gas, chemicals and energy companies.Mosl cited the refinery’s water use inwritten evidenceto a House of Lords committee as an example of “the high volume of water wastage in industry that is not disincentivised by government or the regulatory framework”.Mosl did not name the refinery but described its location, which was also visible on its map of supply points.ExxonMobil disputed Mosl’s figures, saying its water use was commercially confidential. Mosl said it planned to ask the committee to redact parts of its evidence. During reporting, Mosl also removed a report and its supply point map from its website.The refinery said the “vast majority” of the water it used came from the Solent strait for cooling, while “industrial water” was used for processes that could not easily be reduced without shutting down operating units. Potable water accounted for less than 1% of total consumption, it said.double quotation markIt’s surely an injustice that petrochemical and fossil fuel companies most responsible for the climate crisis are also draining … water suppliesRichard Benwell, Wildlife and Countryside LinkApart from refineries, other major users of the public water supply include paper mills and companies in the chemicals and soft drinks industries. But the overall picture of business water use is incomplete. One in 10 businesses are not metered, meaning their use is not measured or reported. Of those that are metered, only 11% have smart meters.Despite Mosl collecting data on water taken from the public supply, it is not free to share all of it, even with government departments, according to Mosl’s chief executive, Sarah McMath.McMath told the House of Lords committee that when the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) or theEnvironment Agencyrequested data, Mosl had to negotiate a bespoke agreement to share it.Mosl was working with the water regulator, Ofwat, to change this, she said, so that data would be shared when it would benefit “the environment or society”.A lack of data is already affecting national water planning. Gaps in local authority growth plans, combined with what the Environment Agency and Ofwat describe as “commercial secrecy, especially in the energy sector”, mean plans are often based on assumptions.The Environment Agency and Ofwat are calling for mandatory reporting of current and projected water use across all sectors to improve water security.A spokesperson for Mosl said: “Our data highlights both the opportunities and regulatory barriers to incentivising businesses to use less water. Rather than focusing on individual users – many of whom are actively seeking to reduce their water demand – we should focus on creating the right conditions to invest in water efficiency and increase water reuse where it is safe and practical.”Water resources planning assumes business water consumption will fall by 9% by 2038 and 15% by 2050.But the trade body Water UK argues the assumption is unrealistic asdemand grows from new homes, asdatacentres, hydrogen production and other developments. It wants water companies to be able to plan for projected demand rather than government reduction targets.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markAnyone can take up to 20,000 litres a day from a stream, borehole or spring without a licence or reporting itCompanies are not required to report all their water use, and for some, the more water they use, the cheaper each unit becomes.One operator told Mosl that a single UK datacentre uses 219m litres a year. It also has a tankered-water supply on standby if its mains connection fails, as well as its own borehole as a backup.Businesses can also take water directly from rivers, lakes, aquifers and the sea via abstraction . This is regulated separately by the Environment Agency.Some abstraction is invisible. Anyone can take up to 20,000 litres a day from a stream, borehole or spring without a licence or reporting it. The gap covers an estimated 850,000 people and organisations across England, mostly on farms and in rural areas.Richard Benwell, the chief executive of the NGO coalition Wildlife and Countryside Link, said: “It’s surely an injustice that petrochemical and fossil fuel companies most responsible for the climate crisis are also draining … water supplies and drawing more water from our parched environment.The water campaigner Feargal Sharkey said: “Yet again, regulatory ineptitude is allowed to triumph over the needs of people and the environment. While water supplies run dry, corporate bank accounts are flooded with the proceeds of corporate greed.”Defra said the government was taking “decisive action to secure water supplies”, including planning to build nine reservoirs and investing in infrastructure.A Water UK spokesperson said: “Supplies are increasingly at risk because England’s official forecasts for how much water the country needs rely on flawed assumptions. The water needed by fast-growing datacentres is explicitly excluded from the forecasts.“At the same time, lower water bills have been prioritised over building a resilient system, meaning in some places water companies only have 2% of water spare to deal with increased demand.”The Environment Agency said abstraction licences had strict conditions and were reviewed regularly, and that it was working towards the 9% reduction in business water use from the public supply.Meanwhile, England’s water companies are losing about 2.2bn litres of water a day through leaking pipes.Get in touchContact the Guardian Business teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. Scroll down and click onSecure Messaging.When asked who you wish to contact please select the ‘Business (UK & Global)’ team.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsWaterOil and gas companiesChemical industryWater industryEnglandEnvironment AgencyEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: British army told to halt non-essential training exercises to save money | British army | The Guardian
description: Collective training exercises for UK-based units to be suspended for most of this year amid budget pressures
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Collective training exercises for UK-based units to be suspended for most of this year amid budget pressures
Content: The cancelled exercises reportedly include those involving tanks and Apache helicopters.Photograph: Andrew Harker/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe cancelled exercises reportedly include those involving tanks and Apache helicopters.Photograph: Andrew Harker/AlamyBritish armyBritish army told to halt non-essential training exercises to save moneyCollective training exercises for UK-based units to be suspended for most of this year amid budget pressuresJamie GriersonFri 4 Sep 2026 02.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 14.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBritish armyhas been ordered to halt non-essential training exercises in an effort to save money.Troops preparing to be deployed or on deployments, those who are on standby or in a quick-reaction role will continue to train as normal. But collective training exercises for UK-based units are being suspended for most of this year amid budget pressures.Cancelled exercises include those involving tanks and Apache helicopters, according to reports in theTimesandBBC.The army did not deny the cuts and said a training regime informed by lessons from the Ukraine conflict – such as on drone warfare and modernisation – was being prioritised.An army spokesperson said: “Our training continues and we are prioritising activity that contributes most directly to readiness, deployability and operational effectiveness. We are also investing £2bn to transform training for the British army over the next 15 years.”Andy Burnham is under pressure to increase defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030, rising to 3.5% by 2035.At prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, Burnham was urged by the chair of the Commons defence select committee, the Labour MP Tan Singh Dhesi, to “urgently commit to charting a pathway to reaching 3% of GDP spend on defence by 2030 which, as his chancellor rightly noted, is critical to keeping our country safe”. Dhesi told the prime minister that “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”, when it came to funding the UK’s armed forcesPlans set out in the defence investment plan (Dip) include defence spending rising to 2.7% of GDP by 2027-28, but there are no firm details on how further increases will be achieved beyond that date.The Treasury has consistently said the government will set out plans for reaching 3% and 3.5% at the spending review, due to take place next year.The chancellor, John Healey,resigned from Keir Starmer’s government as defence secretary in June, in protest against what he argued was the then prime minister’s failure to adequately fund defence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut in his new post in No 11 Downing Street, Healey has made clearhe will wait until next year’s spending reviewbefore presenting a plan to meet Labour’s pledge of devoting 3.5% of GDP to defence by 2035.Healey will present his first budget on 28 October and needs to find approximately £1.4bn a year over the next three yearsto pay for Starmer’s defence investment plan– which Healey in his last job derided as inadequate.Explore more on these topicsBritish armyMilitaryDefence policyJohn HealeyPublic financenewsShareReuse this content

title: Canary staff not paid amid fears for news website’s future | The Canary | The Guardian
description: Outlet faced significant financial challenges after it had funds blocked by bank without explanation
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Outlet faced significant financial challenges after it had funds blocked by bank without explanation
Content: The Canary website was founded in 2015 against a backdrop of support for the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn.Photograph: The CanaryView image in fullscreenThe Canary website was founded in 2015 against a backdrop of support for the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn.Photograph: The CanaryThe CanaryCanary staff not paid amid fears for news website’s futureOutlet faced significant financial challenges after it had funds blocked by bank without explanationBen QuinnPolitical correspondentFri 4 Sep 2026 11.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorkers at the leftwing news outlet the Canary fear it will not survive beyond this year amid access to funds being blocked and allegations of financial mismanagement and internal turmoil.The site, which was founded in 2015 against a backdrop of the wave of support for the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn, appeared set to expand after a multimillion-pound injection of funds last year.But the outlet faced significant financial challenges in July after it announced thatit was unable to pay staffand contractors as a result of Lloyds Bank unexpectedly blocking access to “a substantial amount” of its money. The bank did not give a reason.A number of staff at the outlet were not paid again at the end of August. “Any payment difficulties have been solely due to our ongoing debanking issues,” a Canary spokesperson told the Guardian.Some journalists at the Canary, however, have said they believe the banking issues had been used to distract from wider financial mismanagement.They claim the funding, believed to be more than £2m, has been squandered on projects including a short-lived newspaper and the purchase of other websites.Staff at the outlet, where there are about 50 full-time and part-time jobs, have moved to unionise by forming a branch of theNational Union of Journalists(NUJ). Over the summer a full staff meeting was told that the new funding had all but gone and they were all facing the possibility of redundancy, with about £400,000 left to see the Canary through to December.Since the Canary faced issues with access to its funds, staff say they have been notified that late payments of pension contributions by the company have been reported by the National Employment Savings Trust (Nest), the government-backed workplace pension scheme that helps employers meet their legal duty of automatic enrolment.It is understood that tensions have also risen after, in the spring, workers say, they were asked by management to sign “non-negotiable” non-disclosure agreements, and told that if they refused they would be subject to changes to their employment contracts.The site describes itself as anti-austerity, anti-Zionist and pro-freedom of expression, among other things. Steve Topple, the outlet’s chief executive, told staff in May that he and others in the management team had serious concerns about the integrity of the Canary as an organisation “and also the level of reputational risk”.“We are at a time when we are doing things that are putting a massive target on our backs, and I am expecting the full force of the system to be placed upon us in due course,” he wrote in a message which also said he would not tolerate the leaking of confidential information beyond the organisation.Staff at the website said in 2022 that they had “overthrown” management and were running the organisation as a cooperative. That structure was later dissolved.Some had hoped that the title’s longer term future had been secured after Cecil Hetherington, the founder of the Northern Irish classifieds website Used Cars NI and chair of the house-sale platform PropertyPal, became a major shareholder, contributing an estimated £2m.“We were told originally that Steve had taken on a donation from Cecil Hetherington, but then the ‘debanking’ happened and things changed,” said one worker, referring to the period in which funds were blocked by Lloyds.“Payments have been late for the last three months, wages and invoices have been late. Even basic stuff hasn’t been taken care of, with the result that the website went down at one point.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We were told that only about £400,000 was left out of the £2m.”A spokesperson for the NUJ said: “The NUJ’s concern is, and always has been, for the interests of its members and we are working with all our members at the Canary.“We have spoken with Steve Topple and we are working together to ensure the continued stability of the Canary. It’s in that context that we are promoting a constructive relationship.”Topple said: “Lloyds debanked the Canary and closed its account without warning earlier this year, confiscating and holding all of the company’s cash reserves.“This has resulted in severe financial and emotional stress on the company and its employees. We are working through the financial disruption caused by the closure of our bank account and are liaising closely with staff to achieve an equitable balance between meeting our current commitments and safeguarding the organisation’s future sustainability. We have tried to be as open as possible with staff, while balancing the need for confidentiality and avoiding unnecessary upset.“We have undoubtedly made mistakes in our internal communications, and we apologise to everyone in Canary Media Limited and our readers for that. We are currently in discussions with our employees to address their very understandable concerns and would appreciate the privacy to do that.”Get in touchContact Ben Quinn about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Ben using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. title: Milky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomers | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: Exhibition opens in former home of William Herschel, who discovered Uranus, and his comet-spotting sibling Caroline
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Exhibition opens in former home of William Herschel, who discovered Uranus, and his comet-spotting sibling Caroline
Content: Artist Grace Weir, left, in the garden of the Herschel Museum of Astronomy in Bath with museum curator Bridget de Leon.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenArtist Grace Weir, left, in the garden of the Herschel Museum of Astronomy in Bath with museum curator Bridget de Leon.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianAstronomyMilky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomersExhibition opens in former home of William Herschel, who discovered Uranus, and his comet-spotting sibling CarolineSteven MorrisFri 4 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 14.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the garden of their Georgian townhouse in Bath in the late 18th century, a brother and sister made a series of extraordinary astronomical discoveries.A new art show in the house where the siblings – William and Caroline Herschel – worked and lived highlights their pioneering spirit and their domestic arrangements.View image in fullscreenDetail of painting of William Herschel.The Irish artistGrace Weir, who created the exhibition in what is now theHerschel Museum of Astronomy, said she was deeply interested in the science that went on at the house, including the discovery of the planet Uranus, and fascinated that it took place in such a cosy environment.“It is a home,” Weir said. “Science does not take place in a vacuum. They would have had conversations about their discoveries across the dining table.”One of her artworks, On the Construction of Heavens, was inspired by William Herschel’s drawing of the Milky Way in 1785.Weir has had a copy of the drawing embroidered on to an antique linen tablecloth, which is laid over the family dining table. “William and Caroline must have spoken about the shape of the Milky Way right here,” Weir said. “That would have been an unusual thing to talk about back then.”View image in fullscreen‘They would have had conversations about their discoveries across the dining table,’ says Weir.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianIn the basement workshop, where William Herschel built his own telescopes, Weir has installed an LED digital counter that records the distance of Uranus from the Earth as it changes.A key element of the show is to make sure Caroline Herschel gets her share of the credit for the pair’s advances in science.View image in fullscreenDetail of a print of Caroline Herschel.William Herschel was a self-taught amateur astronomer who came to Bath from Germany in 1777. His sister followed, initially as a housekeeper.She quickly became his assistant, recording his findings, helping him with calculations, keeping his telescopes in order but then made discoveries of her own, finding eight comets and becoming the first woman inEnglandto be paid as an astronomer.One of the most striking pieces Weir has created is a tribute to Caroline Herschel’s comet-spotting abilities. Called An Imperfect Account, it features a piece of meteorite and a piece of obsidian in the shape of one of Caroline’s worry beads.Weir said: “William had to persuade her mother to let her come to Bath. He recognised her intelligence and once she got here, they were incredibly collaborative. They drove each other along, they understood each other.”View image in fullscreenWeir’s artwork An Imperfect Account featuring a piece of meteorite and a piece of obsidian.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianThe pieces created by Weir are scattered around the house, meaning the visitor has to look for them. Weir said people were losing the art of observing closely. “The Herschels were masters of long looking, something we are losing by scrolling,” she said.Amy Frost, a senior curator at Bath Preservation Trust, said it was the first time in the museum’s history that contemporary site-specific artworks had been integrated. “It’s really exciting for us – it feels like a thread being created through time,” she said.The exhibition, called The As-Yet Unseen (a quote by William Herschel predicting the discovery of the planet Neptune), runs from 5 September until 3 January 2027. A second exhibition studying the work in photography of William’s son, John Herschel, also runs until January. For full details, seehere.Explore more on these topicsAstronomySpaceExhibitionsMuseumsEnglandShareReuse this content

title: Democrats demand DHS documents in investigation into Rohingya refugee’s death | New York | The Guardian
description: Lawmakers condemn agency for ‘obstructing the pursuit of juice’ over death of nearly blind Nurul Amin Shah Alam
Author: Lok Darjee
Headline: Lawmakers condemn agency for ‘obstructing the pursuit of juice’ over death of nearly blind Nurul Amin Shah Alam
Content: A memorial to Nurul Amin Shah Alam in February.Photograph: Craig Ruttle/ReutersView image in fullscreenA memorial to Nurul Amin Shah Alam in February.Photograph: Craig Ruttle/ReutersNew YorkDemocrats demand DHS documents in investigation into Rohingya refugee’s deathLawmakers condemn agency for ‘obstructing the pursuit of juice’ over death of nearly blind Nurul Amin Shah AlamLok DarjeeFri 4 Sep 2026 16.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDemocratic lawmakers are demanding that the Department of Homeland Security turn over records and fully cooperate with an investigation into the death ofNurul Amin Shah Alam,a nearly blind Rohingya refugee who died afterUS border agents lefthim outside a closed coffee shop on a freezing night in Buffalo earlier this year.At a press conference in Buffalo on Friday, standing just a few feet away from where Shah was found dead, Tim Kennedy ofNew Yorkwas joined by Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the ranking Democrat on the House homeland security committee, Lou Correa of California, and Nellie Pou of New Jersey in calling on DHS to cooperate with the Erie county district attorney’s investigation.Kennedy said: “The Erie county medical examiner has ruled his death a homicide, yet DHS still won’t hand over a single meaningful record. Not to my office, not to attorney general [Tish] James, and not to the Erie county district attorney. Simply put, they are obstructing the pursuit of justice by local law enforcement.”Kennedy added: “Mr Shah Alam’s family deserves to see justice served by our legal system. I won’t stop demanding it until DHS complies.”Shah Alam, 56, was aRohingya refugeewho had lost much of his sight and spoke little English. On 19 February, after his release from the Erie county holding center, he was taken into the custody of US border patrol agents while his family waited outside the jail expecting to bring him home.Hours later, agents left Shah Alam outside a closed Tim Hortons coffee shop. His family and attorneys were not told where he had been taken or where agents had left him. Five days later, Shah Alam wasfound deadroughly four miles away.In April, the Erie county medical examinerruled his death a homicide, determining that he died from complications of a perforated duodenal ulcer precipitated by hypothermia and dehydration. The district attorney’s office is continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding his death.Kennedy has also sought legislative changes in response to the case. In June, he introduced theDHS Release Transparency Act, which would require immigration authorities to notify a detainee’s designated family member, attorney, or other contact before the person’s release and provide information about where the individual is being released.In March, New York attorney general Letitia James opened a formal investigation into Shah’s death. But in August, Jamesclosed the criminal investigation, citing the refusal of US Customs and Border Protection to cooperate.According to a letter obtained byInvestigative Post, James had requested that CBP identify the agents who “retrieved and released Mr Shah Alam” and produce “all records related to the detainer, transport, custody, dispatch communications, GPS/vehicle data, body-worn camera footage, and incident reports.”CBP declined to share any information, according to anInvestigative post.The New York attorney general’s office then referred the investigation to the Erie county district attorney.On 2 September, Kennedy and Thompson sent a formal letter to DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin, who had said during his confirmation hearing in March that thedepartment was investigating Shah’s death.In the letter to Mullin, the lawmakers demanded that “DHS fully comply with the Erie county DA’s investigation”. The lawmakers wrote that six months after Shah’s death, they had not received “a single meaningful or substantive response” from DHS, despite multiple oversight letters to the department.Speaking at the press conference, Thompson added: “If DHS has nothing to hide, then they need to turn over the records and cooperate fully with the Erie County law enforcement. It is that simple.”Explore more on these topicsNew YorkTrump administrationDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet floods | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metres
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metres
Content: 0:51Workers pulled alive from hydropower tunnel nine days after Nepal flood disaster – videoNepal-Tibet flood disasterTwo workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet floodsOfficials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metresHannah Ellis-PetersenandGaurav Pokharelin KathmanduFri 4 Sep 2026 09.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 00.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days afterdeadly flash floodsburied the projects in deep mud and left them trapped.The workers were rescued during an operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a hydropower project in one of the areas worst affected by last week’sfloods, according to the army spokesperson Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet.Sanjay Shah, a foreman, was the first to be rescued and was taken to the army barracks in Trishuli. Another person, identified as Kabir Maharjan, a project supervisor, was also pulled from the tunnel. They were recovered from a depth of 170 metres (558ft) inside the tunnel, Basnet said.A senior police official confirmed that a body had also been found during the rescue operation, which has yet to be identified. By Friday afternoon, police confirmed they had halted the search as they had found no more signs of life.After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districtsRead moreNepal’s army released images of Shah being pulled from the small dark entrance of a tunnel. He emerged covered in mud but conscious and was carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.Speaking to army officials after he was rescued, Shah’s first question was: “What day is it?”Shah said he had been in the tunnel’s control room at the time of the flood, alongside about 40 to 45 others. “Since I was in the control room, my responsibility was to save everyone’s lives,” he said. “After such an accident, I couldn’t just run away by myself. I had to save everyone.”View image in fullscreenA survivor is carried out after being rescued from inside the tunnel.Photograph: Nepal Army/ReutersHe said that after realising there had been a major accident, he raced through the tunnel telling people to run and save themselves. “In doing so, I lost time. In the end, I couldn’t get out myself,” he said.To keep himself calm in the darkness of the tunnel, Shah said he spent his time chanting mantras. He said that while trapped, he had heard the voices of three or four others.“We were communicating by shouting to each other from nearby. There could also be people inside the powerhouse. Some of them may not have been able to escape,” he said.Satellite images showing before and after of Rasuwagadhi hydropower plantOfficials said the two men had been flown to a hospital in Kathmandu. Shah was said to be stable but Maharjan was in a critical condition and had been transferred to intensive care.Hirashova Maharjan, Kabir’s wife, said he had been in shock at first and was not talking, but had since said “a few words”. She said he had an injury to his leg and was extremely jaundiced.“He did not even recognise me initially. He only said: ‘Where am I? What happened to me?’ He did not say anything else,” she said. “He is better now. He said he wanted some water, so I gave him water. Then I asked him if he recognised me, and he said yes. He nodded his head.”“We had almost lost hope,” she said, adding that when she saw the photos of him being pulled from the tunnel, “I was so happy that I cried.”View image in fullscreenHirashova Maharjan, left, with a family member after visiting her husband in hospital in Kathmandu on Friday.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesMost of the hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the valley last week, triggered by ‌thecollapse of a melting glacieron the border between Nepal andChina-controlled Tibet.At least 1,287 people were killedin the floodsand more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.‘Everyone seems to have forgotten’: In Tibet, flood-hit families search for the missing and grapple with China’s silenceRead moreRescue efforts have increasingly centred on the hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week in air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued across several projects.Large boulders and flood waters had deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels.Speaking over the phone from the rescue site, Amrit Thapa, deputy superintendent of the armed police force, who is part of the seven-person search and rescue team, said they had managed to crawl the length of the tunnel looking for survivors. They were accompanied by a team from the Nepal army.“The team crawled through areas for about 10 to 15 metres and reached the main section,” said Thapa. “When we went to the final point, we found a body on the remaining upper level.”Thapa said that “except for two sections, the entire tunnel was filled with debris. After checking everything, we did not hear any further voices. We also searched the entire powerhouse area, but so far, nothing else has been found.”View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of damage in a village in Rasuwa district following the flash floods.Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPAArmy and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try to clear debris from the tunnel entrance. At least 550 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal.In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with about 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels.Rescue efforts have also focused on Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, where Nepali authorities said they were confident that 46 workers trapped in an underground chamber in the plant were still alive.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Colombia president provokes disgust by posing with bodies of ‘terrorists’ | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Abelardo De La Espriella posts video of himself with rows of body bags as performative populism continues to sweep Americas
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Abelardo De La Espriella posts video of himself with rows of body bags as performative populism continues to sweep Americas
Content: Still from video posted on social media by Abelardo De La Espriella (centre).Photograph: Abelardo De La EspriellaView image in fullscreenStill from video posted on social media by Abelardo De La Espriella (centre).Photograph: Abelardo De La EspriellaColombiaColombia president provokes disgust by posing with bodies of ‘terrorists’Abelardo De La Espriella posts video of himself with rows of body bags as performative populism continues to sweep AmericasTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroFri 4 Sep 2026 09.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColombia’s hardline president, Abelardo De La Espriella, has provoked outrage after posting a video on social media in which he strides through rows of white body bags that he says contained the corpses of 23 “neutralised” guerrillas.De La Espriella took power last month vowing “all-out war” against illegal armed groups and he publishedthe footageon Thursday in an apparent attempt to show he was fulfilling that pledge.Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?Read more“I promised to confront terrorism without hesitation and I’m keeping that promise,” the far-right politician wrote above the video. “I did not come to play nice with murderers, extortionists and child recruiters. I came to defeat them … Long live Christ the king!”Celebrating the military operation in the Colombian Amazon during which the 23 alleged terrorists were killed, De La Espriella declared: “We are utterly determined to destroy you, who are a cancer.”The body bag footage, set to a stirring Hollywood-style score, was condemned by human rights activists and the president’s political opponents.Iván Cepeda, the leftwing candidate beaten by De La Espriella in June’s election,wrote on X: “He strolls among the bags with the corpses. He nearly treads on them with contempt. He calls himself a Christian but in reality he’s an unscrupulous being lacking the slightest sense of humanity.”View image in fullscreenIván Cepeda at a campaign rally in Bogotá in June.Photograph: Mauricio Dueñas Castañeda/EPAThe leftwing lawmaker Daniel Monroy accused the president of “necropolitics”.He wrote: “This is one of the most bizarre things we’ve seen. Strolling among the dead, while invoking the name of God, just to justify an unnecessary spectacle.”De La Espriella’s predecessor Gustavo Petro tweeted: “This is called turning death into a trophy – something only soulless people can do … The soulless find it easy to kill for the sake of killing.”De La Espriella hit back at his critics, posting: “Forgiving terrorists is God’s business. Sending them to meet him – if that’s where they’re headed – is the president’s job.”De La Espriella’s post captured the bellicose and performative political zeitgeist sweeping theAmericas, where a growing number of rightwing populists are seeking to woo voters with promises of ferocious, TikTokable crackdowns on crime.The genre has been pioneered by El Salvador’s authoritarian president, Nayib Bukele, with slick videos of hisnotorious mega-prison, and Donald Trump, who has repeatedly published footage showing allegeddrug boats being blitzedin the Caribbean and Pacific.Ahead of Brazil’s October elections, several candidates are promising lethal attacks on the drug traffickers who control Rio de Janeiro’s favelas. “We’re going to stain the ground red with the blood of these lowlifes,” one candidate, Renan Santos, said recently, promising “a bloodbath” if he won power.Flávio Bolsonaro, the main challenger to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has vowed to wage war on “narco-terrorists”, although he and close allies have themselves been accused of having ties to organised crime. “Criminals will be taken out of circulation, either standing up or lying down,” Bolsonaro has said.In Rio, Felipe Curi, a former police chief running for congress, has posted AI-generated videos depicting him shooting armed men in the favelas. Campaignpropagandafeatures his image superimposed on pictures of the corpses of some of the 122 people killed during the city’sdeadliest ever police raids. “I arrest crooks,” Curi boasts in one video, “and I neutralise them if they react.”Explore more on these topicsColombiaAmericasThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Unimaginable grief’: Iranian town left devastated after US strike on wedding  | Iran | The Guardian
description: Mourning turns to anger as residents of Kuhestak say Baloch communities are being placed in path of conflict
Author: Deepa Parent
Headline: Mourning turns to anger as residents of Kuhestak say Baloch communities are being placed in path of conflict
Content: Mourners gather around the coffin of one of the victims of a reported US strike on a wedding party in Kuhestak, Iran. At least four people were killed and 60 injured.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMourners gather around the coffin of one of the victims of a reported US strike on a wedding party in Kuhestak, Iran. At least four people were killed and 60 injured.Photograph: Getty ImagesIran‘Unimaginable grief’: Iranian town left devastated after US strike on weddingMourning turns to anger as residents of Kuhestak say Baloch communities are being placed in path of conflictDeepa ParentFri 4 Sep 2026 06.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople in Kuhestak, a predominantly Baloch city in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, are mourning after astrike on a weddingkilled at least four people, including a child, and injured more than 60, according to local authorities.The blast hit at around 9.30pm on 1 September, turning a night of celebration into one of devastation for the small coastal community, which is on the strait of Hormuz.In the aftermath, videos shared on social media by friends and relatives of the wedding couple showed rubble, flower garlands and decorations scattered among debris and bloodied shoes.Asked about the strike on Thursday, the US vice-president, JD Vance, said the US would never target civilians in combat but that “sometimes things happen”, adding that he was sceptical of Iran’s reports. He did not acknowledge that the killings had been confirmed by an internationally recognised humanitarian body.According to Iranian state media and people interviewed by the Guardian, the house belonged to Ali Mallahi, a local fisher who was celebrating his daughter’s wedding.In a video published by state media, Mallahi stood amid the rubble of what had been his home and said he was saddened by the attack but thanked God that the casualties weren’t higher.Residents said the celebrations had only just begun. Friends and family were waiting for the bride and groom, and many guests had yet to arrive for the henna ceremony.View image in fullscreenA woman weeps during a mass funeral in Kuhestak.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/APWitnesses who spoke to the Guardian said the attack had left residents angry and in deep mourning.Ahmad*, a local barber who witnessed the aftermath, said the entire neighbourhood had been devastated by what happened.“I don’t really have words. Ours is a small town and we all know each other and are brothers. We are all mourning. I visited the house and the media won’t report it, but it wasn’t just one house. Many houses around the site have been damaged and neighbours were directly hit by sharp objects when the explosions happened”.“We are not carrying coffins on our shoulders, we are carrying the dark future that awaits us all in the south,” Ahmad added.Moein Arjomand, director of the Balochistan Human Rights Documentation Network, said local responders were facing growing obstacles investigating the explosion.“Our team has been facing a lot of difficulties due to the internet [shutdown] and witnesses and relatives telling us they were banned from speaking to any foreign rights groups and foreign media,” he said. “I tried arranging interviews for international media with the relatives, but they are worried about the consequences and I couldn’t arrange them.”Despite the internet restrictions and apparent warnings against speaking out, locals and relatives of the couple have continued sharing videos documenting the aftermath on social media.In one video, Yaqoob Mallahi, a relative of the bride, shared footage of his seven-year-old son, Sepehr, lying in a hospital bed with his head bandaged.View image in fullscreenDamaged buildings after the strike on a wedding party. Asked whether the US was responsible, JD Vance, the US vice-president, said ‘sometimes things happen’.Photograph: Getty ImagesArjomand said at least six victims remained in serious condition in the intensive care unit of a hospital in Minab, about 18 miles (30km) away.“Bandar-e-Kuhestak is a small town and the local clinic is not equipped to handle casualties like this, so the injured were taken to the hospital in Minab,” Arjomand said.A video posted by local activists showed the family of Amir Mohammad Karimi, the four-year-old victim, mourning over his body as he was buried on Thursday.A 16-year-old boy, Mohammad Mallahi, was also killed by shrapnel while riding his motorbike nearby. Videos of his funeral, attended by dozens of local people, were shared online.“We have another funeral on Friday, this time a young woman, and we will all be there,” Ahmad said. “I can only pray to Allah that no more of our blood is shed and our injured come back home from the hospital.”Ahmad was referring to Asiyeh Molainejad, 22, another relative of the bride who was declared dead on Thursday.Beyond the immediate grief, the attack deepened a sense among some Baloch residents and activists that civilian deaths in their communities receive comparatively little attention.View image in fullscreenMen hold red roses as they attend a mass funeral  in Kuhestak.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/APFarzin Kadkhodaei, a human rights activist from Balochistan, said the circumstances of the deaths had made the loss particularly painful.“The human cost is devastating. These were Baloch civilians gathered for a wedding, and losing their lives in the middle of what should have been a joyful occasion is heartbreaking,” he said. “Their families are now left with unimaginable grief, while the injured have to live with the physical and emotional consequences.”Chakar Baloch, 35, a fisher, said the attack reinforced a feeling among local people that civilians living along the Makran coast were being placed in the path of conflicts over which they had little control. “My overall view is that we are the victims. We are the people who live along the Makran coast and for years we’ve gone out to sea, struggled to earn our bread, and just wanted to stay alive,” he said.When asked if local people were demanding answers about the strike, a Baloch resident of Sirik said western media did not understand their plight. “Who do you want me to demand answers from?” she said. “From the US that has attacked us in this war? Or the regime which has brought this war to our doorsteps? Tell me from whom I can demand and I will answer your questions.”Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Populism poses serious challenge to independent central banks, Bailey says | Bank of England | The Guardian
description: Bank of England governor says central bankers must explain decisions or risk being seen as ‘unrepresentative elite’
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Bank of England governor says central bankers must explain decisions or risk being seen as ‘unrepresentative elite’
Content: Insulating the Bank from politics had made it better able to fulfil its role of maintaining the ‘monetary and financial conditions that make sustained prosperity possible’, Andrew Bailey said.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenInsulating the Bank from politics had made it better able to fulfil its role of maintaining the ‘monetary and financial conditions that make sustained prosperity possible’, Andrew Bailey said.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPABank of EnglandPopulism poses serious challenge to independent central banks, Bailey saysBank of England governor says central bankers must explain decisions or risk being seen as ‘unrepresentative elite’Heather StewartFri 4 Sep 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 14.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe governor of theBank of Englandhas said the rise of populist politicians presents a serious challenge to independent central banks.As Nigel Farage’s Reform UKgathered for its annual conferencein Birmingham, Andrew Bailey said central bankers must be prepared to explain their decisions to the public or risk being attacked as an “unrepresentative elite”.Bailey was speaking at a conference at the London School ofEconomics. In an address peppered with historical references, from Alexander Hamilton to Thomas Hobbes, he said central banks must not take their “legitimacy for granted”.Bailey said populist parties’ pitch for power “often rests on the claim that a particular political movement alone represents the authentic will of the people. Any institution seen to get in the way becomes an unrepresentative elite standing between the people and their will, and thus an obstacle to popular sovereignty.”He added: “This is a serious challenge. We have developed systems of government (in the broadest sense of this term) in which legitimacy rests in the plurality of society, not in the preferences of any single group within it.”Populist parties, especially of the right, have been riding high on both sides of the Atlantic in recent years. Attacking traditional institutions – including central banks – often forms part of their platform.Farage has previously suggested he wouldlike to replace Baileyif Reform comes to power. In the US, Donald Trump repeatedly launched tirades against the former Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell over the central bank’s failure to cut interest rates.View image in fullscreenNigel Farage has previously suggested he would like to replace Andrew Bailey if Reform came to powerPhotograph: Thomas Krych/APBailey was among the international central bankers who signed a joint statement defending Powell against Trump’s criticism and stressing the importance of independence.The Bank of England was made independent by the Labour government in 1997, handing decisions on interest rates from the chancellor to a nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC) chaired by the governor.After the 2008 global financial crisis, which led to a significant proportion of the UK banking sector being nationalised at taxpayer expense, the Bank of England was given additional responsibilities for financial stability.Bailey said on Friday that insulating the Bank from politics had made it better able to fulfil its role of maintaining “the monetary and financial conditions that make sustained prosperity possible”.He said: “Institutions that exercise significant authority should expect scrutiny. Such scrutiny is a sign of democratic health. But we should also recognise what is at stake.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe MPC is split over how to respond to rising inflation as a result of the Iran war.
