Bailey has stressed that in a weak jobs market, he does not yet see signs of the “second-round effects” that can embed inflation throughout the economy as workers bid up their wages to keep pace.The MPCvoted to keep interest rates on holdat 3.75% at its last meeting in July. But three members voted for a rate rise, including the Bank’s hawkish chief economist, Huw Pill, whoused a speech on Thursdayto reiterate that in the face of rising inflation, Threadneedle Street should act “clearly, promptly and decisively”.At its next policy meeting on 17 September, the Bank is also expected to announce whether it will press ahead with its controversial policy of quantitative tightening. The Bank has been progressively selling off the bonds it acquired though the emergency policy of quantitative easing – creating money to help stave off recession.Critics, from Reform to leftwing thinktanks, have argued that these sales tend to drive up the yield, or interest rate, on government bonds, which move in the opposite direction to prices. That makes it more expensive for the government to borrow, a pressing issue at a time offebrile bond markets.Bailey will appear before MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee next week to explain his thinking.Explore more on these topicsBank of EnglandAndrew BaileyReform UKEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: How will bond market turmoil affect your mortgage, pension and savings in UK? | Bonds | The Guardian
description: Sell-off raises concerns of higher borrowing costs for households. Here’s what it could mean
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Sell-off raises concerns of higher borrowing costs for households. Here’s what it could mean
Content: Home loans are vulnerable to uncertainty in the financial markets.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHome loans are vulnerable to uncertainty in the financial markets.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesBondsExplainerHow will bond market turmoil affect your mortgage, pension and savings in UK?Sell-off raises concerns of higher borrowing costs for households. Here’s what it could meanZoe WoodandRupert JonesFri 4 Sep 2026 03.56 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThebond market sell-offhas sparked fresh fears of higher borrowing costs for UK households. We look at what the turmoil in financial markets could mean for your mortgage, pension and savings.Cost and choice of home loansExperts think that the pricing on new fixed-rate mortgages could start rising again as a result of the bond market turbulence. That is because lenders get funding for home loans from the money markets.Fixed mortgage rates are largely influenced by “swap rates” rather than the Bank of England base rate. These wholesale rates can react rapidly to changing inflation expectations and financial market uncertainty.The spike in UK government borrowing costs has caused swap rates to jump sharply over the past week.On Thursday, Coventry Building Society was the first notable player to move, warning brokers of its intention to hike fixed-rate deals for new and existing borrowers from Monday. Other lenders are expected to reprice their mortgages in the coming days.This is Groundhog Day for borrowers, many of whom will feel as if they have been down this road before. But so far, the reaction from lenders has not been on the same scale as in the wake of theLiz Truss government’s disastrous mini budget in 2022, or even this spring, when the outbreak of war in the Middle East causedan economic storm.But Rachel Springall, a finance expert at the data provider Moneyfacts, says the jump in swap rates does “not bode well for borrowers, as lenders use swap rates as a key influence to reprice their fixed-rate mortgages”.With the majority of existing mortgage holders on a fixed-rate product, the current situation is a bigger deal if you need to remortgage soon or are trying to buy your first home. On Thursday, the average rate on a new two-year fixed-rate mortgage stood at 5.59%, while the typical rate on a five-year deal was 5.63%. In April these rates were at 5.9% and 5.78% respectively.David Stirling, an independent financial adviser at Belfast-based Mint Wealth, said: “Coventry won’t be the last, as lenders watch each other like hawks, and once one has repriced, the rest follow within a week purely to avoid being the cheapest rate on the market and getting swamped with applications they can’t fund at that price.“My advice to anyone looking to remortgage or purchase right now is simple: lock in your offer of a rate now.”PensionsIf you are aged under 50 and are saving into a pension, it is unlikely any of your money will be in bonds. It is instead probably going into stock market-based investments, and any short-term fall in the FTSE (it actually rose on Thursday after falling back earlier in the week) could be good news as you will get more shares for your money.If you are retired, you may have investments in government bonds (gilts) for the income they provide. These investors do not need to worry about changing prices and yields as they will still get the fixed cash payment – called a coupon – as expected. But the current turmoil is potentially a bigger worry for workers approaching retirement.It is very common for more of members’ pension pots to be moved into gilts as their retirement date gets nearer. If this is the case, and it is now time to sell those gilts, the investor could get less than they bargained for.“If you are closer to retirement, it’s worth reviewing what you are invested in, especially if you’re in a ‘lifestyling’ strategy that moves you out of equities into bonds the closer you get to retirement,” said Helen Morrissey, head of retirement analysis at the investment platform Hargreaves Lansdown.For younger workers with perhaps several decades to go until retirement, keep calm and carry on is not a bad message. You will be invested in a pension for a long time and will experience several periods of market turbulence, says Morrissey. “Taking kneejerk actions, such as changing investments or stopping contributions, can potentially make things worse by locking in losses.”Bear in mind that higher gilt yields should result in lower annuity prices, so anyone planning to trade in their pension for an annuity may not be worse off. (An annuity is a product that converts an individual’s pension pot into a regular, guaranteed income for the rest of their life).Annuity rates are usually closely linked to 15-year gilt yields, which have this week hit 28-year highs.Andrew King, pension technical specialist at Evelyn Partners, says a healthy 65-year-old buying a single-life level annuity with a five-year guarantee can now secure just over £8,000 of income with £100,000 in pension savings, compared with well below £5,000 a decade ago.SavingsThe most important thing for savings rates is the Bank of England base rate and where the markets expect it to be in the future.The money markets expect the Bank of England to leave interest rates on hold at 3.75% at its next policy decision on 17 September. However, the City expects one rate rise before the end of the year, and two more hikes in 2027.At the moment, the top-paying easy-access savings accounts pay about 4.5% interest or thereabouts.Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at the investment platform AJ Bell, says the current market gyrations tend to be good news for savings deals as banks usually react by increasing their interest rates. “This particularly affects fixed rate accounts, so we tend to see them move first and fastest.”“The market is already impressively competitive at the moment, so the reaction may not be particularly dramatic. However, the movements in gilt yields have actually pushed the best five-year fixed [savings] rate over 5%, and we are likely to keep seeing rates nudge up from here.”Explore more on these topicsBondsMortgagesPensionsSavings ratesInvestmentsSavingsexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Volkswagen to cut further 50,000 jobs as it ends row with union over revival plan | Volkswagen (VW) | The Guardian
description: Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructure
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructure
Content: Protesters against proposed VW job cuts outside the company’s Zwickau factory in Saxony in July.Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters against proposed VW job cuts outside the company’s Zwickau factory in Saxony in July.Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty ImagesVolkswagen (VW)Volkswagen to cut further 50,000 jobs as it ends row with union over revival planUnder-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructurePatrick Daly,Lisa O’CarrollandMark SweneyFri 4 Sep 2026 05.43 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe car company Volkswagen has approved controversial plans to shed 100,000 jobs in a battle for survival as it faces fierce competition from Chinese rivals.After the latest round of talks this week, the company announced a further 50,000 job cuts and agreed a staggered end to current production at four German plants: Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and the Audi site in Neckarsulm between 2031 to 2034. There are no specific plans beyond that.Theagreementcame as a surprise after a meeting of shareholders, unions, and state representatives on the supervisory board in what was seen as a considerable test for the German carmaker’s chief executive, Oliver Blume.He had gone as far as to arrange an emergency meeting if the package was rejected in preparation for a potential showdown with unions.“This is a strong signal for the future,” said Blume, who now has a mandate for what the company previously called the “most strategically profound transformation programme” in the history of the VW group.He was booed last month by staff during a tour of the company’s headquarters in Wolfsburg, northernGermany, as part of a dialogue about the need to address the company’s financial challenges.IG Metall, the company’s biggest staff union and representative on the supervisory board, said concessions had been made on both sides to avert “a dangerous escalation of the conflict”.Chief among these was a stay of execution for four plants threatened with closure in exchange for an agreement on staff reductions. The deal includes a sweeping cost-cutting plan to cut a further 50,000 positions by 2030, bringing the total job losses in the pipeline to 100,000.“Concrete solutions must now be developed for all locations … we expect the board to now do its homework based on the compromise reached and deliver results promptly,” said Christiane Benner, the first chair of IG Metall, and Daniela Cavallo , the chair of the General and Group Works Councils of VW.Blume said the company would be investing “a three-figure billion sum” in the next few years “to make our iconic brands even more attractive, stronger and more competitive”.View image in fullscreenOliver Blume, the chief executive of VW, was booed last month by staff during a tour of the company’s headquarters in Wolfsburg.Photograph: Liesa Johannssen/ReutersThe supervisory board acknowledged that there was over capacity inEuropeto produce 500,000 vehicles for which there was no market.Plans to turn a plant in Osnabrück into a defence factory were abandoned this year after objections from Qatari investors.The number of car models VW group produces, which includes the Bentley and Audi brands, will be slashed by half. “It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities,” VW said.The total of 100,000 cuts will be the largest restructuring ever carried out in the global automotive industry and amounts to about 15% of the carmaker’s employees.Volkswagen employs more than 650,000 people across all its brands, which also includes Skoda, Seat, Porsche, Cupra and Lamborghini.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnalysts at Deutsche Bank said the approval of the restructuring plan was a “fundamental breakthrough” and proved wrong investors who believed the carmaker to be “unfixable”.“The unanimous approval is, in our view, a fundamental breakthrough and a much-better-than feared outcome,” the analysts said in a note to investors on Friday.“To be clear [the] agreement does not solve Volkswagen’s challenges overnight. Execution remains key. The market debate was never about whether Volkswagen had challenges. It was about whether those challenges could realistically be addressed within Volkswagen’s complex governance structure. [The] agreement does not end that debate, but it provides the strongest evidence yet that the answer may be yes.”VW has facedincreasing pressure from Chinese competition in Europe, decreasing sales in China and hefty US tariffs. Even before that, it was struggling for years with falling profits and overproduction in Europe.Analysts at Citi called the deal a “brave and rational plan”, adding that it was a “realistic decision for all concerned”.“Given VW’s German plant competitiveness and lack of global revenue opportunities, VW simply had no other choice,” the analysts said. “Given VW’s supervisory board structure, this illustrates also the responsibility the workers council has taken for ensuring the long-term survivability of the VW core business in Europe.”Shares in VW rose 8% in early trading on Friday.The tough market in China has also hit other carmakers. BMW, for example, cut its profit guidance for this year because of the disruption caused by the Iran war and the company’s struggles in the Chinese market.Explore more on these topicsVolkswagen (VW)Automotive industryManufacturing sectorGermanyEuropeJob lossesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Health-tracking smart ring maker Oura to list on US stock market | Technology sector | The Guardian
description: Valuation above $11bn expected for firm whose fans include Prince Harry, Jennifer Aniston and Kim Kardashian
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Valuation above $11bn expected for firm whose fans include Prince Harry, Jennifer Aniston and Kim Kardashian
Content: The American tennis player Taylor Fritz wears an Oura Ring during this month’s US Open.Photograph: Sarah Stier/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe American tennis player Taylor Fritz wears an Oura Ring during this month’s US Open.Photograph: Sarah Stier/Getty ImagesTechnology sectorHealth-tracking smart ring maker Oura to list on US stock marketValuation above $11bn expected for firm whose fans include Prince Harry, Jennifer Aniston and Kim KardashianMark SweneyFri 4 Sep 2026 05.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFans of Oura are accustomed to using its trendy smart rings to fastidiously monitor their health but now investors are preparing to track a new metric: its share price.The company’s filing to list imminently on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York was made public on Thursday.Founded in Finland in 2013 and now headquartered in San Francisco, Oura makes smart rings that have become amust-have itemamong wellbeing enthusiasts, with celebrity fans and ambassadors including Jennifer Aniston, Prince Harry, Kim Kardashian and the Spider-Man actor Tom Holland.The ring allows users to track metrics including heart rate, temperature and sleep quality.View image in fullscreenPrince Harry wears a Oura ring while on a beach in Australia with his wife, Meghan, in 2018.Photograph: Scott Barbour/Getty ImagesThe rings sell for $349 to $499 (about £258-£360), with subscribers then paying $5.99 a month or $69.99 a year for full access to data on their health. The US filing showed a thriving, high-margin business, which brought in $1.21bn in revenue in the nine months to 30 June, up 74% year on year.Oura made its first profit only last year, notching up $1.6m, and followed that with a $60.8m profit in the nine months to the end of June. It is aiming to list on the Nasdaq as soon as later this month, with a valuation expected well above the $11bn it was valued at when it raised $900m last year.Of particular appeal to investors is the after-sales subscription business, which the company said has reached a base of 5 million users, doubling year on year, and which had gross margins of 89% in the nine months to 30 June.Membership revenue came to $240.5m over the nine months, up 121% year over year and hardware sales accounted for about 80% of revenues. Subscribers opened the app more than 3.5 times a day on average, the company said. The former Friends star Aniston has said publicly she is “addicted” to checking her Oura stats.View image in fullscreenThe Oura Ring 5, which went on sale in May.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSubscribers are skewed towards women, who account for 72%, and 42% of the total base are aged 30 to 45, with 31% under 29.Oura said it has collected almost 42bn hours of biometric physiological data from users across 50 metrics.The latest product, Oura Ring 5, went on sale in May at $399 and is 40%smaller than its predecessor. It records heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature and motion, tracking more than 50 metrics involved in sleep, activity, readiness, stress, resilience, heart and women’s health.Explore more on these topicsTechnology sectorIPOsStock marketsFinlandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Why not try to be the best in the world, just for the fun of it?’ Art Garfunkel on a rich, restless life – and reconciling with Paul Simon | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: He taught maths and walked across Europe, trying to leave his demons behind. As he goes back on tour aged 84, the folk-pop legend explains how he came back to singing
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: He taught maths and walked across Europe, trying to leave his demons behind. As he goes back on tour aged 84, the folk-pop legend explains how he came back to singing
Content: ‘You reach this high point of pure joy’ … Art Garfunkel.Photograph: Troy Jensen/Contour by Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘You reach this high point of pure joy’ … Art Garfunkel.Photograph: Troy Jensen/Contour by Getty ImagesPop and rockInterview‘Why not try to be the best in the world, just for the fun of it?’ Art Garfunkel on a rich, restless life – and reconciling with Paul SimonDave SimpsonHe taught maths and walked across Europe, trying to leave his demons behind. As he goes back on tour aged 84, the folk-pop legend explains how he came back to singingFri 4 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsArt Garfunkelis keen to point out, “I am a singer – there, use that as the title of your article” – but he was neverjusta singer. “I’ve been an actor. I am a writer,” he continues. “I’ve walked across countries, taken freighters across oceans. I’ve read the dictionary. I’ve read two books a month for 60 years: Darwin, Herodotus, Balzac, Proust, Tolstoy. I’ve taught maths. I have two great kids and I’m a great father, but it always does seem to come back to the singing.”Which is understandable, given that in Simon and Garfunkel (with songwriter Paul Simon) he sold more albums than any other pop duo in history. Garfunkel’s oft-called “angelic” tones powered classic chart-toppers including The Sound of Silence and Bridge Over Troubled Water, and he became a successful solo artist. However, until a year ago, he was hardly singing at all and hadn’t toured since 2019. “I found myself lying on a pillow in a dream state, thinking about the meaning of being alive,” he reveals. “What is my day? What am I supposed to do with myself?”He realised that the two things that had made him happiest were meeting his wife, Kathryn, in 1985, and singing, especially the point during a show when “it becomes effortless, and you reach this high point of pure joy”. So a friend who worked at an art gallery north of New York suggested he might try singing and telling stories to an audience of 60 people, and see how it felt. “It worked,” Garfunkel enthuses. “After three nights, I thought: I’ll get back to doing this.”View image in fullscreenArt Garfunkel with his wife, Kathryn, in Hollywood, 2008.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty Images for AFIThus, at the age of 84, the polymath is back on the road – he comes to the UK in October – and “singing much more than I have done in two decades”. He made the album Father and Son with his son Art Jr two years ago, and even sang Bridge Over Troubled Water shortly before speaking to me. “In the bathtub at the hotel,” he chuckles, “because there’s reverb, and I sang it as good as I ever sang it in the 60s.”His most recent release is Authorship, a track on a compilation created by the technology companyEleven Labs, which has created an AI model for generating “original compositions” in collaboration with artists. Authorship features a spoken excerpt from Garfunkel’s 2017 memoirWhat Is It All But Luminousover an AI-generated piano backing. Not that he seems to have had too much involvement with the technology. “I think my new management like my writing and wanted to do something with it,” he explains. “I’m the only person left in America without a computer or the internet.”So we’re speaking on a crackly phone line, which gives his dulcet tones an otherworldly quality as he talks about the first time he sang, aged five, in 1946. “I used to sing along to the radio,” he remembers. “Then one day I walked out of kindergarten – the stairwell had lovely reverb – and started singing to myself. I had goosebumps because my voice was pretty. I was having more fun than I’d ever known and I realised: I’m a singer.”Garfunkel gave his first public performance in a talent show in fourth grade. Simon, who was in his year at the same school, was watching. The pair soon became “really tight, laughing all the time”, recording their harmonies in the Garfunkels’ basement in Queens, New York, on a wire recorder. “This is before tape,” he says. “We’d record our harmonies and then put another layer on top. We were very young, but learning to produce.”View image in fullscreenThe early years … Art (left) and Paul in about 1957.Photograph: PictureLux/Hollywood Archive/AlamyAged 16, in 1957, they had their first hit as Tom & Jerry with Hey, Schoolgirl and performed on American Bandstand. “We followed Jerry Lee Lewis, who did Great Balls of Fire,” Garfunkel remembers. “He was a wild man. I remember going to the urinal before going on. One of the dancers asked: ‘Who have we got on today?’ And someone else said: ‘Some jerks calling themselves Tom & Jerry.’ I just stood there, saying nothing.”Tom & Jerry didn’t last and Garfunkel returned to education, where he attained a BA and an MA, and worked towards a mathematics PhD: “I’d have had to go into the army if I hadn’t stayed in college, so that’s what kept me.” However, Simon and Garfunkel had the last laugh when The Sound of Silence rocketed up the charts. “I watched it climb from No 91. When it got to No 5, I called Paul” – who was touring English folk clubs at the time. “‘Paul, the thing we’ve wanted all our lives has happened. You gotta come home.’ The next week we jumped to No 1.”It was the first of many chart-toppers. By his own admission, Garfunkel found the 1960s “wonderful”. He remembers “social evenings with each of the four Beatles. George Harrison took me to his castle, which had a four-storey papier-mache model of the Alps in the back yard. I think the person he’d bought the place from was a bit eccentric.” Garfunkel was also “a workaholic who lived in the studio”, where he laid down an astonishing 300 takes for Bridge Over Troubled Water. “Whatever you do, you gotta do it well,” he shrugs. “Why not try to be the best in the world, just for the fun of it?”View image in fullscreenThe ‘wonderful’ 1960s … Simon (right) and Garfunkel playing live.Photograph: Bernard Gotfryd/Science History Images/AlamyHowever, by 1970 the duo hit troubled waters themselves. In his memoir, Garfunkel admits that he never really forgave Simon for making a single without him in 1958. Conversely, in Alex Gibney’s 2023 documentaryIn Restless Dreams, Simon confesses to a “Freudian trauma” about Garfunkel’s vocals: “My mother said: ‘You have a good voice, but Arthur has a fine voice.’”In 1967, the pair had been working on the soundtrack to The Graduate – which included Mrs Robinson, their second US No 1 – when the film’s director, Mike Nichols, drove up to Garfunkel’s lodgings in a limo, handed him a script for the satirical war comedy Catch-22 and said: “Read this. I see you as an actor, as Lt Nately.”“I’d never acted and was so nervous,” Garfunkel recalls. “But Mike was maybe the most interesting man I ever met and made me feel good, like: ‘At last someone is treating me like the bright fellow I am.’ I was worried about how it would work out socially with all these big, real actors: Alan Arkin, Orson Welles, Jon Voight. But I flew down to Mexico and did a good enough job for Mike to want me to star in his next film, Carnal Knowledge [1971], with Jack Nicholson and Candice Bergen. Jack’s terrific. We still speak from time to time.”View image in fullscreenWith Candice Bergen in Carnal Knowledge.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyAs with music, Garfunkel gave acting “my full concentration, really quite extreme at times”, but Simon grew frustrated with his absences and the duo never recorded together again. After the split Garfunkel became, of all things, a maths teacher.“I wanted to drop out and be normal and live life,” he explains. So he moved to small-town Litchfield, Connecticut, “and I got a job. On the first day of class I told them: I know you all think you’re meeting a celebrity, and I can relate to that, but I want to teach you geometry.” He made a pact that on the last day of term they could ask him anything they wanted, but admits: “I wasn’t very good [at teaching maths]. I know my stuff but I couldn’t motivate them. I didn’t know how to get people to care.”So after six months he left, soon afterwards marrying his first wife, Linda Grossman (they divorced in 1975). He spent the rest of the 70s acting and making “three nice albums”: Angel Clare, Breakaway and Watermark. He notched up the UK’s bestselling single of 1979 with Bright Eyes, the theme from the film Watership Down, but the decade ended with a bump.View image in fullscreenIn Bad Timing.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockThe same year, he starred in Bad Timing, director Nic Roeg’s dark psychological drama in which a troubled young woman kills herself. While Garfunkel was filming in Vienna, Laurie Bird, his partner since 1975 and who is on two of his album covers, took a fatal overdose of Valium in his apartment in New York, aged 25. Even now, 47 years later, he finds this difficult to talk about. “Do I have to revisit it, Dave? My worst year?” But eventually he says: “I don’t know how to describe her other than that she was quiet, into herself, beautiful. I was in love with her. It took me years to get over that.”For several years, he walked away from music – literally. In 1982, in Japan, he “hatched the idea of leaving my old life behind and walking across the country. I stashed my stuff and started walking. Twelve miles later I looked for a place to stay. It’s crazy, but I was walking something off.”He subsequently walked across the US and Europe, beginning “across Central Park and my alma mater, Columbia University, and up the George Washington Bridge. In Europe, I started in western Ireland at Shannon airport, crossed Ireland in eight days and took a ferry to south-west Wales. I passed Dylan Thomas’s house, came to England and then crossed the Channel.” He chuckles. “You know, I’m the son of a travelling salesman. He sold winter coats.”In the Appalachian mountains, Garfunkel sang to cows: “They heard me singing, and just walked down the hill.” Wonderfully, when he was stopped by cops in Wyoming, he recited Thomas Jefferson’s Declaration of Independence. “They rolled down the window,” he says. “You know that tone of voice they have: ‘What are you doing, sir?’ I found myself saying: ‘Every American has the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. So I am in the pursuit of happiness, officer.’ And they said: ‘Uh, we were just checking, sir. You get strange folk out here.’” Eventually, he walked off the dark clouds: he married Kathryn Cermak, a model, singer and actor, in 1988 and returned to music.The 1981 New York concert.There have been sporadic reunions with Simon – most famously at New York’s Central Park in 1981, where they sang to half a million people – but they last toured in 2010 and then stopped speaking. Then, in 2025, Garfunkel revealed that they’d had dinner, hugs, he’d ended up in tears and they’d made plans to meet again.“That was about a year ago and I haven’t seen him in the last year,” he says. But he is curious to hear about his old friend’s recent tour: “Did he speak much? How many musicians did he have?” However, he doesn’t wish to discuss the seemingly unlikely prospect of another tour together. “You know what I think is more interesting?Walkingfrom western Ireland to Istanbul,” he says. “But yes, we got together. Who knows what the future will bring? Life is a surprise. I don’t know what happens next month. I don’t know what happens after we die.”‘I never said I was going to retire ...’ Paul Simon on disability, drive and the mystery behind his greatest songsRead moreGarfunkel frets about big issues, such as global heating, the human race and those in power. “I don’t like America’s position at all,” he says. “I’m not aboard, and I’m thinking of leaving the country, frankly. It’s real that the planet is getting warmer, that the water’s rising, that so many people are starving. When Donald Trump took over Venezuela, are those the new rules? Just take over a country and run it? It’s shocking, and you think: how on earth are we gonna change the presidency? But Trump won’t last for ever. So we’ve got to hope.”Meanwhile, two months short of his 85th birthday, he still has things he’d love to do: “Sail around the world, see India and China, sing in South America.” But, he says pointedly, “I don’t wanna go into space.”“I hope I come across as philosophical,” he concludes. “I’m a thinker, a book reader, a walker, but mostly I’m a singer. I’m always very nervous, behind the curtain. Then I walk out and hear the applause and I flip from fear to confidence right there.”Art Garfunkel’sWhat a Wonderful World tourbegins on 1 October in Los Angeles and goes to the UK, France, Germany and JapanExplore more on these topicsPop and rockArt GarfunkelPaul SimonWalkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Story review – thrilling drama of race, truth and the pursuit of headlines | Stage | The Guardian
description: Letitia Wright plays the ambitious young reporter seduced into cutting corners with contentious reporting in a brilliantly kinetic production
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Letitia Wright plays the ambitious young reporter seduced into cutting corners with contentious reporting in a brilliantly kinetic production
Content: Tough cookie … Letitia Wright  in The Story at the National Theatre.Photograph: Feruza AfewerkiView image in fullscreenTough cookie … Letitia Wright  in The Story at the National Theatre.Photograph: Feruza AfewerkiStageReviewThe Story review – thrilling drama of race, truth and the pursuit of headlinesNational Theatre, LondonLetitia Wright plays the ambitious young reporter seduced into cutting corners with contentious reporting in a brilliantly kinetic productionArifa AkbarFri 4 Sep 2026 07.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 07.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTracey Scott Wilson’s play follows in the fine tradition of the fast-paced newsroom drama, beginning with the cold-blooded murder of a white schoolteacher by an unknown Black assailant as his pregnant wife watches. Cue moral panic, rolling news and the entry of a fiery young journalist determined to solve the case.That is where the Watergate-style investigative blueprint warps because Yvonne (Letitia Wright, of Black Panther fame) is no simple hero in pursuit of truth. She is an ambitious Black woman, assigned to an enclave of a newspaper reserved for Black journalists. Her imperious editor, Pat (Lorraine Toussaint) is after positive news stories on the Black community while her white editor boyfriend, Jeff (Wilf Scolding) promises her a bigger gig if she proves herself worthy.Neither Yvonne nor the press come out of it with their integrity intact: she lies and invents (her character is based on Janet Cooke, a journalist for the Washington Post discredited for making up a Pulitzer prize-winning story in 1981), while the media is shown to be motivated by editorialising and reshaping the facts to suit their needs.View image in fullscreenCaught in the crosshairs of race politics … The Story at the National Theatre.Photograph: Feruza AfewerkiThe story beneath The Story is one of media spin and fake news caught in the crosshairs of racial politics. Yvonne and Pat represent opposite ends of the same spectrum: the former wants to be seen as a “reporter rather than a Black reporter” while Pat speaks of the lack of diversity in the newsroom and the historical struggle to be represented authentically.The themes to Wilson’s 2003 play could not be more apposite today, particularly in relation to the barrage of press coverage in the lead up to the death of Black academic, Jason Arday. Director Clint Dyer’s production has great forward momentum and kinetic pace, with a slick performance from Wright as a tough cookie with no cracks in her armour. It is highly theatrical with fast cuts between scenes and a doubling of action so you see dual scenarios playing out at once, especially in the thrillingly adrenalised first half, although it is so fast and complex at times that you lose the thread.‘There’s always a fresh fury’: Tracey Scott Wilson on Black America and her play about a fraudulent journalistRead moreThe decision to keep the drama in its original timeframe means there is no mention of social media or the internet – the prevailing means of news consumption today. So recurring scenes of reporters brandishing microphones and headline news projected on to the enormous backdrop of the Olivier auditorium feels old-school. Yet it keeps its relevance within this period setting; what emerges as the story beneath The Story now is not so much a revelation on the nature of news journalism, but a dual portrait of Black female ambition. You see through both Yvonne and Pat how this is stymied or made smaller by huge, patriarchal forces. Between these two characters and Black news reporter, Neil (Ashley Thomas), who is intent on revealing the truth, a complicated exploration of authenticity arises – who has the right to represent the Black community, and who to critique it?The second half of the production is more strained as it slows its pace to draw out its messages, and you wish for more texture in all the characters. Yet it is excitingly staged theatre with an ambition as bold as Yvonne’s, seeking to say so much about women, race and the media that still feels incredibly timely.A final, haunting, scene cuts away from the news frenzy to draw our eye to what is happening on the street, beyond the spin and the chasm between the two. That gulf – between reality and its representation in a woefully (or wilfully) out-of-touch press – is surely the story of today.At theNational Theatre, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreLetitia WrightNational TheatreRacereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Basics of Philosophy review – Paul Schrader back to his cool, cruel best | Movies | The Guardian
description: When a figure from his past turns up to a family funeral, a college professor faces an agonising dilemma that makes him question his own morality and whether he can change
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: When a figure from his past turns up to a family funeral, a college professor faces an agonising dilemma that makes him question his own morality and whether he can change
Content: Growing malaise … Jack Huston as John Jorrisen and Sofia Boutella as Rebecca Richards in The Basics of Philosophy.Photograph: Noora FilmsView image in fullscreenGrowing malaise … Jack Huston as John Jorrisen and Sofia Boutella as Rebecca Richards in The Basics of Philosophy.Photograph: Noora FilmsMoviesReviewThe Basics of Philosophy review – Paul Schrader back to his cool, cruel bestVenice film festivalWhen a figure from his past turns up to a family funeral, a college professor faces an agonising dilemma that makes him question his own morality and whether he can changePeter BradshawFri 4 Sep 2026 15.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePaul Schrader is back with his most successful picture sinceFirst Reformedin 2018. It’s a stereotypical Schrader study of masculinity in some ways, about a man agonising over moral choice and ethical behaviour while – as so often in Schrader’s movies – reading and writing philosophy in an austerely furnished room. And yet there is nothing abstract about the issue he faces here. The film moves with a determined suspenseful tread, everything hangs together right up to the queasy final shot and Schrader flavours everything with a streak of melodrama and even a kind of gaunt black comedy. Karl Glusman’s cameo is surely the weirdest thing at Venice this year.The scene is a blandly prestigious liberal arts college, presided over by a genial, grey-haired dean, played in cameo byRichard Gere. John Jorrisen, played by Jack Huston, is the star of the philosophy faculty, enjoying agreeable mid-career success, working on a book about Spinoza. He is cordially resigned to bored students showing up to his “The Basics Of Philosophy” course for what they assume will be easy extra credit, attracted by that undemanding word “basic”.But it is John’s task to show them that philosophy is basic, that all philosophy is philosophy 101, that the challenge is to recognise the primacy of moral simplicity over specious supposed difficulty. He is particularly exercised by the question of whether anyone can really change.John is also dating a stylish colleague in the psychology department called Prof Rebecca Richards (Sofia Boutella), a single mum to whose 14-year-old son he shows every sign of becoming a conscientious stepdad. Yet something is wrong. John keeps taking Rebecca to unrelaxed formal restaurants and failing to stay over afterwards because he supposedly needs to work on his book on Spinoza – who is a stern moral presence. A mutinous student demanding a higher grade sneers that she knows “what he did”. Is she bluffing?John’s growing malaise comes to a crisis with the death of his wealthy, overbearing father Melvyn (Bill Pullman) who abandoned his own dreams of studying philosophy in favour of a lucrative business career. He is seen in flashbacks which are in a soft black-and-white, perhaps partly to make it easier for Huston to play John’s much younger self: the late-teen-early-20s version.John is astonished to see among the funeral congregation a certain man, Miguel Vasque (Daniel Zovatto), who is the key to his unease – and those concerned about spoilers should look away now. Miguel was the son of Melvyn’s gardener and when Miguel was the age Rebecca’s son is now, John sexually abused him; his father had to pay for Miguel’s private school and college education to cover it up – or, at all events, to make amends, as no one would believe Miguel’s word against Melvyn’s if it came to a police action.John is horrified by the agonised dilemma which this has brought up. He has naturally convinced himself over the years that he is not of course a child abuser or a paedophile. But Schrader shows us how he may need to triangulate this self-image with the reality of his ongoing fear by telling himself that he simply does not fit into a heterosexual template; perhaps his sexual identity needs to be rethought, though this would of course be on a consenting legal basis. But is even that real?And all the time he is digging himself deeper into a nightmare by reconnecting with Miguel. Could it be that he can make a grotesque kind of peace with his secret past by imagining himself in love with him? And he starts to ponder the awful final question that change might be impossible; if he is an abuser who will at some stage inevitably revert to type, then should he consider Socrates’ attitude to taking your own life, the coward’s or hero’s way out?Schrader takes all this at a cool, cruel pace: the film has the thriller’s beady-eyed focus on what’s going to happen next, along with a dramatic sense of the perplexed inner man, the man who complacently thinks of himself as a philosopher, an intellectual who is detached from sordid faults, who has insight and perspective. And so he may indeed have, but they may be entirely irrelevant to his destiny. Schrader takes us to an elegant, indirectly macabre finale; this is a very disquieting portrait.The Basics of Philosophy screened at theVenice film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsPaul SchraderRichard GereVenice film festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Gal Gadot’s Wonder Woman was one of DC’s few successes. It’s a mystery why she got the chop | Movies | The Guardian
description: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s regime had good reasons to ditch Ben Affleck’s Batman and Henry Cavill’s Superman. Other choices have been much harder to fathom
Author: Ben Child
Headline: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s regime had good reasons to ditch Ben Affleck’s Batman and Henry Cavill’s Superman. Other choices have been much harder to fathom
Content: ‘It was not handled elegantly’ … Gal Gadot as Wonder Woman.Photograph: Warner Bros/AllstarView image in fullscreen‘It was not handled elegantly’ … Gal Gadot as Wonder Woman.Photograph: Warner Bros/AllstarWeek in geekMoviesGal Gadot’s Wonder Woman was one of DC’s few successes. It’s a mystery why she got the chopBen ChildJames Gunn and Peter Safran’s regime had good reasons to ditch Ben Affleck’s Batman and Henry Cavill’s Superman. Other choices have been much harder to fathomFri 4 Sep 2026 06.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.17 EDTShareThere was never going to be a completely painless way to break up the old DC gang. Warner Bros’ DC Extended Universe probably needed to be ruthlessly ripped apart in order to create space for James Gunn and Peter Safran’s brand-new DCU. We almost certainly did need a clean break from the likes of Ben Affleck (Batman) andHenry Cavill(Superman), if only to persuade audiences that this really was a proper reboot. The question, as Gal Gadot may have been pondering this week, is quite why some of the old universe’s supporting players were smuggled safely into the new continuity while others were left sprawling amid the ruins.Speaking on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, Gadot, who starred in two solo Wonder Woman movies for director Patty Jenkins, revealed that nobody at DC Studios ever formally told her she had been dropped. One minute, Gadot says, she was being assured by Gunn and Safran that they would develop a third instalment with her; the next, she was looking on in mounting alarm as the entire infrastructure of the previous DC continuum was blown to smithereens. “They were like, ‘We’re going to develop it with you, the third one,’” she said. “But I saw the way everybody else was handled, right? And I, you know – the Henry [Cavill] situation was unfortunate. I was in the middle of that. The Henry situation was not handled elegantly, to say the least. Same with Patty – it was not handled elegantly.”Gadot, most would accept, has a bit of a point here, even ifsources close to DC Studios told Variety at the time that no outright promises were ever made to her.Cavill was brought back by the previous DC regime for a cameo at the end of the 2022 Dwayne Johnson superhero vehicle Black Adam,and even encouraged to announce publicly that he was Superman again–only for Gunn and Safran to tell him a few weeks later that they were recasting the role. Jenkins submitted a treatment for Wonder Woman 3 that the studio rejected as the new DCU took shape, and was later forced to denyreports that she had walked away from the film. Against such backdrops, it is hardly surprising that Gadot decided the writing was on the wall and moved on to other projects, though she says she holds no grudges. “I feel like we’re all adults and it’s all good,” she told the podcast. “It’s not even about them. They are there and they’re there to do what they believe in.”View image in fullscreenSuperhero sundown … Henry Cavill, Gal Gadot and Ben Affleck in Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice.Photograph: Warner Bros./AllstarThere’s plenty to explore here, not least because Gadot’s Wonder Woman was one of the few major box office and critical successes of Warner Bros’ previous DC universe. If there was room in the new DCU for John Cena’s Peacemaker, who survived into a second small-screen season in the new reality, and evenXolo Maridueña’s Blue Beetle (who will now appear in the upcoming Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow), why was there no room for the actor who anchored 2017’s Wonder Woman, the old regime’s best-received film? The simple answer is that DC’s holy trinity – Cavill’s Superman, Affleck’s Batman and Gadot’s Wonder Woman – were the central faces of the old Zack Snyder-led DC-verse. Discarding all three announced that Gunn was building his own world, while retaining peripheral figures did not threaten the brave new reality.Gadot may also have suffered due to the lukewarm reception for 2020’sWonder Woman1984, although its box-office performance is almost meaningless because it opened during the pandemic and simultaneously appeared on HBO Max. In any case, one average sequel should not have made Gadot herself completely unusable, and probably wouldn’t have done if the entire DC cinematic universe had not been fed into an industrial woodchipper around her.There is also the continuity problem. Keeping the old universe’s Wonder Woman while replacing its Batman and Superman might have confused audiences and made the new universe feel like a patch-up job. And yet Peacemaker season two has already demonstrated Gunn’s willingness to rewrite inconvenient history and expect everyone to get on with it. The studio chief has left the door open for Margot Robbie to return as Harley Quinn, though there are currently few signs she will.What then really is the difference between the two DC realities, other than that the new one offers the convenient opportunity to dispense with certain superheroes that were not immediately connecting with audiences? Is David Corenswet’s Kal-El really so much more intriguing than Cavill’s? Will forthcoming Batman film The Brave and the Bold finally give us a version of the Dark Knight who can turn up alongside other superheroes without spending the first hour trying to murder one of them and the second demanding to know his mother’s first name?For now, the only iron law of Gunn’s new universe appears to be that continuity is infinitely flexible provided you were already in his contacts book when the apocalypse arrived. Gadot, despite fronting one of the old regime’s few unqualified triumphs, apparently was not. That may be a perfectly defensible way to repopulate a superhero franchise; it is rather harder to explain why nobody thought to tell Wonder Woman.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekWonder WomanGal GadotDC ComicsJames GunnHenry CavillPatty JenkinscommentShareReuse this content

title: 15/18 A Place to Heal review – heartfelt docu-realist study of a French teen psychiatric facility | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Cédric Kahn combines compassion with coolly detailed forensic scrutiny in this genre-challenging film which puts a troubled love triangle at the centre of the story
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Director Cédric Kahn combines compassion with coolly detailed forensic scrutiny in this genre-challenging film which puts a troubled love triangle at the centre of the story
Content: Institutional drama … 15/18 A Place to Heal.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalView image in fullscreenInstitutional drama … 15/18 A Place to Heal.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalMoviesReview15/18 A Place to Heal review – heartfelt docu-realist study of a French teen psychiatric facilityVenice film festivalDirector Cédric Kahn combines compassion with coolly detailed forensic scrutiny in this genre-challenging film which puts a troubled love triangle at the centre of the storyPeter BradshawFri 4 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVeteran French director Cédric Kahn brings us a movie in a classic French vein: a docu-realist study of an institution, in this case a state psychiatric facility for teenagers between 15 and 18; with scenes in treatment suites, recreation areas, dorms and interview rooms. It’s something to compare perhaps withLaurent Cantet’s The Class, orNicolas Philibert’s On the Adamant, or Canadian film-makerDenis Côte’s That Kind of Summer.Kahn’s film is powerful and committed, although sometimes the acting comes close to shouty improv youth theatre. The tone is of course one of compassion, combined with coolly detailed forensic scrutiny, though audiences might be intrigued at Kahn’s use of Purcell’s Funeral Sentences on the soundtrack, music notably used by Kubrick in A Clockwork Orange, a film in which delinquent youth are treated more roughly. Kahn himself plays one of the senior medical staff, part of the gallery of authority figures – doctors, nurses, orderlies, therapists and a nervous intern – who are almost as affected by the institutional drama as the troubled young people themselves.There is a diverse ensemble cast of patients here, but a love-triangle of three is at the centre. Lucia (Malou Khebizi) is a defiantly sexualised wild child with a clear issue of abuse in her background, permanently at war with her mum, involved in chaotic abuse for which the term “sex work” is not entirely accurate. She immediately takes a shine to Enzo (Kenji Peyran), in custody for stabbing a social worker, and he in turn forms an intense though probably predatory and self-serving relationship with abuse survivor Eloïse (Zoé Monpart), who is quiet, and more likely to be submissively grateful for his repeated declarations of love, and to be a more reliable partner for his planned escape attempt.This attempt effectively forms the final act of the film, taking it out of the enclosed institutional location in a way that challenges the genre, and which gives Eloïse a powerful final moment. It’s a heartfelt and high-minded film.15/18 A Place to Heal screened at theVenice film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFranceVenice film festivalEuropeFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Men calling us woke need our show more than most’: punks Piss on finding strength in visceral confrontations of sexual violence | Music | The Guardian
description: The Vancouver band earned a cult fandom for their uncompromising gigs. As they ready their brutal debut album, they discuss subverting audience expectations and the nightly toll of excavating trauma onstage
Author: Emma Garland
Headline: The Vancouver band earned a cult fandom for their uncompromising gigs. As they ready their brutal debut album, they discuss subverting audience expectations and the nightly toll of excavating trauma onstage
Content: Taylor Zantingh of Piss performing at Hit the City festival in Eindhoven, August 2026.Photograph: Kirsten HeskampView image in fullscreenTaylor Zantingh of Piss performing at Hit the City festival in Eindhoven, August 2026.Photograph: Kirsten HeskampMusicInterview‘Men calling us woke need our show more than most’: punks Piss on finding strength in visceral confrontations of sexual violenceEmma GarlandThe Vancouver band earned a cult fandom for their uncompromising gigs. As they ready their brutal debut album, they discuss subverting audience expectations and the nightly toll of excavating trauma onstageFri 4 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’d be hard pressed to find a band with fewer airs and graces than Piss. First, there’s the unavoidable matter of their name, which they style in all caps, no nonsense; a word that scans as vulgar and combative but also somewhat facetious when displayed on their merch in loopy cursive, sometimes decorated with bows. The Vancouver quartet’s music is a merciless cyclone of hardcore, poetry, sound collage and performance art that revolves entirely around singer Taylor Zantingh’s experiences with sexual violence.On stage at Eindhoven’s Hit the City festival in late August, the band greets the stacked crowd with a trigger warning before drummer Garreth Roberts, bassist Gavin Moya and guitarist Tyler Paterson launch into pulverising fits of noise-punk, broken up by audio samples of children laughing and feminist writer Andrea Dworkin talking about pornography. Zantingh hurls herself around, clutching at her stomach and flinging her pigtails before winding down to a nervous, twitching standstill. The intense set is finely tuned to present a narrative of gender-based violence not as entertainment, but as lived experience. They play it exactly the same every night, and have done for the last two years.Piss: Time Loop at Hot Slit – video“I think a lot of people are like, ‘I’m going to see a band called Piss, this is going to be craaaazy!’ And it’s crazy in a different way than they expect,” Zantingh tells me before the show, over chamomile tea. “People come for one thing and then they’re forced to listen to me for half an hour.”The buzz around Piss usually takes bands of their ilk several album cycles to drum up, yet they have released next to no music: a four-track demo on Bandcamp, a few professionally recorded sets and radio appearances on YouTube and some viral fan-filmed clips. Since forming in 2024, their reputation has grown through their live performance, prompting Sub Pop to sign them; their debut album You Made Me / Skin on Linen arrives in October.Recorded over a handful of days in winter 2024, the album was made to mirror the Piss live experience as closely as possible. Throughout, you’ll hear Zantingh gasp for breath or struggle to get words out, lacing traumatic recollections with disturbing imagery of “fingers sewn in the wrong places” and kids “practising blowjobs on glue sticks”. The songs combine Bikini Kill and Fugazi’s DIY approach to “making personal things political” with the uranium-heavy sonics of Chat Pile or Swans. Paterson, who is primarily responsible for shaping the instrumentals, likens his process to scoring a film. “The influences came from a lot of places to uphold the narrative that Tay is weaving,” he says. “The feelings and intention come first, and the sound comes after.”View image in fullscreen‘I have never known how long I’m gonna be able to physically and emotionally do this’ … Piss.Photograph: PRThe way Piss use music, performance art and other voices is fundamental, Zantingh says, because the subject matter is too “monstrous” to be described in words alone. Placing her voice in chorus with a range of others – activists, philosophers, militants, psychoanalysts and transgressive literary figures, including French philosopher Manon Garcia speaking about the trial of Gisèle Pelicot – leaves things open to interpretation. “One reason I feel so strong when I’m on stage is because I’ve found the right way to communicate it, versus trying to confess these things in a literal sense. When I’m telling [the audience] how these events still hurt me today, and they’re watching me hurt myself in real time, they’re watching that injury in a very tangible way.”While Piss try to provide as many access points to their music as possible, it is, at every level, deeply uncomfortable. When I describe their twisted instrumentals as “gross”, drummer Garreth Roberts says, “That’s Ty’s [guitarist Tyler Paterson] favourite word!” Zantingh’s voice jolts unpredictably from soft spoken-word to chainsaw shriek. All lyrics and samples (which they consider a reading list) are also prominently subtitled in their videos, for accessibility and so the subject matter doesn’t take a backseat to the visuals. “I’d like to be able to print them out so people can have them at the shows – almost like a little programme, like when you go to church,” says Zantingh.‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reuniteRead moreIn the queue before the gig, a number of men were sniggering about the name Piss. I wonder whether the band feel their music is always met on its own terms. Zantingh recalls seeing two older men at the front of a festival set. “When I was doing the trigger warning they were like, ‘Woke!’ and then walked off,” she says with a weary smile. “The irony is they probably need that show more than most people there, but I accepted early on that the people I want to play the set for might not be the people I can have the most impact on.”On the precipice of a debut album release through one of the most revered independent labels, Piss find themselves contemplating an uncertain future. “Part of the reason we waited so long to release the record is because I don’t know, and I have never known, how long I’m gonna be able to physically and emotionally do this,” Zantingh states plainly. “I spend my life trying to turn my pain into something beautiful,” she screams on I Wanted to Be a Singer.“The foundation of Piss is built on my suffering,” she continues. “We literally cannot exist the way that we exist if you remove that.” That might be unsustainable in the long run, but for now, she says, “it’s exactly what it’s supposed to be”.You Made Me / Skin on Linen is released via Sub Pop on 30 October. Pissare atBrighton Psych fest on 4 September, End of the Road on 6 September and then tour North America and EuropeInformation and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsMusicPunkRape and sexual assaultPerformance artinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Berlin Philharmonic/ Petrenko/ Hadelich review – flawless musical beauty | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: In their second Proms concert, the Berlin Phil brought Beethoven’s Violin Concerto (with Augustin Hadelich the virtuosic and breathtaking soloist), and a detailed and compelling take on Scriabin’s third symphony
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: In their second Proms concert, the Berlin Phil brought Beethoven’s Violin Concerto (with Augustin Hadelich the virtuosic and breathtaking soloist), and a detailed and compelling take on Scriabin’s third symphony
Content: A masterclass … Augustin Hadelich and Kirill Petrenko with the Berlin Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenA masterclass … Augustin Hadelich and Kirill Petrenko with the Berlin Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewBerlin Philharmonic/ Petrenko/ Hadelich review – flawless musical beautyRoyal Albert Hall, LondonIn theirsecond Proms concert, the Berlin Phil brought Beethoven’s Violin Concerto (with Augustin Hadelich the virtuosic and breathtaking soloist), and a detailed and compelling take on Scriabin’s third symphonyFlora WillsonFri 4 Sep 2026 07.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s the clarity that hits you first. The soft thuds of timpani that open Beethoven’s Violin Concerto landed from the back of the stage with the immediacy of taps on the shoulder, quietly urgent. The string sound was simultaneously luminous and translucent. Pizzicato bass-lines were shaped as if the main event and bubbled upwards through the rest of the texture. You’ll hear orchestral playing to match this on high-end studio recordings, of course, where the entire process can be geared to achieving such crystalline polish. And the BBC’s sound engineers can work miracles in real time on radio broadcasts of Proms performances. But to produce such lucidity live – particularly in the Royal Albert Hall, with its monumental bathroom acoustic – is another thing entirely.View image in fullscreenAngular and majestic … Kirill Petrenko conducts the Berlin Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouFor that, you need an orchestra ofthe calibre of the Berlin Philharmonicunder its chief conductorKirill Petrenko. But violinistAugustin Hadelichalso served up his own brand of astonishingly flawless musical beauty as the soloist in the Beethoven. In the first movement, his rising octaves appeared to float out of the orchestra, his bowing inaudible – the kind of violin-playing, in fact, that appears to defy the laws of physics. The slow movement was a masterclass in bel canto, the third a biting, bouncing romp as both Hadelich and Petrenko pushed gleefully through the rondo theme. The apparent ease of Hadelich’s virtuosity – all his energy seemingly focused on phrasing and dialogue with the orchestra – was nothing short of breathtaking.Where Beethoven’s Violin Concerto is conventional programming by any measure,Scriabin’s Symphony No 3 in C minor, “The Divine Poem”, doesn’t get out much. That’s probably just as well, given its tendency towards late-Romantic colour saturation – the musical equivalent to eating an entire box of champagne truffles in a single sitting. But once again Petrenko eked out the details: glistening shimmers of violin, razor-edged tuba, bright flares of horn cutting through the sensuous haze. His movements were by turn angular and majestic – a touch of waltzing here, a vigorous jab towards a soloist there – as he conjured with sound, before finally allowing the vast orchestra to bloom into a magnificent closing apotheosis.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicBerlin PhilharmonicKirill PetrenkoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the churning darkness of Barcelona producer Nueen and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Nacho Pezzati’s new album Swerved taps into the moody ambience of the UK north-west underground, ratcheting a tangible and thrilling sense of unease
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Nacho Pezzati’s new album Swerved taps into the moody ambience of the UK north-west underground, ratcheting a tangible and thrilling sense of unease
Content: Tangible unease … Nueen.Photograph: PR IMAGEView image in fullscreenTangible unease … Nueen.Photograph: PR IMAGEAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the churning darkness of Barcelona producer Nueen and the week’s best new tracksNacho Pezzati’s new album Swerved taps into the moody ambience of the UK north-west underground, ratcheting a tangible and thrilling sense of uneaseHugh Morris,Ben Beaumont-ThomasandLaura SnapesFri 4 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromBarcelona, SpainRecommend if you likeSpace Afrika, Shackleton, PurelinkUp nextSwerved out nowSwerved, by Barcelona-based producer Nueen (Nacho Pezzati) is a bassy, moody, darkly ambient album that travels through R&B, drill, cloud rap and dub without any obvious changes in its grey-black weather. But this is slowly churning music, on the brink of rot. By the 10th track, Copicat, the unease is tangible; after a slow, agonising ratcheting build of fanbelt hi-hats, the album’s only drop arrives with the weight and power of a cloudburst. It’s thrilling.Swerved follows Nueen’s 2024 Hyperdub debutYou Said You’d Hold My Hand Through the Firewith rapper Iceboy Violet, and fans of thenorth-west undergroundwill recognise many of its themes. On Atmosphere Is My Style, a drawling Loraine James touches on the dislocation and confusion heard in Rainy Miller’s music. Two tracks featuring Manchester’s RenzNiro hit swaggering and confessional notes, similar to his recent album No Weapon Shall Prosper, and Swerved as a whole feels bathed in the humid ambience of Space Afrika. Nueen synthesises all these approaches, and takes stock, before breaking new ground.The paths he heads down are guided by impressive vocal features. Cloud rapper XzavierStone pulls the sound in an Auto-Tune R&B direction on two tracks, and Baltimore singer Dawuna moans through the hot’n’heavy highlight Shm, which sounds like a lost D’Angelo joint. (Check out the latter’s Bandcamp-onlyAfrican Family Laptop Musickfor more.) Nueen breaks into new territories for an established sound without disrupting an album’s subtle cycles: through heating, simmering, and cooling.Hugh MorrisThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenCandid … Ceebo (right) and Blanco.Photograph: Finn HarneyCeebo x Blanco – Gets Like DatTwo British MCs on rich, riveting form: the flows are as energised as a club track but the beat is mournful, as each of them gets candid about the fear and paranoia of failing in the rap game.BBTKali Malone – Heavy With FruitThe heady Colorado composer jettisoned theory for intuitive emotion on her new album, recorded on the organ at Bach’s resting place. Heavy With Fruit flickers like embers, the dying molten core of something.LSKiko Mizuhara– Feelin’ WeeJohn Carroll Kirby lays down puckish, squelchy keys under the Japanese-American actor-model’s cheeky song about love’s elusiveness, synths pinging to life like daisies bursting at warp-speed through the earth.LSCorto.alto – Noblehill (ft Jacob Alon)Mercury-nominated for his 2024 debut, the Scottish jazz artist closes out his new album Some Small Fortune with this extraordinarily deft ballad, Jacob Alon swooping through a pattering rainshower of strings, piano and breakbeats.BBTDiiv – Kid“Everyone is a little kid,” Zachary Cole Smith whispers on fragile shoegaze that – despite producer AG Cook’s synth toybox puckering away in the background – invites a typically cosy, satisfying kind of wallowing.LSPiss – Time Loop at Hot SlitThe uncompromisingly named Vancouver punk band make good on signing to Sub Pop, singer Taylor Zantingh howling “women don’t come” over thrashing guitar and drums that viscerally stumble under their own weight.LSSilvan Strauss – That’s Who?!? (Fast Barista)Fans of Squarepusher’s electro-skronk opus Music is Rotted One Note will thrill to the Hamburg drummer’s joyous new LP Sprinting, with acid jazz played with the breakneck pace and brittle funk of Chicago footwork.BBTSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sairie: Beneath the Spreading Tree review – exquisite 70s-inflected folk heralds a move into autumn’s chill | Folk music | The Guardian
description: Singer Emma Morton brings an indie-girl chorister’s brightness to this captivating debut album, on songs with hints of darkness that sound ages-old
Author: Jude Rogers
Headline: Singer Emma Morton brings an indie-girl chorister’s brightness to this captivating debut album, on songs with hints of darkness that sound ages-old
Content: ‘An intensity that gradually reveals its perils’ … L to r, Andy Thomas, Emma Morton and Jon Griffin of Sairie.View image in fullscreen‘An intensity that gradually reveals its perils’ … L to r, Andy Thomas, Emma Morton and Jon Griffin of Sairie.Folk album of the monthFolk musicReviewSairie: Beneath the Spreading Tree review – exquisite 70s-inflected folk heralds a move into autumn’s chill(Self-released)Singer Emma Morton brings an indie-girl chorister’s brightness to this captivating debut album, on songs with hints of darkness that sound ages-oldJude RogersFri 4 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 08.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSairie’s debut album begins at this transitional time of year, its glistening psych-folk easing us out of the summer heat towards the coming darkness. In its Pentangle-like opener Song for the Winter, birds’ voices “climb higher”, hills “glow brighter” and waves “call out louder”, and the songs that follow are similarly saturated with colour and energy, creating an intensity that gradually reveals its perils.View image in fullscreenSairie: Beneath the Spreading Tree album coverBased in Brighton, Sairie have released a stack of captivating singles and EPs since 2019, spanning folk, originals and modern covers; one great double A-side released earlier in the year had singer Emma Morton master the ballad May Carol and Françoise Hardy’s Tous Les Garçons et Les Filles. Her tone hooks an 80s indie-pop choirgirl-like brightness in tracks like Harder Than It Seemed, bolstered by Andy Thomas’s meaty bass, and makes you realise this style might have its roots in folk singers such as Maddy Pryor. It also channels the twisted beauty of Josephine Foster on songs such as The Breeze on the Meadow, where a wasp-like drone from Jon Griffin’s harmonium, Maria Marzaioli’s violin and Alice Eldridge’s cello amplifies hints of strangeness.The band’s musicianship is fantastic throughout, as are their shivery arrangements, which present like finely wrought 1970s curios while swerving pastiche. Alongside dense, rich takes on traditional songs like The Gairdner and the title track (its story echoing the execution tale of the Scottish ballad, Gilderoy), they also exquisitely mix sweetness and doom. The Griffin-led Three Knots sounds like a sugar-coated duet before its descent into the depths, while The Green Light captures the giddy minutiae of falling in love when you’re young (“What makes your heart beat fast and slow?”) before a subtle but devastating shift in its story. Sairie’s new songs have ancient balladry tightly coiled in their DNA, arriving like they’ve lived rich, long lives already.Also out this monthIn Thin Air (Hudson)is the third outing bySpell Songs,the ongoing project betweenwriter Robert Macfarlane, artist Jackie Morris, and a premier league of folk musicians, including Karine Polwart, Kris Drever and Seckou Keita. Exploring the splendours and mysteries of birdlife as populations decline, the album’s highlights include An Calman (The Dove), a patchwork of double bass, soft drums, coos and breaths, and Flight, a euphoric ode to global migrations. Soundings Folk Club founderElanor Moss’s debut album, The Knife, the Needle (Merge), is an arresting, shivery collection, softly orchestrated with guitars, strings and horns, creating an autumnal sound world recalling the work of Bridget St John and Vashti Bunyan. Scottish rabble-rousersShooglenifty’s 10th album, Stamina Island (Shoogle), is quite different: a rock-fuelled celebration of community ownership, spirit and survival on the Isle of Eigg, featuring Ciarán Ryan going full Slash from Guns N’ Roses, shredding jigs on the banjo.Explore more on these topicsFolk musicFolk album of the monthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The best recent poetry – review roundup | Books | The Guardian
description: Fetch by Colin Bramwell; Girling by Eve Esfandiari-Denney; The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber by Jay Gao; Belling the Leopard by Clementine Ewokolo Burnley; The Matter by Padraig Regan
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fetch by Colin Bramwell; Girling by Eve Esfandiari-Denney; The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber by Jay Gao; Belling the Leopard by Clementine Ewokolo Burnley; The Matter by Padraig Regan
Content: Jay Gao’s poems embody a tree’s form in The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber.Photograph: Jackyenjoyphotography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJay Gao’s poems embody a tree’s form in The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber.Photograph: Jackyenjoyphotography/Getty ImagesPoetry roundupBooksReviewThe best recent poetry – review roundupFetch by Colin Bramwell;  Girling by Eve Esfandiari-Denney; The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber by Jay Gao; Belling the Leopard by Clementine Ewokolo Burnley; The Matter by Padraig ReganOluwaseun OlayiwolaFri 4 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenFetchby Colin Bramwell(And Other Stories, £14.99)Bramwell’s translation of Fernando Pessoa’s work into Scots won him considerable recognition: it took the Oxford Weidenfeld Translation prize and the Highland Book Prize. Between source and target language, there is always a gap; the translator endeavours within that gap to identify meaning and intention, and that is the difficult work of translation. Fetch, Bramwell’s own debut collection, lyrically thematises this gap in the poet-human’s condition: “I’m an instrument for something else / a digital piano that if you opened it up / you wouldn’t understand the wiring.” Fetch (in Celtic folklore, a doppelganger) is by turns solemnly tender, comically worldly, literarily devout. Here you’ll find deep engagement with Russian poets such as Osip Mandelstam and AnnaAkhmatova, poems that fuse Scots and English, alongside filial memories and premonitions of fatherhood. “Death is certain, but back then I was too young for that shit.” For a debut, Bramwell’s poetics convey an uncanny sense of wisdom, patience and, eventually, peace.View image in fullscreenGirlingby Eve Esfandiari-Denney(Fitzcarraldo, £12.99)Before theme and subject, there is the pure, iridescent beauty of Esfandiari-Denney’s sentences; a singular voice that is alluring and sensuous, pleasurable to follow to whichever subject the poet chooses. The subjects are girlhood-cum-womanhood, the line between debilitating illness and delusional wellness (“thank god / you invested / in lion’s mane”), the flickering concept of free will for a species so programmed by genes: “I have wondered to what extent my cancer diagnosis is my mother’s, or my grandmother’s cell mutation, before my own … I look up from a cigarette mid-sentence…” The collection hybridises recognisable prose forms: the essay, the diary, the text message, the anecdote. These are interspliced with short-lined lyric poems that startle because of the bubbly voice from which they come: “I hope it’s ok to die. I can / become something / like actualised metaphor.” The magic of this collection is that it is never highfalutin, finding a way to make an ending like “DJ are you listening did you read to the end will you blow my voice a kiss” powerfully funny and moving.View image in fullscreenThe Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumberby Jay Gao(Carcanet, £12.99)“This is how the buried live. Poetry”. The title of this collection alone will illuminate what kind of poet Gao is: insistent, sprawling, and conceptually daring. The poems in this collection are notspokenby a tree, but rather embody a tree’s form, each line like a budding leaf, simultaneously discreet, and genetically preordained by the bark from which it sprouts: “Mustering diction in the interest of the non-human”; “On the horizon, a filthy war dog shakes her remaindered vernal atoms free”; or, one of my favourite lines, “You wanted the intimacy of two words who shared a sound to unsecure that wild”. Every couple of pages there are “splinters”, single words with ultra-long dashes that could grammatically and sonically replace a word in the preceding line: “A splinter of duration lodged inside times’ ruche, awaiting salvage …” is followed by a page-long em-dash before the word “selvedge”. Gao joins the ranks of poets such as CD Wright and Lyn Hejinian: not for the faint of heart, but an endless well of brilliance and deep feeling if one can undergo their clause-by-clause compressive inventions.View image in fullscreenBelling the Leopardby Clementine Ewokolo Burnley(Bloodaxe, £14)There’s an imaginative heaviness to Belling the Leopard, so composed of the proper names of people, places and things that each poem feels like a constructed miniature: “Liberated Africans, Jamaicans, and English / missionaries lived side by side in eight / corrugated iron shelters shipped / from Clarence.” The forced migrations and enslavement of colonialism create a latticework of place across the collection, which is Burnley’s primary structuring principle. Between the Caribbean, western Africa and western Europe, Burnley describes the intimate violence and domestic and cultural fallout of their comingling histories: “All the flights from Africa used to transit through a European capital city. Ethiopian Airlines no longer touches down in the nine hours it takes to fly from Turtle Island to Togo. Sometimes the border agencies use commercial flights for deportations.” At times, this debut collection feels overwritten, certain narratives more like onslaughts of information and impression with little effect. It is at its best when memory and lyric fuse, where the line between recounting and reshaping blurs: “We rub each other raw in the same spots / and if you’re starting to lose / arguments, I notice I no longer need to win.” There’s much to admire here.View image in fullscreenThe Matterby Padraig Regan(Carcanet, £12.99)Regan’s sophomore collection echoes the structure of their first: lyric poem sequences with a long(ish) essay splitting up the sections. Here, they intensify their engagements with the material world, “chiefly animals, minerals and vegetables”. Lines from the poem A Venus Flower Basket sum up the stylistic changes Regan has made, from parsed syntactical lines to more high-octane fragmentations: “Drowned Arachne! / except: what it spins / it is. & who wouldn’t / want to wear their bones / on the outside / if they could sparkle”. Elsewhere, the poet addresses Gogotte, a naturally occurring “concretion of very fine, very pure sands”, primarily found in France. Gogotte has a way of looking like finely sculpted ceramic work, allowing the poet to drift from the geological to musings on the body’s evanescence, gay saunas, and language itself: “I am a poet, Gogotte: I spend my life trying to come up with verbal structures commensurate with the unstructurable mess of being-in-the world.” Though the collection can feel unevenly motley in some aspects, Regan has a knack for startling detail and lush description, as in the poem A Belemnite: “An off white seam runs jagged / down its length / like an injury; // its surface is a register / of glances & impacts / against whose grain I read the // long, posthumous biography”. This voice can be spellbinding.Explore more on these topicsBooksPoetry roundupPoetryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Golden Hours by Louisa Young review – this continuation of the Cazalet Chronicles is a total delight | Fiction | The Guardian
