description: Elizabeth Jane Howard’s niece has picked up the thread of her much-loved family saga series, taking the story into the 1960s
Author: Ella Risbridger
Headline: Elizabeth Jane Howard’s niece has picked up the thread of her much-loved family saga series, taking the story into the 1960s
Content: Frank clarity … Louisa Young.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFrank clarity … Louisa Young.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Golden Hours by Louisa Young review – this continuation of the Cazalet Chronicles is a total delightElizabeth Jane Howard’s niece has picked up the thread of her much-loved family saga series, taking the story into the 1960sElla RisbridgerFri 4 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 03.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElizabeth Jane Howard’s beloved family saga the Cazalet Chronicles spans three decades in the life of the upper-middle-class Cazalet family. The first four books, written in the 1990s, run from a bucolic prewar 1937 to a bruising 1947, while the fifth, 2013’sAll Change, skips ahead, sitting lonely in 1956. The books are exquisite doll’s houses of feeling and object: both period detail and eternal emotion are rendered precisely and vigorously in Howard’s lovely prose. “Panoramic, expansive, intriguing as social history and generous in their storytelling,”Hilary Mantel wrote in the Guardian. The enormous cast of characters – four late-Victorian siblings, their parents, their children and partners and ex-partners and servants and friends and lovers and enemies and cars and houses – sprawl deliciously over the years. The family fortunes rise and fall. Marriages fail; deaths occur; babies are born; people fall in love. Things change; things stay the same.Written a decade after the death of the original author, The Golden Hours by Louisa Young adds a sixth to this quintet. As with all Cazalet novels, to describe the plot would be impossible: it is simply that many people, whom we have come to love over the course of the previous novels, live their lives, now in the early 1960s.Polly, first encountered as a serious and beautiful child almost 30 years earlier, is now the chatelaine of a falling-down country house. This house has replaced the original Home Place as the centre of family life: it’s Christmas, and the siblings gather at Polly’s home. The next generation take up much of the narrative, picking up the loose threads that Howard set down: what will Louisedowith her life? Can Clary and Zoe and Rupert and Archiereallyall live together in one house? And what, for the love of God, is going to happen to Neville?double quotation markIt achieves a startling mimicry of Howard’s voice that drew even this sceptical reader along for the rideThere is little more controversial, to the serious reader, than a so-called “continuation novel”: a sequel written by somebody else, with little or no input from the original creator (who is mostly, in such cases, beyond the grave). Can it be done?Shouldit be done? Can creations continue to live without their creators? Mortality need not present a challenge to those readers who wish for more (or publishers who wish for more of their money). Eoin Colfer was given the keys to the Hitchhiker’s Guide; Sophie Hannah became Poirot’s posthumous puppeteer. Sebastian Faulks, an overachiever, has been both BondandJeeves. Young has two significant advantages: first, this is her 16th book; second, Howard was Young’s own personal beloved “Aunt Jane”. There is something pleasing about a family saga being continued by the author’s own family – but the stakes are, perhaps, even higher.Happily, however, Young’s gamble has paid off: The Golden Hours is a total delight. It is not the flawless The Light Years, but it is not remotely out of place in the series. It takes a couple of chapters to settle fully into Howard’s voice, but achieves a startling mimicry that drew even this sceptical reader along for the ride. Young tackles several of the trickier problems posed by Howard – Neville again! – without shying away from her frank clarity into the human mind. If the dialogue is occasionally a little more contrived than Howard’s, and a few of the forays into big-picture thinking verge on the glib (“the problem wasn’t what you were, it was how people treated you for what you were”), then these things can be forgiven for the sheer pleasure of coming home.And if things are different, well, then things are different. Any series written over 23 years will trace not just the ways the characters change, but the ways the writer changed in the writing. There is, perhaps, a greater gulf between The Light Years and Howard’s final novel All Change than between All Change and The Golden Hours; or even between The Light Years and The Golden Hours.Writers change, as indeed people change; and yet humanity stays the same. And this is, in many ways, the great unifying theme of this book and the series as a whole. “Are things exactly the same, or mortally different?” muses one-time chauffeur Tonbridge. Another character quotes the Oracle at Delphi: “Know Thyselfon one end;Things Changeon the other …”And this, perhaps, is the secret to writing a great continuation – or, in fact, the secret to writing anything. Things change; know thyself. Young understands both. A new generation takes up the mantle of the next generation of Cazalets: with a seventh and eighth volume promised, long may it continue.The Golden Hours by Louisa Young is published by Mantle (£20). title: Kevin Powers: ‘I was ready to abandon Infinite Jest a thousand times’ | Books | The Guardian
description: The American author on falling in love with The Great Gatsby, being inspired by Dylan Thomas – and the memoir of a canoe trip in Texas he comes back to
Author: Kevin Powers
Headline: The American author on falling in love with The Great Gatsby, being inspired by Dylan Thomas – and the memoir of a canoe trip in Texas he comes back to
Content: ‘If I’m honest, I think I read to be made uncomfortable’ … Kevin Powers.Photograph: Buffalo Sojka StudioView image in fullscreen‘If I’m honest, I think I read to be made uncomfortable’ … Kevin Powers.Photograph: Buffalo Sojka StudioThe books of my lifeBooksKevin Powers: ‘I was ready to abandon Infinite Jest a thousand times’The American author on falling in love with The Great Gatsby, being inspired by Dylan Thomas – and the memoir of a canoe trip in Texas he comes back toKevin PowersFri 4 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryThe deaths of Old Dan and Little Ann in Wilson Rawls’s Where the Red Fern Grows were etched into my being as a first grader in Chesterfield County, Virginia.My favourite book growing upStephen King’s The Stand. I completely lost myself in the story. I don’t think I realised at the time what a rare gift it is to have that experience.The book that changed me as a teenagerWhen I was 12 or 13, I wandered into the modest poetry section of our local used bookstore and was drawn to the cover art of Dylan Thomas’s Collected Poems. I flipped it open and read, “Now as I was young and easy under the apple boughs …” I won’t pretend I was a sophisticated reader of poetry at the time, but the music was undeniable. I wrote my first attempt at poetry that night and knew from that moment I would chase that music for the rest of my life.The writer who changed my mindI read GK Chesterton’s Orthodoxy when I was in my early 20s. His framing of tradition as democracy extended to the dead was something I’d never considered, and frankly, found quite persuasive. My politics didn’t change, but I discovered how essential it is to have your ideas challenged, and how foolish it is to believe your opinions are correct simply because you are the one who holds them.The book that made me want to be a writerF Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby, at school, when I was 15 or 16. I fell so deeply in love with the book that, and this is somewhat embarrassing to admit, I would type out sentences from it on my family’s old desktop computer just to see what it felt like.The book or author I came back toI had a friend in graduate school who was such an evangelist for David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest that he would give me pep talks each of the thousand times I was ready to abandon it. When I finally got to Don Gately’s portion of the narrative, the book completely opened up to me, and I now deeply admire it.The book I rereadI moved to Texas in my 20s and was recommended John Graves’s Goodbye to a River, a memoir of a final canoe trip down the Brazos River before it was meant to be dammed up. The writing is exquisite. For me it’s the platonic ideal of a book as the record of a mind at work. I’ve reread it every year or two ever since.The book I could never read againThomas Wolfe’s Look Homeward, Angel was another transformative work I read as a teenager. I’m afraid I wouldn’t like it if I read it again, and I don’t want to take that joy away from my 16-year-old self.The book I discovered later in lifeI read Pär Lagerkvist’s Barabbas only a few years ago, and it has become a touchstone for clarity in my own writing. There are scenes that are among the most deeply moving yet plainly told as anything I’ve ever read.The book I am currently readingI just finished Foster by Claire Keegan and immediately ordered everything she’s ever published.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy comfort readIf I’m honest, I think I read to be made uncomfortable.Children of the Wild by Kevin Powers is published by Atlantic. title: Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar | Games | The Guardian
description: As one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousands
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousands
Content: Single Pokémon cards for sale, locked in a cabinet.Photograph: Daniella LucasView image in fullscreenSingle Pokémon cards for sale, locked in a cabinet.Photograph: Daniella LucasGamesThieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soarAs one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousandsDaniella LucasFri 4 Sep 2026 05.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePokémon’s success over the last 30 years has seen it grow from a much-loved Game Boy classic, to a world-dominating brand with TV shows, spin-off games, toys and even a theme park. The trading card game is a huge part of that, with more than85bn cardsprinted over its lifetime, and the appetite for them shows no signs of slowing down. Packs get snapped up after release so quickly it’s nowalmost impossible to find them in shops, and a booming resale market is driving the hobby into murky waters.One card recently sold for aneye-watering £12m, and an increasing number of people have gotten into the collecting business on the hunt for huge profits, leading toa rise in thefts targeting card shops. More recently though, some small businesses have reported that their sales have been hit by thieves targeting envelopes within Royal Mail, leading to thousands in lost revenue.Ben Thyer, owner of Bath TCG – a card specialist store in the Bath area, is one of those affected. “We always get the odd parcel going missing, but because it was sporadic, we put that down to unfortunate incidents,” Thyer tells the Guardian. “Then [in late July], we had a message [from a customer] with pictures of a cut-open envelope, and the cards were missing. Then there was a second, and then a third, and then there were seven – all of them from the same batch shipped on the same day. We asked for images from each person, and every envelope had been Sellotaped … we don’t use Sellotape because we have brand new envelopes, and we use our own labels over the seals. It’s clear someone had done it deliberately.”View image in fullscreenBath TCG - an independent shop specialising in trading card games.Photograph: Daniella LucasThe images, seen by the Guardian, show that the mailed envelopes were tampered with in the exact same way. Thyer considers it clear that this was a targeted theft rather than a coincidence. Fortunately, those particular cards weren’t of high value, but he has since had to close down online card sales, considering the risk of theft and damaged reputation to his business to be too high. By stopping those sales he has now lost out on £4,000-6,000 of potential revenue, a huge amount for a small business.Bath TCG is not the only card sales business to be affected, and the issue is not just affecting Pokémon cards. Daniel Stack, director of Mana Rock Games – a specialist in selling Magic: The Gathering cards – has also had issues withRoyal Mailitems going missing. His business is also based in Bath and was affected over similar dates to Bath TCG’s.“I realised it was theft when two customers in different parts of the country sent me pictures of their packages already open with the contents missing, within minutes of each other,” Stack said. “We’d previously had one sent to France turn up the same way a couple of weeks before, but I put it down to the buyer taking a bit of a chance that I’d have no way to hold them to account for pretending there had been an issue. In total we’ve had about £120-worth stolen so far – we had previously sent over 1,200 orders without any issues.”View image in fullscreenSome of BathTCG’s stock.Photograph: Daniella LucasStack also halted online sales for a week, costing him £500 in revenue. Other sellers in the area havementioned similar problemsto him. Unfortunately, as most card businesses in the UK useCardMarketto sell online, it’s the buyer who picks the delivery method, and most often they use Royal Mail services. Cards are often sent in distinctive hard-backed envelopes to protect the contents, often with shop branding on stickers or seals.Royal Mail is investigating the issue and liaising with the affected businesses. A spokesperson told the Guardian: “The safety and security of mail is a top priority and we take any reports of theft very seriously. We investigate concerns thoroughly and take action where necessary, including working with law enforcement.” Investigations are still ongoing; in the meantime, businesses must choose between risking theft and damaged reputation for their stores, or halting online sales and losing revenue.With a new, highly sought-after 30th anniversaryPokémoncard set due to release this month, retailers are already anticipating an increase in scalper and reselling activity, leading to even more potential for thieves to target those selling cards online. We asked the Pokémon Company for comment on how they’re dealing with increased demand and the rise in thefts, but they have yet to respond.Explore more on these topicsGamesPokémonCrimeRoyal MailnewsShareReuse this content

title: The must-see Bayeux masterpiece, Colombia’s chronicler and a Manchester odyssey – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The Bayeux tapestry arrives, the Americas go mainstream and modern, and Manchester threads its way to Korea and India
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The Bayeux tapestry arrives, the Americas go mainstream and modern, and Manchester threads its way to Korea and India
Content: All human life and more … the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Isogood_patrick/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAll human life and more … the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Isogood_patrick/ShutterstockArt Weekly newsletterArt and designThe must-see Bayeux masterpiece, Colombia’s chronicler and a Manchester odyssey – the week in artThe Bayeux tapestry arrives, the Americas go mainstream and modern, and Manchester threads its way to Korea and India –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 4 Sep 2026 07.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekThe BayeuxtapestryBlood and thunder, friendship and betrayal, marginal monsters and raw sex – all human life and more is depicted in this medieval artistic masterpiece that tells an epic national story with unrivalled punch and power.British Museum, London, from 10 September until 11 July 2027Also showingEmma ReyesA look back at this Colombian painter who brought the subaltern cultures of the Americas into the mainstream of modern art.White Cube Mason’s Yard, London, until 3 OctoberJimmy WrightThere’s an alluring tint of Van Gogh’s Sunflowers to this artist’s recent works.Thomas Dane Gallery, London, until 1 OctoberCatherine MurphyTough no-nonsense realism is taken to the point of surrealism in Murphy’s paintings.Sadie Coles HQ, London, until 7 NovemberEntangled and WovenIf the Bayeux tapestry makes you wonder how textile art is faring, here’s a show threading that theme from India and Korea to Manchester.Whitworth, Manchester, until 3 January 2027Image of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Temi AdegbayibPhotography began as a hobby for Temi Adegbayibi after he started photographing his cousin’s band Ezra Collective. But perseverance, confidence, skill and talent has seen the 26-year-old’s work – which captures the movement, intimacy and joy of performing, particularly in his images of Black musicians – exhibited at the Royal Albert Hall. The photograph above shows Adegbayibi “trying to capture the energy of a drum solo”.Read more hereWhat we learnedAn Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace was stolen in a smash-and-grab raidJackson Pollock’s Blue Poles sparked one of Australia’s most enduring culture warsWilem Frischmann, one of architecture’s most daring engineers, has died aged 95The theft of Renaissance art by Messina from a Sicilian museum baffled investigatorsWoo Jin Joo uses London junk to bring a spirit of playfulness to the art worldThe graffiti artist Helch, who has died, left an indelible mark on high-rise BritainVisitors to Nostell, in West Yorkshire, will be able to watch cutting-edge research on a rare painting of Thomas MoreSculptor Maurizio Cattelan, who had his golden loo stolen and $6m banana eaten, is bringing Hitler and a pope to BerlinMasterpiece of the weekThe Story of David and Goliath by Francesco Pesellino, c 1445-55View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Bruce/© The National Gallery, LondonThis Renaissance painting of conflict was created more than 400 years after the Bayeux tapestry. But for all its greater sophistication and especially its command of the new science of perspective, you can’t really say it is a clearer or more emotionally powerful visual narrative. If anything, Pesellino’s painting is harder to make sense of. Because the Bayeux tapestry tells its tale in a completely linear way, unfolding stage by stage, with no layers of action, it is wonderfully easy to follow. Here, the story’s progress is chaotically clogged with crowd scenes and landscapes in depth. So even though the figures are much more muscled and their faces better drawn, some raw simplicity is lost. At another level, nothing has changed: this is still a medieval artwork from an epoch when horses and battles, castles and armour were the most glamorous themes in art.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Wallace’s dog Gromit was nearly a cat, reveals creator as Aardman turns 50 | Wallace & Gromit | The Guardian
description: Nick Park began modelling the character as a feline, before finding it too difficult and changing him to a dog
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Nick Park began modelling the character as a feline, before finding it too difficult and changing him to a dog
Content: Wallace and Gromit in A Grand Day Out, which was released in 1989.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyView image in fullscreenWallace and Gromit in A Grand Day Out, which was released in 1989.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyWallace & GromitWallace’s dog Gromit was nearly a cat, reveals creator as Aardman turns 50Nick Park began modelling the character as a feline, before finding it too difficult and changing him to a dogJamie GriersonandSteven MorrisFri 4 Sep 2026 07.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe creator of Wallace and Gromit has revealed that the world’s most famous stop-motion animated dog was nearly a cat.As Aardman Animations marks its 50th anniversary, Nick Park, who joined the studio in 1985,told the BBChe had originally modelled Gromit as a feline companion for Wallace.“I had this idea of an English guy who builds a rocket in the basement of his house,” said Park. “I was thinking he may have a pet, probably a cat. I started modelling the cat and it was just very difficult, so I thought I’d do a dog instead.”Sean Clarke, Aardman’s managing director, told the broadcaster another of its characters, Shaun the Sheep, nearly spoke. The Wallace and Gromit spinoff – in effect a silent comedy with little or no dialogue – has been another success for the studio.The Wallace and Gromit specials are firmly embedded in British popular culture and have had a surge of Oscar and Bafta wins. The studio includes Chicken Run, Early Man and Flushed Away among its other successes.Chicken Run was the highest-grossing stop-motion film of all time, while Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl becameone of the BBC’s most-watched scripted showsin two decades after it aired on Christmas Day in 2024.Peter Lord and David Sproxton launched Aardman’s studio in Bristol in 1976 with another beloved British children’s character: Morph.View image in fullscreenAardman puppets are among the 220 lots up for auction this month to celebrate the studio’s 50th anniversary.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAA number of exhibitions have marked the 50th anniversary this year, at venues including M Shed in Bristol’s harbourside and the Young V&A in east London. The Royal Mint released a collectible 50p coin.The exhibition in Bristol, open until 13 September, maps howAardman rose from modest beginningsin the city and began to win the nation’s hearts and minds by moulding Morph for the children’s programme Take Hart, before going global.More than 150 items are on display at the Young V&A in Bethnal Green, including never-before-seen models, sets and storyboards from Aardman’s archives.They include meticulous models such as Gromit’s vegetable patch, the museum from The Wrong Trousers and a remarkably large and detailed ship from 2012’s The Pirates! In an Adventure with Scientists!Original Aardman models including Wallace and Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Morph are being auctioned to celebrate the anniversary. There are more than 220 lots, with each starting at £100.Wallace, Gromit and the villain Feathers McGraw, used in Vengeance Most Fowl, will be included in the sale, as well as a Shaun puppet from the film Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom, which is released this month.Ngaio Harding-Hill, Aardman’s director of attractions, live experiences and archive, said: “The Aardman 50th anniversary auction is an unprecedented opportunity to own a part of the studio’s 50-year history.“The collection has been carefully curated by the studio’s creative talent and includes contributions, such as an original Nick Park sketch, produced in celebration of this unique moment to connect with our fans.”Bidding begins on 4 September and the auction concludes on 24 September, with a live event open to online, absentee and telephone bidding around the world.The proceeds will be invested in talent development initiatives at Aardman, including bursaries at its training facility, the Aardman Academy, skills development programmes and opportunities for emerging film-makers.Explore more on these topicsWallace & GromitAardmanAnimation on TVTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Latcho Drom director Tony Gatlif dies aged 77 | Movies | The Guardian
description: Film-maker acclaimed for his celebrations of Roma culture had been working on a ‘historical film project’ in Provence
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Film-maker acclaimed for his celebrations of Roma culture had been working on a ‘historical film project’ in Provence
Content: Tony Gatlif in 2025.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTony Gatlif in 2025.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesMoviesLatcho Drom director Tony Gatlif dies aged 77Film-maker acclaimed for his celebrations of Roma culture had been working on a ‘historical film project’ in ProvenceAndrew Pulverand agenciesFri 4 Sep 2026 09.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 09.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTony Gatlif, the French director of more than 20 films that mostly concentrated on celebrating Roma culture across the world, has died aged 77.His family said in a statement to AFP that Gatlif died on Wednesday of “a health issue” while working on a “historical film project” in Arles in Provence,France. “The beauty of his films, his generosity, his joy, his poetry, and his love of music will remain with us forever.”The statement, from his wife, children and grandchildren wished him “Latcho Drom”, a Roma phrase meaning “safe journey”.Latcho Drom is also the title of Gatlif’s breakthrough 1993 film, a celebration of Roma music that moves from India to Spain, and which won the Un Certain Regard award at the Cannes film festival that year.Gatlif had more success in 1997 with Gadjo Dilo, which featured Romain Duris as a Frenchman who is searching for a Roma singer in Romania; it won a Silver Leopard at the Locarno film festival and a César award for best original music.View image in fullscreen‘His joy, his poetry, and his love of music will remain with us forever’ … Latcho Drom.Photograph: Handout/HANDOUTGatlif was born Michel Dahmani in 1948 in Algeria, of part Berber and part Roma heritage. He left Algeria for France in 1960 during the Algerian war of independence and had a tough life as a rootless teenager, telling AFP: “I used to be violent; you didn’t want to mess with me; I was a bad kid … I wouldn’t listen to anyone; to me, adults – everyone – were enemies.” He changed his name to Gatlif, after a park in Algiers, after being stopped by the police as a 12-year-old.Among his later films,Exils, also starring Duris, explored his Algerian heritage, and won the best director award at Cannes in 2004.Catherine Pégard, France’s minister of culture said that Gatlif “had a fondness for the road less travelled, for blurring borders, and for lives that too often go unnoticed”. She added: “He filmed music, movement, exile, and freedom with an energy that was uniquely his own.”Explore more on these topicsFilmFranceRoma, Gypsies and TravellersEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Queer Edward II review – funny, touching time capsule of Derek Jarman at work | Movies | The Guardian
description: Venice film festival: Filmed during the making of his queer royal feature, while the director was living with HIV, the candid footage includes uproarious scenes at a Cliff Richard rehearsal
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Venice film festival: Filmed during the making of his queer royal feature, while the director was living with HIV, the candid footage includes uproarious scenes at a Cliff Richard rehearsal
Content: Beaming patrician authority … Derek Jarman in Queer Edward II.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalView image in fullscreenBeaming patrician authority … Derek Jarman in Queer Edward II.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalMoviesReviewQueer Edward II review – funny, touching time capsule of Derek Jarman at workVenice film festival: Filmed during the making of his queer royal feature, while the director was living with HIV, the candid footage includes uproarious scenes at a Cliff Richard rehearsalPeter Bradshawin VeniceFri 4 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere could hardly be a more vivid time-capsule film about the publicly funded British arts scene in the early 1990s than this engrossing fly-on-the-wall documentary about Derek Jarman and his movie Edward II. Based on the play byChristopher Marlowe, it is about the 14th-century English king and his love affair with his court favourite, Piers Gaveston, with Steven Waddington and Andrew Tiernan as the leads and Tilda Swinton as Queen Isabella.This film uses the tremendously funny and candid making-of footage shot at the time by Seamus McGarvey, who had worked as a camera assistant on earlier Jarman films War Requiem and The Garden, and whose distinguished career as a cinematographer lay ahead. Jarman emerges as an effortless leader with a beaming patrician authority, rather like David Lean or Richard Attenborough, the kind of chief whom subordinates instinctively wish to please while keeping from him the grubby problems that they themselves have to deal with, such as paying quarrelsome extras or handling tabloid press questions. Jarman had had his HIV diagnosis for five years at this stage, managing the situation with meds which McGarvey’s camera notices.Jarman’s tightly budgeted movie was composed in the formalised theatrical setpiece style that Peter Greenaway favoured in the same period; he intended a radically confrontational piece of Brechtian queer cinema, reinventing the Marlowe play as a movie insurgency against homophobia, Section 28, the (declining but still present) indifference to HIV/Aids research, and age-of-consent inequality. Jarman used Peter Tatchell’s OutRage! protesters as extras in the movie studio, effectively making the film and the street protests part and parcel of each other. This was to lead to one of the most bizarre and chaotic footnotes in British movie history, amusingly shown here in all its uproarious craziness: the OutRage! shock troops stormed into the studios next door where Cliff Richard happened to be rehearsing, demanding that he out himself.The “outing” debate now in fact looks very dated and this is the one moment where you can sense that Jarman thinks that the OutRage! protesters got it wrong by harassing and bullying Cliff Richard; we see him assuring his own team later that Tatchell gave them a real telling off for this. (Did Tatchell actually do anything of the kind? Or is that what Jarman felt ought to have happened?) It’s an absorbing and affecting portrait of a dedicated artist at work.Queer Edward II screened at theVenice film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsDerek JarmanChristopher MarlowePeter TatchellLGBTQ+ rightsVenice film festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I didn’t know I was pregnant until I gave birth | Life and style | The Guardian
description: There’d been no morning sickness, cravings or tiredness. My mum didn’t believe I’d had a baby – even after seeing her on FaceTime
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: There’d been no morning sickness, cravings or tiredness. My mum didn’t believe I’d had a baby – even after seeing her on FaceTime
Content: Aubrie Morris with her daughter, Navie.Photograph: Danielle Villasana/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAubrie Morris with her daughter, Navie.Photograph: Danielle Villasana/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: I didn’t know I was pregnant until I gave birthThere’d been no morning sickness, cravings or tiredness. My mum didn’t believe I’d had a baby – even after seeing her on FaceTimeAubrie MorrisFri 4 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 12.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was 19, I went to college in Texas, where I met my ­boyfriend Preston. It was 2023 and I had big plans. After ­finishing my degree in criminal justice, I wanted to go to law school. I wasn’t in a rush to get married or have kids. My mum had drilled into me a fear of getting pregnant at a young age. I was on the pill and careful with contraception.In May 2025, I took a trip to London, returning to campus in August after the summer holidays. I noticed I was slowly gaining weight; by January this year I’d gained 10lb. I put it down to my late-night snacking and lack of exercise.But then on 20 February, after I had returned to my apartment following my morning class, I felt cramps in my lower stomach. At 1pm, I took some ibuprofen.At 6.20pm, I felt a sudden urge to go to the toilet. After sitting there for a while with nothing happening, I stood up, assuming I was constipated. Then, I felt something strange happening between my legs. I looked down and saw something bulging out of me. I froze. I thought it was a tumour and that I was going to die.double quotation markThe operator asked if I’d had a girl or a boy. I hadn’t registered the fact I’d had a daughterBut then I felt the urge to push – and suddenly there was a baby’s head between my thighs. I was terrified, but primal instinct took over. I waddled to my bedroom and grabbed a clean towel. I laid it down and dropped to my hands and knees. The adrenaline was pumping so hard that I don’t remember feeling pain. Three quick pushes later, I was able to grab my baby. Laying her on the floor in front of me, I rubbed her chest to help her cry. I did it all without thinking. Then I called 911.I explained to the operator that I’d just had a baby I hadn’t known I was pregnant with – I have no idea how I remained so calm. The operator asked if I’d had a girl or a boy. I hadn’t registered the fact I’d had a daughter.Experience: my daughters were born conjoined at the headRead moreHe stayed on the phone for the three minutes it took the paramedics to arrive. In that time, I took a picture of the baby and sent it to Preston. I told him I’d just given birth and he needed to get to the hospital. When the ambulance arrived, all I could think was: how am I going to tell my mum?At the hospital, the baby and I were both checked over. When Preston came running through the doors, he was in shock. We tried to get to grips with what was happening. A doctor explained I’d had a cryptic pregnancy, when a woman has no idea she’s pregnant. The placenta had been at the front, making it harder for me to feel any movement.I realised she must have been conceived just before I went to London. But apart from the weight gain, there hadn’t been any other signs. I’d continued taking the pill and had my regular bleed each month; there’d been no morning sickness, cravings, bloating or tiredness.Given Preston’s and my ages and finances, we thought adoption would be best. But the next day, he walked into my room with a stuffed animal, and he’d clearly been crying. He wanted to keep her. I was relieved – I felt the same. We named her Navie.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe were discharged four days later and went to live with Preston in his apartment. We didn’t tell our parents until Navie was eight days old. At first, my mum didn’t believe me, even when I showed her Navie on FaceTime. It was only when I held up my hospital bracelet that she realised it was true. She cried tears of happiness. I’d had nothing to be worried about.Two weeks after giving birth, postpartum depression hit me hard and Navie and I moved in with my mum for a few weeks.After that, my connection with Navie grew. I loved taking care of her, even though it was a steep learning curve.I had to pause my studies, but I’ll be back at college this autumn to graduate in December. Now, I look at Navie and think, “I can’t believe I carried you for nine months and had no clue.” Motherhood at 21 was never my plan. But she’s shown me that the biggest surprises can turn out to be the greatest blessings.As told to Kate GrahamDo you have an experience to share? title: The best hair dryers for smooth, speedy styling at home – whatever your hair type | Hair care | The Guardian
description: Want every day to be a good hair day? We tested 22 hair dryers to find the best, from gentle diffusers to high-speed and travel-ready models
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: Want every day to be a good hair day? We tested 22 hair dryers to find the best, from gentle diffusers to high-speed and travel-ready models
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHair careReviewThe best hair dryers for smooth, speedy styling at home – whatever your hair typeWant every day to be a good hair day? We tested 22 hair dryers to find the best, from gentle diffusers to high-speed and travel-ready modelsThe best hot brushes, tried and tested by our expertSarah MatthewsFri 4 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn my years of reviewing beauty tech, it was upgrading my hair dryer that made the biggest difference to my routine. I used to dread hair-wash days: the chore of shampooing, conditioning and rinsing my hair, plus the time – and aching arms – spent getting it dry again.My clunky, bargain-bucket hair dryer of seven years was weighty, deafeningly loud, and took a painstaking 20 minutes to dry my hair. So happier days really did arrive when I switched to a new model.My current hair dryer uses a lightweight digital motor that’s not only far quieter, but is also powerful enough to dry my hair in just five minutes. It seems modern hair dryers have stepped up their game. Here, you’ll find the best hair dryers I’ve tested, from gentle options with diffusers for curly hair to ultra-fast models that shave significant time off your morning routine. You’ll also find expert hair-drying guidance from celebrity hairstylist Melissa Timperley.At a glanceBest hair dryer overallHershesonsThe Great£235 at HershesonsBest budget hair dryerBaBylissHydro-Fusion£59.99 at John LewisBest hair dryer for curly hairPanasonicNanoe Moisture+ EH NA0J£199.99 at AmazonBest hair dryer for sensitive scalpsDysonSupersonic NuralStraight and wavy, £349.99 at John LewisBest lightweight hair dryerElectric Head JogFutaria£139.95 at AmazonBest travel hair dryerDysonSupersonic Travel£249.99 at DysonWhy you should trust meI’ve been reviewing beauty products for four years and have amassed a near-encyclopaedic knowledge of hair care. I’ve attended countless styling masterclasses, interviewed hair stylists, and completed a cosmetic science course where I learned exactly how hair growth, styling and care work at a cellular level.I’ve tested and reviewed about 70 hair-styling tools – including hair dryers, curlers,hot brushes, wavers andstraighteners– from big-name brands and newcomers alike. And perhaps most impressively, I’ve walked away with my hair healthy and intact.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach hair dryer was tested for speed and sound levels.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianHaving researched the most popular brands and models, I put 22 hair dryers through their paces for this test. I also spoke to a hair stylist to find out what she looks for in a hair dryer, before cherrypicking the best 12 from my tests to include here.I used an anemometer to test each model’s maximum wind speed, which ranged from a measly 16 metres a second (m/s) to a mind-boggling 43.8m/s, and also a sound meter to measure noise levels from 15cm away.Claims of “enhanced shine or smoothness” aren’t quantifiable, but I did use every hair dryer to complete the same task, noting how long it took to rough-dry hair and then to finish. I also tried my hand at using a round brush to achieve a smooth, bouncy blowout. While I’m no professional at this, it allowed me to make a judgment about how easy a hair dryer’s controls are to use, how precise and versatile its settings are, and comfort levels over the course of styling.When testing was complete, I returned the samples to the manufacturers who sent them. If samples could not be returned, they were sent to the RedbridgeReach Out domestic abuse service, which provides support and refuge for survivors.The best hair dryersView image in fullscreenBlown away: the hair dryers vying for approval.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianBest hair dryer overall:Hershesons The GreatHershesonsThe Greatfrom£235£235 at Hershesons£235 at AmazonWhat we loveFast; lightweight; good results on all hair typesWhat we don’t loveArchaic push-on attachmentsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£235 at Hershesons£235 at AmazonTesting the Hershesons the Great hair dryer confirmed my belief that there’s no need to reinvent the wheel. This hair dryer perfects the basics and irons out any common niggles. It’s the lightest option I’ve ever tested, almost the quickest – and an easy recommendation.Why we love itThe Great hair dryer has four speeds, three heat settings and a cool shot. It reached a super-fast 38.4m/s in my tests, rough-drying my hair in less than five minutes, and leaving it soft and healthy-looking.You change the settings using buttons on the hair dryer’s handle, which can then be locked into place. This is unlike button controls on other models, which can be accidentally pressed mid-use.One distinctive feature of the Hershesons hair dryer, and something that goes a long way to justify its premium price, is its heat-proof mat. This will automatically switch off the dryer when it’s placed on to it, resuming again once it’s lifted. I found this invaluable when blow-drying my hair with a round brush, since I could plonk the hair dryer down to section my hair without having to faff around with the controls.Add on two concentrator nozzles, a diffuser, a fabric bag and a sturdier storage case, and the Great is a hair dryer that truly feels designed with the user in mind.It’s a shame that …it’s so expensive. Next to hair dryers with magnetic attachments, the push-on system here also felt archaic and made it more difficult to switch out tools.Weight (without wire):294gCord length:2.75mHeat settings (including cool shot):fourSpeed settings:fourAttachments:concentrator nozzles and a diffuserMaximum wind speed:38.4m/sVolume range:82-86dBHershesonsThe Greatfrom£235£235 at Hershesons£235 at AmazonWhat we loveFast; lightweight; good results on all hair typesWhat we don’t loveArchaic push-on attachmentsBest budget hair dryer:BaByliss Hydro-FusionBaBylissHydro-Fusionfrom£59.99£59.99 at John Lewis£60 at ArgosWhat we love:Smooth results, sensible price, quiet operationWhat we don’t loveNo high-tech featuresView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£59.99 at John Lewis£60 at ArgosIf you ever struggle with frizzy hair after blow-drying, chances are you need an ionic dryer. This budget-friendly BaByliss option has a good range of speed and heat settings, a concentrator nozzle and a diffuser, making it suitable for numerous hair types. Furthermore, thanks to its 2,100W motor, its 26.4m/s maximum wind speed rivals some of the pricier options on this page.Why we love itIt was immediately clear that the Hydro-Fusion was well built and powerful. It rough-dried my hair in about 10 minutes, leaving it feeling healthy and totally free from frizz and flyaways. Despite this power, it’s quieter than many of the models here, too.Attachments securely clicked into place and stayed on without issue while I completed my round-brush blow-dry test. I found the hair dryer’s two speed settings offered plenty of control for more precise styling, and the cool shot came through quickly compared with other cheaper hair dryers I’ve tested. Once styled, my hair was bouncy and shiny, with a frizz-free finish that lasted multiple days.It’s a shame that …its design is pretty basic; there are no frills here. A few more colour options would have been welcome, too, but you’re unlikely to find a better hair dryer for the price.Weight (without wire):430gCord length:2.5mHeat settings (including cool shot):fourSpeed settings:twoAttachments:concentrator nozzle and a diffuserMaximum wind speed:26.4m/sVolume range:78-85dBBaBylissHydro-Fusionfrom£59.99£59.99 at John Lewis£60 at ArgosWhat we love:Smooth results, sensible price, quiet operationWhat we don’t loveNo high-tech featuresBest hair dryer for curly hair:Panasonic Nanoe Moisture+ EH NA0JPanasonicNanoe Moisture+ EH NA0J£199.99£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMoisturising tech, with smooth healthy resultsWhat we don’t loveConfusing settingsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£199.99 at AmazonAs counterintuitive as it sounds, this hair dryer adds moisture to your hair. Panasonic’s Nanoe technology creates microscopic water droplets that penetrate the hair’s cuticle to add extra moisture to the hair’s deepest layers. It claims this helps to reduce colour fading, flyaways, split ends and breakage.Why we love itI tested the Panasonic EH NA0J hair dryer after several hair washes and found its distinctive shape intuitive to use. For rough-drying, I used heat and the fastest speed setting (23.4m/s), and was impressed at how quickly the hair dryer worked its magic (in about 10 minutes).Compared with the other models here, the Nanoe appeared to separate wet clumps of hair into smaller sections, drying strands faster. Despite using the one and only heat setting, my hair felt smooth and healthy after a rough dry. And when attempting the round-brush blow-dry, the Nanoe set the style quickly using its cool shot.This hair dryer is particularly good at gently diffusing curly and coily hair types. The diffuser attachment locks securely on to the front of the body, and its long prongs are well designed to spread air gently from the root to the tip of a curl. Add in its moisturising capabilities, and you’ll be left with soft, shiny, healthier curls with each use.It’s a shame that …it has only one heat setting. Instead, the Nanoe offers multiple modes: alternating hot and cold for preserving shine; a Scalp Care mode and a Skin Care mode. These won’t be right for everyone, particularly if you like adjusting the heat levels manually. But if your hair needs extra nourishment, this hair dryer is worth a shot.Weight (without wire):460gCord length:2.7mHeat settings (includingcool shot):one (plus scalp care and alternating modes)Speed settings:threeAttachments:concentrator nozzle and a diffuserMaximum wind speed:23.4m/sVolume range:73-84dBPanasonicNanoe Moisture+ EH NA0J£199.99£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMoisturising tech, with smooth healthy resultsWhat we don’t loveConfusing settingsBest hair dryer for sensitive scalps:Dyson Supersonic NuralDysonSupersonic Nuralfrom£349.99Straight and wavy, £349.99 at John LewisCurly and coily, £399.99 at DysonWhat we loveGreat scalp care; luxury design; healthy stylingWhat we don’t loveHigh price, with marginally slower speedsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianStraight and wavy, £349.99 at John LewisCurly and coily, £399.99 at DysonDyson was once best known for its vacuum cleaners, but in recent years has cultivated a reputation for luxury hair styling tools. The 2016 Dyson Supersonic was the brand’s first hair care product, with a distinctive design that ripped up the hair dryer rulebook. And in 2024, Dyson launched the Supersonic Nural, which mirrors the original design but adds some handy scalp care features.Why we love itThe Supersonic Nural had to do some heavy lifting to justify its high price tag. It looks just like its predecessor aside from a small sensor in the middle, which controls the Nural’s new Scalp Protect mode. This tweaks the temperature of the air based on the hair dryer’s proximity to the scalp, ensuring you never burn your scalp or frazzle the delicate hairs at the hairline.As someone with a fussy scalp, I often find the highest temperatures of hair dryers too harsh, but this ensured I was completely comfortable throughout drying. At the same time, it dried the lengths of my hair without frazzling them or causing unnecessary damage. You can also switch this mode on and off if you prefer to control the temperature yourself.There are three speeds and four temperatures, and the button controls are intuitive. Its evenly weighted design was comfortable to hold, its motor was very quiet, and I found its magnetic attachments convenient and easy to use. I particularly liked the flyaway attachment, which quickly and comfortably smoothed down my frizz and flyaways after rough-drying my hair.It’s a shame that …it’s very expensive and the hair dryer wasn’t quite as quick as others I’ve tested. It took about seven minutes to blow dry my hair, but I was grateful that it could take care of my scalp without me having to make adjustments. It’s easily the best option for those with sensitive scalps.Weight (without wire):485gCord length:2.8mHeat settings (including cool shot):fourSpeed settings:threeAttachments:concentrator nozzle, diffuser, flyaway attachment, gentle air attachment and a wide-tooth combMaximum wind speed:29.2m/sVolume range:75-81dBRead our fullDyson Supersonic Nural reviewDysonSupersonic Nuralfrom£349.99Straight and wavy, £349.99 at John LewisCurly and coily, £399.99 at DysonWhat we loveGreat scalp care; luxury design; healthy stylingWhat we don’t loveHigh price, with marginally slower speedsBest lightweight hair dryer:Electric Head Jog FutariaElectric Head JogFutaria£139.95£139.95 at AmazonWhat we loveFast drying; lightweight; sensible priceWhat we don’t loveCould be too powerful for someView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£139.95 at AmazonThis is the fastest hair dryer I’ve ever tested, and weighing 304g, the Futaria is just 10g heavier than the lightest option – the Hershesons above. It was the dark horse here; I hadn’t encountered Head Jog before testing, but with its fast wind speeds of 43.8m/s and reasonable price, it’s an easy favourite.Why we love itThe Futaria hair dryer packs a serious punch, rough-drying my hair in a blisteringly quick four minutes. Thanks to its three speeds and four heat settings, I could master a precise round-brush blow-dry without much effort at all. Personally, I found the wider concentrator nozzle best for styling larger sections of hair, which sped up the process even further.The digital motor also makes the Futaria relatively quiet, and despite its light weight, the design feels sturdy and evenly weighted, plus its rear filter is easy to clean and maintain. As such, this model is perfect for use in busy salons to reduce wrist strain and maximise time efficiency. And those of us at home will also benefit from the dryer’s sleek design, which is available in blue, pink and black.It’s a shame that …since it’s tailored to professional stylists, it’s not as widely stocked as other hair dryers. Also, those concerned about damage may find the knock-your-socks-off power a little much. That said, if you’re careful with the highest intensity settings and use a heat protection spray, you shouldn’t fry your hair.Weight (without wire):304gCord length:3mHeat settings (including cool shot):fourSpeed settings:threeAttachments:twoconcentrator nozzles and a diffuserMaximum wind speed:43.8m/sVolume range:78-84dBElectric Head JogFutaria£139.95£139.95 at AmazonWhat we loveFast drying; lightweight; sensible priceWhat we don’t loveCould be too powerful for someBest travel hair dryer:Dyson Supersonic TravelDysonSupersonic Travelfrom£249.99£249.99 at Dyson£249.99 at John LewisWhat we loveUniversal voltage and fast; smooth stylingWhat we don’t loveIts high priceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lise Smith/Thr Guardian£249.99 at Dyson£249.99 at John LewisI’ve sat by draughty windows that could dry my hair quicker than a hotel hair dryer, so when Dyson announced it was launching a travel-size Supersonic, I was all ears. If you can afford it, it’s easily the best dual-voltage travel hair dryer on the market, with heat monitoring, fast speeds, versatile controls and a build that Dyson claims is 25% lighter and 32% smaller than the original. And, of course, it has the luxury design Dyson is known for.Why we love itAside from its dinky size and weight, it has the same intuitive controls as Dyson’s other hair dryers. That includes two button-controlled heat and speed settings, and a power switch on the handle. That’s fewer options than the full-size model, but more versatility than other travel dryers.It packs a punch, too. Its motor spat out air at an impressive 18.4m/s on its highest speed, which is enough to rival some of the full-size options here. Rough-drying my hair took 10 minutes and, using the nozzle provided, a round-brush blow dry left my hair feeling smooth, sleek and healthy. That’s partly because of the hair dryer’s built-in heat-monitoring system, which helps keep styling temperatures healthy and consistent.And, if you’ve already splashed the cash on a Dyson Supersonic or Nural, the travel dryer is compatible with all existing full-size attachments. If you travel often and hair health is a priority, this is a well-engineered travel dryer that gives you almost all the benefits of the Supersonic on the go.It’s a shame that …it’s so expensive – some full-size options here are far better value, so worth considering above the Dyson. Occasional travellers are likely to be just fine with a cheaper travel model, or a lightweight hair dryer they can easily pack.Weight (without wire):330gCord length:2mHeat settings (including cool shot):threeSpeed settings:twoAttachments:concentrator nozzleMaximum wind speed:18.4m/sVolume range:85-89dBRead our fullDyson Supersonic Travel reviewDysonSupersonic Travelfrom£249.99£249.99 at Dyson£249.99 at John LewisWhat we loveUniversal voltage and fast; smooth stylingWhat we don’t loveIts high priceThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘My hair was left with gorgeous shine’: the Cloud Nine Airshot Pro.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianParlux 3200 PlusParlux3200 Plusfrom£104.63£147.89 at Sally Beauty£104.63 at AmazonWhat we loveGlossy finish, tactile controlsWhat we don’t loveHeavier than othersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£147.89 at Sally Beauty£104.63 at AmazonBest for:fuss-free stylingItalian brand Parlux is well known for making high-quality, powerful, long-lasting hair dryers. According to the brand, the Parlux 3200 Plus (previously Compact) is the most widely used professional hair dryer on the market. I found it well balanced and comfortable in the hand and liked its tactile, retro-feeling switches.During testing, it dried my hair incredibly quickly, leaving a glossy, frizz-free finish. That’s thanks to the inclusion of Parlux’s K-lamination motor, which provides the power of a 2,800W motor while using only 1,900W. The hair dryer is available in a wide range of colours, and is a stylish option – if you can look past the box, which looks freshly fished from the early 2000s.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s heavier than other options here, plus it lacks the design refinements of more expensive models.Weight (without wire):588g;cord length:3m;heat settings (includingcool shot):three;speed settings:two;attachments:two concentrator nozzles;maximum wind speed: 26m/s;volume range:80-85dBParlux3200 Plusfrom£104.63£147.89 at Sally Beauty£104.63 at AmazonWhat we loveGlossy finish, tactile controlsWhat we don’t loveHeavier than othersCloud Nine the Airshot ProCloud NineThe Airshot Profrom£199£299 at Very£199 at AmazonWhat we loveQuiet operation with shiny resultsWhat we don’t loveNo dedicated cool-shot buttonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£299 at Very£199 at AmazonBest for:quiet operationTaking the highest and lowest noise levels into account, the Airshot Pro is the quietest hair dryer I’ve tested. In addition, my hair was left with gorgeous shine thanks to the Sericite-infused heat tech that features in Cloud Nine’s heat-styling tools.As well as offering a great range of temperature controls, with a continuous cool-shot option, the Airshot’s magnetic concentrator nozzle and diffuser attachments proved secure and suited to a range of hair types.It didn’t make the final cut because …it lacks a dedicated cool-shot button, and it’s not as speedy as others in this price range. Still, some may be swayed by its quiet operation.Weight (without wire):448g;cord length:3m;heat settings (including cool shot):four;speed settings:three;attachments:two concentrator nozzles, diffuser;maximum wind speed: 23.8m/s;volume range:75-79dBCloud NineThe Airshot Profrom£199£299 at Very£199 at AmazonWhat we loveQuiet operation with shiny resultsWhat we don’t loveNo dedicated cool-shot buttonGHD SpeedGHDSpeedfrom£263.12£299 at GHD£263.12 at AmazonWhat we loveFast styling; versatile controls; stylish lookWhat we don’t loveHeavy weight; top-heavy build; high priceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£299 at GHDFrom £263.12 at AmazonBest for:quickly smoothing very thick hairGHD hair dryers have historically been some of the best you can buy, and the GHD Speed is a huge step up for the brand in terms of features, design and price.It has four heat settings, plus a cool-shot button and four speeds, and there’s a handy lock switch to prevent you from accidentally changing the settings by pressing buttons mid-styling. It also includes GHD’s “halo” technology, which produces a ring of cool air around the central heated airflow. The company claims this cools the hair’s temperature by 20C, which may help limit damage from drying.This hair dryer comes with one magnetic concentrator nozzle, and other attachments aresold separately from £15. The included nozzle clipped on securely and swivelled around to help get the perfect angle for styling. It also features two channels to accommodate the “halo” of cool air. The dryer took just 10 minutes to get my long, thick hair from wet to styled, with a long-lasting smooth finish – not too shabby.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s heavy, with a slightly odd, top-heavy weighting. The contoured handle and controls also feel more suited to professional use, rather than for personal use; it’s not as comfortable to point towards your own head as it is to point it away from you. I also noticed the dryer creating more frizz around the root for me, where my new hair growth is. For such a high price, I expected better than that.Weight (without wire):620g;cord length:3m;heat settings (including cool shot):five;speed settings:four;attachments:concentrator nozzle;maximum wind speed:24.3m/s;volume range:85-92dBGHDSpeedfrom£263.12£299 at GHD£263.12 at AmazonWhat we loveFast styling; versatile controls; stylish lookWhat we don’t loveHeavy weight; top-heavy build; high priceBellissima B-travelBellissimaB-travelfrom£29.99£29.99 at Boots£30 at AOWhat we loveFast, compact and lightWhat we don’t loveHeat and speed settings are linkedView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£29.99 at Boots£30 at AOBest for:occasional travellersThe dinky Bellissima B-travel hair dryer is a brilliant option for trips and holidays. It has dual-voltage controls, so you can use it wherever you are in the world. Its folding handle and carry case keep everything safe in transit, and it feels very sturdy considering its price.Unlike most hotel hair dryers, which only let out a pathetic trickle of air, this hair dryer provides wind speeds of up to 18.9m/s – faster than some full-size options I’ve reviewed (and a tad faster than the Dyson Supersonic Travel above). That’s highly impressive given the hair dryer’s light weight. You also get a concentrator nozzle for precision styling and two speed options.It didn’t make the final cut because …there’s one control switch, so you can’t adjust the heat setting independently from the speed settings, and the difference between the two heat settings is negligible. Its travel-based use case is limited; you’d be better off investing in an alternative with multiple temperature settings to use at home.Weight (without wire):305g;cord length:1.8m;heat settings (includingcool shot):two;speed settings:two;attachments:concentrator nozzle;maximum wind speed: 18.9m/s;volume range:79-84dBBellissimaB-travelfrom£29.99£29.99 at Boots£30 at AOWhat we loveFast, compact and lightWhat we don’t loveHeat and speed settings are linkedGtech DryOnicGtechDryOnicfrom£119£119 at AO£119 at CurrysWhat we loveClear heat settings with precise controlsWhat we don’t loveCord isn’t long; it really needs a settings lockView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£119 at AO£119 at CurrysBest for:precise temperature controlsOne of my biggest bugbears with hair dryers is that you never quite know how much heat you’re using on your hair. Thankfully, the Gtech DryOnic has a screen on the back that displays the airflow setting and its temperature. With temperatures that range from 40C to 100C, you can make precise adjustments for your hair type.I found the various airflow settings useful and liked how securely the magnetic concentrator nozzle and diffuser attachments fitted on to the dryer. After styling, my hair felt soft and hydrated, with minimal frizz.It didn’t makethe final cut because …it’s not quite as quick as others here at a similar price, and its 2m cord isn’t quite long enough for my liking. I also found it too easy to accidentally press the buttons and change the temperature midway through styling.Weight (without wire):426g;cord length:2m;heat settings (including cool shot):five;speed settings:four;attachments:concentrator nozzle and diffuser;maximum wind speed: 18.8m/s;volume range:78-85dBGtechDryOnicfrom£119£119 at AO£119 at CurrysWhat we loveClear heat settings with precise controlsWhat we don’t loveCord isn’t long; it really needs a settings lockRemington Shine TherapyRemingtonShine Therapyfrom£18£18 at AO£18 at AmazonWhat we loveBudget price; good settings and attachmentsWhat we don’t loveHigher noise levels with a short cordView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£18 at AO£18 at AmazonBest for:tight budgetsThis lesser-known hair dryer is the sister product to the popular Remington Shine Therapyhair straighteners. It offers equally brilliant value and is designed to add shine to the hair using ionic technology.While difficult to quantify in tests, I found the hair dryer did dry my hair relatively quickly and left it shiny and smooth after a round-brush blow-dry. Multiple heat and speed settings, plus a concentrator nozzle and diffuser attachment, make it a good option for all hair types.It didn’t make the final cut because …of its short 1.8m cord and the fact that it’s pretty noisy compared with other models here. That said, it can’t be beaten on price and is a sensible choice if you’re hoping to upgrade an old hair dryer on a budget.Weight (without wire):449g;cord length:1.8m;heat/cool settings:four;speed settings:two;attachments:concentrator nozzle and diffuser;maximum wind speed:18.6m/s;volume range:84-89dBRemingtonShine Therapyfrom£18£18 at AO£18 at AmazonWhat we loveBudget price; good settings and attachmentsWhat we don’t loveHigher noise levels with a short cordWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianIinterviewed Melissa Timperley, hair stylist and founder ofMelissa Salons, to discover her tips for choosing a hair dryer. “When it comes to protecting your hair and achieving the style you want, the tool you use matters just as much as the products you pair it with,” she says.What features should I look for?According to Timperley, the key features are adjustable speed and heat settings, which “allow for better control and protection, depending on your hair type and styling needs”. Look for hair dryers with a cool-shot button, too, which “help to smooth the cuticle and set your style”.Design-wise, consider weight, which is “especially important for longer hair or professional use” to prevent armstrain. Also look for a dryer that has a removable or self-cleaning filter, as “this makes cleaning and maintenance easy, which helps preserve motor life”.What to avoid when choosing a dryerTimperley warns that there are some features, or omissions, that could be detrimental to hair health. It’s best to avoid “single-setting dryers that don’t allow heat or speed control”, as well as low-wattage dryers under 1,800W, because “they often take longer to dry hair, exposing it to heat for too long”.However, some of the dryers I’ve chosen here are below 1,800W. That’s because these use digital motors, which are smaller and lighter than brushed motors and produce faster airflow. That means, in those cases, the difference in drying speeds is negligible.She also warns against buying “heavy, bulky dryers that are uncomfortable to use regularly” and “poor-quality nozzles or diffusers that don’t fit securely or distribute air properly”.Put simply, she says: “If the dryer doesn’t clearly list its motor type, wattage or heat settings, that’s a red flag.”What makes a hair dryer good for different hair types?Picking out the right hair dryer for your hair type can be challenging. “The best hair dryers cater to your hair’s specific needs – whether that’s smoothing frizz, protecting fine strands or cutting through thick, coarse textures,” says Timperley.For fine or damaged hair, Timperley advises looking for “lower heat settings and a ceramic or tourmaline dryer that distributes heat more gently”. For thick or coarse hair, “higher wattage and powerful airflow are essential – infrared, ionic and titanium dryers are great for cutting drying time without excessive heat”. And finally, for curly or textured hair, “a diffuser attachment is key, as is a dryer that offers heat control without sacrificing volume or natural texture”.What’s the difference between ionic and ceramic hair dryers?“Ionic hair dryers emit negative ions that help break down water molecules faster, reducing frizz,” says Timperley. “They’re great for smoothing and shine, especially if you have thick, frizzy or unruly hair.”Conversely, “ceramic hair dryers use ceramic heating elements to distribute heat evenly, which helps prevent hotspots and damage. They’re ideal for fine or delicate hair.”“Some of the best hair dryers,” says Timperley, “combine both technologies, giving you faster drying without sacrificing hair health.”What to do with your old hair dryer?If it still works and is in good condition, you can donate your old hair dryer to a charity shop or shelter. TheBritish Red Crossoften accepts small electrical items, including hair dryers. Be sure to clean out any dust from the rear filter and remove any hair from brush attachments before you pass it on.If your hair dryer is dead, don’t throw it in your normal bin. Take it to your local recycling centre, which you can find usingRecycle Your Electricals. Alternatively, Currys offers afree recycling servicein-store for electrical items, including those you didn’t buy from it.How to stop your hair dryer from damaging your hair?A common misconception is that heat protection is only necessary when using heat styling tools, such as hair straighteners or curlers, but the heat from your hair dryer can be just as damaging. Always prepare wet hair using a heat protection cream or spray before drying. According to Timperley, “this creates a protective barrier between the hair and heat, while helping to smooth and condition the strands.”“Avoid automatically reaching for the highest heat setting,” continues Timperley. “Prolonged exposure to excessive heat can weaken the hair cuticle, leading to dryness, frizz, breakage and a loss of shine over time.” As a rule, opt for the lower heat settings as long as they still allow you to achieve the style you want, and keep the dryer moving constantly to avoid frazzling small sections of hair.Unlike traditional heat stylers, styling with a hair dryer offers the best results when the hair is about 80% dry. Timperley warns, “once a section is fully dry, additional heat offers little styling benefit and significantly increases the risk of damage.” She recommends re-dampening any hair strands you’re unhappy with and restyling for the healthiest results.For more:The best hair masks for every hair typeDyson Supersonic Nural hair dryer reviewDyson Supersonic Travel hair dryer reviewThe best hair oils, capsules and serumsSarah Matthews is aconsumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling, hair removal,light therapyandskincaretools.
