title: The best backpacks in the UK for work, travel and wild adventure – tested | Walking | The Guardian
description: Whether you want a smart-but-stylish commuter rucksack or a hike-friendly pack, our writer lugged 16 over hundreds of miles to find the best bags for your buck
Author: Pete Wise
Headline: Whether you want a smart-but-stylish commuter rucksack or a hike-friendly pack, our writer lugged 16 over hundreds of miles to find the best bags for your buck
Content: Pack leader: writer Pete sizes up the contenders near the Ribblehead viaduct.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPack leader: writer Pete sizes up the contenders near the Ribblehead viaduct.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterWalkingThe best backpacks in the UK for work, travel and wild adventure – testedWhether you want a smart-but-stylish commuter rucksack or a hike-friendly pack, our writer lugged 16 over hundreds of miles to find the best bags for your buckThe best travel mugs for taking hot drinks on the goPete WiseFri 4 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChart your course through a fun, active or productive day, and you’ll often find cause to carry things. Backpacks are arguably the best people-powered way to do it, used by pretty much everyone from Napoleonic soldiers andÖtzi the Icemanto ultra-marathoner Courtney Dauwalter, as well as innumerable workers, students and travellers.The best backpack to choose depends on which elements of your own world you wish to carry, and where you’re planning to take them. You can choose between smart-looking options suitable for work and travel, hiking-focused day packs and trail packs designed for outdoor itineraries, and versatile backpacks with water-resistant materials and a high storage capacity.A lifetime of using backpacks (and several months testing them) has taught me that these bags are just about as diverse as our daily needs and occasional adventures, with only the two shoulder straps in common. I’ve walked and travelled hundreds of miles in a range of backpacks to bring you the selection below, which includes recommendations for everyday, travel and outdoorsy use. Your next shoulder-worn companion is in the bag.At a glanceBest backpack overallColumbiaTitanium Triple Canyon 24l£67.93 at AmazonBest budget backpackBerghausElect U25£33 at ArgosBest investment backpackCarl FriedrikCity-hopper£525 at Carl FriedrikBest durable backpackWingbackEveryday Pack£325 at WingbackBest backpack for adventurous activitiesDare2bTorrek Mountain 25l£51.99 at AmazonBest high-capacity backpackMountain WarehouseTraveller 60l + 20l£69.99 at AmazonWhy you should trust mePeople have told me they rarely see me without a backpack. My hairdresser once said that I’d arrived for a trim looking ready for a Himalayan trek. Usually, I’ll respond by saying that daily life demands a lot of stuff: I need a laptop and tech accessories for work, awaterproof coator miniumbrellato keep off the rain, books, sportswear, old sweet wrappers and so on. I also hike and camp, so I often use larger and more rugged hiking rucksacks, too.On the bus home from Leeds city centre, I’ll often have a backpack across my legs with a laptop perched on top of it, so that I can write product review notes for the Filter without searing a large rectangle into my body. I’ve written this publication’s guides to items includingtravel pillows,cordless drillsandcat toys. It’s a simple pleasure to help people choose things they’ll like.How I testedOn the trail: Pete Wise tries out one of the backpacksMy daily life over a few months of summer 2026 gave me ample opportunity to test 16 backpacks, which I whittled down to my 10 favourites. I used each backpack in situations suited to its intended use, using some for work or for travel, and others for hiking or camping. I tested each rucksack under different loads and in various weather conditions, taking note of its internal organisation, capacity and comfort.For an additional test, I took all of the backpacks on a train journey to assess how easy they were to pack and unpack in a busy, confined setting, under time pressure. We chose to travel on the Settle to Carlisle line, which wends through 73 miles of Yorkshire Dales and Cumbrian countryside, past the Yorkshire Three Peaks and over the spectacular Ribblehead viaduct. Thanks to photographer Christian Hopewell for capturing the scenic fun.View image in fullscreenPack mentality: the rucksacks lined up and ready for testing.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianBackpacks not returned to the manufacturer after testing were donated toCat Action Trust 1977, Leeds, for its next yard sale. The charity’s previous event, which sawmy top-rated packing cubesflying off the shelves, raised more than £550 towards care for feral cats.The Settle-Carlisle Railway iscelebrating its 150th anniversarythis year.Day Ranger ticketsallowing multiple stops along some of the most scenic sections of the line cost £15.10 each for an adult.The best backpacks of 2026Train of thought: Pete Wise tests how the backpacks handle life on the moveBest backpack overall:Columbia Titanium Triple Canyon 24lColumbiaTitanium Triple Canyon 24lfrom£67.93£100 at Columbia£67.93 at AmazonWhat we loveExcels during tough day hikesWhat we don’t loveInternal organisation could be betterView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£100 at ColumbiaFrom £67.93 at AmazonPracticality personified, the Triple Canyon is the backpack that left me best prepared for a broad range of contexts, from rugged day hikes to rainy urban errands. It has a small, shielded opening at the top for the tube from a hydration pack, and the adjustable straps on the sides will help you achieve a streamlined fit, however much you’ve filled the bag.Why we love itI found this bag delightfully comfortable during testing, whether I was carrying it on a walk in the Yorkshire Dales or lugging books home from the library. The material is smooth, robust and cool to the touch, and the back has a good balance of stiffness and softness, which prevents hard or heavy objects inside the backpack from making themselves felt.The rain cover, stowed in its dedicated Velcro-fastened bottom pocket, provides a welcome insurance against moderate to heavy rain, while the backpack’s Omni-Shield coating also gives a good degree of water resistance.It’s a shame that …the internal organisation was not the most convenient on days when I mixed work with leisure. My football boots had to go into the same main compartment as my laptop.Capacity:24lWeight:579gWaterproof?No, but the material is water resistant and a waterproof cover is includedColumbiaTitanium Triple Canyon 24lfrom£67.93£100 at Columbia£67.93 at AmazonWhat we loveExcels during tough day hikesWhat we don’t loveInternal organisation could be betterBest budget backpack:Berghaus Elect U25BerghausElect U25from£33£33 at Argos£50 at BerghausWhat we loveSuitable for study, work and walksWhat we don’t loveCapacity occasionally lackingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£33 at Argos£50 at BerghausA versatile basic backpack that’s equally well suited to everyday use and casual day hikes, the Berghaus Elect U25 proved consistently convenient during testing, and it easily fit on to overhead luggage racks on the Settle-Carlisle Railway. I was instantly taken with its rich colour and comfy straps.Why we love itThe internal organisation is ideal for school, university or office use, with compartments and sleeves that nicely accommodate pens, apower bankand alaptop(though it was a tight fit for my 17in workhorse).There’s also a zipped pocket on the top that keeps small items easily accessible, and the cinchable bungee cord looped around the outward-facing side effectively expands the carrying capacity, providing a place to store light but bulky items such as clothing – especially wet items that you don’t want to put inside the bag.Although the materials aren’t luxurious, they feel pleasant and perform well. Reflective polyester is used on the front, while woven fabric on the sides and a breathable mesh on the back provide strength and comfort, respectively. The bag isn’t waterproof, but it successfully kept its contents dry during light showers.It’s a shame that …the capacity isn’t big enough for a busy day involving multiple activities (or lots of items). Still, I found it adequate for most occasions.Capacity:25lWeight:400gWaterproof?No, but it’s slightly water resistantBerghausElect U25from£33£33 at Argos£50 at BerghausWhat we loveSuitable for study, work and walksWhat we don’t loveCapacity occasionally lackingBest investment backpack:Carl Friedrik City-hopperCarl FriedrikCity-hopper£525£525 at Carl FriedrikWhat we loveBeautiful design and materialsWhat we don’t loveThe high priceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£525 at Carl FriedrikCurrently on preorder for 2-5 OctoberIt’s an investment, but this Carl Friedrik stunner is a smart backpack to cherish, impeccably constructed from nubuck leather (or nylon, at a lower price), with space for everyday essentials such as awater bottle, laptop and items of clothing.Why we love itOf all the many backpacks I’ve owned and used, this is my favourite smart option for workdays. The nubuck is soft and beautiful, the nickel-plated clip that folds down the top section looks great and feels satisfyingly chunky, and the storage options are just right for daily life. Thoughtful details abound, including the tougher, wear-resistant leather patches on the bottom of the bag, and the sleeve-like section on the back which slides handily over asuitcasehandle.I’ve found that there’s more space in the City-hopper than its neat appearance suggests. The internal side pocket is great for drinks bottles (up to 750ml), the outer pocket is fairly roomy, and you can cram larger loads into the bag by simply relying on the main compartment’s zip closure, rather than folding the material and buckling it down. I always carry awaterproof backpack coverinside mine, in case I need to protect the material and stored items from rain showers.It’s a shame that …this backpack costs such a lot. Most of the other models featured in this guide are far cheaper.Capacity:23lWeight:1.8kgWaterproof?NoCarl FriedrikCity-hopper£525£525 at Carl FriedrikWhat we loveBeautiful design and materialsWhat we don’t loveThe high priceBest durable backpack:Wingback Everyday PackWingbackEveryday Pack£325£325 at WingbackWhat we loveBuilt to last a lifetimeWhat we don’t loveNot the comfiest strapsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£325 at WingbackOn preorder for OctoberIf you’re anything like me, you’ll wear out your rucksacks fairly quickly. Whether through clumsy misadventure or weathering, the materials become grubby and dishevelled. This new backpack from Wingback aims to endure far longer, with a tough recycled fabric shell, a nylon lining reinforced with yarn the manufacturer claims is 15 times stronger than steel, and a lifetime guarantee.Why we love itThis bag proved tough during my testing. The material came out of a spell on the sidelines of a five-a-side without a scuff, despite my friend blasting the football at it, and the waterproof outer material held up during rain showers, keeping its contents dry.I had no trouble dividing my day-to-day items into the well-considered organisation options, which include a “floating” laptop sleeve that can sit behind or in front of other items, a roomy main compartment that easily accommodated my sportswear, a small pocket on the top that’s perfect for storing snacks, and a surprisingly capacious front pocket that could carry most water bottles ortravel mugswith room to spare. The chunky, heavyweight zippers and titanium buckles finish the whole thing off beautifully.It’s a shame that …the straps feel a little stiff and harsh on the shoulders. This is also one of the more expensive options I’ve tested – but its durability should keep the cost per wear reasonable.Capacity:21lWeight:1.35kgWaterproof?Yes, waterproof shell with a PFC-free DWR coatingWingbackEveryday Pack£325£325 at WingbackWhat we loveBuilt to last a lifetimeWhat we don’t loveNot the comfiest strapsBest backpack for adventurous activities:Dare2b Torrek Mountain 25lDare2bTorrek Mountain 25l£51.99£51.99 at AmazonWhat we loveWell-balanced and lightweightWhat we don’t loveDifficult to colour-coordinate with jacketsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£51.99 at AmazonI’ve owned one of these backpacks for almost a year, and it has become my trusted choice for relatively high-octane outdoor activities, such as scrambling, abseiling and ridge-walking.Why we love itThe rucksack is light and has a tall, narrow profile, which I’ve found helpful when trying to keep my balance during moments of mild peril. It has loops for walking poles, plus a whistle integrated into one of the chest straps.This is a good backpack for short hikes where you’ll only need relatively few items, such as snacks, thermal layers, a head torch, map and compass. I also use mine for swimming gear, as the bag fits easily inside a locker while accommodating towels and swimwear. The small pocket at the top is useful for storing valuables, and the two mesh side pockets are handy for drinks bottles.This is a lightweight backpack however you wear it, and using the waist and chest straps makes it feel “barely there”.It’s a shame that …in my opinion, neither of the two colourways goes well with many outfits. However, you probably won’t care about that up a mountain.Capacity:25lWeight:620gWaterproof?No, but the material is water repellent and showerproofDare2bTorrek Mountain 25l£51.99£51.99 at AmazonWhat we loveWell-balanced and lightweightWhat we don’t loveDifficult to colour-coordinate with jacketsBest high-capacity backpack:Mountain Warehouse Traveller 60l + 20lMountain WarehouseTraveller 60l + 20lfrom£69.99£69.99 at Mountain Warehouse£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMonumental carrying capacityWhat we don’t loveNot blessed with good looksView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£69.99 at Mountain WarehouseFrom £69.99 at AmazonMountainous in form and warehouse-like in its storage capacity, this is surely the quintessential Mountain Warehouse backpack. But it’s actually two backpacks in one: a 60l main backpack with multiple sections, plus a 20l day pack that attaches via a zip and can be removed for carrying lighter loads during a trip.Why we love itI found this large backpack useful when camping, as I could fit a large amount of kit inside with room to spare, while looping my two-persontentthrough the straps near the bottom of the bag.There are abundant options to organise your things, including the two zipped pockets of the smaller backpack, elasticated sections that can hold multiple drinks bottles, and a couple of spaces inside the main compartment.The fabric and fastenings are simple, but they feel about as robust as you could expect given the reasonable price. Thanks to the generous padding on the straps and at the lower back, I never felt uncomfortable while carrying this pack, despite filling it with a weekend’s worth of belongings.It’s a shame that …this backpack isn’t the easiest on the eye, and its size can make it awkward to carry on a busy train.Capacity:80l (60l + 20l)Weight:2.43kgWaterproof?No, but the fabric is water resistant and a rain cover is includedMountain WarehouseTraveller 60l + 20lfrom£69.99£69.99 at Mountain Warehouse£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMonumental carrying capacityWhat we don’t loveNot blessed with good looksThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Basic but effective’: the EMS Glacier lightweight rolltop.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianMontane Trailblazer 44lMontaneTrailblazer 44lfrom£140£140 at Montane£140 at Ellis BrighamWhat we loveIt’s incredibly comfyWhat we don’t loveStruggles under heavy loadsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£140 at Montane£140 at Ellis BrighamBest for:longer hikesThis is the most blissfully comfortable backpack I’ve tested, with soft materials, slightly stretchy straps and exceptionally breathable fabric against the wearer’s back. On long hikes, these attributes added up to a happier experience.As with most hiking packs, the Trailblazer is at its best when fully buckled to your torso. The waist strap is pretty standard-issue, while the chest strap has a height-adjustable clip-on closure that I found helpful in securing a comfy fit.It didn’t make the final cut because…the same “give” that makes this backpack so comfy means it sits awkwardly when filled with heavy things, as I discovered when I used it to carry a weekly supermarket shop. This doesn’t detract from the fact that this bag is brilliant for carrying bulky but light items, such as clothing and snacks.Capacity:44l;weight:1.09kg;waterproof?No, but the material is water resistant with a PFC-free DWR coatingMontaneTrailblazer 44lfrom£140£140 at Montane£140 at Ellis BrighamWhat we loveIt’s incredibly comfyWhat we don’t loveStruggles under heavy loadsHelly Hansen Stockholm backpack, 28lHelly HansenStockholm backpack, 28lfrom£44.99£75 at Helly Hansen£44.99 at AmazonWhat we loveLooks great and feels comfortableWhat we don’t loveLimited internal organisationView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£75 at Helly Hansen£44.99 at AmazonBest for:everyday style and comfortNeat and slender while in storage, but surprisingly roomy when you need it, this is a highly convenient backpack from Helly Hansen. The fabric comes to life in sunlight with vibrant colour (in my sample’s case, navy, but I also like thewildberrycolourway).I sometimes find rolltop rucksacks a faff to close, but this one works neatly, with dual straps and buckles to hold down the folded fabric. The fabric provides good resistance to moderate rain, and the rubbery base section gives the material some protection when the bag is placed on the ground.It didn’t make the final cut because…there are only two large compartments (one of which is a laptop sleeve) and one front pocket. That’s great for users who like a straightforward backpack, but not when you need to quickly find one of many stored items.Capacity:28l;weight:1kg;waterproof?No, but it’s water resistantHelly HansenStockholm backpack, 28lfrom£44.99£75 at Helly Hansen£44.99 at AmazonWhat we loveLooks great and feels comfortableWhat we don’t loveLimited internal organisationStubble & Co Hybrid backpack 30lStubble & CoHybrid backpack 30lfrom£175£175 at Stubble£175 at SelfridgesWhat we lovePerfect for commuting and business travelWhat we don’t loveLacks well-suited drink storageView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£175 at Stubble£175 at SelfridgesBest for:commuting and business travelThis is probably the smartest-looking backpack I’ve tested that offers both robust protection against the elements and travel-friendly features, which makes it a great pick for carrying equipment and essentials to the workplace or further afield.The main compartment has compression straps, so you can use the bag effectively as an item ofcarry-on luggage, and the laptop and tablet sleeves generously accommodate your favoured devices for productivity, creativity and perhaps the occasional in-transit streaming binge. I found the straps comfortable during testing.It didn’t make the cut because…as with several others here, it lacks a well-suited space for adrinks bottle, although you can fit a few side by side in the front pocket.Capacity:30l;weight:1.5kg;waterproof?Not quite, but it has waterproof fabric and water-resistant zipsStubble & CoHybrid backpack 30lfrom£175£175 at Stubble£175 at SelfridgesWhat we lovePerfect for commuting and business travelWhat we don’t loveLacks well-suited drink storageEMS Glacier lightweight rolltop 20lEMSGlacier lightweight rolltop 20lfrom£49.99£49.99 at Mountain Warehouse£49.99 at DebenhamsWhat we loveLight and compactWhat we don’t loveStingy side pocketsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£49.99 at Mountain Warehouse£49.99 at DebenhamsBest for:a lightweight optionNeed a small, feather-light backpack to sling into a larger pack you’re taking on a camping trip? This rolltop model from EMS is a good choice, as it can be folded up to squish into a particularly tight space.I found this bag to be a basic but effective option for day hikes. The bungee cord on the front is useful for stowing unwanted layers during strenuous exercise, and the rolltop closure works just as it should. It’s impressively adjustable for its size, with waist and chest straps to ensure a stable fit and comfortable weight distribution.It didn’t make the final cut because…the side pockets are stingy.Capacity:20l;weight:680g;waterproof?No, but it is water resistantEMSGlacier lightweight rolltop 20lfrom£49.99£49.99 at Mountain Warehouse£49.99 at DebenhamsWhat we loveLight and compactWhat we don’t loveStingy side pocketsWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenHarness the power: shoulder, waist and chest straps help distribute your backpack’s load more evenly.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianAre backpacks better for your body?Backpacks can placeless strain on the bodythan comparable types of bags such as shoulder bags or satchels. The two straps of a backpack can distribute weight across the shoulders, rather than overloading one shoulder. Plus, using a backpack’s available chest or waist straps helps distribute the load across the torso.Making full use of a backpack’s adjustment features is essential to getting the best possible fit and minimising discomfort. Tighten the shoulder straps enough to make the bag rest against your back, but not so closely that it limits movement. If your backpack has them, cinch the chest strap (or sternum strap) across the top of your chest, and secure the waist strap around the tops of your hip bones. Ideally, your hips will bear as much weight than your shoulders do.Some backpacks are sold as men’s or women’s, with specific designs that account for average differences in male and female proportions. Fit is individual, however, and the best option is the one that fits your body comfortably. I tested unisex backpacks for this article.Are backpacks waterproof?Most backpacks have some level of water resistance, so they can withstand a certain amount of rain before letting water through. However, only a minority of backpacks are waterproof to the same extent asthe most effective waterproof jackets. Where relevant, the level of water resistance or waterproofness should be indicated in the manufacturer’s product description, usually as a specification such as “hydrostatic head” (which tells you how much water pressure is needed to cause a material to let water through, in millimetres).You can protect a backpack from wet weather by using it with a rain cover, which is a detachable accessory that fits tightly over the bag. Some backpacks come with a rain cover in a dedicated storage pocket. If your rucksack doesn’t include a rain cover, I would recommend getting one. I’ve been usingthisFjällrävenmodelfor more than five years, and it still keeps my day-to-day backpacks perfectly dry.For more, read our guides to thebest carry-on luggageand thebest suitcases for your next holidayPete Wise is a writer from Leeds. A frequent contributor to the Filter, Pete has undertaken some of our most intrepid product-reviewing quests, including testingtravel mugson a trampette and stress-testingsuitcasesby hurling them from a ladder. His best and most challenging backpack-toting adventure of 2026 was a hike across the North PenninesExplore more on these topicsWalkingThe FilterFitnessHobbiesHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

description: Thoroughly British, a bit rustic, and very much an early-autumn treat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Thoroughly British, a bit rustic, and very much an early-autumn treat
Content: Pignut’s hedgerow highball.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenPignut’s hedgerow highball.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Pignut’s hedgerow highball – recipeThoroughly British, a bit rustic, and very much an early-autumn treatLaurissa HeywoodFri 4 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis easy, food-friendly drink is built around the flavours of the countryside – sharp apple, local honey, garden herbs – rather than imported citrus. A touch of blackberry gives colour and depth without turning it too sweet, and echoes the kind of preserves and foraged fruit that run through our food menu.Hedgerow highballServes140ml London dry gin– any classic dry one will do50ml cloudy apple juice, ideally a tart one1 tsp local honey1 tsp blackberry jam or preserve2 small sprigs fresh thymeSparkling wine, to top1 blackberry, or 1 thin apple slice, to garnishMeasure the gin, apple juice, honey and jam into a cocktail shaker or jam jar filled with ice, then add the thyme and shake hard for about 10 seconds, so the honey and jam dissolve. Fine strain into an ice-filled highball glass, top with sparkling wine (ideally a local one), garnish with a blackberry or slice of apple, and serve.Laurissa Heywood, co-owner,Pignut & The Hare, Scawton, North YorkshireExplore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodFruitAutumn food and drinkBritish food and drinkWinerecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for brown butter apple and blackberry bars | Food | The Guardian
description: A bar for the bountiful season, with a rubbly oat crust, a soft fruit filling and a crisp topping
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: A bar for the bountiful season, with a rubbly oat crust, a soft fruit filling and a crisp topping
Content: Helen Goh’s brown butter apple and blackberry bars.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s brown butter apple and blackberry bars.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotFoodHelen Goh’s recipe for brown butter apple and blackberry barsA bar for the bountiful season, with a rubbly oat crust, a soft fruit filling and a crisp toppingHelen GohFri 4 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeptember is always a wistful time for me. Summer has all but slipped away, the days are noticeably shorter and the children are heading back to school. But there is comfort, too, in settling back into familiar routines. These bars, with their buttery oat crust, soft fruit filling and crisp, golden topping, are just the sort of thing to have waiting for whenever everyone drifts home. I like to use a mixture of apples – some that soften and collapse into the filling, others that hold their shape – to give the bars a little more texture and interest.Brown butter apple and blackberry barsThese will keep for up to three days in an airtight container, and also freeze well, wrapped individually for convenience.Prep10 minCook1 hr 20 minMakes12 barsFor the crumb base and topping250g unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing1 tsp anise seeds(optional)220g plain flour95g rolled oats80g oat flour, or blitz rolled oats until finely ground150g light brown sugar½ tsp fine sea saltFor the fruit filling750g apples(5-6 medium apples), peeled, cored and cut into 1cm dice (about 600g net weight)80g caster sugarFinely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemon3tbsp lemon juiceSeeds from ½ vanilla bean pod, or ½tsp vanilla bean paste1 bay leaf1 cinnamon stick1 pinchfine sea salt1½ tbsp cornflour300g blackberriesGrease and line a 20cm x 30cm baking tin with greaseproof paper, leaving enough overhang to help lift out the bars later. Put the butter in a medium saucepan on a medium heat and cook, swirling the pan occasionally, for about five minutes, until it smells nutty and the milk solids turn a deep golden brown. Take off the heat, stir in the anise seeds, if using, then leave to cool for five minutes.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Meanwhile, mix the plain flour, rolled oats, oat flour, brown sugar and salt in a large bowl. Pour over the browned butter, including all the toasted milk solids, and mix until evenly moistened. The mixture should resemble damp sand and hold together when squeezed.Reserve about 350g of the crumb mix for the topping, then tip the rest into the lined tin, pressing firmly into an even layer ; use the base of a measuring cup or back of a spoon. This will help the bars hold together neatly when slicing. Bake for 18 minutes, until lightly golden around the edges.While the base is in the oven, make the filling. Put the diced apples, sugar, lemon zest and juice, vanilla, bay, cinnamon and salt in a large, deep frying pan on medium-high heat and cook, stirring occasionally, for five minutes, until the apples have softened slightly but still hold their shape.Mix the cornflour with a tablespoon of water to make a smooth slurry, then stir into the apples. Cook for 30 seconds, until the juices thicken, then gently fold in the blackberries, just long enough for some to soften and colour the apples, while leaving plenty still whole. Discard the bay leaf and cinnamon stick.Spread the fruit evenly over the baked base, then squeeze handfuls of the reserved crumb into irregular clusters and scatter over the fruit. A few gaps are nice so the fruit can peek through. Bake for 40-45 minutes, until the topping is deeply golden and the fruit juices are bubbling around the edges. Leave to cool completely in the tin before slicing into bars.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotBakingFruitSnacksBritish food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: New Zealand drugs regulator approves use of MDMA to treat severe PTSD | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: New Zealand decision follows Australian approval in 2023 of psychedelics to treat PTSD and treatment-resistant depression
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: New Zealand decision follows Australian approval in 2023 of psychedelics to treat PTSD and treatment-resistant depression
Content: Consumed primarily for its euphoric effects, MDMA has now been approved in New Zealand to treat trauma.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConsumed primarily for its euphoric effects, MDMA has now been approved in New Zealand to treat trauma.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesNew ZealandNew Zealand drugs regulator approves use of MDMA to treat severe PTSDNew Zealand decision follows Australian approval in 2023 of psychedelics to treat PTSD and treatment-resistant depressionAgence France-PresseFri 4 Sep 2026 00.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo psychiatrists inNew Zealandwon approval on Friday to prescribe pharmaceutical-grade MDMA to people with severe post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).The move by New Zealand’s pharmaceutical regulatory body Medsafe makes the country only the second worldwide to approve the party drug for use in treating PTSD, following Australia in 2023.“PTSD ruins lives and is difficult to treat,” said the deputy prime minister, David Seymour, who last year backed the approval of magic mushrooms to treat people with severe depression. “MDMA can be very effective at treating it through psychedelic-assisted therapy.”Australian approval of MDMA and psilocybin a ‘baby step in the right direction’, medical experts sayRead moreNew Zealand is committed to opening up access to “innovative treatments”, Seymour said.PTSD is a mental health condition that develops after a person experiences or is threatened by traumatic events such as death, combat or sexual assault.There are clinical trials in the United States after the Food and Drug Administration rejected legalising MDMA’s medicinal use in 2024, saying there was not enough evidence it was safe or effective.Pharmaceutical treatment options for PTSD in the US have so far been limited to two antidepressants that require three months of dosing to take effect. Response rates to the medications have been uneven.A study in Israel last year found that MDMA taken by partygoers at the Nova music festival when hundreds were killed by Hamas in the 7 October attacks had been helpful in cushioning the impact of the trauma they endured.Wellington’s Ministry ofHealthsaid MDMA-assisted treatment would be combined with psychotherapy and stressed that patients would not be supplied drugs to take home.“Treatment takes place in a controlled clinical setting under the care of an authorised psychiatrist and forms part of a comprehensive treatment plan,” the ministry said.Any patients would have to be aged 18 or older, it added.Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandDrugsMental healthHealthPsychiatrynewsShareReuse this content

title: For Gloria Steinem, fashion was about much more than aesthetics | Feminism | The Guardian
description: In an era when feminists were stereotyped as unattractive, the pioneering writer’s style created a Trojan horse
Author: Morwenna Ferrier
Headline: In an era when feminists were stereotyped as unattractive, the pioneering writer’s style created a Trojan horse
Content: Steinem speaking at the Democratic National Convention, 1972. Photograph: John Olson/Getty ImagesIn an era when feminists were stereotyped as unattractive, the pioneering writer’s style created a Trojan horseGloria Steinem obituaryGloria Steinem: A life in picturesByMorwenna FerrierFri 4 Sep 2026 09.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen people wanted to dismiss Gloria Steinem, they spoke about how she looked. Talking about the pioneering activist and journalist who turned feminism into a major civil rights movement, it might seem reductive to focus on her glasses.But after Steinem –whose death at 92 was announced on Thursday– wore them on the cover of Newsweek in 1971 next to the cover-line The New Woman, the lightly tinted aviators – often worn over her hair – became an accidental form of self-branding that made her instantly recognisable. They were as indelibly linked to her legacy as Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s jabots or even Anna Wintour’s sunglasses. They also became one of her greatest weapons.View image in fullscreenSteinem on the cover of Newsweek on 16 August 1971.Photograph: NW Media Holdings CorpNever mind that she had to wear them. Coming from a nearsighted family, she bought the oversized men’s wire Ray-Ban Bausch & Lomb aviators in the late ’60s because she found standard women’s frames too small.“People were always pinching me on the cheek and so I felt I had a very fat face,”she told Teen Voguein 2011. “Those things were undercurrent somewhere, you know, causing me to wear my hair down and wear big glasses.” She was also an anxious public speaker, and liked to hide behind them.View image in fullscreenAnna Wintour, Gloria Steinem, Savannah Guthrie and Mindy Kaling attend the Michael Kors Collection Fall/Winter 2023 Runway Show in New York, February 2023.Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images  for Michael KorsIn the end, along with the centre-parted hair, the bell-bottoms, ribbed polo necks and low-slung concho belts, her look would become a sort of aesthetic armour which charmed and disarmed her critics.It was never about fashion. To Steinem, getting dressed and indeed controlling one’s image were simply part of a woman’s right to choose; clothing as agency. Today’s politicians strategically use clothes to shape public opinion, but Steinem’s style was less about optics and more about creating a Trojan horse. Because once she had our attention, whether at a rally or on TV, she could quickly pivot to delivering uncompromising messages on reproductive rights or systemic sexism.View image in fullscreenSteinem at a fundraiser and rally for the California state senate candidate Catherine O’Neill at actor Lorne Greene’s LA house in 1972.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesDuring the height of the women’s lib movement, her bohemian-tinged wardrobe reflected the fashion of its era. But it also felt relatable. She was the poster girl for politicised youth: Love Story prep meets downtown thrift store. This was particularly pertinent given how relentlessly the mainstream media stereotyped feminists as unattractive. Steinem understood the media landscape better than many, and used her personal image to challenge the patriarchal assumption that smart women should blend into the background – or even that feminists looked like bra-burning radicals.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Brenda Vaccaro, Lynn Redgrave, Liz Torres and Lee Grant dressed as Steinem in the CBS television special The Shape of Things in 1973.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesYet Steinem’s look was scrutinised like that of no other woman in politics, often by other women. Even at the height of her career, the Washington Post columnist Maxine Cheshire described Steinem as“the miniskirted pinup girl of the intelligentsia”.In the early days of Ms magazine, which she founded in 1971, she indeed wore miniskirts, but became more famous for her tight high-waisted jeans, which she described as “anti-fashion” but were largely about practicality. At the women’s conventions, they were putting the tables out, printing flyers. She wore what she wore because it was easier to do her job.View image in fullscreenSteinem wearing overblouse and matching skirt by Sloat, 1964.Photograph: Frances McLaughlin-Gill/Conde Nast/Getty ImagesHer influence on fashion might be more cultural than actual – her blond-streaked hair has even been adopted by gen Z – but she certainly wielded influence over the industry. Unsurprisingly, she turned up on various fashion mood boards, including those of the designers Roland Mouret and Michael Kors. In turn, Steinem occasionally also wore Kors pieces. Her fringed jackets and boho-inflected blouses wouldn’t look out of place on a Celine or Chloe catwalk today.Steinem herself had some interest in trends, but was largely influenced by Audrey Hepburn, Wonder Woman and women she met around the world. As she once said: “Fashion in the past meant conforming and losing oneself; fashion in the present means being unique and finding oneself.”As she got older, the hair got shorter and the clothes grew more sober. In the spirit of Steve Jobs, she leaned towards an all-black get-up, something she “inherited” fromother New Yorkers, she said earlier this year. “You didn’t have to worry about what matched what.”View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem and Michael Kors at the Michael Kors collection fall/winter 2023 runway show in New York.Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images  for Michael KorsBut she always played with accessories, zhushing up her bodysuits with waist-grazing necklaces, though her real weapon were the belts, worn partly because you didn’t have to change your clothes, and partly because they had “a resonance from the past before patriarchy came along”, as she told Lena Dunham in 2015. It was also a great way to offset the activism pins, little signifiers which she integrated directly into her wardrobe, though her greatest “statement” look was probably the “I had an abortion” T-shirt she wore aged 70 (Steinem had an illegal abortion aged 22).View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem in East Hampton, New York in 1970.Photograph: Naomi Lasdon/Newsday/Getty ImagesEarlier this year, Steinem opened up her New York brownstone to auction off 40 personal belongings to raise money for her foundation. Pieces included enamel and silver-tone belts, block-printed jackets and various fringed jackets with activist pins still attached. But the clue was always in the sell – “Own a piece of history”, it read. And as someone who ultimately proved that a woman didn’t have to disguise her femininity to be taken seriously as an intellectual and political force, what a history that was.Explore more on these topicsFeminismWomenNewspapersMagazinesNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Will we have to choose different plants for hotter, drier summers? | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: Increasing heatwaves mean we need to rethink what we grow. The good news? You can still go cottagecore
Author: Alice Vincent
Headline: Increasing heatwaves mean we need to rethink what we grow. The good news? You can still go cottagecore
Content: Hollyhocks did well in the heat.Photograph: Alex Manders/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHollyhocks did well in the heat.Photograph: Alex Manders/Getty ImagesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Gardening adviceWill we have to choose different plants for hotter, drier summers?Increasing heatwaves mean we need to rethink what we grow. The good news? You can still go cottagecoreAlice VincentFri 4 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe only spot-watering my garden has seen in recent months was done by the builder in a quiet moment. I hadn’t asked him to, but I think he saw the state of things and took pity on an acer I’d given up on. I explained I’d been using the drought as an, admittedly extreme, experiment to find which plants are resilient to multiple heatwaves, but said he was welcome to take the acer back to his well-irrigated garden.My observations are that the roses hung in there. Not flowering, as I’ve seen others doing, but mine are probably younger. The wildflower meadow has been surprisingly floriferous; it’s been a good year for zinnias – although not good enough to make me like them. The volunteer buddleja that was hacked to the ground in April made an Oasis-worthy comeback.Euphorbias,meconopsis,sage,erigeron: all fine. Volunteer robinia saplings loved life. Verbascum coped. My son has been eating passion fruit straight from the vine.double quotation markHoneysuckle, roses and hollyhocks – many drought-tolerant plants are cottage garden favouritesThe reason so many of us find gardening relaxing, I think, is because it is one of the ultimate acts of observation. Consider every time you embark on a spontaneous tour of the garden with a friend or family member, how nice it is to potter about pointing things out or discussing how something is growing. This summer has been brutal for many reasons, but ignoring the wake-up call for changing how we grow things is daft. The English garden needs to be one that can survive two months without rain, just as much as flash flooding.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI used to be intimidated by roses. But they are not as high-maintenance as you thinkRead moreGarden designer and author Jack Wallington has collected responses from others who have been watching their gardens dessicate with a mixture of horror and fascination. Over on his newsletter,Wild Way, he’s collated a list of truly drought-tolerant plants from their feedback. What’s notable is how many of them are traditional cottage garden plants: honeysuckle, roses, hollyhocks and ferns, peonies, geraniums and ivy. If you still want to go cottagecore, you can.But what’s perhaps more interesting is all the other plants you may not have previously considered, which are thriving.California poppiesfor colour hits,Calamagrostis‘Karl Foerster’– a particularly beautiful grass that I’ve grown in part-shade as well as full sun – for perennial structure and texture.Gaura lindheimeriand‘Whirling butterflies’, which I find endlessly pretty, and even hydrangeas (notorious moisture-suckers), which I saw looking fantastic in a friend’s garden recently.September marks the start of the planting season. Before choosing plants for your garden, it’s best to consider how much water they’re really going to need.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Seeds of hope: how a local farming project is offering a lifeline to Gaza | Farming | The Guardian
description: Family-run Al-Qarara Seed Bank is helping to counter acute food insecurity after being destroyed in the war
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Family-run Al-Qarara Seed Bank is helping to counter acute food insecurity after being destroyed in the war
Content: Hanadi Salama Muhanna, 38, daughter of seed bank owner Salama Muhanna, holds seeds at the Al-Qarara Seed Bank in Deir al-Balah, Gaza.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersView image in fullscreenHanadi Salama Muhanna, 38, daughter of seed bank owner Salama Muhanna, holds seeds at the Al-Qarara Seed Bank in Deir al-Balah, Gaza.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersFarmingSeeds of hope: how a local farming project is offering a lifeline to GazaFamily-run Al-Qarara Seed Bank is striving to help Palestinians gain sovereignty over their food securityTamara DavisonFri 4 Sep 2026 08.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSalama Ayesh Muhanna still remembers the first seeds he planted on his family’s land in al-Qarara,Gaza. At just 17, Muhanna had proudly sprouted cucumbers.“I was very happy because I saw the results,” Muhanna says. “We were farmers at heart.”Now 71, he is an agronomist, a community leader and the founder of the Al-Qarara Seed Bank.The original project, founded in 2017, was situated near the eastern border of Gaza in al-Qarara, an area now completely flattened and inaccessible. Back then, Muhanna had a large home, olive trees, land of his own, and a successful seed bank operation with dedicated storage and equipment. Everything was destroyed early in Israel’s brutal military campaign, but after being displaced to Deir al-Balah in 2024, Muhanna and his daughter Hanadi, 38, are now hard at work, regrowing seed collections at Gaza’s only seed bank.Outside the tent where they currently live in a displacement camp, summer temperatures climb to almost 35C. Another tent houses their small but growing collection of open-pollinated, non-GMO seeds, including local wheat and vegetables such as okra and spinach.View image in fullscreenSalama Muhanna with his daughter Hanadi inside the seed bank.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersEach day, Muhanna rises early to check on the project, a 200-metre-wide plot of land where the family lives, collects seeds, and experiments with new crops. He inspects the seeds to assess their quality, waters crops and checks on seedlings. As the manager of the seed bank, Hanadi deals with local farmers and oversees the growing seed collection – all while studying agriculture and food sovereignty online via a programme partly tied to Coventry University and the Gaza Urban Agriculture Forum. Muhanna jokes that his hard-working daughter will be “managing her father” by next year.The project has two main aims. One is to collect and preserve the seeds of local plants that may thrive better in this landscape. “The war forced farmers to resort to local seeds,” says Hanadi, because of the ongoing blockades on seed imports, rocketing food prices and growing hunger across Gaza. Yet it appears that this focus on local seed varieties – “baladi” seeds – may prove more effective. That, Muhanna says, is because “local seeds are resistant to drought, fungi, and pests”.“During the war, they’ve been our lifeline,” he adds.The project’s other aim is to create a node for seed distribution for farmers who need to save every possible penny. The seeds, once collected, are distributed among Palestinian farmers and families in Deir al-Balah who then return the same amount after harvest. Approximately 200 farmers have so far benefited thanks to Muhanna and Hanadi’s seeds, with support from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). Beyond multiplying seed collections, it is helping Palestinian farmers reclaim agricultural agency and self-reliance – providing for families despite devastating restrictions on resources including vital humanitarian aid.View image in fullscreenMuhanna says the seeds could be key to future food sovereignty in Gaza.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersThe seeds are deeply connected to memories of the Palestinian land Muhanna has always called home – and could, he hopes, be key to future food sovereignty in Gaza. “The pumpkin plant reminds me of my father and mother,” he says. “It grew on the vineyard where we lived when I was little.”The needs have never been more urgent. At least 1.2 million people in Gaza now face acute food insecurity amid an escalating humanitarian crisis, according to anew reportby the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC). Despitegrowing alarmamong humanitarian organisations, Israel continues to block access to agricultural land and the import of seeds and organic fertiliser. Meanwhile, dwindling water supplies, degraded soil and deadly remnants of explosives make farming a treacherous practice.“Walking in the streets is unsafe, and walking on the land is unsafe,” Muhanna says, adding that the psychological impact affects their work. “The war destroyed my hope.”Despite immense challenges, the family know their seeds are helping the community while preserving indigenous species against agricultural monopolies, and safeguarding Palestine’s agricultural heritage.As Muhanna puts it, seeds are “my identity, my patriotism, my nationality”.Pat Griffiths, ICRC’ spokesperson in Jerusalem, said: “This is about agency. It’s about dignity. It’s about being less dependent on what is or is not allowed to enter Gaza. As the occupying power, Israel has an obligation to make sure that Palestinians in Gaza have access to the food, goods and items that they need to live.”There is still a long way to go in returning the seed bank to its former size. Muhanna says that before the war, they had about 42 types of local seeds. “Now we have about 28.”There is also another looming challenge that could affect the seed bank’s future.View image in fullscreenSalama Muhanna inside the seed bank: ‘During the war, they’ve been our lifeline.’Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters“Climate change is what controls us,” Muhanna says, as he sips his tea and shelters inside from the sun. “When the weather is hot, the seeds spoil.” Sometimes he has to plant almost a month later than normal, delaying harvests in a race against time to gather resilient seeds for the future. Still they keep going, experimenting in their fields to see which local seeds produce the best yields. And with almost 2.5 tonnes of seeds collected so far – better than last year – there are signs that the efforts are working.With each seed, there is hope in Gaza that sovereignty over food security can soon take root.“Any country in the world that doesn’t have sovereignty over food security isn’t a country,” Muhanna says. “If we establish sovereignty over food security, then we’ll be a real country.”Explore more on these topicsFarmingGazaMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineFood securityfeaturesShareReuse this content
