title: UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale | Africa | The Guardian
description: Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland
Content: Africa on the traditional world map based on the Mercator projection, left, and on the 2018 Equal Earth map, right.Composite: equal-earth.com, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAfrica on the traditional world map based on the Mercator projection, left, and on the 2018 Equal Earth map, right.Composite: equal-earth.com, Getty ImagesAfricaUN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scaleTogo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to GreenlandEromo Egbejulein AbidjanFri 4 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 22.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUnited Nationshas voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design.At the session, 164 countries voted in favour of the resolution. Only the US voted no, with its representative saying the resolution was “superfluous”. There were six abstentions.UN resolutions are non-enforceable, so countries and institutions will not be mandated to use only the new projection or forbidden from using the old one. However, the outcome is expected to result in an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.View image in fullscreenThe 1569 map by Gerardus Mercator (1512-1594) has remained the global standard.Photograph: Stock Montage/Getty ImagesTogo, which spearheaded a campaign for the resolution on behalf of theAfrican Union, said the resolution “recognises and affirms that disproportionate cartographic representations, particularly those resulting from the Mercator projection, have had lasting cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic effects, contributing to a drastic reduction in the perceived size of Africa and other regions of the world in the global collective imagination”.Speaking before the resolution passed, Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality.”The Mercator layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later, it remains the global standard.Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map showsAfricaas being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says apetitionon Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.On Friday, before the vote, France’s foreign minister spoke in support of the resolution. “[We] will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists,” Jean-Noël Barrot said during a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris, in a move seen as part of France’s push to increase goodwill among its former colonies.France will now use the Eckert IV projection, which is close to the Equal Earth projection recommended in the resolution.View image in fullscreenA comparison of the Mercator and the Eckert IV mapsIllustration: French foreign ministryHistorians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.View image in fullscreenThe 1973 Gall-Peters world map has been used as an alternative to the Mercator.Photograph: Michael Schmeling/AlamySome argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This is said to have reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.View image in fullscreenThe 2018 Equal Earth Map.Photograph: equal-earth.comTogo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign promoted the use of the 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.Some analysts agree. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.He said: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”View image in fullscreenA map of Africa from Mercator’s atlas dating from between 1595 and 1602.Photograph: Royal Geographical Society/Getty ImagesTogo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.Speaking before the vote, Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say: why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”Explore more on these topicsAfricaUnited NationsTogoAfrican UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s ‘retribution’ could now include Falklands as favor to Milei – and revenge on the UK | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: US president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands
Content: The Falkland Islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, on 16 March 2026.Photograph: Ricardo Mazalán/APView image in fullscreenThe Falkland Islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, on 16 March 2026.Photograph: Ricardo Mazalán/APDonald TrumpAnalysisTrump’s ‘retribution’ could now include Falklands as favor to Milei – and revenge on the UKRobert Taitin WashingtonUS president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islandsFri 4 Sep 2026 16.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 21.01 EDTShareDonald Trumphas long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” hedeclaredto an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House.It is unlikelyArgentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time.But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president.Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas.Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland IslandsRead moreThe centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory.Britain reclaimed them after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender.An uneasy peace has reigned in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their fewer than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British.This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over theFalkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now?Milei jumped onTrump’s commentthat he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control.Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’sdeep-rooted suspicions of Britainand its imperial past.The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked.And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf.In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday.“Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said, ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets.It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump.Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China.Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran.He has repeatedlythreatened to bombor “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping.The White House also announcedthe withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germanyafter the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict.Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally.Turbulence under TrumpBut Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side.Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did.Javier Milei: ‘winds of change’ support Argentina’s claim to Falkland IslandsRead moreThis time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him.But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of afamous speechin 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa.“The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.”In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced.He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor which may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses.Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes.But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpArgentinaFalkland IslandsTrump administrationUS foreign policyUS politicsAmericasanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Colombia president provokes disgust by posing with bodies of ‘terrorists’ | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Abelardo De La Espriella posts video of himself with rows of body bags as performative populism continues to sweep Americas
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Abelardo De La Espriella posts video of himself with rows of body bags as performative populism continues to sweep Americas
Content: Still from video posted on social media by Abelardo De La Espriella (centre).Photograph: Abelardo De La EspriellaView image in fullscreenStill from video posted on social media by Abelardo De La Espriella (centre).Photograph: Abelardo De La EspriellaColombiaColombia president provokes disgust by posing with bodies of ‘terrorists’Abelardo De La Espriella posts video of himself with rows of body bags as performative populism continues to sweep AmericasTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroFri 4 Sep 2026 09.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColombia’s hardline president, Abelardo De La Espriella, has provoked outrage after posting a video on social media in which he strides through rows of white body bags that he says contained the corpses of 23 “neutralised” guerrillas.De La Espriella took power last month vowing “all-out war” against illegal armed groups and he publishedthe footageon Thursday in an apparent attempt to show he was fulfilling that pledge.Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?Read more“I promised to confront terrorism without hesitation and I’m keeping that promise,” the far-right politician wrote above the video. “I did not come to play nice with murderers, extortionists and child recruiters. I came to defeat them … Long live Christ the king!”Celebrating the military operation in the Colombian Amazon during which the 23 alleged terrorists were killed, De La Espriella declared: “We are utterly determined to destroy you, who are a cancer.”The body bag footage, set to a stirring Hollywood-style score, was condemned by human rights activists and the president’s political opponents.Iván Cepeda, the leftwing candidate beaten by De La Espriella in June’s election,wrote on X: “He strolls among the bags with the corpses. He nearly treads on them with contempt. He calls himself a Christian but in reality he’s an unscrupulous being lacking the slightest sense of humanity.”View image in fullscreenIván Cepeda at a campaign rally in Bogotá in June.Photograph: Mauricio Dueñas Castañeda/EPAThe leftwing lawmaker Daniel Monroy accused the president of “necropolitics”.He wrote: “This is one of the most bizarre things we’ve seen. Strolling among the dead, while invoking the name of God, just to justify an unnecessary spectacle.”De La Espriella’s predecessor Gustavo Petro tweeted: “This is called turning death into a trophy – something only soulless people can do … The soulless find it easy to kill for the sake of killing.”De La Espriella hit back at his critics, posting: “Forgiving terrorists is God’s business. Sending them to meet him – if that’s where they’re headed – is the president’s job.”De La Espriella’s post captured the bellicose and performative political zeitgeist sweeping theAmericas, where a growing number of rightwing populists are seeking to woo voters with promises of ferocious, TikTokable crackdowns on crime.The genre has been pioneered by El Salvador’s authoritarian president, Nayib Bukele, with slick videos of hisnotorious mega-prison, and Donald Trump, who has repeatedly published footage showing allegeddrug boats being blitzedin the Caribbean and Pacific.Ahead of Brazil’s October elections, several candidates are promising lethal attacks on the drug traffickers who control Rio de Janeiro’s favelas. “We’re going to stain the ground red with the blood of these lowlifes,” one candidate, Renan Santos, said recently, promising “a bloodbath” if he won power.Flávio Bolsonaro, the main challenger to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has vowed to wage war on “narco-terrorists”, although he and close allies have themselves been accused of having ties to organised crime. “Criminals will be taken out of circulation, either standing up or lying down,” Bolsonaro has said.In Rio, Felipe Curi, a former police chief running for congress, has posted AI-generated videos depicting him shooting armed men in the favelas. Campaignpropagandafeatures his image superimposed on pictures of the corpses of some of the 122 people killed during the city’sdeadliest ever police raids. “I arrest crooks,” Curi boasts in one video, “and I neutralise them if they react.”Explore more on these topicsColombiaAmericasThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Javier Milei: ‘winds of change’ support Argentina’s claim to Falkland Islands | Argentina | The Guardian
description: President cites Trump’s suggestion that he might reconsider US stance on British sovereignty and threatens swifter sanctions on UK oil interests
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: President cites Trump’s suggestion that he might reconsider US stance on British sovereignty and threatens swifter sanctions on UK oil interests
Content: Supporters had expected Milei to use his address to announce an unprecedented US endorsement of Argentina’s claim.Photograph: Juan Mabromata/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSupporters had expected Milei to use his address to announce an unprecedented US endorsement of Argentina’s claim.Photograph: Juan Mabromata/AFP/Getty ImagesArgentinaJavier Milei: ‘winds of change’ support Argentina’s claim to Falkland IslandsPresident cites Trump’s suggestion that he might reconsider US stance on British sovereignty and threatens swifter sanctions on UK oil interestsTiago RogeroSouth America correspondentFri 4 Sep 2026 05.31 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 01.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePresident Javier Milei has said “winds of change” favourable to Argentina’s claim to the Falkland Islands are blowing around the world in a televised address, citing signs thatDonald Trump may reconsider the US positionon the islands’ sovereignty.“Recently, President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas,” he said, using the Argentinian name for the islands.The Argentinian president said the UK was facing “multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. It is clear that they are on a path of decline. Argentina’s future, however, is flourishing and will prevail.”Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland IslandsRead moreEarlier on Thursday, the British outlet GB News asked Trump if he would “come to the UK’s aid” during a potential territorial dispute with Argentina over theFalkland Islands, and hinted that he would not, adding that the UK “weren’t there to help me [with Iran]”.Supporters had expected Milei to use his address to the nation on Thursday night to announce an unprecedented US endorsement of Argentina’s sovereignty claim over the Falklands.Instead, the far-right self-styled libertarian merely referred to Trump’s words last Monday. Asked at the White House whether he was reviewing the US position on the islands, the US president had said: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”Milei portrayed Trump’s response as a “threat” that was “not innocuous”.“The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina is a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” he said.View image in fullscreenStanley, the capital of the Falkland Islands. In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the islanders voted to remain a British overseas territory.Photograph: Rob Carter/AlamyThe US has formally recognised the UK’s de facto administration of the islands but has not taken a formal position on sovereignty. The first reports of a possible revision emerged in April, when an internal Pentagon emailreported by Reutersraised the prospect of Washington reconsidering its stance as one possible way of punishing Nato allies that declined to join the Iran war.In Thursday’s interview, Trump said of the UK: “Your country was not there to help me. We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader [Keir Starmer], ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said, ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”Despite the expectations created by Milei and his supporters – the president summoned all his ministers to stand alongside him – the main new elements of the speech were a few decrees he announced.One of them was to speed up sanctions “against those participating in oil extraction initiatives”, specifically citing an offshore oil project in the North Falkland Basin led by the Israeli company Navitas alongside its British partner, Rockhopper. Milei claimed the project violated a UN call for neither Argentina nor the UK to take unilateral action in the territory.Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?Read moreDespite his “radical” austerity policies, Milei also said he would sign an emergency decree to increase resources for the defence ministry, prioritising the construction of an integrated naval base in Tierra del Fuego. The project to build a base there predates Milei, and construction began in 2022.The UK said earlier this week that its position on the Falklands was “longstanding and unwavering”. It said in a statement: “Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders’ right to self-determination is paramount. The UK’s position is clear. The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory.”Some analysts had already viewed Milei’s embrace of the Malvinas cause as another attempt tocreate a “smokescreen”, at the lowest point of his popularity since taking office. He is expected to seek re-election next year.Amid corruption allegations involving members of his government, and poor economic results – his “chainsaw” austerity policies have brought inflation under control, but unemployment and poverty have risen – the far-right president has increasingly turned up the volume on controversial measures. These include claims of ananti-Argentina campaigndating back to the World Cup, attacks on Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and animmigration crackdownmodelled on the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).Many have noted that his interest in the Falklands issue is recent. Milei had long described himself as a great admirer of Margaret Thatcher, the British prime minister during the 1982 Falklands war, and only began adopting a public pro-sovereignty stance a few months ago, after reports emerged that the US might be reconsidering its position.He also dismissed the principle of self-determination invoked by the UK. In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the islanders voted to remain a British overseas territory.Echoing thesame phrase used by Argentina’s national football teamon a banner celebrating their victory over England in the World Cup semi-final, Milei said: “The Malvinas are Argentinian.”Explore more on these topicsArgentinaJavier MileiFalkland IslandsAmericasUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK hits back at Argentinian Falklands claim and insists islands remain British | Falkland Islands | The Guardian
description: Ed Miliband says Britain’s position remains ‘unwavering’ in response to remarks by Argentina’s president
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Ed Miliband says Britain’s position remains ‘unwavering’ in response to remarks by Argentina’s president
Content: Javier Milei making a television address on Thursday in which he said the ‘winds of change’ favoured his country’s claim to the Falklands.Photograph: Argentina's presidency press office/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJavier Milei making a television address on Thursday in which he said the ‘winds of change’ favoured his country’s claim to the Falklands.Photograph: Argentina's presidency press office/AFP/Getty ImagesFalkland IslandsUK hits back at Argentinian Falklands claim and insists islands remain BritishEd Miliband says Britain’s position remains ‘unwavering’ in response to remarks by Argentina’s presidentUK politics live – latest updatesKiran StaceyPolicy editorFri 4 Sep 2026 05.24 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish ministers have hit back after theArgentinian president said“winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the Falklands were “blowing around the world”.The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the UK would “resolutely uphold” the self-determination of the islands after the Argentinian president,Javier Milei, said his country needed to take them back.Miliband said in a post on X: “The UK’s position on theFalkland Islandsis unwavering. The islands are British and will remain so because that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders.“Their right of self-determination is paramount, grounded in international law and we will resolutely uphold it.”Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said Milei’s statement “tells us more about domestic politics inArgentinathan it does about the Falkland Islands”.Headded on X: “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British. Our commitment to the Falklands is absolute and unshakeable.”Lucy Powell, the education secretary, also insisted the islands were British, adding: “We will defend the right of those who live in the Falkland Islands to determine their own future.”The latest diplomatic spat over the south Atlantic archipelago came after comments by the US president, Donald Trump, who has cast doubt on American support for British control of the islands.View image in fullscreenMount Tumbledown behind Stanley on the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls Malvinas.Photograph: Ricardo Mazalán/APThe US has traditionally remained neutral on the Falklands’ sovereignty, while recognising Britain’s de facto control over them.Britain and Argentina fought a war over the islands in 1982, when British forces defeated Argentinian troops, who had landed there to stake a territorial claim.In more recent years, the British oil company Rockhopper and the Israeli company Navitas have been developing the Sea Lion oilfield, 140 miles to the north of the islands.Asked on Monday whether he could review British sovereignty over the islands as a way to push the UK to spend more on defence,Trump said: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”On Thursday, when questioned about whether the US would back the UK in the event of an Argentinian invasion, he referred to the government’s refusal to let him use British bases in his initial attack on Iran earlier this year.“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”He added: “The Falklands is very interesting because your country is not the same country it was 20 years ago, 25 years ago. That was a long time [ago], you went there and you just took it back very quickly. There was no games, so I don’t know if you’re prepared to do that.”On Thursday night, Milei highlighted Trump’s comments, saying: “President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas [the Argentinian name for the Falklands].”He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.Rockhopper’s shares dropped 7% in early trading on Friday.Explore more on these topicsFalkland IslandsJavier MileiArgentinaForeign policyDefence policyTrump administrationEd MilibandnewsShareReuse this content

title: South Korea pushes back on reports it is readying Hormuz deployment amid US pressure | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Seoul reportedly seeking parliamentary approval to send military assets to Middle East but president’s office plays down claims
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Seoul reportedly seeking parliamentary approval to send military assets to Middle East but president’s office plays down claims
Content: South Korean and US military forces taking part in a joint drill near the Southern Han River in Yeoju, South Korea.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSouth Korean and US military forces taking part in a joint drill near the Southern Han River in Yeoju, South Korea.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesSouth KoreaSouth Korea pushes back on reports it is readying Hormuz deployment amid US pressureSeoul reportedly seeking parliamentary approval to send military assets to Middle East but president’s office plays down claimsRaphael Rashidin SeoulFri 4 Sep 2026 03.47 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 05.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military assets to the strait of Hormuz amid pressure fromDonald Trumpover Seoul’s reluctance to provide support in the region, according to domestic media reports.Citing unnamed government and military sources, the reports published on Thursday and Friday said preparations were under way and that the government intended to seek parliamentary approval for a new deployment. The reports, which appeared in major South Korean outlets, said the exact scale and timing had not been agreed.But the presidential office pushed back, telling the Guardian that such reports were “different from the facts” and that “nothing related to the matter has been decided”, though it said the review was “continuing”.An official said: “Our government has been closely discussing with the international community ways to make practical contributions for the speedy restoration of free navigation in the strait of Hormuz and peace and stability in the Middle East.”Trump’s call for allied deployment to strait of Hormuz meets muted responseRead moreAccording to reports, the assets under consideration include a P-8 Poseidon aircraft, which would mark South Korea’s first overseas deployment of a maritime patrol aircraft, and a naval logistics support ship to provide rear support.One outlet, Seoul Broadcasting System, additionally reported that an explosive ordnance disposal team from the navy’s underwater demolition unit was part of the package.Any new deployment in principle would require review by the national security council, a cabinet resolution and approval from the national assembly.South Koreais highly dependenton the strait of Hormuz, importing more than 90% of its primary energy, including roughly 70% of crude oil through the waterway.View image in fullscreenThe office of South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, said ‘nothing related to the matter has been decided’ in response to the media reports.Photograph: YONHAP/EPAIn 2020, the government of the then president, Moon Jae-in, expanded the mandate of an existing anti-piracy unit off the coast of Somalia to cover the strait of Hormuz, rather than seeking parliamentary approval for a new deployment.South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, in March told parliament that any deployment to the strait would require the national assembly’s consent given how different the mission would be from the unit’s existing anti-piracy mandate.The reports come amid growing strains in the US-South Korea alliance. Trump has repeatedly complained in public that Seoul turned down his request for help over Iran,claiming in Augustthat South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had told him “No, thanks” despite the US stationingtens of thousands of troops on the peninsula.Days later, he ordered the Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises to be scaled back,shortening the drills by six days.Relations between the two allies have also been strained by delays implementing a $350bn investment package Seoul agreed with Washington last year, reports that the US hadrestricted intelligence sharingwith South Korea, and by a dispute over adata breach at the South Korean e-commerce company Coupang.Separately, Seoul has expressed interest in taking part in any renewed US-North Korea diplomacy, as Trump signalsopenness to another meetingwith Kim Jong-un.Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaDonald TrumpAsia PacificUS foreign policyStrait of HormuznewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s housing prices are trending down. See which suburbs have had the biggest falls | Housing | The Guardian
description: Cotality says prices have declined in most capital cities over winter. Search the data to see how they have changed in your area
Author: Nick Evershed
Headline: Cotality says prices have declined in most capital cities over winter. Search the data to see how they have changed in your area
Content: New houses and land for sale at a housing development in San Remo, Victoria.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenNew houses and land for sale at a housing development in San Remo, Victoria.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPThe CrunchHousingAustralia’s housing prices are trending down. See which suburbs have had the biggest fallsCotality says prices have declined in most capital cities over winter. Search the data to see how they have changed in your areaGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastNick EvershedandJonathan BarrettFri 4 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s property market is facing a rare price correction, as rising interest rates andless favourable tax settings for investorsaccelerate a downturn.Most capital cities recorded winter price falls, according to Cotality data, with Sydney leading the decline. That weakness is expected to continue, as higher inflation could lead tofurther interest rate hikes, denting demand.But the recent price falls are not uniform.In general, suburbs that previously recorded the biggest price increases also cooled the fastest. More affordable homes are also more likely to hold their value, given they are in demand by first home buyers aided by the government’s low-deposit scheme.Those who have owned their properties for longer are also likely to be sitting on significant gains, even after the recent falls.In some cities, including Brisbane, Perth and Darwin, home values are still up more than 10% over the past 12 months.And the falls have not done much to makeAustralian homes more affordable for prospective homeowners, given rising mortgage repayment rates have cut borrowing capacity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe CrunchOur data journalists showcase the most important charts and dataviz from the Guardian and around the web, free every fortnightEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAMP notes that while home prices have fallen recently, “it’s just a flick off the top after a 50% surge since the pandemic”.Explore more on these topicsHousingThe CrunchnewsShareReuse this content

title: Charles Perrottet denies asking brother as premier to appoint cabinet minister, Icac hears  | New South Wales politics | The Guardian
description: Charles says claims by developer Jean Nassif in an intercepted phone call that ‘we’re reshuffling the government’ did not reflect promises allegedly made to Nassif
Author: Penry Buckley
Headline: Charles says claims by developer Jean Nassif in an intercepted phone call that ‘we’re reshuffling the government’ did not reflect promises allegedly made to Nassif
Content: Charles Perrottet told Icac that claims by developer Jean Nassif heard on an intercepted phone call were not consistent with promises allegedly made to Nassif.Photograph: Nadir Kinani/AAPView image in fullscreenCharles Perrottet told Icac that claims by developer Jean Nassif heard on an intercepted phone call were not consistent with promises allegedly made to Nassif.Photograph: Nadir Kinani/AAPNew South Wales politicsCharles Perrottet denies asking brother as premier to appoint cabinet minister, Icac hearsCharles says claims by developer Jean Nassif in an intercepted phone call that ‘we’re reshuffling the government’ did not reflect promises allegedly made to NassifFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPenry BuckleyFri 4 Sep 2026 02.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 06.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe younger brother ofDominic Perrottethas denied asking his brother to appoint a cabinet minister to achieve outcomes for a property developer, a corruption inquiry has heard.Charles Perrottet told theIndependent Commission Against Corruption(Icac) on Friday that claims made in an intercepted phone call featuring developer Jean Nassif days before his brother became the NSW premier – in which Nassif described Dominic Perrottet as “my boy” – did not reflect promises allegedly made to Nassif.Dominic Perrottet is not a person of interest in Icac’s inquiry and is not accused of any wrongdoing.As part of its inquiry into alleged corruption in the NSW Liberals, Icac is investigating the allegation that conservative factional figures Charles Perrottet, Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis received prohibited donations totalling $2m from Nassif or his company Toplace between 2020 and 2023 in exchange for political outcomes.Those outcomes allegedly included damage to the career of David Elliott, a former NSW Liberal minister, who had opposed Nassif’s developments and the removal of the former building commissioner David Chandler, who was scrutinising defects in Toplace apartments.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailOn Friday, the commission heard a phone call featuring Nassif, lawfully intercepted by police, made on 2 October 2021. Three days later, Dominic Perrottet was chosen as premier by Liberal MPs, defeating Rob Stokes, under a deal Charles Perrottet helped broker between conservative and moderate factions.In the call, Nassif allegedly told a relative: “This week is going to be the worst week of my life … because we’re reshuffling the government.”“We thought we [had] done it, then this wanker the police minister he did it, and he had a caucus, and he convinced Rob Stokes to challenge my boy,” Nassif continued, saying he supported Perrottet’s campaign. “They’re my people, they’re the right wing.”Nassif told the relative he had been promised that then police minister Elliott and the then fair trading minister Kevin Anderson would be removed.“I put my lady in his position [sic], the consumer affairs minister … then I’m gonna … have to step on fucking David Chandler and get rid of him.”The former NSW fair trading minister Eleni Petinos has previously told the inquiry shemay have been used by fellow Liberals, including Chris Spence and Charles Perrotet, to get rid of Chandler, including attempts to persuade her Chandler was “dodgy”. She is not named in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.Property developer claimed ‘the premier is my best friend’ in tapped phone call, Icac hearsRead moreOn Friday, Charles Perrottet told counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, that following his brother’s accession as premier, he did not discuss the makeup of his cabinet with him. He later said he did recall “a conversation about the balance of women in the cabinet”, which he said he did not include names.He said he did not discuss Petinos, or put her forward for the fair trading portfolio. “Dom would have made his own decisions,” he said. He said he did not recall having a conversation with Nassif about Petinos.In another intercepted phone call to an unnamed person in January 2022, after Elliott had been moved to transport in a reshuffle the previous month, Nassif claimed he had “stripped him from his police ministry”.“I’m gonna fuck everyone. The commissioner, [in] a couple of weeks he’ll be gone.”Charles Perrottet, acknowledging that “commissioner” probably referred to Chandler, said: “You can’t take this seriously.”Chandler resigned in July 2022 citing concerns with Petinos, who was sacked in that month amid bullying allegations which she denied at the time. Chandler, who was later persuaded to reverse his resignation, is not a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.Charles Perrottet has repeatedly denied taking payments from Nassif for political outcomes, saying he would regularly lie to the developer, adding a “political flavour” to advice in order to chase payments for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, a firm controlled by Greenwood and Ellis.Charles Perrottet has previously told the inquiry he agreed that his wife, Anita Perrottet, would be remunerated for advice he had provided to Nassif through her business Macquarie Consulting via payments from lobbying companies Beckington, controlled by Ellis and Greenwood, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood.But on Friday he denied that a spreadsheet created by Ellis showed that $2m from Toplace would be evenly distributed between the three men. Anita Perrottet has told Icac payments of $660,999 to her were for genuine “strategic and marketing advice”.Charles Perrottet rejected the suggestion that his wife had lied to the commission about what the payments were for, saying he was not sure how much he may have disclosed to her.Dwyer suggested he had “outsmarted” himself “by not getting your stories entirely straight, because you fabricated evidence with Anita that you’ve given to this inquiry”.“Not at all,” said Charles Perrottet. As questioning came to a close, he accepted Dwyer’s suggestion that “sometimes in politics you say things that aren’t 100% the truth”.Dwyer said: “But you know, don’t you, that in the witness box in this commission you are obliged to tell the truth by law, 100% of the time.“I suggest you that you that you have repeatedly given false evidence under oath, and you have encouraged your wife Anita to give false evidence under oath.” He rejected this.Nassif, who fled Australia for rural Lebanon in 2022, withdrew from an expected appearance by video link on Friday after providing a medical certificate. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.Greenwood will appear before the commission again next week.The inquiry continues.Explore more on these topicsNew South Wales politicsDominic PerrottetIndependent Commission Against CorruptionNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australian ski resorts to close up to a month early due to global heating and El Niño | Australia weather | The Guardian
description: ‘Challenging’ weather conditions and lack of snowfall are being blamed after a winter that broke multiple heat records
Author: Graham Readfearn
Headline: ‘Challenging’ weather conditions and lack of snowfall are being blamed after a winter that broke multiple heat records
Content: Snow at Mount Buffalo, Victoria in July.Photograph: Marni Cordell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSnow at Mount Buffalo, Victoria in July.Photograph: Marni Cordell/The GuardianAustralia weatherAustralian ski resorts to close up to a month early due to global heating and El Niño‘Challenging’ weather conditions and lack of snowfall are being blamed after a winter that broke multiple heat recordsSign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereGraham ReadfearnEnvironment and climate correspondentFri 4 Sep 2026 02.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 02.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMajor Australian alpine resorts are closing their ski operations up to a month early after a winter that broke multiple records for heat with limited snow falls being washed away by rain.Predictions in June thata building El Niño could combine with global heating for a challenging ski season came to pass, with seven resorts either already closed or announcing ski lifts will stop operating this weekend.This week the Victorian resorts of Mount Buller, Mount Hotham and Falls Creek, together with Charlotte Pass in New South Wales, all announced ski operations would end this weekend.The Victorian resort of Mount Baw Baw, the NSW resort at Selwyn and Tasmania’s Ben Lomond have already closed. Resorts typically aim to stay open until the first weekend of October.Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletterResorts blamed “challenging” weather conditions and lack of snowfall. Two other major NSW resorts at Perisher and Thredbo remain open.“The season was frankly a shocker. This was the fourth disappointing season since 2020,” said Dr Andrew Watkins, a climate scientist and adjunct professor at the Monash University and a science adviser to the campaign group Protect our Winters.“The problems were El Niño and climate change. It was not that dry this year, but the problem was the warmth. The heat just did us in.”Watkins, who is also a keen skier, said winter temperatures had been too high and precipitation that might have fallen as snow, had instead fallen as rain.“Rain is the natural enemy of a snowpack. It melts it and then washes it away,” he said.0:40Footage shows first snow of the year falling at Perisher ski resort in New South Wales – videoData from the Bureau of Meteorology show Falls Creek and Mount Hotham had their wettest winters in more than 30 years but, together with Mount Buller, they also had their warmest winters on record for average maximum and minimum temperatures.Watkins said data from weather observations at Cabramurra in Kosciuszko national park suggested alpine winters had warmed by about 2C since the 1960s.He said that temperature rise would have been the difference between precipitation falling as rain instead of snow. “It would have been a bumper season if it had been 50 years ago,” he said.The El Niño currently in place in the Pacific Ocean can promote hotter and drier temperatures in Australia’s south-east in winter and spring.This weekthe bureau forecast the current El Niño would be the strongest on recordand Australian scientists said climate change had made the strength of the event six times more likely.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoM forecasts strongest El Niño on record as research points to ‘alarming’ climate change influenceRead moreA bureau spokesperson said this winter’s heat was consistent “with a developing strong El Niño” and the season had seen long periods of high pressure in the Tasman Sea that directed warmer air from the north over alpine regions.“But winter 2026 also experienced relatively warm nights, with cloud cover and moist soils resulting in less overnight cooling,” the spokesperson said.“This is in contrast with historical El Niño events. This is all occurring against the background of a globally warmer climate, with daily global surface air temperatures since June close to or above the record levels in 2024.”New South Wales, Tasmania and Victoria all recorded their hottest winters on record this year.In July, many ski resorts broke all-time heat records for the month with temperaturesduring one hot spell up to 12C above average.Climate scientists have been warning for decades that global heating will create a challenging future for Australia’s ski resorts and alpine habitats.Josh Elliott, chief executive at the representative bodySnowResorts Australia, said there was “no question it has been a challenging season for natural snowfall”.“This winter was shaped by a combination of abnormally warm weather and climatic variability, but it’s important to remember that in any outdoor environment, that variability can result in some seasons being better than others.“This is an abnormal season and shouldn’t be considered in isolation as a reflection of what future seasons will look like.”He said skiing, snowboarding and snow play had still been available in NSW, Victoria and the ACT “since the June long weekend, with all resorts across Australia operating through the July school holidays and beyond”.“What this season has shown is the importance and value of the investment resorts have made in snow making, with underlying demand for snow holidays remaining strong through July and August.”Explore more on these topicsAustralia weatherSnowClimate crisisEl Niño southern oscillationnewsShareReuse this content

title: EV sales outpace petrol cars for first time as Australians dodge soaring fuel costs | Environment | The Guardian
description: New record for Australia as more than 27,000 EVs sold in August, driven by the rising cost of fuel and new government policy
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: New record for Australia as more than 27,000 EVs sold in August, driven by the rising cost of fuel and new government policy
Content: The rise in EV sales in Australia has been helped by the war in Iran pushing up oil prices and the introduction last year of a federal vehicle emissions standard.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenThe rise in EV sales in Australia has been helped by the war in Iran pushing up oil prices and the introduction last year of a federal vehicle emissions standard.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPEnvironmentEV sales outpace petrol cars for first time as Australians dodge soaring fuel costsNew record for Australia as more than 27,000 EVs sold in August, driven by the rising cost of fuel and new government policyFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAdam MortonThu 3 Sep 2026 23.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 23.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElectric vehicle sales in Australia exceeded petrol cars for the first time last month as a transformation driven by high fuel prices and government policy encouraging clean car uptake accelerated.More than 27,000 EVs were sold in August, a new record for a single month and representing 24.9% of new cars sold. The climate-friendly technology surpassed both petrol vehicles (nearly 26,000 sold) and diesel cars (23,600).If plug-in hybrids were added, the proportion of new cars with a plug jumped to 36% of sales.The rise in EVs has been helped by two factors – the war in Iran pushing up oil prices and making running a petrol car significantly more expensive, and the introduction last year of a federal vehicle emissions standard that required auto companies to cut average tailpipe emissions year-on-year. The latter has triggered a big increase in the number of models of low and zero-emission cars available at a range of prices.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAustralia had previously trailed most OECD countries in EV take-up, and the technology has been the focus of political scare campaigns, including former prime minister Scott Morrison claiming in 2019 that introducing a vehicle emissions standard would “end the weekend”. They made up less than 2% of sales just four years ago and about 8% last year.The climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, said EV sales surpassing petrol cars was a “landmark moment”.“Australians have seen through the scare campaigns and are voting with their wallets for cars that are cheaper to run, cleaner and reduce their exposure to international petrol price shocks,” he said.Toyota was Australians’ most popular car brand in August, followed by Chinese EV manufacturer BYD and trillionaire Elon Musk’s Tesla. Five of the top 10 brands were Chinese: BYD, GWM, MG, Geely and Cheery. The Tesla Model Y was the most popular new model, with more than 6,400 sold.The Electric Vehicle Council said there had been a “structural shift in the way Australians choose their cars”, with both economic and environmental benefits driving the change.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe council’s chief executive, Julie Delvecchio, said there were now nearly 200 EV models on offer. “The priority now is to make the benefits of going electric accessible to more Australians, including people in regional communities, apartment residents and the 30% of Australians who rent their home,” she said.The Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries CEO, Tony Weber, said consumer choice and competition were rapidly reshaping the new-vehicle market and infrastructure settings needed to keep pace.“Accessible and dependable charging will remain critical to consumer confidence, particularly on highways, in rural and regional areas and for motorists without access to charging at home,” he said.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentElectric vehiclesElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian drone strike on Ukraine’s security services HQ is a ‘major escalation’, says Ukraine’s foreign minister – as it happened | World news | The Guardian
description: Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported a Russian drone hit the headquarter of the security service of Ukraine, in Kyiv
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported a Russian drone hit the headquarter of the security service of Ukraine, in Kyiv
Content: 09.17 EDTRussian drone strikes Ukraine's SBU security services HQ, Zelenskyy says, as he orders retaliationUkraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has just reported a Russian drone hit the headquarter of the Security Service ofUkraine, SBU, in central Kyiv.In a post on X, hesaid:“I spoke with the Head of the Security Service of Ukraine,Oleksandr Poklad.Unfortunately, a Russian drone struck the central building of the Security Service of Ukraine on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv, across from St. Sophia Cathedral.All emergency services are on the scene.Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance.Thedrone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Servicein that building.I instructed Poklad to deliveran appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. title: Russia strikes Ukraine intelligence HQ in ‘major escalation’ | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has told SBU to deliver ‘appropriate, tangible response’ to Kyiv strike
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has told SBU to deliver ‘appropriate, tangible response’ to Kyiv strike
Content: The Russian drone attack struck near St Sophia's Cathedral, a world heritage site.Photograph: Mark Edward Harris/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Russian drone attack struck near St Sophia's Cathedral, a world heritage site.Photograph: Mark Edward Harris/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockUkraineRussia strikes Ukraine intelligence HQ in ‘major escalation’Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has told SBU to deliver ‘appropriate, tangible response’ to Kyiv strikeAmy Hawkinsin KyivFri 4 Sep 2026 11.37 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head office of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency has been hit in a Russian drone attack, sending plumes of black smoke rising into the air in the heart of Kyiv.Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he had instructed the SBU to deliver an “appropriate, tangible response” to the strike, while the foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, described it as a “major escalation”.The streets around the SBU headquarters were cordoned off shortly after Friday’s attack, with armed officers patrolling the area.Numerous ambulances and emergency services vehicles were stationed around the site, which is close to St Sophia Cathedral, a Unesco world heritage site.“Unfortunately, a Russian drone hit the central building of the SBU on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv, opposite the St Sophia Cathedral,” Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram. “The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building.”Kyiv has been undera barrage of daily drone and missile attacksfrom Russia for over a week. Zelenskyy on Friday called for Russia to halt its attacks during a visit of US negotiators, Steve Witkoff ‌and Jared Kushner, to the city on Sunday and said Ukraine would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace while they were in Moscow.Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors which can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-modeljet-powered droneswhich can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept.It is rare for government buildings in central Kyiv to be reached by Russian strikes, especially in broad daylight. The explosion from the hit on the SBU building could be heard from several blocks away.The incident is likely to intensify theescalating attacksthat Moscow and Kyiv have been launching at each other in recent weeks in efforts to destroy each other’s resilience and morale. It will also raise questions about Kyiv’s ability to defend its key infrastructure against Russia.Sybiha said the attack was “a major escalation that demands resolute responses” and called on international partners to “unequivocally condemn these actions and step up pressure on the Putin regime”.At least nine people were injured in Friday’s strike, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.Stanislav Zavertailo, the co-owner of the nearby Zavertailo cafe, said one of his customers was injured in the strike, which sent shockwaves through his premises, shattering all the windows.“It’s a normal cafe,” he said. The customer was “eating one of our famous poppy seed rolls” when the attack occurred, he added.Staff and customers rushed into an underground shelter after the strike, fearing a double-tap attack, a tactic which Russia has employed, in which a second drone is sent in soon after the first, hitting emergency service workers.An hour later, there had been no second strike, but Zavertailo said he did not feel at ease. “We are all waiting for another attack,” he said.The SBU is responsible for coordinating complex operations against Russia, including last year’sOperation Spiderwebwhich destroyed aircraft worth billions of pounds inside Russia.Friday’s hit was “awful” said a Zavertailo cafe employee who had recently emerged from the underground shelter. As “a person who lives in Ukraine for all this time, it’s just hard”.The strike came two days before Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were expected to visit Kyiv for the first time.US-led diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s four-and-a-half-year invasion have stalled in recent months as the US has shifted its focus towards the war with Iran.Additional reporting by Illia DyadikExplore more on these topicsUkraineEuropeRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Germany urges EU to cut Russians’ holiday visas after sabotage attacks | Germany | The Guardian
description: Belarusian said to have had tourist visa issued by Italy is investigated over alleged attempt to attack Leipzig airport
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Belarusian said to have had tourist visa issued by Italy is investigated over alleged attempt to attack Leipzig airport
Content: An explosive-disarming robot at Leipzig airport in August. Berlin said Russian intelligence was likely to have been behind the alleged plot.Photograph: Axel Schmidt/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn explosive-disarming robot at Leipzig airport in August. Berlin said Russian intelligence was likely to have been behind the alleged plot.Photograph: Axel Schmidt/ReutersGermanyGermany urges EU to cut Russians’ holiday visas after sabotage attacksBelarusian said to have had tourist visa issued by Italy is investigated over alleged attempt to attack Leipzig airportEurope live – latest updatesKate Connollyin Berlin,Lorenzo TondoandPjotr SauerFri 4 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany is urging its European partners to introduce tighter limitations on Russian citizens entering the EU on tourist visas, afterrecent sabotage attacks which Berlin has blamed on Moscow.German authorities are investigating a Belarusian national, who also holds a Russian passport, over the alleged attempt to attack Leipzig airport using drones and explosives.The man is alleged to have entered the Schengen area on a tourist visa issued by the Italian embassy in Minsk, the capital of Belarus. Security sources said he did not appear to have ever travelled throughItaly.Germany’s foreign ministry has complained that too many visas were being issued to Russians.“The number of visas issued for Russian nationals for holidays in theEuropean Unionis too high,” a spokesperson said.Sources close to the government say the sheer number of visas being issued to Russians goes against the spirit of sanctions related to theUkrainewar, and make it impossible to know who is entering the EU and for what purpose.Figures show that Italyissued more Schengen visas than any other country in the bloc in 2025; between them, Italy, France and Spain received three-quarters of all visa applications from Russians,according to Euractiv.Italy issued more visas to Belarusians than any other EU country last year, and the number has risen sharply since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to European Commission statistics analysed by the Italian newswebsite Linkiesta, Italy issued just 2,968 visas to Belarusian citizens in 2021, compared with 50,709 last year.A similar trend can be seen withRussia. Italian visas issued to Russian citizens rose from 63,894 in 2021 to more than 165,000 in 2025, almost tripling despite the war.Germany’s government this week announced measures to hit back at the Kremlin, after it said Russian intelligence was likely to have been behind the alleged Leipzig plot. These included closing the Russian consulate in Bonn, summoning the Russian ambassador to the foreign ministry, and tightening the monitoring of Russia’s shadow fleet of illegal vessels carrying oil in the Baltic Sea.The EU also announced a 22nd package of sanctions, and said it was expanding its list of Russians who would not be allowed to enter the EU.Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, has ordered checks on the visa issued to the Belarusian suspect in the Leipzig case.“There is a process for granting visas, because certain requirements have to be met,” Tajani said. “If people meet those requirements and there is no alert concerning them individually, the visa is granted. If that is what happened, we will try to understand why that visa was issued.”Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and the Czech Republic have all but stopped issuing visas to Russian citizens, adopting national restrictions that go beyond EU measures. But several other member states have continued granting large numbers of visas, in some cases increasing them.“Countries closer to Russia geographically, or with sizeable Russian minorities, are shutting their borders altogether or sharply reducing the number of visas they issue, including to students,” said Eleonora Tafuro Ambrosetti, a senior research fellow and co-head of the Russia, Caucasus and Central Asia Centre at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEurope calls out Russia’s ‘hybrid war’ in public. But how can it make Putin pay?Read moreRoderich Kiesewetter, a leading foreign and security policy expert for the governing CDU in the Bundestag, called on the EU to immediately suspend its tourist visa programme for Russians, calling it “untenable” from both a security and moral perspective.Kiesewetter said the security risk posed was “enormous”. The ability for Russians to move freely within the EU with a visa was being “exploited for espionage and sabotage”, he said.He urged the EU to restrict giving visas to Russians “to the absolute minimum”.“This excessive issuance of tourist visas to Russians contradicts the European strategy of isolating Russia,” he said. “It creates a false impression of normalisation for wealthy Russians, precisely those who benefit from the Kremlin’s reign of terror.” He said it was not right that Russia “wages daily a brutal war of aggression and annihilation against Ukraine while Russians continue to holiday without a care in the EU”.Some anti-war Russian activists in Europe have argued that tightening visa controls for all Russian citizens may do little to curb Moscow’s sabotage campaign.They point to a shift in tactics by Russian intelligence services, which increasingly rely not on professional operatives sent across Europe but on people recruited remotely, often through Telegram channels and paid in cryptocurrency to carry out individual tasks.This allows the Russian intelligence officers directing the operations to remain safely at home. In several recent cases prosecuted in Germany and Lithuania, the alleged recruits were Ukrainian or Baltic citizens rather than Russians.Explore more on these topicsGermanyRussiaItalyUkraineBelarusEuropeEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Deadly escalation in Black Sea attacks prompts fears of even higher food prices | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Russian and Ukrainian strikes in July killed more crew than in whole war to that month, preventing grain exports
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Russian and Ukrainian strikes in July killed more crew than in whole war to that month, preventing grain exports
Content: The burned-out Russian-flagged cargo ship Omskiy-107 lies beached off the Turkish coast near Istanbul.Photograph: Murad Sezer/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe burned-out Russian-flagged cargo ship Omskiy-107 lies beached off the Turkish coast near Istanbul.Photograph: Murad Sezer/ReutersUkraineDeadly escalation in Black Sea attacks prompts fears of even higher food pricesRussian and Ukrainian strikes in July killed more crew than in whole war to that month, preventing grain exportsJoanna PartridgeFri 4 Sep 2026 10.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA summer of hostilities in the Black Sea proved deadly for seafarers, as Russia andUkraineattacked each other’s ships and port infrastructure, preventing vital grain exports and prompting concerns that the conflict will push global food prices even higher.More crew were killed in the Black Sea in July than during the entirety of the war before that month as theconflict has intensified, making the body of water the most dangerous in the world for commercial shipping. This is despite the conflict between the US and Iran, with vessels still being targeted in thestrait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.As many as 23 people died in July as a result of attacks on 35 ships in the Black Sea, according to estimates from the Turkish seafarers’ union Türkiye Denizciler Sendikası.Attacks on vessels continued into August and escalation in the Ukraine war has prompted the head of the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization, to condemn the “deterioration of maritime security around the globe”.Russia firstlaunched waves of attackson port infrastructure and vessels anchored in Ukrainian Black Sea ports in the months after its invasion in 2022,preventing Kyiv from exporting grain. In July, Russia again struck Ukraine’s main grain export hubs of Odesa and Chornomorsk.View image in fullscreenFirefighters tackle a blaze on a civilian vessel hit during Russian missile strikes on Chornomorsk last December.Photograph: State Emergency Service Of Ukraine/ReutersHowever, the recent escalation in the Black Sea and neighbouring Sea of Azov – connected by the Kerch strait – has also resulted from Ukrainian retaliatory attacks. Drones have hit Russian vessels, including tankers Kyiv says belong to a shadow fleet of hundreds of ships used byRussiato evade sanctions on its oil exports. Ukraine has targeted ships and port buildings at the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, vital for oil and grain exports.In a grim illustration of the danger to vessels and their crew, an abandoned Russian-flagged cargo ship – with a burned-out command deck – recently ran aground on Turkey’s Black Sea coast as startled holidaymakers looked on.The Omskiy-107’s crew abandoned ship after it was hit by a Ukrainian drone near Novorossiysk, leaving the unmanned vessel to drift hundreds of miles and end up close to the Bosphorus, the narrow strait straddled by Istanbul that is one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes.View image in fullscreenA damaged Liberian-flagged bulk carrier is escorted by a safety boat through the Bosphorus this week.Photograph: Murad Sezer/ReutersShipping in the region is under increased threat, according to analysts at the maritime risk intelligence firm Vanguard. “Merchant vessels are now more likely to be affected because of the ports they visit, their trading activity and the cargoes they carry. Attacks have also extended beyond ports and their immediate approaches, increasing the risk to vessels across a wider area of the Black Sea,” they said.The precarious maritime situation has already significantly reduced Russian and Ukrainian grain exports, raising concerns the disruption will worsen the impact of other food price shocks and hurt countries reliant on imported wheat, barley and maize.Russia is the world’s largest grain exporter, with its produce mostly going to the Middle East and north Africa, particularly Turkey and Egypt, while Ukraine is the fifth-largest.In July, Russiasuspended shippingin the Sea of Azov after a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks, before deciding to redirect some grain exports to alternative routes such as via the Caspian and Baltic seas and the Pacific. However, more than 70% of Russia’s seaborne grain exports are shipped from Black Sea ports, and a further 20% from the Sea of Azov, according to analysis from Oxford Economics.“I have seen estimates that Russian grain exports were down to 40% of normal export capacity in August,” said Tatiana Orlova, the lead emerging markets economist at Oxford Economics.View image in fullscreenA satellite image shows damage to a grain conveyor, after a Ukrainian drone and missile attack on Novorossiysk last month.Photograph: Vantor/ReutersUkraine, which had a bumper and early grain harvest this year, has also found itself unable to export large volumes through its Black Sea ports. Kyiv exported only a third – about 1.4m tonnes – of the grain it could have exported, using sea, rail, river and road, according to recent comments from Ukraine’s food minister.Global wheat prices have been trading higher in recent weeks, but remain below levels at the beginning of the Ukraine war in 2022.However, analysts say the latest disruption to seaborne grain exports is likely to push prices higher and exacerbate other food supply shocks, including the Iran war andlower European grain yieldsafter extreme summer heat and therapidly developing El Niño weather system.Global food prices are forecast by Oxford Economics to rise by nearly 12% this year and a further 4.8% in 2027.Unlike in 2022, when many big food importing countries were caught napping by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, “a lot of countries have grain stocks, which should help, so there is better preparedness for this kind of shock”, said Orlova. “But it is pretty clear the food price is going to be affected.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaShipping industryWater transportInternational tradeTurkeyGlobal economynewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman, 45, killed in Florence in seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August | Italy | The Guardian
description: Lorena Isceri was thrown off a motorway bridge, allegedly by ex-boyfriend Federico Vella
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Lorena Isceri was thrown off a motorway bridge, allegedly by ex-boyfriend Federico Vella
Content: Lorena Isceri still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted.Photograph: FacebookView image in fullscreenLorena Isceri still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted.Photograph: FacebookItalyWoman, 45, killed in Florence in seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-AugustLorena Isceri was thrown off a motorway bridge, allegedly by ex-boyfriend Federico VellaAngela Giuffridain RomeFri 4 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 45-year-old woman abducted and thrown off a motorway bridge near Florence has become the seventh alleged femicide inItalysince mid-August.Lorena Isceri was abducted on Thursday afternoon, allegedly by her ex-boyfriend, Federico Vella, in the Rifredi area of Florence, before being forced into the boot of his car and driven towards a bridge on the A1 motorway.Isceri, who worked in the veterinary sector, still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted.Vella, 38, stopped the car, snatched the phone and allegedly threw her off the bridge, before jumping off himself.After Isceri’s call to the helpline, police traced her phone signal but arrived too late to prevent her murder. Officers are establishing whether Isceri was killed before she was thrown off the bridge.Isceri’s mother toldSkyTg24that she had last heard from her daughter on Thursday morning, and said she sounded fine. When asked about the relationship with Vella, she said Isceri had spoken to her about it and was “very afraid”.Italian interior ministry data had indicated a downward trend in femicides during the first six months of 2026.Figures compiled by the feminist allianceNon Una di Menoshowed that as of 8 August, 40 women had been killed so far this year.But numbers have risen since 15 August, Italy’s Ferragosto national holiday, with seven women, including Isceri, killed by a current or former partner.Giorgia Meloni’s ruling coalition, which on Friday celebrated becoming the longest-serving government in the history of the Italian republic, had pledged to crack down on gender-based violence after the strong public reaction to the killing ofGiulia Cecchetin, a 22-year-old medical student, by her former boyfriend, in November 2023.Two years later, the government approved a law that for the first time introduced a legal definition of femicide in criminal law, punishing it with life in prison, while increasing sentences for crimes including stalking, sexual violence and the sharing of intimate images without consent.However, a campaign to educate schoolboys about healthy relationships was thwarted after the government made it conditional on parental approval.Luisa Rizzitelli, the Italy coordinator of One Billion Rising, which campaigns to end violence against women, said: “Perhaps Meloni is right to celebrate her government’s longevity, because there is precious little to celebrate in terms of concrete results.“The approach to the tragic issue of male violence against women has been based on security policies while completely lacking strategic, structural programmes for training and prevention. The stubborn refusal to implement sex and relationship education in schools is a major factor fuelling the epidemic of femicides in Italy.”In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123 and thedomestic abuse helplineis 0808 2000 247. In the US, thesuicide prevention lifelineis 988 and thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis on 13 11 14 and the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines can be found viawww.befrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsItalyFemicideViolence against women and girlsEuropeWomennewsShareReuse this content

title: Israelis shoot dead two Palestinian teenagers after settlers encircle village | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Troops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continues
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Troops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continues
