Content: Relatives of Khalil Abu Alia at his funeral in al-Mughayyir, after the 16-year-old was shot on his doorstep by an Israeli rooftop sniper.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRelatives of Khalil Abu Alia at his funeral in al-Mughayyir, after the 16-year-old was shot on his doorstep by an Israeli rooftop sniper.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesWest BankIsraelis shoot dead two Palestinian teenagers after settlers encircle villageTroops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continuesEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemFri 4 Sep 2026 11.12 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraelis have shot dead two teenagers in a Palestinian village encircled by settlers, and Israeli troops have razed an entire village outside Hebron, in the latest attacks in a surge of Israeli terror and ethnic cleansing across the occupiedWest Bank.The shootings targeted Khalil Abu Alia, 16, who was about to start 11th grade at the al-Mughayyir boys school, and 19-year-old Omar al-Nassan, who graduated from the same institution with top marks this summer.The teenagers were killed soon after sunset, when a group of settlers entered the village under police and military escort to steal dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, village residents and Israeli activists said.Snipers took up position on rooftops and one shot Abu Alia in the neck, his English teacher, Waheed Abu Naim, said in a phone interview. The boy was on the doorstep of his home when he was targeted.View image in fullscreenMourners at the funeral ceremony of Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesAl-Nassan was shot twice, the second time in the back, residents and activists said. Both teenagers died before they made it to hospital.A spokesperson for the Israeli military said Israeli police, army and settlers had entered the village to take sheep claimed by settlers from a Palestinian home. The spokesperson provided no evidence of ownership, theft or investigation into stolen goods.View image in fullscreenMourners at the funeral ceremony of Abu Alia and al-Nassan in al-Mughayyir.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesWhen Palestinians resisted seizure of the sheep by throwing stones and cinder blocks, the troops shot them, the spokesperson said. “The forces responded by firing at key instigators in order to remove the threat. Hits were identified.”Abu Alia was killed by a soldier. It was not clear whether Al-Nassan was shot by a soldier or a settler.Video shared with the Guardian shows dozens of settlers approaching the village and appearing to liaise with Israeli troops. The Guardian could not independently verify the date the footage was filmed.Israeli troops and settlers filmed in al-MughayyirIsraeli soldiers and militants had already killed three other students from their school’s 470-strong student body this year.The other victims were a 17-year-old playerfrom the Palestinian youth football teamshot in June, a 14-year-oldgunned down at the school gatein April, and another 14-year-oldkilled outside the village mosquein January.“We don’t know how long these crimes are going to continue,” said Abu Naim, who had taught all five boys, and said many more of his students had been injured by Israeli attacks. His brother was also killed by settlers in April.“This week we are making extra security preparations for the new semester, which starts in three days,” he said. They have built a higher wall around the school, topped by a fence, and strengthened gates to the compound.They are also making teaching contingency plans, because the village has been under tightening siege for the past two weeks.View image in fullscreenFuneral attenders look out from their village of al-Mughayyir at an Israeli hilltop settlement.Photograph: Léo Corrêa/APSince late 2023, Israeli barricades blocked all but one road into the village, and at least eight settler outpostssurround it in all directions.In late August, soldiers and settlers began closing the one remaining lifeline out of al-Mughayyir for hours at a time, setting up a temporary checkpoint near the school in the morning and evening.At least eight families had fled in the past week because they were unable to commute to work, renting flats in other places, Abu Naim said.The school has 26 teachers but only nine live in the village, and they fear the other two-thirds may not be allowed to reach their classrooms on Monday.View image in fullscreenIsraeli troops raiding al-Mughayyir in July after settler attacks.Photograph: Mohammed Torokman/ReutersIn the south Hebron hills, Israeli forces spent the day razing the homes of 12 Palestinian families who lived in the community of Khirbet al-Taban. All 70 residents are now homeless, including 28 children.Israeli troops demolished all buildings and destroyed water cisterns, storage, livestock pens and caves, the Israeli-Palestinian rights group B’Tselem said in a statement.It was the 66th Palestinian community wiped off the map since October 2023, with 18 others partly displaced, the group said. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.“Israel is continuing to erase Palestinian communities at an accelerating pace as part of the ethnic cleansing it is carrying out in the West Bank,” saidYuli Novak, the executive director of B’Tselem. “The world continues to stand by as Palestinians and their lives are left completely exposed to Israeli violence.”A spokesperson for Cogat, the Israeli military agency that manages civilian affairs in occupiedPalestine, said troops were carrying out “enforcement activity” against illegal construction in a military training zone.In 1981 Israel designated the Masafer Yatta area, including Khirbet al-Taban, asFiring Zone 918. It has been working since to push out the roughly 1,200 Palestinian residents who remain. They have been fighting expulsion in Israeli courts for decades, slowing but not stopping demolitions.As Palestinian communities have been wiped out, illegal Israeli settlements have expanded, with 11 outposts inside the firing zone, housing some of the mostnotoriously violentIsraeli settlers. None have been targeted for removal.Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Seeds of hope: how a local farming project is offering a lifeline to Gaza | Farming | The Guardian
description: Family-run Al-Qarara Seed Bank is helping to counter acute food insecurity after being destroyed in the war
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Family-run Al-Qarara Seed Bank is helping to counter acute food insecurity after being destroyed in the war
Content: Hanadi Salama Muhanna, 38, daughter of seed bank owner Salama Muhanna, holds seeds at the Al-Qarara Seed Bank in Deir al-Balah, Gaza.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersView image in fullscreenHanadi Salama Muhanna, 38, daughter of seed bank owner Salama Muhanna, holds seeds at the Al-Qarara Seed Bank in Deir al-Balah, Gaza.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersFarmingSeeds of hope: how a local farming project is offering a lifeline to GazaFamily-run Al-Qarara Seed Bank is striving to help Palestinians gain sovereignty over their food securityTamara DavisonFri 4 Sep 2026 08.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSalama Ayesh Muhanna still remembers the first seeds he planted on his family’s land in al-Qarara,Gaza. At just 17, Muhanna had proudly sprouted cucumbers.“I was very happy because I saw the results,” Muhanna says. “We were farmers at heart.”Now 71, he is an agronomist, a community leader and the founder of the Al-Qarara Seed Bank.The original project, founded in 2017, was situated near the eastern border of Gaza in al-Qarara, an area now completely flattened and inaccessible. Back then, Muhanna had a large home, olive trees, land of his own, and a successful seed bank operation with dedicated storage and equipment. Everything was destroyed early in Israel’s brutal military campaign, but after being displaced to Deir al-Balah in 2024, Muhanna and his daughter Hanadi, 38, are now hard at work, regrowing seed collections at Gaza’s only seed bank.Outside the tent where they currently live in a displacement camp, summer temperatures climb to almost 35C. Another tent houses their small but growing collection of open-pollinated, non-GMO seeds, including local wheat and vegetables such as okra and spinach.View image in fullscreenSalama Muhanna with his daughter Hanadi inside the seed bank.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersEach day, Muhanna rises early to check on the project, a 200-metre-wide plot of land where the family lives, collects seeds, and experiments with new crops. He inspects the seeds to assess their quality, waters crops and checks on seedlings. As the manager of the seed bank, Hanadi deals with local farmers and oversees the growing seed collection – all while studying agriculture and food sovereignty online via a programme partly tied to Coventry University and the Gaza Urban Agriculture Forum. Muhanna jokes that his hard-working daughter will be “managing her father” by next year.The project has two main aims. One is to collect and preserve the seeds of local plants that may thrive better in this landscape. “The war forced farmers to resort to local seeds,” says Hanadi, because of the ongoing blockades on seed imports, rocketing food prices and growing hunger across Gaza. Yet it appears that this focus on local seed varieties – “baladi” seeds – may prove more effective. That, Muhanna says, is because “local seeds are resistant to drought, fungi, and pests”.“During the war, they’ve been our lifeline,” he adds.The project’s other aim is to create a node for seed distribution for farmers who need to save every possible penny. The seeds, once collected, are distributed among Palestinian farmers and families in Deir al-Balah who then return the same amount after harvest. Approximately 200 farmers have so far benefited thanks to Muhanna and Hanadi’s seeds, with support from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). Beyond multiplying seed collections, it is helping Palestinian farmers reclaim agricultural agency and self-reliance – providing for families despite devastating restrictions on resources including vital humanitarian aid.View image in fullscreenMuhanna says the seeds could be key to future food sovereignty in Gaza.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersThe seeds are deeply connected to memories of the Palestinian land Muhanna has always called home – and could, he hopes, be key to future food sovereignty in Gaza. “The pumpkin plant reminds me of my father and mother,” he says. “It grew on the vineyard where we lived when I was little.”The needs have never been more urgent. At least 1.2 million people in Gaza now face acute food insecurity amid an escalating humanitarian crisis, according to anew reportby the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC). Despitegrowing alarmamong humanitarian organisations, Israel continues to block access to agricultural land and the import of seeds and organic fertiliser. Meanwhile, dwindling water supplies, degraded soil and deadly remnants of explosives make farming a treacherous practice.“Walking in the streets is unsafe, and walking on the land is unsafe,” Muhanna says, adding that the psychological impact affects their work. “The war destroyed my hope.”Despite immense challenges, the family know their seeds are helping the community while preserving indigenous species against agricultural monopolies, and safeguarding Palestine’s agricultural heritage.As Muhanna puts it, seeds are “my identity, my patriotism, my nationality”.Pat Griffiths, ICRC’ spokesperson in Jerusalem, said: “This is about agency. It’s about dignity. It’s about being less dependent on what is or is not allowed to enter Gaza. As the occupying power, Israel has an obligation to make sure that Palestinians in Gaza have access to the food, goods and items that they need to live.”There is still a long way to go in returning the seed bank to its former size. Muhanna says that before the war, they had about 42 types of local seeds. “Now we have about 28.”There is also another looming challenge that could affect the seed bank’s future.View image in fullscreenSalama Muhanna inside the seed bank: ‘During the war, they’ve been our lifeline.’Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters“Climate change is what controls us,” Muhanna says, as he sips his tea and shelters inside from the sun. “When the weather is hot, the seeds spoil.” Sometimes he has to plant almost a month later than normal, delaying harvests in a race against time to gather resilient seeds for the future. Still they keep going, experimenting in their fields to see which local seeds produce the best yields. And with almost 2.5 tonnes of seeds collected so far – better than last year – there are signs that the efforts are working.With each seed, there is hope in Gaza that sovereignty over food security can soon take root.“Any country in the world that doesn’t have sovereignty over food security isn’t a country,” Muhanna says. “If we establish sovereignty over food security, then we’ll be a real country.”Explore more on these topicsFarmingGazaMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineFood securityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Unimaginable grief’: Iranian town left devastated after US strike on wedding  | Iran | The Guardian
description: Mourning turns to anger as residents of Kuhestak say Baloch communities are being placed in path of conflict
Author: Deepa Parent
Headline: Mourning turns to anger as residents of Kuhestak say Baloch communities are being placed in path of conflict
Content: Mourners gather around the coffin of one of the victims of a reported US strike on a wedding party in Kuhestak, Iran. At least four people were killed and 60 injured.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMourners gather around the coffin of one of the victims of a reported US strike on a wedding party in Kuhestak, Iran. At least four people were killed and 60 injured.Photograph: Getty ImagesIran‘Unimaginable grief’: Iranian town left devastated after US strike on weddingMourning turns to anger as residents of Kuhestak say Baloch communities are being placed in path of conflictDeepa ParentFri 4 Sep 2026 06.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople in Kuhestak, a predominantly Baloch city in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, are mourning after astrike on a weddingkilled at least four people, including a child, and injured more than 60, according to local authorities.The blast hit at around 9.30pm on 1 September, turning a night of celebration into one of devastation for the small coastal community, which is on the strait of Hormuz.In the aftermath, videos shared on social media by friends and relatives of the wedding couple showed rubble, flower garlands and decorations scattered among debris and bloodied shoes.Asked about the strike on Thursday, the US vice-president, JD Vance, said the US would never target civilians in combat but that “sometimes things happen”, adding that he was sceptical of Iran’s reports. He did not acknowledge that the killings had been confirmed by an internationally recognised humanitarian body.According to Iranian state media and people interviewed by the Guardian, the house belonged to Ali Mallahi, a local fisher who was celebrating his daughter’s wedding.In a video published by state media, Mallahi stood amid the rubble of what had been his home and said he was saddened by the attack but thanked God that the casualties weren’t higher.Residents said the celebrations had only just begun. Friends and family were waiting for the bride and groom, and many guests had yet to arrive for the henna ceremony.View image in fullscreenA woman weeps during a mass funeral in Kuhestak.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/APWitnesses who spoke to the Guardian said the attack had left residents angry and in deep mourning.Ahmad*, a local barber who witnessed the aftermath, said the entire neighbourhood had been devastated by what happened.“I don’t really have words. Ours is a small town and we all know each other and are brothers. We are all mourning. I visited the house and the media won’t report it, but it wasn’t just one house. Many houses around the site have been damaged and neighbours were directly hit by sharp objects when the explosions happened”.“We are not carrying coffins on our shoulders, we are carrying the dark future that awaits us all in the south,” Ahmad added.Moein Arjomand, director of the Balochistan Human Rights Documentation Network, said local responders were facing growing obstacles investigating the explosion.“Our team has been facing a lot of difficulties due to the internet [shutdown] and witnesses and relatives telling us they were banned from speaking to any foreign rights groups and foreign media,” he said. “I tried arranging interviews for international media with the relatives, but they are worried about the consequences and I couldn’t arrange them.”Despite the internet restrictions and apparent warnings against speaking out, locals and relatives of the couple have continued sharing videos documenting the aftermath on social media.In one video, Yaqoob Mallahi, a relative of the bride, shared footage of his seven-year-old son, Sepehr, lying in a hospital bed with his head bandaged.View image in fullscreenDamaged buildings after the strike on a wedding party. Asked whether the US was responsible, JD Vance, the US vice-president, said ‘sometimes things happen’.Photograph: Getty ImagesArjomand said at least six victims remained in serious condition in the intensive care unit of a hospital in Minab, about 18 miles (30km) away.“Bandar-e-Kuhestak is a small town and the local clinic is not equipped to handle casualties like this, so the injured were taken to the hospital in Minab,” Arjomand said.A video posted by local activists showed the family of Amir Mohammad Karimi, the four-year-old victim, mourning over his body as he was buried on Thursday.A 16-year-old boy, Mohammad Mallahi, was also killed by shrapnel while riding his motorbike nearby. Videos of his funeral, attended by dozens of local people, were shared online.“We have another funeral on Friday, this time a young woman, and we will all be there,” Ahmad said. “I can only pray to Allah that no more of our blood is shed and our injured come back home from the hospital.”Ahmad was referring to Asiyeh Molainejad, 22, another relative of the bride who was declared dead on Thursday.Beyond the immediate grief, the attack deepened a sense among some Baloch residents and activists that civilian deaths in their communities receive comparatively little attention.View image in fullscreenMen hold red roses as they attend a mass funeral  in Kuhestak.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/APFarzin Kadkhodaei, a human rights activist from Balochistan, said the circumstances of the deaths had made the loss particularly painful.“The human cost is devastating. These were Baloch civilians gathered for a wedding, and losing their lives in the middle of what should have been a joyful occasion is heartbreaking,” he said. “Their families are now left with unimaginable grief, while the injured have to live with the physical and emotional consequences.”Chakar Baloch, 35, a fisher, said the attack reinforced a feeling among local people that civilians living along the Makran coast were being placed in the path of conflicts over which they had little control. “My overall view is that we are the victims. We are the people who live along the Makran coast and for years we’ve gone out to sea, struggled to earn our bread, and just wanted to stay alive,” he said.When asked if local people were demanding answers about the strike, a Baloch resident of Sirik said western media did not understand their plight. “Who do you want me to demand answers from?” she said. “From the US that has attacked us in this war? Or the regime which has brought this war to our doorsteps? Tell me from whom I can demand and I will answer your questions.”Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet floods | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metres
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metres
Content: 0:51Workers pulled alive from hydropower tunnel nine days after Nepal flood disaster – videoNepal-Tibet flood disasterTwo workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet floodsOfficials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metresHannah Ellis-PetersenandGaurav Pokharelin KathmanduFri 4 Sep 2026 09.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 00.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days afterdeadly flash floodsburied the projects in deep mud and left them trapped.The workers were rescued during an operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a hydropower project in one of the areas worst affected by last week’sfloods, according to the army spokesperson Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet.Sanjay Shah, a foreman, was the first to be rescued and was taken to the army barracks in Trishuli. Another person, identified as Kabir Maharjan, a project supervisor, was also pulled from the tunnel. They were recovered from a depth of 170 metres (558ft) inside the tunnel, Basnet said.A senior police official confirmed that a body had also been found during the rescue operation, which has yet to be identified. By Friday afternoon, police confirmed they had halted the search as they had found no more signs of life.After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districtsRead moreNepal’s army released images of Shah being pulled from the small dark entrance of a tunnel. He emerged covered in mud but conscious and was carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.Speaking to army officials after he was rescued, Shah’s first question was: “What day is it?”Shah said he had been in the tunnel’s control room at the time of the flood, alongside about 40 to 45 others. “Since I was in the control room, my responsibility was to save everyone’s lives,” he said. “After such an accident, I couldn’t just run away by myself. I had to save everyone.”View image in fullscreenA survivor is carried out after being rescued from inside the tunnel.Photograph: Nepal Army/ReutersHe said that after realising there had been a major accident, he raced through the tunnel telling people to run and save themselves. “In doing so, I lost time. In the end, I couldn’t get out myself,” he said.To keep himself calm in the darkness of the tunnel, Shah said he spent his time chanting mantras. He said that while trapped, he had heard the voices of three or four others.“We were communicating by shouting to each other from nearby. There could also be people inside the powerhouse. Some of them may not have been able to escape,” he said.Satellite images showing before and after of Rasuwagadhi hydropower plantOfficials said the two men had been flown to a hospital in Kathmandu. Shah was said to be stable but Maharjan was in a critical condition and had been transferred to intensive care.Hirashova Maharjan, Kabir’s wife, said he had been in shock at first and was not talking, but had since said “a few words”. She said he had an injury to his leg and was extremely jaundiced.“He did not even recognise me initially. He only said: ‘Where am I? What happened to me?’ He did not say anything else,” she said. “He is better now. He said he wanted some water, so I gave him water. Then I asked him if he recognised me, and he said yes. He nodded his head.”“We had almost lost hope,” she said, adding that when she saw the photos of him being pulled from the tunnel, “I was so happy that I cried.”View image in fullscreenHirashova Maharjan, left, with a family member after visiting her husband in hospital in Kathmandu on Friday.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesMost of the hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the valley last week, triggered by ‌thecollapse of a melting glacieron the border between Nepal andChina-controlled Tibet.At least 1,287 people were killedin the floodsand more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.‘Everyone seems to have forgotten’: In Tibet, flood-hit families search for the missing and grapple with China’s silenceRead moreRescue efforts have increasingly centred on the hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week in air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued across several projects.Large boulders and flood waters had deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels.Speaking over the phone from the rescue site, Amrit Thapa, deputy superintendent of the armed police force, who is part of the seven-person search and rescue team, said they had managed to crawl the length of the tunnel looking for survivors. They were accompanied by a team from the Nepal army.“The team crawled through areas for about 10 to 15 metres and reached the main section,” said Thapa. “When we went to the final point, we found a body on the remaining upper level.”Thapa said that “except for two sections, the entire tunnel was filled with debris. After checking everything, we did not hear any further voices. We also searched the entire powerhouse area, but so far, nothing else has been found.”View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of damage in a village in Rasuwa district following the flash floods.Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPAArmy and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try to clear debris from the tunnel entrance. At least 550 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal.In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with about 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels.Rescue efforts have also focused on Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, where Nepali authorities said they were confident that 46 workers trapped in an underground chamber in the plant were still alive.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conference | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Splits emerge within party after resignation of officials reported to police for apparent plot to evade donations law
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Splits emerge within party after resignation of officials reported to police for apparent plot to evade donations law
Content: 1:21'Reform broke no law': Nigel Farage responds to latest donation revelations – videoNigel FarageFarage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conferenceSplits emerge within party after resignation of officials reported to police for apparent plot to evade donations lawRowena Mason,Ben QuinnandPippa CrerarFri 4 Sep 2026 14.16 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage sought to shore up his damaged leadership on Friday as he attempted to distance himself from two of his most senior officials reported to the police for apparently plotting to evade the law on foreign donations.As the scandal engulfed Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham, Farage was forced to suspend close aides Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr after anundercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim.He later acknowledged Jukes and Orr had made “human error” and were “not authorised” to act in the way they did when trying to orchestrate donations to benefit the party from a fake US businessman, who was not permitted to give money.View image in fullscreenDan Jukes, left, speaks to Nigel Farage before an interview in Clacton-on-Sea in July 2024.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersThe Met police are now assessing the evidence after a complaint thatFarage, Orr and Jukes may have broken political funding laws, with sources suggesting a full investigation is highly likely to be launched. They all deny wrongdoing.One possibility would be for the police to extend an existing Met investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.Orr is an associate professor of divinity at the University of Cambridge who had been working for Reform, reporting directly to Farage, since February. In relation to the undercover footage of Orr, a spokesperson for the university said Cambridge was “looking into these matters”. Jukes is Farage’s closest aide, and has been at his side for more than a decade working on communications and strategy.Farage had been introduced by Jukes to the would-be donor from the US promising to give £500,000 despite not being eligible, who was really an undercover reporter. The Reform leader then appeared to endorse the scheme for the impermissible US donor to give money through his son, a UK intermediary, by saying “thank you, both” and “all above board”.11:20Reform donations scandal: is this the final blow for Farage? - The LatestAfter dismissing the sting as a “hoax”, Reform began an organised campaign to limit the damage to Farage personally before his main conference speech, after a summer of scandals over his finances, including anundeclared gift of £5m.Addressing the allegations, the Reform leader responded by reading out a legal statement in which he dismissed the allegations as “a little local difficulty” and described the reports as “an exercise in entrapment”.Farage claimed Orr and Jukes had merely been “contractors” who engaged in “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true”. One party figure,Nadine Dorries, claimed Jukes had merely booked transport and carried bags, despite being a senior adviser integral to Reform’s operations and success for many years.View image in fullscreenA man in chainmail and a crown attends the Reform UK conference.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianWhen it was put to Farage that he had thanked the bogus donors and understood what was going on, he said: “It was the middle of the byelection. I was told I had to go and meet these people. I didn’t have to, but I did. I was told they had a global family trust headquartered in London. I asked the question: is this all above board?”The Reform leader also insisted that the party’s internal processes would have stopped any impermissible donors and said neither Jukes nor Orr should have been carrying out fundraising. He said a suggestion by Jukes in the footage that other foreign donations had been channelled through UK intermediaries was not true and the donors did not exist.The pair were caught out after being filmed by undercover reporters from the group Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, and broadcast by Channel 4 News on the eve of Reform’s party conference.View image in fullscreenFarage’s speech was interrupted by protesters.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianIn the footage, Orr and Jukes appeared to help orchestrate an impermissible donation of £30,000 from the fake US donor, which was used to pay for polling that would benefit Reform and made front pages of national newspapers. The money from an American company was transferred to the polling company JL Partners after being organised at the behest of Reform to boost its policies and political narrative. It was not declared to the Electoral Commission.Jukes went on to discuss whether the US businessman could give £500,000 through a UK intermediary, who was an undercover reporter, and introduced the would-be donors to Farage at a lunch in Clacton over oysters and champagne.Jukes issued a statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals using selective editing who had their own agenda to discreditReform UK.”Orr said: “I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party’s internal investigation into the conduct of the program, with which I will cooperate fully.”The Lib Dems have asked the standards commissioner to investigate Farage’s conduct.The row comprehensively overshadowed the first full day of the party’s conference with every Reform politician repeatedly questioned over the scandal.It also exposed splits at the top of the party, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, strongly distancing himself from Jukes and Orr. He told reporters “anyone who supports Reform is disappointed”, and added of the investigation: “It’s just not something I am personally involved in.”He also launched a personal video about his backstory, leading to speculation he could attempt to run for the leadership as a rival toRobert Jenrickor Richard Tice if Farage were to be forced out over his financial scandals.Reform UK exposé comes just as Farage was hoping to change the narrativeRead moreHowever, some Reform insiders are convinced Farage will part company with Yusuf before long, partly over his ambition and combative style on social media, including one post on X that saw him accused of racism towards a Somalia-born Labour councillor. Farage is understood to have used a rude term about Yusuf recently in relation to his troublemaking on social media.One senior Reform figure said they believed Yusuf would have to go as a precondition for some sort of reconciliation withRupert Lowe, whose party, Restore Britain, has eaten into the party’s voters on the hard right. Farage has recently condemned Lowe as vindictive, but some of their friends believe a rapprochement could be possible if Yusuf were no longer in the party.Reform had wanted the main event to be Farage announcing a deal with the hard-right French National Rally president, Jordan Bardella, to return small boats crossing the Channel if both parties achieve power. However, a press conference was dominated by questions about the foreign donations scandal.View image in fullscreenThe National Rally ​party’s chief, Jordan Bardella, attends a joint press conference with Farage on Friday.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianFarage’s main speech was later delayed by security concerns after climate protesters disrupted Tice’s stage appearance. More activists later repeatedly interrupted his address. While waiting to go on stage, the Reform leader danced and sung with the crowd.He began his speech by calling for Andy Burnham to hold a general election and accusing Labour of planning to put up taxes.The speech was light on policy but Farage at one point hinted he could look at the way judges are appointed in future – suggesting the party could look at a system of political appointments as is the case in the US.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKRupert LoweRichard TiceRobert JenrickNadine DorriesMetropolitan policenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cambridge University examines conduct of academic suspended by Reform UK | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: James Orr, an associate professor, was shown in Channel 4 News footage apparently trying to sidestep electoral law
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: James Orr, an associate professor, was shown in Channel 4 News footage apparently trying to sidestep electoral law
Content: James Orr speaking at a Turning Point USA event in Phoenix, Arizona, in December 2025.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreenJames Orr speaking at a Turning Point USA event in Phoenix, Arizona, in December 2025.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyReform UKCambridge University examines conduct of academic suspended by Reform UKJames Orr, an associate professor, was shown in Channel 4 News footage apparently trying to sidestep electoral lawAnna IsaacandRowena MasonFri 4 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCambridge University has said it is examining the conduct of James Orr, its associate professor and a topReform UKaide, after he was filmed appearing to try to circumvent electoral laws on foreign political donations.Orr, the suspended head of policy for Reform, is one of two senior officials to step aside after claims that he orchestrated a plot to have polling paid for by a foreign firm – something that is impermissible under British electoral law.The academic was filmed by a group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, seemingly attempting to sidestep election laws.In a statement shared with the Guardian, a spokesperson for theUniversity of Cambridgesaid: “The university is looking into these matters.”Orr is an associate professor of religion at Cambridge’s divinity faculty and teaches students at the university.1:15Footage from the Channel 4 News and Verbatim undercover investigation into Reform finances – videoLittle known outside UK and US political circles, Orr has been a highly influential intellectual force within Reform. Hewas labelledthe party’s “philosopher king” by the news organisation Politico.A key attraction for senior figures in Reform when appointing Orr was his high-level US political contacts within the Maga movement. JD Vance, the US vice-president, has called him his “intellectual mentor” and his “British Sherpa”.Footage broadcast by Channel 4 News on Thursday night showed an undercover reporter posing as a UK-based supporter in conversation with Orr.Orr discussed commissioning polling that was secretly organised by Reform, but suggested it be paid for by a US company belonging to the fake supporter’s supposed father.Farage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conferenceRead moreIn a separate clip, Orr can be heard saying of the poll funding arrangement thatNigel Farage“doesn’t know, won’t know” and it is the kind of thing he would “rather not know”.Reform UK initially described the Channel 4 News and Verbatim investigation as a “hoax”.On Thursday evening, Orr posted a video on his X account in which he said: “There is absolutely no way this could amount to a benefit or donation in kind at all.”He dismissed Verbatim as “politically motivated actors trying to discredit a political opponent through dubious legal means”.Still, on Friday morning he and Dan Jukes, a senior aide to Farage who has also denied wrongdoing, stood down pending an internal party investigation into the claims raised by the broadcast.Farage, who was also featured in the investigation meeting with the fake supporters, distanced himself from Orr and Jukes on Friday.The party leader told reporters: “The two individuals involved are not even part of our fundraising team, so they should have gone through the appropriate channels. Checks would have been made and they would never, ever have got to sit down at a table with me.”The Guardian has approached Orr for comment.Explore more on these topicsReform UKUniversity of CambridgeNigel FarageParty fundingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday review | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Nazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his death
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Nazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his death
Content: Nazir Afzal, who was head of the CPS in the north-west of England from 2011 to 2015, is now chancellor of the University of Manchester.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNazir Afzal, who was head of the CPS in the north-west of England from 2011 to 2015, is now chancellor of the University of Manchester.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianJason ArdayCambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday reviewNazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his deathRichard AdamsEducation editorFri 4 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUniversity of Cambridgehas asked Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, to lead the first part of its review into the death of the scholar Jason Arday.Arday died at his home in south London on 14 August, nine days after his resignation as a Cambridge professor amid swirling allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said the time since Arday’s death had been “a period of profound sadness and reflection” for the university, and she sought to defend her institution from criticism.“We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus but given the devastating outcome, we are all asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more. This review will answer that question,” Prentice said.“We are committed to ensuring that any recommendations arising from the review are addressed and adopted with clear accountability for delivering necessary changes.”View image in fullscreenJason Arday was found dead at home in south London on 14 August.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianArday was named professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, with the university highlighting his appointment as the university’s youngest ever black professor at the age of 37.Arday denied accusations of plagiarism levelled against him but on 5 August the university said it would hold an investigation into his academic qualifications.Arday resignedhours after the investigation was announced.Prentice said the review would be in two parts, with the first, led by Afzal, to focus on the support given to Arday in the immediate period before his death.Afzal said: “I am honoured to have been asked to lead part one of this important independent review. At its heart is a person, a family and a community who have been profoundly affected by Professor Arday’s death. It is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity.“My responsibility will be to listen carefully, examine the evidence thoroughly and understand what support, interventions and protections were available to Professor Arday in the period before his death. We must be willing to ask difficult questions, including whether more could and should have been done. This work will be conducted independently and with urgency.”Afzal, a University of Birmingham graduate, is the chancellor of the University of Manchester, having been head of the CPS in the north-west of England during which he prosecuted child exploitation rings in Rochdale. In 2022 he led anindependent review into London fire brigadethat exposed a culture of misogyny, racism and bullying.Prentice said: “I am very grateful to Nazir for agreeing to lead this part of the review. He is a highly respected legal professional who will ask challenging questions about the support that was offered to Professor Arday during his time at Cambridge.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue researchRead moreThe university said the review’s second stage would consider “the wider context of Professor Arday’s time at the university”, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, the university’s response to allegations of research misconduct, and the support it gave to academics “subject to extraordinary public and media scrutiny”.Cambridge said it would appoint an independent external chair for the second part and an expert panel “including individuals with lived experience” to advise the review.It said part one of the review was expected to report within three months, and the second part within six months of establishing the expert panel.Earlier this week, Jacqui Smith, the minister responsible for higher education, told parliament that she was “more than just keeping an eye” on Cambridge’s response to Arday’s death. Smith said England’s higher education regulator, the Office for Students, had the powers to investigate further if necessary.Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayUniversity of CambridgeHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage gives speech at Reform conference after party officials suspended over donations sting – as it happened | Politics | The Guardian
description: James Orr and Dan Jukes, aides to Nigel Farage, stepped down after an investigation by Channel 4 News
Author: Andrew Sparrow
Headline: James Orr and Dan Jukes, aides to Nigel Farage, stepped down after an investigation by Channel 4 News
Content: 04.57 EDTFarage admits conversations filmed undercover 'don't look good', and says he's 'not happy'Here are some more lines fromNigel Farage’s interview with LBC this morning where he gave his response to the undercover report about an apparent Reform UK plot to evade election donations rules. (See9.07am.)Farage insistedReform UKhad not broken any laws – but he admitted aides had said things they “perhaps should not have been said” and conceded he was “not happy” about this.He said:double quotation markThe party has broken no laws. The party has not taken any dodgy money or anything like that whatsoever.However, it is a clear case of entrapment, and they worked at it for a very, very long time, and they got a couple of our contractors to say things that perhaps should not have been said.And as a result of that, you know, they have been removed this morning. And yeah, you know, I’m not happy about it.He rejected the claim that the footage of him discussing a £500,000 donation with fake father-and-son donors (see9am) showed that he was aware of a plan to circumvent electoral law.He said:double quotation markIf you listen to what I said, I said, is this all above board? Is this all legal? I’ve been told it was a global family office based in London. And by the way, I was in the middle of a Clacton by-election. I turned up to see people. I knew nothing about them whatsoever. I meet people all the time.He claimed the three polls featured in the investigation were not commissioned by Reform UK.He said:double quotation markWhilst the poll benefited Reform, it wasn’t commissioned by Reform.It had nothing to do with Reform. It was an independent third party that did it. So that’s nothing. That’s nothing. Polls are funded by overseas people every single week. Every single week.In fact, the report contains footage clearly suggesting the polls were carried out at at the behest of Reform UK.He suggestedLabourand the Tories had a worse record on donations because they in effect sold peerages.He said:double quotation markThe Labour Party and the Conservative Party have been selling peerages for years in return for political donations. Political donations leading to big government contracts.In the world of political funding, all sorts of things have been done over decades that are wrong.He said the party had suspended two aides because their remarks “don’t look good”.He said:double quotation markI promise you, the polling is not even an issue. Nothing. The party has not done anything wrong, but entrapped conversations don’t look good, and that’s why we’ve taken the action we have.Nigel Farage speaking to the media.Photograph: Thomas Krych/APShareUpdated at06.54 EDT

title: Investigations launched into polling firm at centre of Reform UK allegations | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: British Polling Council and Market Research Society announce inquiries into JL Partners, which has been accused of breaking transparency rules
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: British Polling Council and Market Research Society announce inquiries into JL Partners, which has been accused of breaking transparency rules
Content: Nigel Farage, the Reform leader, and his adviser Dan Jukes arrive at the Clacton byelection in August. Jukes and James Orr, the party’s head of policy, were recorded apparently plotting to bypass electoral laws.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenNigel Farage, the Reform leader, and his adviser Dan Jukes arrive at the Clacton byelection in August. Jukes and James Orr, the party’s head of policy, were recorded apparently plotting to bypass electoral laws.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersReform UKInvestigations launched into polling firm at centre of Reform UK allegationsBritish Polling Council and Market Research Society announce inquiries into JL Partners, which has been accused of breaking transparency rulesWhat is the latest finance scandal facing Reform UK?Geraldine McKelvieFri 4 Sep 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA polling firm at the centre of allegations that Reform UKbreached electoral lawis being investigated by two industry bodies.JL Partners, which is run by former Conservative aides, has been accused of breaking transparency rules by failing to declare that three separate polls had been commissioned by the party.The company is a member of the British Polling Council and the Market Research Society, who say the identity of a client commissioning a poll should be disclosed when the results enter the public domain.Both organisations confirmed on Friday that they had launched inquiries into JL Partners. The reviews have come after Channel 4 News broadcast footage gathered by undercover reporters during a year-long investigation into Reform’s finances on Thursday night.Investigative journalists from Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a Reform donor and his American father, who paid for more than £30,000 of polling from JL Partners that generated positive headlines for the party.Nigel Farage, the party leader, was filmed saying the polling was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”.In the footage, Farage appeared to welcome the suggestion of a larger donation to the party. He was told the UK-based son could be registered as the official donor, despite the money originating from his father. Farage said: “Both of you, thank you.”11:20Reform donations scandal: is this the final blow for Farage? - The LatestIn the UK, only those registered on the electoral roll are permitted to donate to political parties, meaning the polls and the proposed larger donation could both be classed as illegal.On Friday, as its annual conference got under way in Birmingham, Reform said it had suspended two senior officials who were filmed as part of the Channel 4 News investigation.James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a senior adviser to Farage, were both recorded apparently plotting to bypass electoral laws.The first poll, conducted in January, related to the Labour government’s aborted plans to cancel some local elections, which Reform strongly opposed. The poll indicated Labour would face heavy defeats if these went ahead.The second, published in April, suggested that two-thirds of voters wanted the then prime minister, Keir Starmer, to resign. The third, released in June, appeared to show that support for Reform among trade union members was drawing level with Labour.JL Partners’ co-founder James Johnson was covertly filmed discussing the Reform polling, telling one of the reporters that his company had done “a little bit of informal rule-bending” in relation to one survey. He admitted that it “should have disclosed who the client was” when publishing the data.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe results of the polling appeared on the front pages of the Times and the Daily Telegraph. Both newspapers said they had not been aware that the polling had been commissioned by Reform.The British Polling Council said on Friday that “all data and research findings made on the basis of social or political polls conducted in the United Kingdom … must include reference to the client commissioning the survey”. It added that it was clear its rules had been breached in relation to the polls paid for by Reform.“According to the programme, this may have been deliberate,” a spokesperson added. “We are seeking further information from the BPC member concerned and expect them to make information available after further consideration.”The Market Research Society said: “MRS is aware of the Channel 4 reporting involving an MRS Company Partner. The matter is being referred to the Market Research Standards Board (MRSB) for review in line with its established complaint procedures.”JL Partners told Channel 4 News: “Despite there being no concern about the accuracy of our work, the report did reveal weaknesses in our procedures. For that reason JL Partners is reviewing those procedures in order to eliminate possible grey areas and ambiguities and strengthen our safeguards for the future.”The company did not respond to follow-up queries from the Guardian.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FarageParty fundingInvestigative journalismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ex-safety manager given 19 months’ prison over five-year-old’s hyperbaric chamber fire death | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Jeffrey Mosteller pleaded no contest to charges relating to burning death of Thomas Cooper in Michigan
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Jeffrey Mosteller pleaded no contest to charges relating to burning death of Thomas Cooper in Michigan
Content: Thomas Cooper.Photograph: GoFundMeView image in fullscreenThomas Cooper.Photograph: GoFundMeMichiganEx-safety manager given 19 months’ prison over five-year-old’s hyperbaric chamber fire deathJeffrey Mosteller pleaded no contest to charges relating to burning death of Thomas Cooper in MichiganMarina DunbarFri 4 Sep 2026 17.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former safety manager has been sentenced to one year and seven months in prison in connection with the death of a five-year-old Michigan boy who waskilledin a fiery January 2025 explosion inside a hyperbaric oxygen chamber.Jeffrey Mosteller, 66, received that sentence after pleading no contest to involuntary manslaughter in Oakland county circuit court inMichiganon Monday.He worked as the safety manager at the Oxford Center, an alternative healthcare facility that treats children with a range of health conditions – including autism, ADHD and autoimmune diseases – using hyperbaric oxygen therapy.Mosteller faced up to 15 years in prison before being handed his 19-month sentence.Five-year-old Thomas Cooper, of Royal Oak, Michigan, was undergoing treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and sleep apnea at the Oxford Center in the Detroit suburb of Troy when a fireeruptedinside the hyperbaric chamber. That triggered an explosion which killed Cooper.According to an expert whoviewed videoof the case, the child had squirmed enough to pull the sheet off a mattress inside the chamber, causing a spark of static electricity. That spark became a flash fire that incinerated him within seconds because of the oxygen-rich environment surrounding him.Cooper’s mother was badly burned on her arms and chest while desperately trying to open the tank.Mosteller is one of four former Oxford Center employees charged in connection with Thomas’s death. The other three were still awaiting trial at the time of his sentence.The Oxford Center founder and chief executive, Tamela Peterson, 58, was charged with second-degree murder. Facility manager Gary Marken, 65, was charged with second-degree murder and involuntary manslaughter. And Aleta Moffitt, 60, who was operating the chamber when it exploded, was charged with involuntary manslaughter and intentionally placing false medical information on a medical records chart.The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has cleared hyperbaric chambers to be marketed as safe and effectivefor 13 disorders, including severe burns, decompression sickness and non-healing wounds. The therapy works by delivering pure oxygen to a person’s body inside a pressurized chamber.Despite its FDA approval in certain cases, hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) has been a growingsource of controversyas the safety of these chambers have been called into question. Many allies of Trump administration health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr have endorsed HBOT, but many others have expressed skepticism towards the treatment’s increasing push into the healthcare mainstream.Cooper’s parents filed a $100mwrongful death lawsuitagainst the clinic and the chamber’s manufacturer over their son’s death.Explore more on these topicsMichiganUS crimeAlternative medicinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Democrats demand DHS documents in investigation into Rohingya refugee’s death | New York | The Guardian
description: Lawmakers condemn agency for ‘obstructing the pursuit of juice’ over death of nearly blind Nurul Amin Shah Alam
Author: Lok Darjee
Headline: Lawmakers condemn agency for ‘obstructing the pursuit of juice’ over death of nearly blind Nurul Amin Shah Alam
Content: A memorial to Nurul Amin Shah Alam in February.Photograph: Craig Ruttle/ReutersView image in fullscreenA memorial to Nurul Amin Shah Alam in February.Photograph: Craig Ruttle/ReutersNew YorkDemocrats demand DHS documents in investigation into Rohingya refugee’s deathLawmakers condemn agency for ‘obstructing the pursuit of juice’ over death of nearly blind Nurul Amin Shah AlamLok DarjeeFri 4 Sep 2026 16.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDemocratic lawmakers are demanding that the Department of Homeland Security turn over records and fully cooperate with an investigation into the death ofNurul Amin Shah Alam,a nearly blind Rohingya refugee who died afterUS border agents lefthim outside a closed coffee shop on a freezing night in Buffalo earlier this year.At a press conference in Buffalo on Friday, standing just a few feet away from where Shah was found dead, Tim Kennedy ofNew Yorkwas joined by Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the ranking Democrat on the House homeland security committee, Lou Correa of California, and Nellie Pou of New Jersey in calling on DHS to cooperate with the Erie county district attorney’s investigation.Kennedy said: “The Erie county medical examiner has ruled his death a homicide, yet DHS still won’t hand over a single meaningful record. Not to my office, not to attorney general [Tish] James, and not to the Erie county district attorney. Simply put, they are obstructing the pursuit of justice by local law enforcement.”Kennedy added: “Mr Shah Alam’s family deserves to see justice served by our legal system. I won’t stop demanding it until DHS complies.”Shah Alam, 56, was aRohingya refugeewho had lost much of his sight and spoke little English. On 19 February, after his release from the Erie county holding center, he was taken into the custody of US border patrol agents while his family waited outside the jail expecting to bring him home.Hours later, agents left Shah Alam outside a closed Tim Hortons coffee shop. His family and attorneys were not told where he had been taken or where agents had left him. Five days later, Shah Alam wasfound deadroughly four miles away.In April, the Erie county medical examinerruled his death a homicide, determining that he died from complications of a perforated duodenal ulcer precipitated by hypothermia and dehydration. The district attorney’s office is continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding his death.Kennedy has also sought legislative changes in response to the case. In June, he introduced theDHS Release Transparency Act, which would require immigration authorities to notify a detainee’s designated family member, attorney, or other contact before the person’s release and provide information about where the individual is being released.In March, New York attorney general Letitia James opened a formal investigation into Shah’s death. But in August, Jamesclosed the criminal investigation, citing the refusal of US Customs and Border Protection to cooperate.According to a letter obtained byInvestigative Post, James had requested that CBP identify the agents who “retrieved and released Mr Shah Alam” and produce “all records related to the detainer, transport, custody, dispatch communications, GPS/vehicle data, body-worn camera footage, and incident reports.”CBP declined to share any information, according to anInvestigative post.The New York attorney general’s office then referred the investigation to the Erie county district attorney.On 2 September, Kennedy and Thompson sent a formal letter to DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin, who had said during his confirmation hearing in March that thedepartment was investigating Shah’s death.In the letter to Mullin, the lawmakers demanded that “DHS fully comply with the Erie county DA’s investigation”. The lawmakers wrote that six months after Shah’s death, they had not received “a single meaningful or substantive response” from DHS, despite multiple oversight letters to the department.Speaking at the press conference, Thompson added: “If DHS has nothing to hide, then they need to turn over the records and cooperate fully with the Erie County law enforcement. It is that simple.”Explore more on these topicsNew YorkTrump administrationDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘There’s no plan’: as instability in global bond markets rises, what are the knock-on effects? | Bonds | The Guardian
description: From mortgages to inflation, concerns about the public finances of major economies have wide-reaching consequences
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: From mortgages to inflation, concerns about the public finances of major economies have wide-reaching consequences
Content: Yields on US Treasury bonds and UK gilts recently hit their highest levels for decades.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenYields on US Treasury bonds and UK gilts recently hit their highest levels for decades.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPABonds‘There’s no plan’: as instability in global bond markets rises, what are the knock-on effects?From mortgages to inflation, concerns about the public finances of major economies have wide-reaching consequencesHeather StewartandPatrick ComminsFri 4 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Donald Trump was asked recently about the threat of rising interest rates on US government debt, he told baffled reporters: “The ultimate intervention is our military. And if we have to use that, we will.”Perhaps not surprisingly, his bellicose words did not soothe fractious bond markets, and his resumption of the bombing campaign against Iran only made matters worse.The past fortnight has seen a wave of instability sweeping through government bond markets in major economies – with knock-on effects for millions of borrowers. The interest rate, or yield, on 10-year US government borrowing hit 4.8% on Friday, up from 4.64% 10 days ago. At one point midweek, the 30-year yield touched its highest level since 2008.Neil Shearing, the chief economist at the consultancy CapitalEconomics, said one impetus for the current wobble had been markets taking a fresh look at the state of US public finances. “There’s been a recalibration,” he said.Graph showing government borrowing costs are increasing in many countriesTotal US government debt hassurged past $40tn(£29.5tn), and annual deficits are forecast to be an eye-watering 6% of GDP for the foreseeable future.Such figures were long deemed barely to matter given the status of US government bonds, or treasuries, as the ultimate safe-haven investment. But as the events that led up to the 2008 financial crisis revealed, things don’t matter in the markets until they do.“I think we are starting to see a more realistic reassessment of the fiscal pressure in the US,” Shearing said. “What marks the US out is that there’s not really an acknowledgment of the fact that there might be a problem. There’s no plan.”Graph showing US government debt is projected to rise sharplyRussell Jones, a veteran bond market analyst at Llewellyn Consulting, said: “The thing about economics is that often markets delay the judgment and, you know, you can’t really time when they suddenly decide that that’s enough.”The US treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s recentfumbled attempts to intervenein financial markets – to help Tokyo prop up the yen and then to calm bond yields – have only added to the sense that policymakers are panicking.Layered on top of these concerns is a more immediate worry about inflation taking off again as a result of renewed hostilities in the Middle East. Oil prices have risen back above $90 a barrel since the US and Iran resumed tit-for-tat attacks.That has increased expectations that central banks will have to raise interest rates – another factor that puts upward pressure on yields.Graph showing oil prices have risen since the start of the US-Iran warEvery pronouncement by policymakers is being closely scrutinised for clues, including a key speech by the new Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, last Friday that was read by markets as signalling a willingness to act.The European Central Bank is expected to lead the charge with a rate rise next week, but markets are telegraphing higher borrowing costs across major economies.That includes the UK, where investors are now pencilling in three quarter-point rate rises over the next 12 months, and Japan, where the decades-long period of deflation and rock-bottom rates is finally coming to an end.A dramatic expansion of borrowing by AI “hyperscalers” in the US, to help fund the massive planned expansion of datacentres, has offered investors an alternative home for their cash – and raised questions about the market’s ability to absorb so much debt simultaneously.Recent calculations by the investment group Vanguard put the value of debt issued by five major tech companies at $135bn (£100bn) this year, up from an average of $35bn between 2020 and 2024.Graph showing rising spending by tech giants including Alphabet, Amazon and MetaThere is potentially an even more fundamental explanation for an upward shift in borrowing costs, too – based on the growing prevalence of inflationary shocks not just as a result of geopolitical chaos but because of the climate emergency.Some economists, including the Bank of England policymaker Swati Dhingra, have argued these increasingly regular shocks, as a result of extreme weather events and resulting economic upheaval, could lead to structurally higher interest rates.Whatever the causes of rising bond yields, the impact is already rippling out worldwide. Public borrowing has increased dramatically in recent years as policymakers have stepped in to cushion consumers against Covid shutdowns, wrestled with sharply higher energy prices since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and stepped up defence spending. That means small changes in global interest rates can have an outsized impact on government budgets.In the UK, where £1 in every £12 of public spending already goes on debt interest, Andy Burnham, the prime minister, was pressed this week by the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, about the rising cost of government borrowing.Higher yields on gilts, as UK government bonds are known, will feed through into predictions of higher interest rate costs for the Treasury ahead of the new chancellor John Healey’s autumn budget.David Aikman, the director of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, urged the government to take the opportunity to implement spending cuts and/or tax increases to help insulate the UK from higher borrowing costs.“There will be a lot of talk about the fiscal rules. I think that’s slightly missing the point,” he said. “The big point here is we’ve just got a lot of debt, whether you’re missing the rules or not. And it means we’re really vulnerable.”On the other side of the world, Australian policymakers have been wrestling with similar challenges. Bond yields have breached 15-year highs just days after the country passed A$1tn in government debt.The timing of the two milestones comes at a difficult time for a Labor government that is under pressure to rein in historically high levels of spending.Falling house prices in a property-obsessed nation are adding to a mood of discontent. Bets have firmed that the Reserve Bank of Australia could deliver another interest rate hike later this month to tame stubbornly high inflation.Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, has been at pains to highlight Australia’s relatively strong budget position internationally. Australia’s debt is equivalent to about half the size of the economy, which pales against other advanced nations. Similarly, the commonwealth is running deficits, but of less than 1% of GDP.Chris Richardson, an independent budget expert, said Australia’s government indebtedness wasn’t “bad by world standards”. “But it’s still a lot of debt. And the higher cost of money means the difficult choices that were there already are that much harder.”For developing countries, these issues are all the more urgent. The International Monetary Fund warned earlier this year that these economies hadbecome more exposedto the risk of higher interest rates, because of the growing importance of lending from short-term investors such as hedge funds, which tend to be more flighty during periods of market volatility.Matthew Martin, of the advocacy group Development Finance International, said: “A lot of these countries are very near the edge, and if they have to go back to the markets and refinance another bond at 1% or 2% higher than it was before, that will mean even less money to spend on climate action, health and education.”If higher yields are sustained, the effects will be felt far beyond the world’s treasuries, muddying the maths for corporate investments and putting upward pressure on mortgage rates, which in the UK have already started to rise.Aikman argued corporate balance sheets worldwide looked less shaky than before the global financial crisis. “We’re not in the place we were in the run-up to 2008,” he said. But he pointed to “pockets” of concern, including the huge scale of debt-fuelled private equity projects that could prove vulnerable in a world of higher rates.By the end of the week, the sell-off sweeping global bond markets appeared to have eased, for now. But it left yields at levels significantly higher than three months ago – and delivered a painful reminder to policymakers, including Burnham, that in globalised financial markets their plans can be buffeted by forces far beyond their control.Explore more on these topicsBondsGiltsGovernment borrowingUS Government borrowingInflationGlobal economyEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maria Bartiromo’s lawyer denies she was fired from Fox News anchor role | Fox News | The Guardian
description: Fox announced host’s departure Thursday but gave no explanation, only saying it was effective immediately
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Fox announced host’s departure Thursday but gave no explanation, only saying it was effective immediately
Content: Fox Business Network's Mornings with Maria show anchor Maria Bartiromo, speaks during an interview, on 9 June 2026, in Washington.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreenFox Business Network's Mornings with Maria show anchor Maria Bartiromo, speaks during an interview, on 9 June 2026, in Washington.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APFox NewsMaria Bartiromo’s lawyer denies she was fired from Fox News anchor roleFox announced host’s departure Thursday but gave no explanation, only saying it was effective immediatelyGaya Guptain New YorkFri 4 Sep 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 14.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaria Bartiromo’s lawyer sharply denied that she was fired from her job atFox Newson Friday, after reports that she was dismissed after divulging the network’s editorial guidance to the White House.Fox announcedBartiromo’s departureon Thursday but provided no explanation, saying only in a statement that it was effective immediately.“Effective today, Maria Bartiromo is no longer with FOX News Media,” the network said in a press release, adding in a statement: “We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 and a half years and wish her all the best on her next chapter.”Fox News Media abruptly ousts longtime anchor Maria BartiromoRead moreShe had been with Fox for more than 12 years and hosted a popular three-hour weekday morning show for the Fox Business network, as well as a Sunday morning show.Status Newsreported on Thursday that Fox instructed senior employees to avoid covering Donald Trump’s July primetime address, where he sharedunproven and false claims about the 2020 election. Bartiromo, an avid Trump supporter, shared that message with the White House, according to Status News, a violation of company policy. Bartiromo was taken off the air shortly after.In a statement, Bryan Freedman, Bartiromo’s attorney, called her, “one of the hardest-working journalists throughout her award-winning career” and denied the claims reported by Status News. Freedman has previously defendedseveral journalists fired from their networks, including Don Lemon at CNN, Megyn Kelly at NBC News and Tucker Carlson at Fox.“The irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false,” Freedman said in a statement. “Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise. Those reporting her firing or the incredulous facts supporting that fiction have exhibited a complete and utter reckless disregard for the truth.”A Fox spokesperson pointed to the company’s original statement and said: “The release speaks for itself.”Several former Fox News employees are now working at the Trump administration, including Trump’s defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. With the recent announcement that Trump’s press secretary, Karoline Leavitt,would be stepping downat the end of August, some have speculated that Bartiromo might be tapped to step into the role.After news broke of her departure, Trumpposted:“I can’t believe Maria Bartiromo is no longer going to have her great show(s) on FoxNews/Business. Three different shows, always number one. Maria is a total professional, and a true warrior. Her fans, of which there are many, will not be happy. God bless you, Maria! President DONALD J. TRUMP”Explore more on these topicsFox NewsDonald TrumpUS television industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: US added 162,000 jobs in August, with unemployment rate holding steady | US unemployment and employment data | The Guardian
description: Number of new jobs being added has been fluctuating, with private companies adding 38,000 jobs in August
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: Number of new jobs being added has been fluctuating, with private companies adding 38,000 jobs in August
Content: A job seeker holds a now hiring flyer as they receive information about education careers in Los Angeles, California, on 29 July 2026.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA job seeker holds a now hiring flyer as they receive information about education careers in Los Angeles, California, on 29 July 2026.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesUS unemployment and employment dataUS added 162,000 jobs in August, with unemployment rate holding steadyNumber of new jobs being added has been fluctuating, with private companies adding 38,000 jobs in AugustLauren ArataniFri 4 Sep 2026 08.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS economyadded 162,000 jobs in August, an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market.The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, still down from its most recent peak of 4.5% last November, according to new data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Despite the relative stability of the unemployment rate, the number of new jobs added to the economy has been fluctuating, going from 214,000 in March down to a 21,000 gain in July and then back up in August.August jobs reportFigures for job growth in June and July were both revised up. After revisions, job growth in June was 31,000 jobs, up from an initial 20,000, and July was revised up by 44,000 jobs, from an initially reported loss of 23,000 to a gain of 21,000.Economists had predicted gains would be at least 50,000 new jobs. Earlier in the week, the payroll firm ADP reported private companies added 38,000 jobs in August, lower than initial expectations and the lowest month for new jobs since January. Meanwhile, outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmasreportedthat layoffs have been going down and are 41% lower than cuts that were announced by this time last year.Economists have pointed out that the labor market appears to be stalled in a “slow hire, slow fire” state, with neither growth nor contractions in jobs.A separate BLS report from earlier this week showed job openings and layoffs had changed little in July. The number of people quitting their jobs also remained flat, suggesting workers are feeling less confident about their ability to find another job.For many Americans feelingfrustratedabout the economy, a lackluster job market feels especially painful when paired with rising prices. US inflation has increased significantly since the start of the war with Iran, with the annual inflation rate going from 2.4% in February to 3.4%in July. In May, price increases reached 4.2%, the highest rate since 2023.In recent weeks, persistent inflation has started to have a domino effect in the US economy after asell-offin the US bond market.
