Yields for US Treasury bonds have been going up since the start of the Iran war, suggesting that investors are concerned about the long-term health of the economy. Higher yields could push up the price of loans, including mortgages, car loans and the interest rate on student debt, making things even more costly for Americans.Economists are expecting at least one interest rate hike from the USFederal Reservebefore the end of the year. Higher interest rates could help lower inflation, but at the risk of destabilizing the labor market.Last week, Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair, gave his debutspeechat the Fed’s symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, where he said the Fed was still committed to getting inflation down to its 2% target rate, but held off on making any firm suggestions on the central bank’s next move.“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” he said. “Otherwise, we have work to do.”Donald Trump on Friday celebrated the new job figures and threatened to “stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit” if the Fed doesn’t lower interest rates.“A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE –IT’S A BETTER CREDIT… Very simple!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “We should have the LOWEST RATE of any country in the World, like ‘the old days’.”Explore more on these topicsUS unemployment and employment dataUS economyInflationUS interest ratesFederal ReserveEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Private equity faces existential crisis in US as unsold companies pile up | Business | The Guardian
description: Private equity firms and the companies they own employ over 13 million, from startups to rural hospitals and large retailers, but experts’ concerns of collapse are growing
Author: Heather Timmons
Headline: Private equity firms and the companies they own employ over 13 million, from startups to rural hospitals and large retailers, but experts’ concerns of collapse are growing
Content: Shoppers pass a closing sale at an Eddie Bauer store in February.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenShoppers pass a closing sale at an Eddie Bauer store in February.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockConsumedBusinessPrivate equity faces existential crisis in US as unsold companies pile upPrivate equity firms and the companies they own employ over 13 million, from startups to rural hospitals and large retailers, but experts’ concerns of collapse are growingHeather TimmonsFri 4 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 17.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRetail stalwarts Saks and Eddie Bauer filed for bankruptcy. Kmart and JoAnn Fabrics are gone for good, a trail of layoffs anddisappointed customersin their wake. Hospital giant Steward Health Care collapsed,costingthousands of jobs and leaving several communities without a local hospital.These once-trusted US companies have one thing in common: they were owned by private equity investors, who load companies with debt when they buy them and squeeze out profits as they restructure.The business model is now facing an existential crisis that may have profound ramifications across the US.Once fringe financial players, private equity investors have bought up vast swathes of US, UK, European and Australian industry, fromlocal dentiststo shopping mall anchors and fast-food chains and even thevideo games company EA.In the US,these firms and the companies they own, employ more than 13 million people in everything from quirky startups like Dave’s Hot Chicken, Two Men and a Truck and School of Rock (allowned by Roark Capital) to the US’s largest pet retailer PetSmart (BC Partners) and classics Birkenstock (purchased byL Catterton in 2021) and Pyrex (owned byCentre Lane Partners).Private equity investors also boughtthousands of healthcare facilitiesin the US in recent years, including non-profit hospice care, rural hospitals and small-town dentists’ offices.But this wave of buyouts is running smack into a wall ofpersistently high interest rates, rising buyout prices and pressure overmoribund returns.Private equity funds are sitting on a “record number of unsold companies, many of which they’ve been unable to sell … or at least unable to sell at the prices that they’re looking for”, said Jim Baker, the executive director of thePrivate Equity Stakeholder Project,an industry watchdog.A bar chart showing that private equity firms are holding on to more than 13,500 unsold US companiesThe US’s over 13,500 unsold companies in private equity portfolios include 2,563 consumer products and services companies, PitchBook data shows, and 1,536 healthcare companies. Hundreds of these have been sitting in PE portfolios for years longer than funds historically like to keep their investments.A growing concern is that “eventually, the companies that have accumulated this much debt are going to collapse”, said Audrey Stienon, Industrial Policy Program Manager at Open Markets, an anti-monopoly thinktank that isexamining private equity’s rolein the greater economy.And often, what private equity buys up “are really, really important businesses”, Stienon said, providing jobs or vital services to local communities. “When they go down, either you need to bail them out, or you need to find someone to save them, or else you’re just stuck with fewer options for consumers down the line.”Executives in the industry argue their deep pockets will help businesses weather any upcoming crisis. “Private equity-backed businesses face the same higher interest rates and economic pressures as other companies, but they also have committed investment partners that can provide additional capital and keep investing through difficult periods,” Will Dunham, the president and CEO of American Investment Council, an industry trade group, said in a statement.“Ultimately, private equity only succeeds when the businesses it invests in succeed over the long term,” he said.High rates, more competitionThink of private equity deals like buying a home, explains Brad Lipton, director of corporate power and financial regulation at the Roosevelt Institute. Investors buy the company with a hefty loan, like a mortgage, but plan to sell in a matter of years.But unlike with a mortgage, the company is on the hook for making payments, not the buyer, and the buyer almost always plans to sell in a few years.“Interest rates being unexpectedly high may have complicated exit strategies,” Lipton said.Private equity firms promise investors higher returns than the stock market, in exchange for holding on to their money for a longer time period, generally 10 years, a business model that’s been the same for decades.“What has changed is that the price of buying a target company has gone through the roof,” as the number of private equity funds increased, explains Rosemary Batt, a Cornell University management and labor professor who studies the industry’s impacts on workers and companies. Healthcare companies that once sold at 11 times EBITDA, a measure of enterprise value, are now priced at 18 times or more, for example.That makes exiting the investment for a profit even more difficult on investors – and on customers and employees.The higher prices for buyouts are “putting even more pressure on PE firms to squeeze the juice out of their portfolio companies”, Batt said, at a time when there’s almost no regulation governing how they do that.“They can engage in financial engineering or just slash and burn on the operating side,” Batt said. “And it takes years for anyone to really see it.”As they hold the company, these investors generally channel free cashflow to “creditors and equityholders, often constraining capital expenditures, worker training, and safety investments”, the University of Chicago’s Business Law Reviewwarns. Tightening macroeconomic conditions can result in forced restructurings “that are costly and value‑destroying for the going concern”.One vulnerable area is rural hospitals and other health provider chains which could face cashflow issues, making debt payments even more difficult, as the Trump administration’s cuts to the Affordable Care Act tax credits and Medicaid bite, warns Pablo Willis, spokesman for the Americans for Tax Fairness, which isadvocating for changesto how private equity managers compensation and the firms overall are taxed.“There’s bound to be a very negative effect,” he said.A lack of financial transparency means it is hard to predict where or when, though. Companies owned by private equity generally don’t disclose their debt levels or other financials unless they go public or issue bonds themselves.“By design, the industry takes place in the shadows,” Lipton said, so “everything has to begin with the thought that we don’t have a lot of clarity.”More bankruptcies aheadIn a hint of the turmoil to come, private equity-backed companies have accounted for the lion’s share of big corporate bankruptcies in 2025 and the first half of 2026, research from the Private Equity Stakeholder Partnership shows.A bar chart showing the number of PE companies that went bankrupt in 2025, by liability totalsThe biggest determinant of whether or not a company will go bankrupt is leverage – the amount of borrowed money explains Edith Hotchkiss, a finance professor at Boston College. Private equity-backed companies are no more likely to default than other similarly leveraged firms, but their business models mean they have more debt.They carry debt of about 50% of their enterprise value,recent studies show.US consumers have felt private equity’s impact through the deteriorating quality of some fast-food outlets and disappearing stores as brands under PE ownership go broke.chart 3Other industries have been hit too. More than 60% of big manufacturing bankruptcies in the US last year were private equity-backed, Baker said, as were an outsized number of healthcare bankruptcies.Still, the number of PE-backed companies entering bankruptcy declined in 2025 from the year before, even as overall bankruptcies climbed,S&P found, as more companies pursued out-of-court settlements.The entire process is disruptive by nature. “By definition there is not enough money to go around to pay” a company’s debts, Roosevelt’s Lipton said. “Someone is going to lose out and all too often that can be workers” who are owed pensions.“It is a cause of concern for workers and consumers left holding the bag,” said Lipton.New rules aheadPrivate equity operates without the rules and regulatory oversight of publicly traded companies. The industry has long argued that because it caters to sophisticated, high-net worth investors, it doesn’t need the same scrutiny.But tens of thousands of layoffs, high bankruptcy rates, and the soaring wealth ofdozens of private equity billionaireshas created bipartisan momentum for more oversight, even before the current interest rate crisis. AndDonald Trump’s pushto allow everyday Americans to invest in the sector through their retirement plans has raised new concerns.Congress’sJune housing billcurbs private equity investments in single-family homes. November’s midterm elections, which are widely expected to deliver one or both houses of Congress to Democrats, could see a sea change for the industry in Washington, while several states are pursuing their own regulation.View image in fullscreenA closed Kmart store stands at Astor Place in 2021 in New York City.Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty Images“For private equity, the question increasingly is not whether Congress will investigate private equity firms and their practices, but rather where the scrutiny will turn to next,” corporate law firm Holland and Knightwarned this month.Multiple bills are circulating on Capitol Hill that would regulate how private equity is taxed, how it can invest in certain industries and how fund managers and investors can take profits.States’ billswould limit private equity in healthcare, scrutinize deals more closely and put caps on debt.The“Let Kids Play” Actseeks to ban private equity from youth community sports, now a “$40bn industry dominated by private equity, with the singular goal of extracting as much profit as possible from families”, it contends.The Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren, one of the industry’s most vocal critics in Washington, is leading ahealthcare billthat seeks criminal penalties for “executives who loot health care entities like nursing homes and hospitals if that looting results in a patient’s death” and clawbacks of PE compensation.Whether US consumers see some relief could depend on what state they live in, or what other issues Congress takes up in the fall. “Even Democrats will be very hard pressed to do much,” if they have any clout in Congress, Batt predicts, because they have so much on their plate. “The best opportunities right now are for local and state level initiatives,” she said.Explore more on these topicsBusinessConsumedRetail industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Isak’s rapid double sinks Ipswich to give Andoni Iraola first Liverpool win | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Two early goals from Alexander Isak gave Liverpool a 2-0 win at Ipswich, Andoni Iraola’s first as head coach
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Two early goals from Alexander Isak gave Liverpool a 2-0 win at Ipswich, Andoni Iraola’s first as head coach
Content: Alexander Isak jumps for after scoring his second goal.Photograph: Dave Shopland/APView image in fullscreenAlexander Isak jumps for after scoring his second goal.Photograph: Dave Shopland/APPremier LeagueIsak’s rapid double sinks Ipswich to give Andoni Iraola first Liverpool winJohn Brewinat Portman RoadFri 4 Sep 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA first win for Andoni Iraola’sLiverpool, the introduction of the latest star signing in Bradley Barcola making for a successful Friday night. Better yet, continuing signs that Alexander Isak, last year’s model, is coming back to life, his two, well-taken early goals securing the three points. That Cody Gakpo, Isak’s supplier, might have been at Manchester City or Tottenham had the transfer runes been right, added further to a sense of renewal. Liverpool’s attackers were full of the speed and invention sorely lacking for much of last season.Once Barcola arrived in the second half, those velocity levels increased yet further, Liverpool playing the attacking style, high on risk and entertainment, the appointment of Iraola promised. “We are starting to get to the way we want to play,” said Isak afterwards.Ipswich Town v Liverpool: Premier League – liveRead moreTravelling Liverpool fans were made to wait for their first glimpse of £123m Barcola, his being on the bench adding further suspense to a deal that took an entire summer to complete.If Ipswich looked to show the “emotional discipline” their manager, Gary O’Neil, said they lacked in losing 5-2 at Old Trafford, little was in evidence in a ruinous opening spell that betrayed the decent performance they went on to put in.How long will Iraola’s doctrines take to embed? Perhaps not as long as feared. Isak, the most expensive player signed under the outgoing sporting director Richard Hughes, looks – at last – to be flowering. To follow his strike against Nottingham Forest, he had scored twice by the 10th minute. “If Alex is fit and is available, he will produce the numbers,” said Iraola.Assisted for both by Gakpo, the finishes were of the gold standard Liverpool invested so heavily in. “Cody was outstanding,” said Virgil van Dijk, sharing the credit. “I said it before the transfer window had closed, he’s important for us, and he will be important this season.” Iraola joined the appreciation society: “I had no doubt with Cody … he knows how much we value him.”“The level is ruthless,” said O’Neil, otherwise exalted by his team’s response to adversity beyond those opening nine minutes. “If you make mistakes against players like Gakpo, Wirtz and Barcola, there’s a chance you will get punished.”Just as at Old Trafford, two Ipswich goals were conceded in quick, damaging succession, the defence far too open and chaotic. After Víctor Muñoz had set off on a long run stopped only by Issa Diop’s last-man tackle, Julio Enciso controlled the ball, taking a beat by standing on the ball, as if calling for calm.Isak, who had a third first-half goal disallowed for offside, made the runs into scoring positions that made his reputation, nothing like the sorry figure of his debut, lost season. Meanwhile, a no-look pass from Ipswich’s captain, Dara O’Shea, straight to Gakpo, betrayed a collective cognitive dissonance.View image in fullscreenBradley Barcola beats Dara O’Shea on his Liverpool debut.Photograph: Dave Shopland/APFlorian Wirtz becoming involved with the tricks and flicks offered another pointer that last summer’s huge Liverpool outlay may not be so wasteful as it appeared in Arne Slot’s dog days. Iraola’s appointment came with a reputation for improving players. Should the Basque get the best from the German, in a similar price bracket to Barcola and Isak, then this week’s pronouncement he is happy with his squad will ring truer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAn obvious gap in the Liverpool squad left by Hughes is a commanding defensive midfielder. Enciso often located space, though suffered for a lack of quality around him. Beyond the break, with O’Neil in full flow, barking at players and officials alike, Ipswich were more confrontational, less admiring of their opponent’s higher skill levels. “I hate having to talk about good performances when you don’t get points because you need to maximise them,” said O’Neil, painting a picture that will not match many other summations of the match.Muñoz, stocky and adventurous, might well prove the answer to the right-wing vacancy left by Mohamed Salah, showing off a ready work ethic before departing in the double substitution that brought Barcola on. Isak also departed, returning after full time to an ovation from fans finally seeing something close to his potential.With Gakpo pushed to centre-forward, Barcola’s first touches came off the left flank, one drop of the shoulder and sprint beyond O’Shea lifting the volume among the away supporters. “He hadn’t played a single minute since the World Cup so we had to be careful,” said Iraola. “He was always a threat.”That burst of Barcola preceded another loss of Ipswich faculties as Leif Davis first pulled Dominik Szoboszlai, and then knocked him over for what appeared a clear penalty. Only an offside ruled by the video assistant protected the Ipswich defender’s modesty. The announcement of that decision brought the loudest cheer of the night from the home contingent.Barcola, even amid the warp speed of thePremier League, showed lightning acceleration when creating a late chance for Gakpo. An impressive cameo and the expectation of far more to come from the player and his new team.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueIpswich TownLiverpoolmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka halts US Open match due to cannabis smell  | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Aryna Sabalenka briefly stopped her US Open match, complaining about the strong smell of cannabis on court
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Aryna Sabalenka briefly stopped her US Open match, complaining about the strong smell of cannabis on court
Content: Aryna Sabalenka needs to win the US Open to retain her No 1 ranking.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersView image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka needs to win the US Open to retain her No 1 ranking.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersUS Open Tennis 2026‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka halts US Open match due to cannabis smell‘It’s tricky to handle when you’re trying to compete’Alcaraz into fourth round after straight sets victoryTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsFri 4 Sep 2026 17.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAryna Sabalenka briefly stopped her match at the US Open to complain about the strong smell of cannabis on her court as she comfortably reached the fourth round in New York.Sabalenka, the two-time defending champion, continued her attempts to rebuild her form as she overcame a challenging test from Kamilla Rakhimova before winning 6-3, 6-4.Early in the match, a smiling Sabalenka approached the chair umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore while leading 3-0, stating “Someone is smoking weed, do you mind … because it’s so strong,” Afterwards, Sabalenka laughed as she described her interaction with the umpire: “I was, like, Guys, you can do whatever, you can smoke whatever, you can relax as much as you can, but please, do not do it around the tennis courts. It’s a bit tricky to handle that smell while you’re trying to compete at your best.”US Open tennis: Alcaraz beats Wu, Sabalenka, Pegula and Medvedev advance on day six – liveRead moreCannabis is legal in New York and weed can be smelled around tournament grounds, as is the case all around the city. This has become a common talking point at the US Open in recent years. Although Sabalenka initially seemed to believe that the smoke may have been coming from a spectator in or right by the crowd, she later said she was unclear about its origins but the smell of cannabis was stronger than she had ever smelt it during her years of competing in New York: “That strong, yeah. Also, because it was a bit windy. I don’t know if it was, like, coming from the crowd or was from the outside because the wind blows it into the stadium. I don’t know. I just hope they’re going to be a bit more aware of that stuff,” she said.Most importantly for Sabalenka, she has returned to the round of 16 without dropping a set and she appears to be finding some rhythm on the court. This victory was spearheaded by a stellar serving performance, with the Belarusian serving 10 aces and facing zero break points. She had arrived in New York in some of her most difficult form for years, having failed to reach a final since spectacularly winning Indian Wells and Miami back-to-back in March. Sabalenka will lose her No 1 ranking, which she has held for 97 weeks, unless she wins her third US Open title in a row and Elena Rybakina, the world No 2, loses before the semi-finals.Although Sabalenka has put together a series of encouraging performances on-court, the added pressure on her shoulders has perhaps been revealed elsewhere. After her dominant second round win over Polina Iatcenko, Sabalenka clashed with a reporter in her post-match press conference when the reporter described her week before the US Open as “parties and fun”.View image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz enjoyed a straightforward win over Yibing Wu.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAThis was the second time during the tournament that a reporter had referenced pre-tournament obligations leading up to the US Open, prompting a forceful response from Sabalenka: “You guys are, like, a joke,” she said. “‘Parties, fun …’ like, why would you even say that? Why would you even think about that? What kind of question is that? Just because I posted, like, some activities with brands, and you think that I’ve been partying, not training?”Sabalenka eventually ended the lengthy, heated exchange by imploring the reporter to: “Think before you say stuff.”A tougher test awaits Sabalenka in the fourth round as she faces the home favourite Taylor Townsend, who followed up her great run to the fourth round last year with another excellent tournament in New York. Townsend defeated the 15th seed Diana Shnaider 6-2, 6-7 (3), 6-3 to return to the fourth round.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDaniil Medvedev, the 2021 men’s singles champion, also continued to find his feet in New York as he reached the fourth round with a 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 victory over the 29th seed Arthur Rinderknetch.Carlos Alcaraz, the men’s defending champion, continues to grow in confidence on his return to tennis from a four-and-a-half month injury layoff and he moved into the fourth round with a 6-3, 6-4, 6-1 win over Wu Yibing of China. Alcaraz, who until the tournament had not competed since injuring his right wrist at the beginning of April, had to hold his nerve and problem solve during some tight moments in the first two sets. However, he elevated his game in those decisive moments and he continues to show that he will be difficult to defeat despite how early it is in his comeback.Alcaraz will next face the 20th seed Tommy Paul, an American player, who overcame the 15th seed Alexander Bublik 6-4, 3-6, 6-7(4), 6-1, 6-3: “To be honest, I’m better than I thought,” Alcaraz said. “Physically, I thought I was going to be bad after the first match but I’m recovering really well, I’m doing great things off the court out be in a good shape and right now I think my level is good. I’ve got the rhythm of the competition. Every time I step on to the court, I give it my all.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Aryna SabalenkaTennisUS Open tennisUS sportsCarlos AlcaraznewsShareReuse this content

title: Cathy Engelbert’s WNBA tenure: the wins and losses that defined her seven years | WNBA | The Guardian
description: From record growth and a landmark media deal to expansion, labor battles and a fractured relationship with players, Engelbert’s tenure was rarely quiet
Author: Stephanie Kaloi
Headline: From record growth and a landmark media deal to expansion, labor battles and a fractured relationship with players, Engelbert’s tenure was rarely quiet
Content: Caitlin Clark poses with WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert after being selected No 1 overall by the Indiana Fever at the 2024 WNBA draft in New York.Photograph: Sarah Stier/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCaitlin Clark poses with WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert after being selected No 1 overall by the Indiana Fever at the 2024 WNBA draft in New York.Photograph: Sarah Stier/Getty ImagesWNBAAnalysisCathy Engelbert’s WNBA tenure: the wins and losses that defined her seven yearsStephanie KaloiFrom record growth and a landmark media deal to expansion, labor battles and a fractured relationship with players, Engelbert’s tenure was rarely quietFri 4 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 14.27 EDTShareWNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbertwill retire from the roleon 31 December, bringing an end to a tenure that began with her appointment as the league’s first commissioner in 2019.“After more than seven years at theWNBAand more than 40 total years in business, I have made the decision to retire as WNBA Commissioner,” Engelbert said in a statement shared by the league. “In 2019, I had the privilege of being appointed the league’s first commissioner and to lead a league with enormous potential yet untapped awareness and significant undervaluation. Over the years, it has been amazing to watch WNBA players thrive and lead the massive cultural surge around women’s sports.”WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert says she will retire at end of yearRead moreEngelbert has not always been popular with players or fans. Her tenure has featured landmark successes as well as bruising controversies. Here is a look at some of the defining moments of her seven years leading the WNBA.The winsEngelbert was thrust into the fire almost immediately when the Covid-19 pandemic threatened her first season in charge. She helped oversee the creation of the “Wubble” at IMG Academy in Florida, allowing the league to stage a shortened 22-game season in 2020. The regular-season schedule has since expanded to 44 games and will grow to 50 in 2027.Engelbert has presided over the WNBA during a period of historic growth, with sharp increases in television audiences, attendance, sponsorship revenue and merchandise sales. It would be nonsensical to deny that her tenure produced enormous results.Engelbert also led the WNBA through a huge expansion from 12 teams to 18 by 2030. The Golden State Valkyries joined the league for the 2025 season, while this year saw the addition of both the Portland Fire and the Toronto Tempo. Teams from Cleveland, Detroit and Philadelphia will join by the decade’s end.But there are two key achievements that will probably come to define Engelbert’s time as commissioner: the league’slandmark $3.1bn media rights dealand the unprecedented collective bargaining agreement (CBA) struck between the league and the players, both of which were negotiated this year.That 11-year media rights deal resulted in an astronomical increase to the league’s annual revenue – to the tune of $281m – and includes partners Amazon, Disney and NBC. The deal also resulted in more than 200 games being streamed or aired live this season (out of 330 total regular-season games).View image in fullscreenWNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert speaks before the 2026 WNBA draft in New York.Photograph: Angelina Katsanis/Getty ImagesThe CBA negotiations between the WNBA and the Women’s National Basketball Players’ Association dominated most of the league’s coverage ahead of the 2026 season. The two partiesreached a verbal agreementin March andratified the deal a week laterafter months of often-contentious negotiations. Though Engelbert was on the receiving end of much of the scrutiny that accompanied those negotiations, she maintained the end result was worth it.WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert has a hard job. Here’s how to make it easier | Jordan RobinsonRead more“It was contentious. Some of that is negotiations and the way negotiations work, and I know I talked about that at draft because, remember at draft we had just finished the negotiations, so it was a little more recent,” Engelbert told reporters during WNBA All-Star Weekend. “And today, I just can’t be more proud of these players: how we were able to have so many players sign million-dollar-plus, multi-year contracts.”She continued: “I think they know that the league is in a really good place, and now they’re in a revenue share with the league, as you know, because that was part of the CBA. So I think I feel like at this and the Orange Carpet … we’re all kind of gelling from that perspective of what’s good for our players is good for our league, and we’ll all benefit from that.”This year’s CBA raised the salary cap from $1.5m to $7m, gave players approximately 20% of shared revenue, increased supermax salaries to $1.4m and established a $300,000 minimum salary. Just as significantly in the short term, after months of increasingly contentious negotiations, the agreement ensured the 2026 season began on time.The league will also continue to reap more benefits thanks to Engelbert’s work as commissioner, including the creation of a fully centralized replay center starting in 2027.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe lossesBut Engelbert’s tenure has also been marked by tensions with players, with her communication – or lack of it – at the heart of much of the criticism directed her way.For example, the Phoenix Mercury’s Alyssa Thomas said she didn’t hear from Engelbert afterreceiving death threatsfollowing a foul interaction with Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark. “A lot of us, myself included, didn’t even know the play took place until after the game, and now we’re being painted as thugs and there’s death threats out on us, so it’s really unacceptable, it’s something that needs to change in this league, and I’m just really sick and tired of it,” Thomas told reporters.She continued: “We still have yet to hear anything from Cathy, it’s no surprise. As usual, she remains silent, and that’s unfortunate when our lives are being threatened.”Thomas isn’t the only player who has spoken about Engelbert’s lack of communication. “My only relationship with Cathy is when she hands me awards, which is great. I love to see her,” A’ja Wilson joked at All-Star Weekend. The moment was funny, but also illuminating.And it would be impossible to forget Napheesa Collier’sblockbuster broadside toward Engelbertat the end of the 2025 season. “This past February, I sat across from [Engelbert] and asked how she planned to address the officiating issues in our league,” Collier told reporters in October. “Her response was, ‘Well, only the losers complain about the refs.’ I also asked how she planned to fix the fact that players like [Clark, Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers], who are clearly driving massive revenue for the league and are making so little for their first four years.View image in fullscreenDawn Staley and Sarah Kustok speak with WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert during the 2022 Commissioner’s Cup championship game in Chicago.Photograph: Jeff Haynes/NBAE/Getty Images“Her response was, ‘[Clark] should be grateful she makes $16m off the court because without the platform that the WNBA gives her, she wouldn’t make anything.’ And in that same conversation, she told me, ‘Players should be on their knees, thanking their lucky stars for the media rights deal that I got them.’”Engelbert, in her availability at All-Star, acknowledged she could have done more. Communication is and was “absolutely something I’ve been talking with the players about, how much they want to hear from us, how much they don’t”, she said. “We do send them a lot of email updates and things like that. They’re a generation that doesn’t check email as much, so we have to get better at a text chain.”She added: “There’s no doubt I need to be better, everybody needs to be better at communication, I think, all the time. So we’ll continue to work on that and communicate.”Engelbert also seemed to chalk much of the complaints up to missed signals. “I figure the players don’t want to hear from us all the time, so we’re going to institute more frequent communications with them when it’s appropriate,” she said.It was a striking disconnect for a commissioner who oversaw such extraordinary growth. Engelbert helped build a WNBA that was richer, larger and more influential than the one she inherited. Yet as the players themselves became more powerful, the distance between them and the league’s commissioner often appeared to grow along with it.Explore more on these topicsWNBABasketballanalysisShareReuse this content

title: The wild world of LSU: from tigers on the field to wooing ex-NFL players  | College sports | The Guardian
description: Recruiting ex-pros. Inflaming Ukraine-Russia tensions. Suing the SEC and being sued back. The school is adapting to a new reality – and also creating a new one
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: Recruiting ex-pros. Inflaming Ukraine-Russia tensions. Suing the SEC and being sued back. The school is adapting to a new reality – and also creating a new one
Content: LSU football coach Lane Kiffin; women’s basketball coach Kim Mulkey; and Louisiana governor Jeff Landry.Composite: Photos by Gus Stark/LSU/University Images via Getty Images; Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images; AP Photo/Gerald HerbertView image in fullscreenLSU football coach Lane Kiffin; women’s basketball coach Kim Mulkey; and Louisiana governor Jeff Landry.Composite: Photos by Gus Stark/LSU/University Images via Getty Images; Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images; AP Photo/Gerald HerbertCollege sportsThe wild world of LSU: from tigers on the field to wooing ex-NFL playersRecruiting ex-pros. Inflaming Ukraine-Russia tensions. Suing the SEC and being sued back. The school is adapting to a new reality – and also creating a new oneAndrew LawrenceFri 4 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1893, a chemistry professor named Charles Coates arrived at Louisiana State University andwrotethat, to his surprise, “there was practically no athletics in the student body: no football, no tennis, and only very little baseball in the spring.” A broad program of sports struck him as the kind of thing a school should have, particularly as US universities were beginning to tout intercollegiate athletics as critical to a balanced higher-ed experience and another way to justify the cost of entry. But 133 years on, sports aren’t merely the main attraction at LSU. They’re the school’sraison d’être, the blinkered obsession that consumes the university and its most prominent ambassadors.Any doubt that the business of educating college students is just a nettlesome distraction from the business of college sports in Baton Rouge has been emphatically dispelled over the past 10 months. On the football side, the school has spent or committed roughly $162m to its last three head coaches: Ed Orgeron,the folksy national champion in 2019who received a $17m buyout when he was fired two years later; Brian Kelly, the unloved underachiever who received a$54m buyoutafter being fired last October; and Lane Kiffin, the Kelly replacement whom it signed to a $91m deal a month later. Clemson, the opponent for LSU’s season opener at home on Saturday, are about to find out what all that money buys.College football is booming, chaotic and more confusing than everRead moreIn March, LSU brought back men’s basketball coach Will Wade, the turnaround artist who became a national emblem of college sports’ old pay-for-play hypocrisy when he wascaught on an FBI wiretapdiscussing a recruiting offer seven years ago. An NCAA dragnet soon uncovered more alleged recruiting improprieties. After LSU fired Wade for cause, he resurfaced at McNeese State, engineering an unlikely reversal of fortune that eventually landed him a lucrative offer to coach back in the big leagues at North Carolina State. That stint lasted all of one 20-win season before the Tigers swooped in and began the process to bring Wade back – despite the fact that someone else wasalready coaching the team.And then there’s Kim Mulkey, grande dame of LSU sports blindness. When the national championship-winning women’s basketball coach brought 17-year-old Anna Minaeva into the fold last month, more than a few eyebrows arched – and not because she plays the same position as junior center Kate Koval. It’s more that Minaeva is Russian, Koval is Ukrainian and the one notable reprieve her father, a drone operator in the Ukrainian military, took from the war was to travel to the United States to watch his daughter play.“I cannot make a decision to not recruit somebody that can help our program because of a conflict between two countries,” Mulkeytold Koval, who then unsurprisingly decided to leave the team. “For me, this war isn’t distant or abstract,” Kovalwroteof her departure. “People close to me have been killed and wounded in Russian attacks, and places where I grew up and first began playing basketball have been destroyed by missile strikes.”Mulkey’s decision to focus on basketball over all other matters would be stunning if this wasn’t the same coach who stuck to sports when one of her former players, Brittney Griner, was facing downan indefinite sentence in a Russian prison. Instead of offering Griner even a few token words of support, Mulkey said she would staysilent on the matter.Fixation on sports certainly isn’t unique to LSU. Travel to any American college, and odds are you’ll notice the stadium well before you do the library. But it wasn’t always that way in Baton Rouge. For much of its history, the university used revenue from athletics, football most glaringly, to underwrite teaching and research – you know,actualcollege work. In 2015, LSU athletics transferred more than $7m to the university to support academic, research and public-service missions as part of afive-year, $36m pledge. Was it a perfect symbiosis? No. But LSU at least could say athletics had become what Coates hoped for – a tide to lift all boats.So what changed? College sports went from a delicate experiment in amateurism that could easily blow up overa team barbecueto a full-blown arms race. Now LSU works overtime to justify its presence in the all-powerful Southeastern Conference (SEC) while competing with the even-better-funded Ohio State, Texas and arch-rival Alabama. Student-athletes have gone from being criminalized for accepting any form of compensation beyond a basic education to cowboy entrepreneurs ina freewheeling name, image and likeness (NIL) erathat, among other things, has thrust former LSU quarterback Jayden Daniels – now of the NFL’s Washington Commanders – in a pitched legal battle with the university over claims to the commercial use ofhis old college jersey number. Athletics revenue that once helped underwrite actual academics is now invested in players and coaches in the race to win at all costs. Administrators like former Alabama coach Nick Saban, who benefitted handsomely from the old way of business, are now working hand-in-glove with the Trump administration toregulate all of this.View image in fullscreenKate Koval, a native of Kyiv, opted to leave the LSU women’s basketball program after the team signed a Russian player.Photograph: Tyler Kaufman/Getty ImagesAll the while, LSU is helping drive the transformation as it adapts to the new normal. Kiffin – whothreatened to take Ole Miss’ best playerswith him after abandoning the Rebels to take the LSU job – has not been bashful about seeking to exploit a loophole that left the door open forformer NFL players to return to college and playfor money that could surpass a rookie contract in the pros. After Kiffin signed a number of players off the NFL’s training-camp waiver wire this month, the SEC scrambled to change its rules to stop the march of professionalsbacksliding to campus. Jack Pyburn, a standout Tigers edge rusher who turned pro earlier this year, was in line to return to school after being cut by Tampa Bay – only for Kansas City to claim him, thwarting an NIL windfall that was due to eclipse his NFL salary.It’s not limited to football. The showpiece of Wade’s incoming men’s basketball recruiting class is RJ Luis Jr, a college standout who wason the Boston Celtics’ rosterduring the 2025 preseason.Dae’Quan Wright, the first player to go from the NFL to the transfer portal, has already practiced with the Tigers as LSU sues the SEC and NCAA over the eligibility ofthese professional ringers, much to the “high level of frustration” among university presidents in the conference at Kiffin’s challenge to the supposed amateur spirit of college sports. Rival coaches aren’t exactly thrilled about the state of play either. “It’s embarrassing,”saidClemson coach Dabo Swinney, patron saint ofold-school amateurism. “We have no rules. There’s no governance. I mean, it’s a joke.”On Thursday night, a Louisiana judge saw it Kiffin and the Tigers’ way (quelle surprise), granting apreliminary injunctionthat clears a path for the NFL ringers to join the team. Earlier this week, the coach assured reporters that his NFL recruiting gambit had the full backing ofhis team– as if these young men, however well recompensed, would dare oppose LSU’s $91m sports lord. “This is how the real world works,” Kiffin deadpanned. The team fanzine echoed the prevailing mood. “You either play the villain or the victim in today’s NCAA,”tweetedthe associate editor at TigerBait.com.Ukrainian star leaves LSU women’s basketball team after signing of Russian recruitRead moreIn this blinkered world, there are more than feudal lords like Kiffin to consider as they bend reality to fit their agendas. As LSU is a state university, it is effectively run by Louisiana’s governor, theMaga-alignedJeff Landry. Besides appointing the board that steers the university, Landry has a heavy hand in hiring and firing the coaches (though he did invite Donald Trumpto pick Kelly’s successor) and insisted oncarting a live tiger into one gamedespite the protests of animal rights groups and the university’s own veterinarians. Landry spearheaded the NIL war chest that is to beLSU’s ace in the holeand backed the lawsuits against the NCAA and SEC; on Thursday, the conference hit back with its ownlawsuit, filed in a federal court inAlabama– for a different kind of home-court advantage, no doubt.And this is all while Landry spearheadsthe great unwokeningin Louisiana and pressures LSU to dismantle much of its DEI policies. The backlash to Landry’s politics has reached the playing field: in May, the NAACP urged Black athletes toreconsider attending public universities in Southern statessuch as Louisiana that were engaged in what it described as efforts to limit, weaken or erase Black voting representation through redistricting. The NAACP offered up HBCUs as an alternative but, alas, the great migration never came. The lure of sports-obsessed schools such as LSU is still too strong to fight.Certainly Coates, the first football coach in LSU history, couldn’t know what he had unleashed. He wanted athletics to lift all boats, but it has swamped campus life entirely. It has driven universities to sacrifice their values for the pursuit of sporting glory, in a game where winning is never enough, and it costs hundreds of millions of dollars to compete at the most basic level. If this is how the real world works now, fans cheer at their own peril.Explore more on these topicsCollege sportsLouisianaUS sportsCollege footballCollege basketballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andy Ruiz Jr once turned boxing upside down. Can he do it again at 36? | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Seven years after springing one of the biggest upsets in boxing history, the Mexican Rocky is back with his old trainer for one final run at the heavyweight summit
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Seven years after springing one of the biggest upsets in boxing history, the Mexican Rocky is back with his old trainer for one final run at the heavyweight summit
Content: Andy Ruiz Jr (left) and Damian Knyba look on after Thursday’s ceremonial weigh-in ahead of their heavyweight fight at the Prudential Center in Newark, New Jersey.Photograph: Matchroom BoxingView image in fullscreenAndy Ruiz Jr (left) and Damian Knyba look on after Thursday’s ceremonial weigh-in ahead of their heavyweight fight at the Prudential Center in Newark, New Jersey.Photograph: Matchroom BoxingBoxingAndy Ruiz Jr once turned boxing upside down. Can he do it again at 36?Seven years after springing one of the biggest upsets in boxing history, the Mexican Rocky is back with his old trainer for one final run at the heavyweight summitBryan Armen Grahamin Newark, New JerseyFri 4 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven years ago, Andy Ruiz Jr became the first fighter of Mexican descent to win the world heavyweight championship in one of the biggest upsets boxing has ever seen,stopping the undefeated Anthony Joshuainside seven rounds at Madison Square Garden.A replacement opponentsummoned on five weeks’ noticewho went off as an 11-1 underdog, Ruiz came off the canvas in the third to knock Joshua down four times before the referee finally waved it off. Hailed as the “Mexican Rocky”, he waslionized as a border-straddling heroin his hometown of Imperial, the dusty agricultural community framed by the mountain ranges and flat deserts of south-eastern California. Hemade the late-night rounds, took an audiencewith Mexico president Andrés Manuel López Obradorand signed a $10m guarantee when Joshua activated his rematch clause. The money, cars, fame and women arrived all at once.Barely six months later, Ruiz was an ex-champion who had taken his place alongside Buster Douglas, Leon Spinks and James J Braddock in heavyweight boxing’s one-and-done club. His 190-day reign ended with a listless points defeat to Joshua in the sand-blown Saudi Arabian city of Diriyah, after three months of partying and a self-abbreviated training camp that left him 15lb heavier than he had been for their first meeting. At a 3am press conference after the fight that ached with pathos, Ruizadmitted he had been overconfidentand had failed to take the rematch seriously, the regret plain on his marked-up face.Ruiz, who turns 37 next week, has fought only three times in the more than six years since, a wilderness period marked by fluctuating weight, injuries and enough false starts to make the most famous win of his career feel like an artifact from another life.On Friday night at the Prudential Center in Newark, about 10 miles west of the Manhattan arena where his life changed forever, Ruiz will launch one final campaign for the heavyweight summit, testing the limits of even boxing’s generous capacity for second chances. He will face the 6ft 7in Damian Knyba in a 12-round non-title fight, his first appearance since a majority draw with Jarrell Miller more than two years ago and the first of a three-fight contract with Eddie Hearn’s promotional company.View image in fullscreenAndy Ruiz Jr throws out the ceremonial first pitch before the Padres’ game against the San Francisco Giants at Petco Park last month in San Diego.Photograph: Matt Thomas/San Diego Padres/Getty ImagesThere was a time when another run at the title was more plausible. Even after losing the WBA, IBF and WBO belts to Joshua, Ruiz was only 30 and remained one of the division’s most naturally gifted offensive fighters, blessed with unusually fast hands and an ability to throw blinding combinations that belied his doughy frame. It was the same contradiction that had followed him since childhood, when opponents routinely underestimated the chubby kid whose hand speed and ring intelligence were apparent in the amateur ranks long before the rest of the world took notice.Manny Robles, the 54-year-old trainer who guided Ruiz through both Joshua fights, is once again in his cornerafter their messy splitamid the wreckage of the rematch. Ruiz had replaced him with Eddy Reynoso, the trainer best known for his partnership with Canelo Álvarez, before his 2021 comeback against Chris Arreola, then switched to Alfredo Osuna for his win over Luis Ortiz the following year. By the time he returned from another long absence to fight Miller in 2024, Ruiz said he was effectively training himself and “half-assing” with “one foot in the water and one foot out”.Their reconciliation began over piña coladas while Ruiz was vacationing with his girlfriend in Tulum. As he reflected on the heavyweight division moving on without him, Ruiz said he swallowed his pride and, a little intoxicated, messaged Robles on Instagram to ask if he would train him again. Robles replied almost immediately that he would, provided Ruiz was prepared to listen, focus and give him “120%” of his time and dedication.“I’m just happy that I reunited with Manny Robles,” Ruiz said Wednesday in Newark. “Before with the other fights and the other opponents that I had, I wasn’t doing the right things that I was supposed to. [He] kind of woke me up, and that’s why we’re here now.”Their reunion has become the most credible evidence that Ruiz’s comeback is different from the fits and starts that came before. Robles said they have spent virtually the entire year in the gym together rather than assembling for a conventional training camp. “This did not start two months ago or three months ago,” Robles said. “It’s been the entire year and it’s been great to get to this point. I’m glad to say I got the old Andy back, and he’s in great shape mentally, physically, spiritually. He’s in a good place.”View image in fullscreenAndy Ruiz Jr knocks down Anthony Joshua in the third round of their heavyweight title fight at New York’s Madison Square Garden on 1 June 2019.Photograph: Al Bello/Getty ImagesThere was at least some evidence for Robles’s optimism at Thursday’s weigh-in. Ruiz came in at a svelte 254.3lb, his lightest since a 2018 win over Kevin Johnson and 29.4lb below the career-high 283.7lb he weighed for the Joshua rematch. Knyba weighed 255.5lb, leaving barely a pound between fighters separated by six inches in height.There have been legitimate obstacles on Ruiz’s road back, including surgeries on his right knee in 2021 and on a torn rotator cuff in 2023. He then broke his right hand during the Miller fight but pressed on through the injury for all 12 rounds. He initially hoped it would heal without an operation before eventually undergoing surgery, another setback that contributed to the 762-day absence that ends on Friday.Ruiz took his recovery slowly, spent time with his five children and worked on property developments with his Mexican-born father, the contractor who introduced him to boxing aged five to tame a hyperactive streak and spent years ferrying him across the border to gyms in Mexicali. He started going to church. Having earned about $17m from the Joshua fights alone, there was no financial imperative. But eventually, as he puts it, he “became tired of being tired” and “bored of being bored”.The timing could hardly be better for a lapsed heavyweight contender attempting to re-enter the frame. It took a quarter-century for boxing to produce the first undisputed heavyweight champion since Lennox Lewis – when Oleksandr Usyk finally unified all four major titlesby outpointing Tyson Furyin May 2024 – and barely two years for the division to splinter completely again. With the 39-year-old Usykhaving vacated his remaining titlesin June, the belts are now scattered among Murat Gassiev (the WBA champion), Agit Kabayel (WBC), Filip Hrgović (IBF) and Daniel Dubois (WBO), creating no shortage of potential pathways back to the top.For a former world champion with a recognizable name and one of the most famous victories of the past decade, a win on Friday could propel Ruiz right back into the championship mix. Even a lucrative rubber match with Joshua, once seemingly fanciful, could be in play after the Englishman’s anticipated November showdown with Fury. (Ruiz’srecently released diss track, which name-checks no fewer than a half-dozen of his heavyweight rivals, suggests he’s not wanting for ambition.)View image in fullscreenAndy Ruiz Jr weighed in at 254.3lb for Friday’s fight against Damian Knyba, his lightest fighting weight since 2018.Photograph: Matchroom BoxingThere is neat symmetry to Ruiz’s return. It was Ruiz himself who messaged Hearn back in 2019, pleading for the opportunity when Miller was removed from the Joshua fightafter testing positivefor performance-enhancing drugs. Now, after fielding offers elsewhere, Ruiz has aligned himself with the promoter whose carefully laid heavyweight plans he turned upside down that night in New York.Hearn makes no secret of the commercial calculus. “It’s a business decision,” he said of Ruiz’s deal with Matchroom. The promoter believes the hand speed, punching power and durability that made Ruiz such an improbable nightmare for Joshua remain intact, while his heritage and history give him a box-office ceiling few heavyweights today can match. “If he gets this right and starts going through the division,” Hearn said, “he’s going to be one of the biggest stars in the sport.”Knyba (17-1, 11 KOs), an enormous fighter even by heavyweight standards who carries an 86in reach, represents the first examination. The New Jersey-based Pole is coming off the lone defeat on his professional ledger, a January stoppage loss to Germany’s Kabayel where he enjoyed promising stretches before the fight was stopped in the third round. At Wednesday’s final press conference, Knyba called the experience proof that he could operate at the elite level and said he expects to face “the most hungry and best version of Andy Ruiz”. A substantial Polish contingent is expected on Friday night, recalling the rollicking crowds that once made two-weight world champion Tomasz Adamek a major draw in Newark.For Ruiz (35-2-1, 22 KOs), the size discrepancy is nothing new. At 6ft 1in, he has spent his entire career looking up at heavyweights with more conventional builds. “[Knyba]’s a giant,” Ruiz said. “That’s why they call me the giant slayer, because I’m always a small guy fighting these big, big guys. But for some reason it works for me.”The matchup also serves a practical purpose. There is little value now in easing Ruiz back in against an opponent who cannot tell him anything about what’s left. As Hearn put it bluntly: “If you’ve got the ambition to really do what you say you want to do, which is to go and win the world heavyweight title again, you have to be beating guys like this.”Ruiz learned seven years ago there are only so many tomorrows a fighter can waste before they run out. At 36 and finally ready to make them count, he’s about to find out how many he has left.Explore more on these topicsBoxingAnthony JoshuaUS sportsOleksandr UsykTyson FuryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Vuelta a España: Wout van Aert battles scorching heat to claim stage 13 victory  | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Belgian star edges out Valentin Paret-Peintre in breakaway while Enric Mas keeps red jersey with 1m 45sec lead
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Belgian star edges out Valentin Paret-Peintre in breakaway while Enric Mas keeps red jersey with 1m 45sec lead
Content: Wout van Aert celebrates after landing his first stage win of this year’s Vuelta a España.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPAView image in fullscreenWout van Aert celebrates after landing his first stage win of this year’s Vuelta a España.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPAVuelta a EspañaVuelta a España: Wout van Aert battles scorching heat to claim stage 13 victoryMas keeps hold of red jersey with 1min 45sec leadKooij claims stage win at Tour of BritainAssociated PressFri 4 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 12.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWout van Aert won his fourth career stage at theVuelta a Españaamid scorching heat on Friday, while Enric Mas kept the red jersey.On a hot and sunny day in southern Spain, Van Aert beat fellow breakaway rider Valentin Paret-Peintre to claim the hilly 192km jaunt from Almuñécar to Loja.The elite Belgian rider stopped the clock after four and a half hours of racing. It was Van Aert’s first win of this edition after he won three stages in 2024. It added to his long list of triumphs, which includes 10 stages of the Tour de France and several one-day classics. It was also the fourth team win for Team Visma Lease a Bike at this edition.Mas, the Movistar leader,kept his leadof one minute 45 seconds over the four-time winner Primoz Roglic. They crossed in a group around three minutes after Van Aert.Riders had to handle more heat as thermometers recorded 36C (97 F) in Loja, where the stage finished. One rider compared the heat to having a “hairdryer blowing in your face”. Another said he spent the day pouring water over himself at every opportunity.View image in fullscreenThe Spanish Movistar cyclist Enric Mas celebrates on the podium wearing the red overall leader’s jersey following stage 13.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPA“It was a very tough stage because of the heat and the hard pace,” the American rider Sepp Kuss, of Visma Lease a Bike, told broadcaster RTVE in fluent Spanish. “If you tried to attack, you just cracked. But we all had to compete in the same conditions. I must also thank the organisers for adding extra spots where we could grab water. If not, it would have been impossible.”Mas has led the race since the Tour de France champion, Tadej Pogacar, withdrew following a crash last Saturday. Mas has finished the Vuelta as runner-up on three occasions, in 2018, 2021 and 2022. He is trying to become the first Spanish rider to win the home race since Alberto Contador in 2014. The key to Mas finally coming out on top will likely rest on him having a big enough lead to withstand Roglič during a time trial on stage 18.Friday’s stage 13 was just south of Granada, where the three-week race will finish on 13 September. On Saturday, riders face a 154km (95m) stage from Jaén to Sierra de la Pandera. “Our goal tomorrow is just keeping the red shirt for the next day,” Mas said.This year’s Vuelta is entirely in southern Spain and without any of its classic mountain finishes in the country’s greener north.Kooij claims stage win at Tour of BritainOlav Kooij edged out Tim Merlier in a chaotic sprint to win stage three of the Tour of Britain in Beverley. Kooij began his charge well down in the pack but, with Thursday’s stage winner Merlier finding himself boxed in, the Dutchman spotted his opportunity down the left and, by the time he belatedly found some room, Merlier could not respond.View image in fullscreenOlav Kooij wins stage three of the Tour of Britain in Beverley.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAIt was an eighth career stage win for Kooij at this race, putting him second in the Tour of Britain’s record books alongside Edvald Boasson Hagen, two behind the all-time record held by Sir Mark Cavendish.After a second consecutive sprint finish to end the 181km stage from Hull, the stage one winner Lewis Askey continues to lead overall. Askey leads by 12 seconds from Tim Wellens, with Matteo Trentin a further seven seconds back in third.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Caitlin Clark’s double-double helps USA rout China in Fiba World Cup opener | Fiba Women's Basketball World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Caitlin Clark finishes with 14 points and 11 assists as the defending champions open their campaign with a 94-61 victory in Berlin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Caitlin Clark finishes with 14 points and 11 assists as the defending champions open their campaign with a 94-61 victory in Berlin
Content: USA’s Caitlin Clark battles China’s Luo Xinyu for the ball during their Fiba Women’s Basketball World Cup group-stage game in Berlin on Friday.Photograph: Virginie Lefour/BELGA MAG/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUSA’s Caitlin Clark battles China’s Luo Xinyu for the ball during their Fiba Women’s Basketball World Cup group-stage game in Berlin on Friday.Photograph: Virginie Lefour/BELGA MAG/AFP/Getty ImagesFiba Women's Basketball World Cup 2026Caitlin Clark’s double-double helps USA rout China in Fiba World Cup openerClark finishes with 14 points and 11 assistsAmericans extend World Cup win streak to 31China’s 7ft 3in Zhang Ziyu scores 13 on debutAgenciesFri 4 Sep 2026 10.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 12.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCaitlin Clark and Paige Bueckers made the most of their World Cup debuts to help the United States rout China in the opener of the tournament.Clark had 14 points and 11 assists and Bueckers added another 14 points as the Americans topped China 94-61 on Friday.Fiba World Cup: what to watch as Team USA and WNBA stars chase goldRead moreIt was the first of likely many times that Clark and Bueckers will play together in the US backcourt over the next decade for the senior national team.“It’s just organic. We know how to play well off of each other,” Bueckers said. “She draws so much defensive attention, so a lot of the defense is worried about her.”Clark loved having so many offensive options, including Bueckers. Everywhere she turned to pass there was a teammate waiting to score.“Obviously being around so many talented players, obviously our guards are incredible and our bigs too, but you know anybody I pass the ball to, it feels like they’re never going to miss a shot,” Clark said. “That’s one of my goals when I come into the game – to facilitate.”Clark’s 11 assists were the most by a US player since Dawn Staley had 12 against Russia in 1998, which tied her for the most ever with Teresa Edwards, who had a dozen against China in 1986.The US beat China for the gold medal in the 2022 World Cup, but that Chinese team didn’t have 7ft 3in Zhang Ziyu. The 19-year-old had her own impressive debut in the World Cup, finishing with 13 points and hitting nine of her 10 free throws.The towering Zhang had just two blocked shots, but made the Americans think twice about driving to the basket. Bueckers took a few foul line jumpers instead of attacking Zhang.“I like to think I’m pretty smart. I thought that a layup over some 7-3 center is probably not the best idea,” Bueckers said, smiling.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClark agreed that Zhang presented a difficult challenge, but the US frontcourt of Breanna Stewart, Napheesa Collier, Aliyah Boston and Angel Reese held their own, collecting a combined 24 rebounds.“This was a different type of basketball game that I probably ever played in my entire life,” Clark said. “I’ve never played against a woman of that size. She obviously presented some challenges for us, but you gotta give our post players a lot of credit.”Reese and Boston also were making their World Cup debut. In total, nine of the 12 players on the American roster, which is full of WNBA All-Stars, were playing in their first World Cup. They were able to keep the US rolling.The win was the 31st in a row for the Americans, who have a day off Saturday before facing Italy on Sunday and the Czech Republic on Monday.“It was great. Obviously the first one we got to shake off our rust,” Bueckers said. “Get back into game shape. Get back into game mode. And it’s our first time playing together as a team, as a unit. So we got a couple of days of practice, but there’s nothing like getting game reps, getting game experience together.”Explore more on these topicsFiba Women's Basketball World Cup 2026BasketballCaitlin ClarkShareReuse this content

title: Gaël Monfils takes final grand slam bow after US Open defeat to Learner Tien | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: The French showman’s 22-year grand slam career ended in a 6-3, 6-4, 6-3 defeat to 20-year-old American Learner Tien
Author: Ella Brockway
Headline: The French showman’s 22-year grand slam career ended in a 6-3, 6-4, 6-3 defeat to 20-year-old American Learner Tien
Content: Fans salute Gael Monfils after his straight-sets defeat by Learner Tien in the second round of the US Open.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAView image in fullscreenFans salute Gael Monfils after his straight-sets defeat by Learner Tien in the second round of the US Open.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Gaël Monfils takes final grand slam bow after US Open defeat to Learner TienFrenchman falls in straight sets to No 14 seedMonfils, 40, will retire at end of 2026 seasonTien reaches US Open third round for first timeElla Brockwayat Flushing MeadowsThu 3 Sep 2026 23.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 01.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt would have felt more fitting if Gaël Monfils went out with a roar, with a five-set epic matching the reputation he has built as tennis’s great showman.He may have preferred the kind of bow he made at his home French Open earlier this year,a thrilling five-set fightbackthat ended well after midnight, or one that had a few more of his dazzling signature shots, likethe mid-air forehandthat stole the show in his first-round win this week.Gaël Monfils, tennis’s great showman, prepares for his final bowRead moreInstead, the final grand slam match of Monfils’s 22-year career was a quieter farewell, a straight-sets 6-3, 6-4, 6-3 second-round US Open defeat to No 14 seed Learner Tien on Thursday night. The 40-year-old has said he will retire after this season, and the result ensured he will finish his career as one of the greatest players to never win a major.The 20-year-old Tien wore Monfils out, forcing him into long rallies and constant movement along the baseline on a muggy night at Louis Armstrong Stadium. The flashes were fewer than usual for the Frenchman, but he still kept the crowd entertained, praising the “unbelievable atmosphere” and saying he was proud to have given it his all.“You always want to give a little bit more, you want to stay a little bit more,” he said. “I gave my absolute all, but Learner was a really tough one tonight.”Monfils came up in the golden age of the men’s tour, in the era of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, Novak Djokovic and Andy Murray. He has won nearly 600 singles matches and collected $25m in earnings, but reached the last four of a grand slam just twice, at Roland Garros in 2008 and here at Flushing Meadows in 2016. And yet his style – the tweeners, the overheads, the movement that swung the momentum of points – attracted just as many fans and as much acclaim as the silverware would have.View image in fullscreenGaël Monfils shares a laugh with Learner Tien after the Frenchman’s second-round defeat at the US Open on Thursday.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersOnce ranked as high as sixth, he has dropped to No 311 and earned entry to this US Open on a wildcard. He had only played two tour-level events since Roland Garros. But through this run, he has been his trademark showman self, coming full-circle from the 18-year-old in a baggy yellow tank top who made his US Open debut in 2005 with a grueling five-set loss to Djokovic.It began in last week’s mixed doubles, where he advanced to the semi-finals playing alongside his wife (and world No 9) Elina Svitolina, and continued against 60th-ranked Paraguayan Adolfo Daniel Vallejo in the first round of the main draw. The 2-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-0 victory there, on the day he turned 40, made him the oldest man to win a US Open match since Jimmy Connors in 1992, and the Armstrong Stadium crowd serenaded the longtime fan favorite by singing “Happy Birthday”.“I’m just me, Gaël Monfils,” he said, when asked how he wanted to be remembered. “I think I have been the same since I came on tour, with a lot of joy. … The most important for me is how my family lived all these year and how they will remind this ride was unbelievable.”Thursday night brought a more difficult challenge, against a composed and smart lefty in Tien. Monfils held his own to start, but he was broken in his third service game and began putting his hands on his knees to rest or leaning over to fix his shoe after points.Tien was content to play long, patient points – he finished with just 20 winners, fewer than Monfils’s 29 – and such a strategy tired his opponent’s legs. In the sixth game of the second set, Monfils leaned over a towel box in the corner of the court after a 20-shot rally. A leaping backhanded volley energized the crowd and Monfils himself, but it couldn’t make up for his 22 unforced errors in the set.View image in fullscreenGaël Monfils is presented with a gift after his second-round defeat by Learner Tien, having announced he will retire at the end of the season.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersBy the third set, even his serve was a taxing effort. He leaned on his racket in front of the baseline before double-faulting twice in the seventh game, where Tien would find the break that swung the match in his favor. The American played remarkable defense in the eighth game, saving break point after a desperate Monfils had held his finger up to the sky asking for just one break following seven unsuccessful previous efforts. (It did not come.)Time, though, comes for all. Tien, who is into the third round at the US Open for the first time, said he felt grateful to share the court with Monfils and jokingly apologized for all of his drop shots.“A couple months ago [in Paris], it was really tough, because you don’t really know what to expect and how you will really react,” Monfils said. “It was a little bit tougher for me to handle my emotion and play and perform, because I said that I want to say good-bye but be able to perform well. … It was much better, much easier for me to handle here.”Tournament organizers presented Monfils with a framed picture in an on-court ceremony. Perhaps he’ll have a new place to hang it soon: ever the master of surprise, he announced in his post-match news conference that his post-tennis life will involve an office job with a Swiss wealth management company.The ceremony closed with a montage of clips from throughout Monfils’s career on the video board. Few moments from Thursday’s match are likely to end up in future reels, but one captured the night’s scene. In the third game of the second set, up 40-0, he delivered a strong serve and went for a no-look slice on the return. At another time, such a shot could have been a showstopping winner. On this night, it lobbed into the net, and Monfils’s only reaction was to close his eyes and laugh. This is 40, his face seemed to say.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026TennisUS Open tennisShareReuse this content

title: Alexia Putellas begins WSL ride as London City outclass Manchester United  | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Alexia Putellas made her Women’s Super League bow as London City Lionesses brushed aside Manchester United in the season opener
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Alexia Putellas made her Women’s Super League bow as London City Lionesses brushed aside Manchester United in the season opener
Content: The talk was all about London City’s new players, but it was one of last season’s big-name signings Daniëlle van de Donk who made the game safe.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe talk was all about London City’s new players, but it was one of last season’s big-name signings Daniëlle van de Donk who made the game safe.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianWomen's Super LeagueAlexia Putellas begins WSL ride as London City outclass Manchester UnitedSuzanne Wrackat Copperjax Community StadiumFri 4 Sep 2026 16.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are few scenarios since Millwall Lionesses broke away from Millwall and became London City Lionesses that would have felt more surreal than the idea ofAlexia Putellas captaining the sideto a statement win in a WSL season-opener in Bromley just seven years later.Here we are though: referees have to get used to the formerly talismanic Barcelona captain stooping to pick up the coin after the toss, as is her custom; players must get used to eyes and cameras looking past them to focus in on the influential No 11; and the two-time Ballon d’Or winnerhas to get used to playing with teammatesnot drilled in a very specific style of play from such an early age that it becomes an inherent part of them.London City claim sponsor deal is record and bigger than some in Premier LeagueRead moreOf course it is a step down to go from the three-time European champions to a team embarking on their second season in the WSL, but off the pitch, with the owner, Michele Kang, committed to giving female athletes the best of everything, the difference will be more negligible, even before the approved new world-class training facility is built.Regardless of what you think of her movements in women’s football,or about private finance investment in it, Kang, who walked the perimeter of the stadium prior to kick-off taking photos with fans in her ‘Kang 27’ emblazoned home shirt, is the antithesis of the owner of last night’s opposition, Jim Ratcliffe,and his dismal references to his women’s teams.View image in fullscreenMichele Kang did the rounds at a sold-out stadium, the first time London City Lionesses have done that since starting to play at Bromley.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianPutellas led the team out to a ­raucous welcome at the sold-out home of Bromley FC, her steely stare only broken to crack a quick smile and share some words with the mascot gripping her hand.In this corner of London’s outskirts, the midfielder experienced her first proper taste of her new reality. At 32 and with her very best years likely behind her, it was a solid rather than showstopper performance. She was outshone by teammates such as Rosa Kafaji and Lucía Corrales, who unfortunately went off on a stretcher late on after overstretching for the ball.“Everybody knows what [Putellas] can create and bring to us,” said the London City manager, Eder Maestre. “It’s not just the things she’s capable of doing, it’s the things she facilitates for other players too.“Having this kind of player in the squad is very important because she represents the highest standards and having her involved in it is not only because of her performance, but also because of the leadership she can bring in terms of helping us to reach that standard. But it is not only about Alexia, she is only one player, and I think the most impactful thing was the way everybody connected, the chemistry that we are building around the players.”View image in fullscreenAlexia Putellas was solid rather than spectacular on her WSL debut.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianMaestre has been tasked with gelling a squad stacked with new players, includingthe former England goalkeeper Mary Earps, who was on the bench with Elene Lete starting.Maestre explained: “Mary had some issues in pre-season so that was why there was inconsistency in game involvement. We have two strong goalkeepers. Today, Elene deserved to be in the lineup. She was very strong in her actions.”Maestre has said the identity he wants to create for the side is “related to all those things we felt when we were playing football as children”.That ethos was evident in their play, with London City on the front foot from the off. Despite not always being pretty, they looked like they were having fun as they pressed and attacked aggressively, and when they broke the deadlock nine minutes in it was not surprising.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlanna Kennedy provided the pressure, rising above a hunkered-down Julia Zigiotti Olme who could only turn the ball into her own net.View image in fullscreenDelphine Cascarino (left), who set up London City Lionesses’ second goal, was named player of the match.Photograph: John Walton/PAIt was a cruel introduction to life in the WSL, and its spotlight, forthe new Manchester United manager, Eva Olid, particularly with Chelsea and Arsenal up next, but on this showing andafter a lacklustre summer transfer window, few games would have offered a kind introduction. United were outclassed in Bromley, conceding 60% possession.They did at least manage three shots, but by the time they did any hopes of a leveller were crushed by the home side, when Mapi León’s corner was worked towards Delphine Cascarino and the French forward’s cross was delightfully flicked into the far corner by Daniëlle van de Donk.“It’s a process,” said Olid. “I think it was something more mental in the first half, we could feel like the players were not believing.“At half-time I say that this is not us, we need the ball to be ourselves … in the second half, we were building through the middle, finding the free player, playing between the lines. That is us, and I can feel my team in the second half.
