It’s my job to help them to believe that we can always be the team of the second half.”There was a late consolation for Olid’s humbled charges deep into added time, when Simi Awujo powered in the loose ball after a free-kick was cleared into empty space, but it could not dampen the enthusiasm of an emphatic performance from Maestre’s side – a performance that is a very solid foundation to build on.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueLondon City LionessesManchester United WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: José Mourinho sick as a Parrott as Real Madrid sunk by Real Betis and Irish supersub | European club football | The Guardian
description: Mbappé sees late penalty saved by Valles while PSG were beaten by league leaders Monaco
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mbappé sees late penalty saved by Valles while PSG were beaten by league leaders Monaco
Content: Troy Parrott celebrates after scoring the winner against Real Madrid.Photograph: Raúl Caro Cadenas/EPAView image in fullscreenTroy Parrott celebrates after scoring the winner against Real Madrid.Photograph: Raúl Caro Cadenas/EPAEuropean club footballJosé Mourinho sick as a Parrott as Real Madrid sunk by Real Betis and Irish supersubMbappé sees late penalty saved by VallesPSG are beaten by league leaders MonacoAgenciesFri 4 Sep 2026 18.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReal Madrid’s perfect start in La Liga ⁠ended on Friday when Real Betis beat them 1-0, with the ⁠substitute Troy Parrott ⁠scoring ​nine minutes from time and goalkeeper Álvaro Valles saving a stoppage-time ⁠penalty from Kylian Mbappé.The clash began at a high tempo but the pace ⁠dropped after the interval in the heat in ​Seville. The Republic of Ireland star Parrott, introduced ‌in the 68th ‌minute, broke the deadlock in the 81st when ‌he reacted quickly after Thibaut Courtois parried a header into his path.Mbappé struck the crossbar four minutes later before the substitute Carlos Espí met a cross from Vinícius Júnior with a spectacular bicycle kick, only for the equaliser to be ruled ​out for offside following a VAR review.Tough start for PSG but Luis Enrique has faith in burst of ‘new energy’ from signingsRead moreNelson Deossa then nearly sealed the victory for hosts Betis with a long-range effort after spotting Courtois ⁠off his line, but the goalkeeper recovered to ​make ​the save.José Mourinho’s Madrid got one ​final opportunity when Natan brought down ​Vinícius inside ‌the area, ​deep ​into stoppage time, but Valles saved Mbappé’s spot-kick to preserve Betis’s lead and secure the three points.“My team played a great game, and sometimes you lose and you don’t know why,” Mourinho said. “We dominated, controlling everything, lots of attacks, lots of chances. If we had drawn we would have been left frustrated, so imagine how we feel after losing.“I don’t know how we lost because we played very well collectively. I cannot fault the attitude of any of my players. We deserved to win but deserving to win does not ⁠give you points. I’m very happy with ​my players, all ​of them. I cannot fault ​any of them individually. As for the penalty, when ​one of us ‌steps up to ​take it, ​we all stand together.“The Betis players are more streetwise than the Madrid players, who are very honest. With the backing of a fantastic crowd, they manage to gain these kinds of advantages.”Paris Saint-Germainlooked to be on their way to their first Ligue 1 win of the season when Marquinhos put the hosts ahead in the 31st minute, butMonacorallied with goals from Flavio Nazinho in the 58th minute and Stanis Idumbo in the 72nd. Monaco lead the table as the only team to win their opening three games.“We clearly deserved to win. That is my opinion,” said Luis Enrique.“I saw the game and it was the typical game in which we were better than the opposition and created a lot more chances, but the opposition goalkeeper was the best player on the pitch.”The US striker Folarin Balogun was left out of Monaco’s squad after the collapse of his proposed transfer to Everton this week, while Lamine Camara played after his move to Chelsea was called off at the last minute.View image in fullscreenPSG’s Fabián Ruiz (left) challenges for the ball with Monaco’s in-demand Lamine Camara.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/APPSG had already drawn 2-2 with Rennes and Lille in their first two games and also lost the French Super Cup to Lens 1-0 last month.The first league defeat came hours after PSG announced contract extensions for coach Luis Enrique and several players. João Neves, Lucas Beraldo, Senny Mayulu and Willian Pacho all signed new deals through to 2031, while Fabián Ruiz had his contract extended until 2028.LyonbeatAuxerre3-1 earlier on Friday and are second in the league, two points behind Monaco and level on points withLille, who won 1-0 atToulouseon Thursday thanks to an Ayase Ueda goal.Assane Diao bagged a brace asComorolled to a 4-1 win atGenoainSerie A. Nico Paz and Martin Baturina also added goals. Cesc Fabregas’ side lead the Italian standings by one point ahead of a pack of six teams who have yet to play this weekend.Como will make their Champions League debut against Leipzig on 10 September, with Manchester United to visit in October and PSG in January.In Germany,Stuttgartromped to a 4-1 win overKölnin theBundesliga.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballReal BetisReal MadridLa LigaParis Saint-GermainLigue 1MonaconewsShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea hit bullseye with Morgan Rogers as Arsenal rue what might have been | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: The Gunners will have a look at what they could have won when the former Villa man lines up against them, having made a flying start for Xabi Alonso’s team
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: The Gunners will have a look at what they could have won when the former Villa man lines up against them, having made a flying start for Xabi Alonso’s team
Content: Arsenal had hoped to get Morgan Rogers for around £80m but Chelsea hijacked their plans with a successful £117m bid.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArsenal had hoped to get Morgan Rogers for around £80m but Chelsea hijacked their plans with a successful £117m bid.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesSportblogChelseaChelsea hit bullseye with Morgan Rogers as Arsenal rue what might have beenThe Gunners will have a look at what they could have won when the former Villa man lines up against them, having made a flying start for Xabi Alonso’s teamJacob SteinbergFri 4 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChelsea thought they had little chance of signing Morgan Rogers at the start of the summer.Xabi Alonsoand the club’s recruitment team had the England international as a priority target but a deal seemed unlikely. Chelsea had endured a disappointing season, missing out on European football after finishing 10th, and their expectation was that Rogers would leave Aston Villa for Arsenal.It was towards the end of the World Cup that Chelsea were made aware of a window of opportunity. AlthoughArsenalcould claim to be London’s top dogs after winning the Premier League they dithered in talks with Villa, raising the prospect of another club stepping in.Mikel Arteta talked about being bold in the market after Arsenal’s defeat by Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final. Arteta wanted more in attack. A new option on the left was a priority; Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli were up for sale and everything pointed towards Arsenal making their move for Rogers at the end of June.Premier League paradox: midfielders are more and more expensive, yet more and more mediocre | Jonathan LiewRead moreYet the lines became blurred. Arsenal had a fee of £80m in mind, while Villa wanted more, particularly after Nottingham Forest sold Elliot Anderson to Manchester City for £116m. Time dragged on. How serious were Arsenal? There was also interest in Julián Alvarez, Vinícius Júnior and Bradley Barcola. Villa waited and the price for Rogers went up. Arsenal, beaten to the punch in the end, will have a look at what they could have won whenChelseaand Rogers visit the Emirates Stadium on Sunday.Chelsea were decisive. They were tracking Rogers before he left Middlesbrough for Villa in February 2024. Joe Shields, one of Chelsea’s five sporting directors, worked with Rogers at Manchester City’s academy. The signing was not done on a whim. Chelsea have a good relationship with Villa’s owners and moved quickly after opening club-to-club talks a day after Rogers played in England’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina. The fee was £117m and Chelsea did not struggle to convince Rogers. Alonso wooed him and the deal was confirmed five days after negotiations began.View image in fullscreenXabi Alonso has put a lot of smiles back on faces at Chelsea after last season’s player rebellions.Photograph: Alex Ferrelly/Crystal Pix/Sports Press Photo/ShutterstockThere was no last-ditch move from Arsenal. They signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34m two days later and focused on other targets. When the window closed, though, Arteta’s options on the left looked a little light. Martinelli and Trossard left but only Tzolis arrived. Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke are alternatives. It is hard not to feel that Arsenal could have done with Rogers, even though Chelsea have paid a high price for him.It remains to be seen whether the 24-year-old can prove he merits becoming the third-most expensive player in English football history. For context, the fee is the consequence of the market threatening to rise out of control and the money spent on many playersstarting to feel meaningless. It is worth pointing out, too, that money flowed back and forth between Chelsea and Villa all summer. Even so the price will follow Rogers around, so it is just as well he has made an excellent start.Rogers has been involved in four of Chelsea’s seven goals in their first two league games. He scored in the3-2 win at Fulhamand later combined with João Pedro to set up Cole Palmer’s goal. He created Pedro Neto’s goal in last weekend’s4-3 win over Brightonand played a key role when Jorrel Hato played in João Pedro to score.Chelsea have thrilled in attack so far, João Pedro, Rogers and Palmer combining to devastating effect. Alonso, an adaptable manager, wants more control but his transitional football has been a delight. Chelsea were mannered and controlled during Enzo Maresca’s time in charge. It is felt that Alonso has recognised the Premier League’s shift towards power and athleticism. Rogers fits into the Spaniard’s system. Thomas Tuchel loves Rogers for his connectivity and pressing. It is significant that England’s energy levels rose in their quarter-final against Norway after the introduction of Rogers and Djed Spence late in the second half.Chelsea needed more strength, more speed. Rogers, able to play anywhere in attacking midfield or as a No 8, looks a better fit in Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 than Enzo Fernández, sold this week to Manchester City for £125m. He has played with Palmer as one of the No 10s but has a responsibility to drift left, a role that is unlikely to have suited Fernández. Arsenal’s impeccable defence will be tested by Chelsea’s front three.The Rogers-Palmer partnership has clicked. They are old friends and banter over the “ice cold” celebration. Rogers is a bubbly character and can get on with anyone. Chelsea are keen to improve the culture in the dressing room. It is felt that Alonso has shifted the mood after last year’s rebellions. The squad are united. It is one of the reasons why Chelsea decided to sell Fernández on deadline day. They did not need the headache of reintegrating the Argentinian.View image in fullscreenCole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, pictured celebrating Chelsea’s fourth goal against Brighton, have forged a promising relationship.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersThis is a fresh start. The signing of Rogers, who was the Professional Footballers’ Association’s young player of the year in 2025, was a sign of Chelsea’s intent. Rogers was one of the best players in the Premier League last season. He grew under Unai Emery and scored whenVilla beat Freiburg in the Europa League finalin May.It was one of Rogers’ less eye-catching goals: a clever jab at the near post from a low cross. There was a period last season when he could not stop scoring from long range but Rogers has spoken about wanting scruffier goals and he arrived at the far post to open his Chelsea account against Fulham.Rogers is embracing the challenge. At Arsenal he would have been slotting into the finished article. Arsenal have reached the summit. Chelsea are beginning their climb under Alonso. Rogers, who has played in the Championship and had a loan in League One, rather liked the idea of starting lower down.Explore more on these topicsChelseaSportblogArsenalXabi AlonsofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Moyes reveals he has never spoken to Everton owner but is defiant after transfer blows | Everton | The Guardian
description: David Moyes has not spoken to the Everton owner and chairm, Dan Friedkin, in the 20 months since he returned to the club as manager
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: David Moyes has not spoken to the Everton owner and chairm, Dan Friedkin, in the 20 months since he returned to the club as manager
Content: David Moyes has had no contact with Dan Friedkin in the 20 months since he returned to the club.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid Moyes has had no contact with Dan Friedkin in the 20 months since he returned to the club.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersEvertonMoyes reveals he has never spoken to Everton owner but is defiant after transfer blowsFriedkin Group under scrutiny after summer of salesMoyes hopes for ‘something special’ with weaker squadAndy HunterFri 4 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Moyes has not spoken to the Everton owner and chair, Dan Friedkin, in the 20 months since he returned to the club as manager. Moyes also issued a defiant response on Friday to Everton’scalamitous end to the transfer window, claiming it could galvanise players and fans to achieve “something special” this season.Moyes exposed an astonishing disconnect at the club when confirming he has had no contact with Friedkin, founder and chief executive of The Friedkin Group, since replacing Sean Dyche as manager in January 2025. TFG president, Marc Watts, is Everton’s executive chair and Rishi Majithia, Friedkin’s son-in-law, is the owner’s day-to-day representative at the club. But with TFG’s ambition forEvertonunder scrutiny after the transfer window, and amid claims they are looking for fresh investment or even to sell the club, Moyes’s revelation raises further questions over the company’s commitment.Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendRead moreThe Everton manager admitted any successful club “needs to be aligned” at the top and added: “We’ve got new owners in who are still feeling their way in the club. I think if we get to know each other more it will get better.” Moyes, whose main point of contact at Everton is the chief executive, Angus Kinnear, was later asked whether he had ever had a conversation with Dan Friedkin. “Er, no,” he replied. So you’ve never met him? “No,” said Moyes.It was TFG’s decision to sell Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest last weekend that started Everton’s dreadful end to the transfer window. They U-turned after a backlash from Evertonians over the deal but Moyes was ultimately left with a weaker squad after the sales of Iliman Ndiaye, Beto, Tim Iroegbunam and Nathan Patterson.“We don’t have a huge squad but sometimes you need to do something special in football and we will attempt to do something special,” Moyes said. “It’s not going to be easy. You know what happens in these situations, there’s only one person who tends to get called out at the end [the manager].“But Everton’s different. I wouldn’t have come back for anybody but Everton. People saw the face of Evertonians last week and it can be really powerful. I would expect them to be really powerful now. Powerful for the team, powerful for the players. We’re going to need extra from them because we’re short. We need them. If they’re not with us, then it’s terrible.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But they are with us. I believe they are with us. I love Everton and always have done. It’s reinvigorated me being back and now there’s a little bump in the road. I need to get over the bump quickly and start looking at how I can make it go smoothly.”Explore more on these topicsEvertonDavid MoyesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nottingham Forest’s Liam Delap: ‘I play at my best on the edge of being horrible’ | Nottingham Forest | The Guardian
description: After a difficult year at Chelsea the striker hopes to get his career back on track at the City Ground. ‘I’ve got to learn and kick on,’ he tells Ben Fisher
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: After a difficult year at Chelsea the striker hopes to get his career back on track at the City Ground. ‘I’ve got to learn and kick on,’ he tells Ben Fisher
Content: Liam Delap before his Nottingham Forest debut at Anfield, where he made an immediate telling contribution off the bench.Photograph: Matt West/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLiam Delap before his Nottingham Forest debut at Anfield, where he made an immediate telling contribution off the bench.Photograph: Matt West/ShutterstockNottingham ForestInterviewNottingham Forest’s Liam Delap: ‘I play at my best on the edge of being horrible’Ben FisherAfter a difficult year at Chelsea the striker hopes to get his career back on track at the City GroundFri 4 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“You can imagine it: he’s a centre-back, I’m a striker,” says Liam Delap,Nottingham Forest’s £45m club-record signing, smiling as he sets the scene. He is reliving taking on his younger brother, Finn, in the garden. These days, they are each other’s biggest supporters – Liam attended Finn’svictory for third-tier Burtonon Wednesday – but as kids there was a friendly rivalry. The elder brother says: “There were probably a lot of tears, a lot of fights … whether it was playing Monopoly or football, it always ended in either the table being flipped or kicking the shit out of each other.”It is a competitive streak that has stuck and Delap is determined to make his presence felt at Forest, for whom he could make his full debut against Tottenham on Saturday. It has been a testing 16 months; he left Chelsea a season into a six-year contract and after one goal in 28 top-flight appearances, a dozen of those starts. “It is never a linear path straight to the top,” Delap says, his right hand taking flight in the City Ground boardroom, the 1979 and 1980 European Cups shimmering behind him. “I just want to get my head down, focus and keep improving because I’m still so young and I have so much to learn. I even at times probably think I’ve been in football a lot longer than I have. I’ve still, hopefully, got a long career ahead.Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendRead more“I think you just have to accept that sometimes things go bad, things happen … it might [prove to] be a good thing, I think. My first loans to Stoke and Preston [from Manchester City, across 2022-23] didn’t really go well at all and it was probably one of the best things that happened because I learnt so much from that season and went to Hull [for 2023-24] and kicked on from there. I’m still young, I’ve still got a lot of learning to do. Sometimes injuries happen, sometimes you don’t play. I don’t think anything is lost … Everyone has rocky moments. I’ve just got to use them to learn and kick on.”Last summer, Delap was hot property. Oliver Glasner tells a story of Delap having proposals from 18 Premier League clubs and jests that the 23-year-old knows every top-flight manager owing to the various Zoom calls he held while deciding his next move. After all, one of those was with Glasner, then at Crystal Palace. Forest wanted him then, too. “It was a tough decision,” recalls Delap. “I remember the conversation we had, I was really impressed and I thought: ‘This guy [Glasner] is really good.’ He spoke incredibly well and you can see he has done really well with the strikers he has had in the past. That definitely stuck in my mind.”Glasner wants Delap to play to his strengths: physicality, power and finishing. He doesn’t mean the forward’s hidden talent: cube roots. At the start of the year a clip of Delap showing off his maths skills went viral. “I didn’t enjoy maths one bit but I was always quite good at it. One of my friends taught me in school how to do it and I didn’t forget it. I hated school, [the] work, but I was always quite intelligent.”The Austrian head coach said it was apparent in conversations with Delap this summer that the player had learnt lessons from a trying year: “I think it shows his attitude and his character that he said: ‘Yeah, I want a team and a club that values my strengths and wants to play to my strengths.’ Because I never want to change a player: it doesn’t make sense to say: ‘OK, now you should play like Messi: false nine, drop into midfield and combine play with one or two touches.”View image in fullscreenLiam Delap scored once in 28 league appearances for Chelsea.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAA tally of 12 goals in the Ipswich side relegated in 2024-25 triggered widespread interest. At that point Delap was talked up as a potential heir to Harry Kane as England’s No 9. He has been capped by his country at every age group and was in the same under-16s team as Jude Bellingham. “As a little kid, all you want to do is play for your country,” Delap says. “So, of course, in my mind that’s where I want to get to. But it’s not as easy as that. I have to work hard and improve and that’s all I can do.”An imposing 6ft 2in striker, Delap has long been viewed as the next big thing. He spearheaded Manchester City to FA Youth Cup victory over Chelsea in 2020, a couple of months after Pep Guardiola handed him his senior City debut aged 17. Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, now teammates at Chelsea, were part of that same under-18s side, together with the new Aston Villa defender Taylor Harwood-Bellis and James McAtee, one of his best friends and now a clubmate again.“He was a No 10 and quite often he would give me the ball and we just had that really good relationship off the pitch and it translated on to the pitch,” Delap says of McAtee. “If we didn’t win, we’d all be fuming. It probably instilled that winning mentality into us early. I think it’s worked because you can see from that team that almost everyone is playing somewhere in the Premier League, abroad, the Championship and that is probably because we pushed each other so much.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDelap made his Forest debut as a substituteat Anfield last weekend, his first notable action a quick throw-in that led to the penalty scored by Morgan Gibbs-White to earn a second-half lead. Only after the 2-2 draw did Glasner discover that Delap’s father, Rory, who played for Southampton and Stoke among others, knew a thing or two about throws. “I said: your father will be proud of you,” says Forest’s head coach. So, has Liam got a mammoth throw in his armoury? “No, I don’t think so,” he replies. “I would never, anyway: I’m a striker, I need to be in the box.”View image in fullscreenLiam Delap was much in demand after impressing with a 12-goal league season at Ipswich.Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Getty ImagesDelap relishes the blood and thunder of battle. Glasner loves how Forest’s marquee signing stands up to centre-backs, making the point that defenders are hardly “hugging and kissing you all the time” in the heat of duels. But Delap, who spent a decade at Derby before joining City, says he has learned to harness his aggression on the field, after periods of getting into trouble when he was a youngster.“You have to be careful, but not shy away from who you are,” he says. “I’m always going to fight for everything, always be aggressive, determined. It goes back to the point about my brother, being little kids in the garden, going at each other: that’s me. Sometimes you need to control it and sometimes you need to be careful, but I think I play at my best when I’m on that edge of being … being horrible.”Explore more on these topicsNottingham ForestinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Chaotic Crystal Palace transfer window leaves Pierre Sage to run the gamut of emotions | Crystal Palace | The Guardian
description: Manager was frustrated not to land defensive targets and lost last-day tug of war but can draw on positives as he seeks his first points
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Manager was frustrated not to land defensive targets and lost last-day tug of war but can draw on positives as he seeks his first points
Content: Pierre Sage with Adam Wharton, one of the key players Crystal Palace managed to keep hold of this summer.Photograph: Daniel Weir/Sports Press Photo/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPierre Sage with Adam Wharton, one of the key players Crystal Palace managed to keep hold of this summer.Photograph: Daniel Weir/Sports Press Photo/ShutterstockCrystal PalaceChaotic Crystal Palace transfer window leaves Pierre Sage to run the gamut of emotionsManager was frustrated not to land defensive targets and lost last-day tug of war but can draw on positives as he seeks his first pointsEd AaronsFri 4 Sep 2026 07.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least Pierre Sage did his research before joining Crystal Palace in June. Having stepped into Oliver Glasner’s shoes after the most successful era in the club’s history, it has not been the easiest transition for the engaging Frenchman following defeatsagainst EvertonandManchester Cityto start the new campaign, and amid uncertainty surrounding the futures of some of the Conference League winners’ key players.Ismaïla Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta ended up staying at Selhurst Park despite interest from Liverpool and Aston Villa respectively, while Palace brought in four new players after missing out to Sunderland for Malick Fofana inone of deadline day’s most dramatic storylines. But Sage is sanguine about experiencing a typically chaotic first transfer window in south London, and relieved to be able to concentrate on events on the pitch before Saturday’s trip to Fulham.Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendRead more“I knew that and I had to deal and adapt to that,” Sage said when asked about Palace’s reputation for doing late deals, a trend that has led to them signing 10 players on the final day in the past three summer windows. “But at the end the most important thing is to have the player or the profile we choose and that’s the case. I think we are in line with what we need.”Glasner, who has been joined at Nottingham Forest from Palace by Daniel Muñoz, made no secret of his dissatisfaction at having to wait until deadline day to bring in players after Palace signed four in his first summer at the club in 2024. It’s not Sage’s style to make a similar fuss, even if he is understood to have expressed frustration over their efforts to recruit a top-class replacement for Maxence Lacroix when the France defenderwas sold to Chelseain July.His favoured target was Ismaëlo Ganiou from Lens, the 21-year-old a key competent in the team that won the Coupe de France and finished second in Ligue 1 under Sage last season. However, Lens were reluctant to sell one of their prized assets and Ganiou signed a new deal at the start of August, forcing Palace to explore other targets.A deal for Joel Ordóñez of Club Brugge broke down as the Ecuador defender is still recovering from a broken foot, while attempts to sign Augsburg’s Chrislain Matsima and Raphaël Le Guen of Brest also came to nothing. The arrival of Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor on loan will help plug the gap, yet there remain major doubts over whether Lacroix’s leadership at the back has been fully replaced.View image in fullscreenOne that got away: Malick Fofana chose Sunderland over Palace on deadline day.Photograph: Jean Catuffe/Getty ImagesHaving failed to lure Mamadou Sangaré from Lens, with the Mali midfielder opting to join Brentford instead, Sage was the driving force in Palace’s attempt to bring in Fofana from another of his former clubs, Lyon. That ultimately proved futile despite a series of phone calls to the Belgium forward on deadline day. “I’m really proud and happy with what the club did for that,” Sage insisted. “We fight a lot and sometimes you cannot give more than this, but we give our best in this situation. At the end, the player chooses.” It remains to be seen whether the signing of the Chile forward Dario Osorio from the Danish club Midtjylland on an initial loan with an obligation to buy next summer for £26m makes up for the disappointment given he plays mainly on the right flank.Palace are well stocked in attacking areas having also signed Dwight McNeil and Evann Guessand – who has been left out of the squad for the Europa League – and kept hold of Sarr. The return of Ben Chilwell and late addition of Quinten Timber to midfield will add depth and are believed to have gone some way to satisfying Sage, not to mention Palace’s rejection of bids from unnamed sides for Adam Wharton. Manchester City and Chelsea were believed to be among those who showed an interest. “The club was strong with the situation, and I think the player is completely in line with that,” he said.But after breaking their transfer record twice in January, for Jørgen Strand Larsen and Brennan Johnson – who was swapped for McNeil, with Everton – Palace’s summer net spend of almost £40m in profit was the second lowest in the division behind Aston Villa. Over the past five seasons, Hull and Coventry have both invested more than Palace’s £90m despite being in the Championship.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSage was quick to reject suggestions he is unhappy with Palace’s summer signings and instead drew on his experiences from watching his parents run their brasserie in Belley, a town in the Ain region of eastern France. “I’m not frustrated – we are not a bank,” he said. “We do with what we have. My parents had a restaurant and I prefer every day there’s a lot of clients but it was not the case sometimes and we have to deal with that every day. In football it’s the same.”View image in fullscreenPierre Sage said of Palace’s transfer window: ‘I’m not frustrated, we’re not a bank.’Photograph: Malcolm Fell/Focus Images Ltd/ShutterstockThe absences of Sarr and Mateta, the latter of which had his hopes of leaving scuppered by a hamstring injury that will keep him out for another three weeks, will not help Palace’s chances against Fulham. Sage expects Sarr back from a groin injury for the game against Ipswich next Saturday but said the Senegal forward “needs time” after being affected by Liverpool’s interest, which led to his agentreleasing a statementcriticising the player’s treatment.It will not have escaped Sage’s attention that Glasner won three times at Craven Cottage in 2025, including aquarter-final victoryon the way to winning the FA Cup. After the week he has had, more of the same would do against another team who have yet to get off the mark in the league this season.Explore more on these topicsCrystal PalacefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: WSL transfer talking points: three things we learned from the data | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Arsenal invested the most as the leading clubs’ spending dwarfed that of the rest of the league but there was a greater emphasis on stability
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: Arsenal invested the most as the leading clubs’ spending dwarfed that of the rest of the league but there was a greater emphasis on stability
Content: Ona Batlle is among the new faces at Arsenal.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOna Batlle is among the new faces at Arsenal.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesWomen's Super LeagueWSL transfer talking points: three things we learned from the dataArsenal invested the most as the leading clubs’ spending dwarfed that of the rest of the league but there was a greater emphasis on stabilityAndrew BeasleyFri 4 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Women’s Super League’s summer transfer window has closed before the start of the 2026-27 season. The finances involved are microscopic compared with the £3.4bn that Premier League clubs spent on new players but the data provides three key points of interest: which club has made the biggest improvement to their squad, who is banking on stability, and how the women’s game has outsmarted its male equivalent.Arsenal have the most improved squadMany transfers in women’s football occur without the fee being disclosed, which deprives us of the conventional shorthand for assessing player quality. Thankfully there is Soccerdonna, the arm of Transfermarkt that covers women’s football. It carries estimated market values of players in euros. Using these, we can see by how much clubs have improved their squads.Arsenal’s new additions have a combined value of €3.9m, slightly more than the €3.5m of talent that London City Lionesses have gained this summer. The entire squads of eight of the 14 teams in the 2026-27 WSL are worth less than these figures, which highlights the impact the new players should have. Indeed, London City’s new two-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas is valued at €1.15m, which is more than the entire Charlton squad and not far behind the roster at Crystal Palace.Chart showing the market value of players at clubs in the 2026-27 Women’s Super LeagueWest Ham could argue they have added the most to their squad as the combined market value of their new players (€1.02m) is more than the corresponding amount for the players who remain from last season (€0.96m). Having finished 10th after winning only three of their opening 19 matches, improvements were clearly required.Clubs have kept more settled squadsWhile supporters are most excited by new signings, departees are just as relevant to the health of a squad. Or at least they are if they made significant contributions in the previous season.West Ham had to make additions as they lost players that contributed 6,322 minutes in the 2025-26 WSL, 29% of their total. Chief among those leaving was the goalkeeper Kinga Szemik, who started 19 of 22 games. Only Martina Fernández (1,950 minutes for Everton) and Keira Flannery (1,891 at Charlton) left current WSL clubs and played more minutes last season.Chart showing minutes played in 2025-26 by players who left Women’s Super League clubs this summerTeams may have learned from 12 months ago. Brighton lost 9,584 minutes of playing time from their 2024-25 squad in the summer 2025 window and went on to finish two places lower last season. Liverpool also said goodbye to a higher share of their playing time than anyone has in this transfer window (6,406 minutes), and started the campaign very slowly.Output could be a greater issue than time played. Manchester City and Aston Villa have both lost players who contributed at least 13 combined goals and assists last season in Kerolin and Kirsty Hanson respectively. The difference between these clubs is that the champions can absorb the cost of that exit far more easily. The 17 goal contributions Villa have lost from last season through players leaving constitute 36.2% of their total, the highest proportion of the teams who were in the WSL in 2025-26.The WSL is far better prepared for transfer windows than the Premier LeagueThe Premier League endured a ridiculous deadline day on Tuesday. Around a sixth of players signed by clubs in the latest transfer window completed their deals on 1 September. Just over a third of the money that went on transfer fees this summer was spent after the 2026-27 season had already begun.Things have been rather more organised in the WSL. Granted, its window closed before the new campaign gets under way and they didn’t have a World Cup clogging up the summer this year. But where the Premier League had completed only 83% of eventual total signings when deadline day began, the WSL made that proportion four weeks ago.Chart showing Women’s Super League players bought in the seven-day periods throughout the summer 2026 transfer windowThe obvious explanation would be that lower-finance deals are easier to complete. Yet Fifa recently revealed global spending on transfer fees in women’s football had increased by 83.6% year-on-year. Spending on agents fees by WSL clubs grew by 75% in the year up to 3 February 2026 too. The transfer business remains efficient even while the sums involved are rapidly increasing.Men’s football will always have much more money but it could benefit from the transfer expertise and planning in the women’s game.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Premier League news: Richarlison refused new contract, Alonso backs James in midfield | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Maresca hails ‘winner’ Fernández but will not make him captain, and De Zerbi defends Richarlison treatment
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Maresca hails ‘winner’ Fernández but will not make him captain, and De Zerbi defends Richarlison treatment
Content: Richarlison has been omitted from Tottenham’s Premier League squad for the season.Photograph: John Walton/PAView image in fullscreenRicharlison has been omitted from Tottenham’s Premier League squad for the season.Photograph: John Walton/PAThe talkSoccerPremier League news: Richarlison refused new contract, Alonso backs James in midfieldTottenham manager Roberto De Zerbi insists his wantaway Brazilian striker ‘decided everything, not me’Guardian sportand Press AssociationFri 4 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1.De Zerbi defends treatment of RicharlisonRoberto De Zerbi insisted he had no choice but to leave Richarlison out of Tottenham’s Premier League squad after the Brazilian declined the offer of a contract extension and repeatedly insisted he wanted to leave the club.Richarlison was Spurs’ leading scorer in the Premier League last season but did not feature in last weekend’s defeat to Newcastle amid discussions of a return to his former club Everton. He eventually rejected that move but, with Tottenham bringing in Omar Marmoush from Manchester City, there was no space for the 29-year-old in De Zerbi’s 25-man list of players he plans to use in the league this campaign.“At the beginning of pre-season I spoke to Richarlison and asked him if he wanted to extend his contract because I was happy to keep him with us,” said De Zerbi. “He didn’t want to. Richarlison is a good player, yes. He was important last season, yes, very important. He’s a good guy, yes. But in the end I had to stop myself putting pressure on the players if the players show me they want to leave. I’m sorry for him, but we have to go to another page and work with Dominic Solanke and Omar Marmoush.”Richarlison has spent the week training separately from the first team, but De Zerbi denied cutting the Brazilian adrift, insisting: “He decided everything. Not me, not the club.”Spurs will have deadline-day arrival Mykhailo Mudryk available for Saturday’s trip to Nottingham Forest, with De Zerbi suggesting the Ukrainian is ready to play up to 30 minutes after signing on loan from Chelsea.Mudryk has not played a competitive match since November 2024, having served a doping suspension. But De Zerbi, who worked with Mudryk at Shakhtar Donetsk, previously said the winger “has the potential to win the Ballon d’Or.”“He’s 25, he’s in the right moment of his career in a top club. I think it’s the right moment for him to show what he can do,” said the Italian. “Mudryk loves football. He lives for football. I have never seen many players like him as a mentality, as a belief, in the work during the week in training. He works double than other teammates.”De Zerbi confirmed fellow new arrival Savio is available again this weekend, but James Maddison is likely to miss out as he recovers from a shoulder fracture. Spurs are yet to score in successive Premier League defeats to Brentford and Newcastle this season.Ben Bloom2.Alonso says sky is limit for James in midfieldXabi Alonso believes Reece James can become one of the best midfielders in the world. James has established a reputation as one of the game’s leading right-backs but has frequently covered in midfield, and Alonso – one of the finest midfielders of his generation – intends to continue using him centrally.James started Chelsea’s first two matches, victories against Fulham in the Premier League and League One Luton in the Carabao Cup, and came on in the win against Brighton in central midfield.Alonso, asked whether James could become one of the world’s best midfielders, said: ‘“I would say so. He’s very comfortable, very confident playing in that position. He has the intelligence to play there. He has the intelligence to connect with teammates around him in the middle to know what’s the best thing before and after you get the ball. And he has this awareness. I remember seeing him play very well in the middle. So yes, we are using him. He will have a lot of minutes in there as a first midfielder.”Alonso prefers to play two central midfielders, whether he fields a back four with a double pivot in front, or a back three with a pair between wing-backs. The loss of Enzo Fernández to Manchester City for £125m on deadline day and the late collapse of a deal for Monaco’s Lamine Camara left the Chelsea manager a player short in midfield, even if Alonso insisted before Sunday’s game at Arsenal that he was satisfied with the transfer business and balance of his squad.He believes James’s leadership traits are most effective in a more advanced position: “He has the capacity to help the teammates around him, so that is very important as well, because he has this presence, this respect from the teammates. When he tells them something, they listen and they follow him. His impact in terms of emotionally, in terms of captain, leadership in the middle, he’s closer to everything and he can play an important role there.”James has been held back by a series of long-term injuries, including a knee problem earlier in his career and repeated hamstring issues that required surgery in 2023. Not competing in Europe will help Chelsea manage his workload.“We need to manage the loads, manage the minutes, with some players there are special cases,” Alonso said. “We need to be aware of that. After that we try to do as much as possible but can’t control all the variables.”Sam Cunningham3.Maresca: Don’t judge Fernández on price tagEnzo Maresca has insisted Enzo Fernández should not be judged by the British record-equalling £125m fee Manchester City paid Chelsea for the midfielder. “Don’t judge players based on how much the club pays for them,” said Maresca. “Not just for Chelsea, for City, for all the clubs – Arsenal, Tottenham …don’t judge a player based on that, because it is not correct. He is a fantastic player.”The manager was asked if the combative midfielder will add a level of streetwiseness to City. “I don’t know if it’s streetwise but he knows how to win,” Maresca said. “When you want to compete or win, it’s much more important to have players that already know how to do that than players who never have done it in the past. Enzo is not the only one. This squad has many players who know how to win titles and compete, and this is what we were looking for.View image in fullscreenEnzo Fernández is not regarded by his new manager as a potential Manchester City captain.Photograph: Manchester City FC“I can promise you that in the last four or five days, four or five players from the squad were asking if he is coming or not because they want him to be with us. It’s very important that he is with us and we are 100% happy with that.”Although Fernández captained Chelsea under Maresca, Rúben Dias will wear the armband at City. The Argentinian is also not part of the squad’s leadership group. “The four captains are Ruben, Erling [Haaland], Marc [Guéhi] and Gianluigi [Donnarumma],” confirmed Maresca. ‘I was also thinking about Phil [Foden] because Phil is one of the guys from the house [a local]. He’s not in that group, but for me he’s also one of the captains, one of the players that belong to that group.”On signing, Fernández said: “I always dreamed of being at a club as big as City”, the implication being that Chelsea are a small club. Maresca was asked if he found this amusing. “He was already in a big club like Chelsea and is happy to be with us now,” said the 46-year-old. “Chelsea are a big club and City are a big club.Of Fernadez’s best position, Maresca said: “I see Enzo as a six, a little bit more deep, or a little higher arriving in the box. It depends a little on what we need during the game and we’re going to use him in different positions.”Jamie Jackson4.Emery omits £25m signing Harwood-BellisUnai Emery conceded omitting Taylor Harwood-Bellis from Aston Villa’s Champions League squad, two days after the defender joined in a £25m deal from Southampton, prompted a “difficult” conversation. Harwood-Bellis and the 17-year-old Brian Madjo were surprisingly left out of Villa’s 23-man squad.Emery spoke to Harwood-Bellis on Thursday to advise the 24-year-old, who has one England cap, that he would not be eligible to play in European competition. Madjo is not expected to play until October owing to a foot injury sustained after scoring in the Super Cup last month, but in that scenario would be injured only for Tuesday’s Champions League opener at Club Brugge.Harwood-Bellis, a deadline-day arrival, was the last of Villa’s 10 summer signings after being identified as a replacement for Ezri Konsa, who joined Arsenal in a £51m deal. It is understood there is no financial reason for the omissions, though Villa’s fight to meet Uefa’s squad-cost rules is ongoing. Emery said he hoped Harwood-Bellis would play in the Champions League later in the season, potentially in February if they advance to the knockout stages, but for now the midfielders Lamare Bogarde and Boubacar Kamara can deputise in at centre-back.“It was difficult,” Emery said of his decision to exclude Harwood-Bellis. “It is hard for him, it is hard for me to tell him my decision, but I did it yesterday. I spoke with Taylor and explained to him why. Of course, it was hard, but he understood it. For other players like Madjo and [Modou Kéba] Cissé, there are different circumstances, Cissé and Madjo are injured. Of course, hopefully Madjo will be available after the break and the next challenge is for him to get inside [the squad] in January.”In February 2025, Emery left Donyell Malen out of his Champions League squad, weeks after the Dutchman joined from Borussia Dortmund, for whom he played in the 2024 final against Real Madrid. In the same window the defender Andrés García, who joined from Levante and is on loan at Getafe, was also omitted.“Taylor arrived as the last one, and we can get the balance [in defence] with Lamare Bogarde, and we can even play Kamara,” Emery said. “We tried to analyse it deeply. Taylor will be here for a long time, and hopefully, we will have the opportunity to play in Europe with us, after January maybe, and the next few years. Madjo is 17 years old and is so, so young. He will have, for sure, more opportunities to play with us this year and the next years in Europe.”Ben Fisher5.No ‘instant fix’ at United, admits CarrickMichael Carrick has admitted one transfer window cannot provide an “instant fix” for Manchester United but said he was “largely happy” with the club’s business, despite being outspent by promoted Hull, Ipswich and Coventry. United spent £155m on central midfielders but failed to sign a left-back, leaving Luke Shaw as the only senior player in that position.United go to Everton on Sunday seeking their first away point, having lost at Hull. There were no signings in the final week of the window, despite a number of inquiries for left-backs. Everton asked about loaning Joshua Zirkzee on deadline day but United deemed it too late to source a replacement striker.“What squad’s ever the perfect squad?” Carrick said. “You’ve always got to find ways of adapting. When you’re building and trying to push, going through a period where we’re trying to get to the top, that’s the ultimate goal. You’ve got to make steps. It’s not going to be one hit where everything is [fixed] and I’m not just talking about players, individuals … I’m talking about the whole thing of improving as a group, improving as a squad. It’s not just an instant fix and you finish top of the league and you stay there.”Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba arrived to bolster the midfield, and Karl Darlow was brought in on a free as a backup goalkeeper. United start their Champions League campaign on Thursday and there are questions over strength in depth.“We went into the window wanting to come out stronger,” Carrick said. “From the group we had last season, we’ve added to that, we’ve done a lot of good work. The situation is what it is in terms of finances and what we can do. The players we brought in I’m delighted with; the quality and level we’ve got I’m really happy with. These other things you can do or could have done, that’s part of evolving the group and trying to push all the time. We had certain things we needed to fill and largely I think we’re in a good group. We’ve a good dynamic in the squad. We’ve got players that are flexible in the team and can play in different positions. Largely pretty happy.”Will UnwinExplore more on these topicsFootballThe talkMichael CarrickManchester UnitedUnai EmeryAston VillaManchester CityTottenham HotspurnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cameron Myers shines in star-studded field to win 1500m at Diamond League final | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Australian beats Olympic champions Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Cole Hocker, while pole vaulter Kurtis Marschall soars over 5.82m to finish third in Brussels
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Australian beats Olympic champions Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Cole Hocker, while pole vaulter Kurtis Marschall soars over 5.82m to finish third in Brussels
Content: Australia’s middle-distance runner Cameron Myers celebrates winning the men’s 1500m at the 2026 World Athletics Diamond League final in Brussels.Photograph: Elias Rom/Belga/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAustralia’s middle-distance runner Cameron Myers celebrates winning the men’s 1500m at the 2026 World Athletics Diamond League final in Brussels.Photograph: Elias Rom/Belga/ShutterstockAthleticsCameron Myers shines in star-studded field to win 1500m at Diamond League finalAustralian beats Olympic champs Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Cole HockerPole vaulter Kurtis Marschall soars over 5.82m to finish third in BrusselsGuardian sportFri 4 Sep 2026 19.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 21.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMiddle-distance runner Cameron Myershas become only the eighth Australian to win a Diamond League final crown with victory in the men’s 1500m in Brussels.The 20-year-old claimed one of the biggest wins of his career to date as he beat a star-studded field that included Olympic champions Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Cole Hocker to continuehis own meteoric rise.Myers timed a late burst down the home straight to perfection and dipped at the line to snatch victory in 3:30.14 ahead of Kenya’s Phanuel Kipkosgei Koech (3:30.18).Amy Hunt left trailing by Julien Alfred in women’s 200m Diamond League finalRead moreIngebrigtsen, on the comeback trail after Achilles surgery in February, dictated the pace of the race and looked on course for a morale-boosting win before ​tiring in the last 30 metres.America’s Ethan Strand edged past the Norwegian in the final few steps to cross the line in 3:30.50 and round out the podium.Myers won the 1500m in Brussels to continue a rich vein of form that includessmashing the national recordwhen crossing first at the Paris Diamond League meet in June.“I’m pretty relieved to be honest! It’s nice to get a win, I’m super pumped,” Myers said.​“I was feeling good. I contemplated making a move on the back straight but I didn’t really need to, so I just waited as long as possible and a gap opened up and I was able to take it.​“It’s pretty cool memorabilia to have a trophy like that.”View image in fullscreenAustralia’s Cameron Myers wins the men’s 1500m ahead of Kenya’s Phanuel Kipkosgei Koech at the Diamond League final.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAPole vaulter Kurtis Marschallfinishedon the podium on Friday night after world record-holder and Olympic champion Armand Duplantis withdraw pre-competition.​Marschall soared over 5.82m to finish in third place on countback behind Norway’s Sondre Guttormsen, while Germany’s Emmanouil Karalis claimed the event with a new meet record of 6.12m.​“It’s another 5.80 and 5.80 doesn’t get enough credit,” Marschall said. “It’s still a hard bar to jump and if you do it when it counts, that’s what really matters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toAustralia SportGet a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports deskEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKurtis Marschall finished third in the men’s pole vault during the World Athletics Diamond League final in Brussels.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images​Lachlan Kennedy ran his fifth sub-10 second 100m of 2026 when flashing to fourth place in 9.99sec (+0.1), finishing just 0.02s off the podium.​Racing from lane one, theCommonwealth championreturned to top form as the race was won by Jamaica’s reigning world champion Oblique Seville in 9.90s.​“Under 10 seconds again in objectively not the best conditions,” Kennedy said. “The crowd was good, the field was good and it was a close race.​“It’s high stakes and not good conditions, but they are the same for everyone else.”​Discus thrower Matthew Denny was another Australian to finish one position shy of the podium as he ended his 2026 campaign with a 68.04m.Denny’s throw was less than a metre short of the podium which was topped by Slovenia’s Kristjan Ceh with a meet record of 71.29m.​Commonwealth champion Rose Daviesalso just missed the podium in the women’s 5,000m, clocking 14:37.47 in the race won by Ethiopia’s Freweyni Hailu in 14:35.20.​Fellow Australians Georgia Griffith was sixth in 14:38.69 and Linden Hall finished in 10th with a personal best time of 14:40.62.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: St Helens miss out on playoffs after Charnley news caps Leigh’s perfect night | Super League | The Guardian
description: St Helens miss out on the playoffs for the first time in over 60 years after a 48-10 defeat at Leigh
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: St Helens miss out on the playoffs for the first time in over 60 years after a 48-10 defeat at Leigh
Content: Josh Charnley touches down for the first try in the thrashing of St Helens which secures Leigh’s place in the Super League playoffs.Photograph: Ed Sykes/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJosh Charnley touches down for the first try in the thrashing of St Helens which secures Leigh’s place in the Super League playoffs.Photograph: Ed Sykes/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueSt Helens miss out on playoffs after Charnley news caps Leigh’s perfect nightLeigh 48-10 St HelensCharnley scores and agrees contract extensionAaron Bowerat Progress With Unity StadiumFri 4 Sep 2026 17.26 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 19.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt ended not so much with a bang, but with a whimper. One of rugby league’s most extraordinary streaks has felt as though it was coming to an inevitable end for quite some time but as it transpired, St Helens’ 64-year run of making the playoffs ultimately concluded in a manner that summarises their fall from grace.You have to go back to 1962 to find an end-of-season playoff series that did not include one of rugby league’s true heavyweight clubs. In theSuper Leagueera, they have won 10 titles and were champions of the world as recently as 2023. But this, sadly, is a shadow of that side – and indeed that club.St Helens’ 60-year playoff record hangs by a thread after thrashing by LeedsRead moreThey have been outsiders all season long for the playoffs, and their hopes were emphatically ended here against a team who themselves have genuine Old Trafford aspirations. Without over a dozen first-team players, Saints’ defensive frailties that have plagued them all season were exposed brutally yet again to ensure they will finish seventh. History for all the wrong reasons.But this was just as significant a night for Leigh as it was for St Helens. These two teams have been on contrasting journeys in recent years with Saints slowly slipping away from being the best team in the world, and the Leopards rising year-on-year to become a genuine Super League threat in 2026. They scored eight tries, four in each half, to blow Saints away in crucial moments and book their playoff spot. They could yet finish fourth and get home advantage in the opening week should they beat Wakefield next Friday. After a slow start, Leigh look genuine contenders.“We’ve got to rely on other teams winning over the weekend and then it’s still mathematically a chance,” their coach, Adrian Lam, said. “But we would have taken this a third of the way through the season so I’ve got to appreciate that.” His side were far too good when it mattered here, with their attack in devastating form all evening.Super League’s all-time top try-scorer, Josh Charnley, opened the scoring with his 281st career try – and celebrated by signing a fake contract extension which was officially announced in the stadium moments later. David Armstrong doubled the lead soon after. There was a brief flurry of resistance from Saints but tries for Jacob Douglas and Tristan Sailor proved a false dawn. They collapsed again as half-time approached, with two more Leigh tries making it 24-10.From there, it always felt unlikely at best that Saints could keep their season alive going into next weekend. “The group are very disappointed but they should be proud,” their interim coach, Eamon O’Carroll said. “The scoreline blew out but there were some St Helens traits in there. But there needs to be changes now.”Those changes will be headlined by the arrival of the Australia coach, Kevin Walters, in 2027 – and he has plenty to work on based on this display. Leigh put the result beyond doubt as the hour mark approached when the outstanding Umyla Hanley scoring his second after Edwin Ipape barged over from close range.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBy then, it was merely a case of how many Leigh would win by. The answer was a resounding 38, as Jacob Alick-Wiencke exposed more timid St Helens defending before Robbie Mulhern strode through to score late on with the kind of ease that has been too common a sight in Saints’ play this season.Sport is cyclical, and history suggests St Helens will be a force again. But there is a major rebuild ahead that suggests that return to the top table is some way off. For the first time in over a generation, the Saints will watch the playoffs with the rest of us as spectators.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueLeigh LeopardsSt HelensRugby leaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Amy Hunt left trailing by Julien Alfred in women’s 200m Diamond League final | Athletics | The Guardian
description: The British sprinter finished third behind the Olympic 100m champion, on a night where the pole vault superstar Mondo Duplantis pulled out with an injury
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The British sprinter finished third behind the Olympic 100m champion, on a night where the pole vault superstar Mondo Duplantis pulled out with an injury
Content: A season’s best for Amy Hunt (right) was not enough to win the Diamond League women’s 200m against the pace set by Julien Alfred (centre).Photograph: Omar Havana/APView image in fullscreenA season’s best for Amy Hunt (right) was not enough to win the Diamond League women’s 200m against the pace set by Julien Alfred (centre).Photograph: Omar Havana/APAthleticsAmy Hunt left trailing by Julien Alfred in women’s 200m Diamond League finalBritish sprinter finishes third behind Olympic 100m championPole vault superstar Mondo Duplantis pulls out with injurySean Ingleat King Baudouin StadiumFri 4 Sep 2026 17.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 21.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s Amy Hunt was given a jolting reminder of the gap between her and the world’s very best female sprinters as she finished nearly half a second behind Julien Alfred in the Diamond League 200m final.But afterwards Hunt insisted that coming third in a season’s best time of 22.16sec, on tired legs on a dank Brussels night, amounted to one of the better races of her career.Cameron Myers shines in star-studded field to win 1500m at Diamond League finalRead more“I’ve shown the last few 200s, I’m getting a lot stronger, and I think I was probably one of the closest athletes up to my personal best tonight,” said Hunt, who won four European gold medals last month in Birmingham. “So on a very freezing cold night in northern Europe, in September, at 10pm – I think that’s probably one of the best 200s I’ve ever done.”Certainly there were plenty of signs for optimism as Hunt made a fast start and was in touch with Alfred around the bend. But then the St Lucian, who won 100m gold in the Paris Olympics, applied the afterburners to take victory in 21.79, with Kyla White of the US second in 22.00 as Hunt faded.“That was the closest I’ve ever been to Julien on the bend, and I thought: ‘Oh my gosh, if I had completely fresh legs, I could really take you on right now,’” said Hunt. “And that’s such an exciting thing to me because she’s such an incredible athlete. She’s so fierce, but also kind. And to know that that was probably the best first half of the race I’ve ever put together makes it really, really exciting for next season.”The race of the night came in the men’s 1500m as the AustralianCameron Myers found his way out of a boxon the home straight, swerved between Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Phanuel Koech, and then got his nose in front to win in 3:30.14.It was vindication of sorts for Myers, who was a little disappointing in taking Commonwealth Games silver in the milebehind Josh Kerrin Glasgow last month. But there was also encouragement for Ingebrigtsen, even though he ran out of steam in the final 30 metres, as his time of 3:30.52 was the quickest since his comeback after missing 11 months due to an achilles injury.View image in fullscreenEmmanouil Karalis broke Mondo Duplantis’s Diamond League pole vault record.Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/ReutersThis Diamond League final also doubled as the 50th memorial meeting to be staged in memory of Ivo Van Damme, the brilliant Belgian athlete who won silver medals over 800m and 1500m at the 1976 Olympics before dying in a car accident later that year, aged just 22.After a lengthy tribute to Van Damme, several of the famous athletes to grace this track – including the nine-time Olympic champion Carl Lewis – were paraded in front of the crowd and Philippe, King of the Belgians.Lewis had taken his place next to the king in time to see the Jamaican world champion Oblique Seville take the men’s 100m in 9.90sec, recovering from a poor start to beat the Commonwealth champion Emmanuel Eseme by three-hundredths of a second.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSoon afterwards another world champion, Emmanuel Wanyonyi, had the crowd standing to applaud as he destroyed a strong field to set a meeting record of 1:41.80 in the men’s 800m.“Today was all about winning and I knew that I would have to run 1:41 to win and I did,” said Wanyonyi, who finished nearly a second ahead of the Algerian Djamel Sedjati, with Britain’s Ben Pattison fifth in 1:44.29. “The conditions weren’t ideal tonight. The wind didn’t bother me that much, I was happy it stopped raining.”Elsewhere Busang Collen Kebinatshipi won the men’s 400m in 43.40, breaking his own Diamond League record, while Emmanouil Karalis broke Mondo Duplantis’s meeting record by clearing 6.12m in the pole vault. But there was disappointment as Duplantis pulled out beforehand with tightness in his leg and admitted that his chances of making the new $10m Ultimate Championships in Budapest next week were in question.“The worst possible thing to do is having to pull out of a competition,” said Duplantis. “My head is everywhere right now. It’s super difficult but that’s the life of an athlete. I try to stay calm and positive. We will see if I can make it to the Ultimate Championships. I don’t have the answer right now.”The two-day meeting will conclude on Saturday, with Audrey Werro’s attempt on the women’s 800m world record topping the bill. There should be British success too, with Georgia Hunter Bell favourite to win the women’s 1500m – and a first prize of $60,000.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content
