title: Surrey beat Yorkshire; Somerset thrash Glamorgan: county cricket, day three – as it happened | Sport | The Guardian
description: Somerset beat Glamorgan by an innings while Surrey triumphed by one wicket at the Oval
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: Somerset beat Glamorgan by an innings while Surrey triumphed by one wicket at the Oval
Content: 6h ago15.25 EDTSomerset's Championship dream alive as Surrey sneak thrillerSomerset’s dreams of a first Championship pennant continue to bubble and squeak, for now sitting pretty at the top of the table with just three rounds to go. The innings victory overGlamorgan, whileNottinghamshirewere hamstrung by the weather and a stoicalLeicestershire, put the spring in a west country step.There were three wickets each for the on-song Jack Leach, Craig Overton and Lewis Gregory, the main resistance coming from Asa Tribe and Sean Dickson, who both made forties, but it was all over before tea.ButWarwickshirewere close on their tails after mopping up at Southampton. A match that had started grubbily forHampshirewith the signing and unsigning of Scott Kuggeleijn finished with them dismissed for 115 and 154 to lose by an innings, flailing below the pack at the bottom of Division One. Chris Woakes whipped out both openers cheaply in Hampshire’s second innings and Manav Suthar pocketed four.There was a high-wire finish at the Oval asSurreysnookeredYorkshireby one wicket and with it the spoils of 19 points to leapfrog them and out of the relegation zone. Surrey’s pursuit of 185 was stop-start-stop and when Ollie Pope went for a 12 that contained only two scoring shots and Ben Foakes was done by a Ben Coad chestnut before lunch, Surrey looked shot. But while Josh Blake’s stoical 43 off 183 balls blocked one end, the tail played shots at the other. With Surrey eight wickets down, and eight runs needed, Auqib Nabi trumpeted Coad out of the ground but was out next ball. Ten scoreless deliveries followed until Dan Worrall finally hoiked a boundary to win.The wretched season at Old Trafford rolled on, as Tom Helm (four for 36) and co bowledMiddlesexto victory. After a promising start in pursuit of 297,Lancashirecrumpled, losing seven for 39. George Balderson had earlier grabbed five for 54 as Middlesex spiralled in a similar manner, buoyed up by a sing-song 37 from Toby Roland-Jones.Nottinghamshire’s campaign was held up by the unlikely figure of the Leicestershirefast bowler Josh Hull, who came in as nightwatcher at Trent Bridge on Thursday night, and had only reached double figures three times in 34 innings. He was finally out after more than five hours at the crease for 97.ShareUpdated at18.56 EDT

title: McLaren and Alpine F1 teams at odds after Briatore outburst over appeal | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Flavio Briatore went on the attack over a Monaco GP decision that went against his driver, with an accusation of a judge’s bias towards McLaren
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Flavio Briatore went on the attack over a Monaco GP decision that went against his driver, with an accusation of a judge’s bias towards McLaren
Content: Flavio Briatore and Andrea Stella in better times.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFlavio Briatore and Andrea Stella in better times.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026McLaren and Alpine F1 teams at odds after Briatore outburst over appealBriatore on the attack over Monaco GP decisionAccusation of judge’s bias towards McLarenGiles Richardsin MonzaFri 4 Sep 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 17.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA furious row has broken out in the buildup to the Italian Grand Prix between the Alpine team executive adviser and de facto team principal, Flavio Briatore, and theMcLarenprincipal, Andrea Stella, after Briatore made extraordinary allegations about McLaren’s influence on an FIA court of appeal decision against his team, claims which Stella dismissed as “insulting”.Early on Friday a decision was released by the court of appeal, finding in favour of McLaren and Red Bull appeals against the result ofthe Monaco GP, prompted by a series of pit lane speeding penalties that were incorrect. The pit lane at Monaco had been incorrectly measured, leading to the penalties, including two for Alpine’s Pierre Gasly. Alpine appealed against those and they were successful, with the Frenchman subsequently awarded third place.Lewis Hamilton ready to rock Monza with ‘phenomenal’ Italian GP win for FerrariRead moreHowever, that decision went to the court of appeal who reversed the decision, demoting Gasly to seventh, with Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar returned to his third place and McLaren’s Oscar Piastri to fourth.Briatore, who had a lifetimeFormula Oneban for fixing the 2008 Singapore Grand Prix overturned, arrived for the press conferenceon Friday in Monza with an A4 piece of paper and, sitting across from Stella, immediately launched into an attack on the judgment, claiming it had been biased.“We accept the decision but what is very strange was four judges in the panel. One of the judges act like a prosecutor,” he said. “This is not a big problem. The problem is he’s linked with the McLaren company, because we have a nice picture of this guy at a speech for McLaren in 2018 in MSO [McLaren Special Operations], Beverly Hills.“He has a foundation, it’s called the One Drop foundation and McLaren gave two, three McLaren cars. This was quite unfair. One of the judges was linked with a team which was protesting us.”MSO is an organisation associated with McLaren automotive, the car manufacturing wing of the company not the racing team. Stella, who was visibly affronted by the accusation, was cold and stony-faced in his reply and suggested there could be consequences for Briatore after the allegations.“I find that this conference is going in this direction, quite insulting for McLaren, for the reputation of a team that deserves a lot of respect,” he said. “If anybody makes these kind of allegations, which seem quite serious, they are going to have to take responsibility for what they are saying in a public forum. The hearing, the whole international court of appeal was conducted to the highest standards, and we should not question this.”View image in fullscreenPierre Gasly was awarded third place at the Monaco GP but it was then taken away on appeal.Photograph: David Davies/PAStella cited Article 1.1.1 of the international sporting code of the FIA, the governing body, under which McLaren and Red Bull had appealed and under the auspices of which the court of appeal had operated.Briatore hit back, going as far as accusing the judge in question by name. “It’s very nice to talk about the point one, one, P2, three, P, P, P. But what is unfair is that the judge was linked with McLaren. This is unfair. The judge normally being completely independent and this judge, the name is Filippo Marchino. Filippo Marchino is a judge, he was very nasty during the hearing, was acting as a prosecutor. And after we found out what is the reason why so nasty, this guy. He is very linked with McLaren.”The court of appeal consists of four people and it is understood the makeup of the panel was known six weeks in advance at which point the parties involved could have objected to those appointed. The FIA issued a statement, stating their procedure for choosing candidates. “The eligibility of candidates for membership of the international tribunal and international court of appeal (ICA) is checked by the eligibility assessment committee, in accordance with the FIA statutes.“The FIA judicial and disciplinary rules provide that for each case before the ICA, a judging panel is constituted, comprising at least three judges. The members of the judging panel are appointed by the president of the ICA.” Marchino is being sought for comment.On the track at Monza, Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton secured a one-two in first practice from Mercedes’ George Russell in third, with his teammate Antonelli in fifth. In the second session, Russell was quickest, one-tenth clear of Leclerc, with Antonelli third, McLaren’s Lando Norris fourth and Hamilton in fifth.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMcLarenMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: USL and players ratify new CBA, raising salaries and introducing 12-month deals  | USL | The Guardian
description: The new pact will grow the base pay in the Championship from $31,000 to $42,000 and include terms for the soon-to-launch first-division USL Premier
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The new pact will grow the base pay in the Championship from $31,000 to $42,000 and include terms for the soon-to-launch first-division USL Premier
Content: Hartford Athletic and Oakland Roots are two clubs in the USL Championship.Photograph: Doug Zimmerman/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHartford Athletic and Oakland Roots are two clubs in the USL Championship.Photograph: Doug Zimmerman/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesUSLUSL and players ratify new CBA, raising salaries and introducing 12-month dealsNew pact includes terms for first-division USL PremierBase pay for Championship grows from $31k to $42kAgreement runs through the 2030 seasonJeff RueterFri 4 Sep 2026 17.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 17.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United Soccer League andUSLPlayers Association announced the ratification of a new collective bargaining agreement for two levels of the organization’s pyramid on Friday, with fresh terms taking effect immediately and running through 2030. The new pact include a second agreement for the second-division USL Championship as well as the first set of terms for the upcoming USL Premier, a first-division sanctioned league scheduled to lauch in 2028.Among the headline items of the deals is the introduction of 12-month contracts for players, a codified first in the US lower divisions. The first USL CBAs worked to standardize 10-month contracts; before then, clubs varied in their commitments to players. Championship players will earn a base compensation (which includes housing) of $42,000 in 2026 – up from $31,000 – with that floor increasing annually over the term of the agreement. The USL Premier will also launch with 12-month contracts and a compensation floor of $67,500 in 2028 with annual increases worked into the CBA.Folding teams, a labor fight, and … expansion? The USL’s structure allows for it all to happenRead more“This collective bargaining agreement is a significant step forward for the USL and our players and reflects the shared commitment on both sides to continue growing the game and advancing professional standards,” USL president and CEO Paul McDonough said in a statement. “It provides long-term stability for our players, clubs and leagues, and greater confidence to invest in the future of the USL.”The agreement also includes refined elements on how group licensing and commercial rights are distributed to involved players, improved medical and professional standards, expanded healthcare to be required for all players, and the introduction of competitive prize money into the USL ecosystem.This is the second CBA for the Championship, with the first having been ratified in 2021.“This was a challenging negotiation, but it was also a measure of how far the sport and its players have come since 2018,” USLPA executive director Connor Tobin said. “When the USLPA was formed that year, we wanted to create an organization in which each player had a voice. … The remarkable progress we have seen for USL players and in American soccer over the last eight years does not happen without the players themselves.”The USL has almost solely organized the professional lower divisions of American soccer since 2018, a year afterthe North American Soccer League’s second iteration ceased operations. There are 25 teams in the Championship and 17 in third-division League One, whose own CBA is set to expire after 2026 but is actively being discussed. The USL also runs a first-division women’s league, the Gainbridge Super League, with its own CBA and eight active clubs. In 2021, League One’s CBA was ratified in the weeks immediately following the Championship’s, using a similar framework but scaled for the level.“A tremendous amount of time and energy went into the bargaining process to reach an agreement that establishes stronger standards for player safety, stability, and the long-term future of the game,” said USLPA president Duke Lacroix, a Colorado Springs Switchbacks defender who represented Haiti at the 2026 World Cup. “Players are the collective voice of this sport, and ratifying this agreement demonstrates the value of having that voice represented at the bargaining table.”Announced in 2025, the USL Premier will be the second first-division sanctioned league in US men’s soccer, alongside Major League Soccer.Tony Scholes, a former executive at Stoke City and the Premier League, will serve as CEO of the new league. The league’s launch will coincide with the introduction of a promotion and relegation model between the USL’s three professional tiers. There has been no substantive detail from the league about how its system will operate and which active teams (likely in the Championship) will be elevated to USL Premier for its first season.Explore more on these topicsUSLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert says she will retire at end of year | WNBA | The Guardian
description: The commissioner announced she will retire after seven years at the helm, a tenure that saw the league experience massive growth but also significant tumult
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The commissioner announced she will retire after seven years at the helm, a tenure that saw the league experience massive growth but also significant tumult
Content: Cathy Engelbert will retire at the end of the year.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APView image in fullscreenCathy Engelbert will retire at the end of the year.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APWNBAWNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert says she will retire at end of yearSeven-year tenure included both growth and tumultInternal and external candidates are on league’s radarAnalysis: Cathy Engelbert’s defining wins and lossesAssociated PressFri 4 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 16.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert is retiring at the end of the year, bringing to a close her seven-plus years at the helm of the league and a stewardship that has been transformative and at times tumultuous.Engelbert is the second-longest tenured WNBA president or commissioner, and she helped negotiate a lucrative collective bargaining agreement this past spring that resulted in the league’s first set of million-dollar player salaries.“Cathy has presided over the WNBA through the most significant period of growth in the league’s 30-year history,” NBA commissioner Adam Silver said Friday when announcing Engelbert’s decision. “We are grateful for Cathy’s leadership and unwavering commitment to the advancement of women’s basketball.”Cathy Engelbert’s WNBA tenure: the wins and losses that defined her seven yearsRead moreEngelbert, who turns 62 in November, told the Associated Press that she has been thinking about retiring for months.“When I first came to the league I intended to do this for 3 1/2 years,” she said in a phone interview. “The 7 1/2 years exceeded that time. This is a really good time given the financial transformation journey we’ve been on. Getting the collective bargaining agreement done, getting a long-term media rights deal done, getting expansion done.”Engelbert insists the decision to leave was solely her own and that she did not feel any pressure to step down from NBA or WNBA stakeholders. She said she has been working on a succession plan over the last few years. While she didn’t give any specifics on who may be considered for the position, Engelbert did say there are both internal and external potential candidates on the league’s radar.“It’s a good time to hand it off to the next leader to take the ‘W’ into a better phase,” she said. “I’m proud of the team we built and everything we accomplished. A leader knows when it’s time to drop the mic and move on after building a powerhouse team in the league office.”Engelbert said she has mixed emotions about leaving.“I love women’s basketball and am not going anywhere yet. We’ll run a real succession process in the remaining four months. If we don’t find someone I’ll stay on,” she said. “I had no transition. I walked in the door and I was by myself as no one transitioned me into this role.“Hopefully I can help this next leader transition in especially considering the elevation of this league.”The WNBA has grown at an exponential rate during Engelbert’s tenure as commissioner, with record television ratings, strong attendance, a new long-term media rights deal and expansion to 18 teams by the end of the decade. Engelbert said the growth of the league has “blown away her expectations” since she stepped into her role after leaving her previous position as chief executive of Deloitte in 2019.Besides the new CBA, the list of things she is most proud of includes getting charter travel for players, keeping the league going during the coronavirus pandemic, the historic media rights deal and exponential increase in the value of WNBA franchises. In 2019, the average value of a WNBA franchise was $10m; in 2026, it is about $460m.Along with the financial gains, however, turmoil and tension have accompanied the WNBA’s growth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlayers say they have seen more social media vitriol directed toward them over the last few years and some don’t feel the league has done enough to ensure their safety. The league also has been at the center of discussions about the eligibility of transgender athletes to play in the league.Engelbert has repeatedly said the online attacks on players are unacceptable and she backs league initiatives to protect players. She also said there should be no confusion on the transgender athletes question.Fiba World Cup: what to watch as Team USA and WNBA stars chase goldRead more“We have no current eligibility issues in the WNBA,” Engelbert said, adding that “if we did, we would have a thoughtful policy discussion with the ‘[players’ association] and the players.”While there was a strained partnership between the commissioner and players during the recent CBA negotiations, Engelbert insists she has a good relationship with them.Talks between the commissioner and players have been complicated. New York Liberty forward Breanna Stewart, vice-president of the WNBA players’ union executive committee, said before the All-Star Game that there is a respect for Engelbert among the players, just not much of a relationship.Engelbert said she is ready to do what most retirees plan: spend more time with family.Explore more on these topicsWNBAUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They disturb the game’: how betting fans are taking over tennis courts | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jeering and heckling are increasingly commonplace, even at grand slams, as spectators try to influence matches
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Jeering and heckling are increasingly commonplace, even at grand slams, as spectators try to influence matches
Content: Players at the US Open report hearing comments intended to put them off as people bet more often on matches.Photograph: Al Bello/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPlayers at the US Open report hearing comments intended to put them off as people bet more often on matches.Photograph: Al Bello/Getty ImagesUS Open Tennis 2026‘They disturb the game’: how betting fans are taking over tennis courtsJeering and heckling are increasingly commonplace, even at grand slams, as spectators try to influence matchesTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsFri 4 Sep 2026 07.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMidway through the first week of the US Open a couple of years ago, Jiri Lehecka’s attempts to find his form were disrupted by incessant taunting from a spectator close by. “There was a guy who sat just behind my bench on a smaller court, court four, and he was talking to me basically for the first three sets, like non-stop,” Lehecka says. “He was talking to me like: ‘You can’t do it. You are tired. He’s better than you are.’”Lehecka maintained his composure and closed out the match, but even as he focused on navigating the intense stress of competition, he believed he understood this spectator’s motivations. The spectator, he thinks, was not there just to cheer for his favourite player: he was a bettor who had put money on Lehecka to lose. He had entered court four solely to influence the outcome of the match.Gaël Monfils takes final grand slam bow after US Open defeat to Learner TienRead more“In that moment, I took it as a motivation, but just out of curiosity, I spoke to the chair umpire and I was like: ‘Do you think this is normal? Can you do something with that?’” says Lehecka. “The reaction was not very powerful. It was: ‘Yeah, I can’t do anything as long as he’s not insulting you.’ It was some person who knew exactly where the line was. So it wasn’t a nice experience. I won that match, but I think that as soon as you start going against the other player instead of cheering for the player you had a bet on, this is wrong.”The presence of disruptive gamblers in the stands at tournaments has been a growing trend in tennis, an additional annoyance that players must navigate. “I think that we can see this, basically, I don’t want to say in every tournament, but in many tournaments, especially in Europe,” says Lehecka.While players report seeing bettors at tournaments around the world, from the grand slams to the lower level WorldTennisTour, where the presence of these individuals are even more conspicuous in the absence of large crowds, certain events have gained notoriety for their presence. At the Italian Open, it has become commonplace to see spectators trying to get into players’ heads. The US Open is another tournament where players have repeatedly reported disruptive gamblers.Lorenzo Musetti, the Italian world No 14, agrees: “It happened a lot of times, not just in Italy, but in every part of the world. Unfortunately, there’s still this problem that we see sometimes, especially in some matches which is pretty clear that there’s some people from the crowd that they bet and are cheering for the ones that maybe it’s not the home favourite or they disturb the game.”View image in fullscreenJiri Lehecka at the US Open in 2024, when he was harassed by a spectator.Photograph: Marek Janikowski/Icon Sport/Getty ImagesLast year, the Swiss player Leandro Riedi angrily confronted someone he believed actually had money on him to win before reporting him to the chair umpire. Naturally, this is a greater problem for lower-ranked players assigned to smaller courts in closer proximity to spectators than the top players on the big stages.Betting is an unavoidable theme in modern tennis that affects all levels of the sport with negative consequences everywhere. After every loss, and even wins, professional players can be subject to abuse, threats and hate speech on social media from gamblers. Betting is also at the heart of corruption within the sport, with many players over the years being banned for throwing matches.But this year’s US Open has thrust the subject further into the spotlight. On the eve of the tournament, the organisation announced a partnership with Kalshi, the sports betting and prediction company that allows users a wide variety of predictions. Almost as soon as the partnership had been announced, the US Open sent push notifications from its app for articles sponsored by Kalshi offering match predictions. While players continue to receive the negative consequences of betting, the US Open profits from the same beast.For now, there is nothing in the rule books of the men’s Association of Tennis Professionals, the Women’s Tennis Association or the grand slams aimed at weeding out disruptive bettors and umpires can only step in if a spectator becomes abusive. Players are split on whether they should accept this situation. Some, like Musetti, argue there is more the sport’s authorities can do. “The only thing that we can do is try to avoid these people … the [tennis governing bodies] have to do something and have some security because we cannot do much on the court,” he says.However, some also feel they should accept that bettors in the stands have become a part of the sport. Jakub Mensik says players simply have to accept these situations. “Sometimes it’s so obvious you can see it,” he says. “It happens to me plenty of times but I know that I cannot do anything because [bettors], those kinds of people, sometimes they don’t know what to do with their lives. They’re just trying to enjoy it and wishing all the other players the worst so it’s part of the game. It’s basically already part of us, part of all of the athletes, and we just unfortunately have to manage it. There is no other way.”View image in fullscreenThe prediction market platform Kalshi is now an official partner of the US Open.Photograph: Martin Lelievre/AFP/Getty ImagesTommy Paul, the American world No 21, similarly believes this is a regular part of professional sport. “I think it’s part of sports,” he says. “You never react to anything. It’s annoying, for sure. Everyone hears it. It’s not like what you want to be hearing at the back of the court, but it’s kind of what we signed up for.”Other players are defiant. During a recent match,Coco Gauffwondered whether an incredibly loud fan was a bettor but she is adamant that no unruly gambler can get into her head: “If they want to come, they can try and see if they can rattle me, but it won’t work.”On the subject of whether he has dealt with this issue in any of his matches, Frances Tiafoe responds with a devilish laugh. “I haven’t gotten that,” he says, smiling. “Yeah. You don’t want me to have that. It would definitely hit headlines. Let me not even get into it. If that happened, it would be fun.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026TennisUS Open tennisSport bettingGamblingUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US military disables ad trackers on troops’ phones amid security fears | US military | The Guardian
description: Senator releases letters from armed forces after reports of location data being used to track US troops in Middle East
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Senator releases letters from armed forces after reports of location data being used to track US troops in Middle East
Content: Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon, Democrat, has pressed the Pentagon on the issue of location data for months.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenSenator Ron Wyden, an Oregon, Democrat, has pressed the Pentagon on the issue of location data for months.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APUS militaryUS military disables ad trackers on troops’ phones amid security fearsSenator releases letters from armed forces after reports of location data being used to track US troops in Middle EastReutersFri 4 Sep 2026 08.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS militaryofficials say they have disabled advertising trackers on a range of phones and computers, according to letters released on Friday by the US senator Ron Wyden and ⁠statements given to Reuters.The development follows reports ​that commercially available location data had been used to target American forces in the Middle East.The air force told Wyden it disabled the advertising identifiers on computers and mobile phones two ⁠months ago. US Special Operations Command said in a separate letter that it had “recently” disabled them on its Windows devices. The army told Reuters that advertising IDs tied to mobile devices had been disabled since earlier this year.Wyden, ⁠an Oregon Democrat, has pressed the Pentagon on the issue for months.Pentagon official overseeing military AI sold millions worth of stock in AI firmRead moreThe disclosures highlight a growing national security concern: that location data collected ​by the advertising industry and sold by data brokers – companies that ‌collate and resell personal data – can ‌be used to track and target military personnel deployed to war zones.The air force and Special Operations Command declined further comment. Similar letters ‌from the army and navy to Wyden said they disabled advertising IDs on military devices but gave no indication of when the restrictions were imposed. The army said in a statement that advertising IDs had been blocked on Windows computers “since before 2021” but that Android and Apple mobile devices had only had it disabled by default “since at least February 2026”.Messages seeking comment from the navy went unreturned.The effort to reduce the location data generated by smartphones comes as military officials weigh increasingly strict restrictions on phone use overall. ‌In July, Reuters reported that some deployed personnel in the Middle East could be ordered to surrender their phones amid concerns that mobile videos they were posting to the internet were helping Iran target American bases in the ​region.Wyden and Representative Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican, sent a letter to the Pentagon on Friday asking for an investigation into whether the military had properly countered the dangers of the location data trade. The letter included the updates from the various service branches on their efforts to disable advertising IDs on military devices.Wyden said in a statement that it was clear that the military’s efforts “have not been effective at ⁠neutralizing this threat”. Harrigan said that US enemies “should not be able to pull out a credit card and ​buy information that helps them track American ​troops”.The Pentagon said in an email it would ​respond to the lawmakers directly.Mobile advertising IDs, often abbreviated MAID, are unique identifiers tied to specific devices that ​can be used to track ‌a person’s activity across mobile ​apps and pinpoint their physical location.Zach ​Edwards, co-founder of the privacy ad tech company DecryptAds, said that efforts to disable MAID on military-operated devices were “definitely a positive thing”.The restrictions “will essentially ensure their location isn’t being included in bulk data sales being done by numerous vendors”, although he cautioned that personnel might still be tracked through apps in other more complicated ways, for example by triangulating technical device details with network data or location information.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryMobile phonesSurveillanceUS national securitynewsShareReuse this content

title: The best hair dryers for smooth, speedy styling at home – whatever your hair type | Hair care | The Guardian
description: Want every day to be a good hair day? We tested 22 hair dryers to find the best, from gentle diffusers to high-speed and travel-ready models
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: Want every day to be a good hair day? We tested 22 hair dryers to find the best, from gentle diffusers to high-speed and travel-ready models
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHair careReviewThe best hair dryers for smooth, speedy styling at home – whatever your hair typeWant every day to be a good hair day? We tested 22 hair dryers to find the best, from gentle diffusers to high-speed and travel-ready modelsThe best hot brushes, tried and tested by our expertSarah MatthewsFri 4 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn my years of reviewing beauty tech, it was upgrading my hair dryer that made the biggest difference to my routine. I used to dread hair-wash days: the chore of shampooing, conditioning and rinsing my hair, plus the time – and aching arms – spent getting it dry again.My clunky, bargain-bucket hair dryer of seven years was weighty, deafeningly loud, and took a painstaking 20 minutes to dry my hair. So happier days really did arrive when I switched to a new model.My current hair dryer uses a lightweight digital motor that’s not only far quieter, but is also powerful enough to dry my hair in just five minutes. It seems modern hair dryers have stepped up their game. Here, you’ll find the best hair dryers I’ve tested, from gentle options with diffusers for curly hair to ultra-fast models that shave significant time off your morning routine. You’ll also find expert hair-drying guidance from celebrity hairstylist Melissa Timperley.At a glanceBest hair dryer overallHershesonsThe Great£235 at HershesonsBest budget hair dryerBaBylissHydro-Fusion£59.99 at John LewisBest hair dryer for curly hairPanasonicNanoe Moisture+ EH NA0J£199.99 at AmazonBest hair dryer for sensitive scalpsDysonSupersonic NuralStraight and wavy, £349.99 at John LewisBest lightweight hair dryerElectric Head JogFutaria£139.95 at AmazonBest travel hair dryerDysonSupersonic Travel£249.99 at DysonWhy you should trust meI’ve been reviewing beauty products for four years and have amassed a near-encyclopaedic knowledge of hair care. I’ve attended countless styling masterclasses, interviewed hair stylists, and completed a cosmetic science course where I learned exactly how hair growth, styling and care work at a cellular level.I’ve tested and reviewed about 70 hair-styling tools – including hair dryers, curlers,hot brushes, wavers andstraighteners– from big-name brands and newcomers alike. And perhaps most impressively, I’ve walked away with my hair healthy and intact.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach hair dryer was tested for speed and sound levels.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianHaving researched the most popular brands and models, I put 22 hair dryers through their paces for this test. I also spoke to a hair stylist to find out what she looks for in a hair dryer, before cherrypicking the best 12 from my tests to include here.I used an anemometer to test each model’s maximum wind speed, which ranged from a measly 16 metres a second (m/s) to a mind-boggling 43.8m/s, and also a sound meter to measure noise levels from 15cm away.Claims of “enhanced shine or smoothness” aren’t quantifiable, but I did use every hair dryer to complete the same task, noting how long it took to rough-dry hair and then to finish. I also tried my hand at using a round brush to achieve a smooth, bouncy blowout. While I’m no professional at this, it allowed me to make a judgment about how easy a hair dryer’s controls are to use, how precise and versatile its settings are, and comfort levels over the course of styling.When testing was complete, I returned the samples to the manufacturers who sent them. If samples could not be returned, they were sent to the RedbridgeReach Out domestic abuse service, which provides support and refuge for survivors.The best hair dryersView image in fullscreenBlown away: the hair dryers vying for approval.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianBest hair dryer overall:Hershesons The GreatHershesonsThe Greatfrom£235£235 at Hershesons£235 at AmazonWhat we loveFast; lightweight; good results on all hair typesWhat we don’t loveArchaic push-on attachmentsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£235 at Hershesons£235 at AmazonTesting the Hershesons the Great hair dryer confirmed my belief that there’s no need to reinvent the wheel. This hair dryer perfects the basics and irons out any common niggles. It’s the lightest option I’ve ever tested, almost the quickest – and an easy recommendation.Why we love itThe Great hair dryer has four speeds, three heat settings and a cool shot. It reached a super-fast 38.4m/s in my tests, rough-drying my hair in less than five minutes, and leaving it soft and healthy-looking.You change the settings using buttons on the hair dryer’s handle, which can then be locked into place. This is unlike button controls on other models, which can be accidentally pressed mid-use.One distinctive feature of the Hershesons hair dryer, and something that goes a long way to justify its premium price, is its heat-proof mat. This will automatically switch off the dryer when it’s placed on to it, resuming again once it’s lifted. I found this invaluable when blow-drying my hair with a round brush, since I could plonk the hair dryer down to section my hair without having to faff around with the controls.Add on two concentrator nozzles, a diffuser, a fabric bag and a sturdier storage case, and the Great is a hair dryer that truly feels designed with the user in mind.It’s a shame that …it’s so expensive. Next to hair dryers with magnetic attachments, the push-on system here also felt archaic and made it more difficult to switch out tools.Weight (without wire):294gCord length:2.75mHeat settings (including cool shot):fourSpeed settings:fourAttachments:concentrator nozzles and a diffuserMaximum wind speed:38.4m/sVolume range:82-86dBHershesonsThe Greatfrom£235£235 at Hershesons£235 at AmazonWhat we loveFast; lightweight; good results on all hair typesWhat we don’t loveArchaic push-on attachmentsBest budget hair dryer:BaByliss Hydro-FusionBaBylissHydro-Fusionfrom£59.99£59.99 at John Lewis£60 at ArgosWhat we love:Smooth results, sensible price, quiet operationWhat we don’t loveNo high-tech featuresView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£59.99 at John Lewis£60 at ArgosIf you ever struggle with frizzy hair after blow-drying, chances are you need an ionic dryer. This budget-friendly BaByliss option has a good range of speed and heat settings, a concentrator nozzle and a diffuser, making it suitable for numerous hair types. Furthermore, thanks to its 2,100W motor, its 26.4m/s maximum wind speed rivals some of the pricier options on this page.Why we love itIt was immediately clear that the Hydro-Fusion was well built and powerful. It rough-dried my hair in about 10 minutes, leaving it feeling healthy and totally free from frizz and flyaways. Despite this power, it’s quieter than many of the models here, too.Attachments securely clicked into place and stayed on without issue while I completed my round-brush blow-dry test. I found the hair dryer’s two speed settings offered plenty of control for more precise styling, and the cool shot came through quickly compared with other cheaper hair dryers I’ve tested. Once styled, my hair was bouncy and shiny, with a frizz-free finish that lasted multiple days.It’s a shame that …its design is pretty basic; there are no frills here. A few more colour options would have been welcome, too, but you’re unlikely to find a better hair dryer for the price.Weight (without wire):430gCord length:2.5mHeat settings (including cool shot):fourSpeed settings:twoAttachments:concentrator nozzle and a diffuserMaximum wind speed:26.4m/sVolume range:78-85dBBaBylissHydro-Fusionfrom£59.99£59.99 at John Lewis£60 at ArgosWhat we love:Smooth results, sensible price, quiet operationWhat we don’t loveNo high-tech featuresBest hair dryer for curly hair:Panasonic Nanoe Moisture+ EH NA0JPanasonicNanoe Moisture+ EH NA0J£199.99£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMoisturising tech, with smooth healthy resultsWhat we don’t loveConfusing settingsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£199.99 at AmazonAs counterintuitive as it sounds, this hair dryer adds moisture to your hair. Panasonic’s Nanoe technology creates microscopic water droplets that penetrate the hair’s cuticle to add extra moisture to the hair’s deepest layers. It claims this helps to reduce colour fading, flyaways, split ends and breakage.Why we love itI tested the Panasonic EH NA0J hair dryer after several hair washes and found its distinctive shape intuitive to use. For rough-drying, I used heat and the fastest speed setting (23.4m/s), and was impressed at how quickly the hair dryer worked its magic (in about 10 minutes).Compared with the other models here, the Nanoe appeared to separate wet clumps of hair into smaller sections, drying strands faster. Despite using the one and only heat setting, my hair felt smooth and healthy after a rough dry. And when attempting the round-brush blow-dry, the Nanoe set the style quickly using its cool shot.This hair dryer is particularly good at gently diffusing curly and coily hair types. The diffuser attachment locks securely on to the front of the body, and its long prongs are well designed to spread air gently from the root to the tip of a curl. Add in its moisturising capabilities, and you’ll be left with soft, shiny, healthier curls with each use.It’s a shame that …it has only one heat setting. Instead, the Nanoe offers multiple modes: alternating hot and cold for preserving shine; a Scalp Care mode and a Skin Care mode. These won’t be right for everyone, particularly if you like adjusting the heat levels manually. But if your hair needs extra nourishment, this hair dryer is worth a shot.Weight (without wire):460gCord length:2.7mHeat settings (includingcool shot):one (plus scalp care and alternating modes)Speed settings:threeAttachments:concentrator nozzle and a diffuserMaximum wind speed:23.4m/sVolume range:73-84dBPanasonicNanoe Moisture+ EH NA0J£199.99£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMoisturising tech, with smooth healthy resultsWhat we don’t loveConfusing settingsBest hair dryer for sensitive scalps:Dyson Supersonic NuralDysonSupersonic Nuralfrom£349.99Straight and wavy, £349.99 at John LewisCurly and coily, £399.99 at DysonWhat we loveGreat scalp care; luxury design; healthy stylingWhat we don’t loveHigh price, with marginally slower speedsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianStraight and wavy, £349.99 at John LewisCurly and coily, £399.99 at DysonDyson was once best known for its vacuum cleaners, but in recent years has cultivated a reputation for luxury hair styling tools. The 2016 Dyson Supersonic was the brand’s first hair care product, with a distinctive design that ripped up the hair dryer rulebook. And in 2024, Dyson launched the Supersonic Nural, which mirrors the original design but adds some handy scalp care features.Why we love itThe Supersonic Nural had to do some heavy lifting to justify its high price tag. It looks just like its predecessor aside from a small sensor in the middle, which controls the Nural’s new Scalp Protect mode. This tweaks the temperature of the air based on the hair dryer’s proximity to the scalp, ensuring you never burn your scalp or frazzle the delicate hairs at the hairline.As someone with a fussy scalp, I often find the highest temperatures of hair dryers too harsh, but this ensured I was completely comfortable throughout drying. At the same time, it dried the lengths of my hair without frazzling them or causing unnecessary damage. You can also switch this mode on and off if you prefer to control the temperature yourself.There are three speeds and four temperatures, and the button controls are intuitive. Its evenly weighted design was comfortable to hold, its motor was very quiet, and I found its magnetic attachments convenient and easy to use. I particularly liked the flyaway attachment, which quickly and comfortably smoothed down my frizz and flyaways after rough-drying my hair.It’s a shame that …it’s very expensive and the hair dryer wasn’t quite as quick as others I’ve tested. It took about seven minutes to blow dry my hair, but I was grateful that it could take care of my scalp without me having to make adjustments. It’s easily the best option for those with sensitive scalps.Weight (without wire):485gCord length:2.8mHeat settings (including cool shot):fourSpeed settings:threeAttachments:concentrator nozzle, diffuser, flyaway attachment, gentle air attachment and a wide-tooth combMaximum wind speed:29.2m/sVolume range:75-81dBRead our fullDyson Supersonic Nural reviewDysonSupersonic Nuralfrom£349.99Straight and wavy, £349.99 at John LewisCurly and coily, £399.99 at DysonWhat we loveGreat scalp care; luxury design; healthy stylingWhat we don’t loveHigh price, with marginally slower speedsBest lightweight hair dryer:Electric Head Jog FutariaElectric Head JogFutaria£139.95£139.95 at AmazonWhat we loveFast drying; lightweight; sensible priceWhat we don’t loveCould be too powerful for someView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£139.95 at AmazonThis is the fastest hair dryer I’ve ever tested, and weighing 304g, the Futaria is just 10g heavier than the lightest option – the Hershesons above. It was the dark horse here; I hadn’t encountered Head Jog before testing, but with its fast wind speeds of 43.8m/s and reasonable price, it’s an easy favourite.Why we love itThe Futaria hair dryer packs a serious punch, rough-drying my hair in a blisteringly quick four minutes. Thanks to its three speeds and four heat settings, I could master a precise round-brush blow-dry without much effort at all. Personally, I found the wider concentrator nozzle best for styling larger sections of hair, which sped up the process even further.The digital motor also makes the Futaria relatively quiet, and despite its light weight, the design feels sturdy and evenly weighted, plus its rear filter is easy to clean and maintain. As such, this model is perfect for use in busy salons to reduce wrist strain and maximise time efficiency. And those of us at home will also benefit from the dryer’s sleek design, which is available in blue, pink and black.It’s a shame that …since it’s tailored to professional stylists, it’s not as widely stocked as other hair dryers. Also, those concerned about damage may find the knock-your-socks-off power a little much. That said, if you’re careful with the highest intensity settings and use a heat protection spray, you shouldn’t fry your hair.Weight (without wire):304gCord length:3mHeat settings (including cool shot):fourSpeed settings:threeAttachments:twoconcentrator nozzles and a diffuserMaximum wind speed:43.8m/sVolume range:78-84dBElectric Head JogFutaria£139.95£139.95 at AmazonWhat we loveFast drying; lightweight; sensible priceWhat we don’t loveCould be too powerful for someBest travel hair dryer:Dyson Supersonic TravelDysonSupersonic Travelfrom£249.99£249.99 at Dyson£249.99 at John LewisWhat we loveUniversal voltage and fast; smooth stylingWhat we don’t loveIts high priceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lise Smith/Thr Guardian£249.99 at Dyson£249.99 at John LewisI’ve sat by draughty windows that could dry my hair quicker than a hotel hair dryer, so when Dyson announced it was launching a travel-size Supersonic, I was all ears. If you can afford it, it’s easily the best dual-voltage travel hair dryer on the market, with heat monitoring, fast speeds, versatile controls and a build that Dyson claims is 25% lighter and 32% smaller than the original. And, of course, it has the luxury design Dyson is known for.Why we love itAside from its dinky size and weight, it has the same intuitive controls as Dyson’s other hair dryers. That includes two button-controlled heat and speed settings, and a power switch on the handle. That’s fewer options than the full-size model, but more versatility than other travel dryers.It packs a punch, too. Its motor spat out air at an impressive 18.4m/s on its highest speed, which is enough to rival some of the full-size options here. Rough-drying my hair took 10 minutes and, using the nozzle provided, a round-brush blow dry left my hair feeling smooth, sleek and healthy. That’s partly because of the hair dryer’s built-in heat-monitoring system, which helps keep styling temperatures healthy and consistent.And, if you’ve already splashed the cash on a Dyson Supersonic or Nural, the travel dryer is compatible with all existing full-size attachments. If you travel often and hair health is a priority, this is a well-engineered travel dryer that gives you almost all the benefits of the Supersonic on the go.It’s a shame that …it’s so expensive – some full-size options here are far better value, so worth considering above the Dyson. Occasional travellers are likely to be just fine with a cheaper travel model, or a lightweight hair dryer they can easily pack.Weight (without wire):330gCord length:2mHeat settings (including cool shot):threeSpeed settings:twoAttachments:concentrator nozzleMaximum wind speed:18.4m/sVolume range:85-89dBRead our fullDyson Supersonic Travel reviewDysonSupersonic Travelfrom£249.99£249.99 at Dyson£249.99 at John LewisWhat we loveUniversal voltage and fast; smooth stylingWhat we don’t loveIts high priceThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘My hair was left with gorgeous shine’: the Cloud Nine Airshot Pro.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianParlux 3200 PlusParlux3200 Plusfrom£104.63£147.89 at Sally Beauty£104.63 at AmazonWhat we loveGlossy finish, tactile controlsWhat we don’t loveHeavier than othersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£147.89 at Sally Beauty£104.63 at AmazonBest for:fuss-free stylingItalian brand Parlux is well known for making high-quality, powerful, long-lasting hair dryers. According to the brand, the Parlux 3200 Plus (previously Compact) is the most widely used professional hair dryer on the market. I found it well balanced and comfortable in the hand and liked its tactile, retro-feeling switches.During testing, it dried my hair incredibly quickly, leaving a glossy, frizz-free finish. That’s thanks to the inclusion of Parlux’s K-lamination motor, which provides the power of a 2,800W motor while using only 1,900W. The hair dryer is available in a wide range of colours, and is a stylish option – if you can look past the box, which looks freshly fished from the early 2000s.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s heavier than other options here, plus it lacks the design refinements of more expensive models.Weight (without wire):588g;cord length:3m;heat settings (includingcool shot):three;speed settings:two;attachments:two concentrator nozzles;maximum wind speed: 26m/s;volume range:80-85dBParlux3200 Plusfrom£104.63£147.89 at Sally Beauty£104.63 at AmazonWhat we loveGlossy finish, tactile controlsWhat we don’t loveHeavier than othersCloud Nine the Airshot ProCloud NineThe Airshot Profrom£199£299 at Very£199 at AmazonWhat we loveQuiet operation with shiny resultsWhat we don’t loveNo dedicated cool-shot buttonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£299 at Very£199 at AmazonBest for:quiet operationTaking the highest and lowest noise levels into account, the Airshot Pro is the quietest hair dryer I’ve tested. In addition, my hair was left with gorgeous shine thanks to the Sericite-infused heat tech that features in Cloud Nine’s heat-styling tools.As well as offering a great range of temperature controls, with a continuous cool-shot option, the Airshot’s magnetic concentrator nozzle and diffuser attachments proved secure and suited to a range of hair types.It didn’t make the final cut because …it lacks a dedicated cool-shot button, and it’s not as speedy as others in this price range. Still, some may be swayed by its quiet operation.Weight (without wire):448g;cord length:3m;heat settings (including cool shot):four;speed settings:three;attachments:two concentrator nozzles, diffuser;maximum wind speed: 23.8m/s;volume range:75-79dBCloud NineThe Airshot Profrom£199£299 at Very£199 at AmazonWhat we loveQuiet operation with shiny resultsWhat we don’t loveNo dedicated cool-shot buttonGHD SpeedGHDSpeedfrom£263.12£299 at GHD£263.12 at AmazonWhat we loveFast styling; versatile controls; stylish lookWhat we don’t loveHeavy weight; top-heavy build; high priceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£299 at GHDFrom £263.12 at AmazonBest for:quickly smoothing very thick hairGHD hair dryers have historically been some of the best you can buy, and the GHD Speed is a huge step up for the brand in terms of features, design and price.It has four heat settings, plus a cool-shot button and four speeds, and there’s a handy lock switch to prevent you from accidentally changing the settings by pressing buttons mid-styling. It also includes GHD’s “halo” technology, which produces a ring of cool air around the central heated airflow. The company claims this cools the hair’s temperature by 20C, which may help limit damage from drying.This hair dryer comes with one magnetic concentrator nozzle, and other attachments aresold separately from £15. The included nozzle clipped on securely and swivelled around to help get the perfect angle for styling. It also features two channels to accommodate the “halo” of cool air. The dryer took just 10 minutes to get my long, thick hair from wet to styled, with a long-lasting smooth finish – not too shabby.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s heavy, with a slightly odd, top-heavy weighting. The contoured handle and controls also feel more suited to professional use, rather than for personal use; it’s not as comfortable to point towards your own head as it is to point it away from you. I also noticed the dryer creating more frizz around the root for me, where my new hair growth is. For such a high price, I expected better than that.Weight (without wire):620g;cord length:3m;heat settings (including cool shot):five;speed settings:four;attachments:concentrator nozzle;maximum wind speed:24.3m/s;volume range:85-92dBGHDSpeedfrom£263.12£299 at GHD£263.12 at AmazonWhat we loveFast styling; versatile controls; stylish lookWhat we don’t loveHeavy weight; top-heavy build; high priceBellissima B-travelBellissimaB-travelfrom£29.99£29.99 at Boots£30 at AOWhat we loveFast, compact and lightWhat we don’t loveHeat and speed settings are linkedView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£29.99 at Boots£30 at AOBest for:occasional travellersThe dinky Bellissima B-travel hair dryer is a brilliant option for trips and holidays. It has dual-voltage controls, so you can use it wherever you are in the world. Its folding handle and carry case keep everything safe in transit, and it feels very sturdy considering its price.Unlike most hotel hair dryers, which only let out a pathetic trickle of air, this hair dryer provides wind speeds of up to 18.9m/s – faster than some full-size options I’ve reviewed (and a tad faster than the Dyson Supersonic Travel above). That’s highly impressive given the hair dryer’s light weight. You also get a concentrator nozzle for precision styling and two speed options.It didn’t make the final cut because …there’s one control switch, so you can’t adjust the heat setting independently from the speed settings, and the difference between the two heat settings is negligible. Its travel-based use case is limited; you’d be better off investing in an alternative with multiple temperature settings to use at home.Weight (without wire):305g;cord length:1.8m;heat settings (includingcool shot):two;speed settings:two;attachments:concentrator nozzle;maximum wind speed: 18.9m/s;volume range:79-84dBBellissimaB-travelfrom£29.99£29.99 at Boots£30 at AOWhat we loveFast, compact and lightWhat we don’t loveHeat and speed settings are linkedGtech DryOnicGtechDryOnicfrom£119£119 at AO£119 at CurrysWhat we loveClear heat settings with precise controlsWhat we don’t loveCord isn’t long; it really needs a settings lockView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£119 at AO£119 at CurrysBest for:precise temperature controlsOne of my biggest bugbears with hair dryers is that you never quite know how much heat you’re using on your hair. Thankfully, the Gtech DryOnic has a screen on the back that displays the airflow setting and its temperature. With temperatures that range from 40C to 100C, you can make precise adjustments for your hair type.I found the various airflow settings useful and liked how securely the magnetic concentrator nozzle and diffuser attachments fitted on to the dryer. After styling, my hair felt soft and hydrated, with minimal frizz.It didn’t makethe final cut because …it’s not quite as quick as others here at a similar price, and its 2m cord isn’t quite long enough for my liking. I also found it too easy to accidentally press the buttons and change the temperature midway through styling.Weight (without wire):426g;cord length:2m;heat settings (including cool shot):five;speed settings:four;attachments:concentrator nozzle and diffuser;maximum wind speed: 18.8m/s;volume range:78-85dBGtechDryOnicfrom£119£119 at AO£119 at CurrysWhat we loveClear heat settings with precise controlsWhat we don’t loveCord isn’t long; it really needs a settings lockRemington Shine TherapyRemingtonShine Therapyfrom£18£18 at AO£18 at AmazonWhat we loveBudget price; good settings and attachmentsWhat we don’t loveHigher noise levels with a short cordView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£18 at AO£18 at AmazonBest for:tight budgetsThis lesser-known hair dryer is the sister product to the popular Remington Shine Therapyhair straighteners. It offers equally brilliant value and is designed to add shine to the hair using ionic technology.While difficult to quantify in tests, I found the hair dryer did dry my hair relatively quickly and left it shiny and smooth after a round-brush blow-dry. Multiple heat and speed settings, plus a concentrator nozzle and diffuser attachment, make it a good option for all hair types.It didn’t make the final cut because …of its short 1.8m cord and the fact that it’s pretty noisy compared with other models here. That said, it can’t be beaten on price and is a sensible choice if you’re hoping to upgrade an old hair dryer on a budget.Weight (without wire):449g;cord length:1.8m;heat/cool settings:four;speed settings:two;attachments:concentrator nozzle and diffuser;maximum wind speed:18.6m/s;volume range:84-89dBRemingtonShine Therapyfrom£18£18 at AO£18 at AmazonWhat we loveBudget price; good settings and attachmentsWhat we don’t loveHigher noise levels with a short cordWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianIinterviewed Melissa Timperley, hair stylist and founder ofMelissa Salons, to discover her tips for choosing a hair dryer. “When it comes to protecting your hair and achieving the style you want, the tool you use matters just as much as the products you pair it with,” she says.What features should I look for?According to Timperley, the key features are adjustable speed and heat settings, which “allow for better control and protection, depending on your hair type and styling needs”. Look for hair dryers with a cool-shot button, too, which “help to smooth the cuticle and set your style”.Design-wise, consider weight, which is “especially important for longer hair or professional use” to prevent armstrain. Also look for a dryer that has a removable or self-cleaning filter, as “this makes cleaning and maintenance easy, which helps preserve motor life”.What to avoid when choosing a dryerTimperley warns that there are some features, or omissions, that could be detrimental to hair health. It’s best to avoid “single-setting dryers that don’t allow heat or speed control”, as well as low-wattage dryers under 1,800W, because “they often take longer to dry hair, exposing it to heat for too long”.However, some of the dryers I’ve chosen here are below 1,800W. That’s because these use digital motors, which are smaller and lighter than brushed motors and produce faster airflow. That means, in those cases, the difference in drying speeds is negligible.She also warns against buying “heavy, bulky dryers that are uncomfortable to use regularly” and “poor-quality nozzles or diffusers that don’t fit securely or distribute air properly”.Put simply, she says: “If the dryer doesn’t clearly list its motor type, wattage or heat settings, that’s a red flag.”What makes a hair dryer good for different hair types?Picking out the right hair dryer for your hair type can be challenging. “The best hair dryers cater to your hair’s specific needs – whether that’s smoothing frizz, protecting fine strands or cutting through thick, coarse textures,” says Timperley.For fine or damaged hair, Timperley advises looking for “lower heat settings and a ceramic or tourmaline dryer that distributes heat more gently”. For thick or coarse hair, “higher wattage and powerful airflow are essential – infrared, ionic and titanium dryers are great for cutting drying time without excessive heat”. And finally, for curly or textured hair, “a diffuser attachment is key, as is a dryer that offers heat control without sacrificing volume or natural texture”.What’s the difference between ionic and ceramic hair dryers?“Ionic hair dryers emit negative ions that help break down water molecules faster, reducing frizz,” says Timperley. “They’re great for smoothing and shine, especially if you have thick, frizzy or unruly hair.”Conversely, “ceramic hair dryers use ceramic heating elements to distribute heat evenly, which helps prevent hotspots and damage. They’re ideal for fine or delicate hair.”“Some of the best hair dryers,” says Timperley, “combine both technologies, giving you faster drying without sacrificing hair health.”What to do with your old hair dryer?If it still works and is in good condition, you can donate your old hair dryer to a charity shop or shelter. TheBritish Red Crossoften accepts small electrical items, including hair dryers. Be sure to clean out any dust from the rear filter and remove any hair from brush attachments before you pass it on.If your hair dryer is dead, don’t throw it in your normal bin. Take it to your local recycling centre, which you can find usingRecycle Your Electricals. Alternatively, Currys offers afree recycling servicein-store for electrical items, including those you didn’t buy from it.How to stop your hair dryer from damaging your hair?A common misconception is that heat protection is only necessary when using heat styling tools, such as hair straighteners or curlers, but the heat from your hair dryer can be just as damaging. Always prepare wet hair using a heat protection cream or spray before drying. According to Timperley, “this creates a protective barrier between the hair and heat, while helping to smooth and condition the strands.”“Avoid automatically reaching for the highest heat setting,” continues Timperley. “Prolonged exposure to excessive heat can weaken the hair cuticle, leading to dryness, frizz, breakage and a loss of shine over time.” As a rule, opt for the lower heat settings as long as they still allow you to achieve the style you want, and keep the dryer moving constantly to avoid frazzling small sections of hair.Unlike traditional heat stylers, styling with a hair dryer offers the best results when the hair is about 80% dry. Timperley warns, “once a section is fully dry, additional heat offers little styling benefit and significantly increases the risk of damage.” She recommends re-dampening any hair strands you’re unhappy with and restyling for the healthiest results.For more:The best hair masks for every hair typeDyson Supersonic Nural hair dryer reviewDyson Supersonic Travel hair dryer reviewThe best hair oils, capsules and serumsSarah Matthews is aconsumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling, hair removal,light therapyandskincaretools. In her spare time, you’ll find her lightly scolding her friends for not wearing SPF or getting sucked into a Vinted wormholeThis article was originally published on 26 August 2025.
