title: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade | Games | The Guardian
description: A string of distractions on the US government’s own website invite you to catch pixelated migrants – showing gaming’s potential to be nastily weaponised
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: A string of distractions on the US government’s own website invite you to catch pixelated migrants – showing gaming’s potential to be nastily weaponised
Content: Fascist fun … A screenshot from one of the White House Arcade games, Build The Wall.Photograph: The White HouseView image in fullscreenFascist fun … A screenshot from one of the White House Arcade games, Build The Wall.Photograph: The White HouseGamesThe Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcadeKeza MacDonaldA string of distractions on the US government’s own website invite you to catch pixelated migrants – showing gaming’s potential to be nastily weaponisedFri 4 Sep 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.41 EDTShareThe Trump White House on Thursday released ahorrible little propaganda arcadevia its website, a collection of nasty riffs on popular games. Wrapped in the cutesy, nostalgic aesthetic of early-90s pixel art, these mindless fascist diversions are harmless-looking, but their intent is stomach-turning: this is the appropriation of play in service of propaganda. It’s just the latest in a series of attempts from Trump’s administration to usevideo game memes and imageryto further its messaging.Having riffed on Halo and Pokémon in social media ads last year, inviting potential ICE recruits to “stop the flood” and “catch ’em all”, this time the administration has ripped off a series of recognisable games. Flappy Bill, perhaps the least gross, is a version of the old mobile hit Flappy Bird, except here you’re an eagle with a scroll in its claws. Supply Line could almost be an educational game about healthy food in schools, where you sort junk food off a conveyor belt destined for school lunches, except for some reason you play as a boxer who becomes more bloodied with every seed-oil containing, ultra-processed food item that you fail to punch into the garbage chute.Then come the really nasty ones: Build the Wall, which warps Tetris into a game where you must fortify the southern border to keep out “the coming horde”, and an evil little take on Snake where you patrol the Rio Grande, collecting brown people who then follow you around in orange jumpsuits. The final game is Trump Savings Tycoon, where you “fill your kids’Trump accounts” by catching bills and gold coins in a net. (The algae-beset Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is depicted in the foreground, inaccurately coloured in blue.)I have played all of them, so that you don’t have to. Build the Wall and Rio Run are actively disgusting, built around the naked dehumanisation of migrants, but mostly these games are just embarrassing. Like most things that come from the Trump White House communications team, they are mean-spirited, unimaginative and lazy. I have a strong suspicion that they are vibe-coded using AI, and I almost hope that they are, because the idea of humans spending their precious time on Earth making these horrid, half-arsed games makes me even sadder than playing them did.Anyone involved in the creation of the original games that the White House Arcade is ripping off is surely cringeing. Members of the original Halo team were moved to speak out on social media after the White House posted a picture ofTrump as Master Chieflast year; I wonder if Sega will have anything to say about this trailer, which opens with a digital chorus singing “Magaaaa”, soundtracking the sorry collection with music that sounds alotlike Sonic’s Green Hill Zone.The leveraging of video games and their imagery for political influence has been under way for some time, beginning perhaps with 2014’sGamergate, an online harassment movement that was stoked by Steve Bannon and far-right website Breitbart. Trump, alongside other rightwing regimes, has had an enormous head start on this front. “The use of video game content, culture and aesthetics for communication is a feature of Trump’s White House, rather than a bug, because much of the modern political right emerged from toxic game communities,” says George Osborn, author of Power Play: Video Games, Politics and the Battle for Global Influence.“Activists who shaped the Gamergate movement have become an established part of the political right … Until now, it seemed to be restricted to social media posting.I estimated that video game-coded posts had approximately twice the reach of a regular White House Instagram post, suggesting it was able to simultaneously rile up audiences offended by its post and delight supporters. But the deployment of an arcade on its website marks a change of course … Now, it appears that Trump’s White House is ready to use games to begin to try to win over audiences – escalating from appropriating video game culture to ensnaring the medium itself for its own ends.”Artists and activists have been using video games to put across political messages for a very long time. I have played games about escaping war-torn countries; about examining the paperwork of desperate people at the border of a fictional eastern bloc country; about running a dictatorship or taking one down. Governments, however, are new players in this space.These games, in line with the Trump administration’s wider social media and communications strategy, are culture-war shitposting. They are almost entirely valueless, and exist more to rile us up than to actually persuade anyone of anything. If we attach too much outrage to them, we are being drawn into someone else’s game; it is deeply unlikely that a round of Rio Run is about to radicalise anyone who isn’t already fully on board with Trump’s whole schtick. But at a time when the Saudi Arabian wealth fund now co-ownsone of the world’s biggest game publishersalongside an investment firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, gaming’s propagandist potential should not be a blind spot.Explore more on these topicsGamescommentShareReuse this content

title: Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar | Games | The Guardian
description: As one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousands
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousands
Content: Single Pokémon cards for sale, locked in a cabinet.Photograph: Daniella LucasView image in fullscreenSingle Pokémon cards for sale, locked in a cabinet.Photograph: Daniella LucasGamesThieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soarAs one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousandsDaniella LucasFri 4 Sep 2026 05.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePokémon’s success over the last 30 years has seen it grow from a much-loved Game Boy classic, to a world-dominating brand with TV shows, spin-off games, toys and even a theme park. The trading card game is a huge part of that, with more than85bn cardsprinted over its lifetime, and the appetite for them shows no signs of slowing down. Packs get snapped up after release so quickly it’s nowalmost impossible to find them in shops, and a booming resale market is driving the hobby into murky waters.One card recently sold for aneye-watering £12m, and an increasing number of people have gotten into the collecting business on the hunt for huge profits, leading toa rise in thefts targeting card shops. More recently though, some small businesses have reported that their sales have been hit by thieves targeting envelopes within Royal Mail, leading to thousands in lost revenue.Ben Thyer, owner of Bath TCG – a card specialist store in the Bath area, is one of those affected. “We always get the odd parcel going missing, but because it was sporadic, we put that down to unfortunate incidents,” Thyer tells the Guardian. “Then [in late July], we had a message [from a customer] with pictures of a cut-open envelope, and the cards were missing. Then there was a second, and then a third, and then there were seven – all of them from the same batch shipped on the same day. We asked for images from each person, and every envelope had been Sellotaped … we don’t use Sellotape because we have brand new envelopes, and we use our own labels over the seals. It’s clear someone had done it deliberately.”View image in fullscreenBath TCG - an independent shop specialising in trading card games.Photograph: Daniella LucasThe images, seen by the Guardian, show that the mailed envelopes were tampered with in the exact same way. Thyer considers it clear that this was a targeted theft rather than a coincidence. Fortunately, those particular cards weren’t of high value, but he has since had to close down online card sales, considering the risk of theft and damaged reputation to his business to be too high. By stopping those sales he has now lost out on £4,000-6,000 of potential revenue, a huge amount for a small business.Bath TCG is not the only card sales business to be affected, and the issue is not just affecting Pokémon cards. Daniel Stack, director of Mana Rock Games – a specialist in selling Magic: The Gathering cards – has also had issues withRoyal Mailitems going missing. His business is also based in Bath and was affected over similar dates to Bath TCG’s.“I realised it was theft when two customers in different parts of the country sent me pictures of their packages already open with the contents missing, within minutes of each other,” Stack said. “We’d previously had one sent to France turn up the same way a couple of weeks before, but I put it down to the buyer taking a bit of a chance that I’d have no way to hold them to account for pretending there had been an issue. In total we’ve had about £120-worth stolen so far – we had previously sent over 1,200 orders without any issues.”View image in fullscreenSome of BathTCG’s stock.Photograph: Daniella LucasStack also halted online sales for a week, costing him £500 in revenue. Other sellers in the area havementioned similar problemsto him. Unfortunately, as most card businesses in the UK useCardMarketto sell online, it’s the buyer who picks the delivery method, and most often they use Royal Mail services. Cards are often sent in distinctive hard-backed envelopes to protect the contents, often with shop branding on stickers or seals.Royal Mail is investigating the issue and liaising with the affected businesses. A spokesperson told the Guardian: “The safety and security of mail is a top priority and we take any reports of theft very seriously. We investigate concerns thoroughly and take action where necessary, including working with law enforcement.” Investigations are still ongoing; in the meantime, businesses must choose between risking theft and damaged reputation for their stores, or halting online sales and losing revenue.With a new, highly sought-after 30th anniversaryPokémoncard set due to release this month, retailers are already anticipating an increase in scalper and reselling activity, leading to even more potential for thieves to target those selling cards online. We asked the Pokémon Company for comment on how they’re dealing with increased demand and the rise in thefts, but they have yet to respond.Explore more on these topicsGamesPokémonCrimeRoyal MailnewsShareReuse this content

title: How much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at all | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: Such is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for voters, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: Such is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for voters, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Donald Trump at a rally and campaign event at Coastal Carolina University, South Carolina, 10 February 2024.Photograph: Randall Hill/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at a rally and campaign event at Coastal Carolina University, South Carolina, 10 February 2024.Photograph: Randall Hill/EPAOpinionDonald TrumpHow much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at allJonathan FreedlandSuch is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for votersFri 4 Sep 2026 12.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.08 EDTShareWhat is Donald Trump playing at? If it’s true that the best way of understanding the behaviour of an organisation is to assume it’scontrolled by a secret cabalof its enemies, perhaps that same logic extends to the current conduct of the president of the United States. Maybe he secretly wants Republicans to lose the looming midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in the US for the next two years and for whichthe first postal ballotswere sent out today.That’s not as mad a theory as it sounds. Indeed, there are at least two reasons why Trump might either be unbothered by Republican defeat in November or even covertly desire it. We’ll come to those, but let’s start with a pattern of behaviour that is hard to explain as anything other than calculated self-sabotage.At the centre of it is the single act that is already defining Trump’s second term: his reckless, failed war of choice against Iran. No matter how many times he declares mission accomplished or claims to have destroyed the Iranian military or to have reopened the strait of Hormuz, the facts keep telling a different story. In the past week, the two sides shifted from an economic standoffback to a shooting war, with the US firing on Iranian targets that included a wedding party, killing four, and Tehran striking out all over the neighbourhood, hitting Iraq, Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain.The impact on US voters is severe, felt most directly through rising petrol prices and grocery bills. But look atthe graphmeasuring the cost the US government must pay to borrow money: it’s been a steep upward climb since 28 February, the day the war began,hitting a fresh high on Tuesday. For consumers, that rise translates into an expected jump in interest rates. It means that many of those casting ballots are likely to be doing so just as they start paying more on their credit card bills and mortgages. Given that Trump was elected in November 2024 on a promise to bring down inflation, it’s hard to think of a worse environment for a governing party about to face the voters’ verdict. And that’s before you consider the disenchantment of the Maga faithful, who thought the whole point of Trump was an end to forever wars in the Middle East.And yet, Iran may not even be the most electorally damaging of Trump’s foreign adventures. He is, and it would once have been absurd to write this sentence, leading his country into a state of war with … Canada. It’s easy to laugh at the petty gestures, such as Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America, a move shamefully followed, and therefore endorsed, byApple and Googlein their map apps. But the economic confrontation is serious – and seriously damaging to Republicans’ electoral prospects.For which US states are hit hardest by Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” response to Trump’s tariffs? Why, it’sMichigan, Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Texas, all of which just happen to have key senate contests this year. Republican candidates in those states now have to explain why a crucial and previously friendly export market – Canada takes nearly a third of Iowa’s exports, for example – has suddenly turned icy.What’s odd is that Trump’s trade wars are also wars of choice, and they are hurting especially badly what should be a reliable Republican constituency: farmers. Take Iowa: Democrats have not won a senate seat in that farming state for nearly 20 years, yet now, thanks to Trump’s tariffs, they have a genuine shot.Still, perhaps the most egregious illustration of Trump’s apparent determination to ruin Republican chances in the midterms is his support for datacentres. Few issues have seen their salience rise so quickly and in such a clear direction: almost overnight, they have become objects of fear and loathing across the country and across the political spectrum, withseven in 10 Americanssaying they would not want one anywhere near where they live. Even among Republicans,there is deep concernover their environmental impact, energy consumption and water use. For others, datacentres have become a lightning rod for a broader anxiety over AI and what it may do to our jobs and our lives. Either way, they are kryptonite to voters.So where does Trump stand? “The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want data centres is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,”the president postedon Monday. In that remark, he not only put himself at odds with most US voters, he insulted them too.It’s almost a talent, this ability of Trump’s to land on the wrong side of so-called 80/20 issues, siding with one-fifth of the electorate against the rest. Likewise, strong majorities oppose his vanity projects, whetherdemolishing the East Wingof the White House to build a ballroom or putting his signature on the dollar bill, yet he persists not only in doing them but in talking about them constantly.And all the while, he has hobbled his party by endorsing radioactively unpopular candidates. Few politicians in the US are more tainted than Ken Paxton, who as attorney general of Texas wasimpeached by his fellow Republicanson a long list of charges that included bribery and abuse of public trust. Yet who did Trump back as the Republicans’ senate choice in Texas? As a result, now even thatred-state stronghold is shaky.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higher | Sina ToossiRead morePut it all together, and these look like the actions of a man who has no fear of the blue wave that seems to be coming and who could not care less if it sweeps away the Republicans’ current majorities in Congress. That’s curious, given how useful it has been for Trump to have Capitol Hill serve as a rubber stamp that, combined with a largely pliant supreme court, has allowed him to rule with the scarcely fettered power of a would-be autocrat. What could explain the insouciance?One answer is that Congress’s most potent weapon – the power of subpoena and investigation – holds no terror for Trump because he knows that the House and Senate have no means to enforce their will. They have no police or troops at their command. They can issue their writs and summonses, and he will simply ignore them – comforted by the near-blanket immunity he has already been granted by the supreme court. If Congress goes after his aides and advisers, he will instruct them to follow his lead, on the promise of a comprehensive presidential pardon protecting them from any and all legal consequences. The only real weapon Congress has – impeachment and removal from office – he knows they will never use. If senate Republicans could acquit him after the 6 January insurrection, as they did, he knows they will never vote to convict him of anything, no matter how great the crime.But that only goes so far. It explains why Trump does not fear Republican defeat in November, but not why he would actively seek it. For that, one has to look into the abyss that passes for the president’s soul. The bestselling new bookRegime Change, by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, spells it out: “If Republicans were wiped out in the 2026 midterm elections, or in 2028, he could simply boast that they couldn’t win without him” on the ballot paper. Such is Trump’s narcissism, he will take an epic Republican defeat in two months’ time not as a repudiation, but as a compliment. And, it seems, he is doing all he can to earn it.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS midterm elections 2026US politicsUS economycommentShareReuse this content

title: Tennessee is about to execute its first woman since 1819. Her case raises troubling questions | Austin Sarat | The Guardian
description: Christa Pike’s planned execution is emblematic of America’s broken death penalty system
Author: Austin Sarat
Headline: Christa Pike’s planned execution is emblematic of America’s broken death penalty system
Content: ‘Like many who end up on death row, Pike had an unspeakably difficult childhood.’Photograph: APView image in fullscreen‘Like many who end up on death row, Pike had an unspeakably difficult childhood.’Photograph: APOpinionTennesseeTennessee is about to execute its first woman since 1819. Her case raises troubling questionsAustin SaratChrista Pike’s planned execution is emblematic of America’s broken death penalty systemFri 4 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.35 EDTShareOn 30 September, the state of Tennesseeplansto put Christa Pike to death. Shewouldbe the third person brought to the death chamber in the Volunteer state this year, one of which was stopped after it was botched.Shewouldjoin 17 others who have been put to death there since 1960. None of them were women.In fact in all of US history, only 578 womenhave been executed, a little more than 3% of our country’s total. The lastone wasAmber McLaughlin, killed in Missouri in 2024. If Pike is killed, it would be Tennessee’sfirst execution of a womansince 1819.So, on the face of it, the fate that awaits Pike is unusual. But on second glance, it displays many of the hallmarks of America’s broken death penalty system.The scourge of the death penalty hangs over America | Austin SaratRead moreLike many who end up on death row, Pikehad an unspeakably difficultchildhood. She was raped and abused and, when not being subject to such horrors, was abandoned and neglected by her parents.So it was not surprising when Pike turned to violence, and with two others committed a murder when she was still a teenager. As the psychologist and trauma expert Bethany Brandexplains: “At 18 years old, her immature, traumatized brain made her exceptionally vulnerable to impulses and extremely poor decisions … Unmedicated and untreated, she was not able to put the ‘brakes on’ her bipolar- and trauma-triggered emotions.”When it came to her trial, Pike’s lawyer failed to present mitigating evidence that was readily available to him and to uncover any new mitigating circumstances. As the professor Deborah Dennoexplains: “Specifically, counsel chose not to present defendant’s social history evidence … claiming that the … materials in particular contained double-edged information,” namely information that might have hurt as well as helped her.And now as she awaits her execution, shehas legitimate concernsthat, given her distinctive medical and emotional problems, when the state tries to kill her, she will face a torturous and cruel death.But so far, courts havechosen to look the other way.If they continue to do so, Pike will take her place among America’s relatively exclusive club of female execution victims. It is such a club because while womencommitabout one in eight homicides in the United States, they tend to commit murders that fall below the threshold of crimes that prosecutors, judges and jurors consider to be the worst of the worst.As the professor Elizabeth Rappaportargues: “Two thirds of women who kill, kill family members and lovers … [and] [t]hese crimes almost never result in death sentences, regardless of the sex of the killer.”Pike was obviously not one of those killers. And her victim was murdered in a gruesome manner.A local television station in Knoxville,Tennessee, saysprosecutors claim Pike “tortured and killed” her victim because Pike thought she was trying to steal Pike’s boyfriend.This crime is reminiscent in its brutality to the onecommittedby Karla Faye Tucker in Texas in 1983. She and her co-defendant killed their victims with a pickaxe.Tucker became something of a celebrity after having a sincere and profound religious conversion on death row. Texas Public Radioreportsthat her case “attracted national attention by many of America’s top televangelists, including Pat Robertson. He appealed to the Texas Governor George W. Bush … to commute Tucker’s sentence,” something that Bush refused to do.Tucker was put to death in 1998,makingher the first woman executed in Texas since 1863.Fast forward to January 2021, when the federal government under Donald TrumpexecutedLisa Montgomery. Here, again the crime for which she was convicted was particularly gruesome.Alabama wants to execute a man by nitrogen hypoxia. That is cruel | Austin SaratRead moreIn 2004, Montgomerycrossedstate lines “ostensibly to purchase a puppy from Bobbie Jo Stinnett, a 23-year-old dog breeder who was eight months pregnant. Instead, Montgomery strangled her, cut her fetus from her womb and tried to pass the surviving baby off as her own.”Like Christa Pike, Montgomery“had brain damage and severe mental illness that was exacerbated by a lifetime of abuse, including child sex trafficking, gang rape and physical abuse largely at the hands of family members”.She was killed by lethal injection, making her just the fourth woman ever executed by the federal government. Itput a woman to deathfor the first time in 1865, when it hanged Mary Surratt for her role in the assassination of Abraham Lincoln.At the time,according to the National Museum of Women’s History, “most people, including the military judges who issued the guilty verdict, could not believe the United States government was going to execute awoman.”There is a bit of that sentiment reflected in the news coverage of Pike’s case. Even as this society seeks to achieve gender equality, thereisstill something unsettling at the prospect of putting a woman to death.In Pike’s case, what should truly be unsettling is not her gender, but rather the prospect of putting to death someone whose crime was as much the product of society’s failure as it was of her criminal intent. For women as well as men, capital punishment offers no solution to the problems that give rise to the most serious crimes.Austin Sarat, associate dean of the faculty and William Nelson Cromwell professor of jurisprudence and political science at Amherst College, is the author of Gruesome Spectacles: Botched Executions and America’s Death PenaltyExplore more on these topicsTennesseeOpinionCapital punishmentGendercommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: Tom Tugendhat is a serious politician. What’s he doing in a Reform-lite Tory frontbench? | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Want to see how small the gene pool of Tory talent is? I give you Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor. Also this week: Starmer’s Fomo, and telly wars
Author: John Crace
Headline: Want to see how small the gene pool of Tory talent is? I give you Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor. Also this week: Starmer’s Fomo, and telly wars
Content: Kemi Badenoch, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately and shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith in Westminster on Thursday.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately and shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith in Westminster on Thursday.Photograph: Yui Mok/PADigested weekPoliticsDigested week: Tom Tugendhat is a serious politician. What’s he doing in a Reform-lite Tory frontbench?John CraceWant to see how small the gene pool of Tory talent is? I give you Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor. Also this week: Starmer’s Fomo, and telly warsFri 4 Sep 2026 07.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTShareMondayIt’s the end of summer and Kemi Badenoch chose to mark the occasion with a reshuffle of her shadow cabinet. Her aim is apparently to get the Tories match fit in case Andy Burnham calls an early general election, but the vibes are much more rearranging the deckchairs on a sinking ship. After all, when the gene pool of talent is that small, there’s not much you can do. James Cleverly got the ball rollingby announcinghe was planning to be the Conservative candidate for London mayor in two years’ time. He may have his work cut out. London is a liberal, multicultural city and unlikely to be won over by a party giving up on net zero and the European convention on human rights.Cleverly’s replacement as shadow housing secretary is Katie Lam, who was only elected two years ago but has been desperate to attract attention by consistently saying the most offensive thing she can think of. This may not end well. Priti Patel’s departure as foreign secretary was no great surprise as she has always been a liability, but Kemi’s decision to appoint Tom Tugendhat in her place did raise eyebrows. Tom has always been from the One Nation side of the party and Kemi didn’t seem to realise that when he said: “If I had known Kemi was this good I wouldn’t have stood against her,” he had merely been joking. He is at least a serious politician in the way Priti never was, but you also can’t help wondering if he is really signed up to Kemi’s Reform-lite Tory agenda. Still, Tom has never been one to shy away from going to war with anyone, so he and Kemi will have something in common.That just leaves the change of shadow chancellor. It goes without saying that Mel Stride had always been endearingly hopeless, but thechoice of Andrew Griffithto take over is bewildering. The Tories always like to play up Griffith’s career in business, but what the rest of the country will be focusing on is that he was the co-author and defender of Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-budget. So maybe his economic judgment is not that sound after all. It should also be remembered that Griffith was Boris Johnson’s “net zero business champion” in 2020; something he and Kemi are also hoping to forget. Maybe the key to understanding Griffith is that he is just a career opportunist who doesn’t really believe in anything. In which case he may fit in just fine.View image in fullscreenTom Tugendhat, the new shadow foreign secretary.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersTuesdayOne politician who won’t be hurrying back to Westminster for the start of the new parliamentary session isKeir Starmer. He has just announced he is standing down as an MP. The only recent former prime minister to remain a backbencher and regularly turn up to debates in the Commons was Theresa May and she cut a somewhat sad figure. Her attendance was impressive but she never appeared to have any friends. Just sitting by herself, lost in her own thoughts. What Keir is thinking now is anyone’s guess. We don’t all get the summer we were hoping for – I certainly didn’t – but Starmer’s must have been borderline surreal. It must be so hard for a prime minister to learn to switch off. One day you’re the centre of attention with constant demands on your time, the next you’re a virtual ghost. A person of little importance. Most former prime ministers have a tormented shadow to them, even years after they have left Downing Street. As if they still can’t believe that the voters or their own MPs have rejected them. Keir will have been expecting to have spent the last six weeks on constant alert. Dealing with world events and travelling the country to convince everyone he was actually working. A prime minister needs to be visible, or their enemies assume they are skiving. Instead, his phone will have gone quiet with no one making any demands on his time. The fear of missing out must have been intense.He might have wished Burnham well in public but in private he wouldn’t have been too sad if Andy was struggling just a little bit. Just about all we did hear about Keir during the break was that he had donated a copy of Tom Baldwin’s biography of himself to the No 10 library. Which felt, somehow a little desperate. Somewhat tragic. Why not break with tradition and leave a work of fiction? Rebecca; or The Age of Innocence. Something that just oozes class. But instead, like many prime ministers, he couldn’t resist giving a rose-tinted version of his deeds that will never be read by anyone. It will survive to collect dust. Which only goes to show that with many politicians, it really is all about them.View image in fullscreenWe don’t all get the summer we were hoping for – but Keir Starmer’s must have been borderline surreal.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesWednesdayMost of us go through life collecting bits and pieces. What others might call clutter. Items that shape the identities of our homes. Starting with the basics. Tables, chairs, beds, chest of drawers, kitchenware, that sort of thing. Then books, televisions and sound systems. But what happens to all this when we die? How much will remain? In my mother’s case, the answer was almost nothing.My mum died last year at the age of 101, her last seven years spent in a care home as her Alzheimer’s prevented her from living on her own. So the house she and my father – he died in 1999 – had bought for their retirement years earlier had to be sold to pay for her care. My sisters and I spent several weekends going through the contents prior to the sale, trying to work out what to keep and what to do with the rest. Almost everything went to a house-clearance firm. We had no use for the beds or the furniture because we all had our own already and didn’t have the space for any more. It was all rather melancholic. There were several items my mum had inherited from her parents that she had always said were quite valuable. We got an expert in who told us they were all cheap reproductions. My grandmother had been ripped off. All we kept were a couple of pictures, some personal effects and a few small items to furnish her new room at the care home.When she died, we had 10 days to clear out her room and almost all of this went too. Her clothes, her chair and a few books that she had never read because of her dementia. The only things that really remained of value to us were her photograph albums. These were her memories. The last surviving physical links not just between us and her, but between her and our father, between her and her parents and grandparents. Many of these photos I had never seen while she had been alive.In generations to come, not even these will remain when people die. Everyone’s photos will be on their phone or laptop. My mum never held with either. We gave her a mobile about 20 years ago but she always refused to use it so there was no point ringing it. So more than a century of a life well lived reduced to almost nothing. Just a few precious keepsakes that mean everything but are of little financial value. And when my sisters and I die, our mum will die again. Dust to dust.ThursdayView image in fullscreenSign reading ‘Lake Ontario, now and always’, unveiled by Ontario premier Doug Ford.Photograph: Carlos Osorio/ReutersThe naming wars have been hotting up. First Donald Trump declared he was renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. Then, during one of his regular hissy fits with the Canadians, hechanged the name of Lake Ontarioto Lake America by presidential decree. You can sense a theme emerging. And earlier this week he was openly fantasising of calling the strait of Hormuz the strait of Trump. Just imagine having so much narcissism and so little imagination.Not so long ago, the Donald came close to calling Greenland America, so there’s no way of really knowing where this one is going to end. Why not call the Atlantic Trump Ocean and the Pacific America Ocean? It’s odds on that he will demand that part of the moon will be named after him when Nasa lands astronauts back on the lunar surface in a few years’ time. Weirdly, many Americans think this behaviour is quite normal.In a spectacular display of presidential brown-nosing, Google even marks the changes on its maps for a US audience. Google Lake Ontario in the UK andyou get Lake Ontario (Lake America). You’d have thought a better response would be to just ignore the president and wait till he went away. Canada has tried being rational. It explained the lake had been called Ontario since the 17th century, long before the USA and Canada existed in their current forms, and was an Iroquoian word meaning “beautiful lake”. All this was far too complicated for The Donald. So now the Canadians have upped their game byputting up giant Lake Ontario signsby the lake, only for Trump to post a video of himself kicking over the sign and replacing it with Lake America. It’s like dealing with a five-year-old.So maybe we’d all be better off treating him like one. At least we’d all have more fun. The Canadians could start by renaming the US half of Lake Superior as Lake Inferior. Mark Carney could sign that off in a day and then Google would be obliged to make the changes on its maps. Maybe. But we could all join in. Burnham could rename the US the United States of Greater England. Pretend independence had always been a big mistake. The perfect 250th anniversary present.FridayView image in fullscreenSuranne Jones as Amy Silva in Vigil.Photograph: Mark Mainz/BBC/World ProductionsThis time of year always makes me feel depressed. The days getting shorter, the weather colder. Most years, this can be offset a little by the start of the Premier League football season. This autumn, not so much. Despite having spent more than a third of a billion pounds on new players, Spurs are at the bottom of the table. Played two, lost two. Goals scored, nil. At least you have to admire the consistency. Yet again we have a manager who is calling for patience, that it will come right in the end. Maybe it will, but it doesn’t feel like it at the moment.Still, on the plus side, we have the new autumn TV schedules with the broadcasters having waited until we had all stopped enjoying ourselves outdoors before giving us something half decent to watch. The current onscreen battle in our house is between the BBC and ITV.Vigilversus Trigger Point. Suranne Jones vVicky McClure. Two dramas on to their third and fourth series respectively that are dominated by badass women tasked with saving the world. We are a lot further into Trigger Point than we are into Vigil, but that’s only because ITV has put the whole series up on its streaming site. And I am loving both in a particularly mindless kind of way. As much for the nonsense as the drama. The entire plot of Vigil depends on the security services turning to the same two Scottish policewomen, who just happen to be in a relationship and have seamless childcare, every time the country is on the verge of war. We are currently both in Scotland and Svalbard, where everyone seems to have a secret to hide.Trigger Point is even wilder. Two bombs go off in central London and no one seems to bat an eye, as all attention is on the one that Vicky has defused. Almost all bombs seem to be neutralised by cutting the red wire. If someone else tries to defuse a bomb then they will almost certainly get blown up. Meanwhile there is a member of the security services who couldn’t be overacting to look suspicious any harder if she tried and no one seems to notice. Thank God for Vicky, or we’d all be screwed.Digested week in picturesView image in fullscreen‘Read my lips. We will never start a foreign war.’Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/APView image in fullscreen‘You’ll never believe who is paying for all this.’Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreen‘That’s one in the eye for the monarchy.’Photograph: Adrian Dennis/WPA Pool/ShutterstockExplore more on these topicsPoliticsDigested weekKemi BadenochConservativesKeir StarmerDonald TrumpCanadacommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s time for Mark Zuckerberg to resign from Meta | Joan Donovan | The Guardian
description: The CEO is the throughline in a history of billion-dollar blunders that have caused real harm, culminating in last week’s settlement
Author: Joan Donovan
Headline: The CEO is the throughline in a history of billion-dollar blunders that have caused real harm, culminating in last week’s settlement
Content: ‘It is clear that this latest settlement is the harbinger of a punishing future ahead for Zuckerberg’s businesses.’Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It is clear that this latest settlement is the harbinger of a punishing future ahead for Zuckerberg’s businesses.’Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesOpinionMark ZuckerbergIt’s time for Mark Zuckerberg to resign from MetaJoan DonovanThe CEO is the throughline in a history of billion-dollar blunders that have caused real harm, culminating in last week’s settlementFri 4 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 16.11 EDTShareLast week, Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook,agreed to a settlementof up to $18bn after dozens of US states accused it of harming children with addictive products. The settlement’sregulatory implicationsfor social media will affect every user, far beyond teens.But if Meta is truly interested in prioritizing the safety of users, the board should request the resignation ofMark Zuckerbergand restructure to put safety above profit.The settlement does little to resolve the scientific question about the degree to which social media is addictive, but instead is the culmination of a battle launched by journalists and independent researchers in 2016 that focused on the digital design of disinformation campaigns powering Brexit in the UK and the US presidential election. Zuckerberg is the one throughline in Meta’s history of billion-dollar blunders that have hurt real people.For the past 15 years, I have studied how science and technology produces social change, forbetterandworse. As the founder ofThe Critical Internet Studies Institute, I lead a team investigating harms caused by emerging technologies. We educate practitioners and professionals about the manifest and latent features of new technologies,warts and all. In 2020, Itestified to Congressabout misinformation as “secondhand smoke”. My comments came weeks after testimony from Facebook’s former director of monetization, who likened the design process of making Meta’s engagement optimization algorithms to the ways tobacco companies made cigarettes more addictive.An $18bn settlement – and Zuckerberg barely blinked. The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soon | Jonathan FreedlandRead moreIn a series of op-eds, congressional briefings and research papers, I extended the tobacco case study to show howcultural attitudesabout smoking as a personal luxury were upended by concepts such as secondhand smoke, and scientific confirmation that tobacco increases risk of cancer, whose true costs were passed on to families, insurance companies, and employers who lost time and resources to combatting smoking. The public health solution did not go as far as to ban smoking, but limited the areas where smoking was allowed, set an age limit for possession, made companies pay for public education campaigns on the hazards of the product, and most importantly, put products behind grumpy cashiers who validate IDs to purchase. Public health campaigns and warning labels were also important strategies.Similarly, social media companies make all kinds of critical decisions about how to deliver content to your feed. Some of those features are algorithmically engineered to increase the likelihood of users remaining on the app.The settlement comes withdesign restrictions; teen accounts are limited to two hours per day, no access from midnight to 6am, and no notifications from school bell to bell. Teen accounts must be linked to a parent’s accounts, amid stronger age verification. It’s still unclear how that will be implemented, but it promises to become a privacy nightmare. While these interventions limit time for 13-18 year olds, they do little to address contentious content, such as how drugs, sex and gambling end up algorithmically recommended.It is clear that this latest settlement is the harbinger of a punishing future ahead for Zuckerberg’s businesses. Meta has litigated a number of issues, while avoiding any serious regulation on content moderation (cost center) or advertising (profit center). Enforcing these new rules for teens will increase costs. Meta has faced billions in settlements or fines for harms ranging fromfailing to protectuser privacyto a2018 security breachto abhorrent outcomes foryoung people’s mental health. Meta has also caused unremunerated harms to other groups, includingamplifying hate speechagainst Rohingya in Myanmar and hosting and algorithmically promoting rampantmedical misinformationand conspiracy theories leading to toxic poisoning and vaccine hesitancy that the World Health Organization labelled an “infodemic”.Zuckerberg’s leadership failures directly led to well-documented damage to civic life, democracy, and global mental and physical health and wellbeing, especially that of young people. Since founding Facebook in 2004, Zuckerberg has been in constant litigation over a number of issues related to ownership and stock early on, which is where he first started to employ a PR strategy todelay, deny and deflectany issues that arise from executives’ decisions to put profit over users’ health. Meta executives lined their pockets off of the tragic and devastating amplification of hate, harassment and incitement.Meanwhile, it has produced a cadre of whistleblowers, with more to come now that it’s clear these executives’ choices led to “real-world harm”, a Silicon Valley term of art that separates cyberspace from meatspace.The settlement comes on the heels of last week’s damning hearings, where one of those whistleblowers, Arturo Béjar,boldly stated: “You just cannot trust Mark Zuckerberg with kids.” Béjar was a lead on safety at Instagram when his teen daughter was the victim of unwanted sexist harassment and profanity on Instagram. Because of his role at Meta, he had real data for accurate measurements of harms on Instagram including the effectiveness of different algorithmic interventions on growth, engagement and user experience.An $18bn settlement is a drop in the ocean for Meta – but the tide will still come for it | Chris Stokel-WalkerRead moreBéjar estimated he hadmet with Zuckerbergmore than 100 times before becoming a whistleblower. Many whistleblowers’ stories begin with an ardent attempt to fix the problems through the correct channels and a refusal from higher-ups to tackle the issue. Ironically, whistleblowers tend to be rule followers who become increasingly indignant as their concerns are met with a workplace culture of ambivalence or advance compliance.In December 2023, I experienced intense professional blowback in academia after obtaining documents culled from another whistleblower, Frances Haugen, which I intended to publish in a publicly accessible database. I acquired the documents legally and used my expertise to help tech insiders, journalists, researchers and Washington DC staffers understand what the Haugen documents did, and importantly did not, say about Meta’s liability and knowledge of product problems. But the message was clear: Meta, then called Facebook,knew of the damage Instagramcaused to teenage girls.And yet, through every scandal, Zuckerberg’s net worth has climbed to nearly$200bn, according to Forbes. Fines mean nothing to those with wealth like his, so the first step to safeguard society is to give Meta a fresh start without Zuckerberg’s influence on future products. His vision for “a future for everyone” is an incredibly facile utopia, where AI agents run your life and you just slop your way through it.Beyond the courts, Meta could triage the situation by calling for Zuckerberg to voluntarily resign. Ushering in hope for the future of technology requires changing Meta’s leadership now, so that the future is collectively imagined and built upon a new reputation and commitment.Zuckerberg does not deserve another chance simply because he can afford it. We as a society ultimately pay for his mistakes. Now is the time for shareholders to speak up and push back on Zuckerberg’s dominance and control.Joan Donovan is an assistant professor of journalism at Boston University who studies how technology impacts society. She is the founder of theCritical Internet Studies Institute, where she leads a project on political violence and social movementsThis article was amended on 4 September 2026. An earlier version described Facebook’s former director of marketing as an executive.Explore more on these topicsMark ZuckerbergOpinionMetaFacebookSocial networkingcommentShareReuse this content

title: As AI madness encroaches, we need human connection more than ever. But we’ll have to fight for it | Van Badham | The Guardian
description: We don’t want the isolating, automated outputs tech lords are selling us. We’re yearning for a shared frame of reference
Author: Van Badham
Headline: We don’t want the isolating, automated outputs tech lords are selling us. We’re yearning for a shared frame of reference
Content: Elon Musk, the trillionaire owner of social media platform X, has mooted making an ‘AI Odyssey’. Van Badham writes that as AI regulation is debated, we should ‘take a wild, political stand for authentic preference over forced consumption’.Photograph: Anton Dos Ventos/AlamyView image in fullscreenElon Musk, the trillionaire owner of social media platform X, has mooted making an ‘AI Odyssey’. Van Badham writes that as AI regulation is debated, we should ‘take a wild, political stand for authentic preference over forced consumption’.Photograph: Anton Dos Ventos/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)As AI madness encroaches, we need human connection more than ever. But we’ll have to fight for itVan BadhamWe don’t want the isolating, automated outputs tech lords are selling us. We’re yearning for a shared frame of referenceFri 4 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 20.16 EDTShareIhave a cherished memory of a family trip to the movies. In the Australian tradition, we bought choc-top ice-creams, chattered through pre-show trailers and a hush fell on the full house as the movie started.It wasChristopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, on film, only a couple of weeks ago, months after its release.In an AI-supercharged world of algorithmic recommendations and atomised cultural space, I’ve come to suspect The Odyssey’s ongoingpopular appealis no longer its Greeks with gifts, or superstar director.It’s the increasingly rare opportunity to share even a single cultural reference with other people. Despite our human instinct for interaction, we live in a global moment wherehealth authoritiesbelieve social isolation is an epidemic.Yet in the same city of my fun night at the cinema, this week it wasnewsthat Australia’s Macquarie University has introduced an AI chatbot into the weekly teaching of two mandatory psychology subjects.Lost jobs, inequality, rogue agents: why are we accepting oligarchs’ AI agenda? | Robert ReichRead moreDisplacing human beings from what should be stable jobs isn’t the only outrage here.As someone whose dainty, addled, depressive brain obliges tender care from trained professionals, Macquarie, please record this data in your feedback corpus: I cannot trust or validate the insight of a supposed expert whose contact with adult realities has been compromised by being taught by a machine.If I want a chatbot to talk me out of a panic spiral, I’ll consult it within my already-paid-for subscription service whenI’m freaking out at midnightlike a normal person, thank you.Far more positive social impacts can be measured from Australia’s academics’ union, this week takingstrike actionat the University of Sydney against the encroach of AI madness.“We want enforceable protections against AI being used to cut jobs, intensify workloads, undermine academic and professional judgement, or replace work and human interaction that are fundamental to a university,” said the NTEU’s Vince Caughley.Solidarity, brother. My gratitude extends to Australia’s writers’ union, theAWG, as well as itsentertainment and communications union, theUS actors’ unionandWriters Guild of America,Canada’s performance union,Germany’s service workers union and actors’ union, an alliance ofItaly’s dubbing unions and all industrial organisations striking AI-use agreements not merely to protect their members’ workplace rights, but to remain on the side of public opinion.Because studies repeatedly suggest consumers don’t want the isolating, automated outputs being sold to them.double quotation markWe missed the boat on regulating social media. Nazis, radicalisation and deadly misinformation sailed inIn the world of commercial literature,one study found“consumers perceived human-written books more positively in all investigated dimensions than ones written by AI”. While other researchers have found the intrusion of AI titles to Amazon is now as many as 20% of its ebook catalogue,the same studyshows they only made up 12% of sales and 10% of bestsellers in their genre. A considerable underperformance.In music, global consultancy Bain learned that62% of consumerswould not engage with music generated by AI.French streaming service Deezer revealed fully AI-generated music constituted as much as 18% of its daily uploads but amounted only to about 0.5% of listening – whilethe Guardian reportedthat up to 70% of those streams appeared fraudulent.Bain found the only majority tolerance for AI content was in video games: 71%did not want AI in their books, and 65% did not want it in their news and magazines.Similarly, in sales, studies show that telling customers beforehand they are engaging with chatbots in outbound callsreduces purchase rates by 79.7%. In 2025,Deloittelearned 74% of customers preferred human interaction even for routine banking questions. In anotherinternational 2025 study, chatbots were the least popular form of customer service engagement: a mere 8% of respondents chose them voluntarily.Consumer sentiment backlash is registering faster than the slow pace of democratic governance. Governments have struggled with the speed of tech encroach, with regulation lagging in the face of relentless economic and political pressure from the world’s mostaggressively overcapitalised, cashed-updipshits who own all this stuff. Australia is considering its approaches to AI regulation, butit does not have it yet.‘If you build something vastly smarter than you, it better be on your side’: can we stop AI from deceiving us?Read moreFriends, we missed the boat on regulating social media. Nazis, radicalisation, deadly health misinformation andaddictive and dangerous productssailed in.As more comprehensive AI regulation is debated, the Australian government is mooting community calls for defaultopt-in obligationson platform algorithms, to stop the use of apps being conditional on what preferred form of slop its tech lord wants to shove into your consciousness.We should all support it, if just to take a wild, political stand for authentic preference over forced consumption. Elon Musk has mooted making an “AI Odyssey”, and if you think the algorithm he paid $44bn for will let you escape that horror show, there are some relevant scenes fromA Clockwork OrangeI suggest you try to catch at a midnight screening.Cinema, writing, education, psychology and, yes, even shopping and banking facilitate human interactions.Unless the clients of AI’s robots are also robots, I have to ask: just who are y’all making products for?Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionSocial mediaChatbotscommentShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Farage meeting a ‘shadowy foreign donor’? It can only be another establishment stitch-up | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: The only thing more dodgy than Reform’s financial dealings is the egregious lunchtime combination of oysters, Guinness and champagne, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: The only thing more dodgy than Reform’s financial dealings is the egregious lunchtime combination of oysters, Guinness and champagne, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Nigel Farage with his adviser Dan Jukes, who has just ‘stepped down, pending an investigation’, Clacton-on-Sea, 2 July 2024.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenNigel Farage with his adviser Dan Jukes, who has just ‘stepped down, pending an investigation’, Clacton-on-Sea, 2 July 2024.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersOpinionNigel FarageNigel Farage meeting a ‘shadowy foreign donor’? It can only be another establishment stitch-upMarina HydeThe only thing more dodgy than Reform’s financial dealings is the egregious lunchtime combination of oysters, Guinness and champagneFri 4 Sep 2026 09.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.10 EDTShareHow many sarcastic air quotes is too many for quotingNigel Farage’s suggestionthat Reform have been ““““““““hoaxed”””””””” by some undercover investigators into appearing to seek to get round electoral law to bag a £500k donation from a foreigner, as well as commissioning off-the-books polling and failing to identify it to newspapers? I don’t feel eight was too many. I could run to nine. Amazing, really, that it’s been as long as a few weeks since Farage had a crash-out and forced a byelection. All any of us wants is for Nigel to once again resign after a staged shitfit and ask a few thousand members of the public to judge him.For whatever reason, though, the law of our country does not amount to an “ONLY THE PEOPLE OF CLACTON CAN JUDGE ME” tattoo, and so it is that as Reform’s conference gets under way today, the party has been reported to the police for allegedly using foreign money to fund its activities. It’s all based ona covert stingcarried out by Verbatim – an investigative group founded by journalists from the non-profit Centre for Climate Reporting – and broadcast last night on Channel 4 News.Though Farage has some very significant walk-on parts in this secretly filmed footage, the chief protagonists in the hokey cokey are James Orr, the party’s director of policy, and Nigel’s right-hand man Dan Jukes. Jukes is one of the many Farage aides to physically resemble an Apprentice candidate who crashes out in week four after miscalculating quantities in the sweetshop task. Still, he’d make a lovely Rolf in a regional production of The Sound of Music. And, happily, would now have the time to really commit to the role.“If Nigel makes it to No 10,” he honks at one point during filming carried out by an undercover “donor”, “you’re having a pint with who’s effectively going to be his chief of staff in No 10. If that isn’t a business interest, I don’t know what is.” As it turns out, the guy is effectively having a pint with someone the party chair, Lee Anderson, this morning said was “gone” with “no chance of them coming back”. Slightly less definitively, the official party statement said that Jukes and Orr had stepped down pending an internal investigation. Can’t imagine what form that will take. I always picture Reform’s internal affairs department as a toy phone ringing out in an abandoned wendy house.But perhaps this sort of thing is the job of flailing enforcer/terminal shitposter Zia Yusuf, who this week could be found branding a possible Labour byelection candidate for Keir Starmer’s vacated Holborn and St Pancras seat as something other than the tireless community servant her career has thus far marked her out as. Or as Zia put it: “The front runner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former Prime Minister Keir Starmer in our Parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what is happening?” If not, certainly one to discuss with that much-vaunted recent defector to Reform, the Iraq-born Nadhim Zahawi. Still, the episode does at least confirm Yusuf as the biggest Pick-Me in British politics. He’s really not like the other children of immigrants, you see – he actually enjoys being racist for approval.Back to the undercover investigation, though, whicha highly defensive Reform statement whingeswas “perpetuated by foreign-funded climate-change activists posing as would-be party donors”. Foreign-funded! That’s a bit rich in the circumstances. But the real standout bit of footage for many will be the moment when Orr laments: “We just don’t have British resident donors, British entities, that would support us. That’s the grim reality.” From the horse’s mouth, then, comes apparent confirmation that Reform is funded by foreign-based money for reasons on which we can only speculate.It’s often the incidental details that seem most weirdly illuminating. Take the scene when the fake American donor finally journeys to some sort of Clacton beer garden, where he and Farage and co seem to have settled themselves in one of a row of cursed teak gazebos. Here, Nigel chortles about “Guinness with a champagne top”, confirming his undying addiction to an even more annoying brand of alcohol-based identity politics than a Gin O’Clock poster.He’ll no doubt be butching it out with a drink at the Reform conference this weekend. The rest of the country might do well to once again ponder the 64,000-of-indeterminately-sourced-dollars question: why does this sort of thing keep happening to Farage and his party? Is it because of a byzantine conspiracy involving climate activists, “the establishment”, the deep state and Big Gazebo? Or is it because they are just endlessly, repeatedly and ineptly dodgy? Watching the footage, it’s fairly difficult to conclude anything other than that we are dealing with a bunch of preposterously self-regarding amateurs.We’ll have to see if this latest exposure further fans the anger that has been radiating off Farage all summer, ever since hisundeclared £5m giftfrom a Thai-based crypto billionaire was revealed. As discussed here before, I am ever-more convinced that Farage is too mentally fragile for the highest office – indeed, leading anything other than an insurgent party seems to be either spinning him out or finding him out. Today’s attempt to shift focus saw him promise to declare a “national emergency” in the event he becomes prime minister. On the basis of all we keep discovering about him, you can’t argue with that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarina Hyde is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Andy Burnham presents his new government as more leftwing than Keir Starmer’s. In reality, it’s barely moved at all | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: The prime minister talks the talk about reversing decades of privatisation and austerity, but we’re yet to see any policies to this end, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: The prime minister talks the talk about reversing decades of privatisation and austerity, but we’re yet to see any policies to this end, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Keir Starmer and Andy Burnham in Manchester, 12 May 2024.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKeir Starmer and Andy Burnham in Manchester, 12 May 2024.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham presents his new government as more leftwing than Keir Starmer’s. In reality, it’s barely moved at allOwen JonesThe prime minister talks the talk about reversing decades of privatisation and austerity, but we’re yet to see any policies to this endFri 4 Sep 2026 07.57 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.21 EDTShareIf Starmerism sought to present theLabourgovernment as more rightwing than it is, Burnhamism seeks to do the opposite.The change in rhetoric is certainly stark. Unlike his sulking predecessor, the new prime minister offers both an analysis and a vision. British stagnation and decline,Andy Burnhamcorrectly told the House of Commons, can be explained by a series of “wrong turns” taken from the 1980s onwards: the privatisation of economic power, the deindustrialisation of the country and the ruinous austerity that followed the 2008 crash.The solution, Burnham suggests, is public control of the essentials, the devolution of power and the rebirth of industry – to rebuild living standards and the economy and give long-abandoned communities a future. Keir Starmer, by contrast, had no vision, relying instead on a technocratic image of competence that was swiftly shattered by one fiasco after another. That left him defined by his opponents, and the electorate baffled as to where his government was headed.The Starmer project foregrounded all of the government’s reactionary elements and buried its social-democratic features. Stringent fiscal rules, the assault on the winter fuel allowance, the attack on disability benefits, the construction of one of Europe’s most punitive asylum regimes, the arrest of pensioners who opposed Israel’s genocide: all became headline policies by design.Now consider what they shouted least about: the semi-nationalisation of the railways, the creation of the publicly run Great British Energy, modest improvements to workers’ and renters’ rights, and some progressive taxation measures, such as hiking capital gains tax.That was for a reason: defining itself against the left was the core strategy of Starmerism. When, in opposition, Starmer committed to retaining the Tories’ two-child benefit cap – even though it plunged hundreds of thousands of children into poverty – his advisers believed, as the journalist Andrew Marrput it, that “the public will notice him standing up to the left”.Starmer junked the radical policy commitments he made to become leader and claimed Labour had gone “from a party of dogma to a party of patriotism” and “from a party of protest to a party of public service”. Labour voters defected en masse to Zack Polanski’s Greens, first in the Gorton and Denton byelection and then in June’s local elections. Starmer’s strategy of insulting progressive voters and their values succeeded in plunging Labour into an existential crisis.Burnham, then, takes the opposite tack, having understood that, in the Britain of the 2020s, the left is a significant political constituency that Labour must appeal to, rather than wilfully alienate.He bemoansthe Starmerite purge of leftwingers, such as economist Faiza Shaheen and former Labour mayor Jamie Driscoll. He sells himself not as a factionalist but as “a Labour politician that’s about unifying people”. Notably, when Jeremy Corbyn asked the prime minister a question about rent controls in the House of Commons, Burnham called the expelled former leader “my right honourable friend”: by parliamentary convention, “friend” is reserved for members of one’s own party.The presentation has certainly changed. But what about the substance? When he stood in the Makerfield byelection in June, Burnhamsaidthat public ownership “is what should be done” in the case of Thames Water. Last week, he backtracked:“I’ve deliberately talked about public control rather than necessarily nationalisation.”It is certainly true that “public control” has been his preferred formula. It allows voters – whooverwhelmingly supportnationalisation – to believe it means public ownership. But as he told Newsnightthis year, it could mean anything from “much tougher regulation” to “public ownership”. That simply allows the existing approach to be rebranded.During his byelection campaign, Burnham demanded that the government’s £39bn Affordable Housing Programme be entirely reserved for council and social housing.In office, his government allocated 40% of the first £10bn tranche to other types of housing – continuity with his predecessor’s approach.Before his victorious return to parliament, Burnham had backed a £500,000 cap on donations to political parties.In power, he has U-turned.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile just a few months ago, Burnham had said he had “long been persuaded” by the case for a land value tax, andproposedit as a replacement for the “iniquitous” council tax, as prime minister he declared: “That won’t be happening.” He has already embraced fiscal rules that block the investment needed for resource-starved public services and infrastructure.Burnham apologised for Labour’s positioning on Gaza, but notably only for its record in opposition. He avoided stating that Israel had committed war crimes, with all the legal obligations that would impose on the government. His new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, now touts sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank, but these are small, piecemeal measures that avoid imposing tough measures on Israel itself.If vibes are your thing, then Burnhamism is a political sensation. Alas, what should matter is the substance. Our prime minister is correct that Britain took a series of wrong turns from the 1980s onwards. The logical conclusion arising from that is that the country needs a new economic model. Burnham has traced the path that led Britain here with admirable clarity. What remains unclear is whether he is prepared to leave it.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Britain’s schools are failing its young people – and 1m Neets are paying the price | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: Obsessed with exams, devoid of vocational training: there is a total mismatch between schools and life beyond their gates, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: Obsessed with exams, devoid of vocational training: there is a total mismatch between schools and life beyond their gates, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Young people speaking with National Careers Service advisers at the Manchester Job Show, April 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYoung people speaking with National Careers Service advisers at the Manchester Job Show, April 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionEducationBritain’s schools are failing its young people – and 1m Neets are paying the priceSimon JenkinsObsessed with exams, devoid of vocational training: there is a total mismatch between schools and life beyond their gatesFri 4 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTShareBlame the schools.Alan Milburn’s report on Neets, published in May, was one of the most damning comments on the welfare state I have read. It described a new generation of a million mostly poor Britons now encouraged to fare worse, not better, than their parents. This means,said Milburn, that “the great British promise” – the advance of generations – is being broken. A sizeable chunk of the population is going backwards.The number of young people not in education, employment or training – one in eight of all 16- to 24-year-olds – is rising fast and will be 1.25 million by 2030. More than 80% of them claim to want to find a job, education or training. A third even have “good GCSEs”, but 44% of them are on state benefits, now costing £8.1bn. Many of them suffer from anxiety and other disabilities, according to the NHS. The number of young people with special educational needs has doubled in 10 years. Mental ill-health is bordering on pandemic levels.The Neets crisis is a gift to politicians. There is always someone else to blame. The most obvious target is Labour’s curiously punitive treatment of small businesses and casual or unskilled jobs. Curbing zero-hours contracts and proposing first-day job security are measures that seem almost targeted at keeping Neets out of work.But the complaint ringing ever louder from employers is that young people leaving school are unready for work and life in the real world. August’sDepartment for Work and Pensions surveyof employers’ views is an indictment. More than 90% thought the education system should offer more vocational pathways to young people. They pleaded for the young to understand personal motivation, teamwork and time management. They believed schools were too focused on ensuring children and young people passed exams, and lacked anything passing for careers guidance.Reading these reports leaves an eerie sense of a total mismatch between schools and the social and economic life of the community beyond their gates. They seem like monastic institutions, fixated on their own seasons and periods, and on “subjects” handed down from the past. Above all, they love to measure what they teach, even if it has nothing to do with their pupils’ futures.If I were an employer I would want new entrants educated in handling money, public affairs, the law, crime and punishment. They should learn about citizenship, the economy and the environment. They should know about public health and their own physical and mental wellbeing. They should be taught elementary ethics and the meaning of morality.This should be just a beginning. What Neets most clearly lack is self-confidence.The new oracy movementis pleading for practical lessons in getting the young to talk clearly and present themselves to others. They should learn to articulate views and listen to others and learn how to agree and disagree. I cannot imagine a more critical skill, yet it is virtually untaught in schools. The reason, of course, is that authority cannot measure it. There is no league table for confidence.Here the temperature rises. I used to notice pupils at my local secondary breaking up for the day. They would burst through the gates conversing in twos, threes or larger groups. These groups would merge and dissolve down the street like clouds. I liked to see them as a metaphor for the economy at work.Today those same groups are quite different, composed of pupils with heads buried in phones and with just a few of them shouting into the air. The American social psychologist Jonathan Haidt, inThe Anxious Generation, finds this a universal facet of younger generations on both sides of the Atlantic. Social media is denying them the art of conversation, of intellectual tolerance. It is electronic introversion and there is no GCSE in that – let alone a job interview. These phones must disappear.Milburn’s Neets report is interim. It poses the problem. We await his solution this autumn. It will doubtless elevate the importance of technical and vocational education alongside the cult of the academic subject. Nothing would aid this more than to end the disastrous merging of universities and technology colleges that took place 30 years ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs it too much to dream that Milburn might look deeper? For more than a century, education’s radicals, such as Rudolf Steiner, Maria Montessori and John Dewey, have sought to bring a fresh relevance to what is taught in schools. Reading, writing and arithmetic remain necessities, but they are primary-stage skills usually acquired before the teens.Secondary curriculums emerged from the 19th-century academies and have remained little changed ever since. They rank as noble pastimes much to be cherished, but they have scant relevance to the future lives and livelihoods of most pupils. Teaching, the world’s most conservative profession, merely clings to them. Britain’s Neets are the most unjustly treated victims.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEducationOpinionSchoolsYoung peopleYouth unemploymentApprenticeshipscommentShareReuse this content

title: When does rage help us, and when does it harm us? Ukraine has taught me the answers | Charlotte Higgins | The Guardian
description: Fury at Russia’s death and destruction has fuelled art, action and resistance. But eventually, rage’s fire is all-consuming, says the Guardian’s chief culture writer, Charlotte Higgins
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: Fury at Russia’s death and destruction has fuelled art, action and resistance. But eventually, rage’s fire is all-consuming, says the Guardian’s chief culture writer, Charlotte Higgins
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionCultureWhen does rage help us, and when does it harm us? Ukraine has taught me the answersCharlotte HigginsFury at Russia’s death and destruction has fuelled art, action and resistance. But eventually, rage’s fire is all-consumingFri 4 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.49 EDTShareTwice, I have heard Ukrainians perform Verdi’s Requiem. Oncein Lviv, last Maundy Thursday, and once last month, under the great dome of St Paul’s Cathedral in London. InSt Paul’s, performed by the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra with the Philharmonia Chorus, the greatDies irae– “day of anger” – unfurled in an operatic gale of fury, reverberating so powerfully around Wren’s lofty spaces that the music felt like thunder echoing between mountain peaks.In Lviv, where it was performed by a Ukrainian chorus and orchestra, the evening began with a call to remember the war dead. Lviv’s lay a mile up the road: 153 graves when I first visited in autumn 2022, and by this year more than 1,000. Ranks and ranks of soldiers killed in their 20s, 30s and 40s, each grave planted with flowers and plants, flags flying above. On that occasion,Dies irae– in the more sober acoustic of the Lviv Philharmonic Hall – seemed to contain the furious ache of grief. Certainly I have never heard a more wrathful day of anger.I have thought a lot about Ukrainian rage. This was a rage againstRussiaand Russians, and it burned with a fury that was at times hard to step close to. Ukrainians, too, have sometimes been taken aback by the depth of their anger. Oleksandr Mykhed, an author now in the armed forces, has written a wartime alphabet book for children in which L stands forlyut, rage. He defines it as a “special mixture of feelings when the desire to defend what is yours, hatred for the enemy and enduring love for your own people are mixed in equal proportions”. This complicated, extreme cocktail of feelings is not a peacetime emotion, nor an easy one.View image in fullscreenUkrainian Freedom Orchestra founder and conductor Keri-Lynn Wilson at the St Paul’s concert in London on 18 August.Photograph: Frances MarshallI found myself making sense of it through literature, specifically Homer’s epic poems. Epics need fuel to motor them on their poetic journey. They also need delay, so that they become long poems, not short ones. Inthe Odyssey, the fuel of the poem is desire – the desire to get home – and the delay is the divine malevolence that brings many obstacles in Odysseus’s path.
