But in the Iliad, set during the Trojan war, Achilles’ rage is the fuel of the poem: first his outrage as a subordinate insulted by his commander, later the raging grief of a man who has lost his dearest friend in battle. Grief and rage are cousins; that is also clear to me in Ukraine.It would be wrong to suggest that Ukrainian rage is like Achilles’. His veers beyond the human, into the supersize, mythical emotional zone inhabited by the children of the gods. But I found myself thinking about the vastness of this Homeric rage when encountering the fury of Ukrainians at civilians killed, cities bombed, people raped and tortured. The poet Iryna Shuvalova, in an interview with the writer Kateryna Iakovlenko for Suspilne, the Ukrainian national broadcaster, said rage was “pouring out of us as a reaction to the incredible trauma, the blow, the provocation, the terrible losses”.View image in fullscreenIryna Shuvalova’s poem February deals with to the month of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Photograph: Olga ZakrevskaShuvalova’s poemFebruary– referring to the month of the full-scale invasion in 2022 – begins gently, wryly, by pointing out that “we planned to get through February / like any other month— / only shorter”. But then the invasion begins, and “instead, the river roars and grabs us by the legs / this red slippery foaming / February-fury”. The translators, Amelia Glaser and Yuliya Ilchuk, used the phrase “February-fury” to mimic the echo in Ukrainian betweenlyutyy, the word for February, andlyuta, raging. For me, the immediate resonance of Shuvalova’s blood-soaked river is Homer’s Scamander River, choked in blood and the corpses of the war dead.And what is the “day of anger” that powers Verdi’s Requiem? The words, no longer often used as part of a requiem mass, are from a medieval Latin poem that summons up the chaos and terror of the Earth’s final dissolution. The intensity of its expression – the visceral, gut-felt outpouring – that I heard in those Ukrainian performances of the work reminded me of Homeric wrath, although it is a rage that has a different force. The anger of theDies iraeis a kind of world-fury produced when everything is disrupted, put out of order by human actions. A world locked into war, perhaps.I am not a Christian, and the values of Homer’s Iliad are alien to me. But I think perhaps there are different orders of rage. Some rage is trivial and petty; the everyday rage of frustration and aggression. But Mykhed told me of a generative rage: a rage that produces action, that fuels resistance. His rage provided him with the impetus and energy to write his bookThe Language of War. He told me that he wanted his rage-filled book about the first year of the full-scale invasion of his country to be “a time capsule for myself so that I know where I’ve been, when in five years or 10 years, my rage won’t be so sharp”.The feeling, he said, is specifically “not hatred, it is rage, because hatred doesn’t give you power, it’s more chaotic. But rage gives you words.” In 1981, Audre Lordewrote urgentlyof the fury provoked into flame by racism – a fury that could alienate and be resented by white people. Black women, she wrote, “tremble their rage under harness”. But pulled into service, channelled towards action and words, anger “is loaded with information and energy”. So it has been for Ukrainians: rage turned into action fuelled resistance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenOleksandr Mykhed has written a wartime alphabet book for children in which L stands forlyut(rage).Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianBut now, in 2026, Ukrainian rage burns low, at least among my friends. The fire cannot be sustained; it would consume you in its overwhelming heat. What is left? Fatigue, emptiness, an alertness to the dreadful idea that however bad things are now, they could get worse. “I feel like anything is possible – nuclear war, anything,” Iakovlenko told me. “Everything that was written in books and in films is actually happening to us.”Sasha Dovzhyk, the director of Index, Ukraine’s Institute for Documentation and Exchange, told me that she felt “pure spite and grit and grim determination and a memory of what it felt like to have feelings and a loyalty to that past version of the self who felt rage”. She missed rage, she told me. Rage and grief gave her the power to write her forthcoming book,Apocalypse Baroque: Tales from Ukraine at War, which mixes genres – documentary and fairytales – with rageous energy. Maybe rage sometimes brings one too close to the perilous realm of myth, to the destructiveness of an Achilles. But if you can tame the wild horse of rage, it can be ridden, for a while.Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writer and the author ofUkrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War, published by Jonathan Cape. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.comOn Wednesday 30 September,join Charlotte Higginsand our panel of acclaimed Ukrainian writers to reflect on the profound connections between war, art and life. With Olia Hercules, Sasha Dovzhyk and Olesya Khromeychuk. Book ticketshereExplore more on these topicsCultureOpinionUkraineGiuseppe VerdiPoetryHomerRussiaEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Capitalism is dying’: in Luton, these former car workers have a moral tale for our times | Aditya Chakrabortty | The Guardian
description: Abandoned by the company they worked for, let down by Labour and their unions – now they watch their friends turn to Reform for answers, says Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty
Author: Aditya Chakrabortty
Headline: Abandoned by the company they worked for, let down by Labour and their unions – now they watch their friends turn to Reform for answers, says Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty
Content: Former Vauxhall workers at the closed site: (from left) Mohammed Hussain, Malik Mahmood, Gary Reay, Paul Geary and Gerald Shalvey, Luton, 28 August 2026.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFormer Vauxhall workers at the closed site: (from left) Mohammed Hussain, Malik Mahmood, Gary Reay, Paul Geary and Gerald Shalvey, Luton, 28 August 2026.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianOpinionAutomotive industry‘Capitalism is dying’: in Luton, these former car workers have a moral tale for our timesAditya ChakraborttyAbandoned by the company they worked for, let down by Labour and their unions – now they watch their friends turn to Reform for answersFri 4 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 08.50 EDTShareAfter everything, why would anyone still back Nigel Farage? In some of the comments below my piecelast weekabout Reform UK, I spot the usual answers: Farage’s supporters are dim, racist, deplorable. Yet away from Westminster and the news cycle, Reform voters are being manufactured – not with headlines or crypto funds but through the failure of institutions they once trusted to protect them. To see what I mean, leave SW1 and go 40 miles up the road, to Luton.In a deserted hotel bar, five men are reminiscing about how their world ended. Their minds are on a Friday afternoon in March last year, as the place where they had worked for two or three decades apiece, making friends and even meeting future wives, is about to shut for good.Vauxhall came to Luton not long after the death of Queen Victoria; it helped build the town and gave it an economy and an identity. At its peak in 1971, the company directly employed 37,000 staff in Britain, mostly in Luton. Nowit is leaving. On this afternoon, these men and so many of their soon-to-be ex-workmates are crowded around the assembly line. As the last white van comes off, they clap and cheer with pride for what they had been part of. Some cry. “It’s as if you had lost someone in your family,” remembers Paul Geary, whose ties with this place are four generations deep.“It’s such a chunk of your life,” says Gerald Shalvey, who gave the company 34 years of his. Later, he walks back out on to the line and surveys the site where until this afternoon 1,600 people had worked. For the first time ever, the machinery is still and he hears nothing but silence: “an industrial graveyard”. Then he wonders what comes next, for him, his mates and his town.For the hard right and far right alike, Luton is a contemporary hell. The star of countless memes and YouTube films, it spells migrants, Muslims and growing poverty. For some key players, the connection is personal. Luton boy Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson, has talked of how his stepfather worked atVauxhall. Andrew Tate grew up in what he calls “the worst area of the worst town” (actually, the same estate as Geary). They lived through Luton’s long decline; then they monetised it.The ex-Vauxhall workers talking to me are nothing to do with the rightward exploitation. But since their factory’s closure, they have seen fellow union members switch in droves from voting for Keir Starmer in 2024 to backing Farage. It’s not just Labour; their disgust is at a society they feel has let them and their families go under. A similar process is at work in other “industrial graveyards” from Grangemouth to Port Talbot and across the west.View image in fullscreenA sign outside the former Vauxhall plant in Luton.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianIn the east German province of Saxony-Anhalt, the far right looks set this weekendto win governing powerfor the first time in decades. Its current state premier, Sven Schulze,knows why: “We’ve seen how quickly we can lose our jobs, how quickly a company can disappear. That’s the experience east Germans have had, and it’s far deeper than west Germans think.”There isn’t the space here to look closely at how Vauxhall left Luton, but the final episode comes in three parts. First, the then boss of the company’s owner, Stellantis, visits the plant early in 2023 and tells staff they need to halve manufacturing coststo compete with employees in Turkey. Whether Luton lives or dies is in their hands, he says, ending: “Good luck”. (These events were recalled by several employees and were not disputed by Stellantis.) Workers and managers collaborate and through a lot of sacrifice almost halve costs. It makes no odds: late in 2024, Stellantisannounces it will closea plant that is profitable. Only Ellesmere Port will be kept open.“Corporate greed,” say the trade unionists, who make counter-proposal after counter-proposal, to no avail. Some Unite members grumble to me about their leaders not fighting hard enough, and cite among examples a key meeting with the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, which the Unite head, Sharon Graham, did not attend but sent an aide. (When I checked this with Unite’s press office, it replied with lawyers’ letters and a statement saying Graham had “a pre-arranged meeting” but that she had negotiated directly with both Starmer and Reynolds on a government package of support to keepLutonopen.)Labour ministers make clear they will “support” Stellantis financially and otherwise to stay at Luton. But in dealing with this multinational carmaker, a G7 government does not have much more sway than a shop-floor steward. At the start of 2025, a frustrated Reynolds writes to a Luton MP that “despite these repeated offers from my department, Stellantis have been unwilling to engage in any discussions”. Then comes that Friday afternoon in March. As their factory closes for ever, workers are given a commemorative brochure and a medal made of scrap metal.Now see this from a Luton worker’s point of view. The company to whom you’ve given half your life has first castigated you for not being as cheap as your Turkish counterparts, then upped and left. The union to whom you pay your subs wasn’t able to stop it going. Also impotent was the Labour government you voted for – again. Luton lost its car plant under Tony Blair, it lost its van plant under Starmer. Now you’re out of work, and – in the case of Mohammed Hussain, sitting next to me – you’ve just bought a house with a hefty mortgage. More than a year later, he’s still out of work.Throughout our conversation, one man has barely spoken. Malik Mahmoodcleaned at Vauxhall for 26 years; only now do his words come, in fits and starts.View image in fullscreenFormer Vauxhall worker Gary Reay outside the closed Luton plant.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“One year I struggled for work.” He went for so many jobs – “50? 60? Fucking loads” – but this honest man with a quarter-century of loyal service found no takers. The big black mark, he thought, was age: Mahmood is deep into his 60s. After months of burning through his Vauxhall payout, he took jobseeker’s allowance, walking through the town to sign on, getting £84 a week and an inquisition from jobcentre staff. He mimics them – “What you did? Have you found a job?” His face is etched with years of hard work and worry.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA few months ago, Unite published aninternal reporton the lessons from the closure of Vauxhall Luton. It’s a rare document, not least because trade unions like to celebrate victories rather than dwell on defeats, and this is its first mention anywhere in the press. At its heart is a survey of ex-Vauxhall workers and the finding that, a year after closure, like Mahmood and Hussain, 30% were still unemployed. At the same time, the report found, those ex-workers switched their politics. Less than 10% backed Labour as of this spring; more than 50% supported Farage.In June, Mahmood finally landed a position in one of the new warehouses out of town. Now he depends on a mate to give him a lift into work, and his pay today is £1,000 a month lower than it was 18 months ago. This is typical of other Vauxhall survivors, the Unite report shows: even the winners have lost out. Getting laid off in a cost of living crisis is expensive, and the men here today rely on family members for help, and cut back on heating and groceries.In the late 1960s, a group of sociologists visited then booming Luton, interviewing workers at Vauxhall and elsewhere for a renowned series of books, titled The Affluent Worker. Its central question was: when the working classes get middle-class salaries and mod cons, what happens to their class identity? Sixty years later, Britain is running the experiment in reverse, driving working-class families into deprivation and smashing up their communities. The results are not yet in, but they look bad.The closure of Vauxhall Luton leaves a “vacuum”, says Geary: economically, socially and politically. “These were solid jobs with pensions and you were getting good money. You could get qualifications, a mortgage. What are the kids going to train at school to be? All on social media?” That vacuum, he says, is where the hard right and far right step in.None of them set much store by Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain. The workers have gone, and so have their skills. The economic models these guys discuss now are Donald Trump’s protectionism and Beijing’s historic public investment. European social democracy doesn’t rate a mention. “The system of capitalism is dying because people are seeing it’s not worked,” says Gary Reay.We end by doing the photos, walking along the road that was once all Vauxhall. To get from one end of the site to the other was once a 15-minute walk filled with noise and people. Now the only sound is planes screaming away to holiday destinations. Shalvey points out the large Vauxhall badge still hanging from a brick wall. “What a waste,” he says. “What an idiotic waste of potential.”Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAutomotive industryOpinionLutonVauxhallUnemploymentLabourReform UKFar rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: Albanese’s resources minister celebrating the Beetaloo carbon bomb is a hell of a choice. Labor can’t say it wasn’t warned | Adam Morton | The Guardian
description: Scientists will be able to estimate the amount of heating and destruction caused by the gas ultimately drawn from the Beetaloo
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: Scientists will be able to estimate the amount of heating and destruction caused by the gas ultimately drawn from the Beetaloo
Content: The Northern Territory mining and energy minister, Gerard Maley, the Tamboran Resources chief executive, Todd Abbott, Australia's resources minister, Madeleine King, and the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, turn on the gas supply to Darwin from the Beetaloo basin.Photograph: Helen Clark/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Northern Territory mining and energy minister, Gerard Maley, the Tamboran Resources chief executive, Todd Abbott, Australia's resources minister, Madeleine King, and the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, turn on the gas supply to Darwin from the Beetaloo basin.Photograph: Helen Clark/ReutersClear airClimate crisisAlbanese’s resources minister celebrating the Beetaloo carbon bomb is a hell of a choice. Labor can’t say it wasn’t warnedAdam MortonScientists will be able to estimate the amount of heating and destruction caused by the gas ultimately drawn from the BeetalooGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 3 Sep 2026 22.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 02.30 EDTShareAgiant chunk of glacier-covered mountain has collapsed with catastrophic effect and, whatever the mechanics of the disaster in Nepal’s Langtang national park, this is what human-caused climate crisis looks like. The likelihood of it happening again will rise as temperatures increase and the ice within rock and soil formations melts.Anthony Albanese was in Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum, speaking with the leaders of countries that could lose some or all of their homelands this century due to sea-level rise driven by emissions from burning fossil fuels.Meanwhile, a senior member of his Labor government visited the Northern Territory outback andposed for photos laughing alongside the NT chief ministeras they jointly turned the tap to release the first gas from what is potentially one of the world’s largest fossil fuel reservoirs.We could ask how history will look on this, but why wait? We have a good idea now.double quotation markNone of the trio acknowledged what else extracting and burning that gas would mean: the release of a globally and historically huge amount of heat-trapping pollutionThe image of the federal resources minister, Madeleine King, marking the opening of the Beetaloo basin alongside the Country Liberal party’s Lia Finocchiaro received only passing attention in national discussion this week, but my guess is it will linger.At some point, scientists will be able to estimate the amount of heating and destruction caused by the gas that is ultimately drawn from the Beetaloo. The celebratory photo may come to be seen as real-time evidence of how some political leaders felt about that prospect.Very obviously, they won’t be able to say they weren’t warned.The first gas being drawn from the Beetaloo basin is a significant and long-promised moment. The Beetaloo is huge, spread across about 28,000 square kilometres of Indigenous and pastoral land between Katherine and Tennant Creek, roughly 500km south-east of Darwin. It is home to shale gas, which means the fossil fuel is trapped inside sedimentary rock and can be extracted through fracking – a highly contentious process.Estimates of the scale of the basin vary. Todd Abbott – the chief executive of Tamboran Resources, the company behind the first Beetaloo development – stood alongside King and Finocchiaro this week as he told reporters that the sub-basin contained about 200 trillion cubic feet of gas, making it the world’s largest non-oil gas field outside the Middle East or Russia. He said that was enough gas to power every home in Sydney 20 times over for more than a century.None of the trio acknowledged what else extracting and burning that gas would mean: the release of a globally and historically huge amount of heat-trapping pollution that would have a real impact on lives, livelihoods and ecosystems.Few people believe the Beetaloo will be developed to its full extent and the pilot project launched this week, while locally significant, is relatively small. But the goal is mass extraction, and some experts didn’t think it would get this far. Several projects are in the works. Its potential expansion should be taken seriously.The datacentre power spat highlights a hidden truth: we’re not building renewables fast enough to meet our needs | Alison ReeveRead moreThere is a strong case it has only come this far due to politicians prioritising gas industry demands by offering taxpayer support, weakening climate policies andpushing aside concerns about the impact on culture and water resources raised by some traditional owners. This has been demonstrated through reporting by the Guardian’s Lisa Cox, among others.In 2018, when the NT was considering lifting a moratorium on fracking, a government inquiry recommended that any shale gas development should not be allowed to increase Australia’s net emissions. That meant the full emissions released in the country from extracting, processing, transporting and burning the gas must be offset through the purchase of carbon credits.Carbon credits are controversial for a range of reasons, but they have at least one unarguable effect – laws forcing industry to buy them increases the cost of fossil fuel developments as polluters pay a cost for their pollution. That might not hurt a company of the scale of Woodside, but it makes marginal projects harder to get off the ground.The then NT Labor administration claimed it backed this recommendation, but documents show it abandoned itafter the gas industry objected.It also signed a contract to buy gas from the Tamboran pilot development to use in Darwin. Would it have launched this week without taxpayer underwriting? It seems unlikely.The Country Liberal party supported Labor’s stance and doubled down after it was elected by stripping away support for cleaner alternatives. It scrapped a renewable energy target of 50% by 2030 that it backed in opposition and abandoned a promised emissions reduction target.It maintained its position as the NT suffered through an unprecedented five overlapping natural disasters last wet season, including flooding that displaced some Aboriginal communities on the Daly River for months. Rather than reconsider its fossil fuel stance, the CLP released a climate resilience plan that, in its first listed action, committed to accelerate production of Beetaloo gas.Projects that result from this will not be required to limit emissions under NT law. Some will fall under the safeguard mechanism, a federal climate policy, but analysis suggests itwill have little affect on emissions from Beetaloo gas in the next few years.Finocchiaro declared the start of pilot production a landmark day that would change the future of the local economy, largely because it would address energy affordability worries. She then tempered this a little by saying prices would “stabilise over the long term”.View image in fullscreenThe NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPWho knows what that means? The reality is that gas is routinely the most expensive form of energy used in Australia and far more costly in most cases than firmed renewable energy. Production at new basins such as the Beetaloowill be more expensive again.That cost will multiply if an industry dream of a federally backed, multibillion-dollar gas pipeline from Beetaloo to the east coast goes ahead. With demand for gas in the eastern states falling that seems unlikely, and suggests whatever gas is produced in the Beetaloo will be for local use or exported.On cost grounds alone, it would be logical to be working hard to reduce gas demand. Instead, the NT chief minister is arguing she can provide cheap fuel for datacentres, while attacking suggestions otherwise.A question for the Albanese government is: what exactly is its minister celebrating here? Asked on Tuesday about criticisms she was backing a “carbon bomb”, Kingoffered a word saladin which she said Labor was “dealing with climate change” while also supporting gas.She didn’t mention a UN Environment Programme report this week said the Paris agreement goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels – which Laborsays it still strongly supports– will inevitably be passed, and a temperature rise that peaks at 1.8C isnow the most optimistic future available.Every extra fraction of a degree intensifies the risks from extreme weather, glacier melt and coastal and island submersion. Human health, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies could all be severely damaged.Limiting that requires immediate and sustained emissions cuts alongside strategies to draw CO2from the atmosphere. Australia can’t do that on its own. But chuckling while opening a new gas basin – and while climate-friendly options are being ignored – is what you might call a hell of a choice.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisClear airEnergycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t know if I’d ever have sex again’: inside Sharon Horgan’s excruciating post-divorce comedy | Television | The Guardian
description: Horgan’s hilarious new show probes the perils of ageing and the horror of being single again – and it has sex scenes so wild you’ll be laughing for weeks. The creator and her co-stars open up about Youth
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Horgan’s hilarious new show probes the perils of ageing and the horror of being single again – and it has sex scenes so wild you’ll be laughing for weeks. The creator and her co-stars open up about Youth
Content: It’s complicated … Rupert Friend as Patrick and Sharon Horgan as Alex in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBOView image in fullscreenIt’s complicated … Rupert Friend as Patrick and Sharon Horgan as Alex in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBOTelevisionInterview‘I didn’t know if I’d ever have sex again’: inside Sharon Horgan’s excruciating post-divorce comedyZoe WilliamsHorgan’s hilarious new show probes the perils of ageing and the horror of being single again – and it has sex scenes so wild you’ll be laughing for weeks. The creator and her co-stars open up about YouthFri 4 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 09.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenSharon Horganwalked into HBO to pitch her new series, Youth, she basically just said “sandwich generation” to them. Alex, the protagonist, is squished between a teenage son and two elderly parents. That’s the classic; the rest of it – the recent divorce, the dating hell, the busy, creative professional life full of pricks – is the icing on the sandwich (if you like). Horgan had been incubating some of the characters for five years, but “honestly”, she tells me, “I said about three sentences and a week later, they said yes. I’ve never had that experience before.”You might think you can imagine it, but Youth is unlike any portrait you’ve ever seen in the gallery of (for brevity) menopausal women doing everything for everyone. There’s an urgency and valour to it that is very much drawn from Horgan’s own experience. “Everything just changed for me when I hit my 50s,” she says. “I was very bamboozled but I really had a hunger to make time count.” Not every situation is lifted directly from her own life, post-divorce – she’s also borrowing from her friends, she emphasises – but in general terms, the pressures, the worries, the outrages, the surprise and the delight are all so exquisitely drawn that even if it’s not Horgan herself, you hope someone, somewhere, is living this in real life.View image in fullscreen‘She could have chemistry with a toaster’ … Sharon Horgan.I caught some of the shooting on a blowy day in April this year, in east London. Horgan and her co-starRupert Friendwere filming a crux scene. Friend plays Patrick, slightly younger than Horgan’s Alex, a little indecisive and shambling. “He’s not a Prince Charming character. I don’t think I’m the answer to all her ills,” he says, walking around a little park in between takes. Patrick wants to be with Alex, but he also thinks he wants children and there’s no way she’s going back there again, even if she could. “Sharon flips the proverbial biological clock on its head,” he says. “Men think it doesn’t apply to them because they ostensibly can make children all the way through. He’s never considered that it’s not his clock.”Nothing passes between Alex and Patrick that’s overstated or even out of the ordinary, unless you count the fact that she gets hit by a cyclist as she walks away. But when it slots into the finished show, it is, like every other scene, hilarious. I just do not know how Horgan does what she does – which is what every one of her co-stars says about her. “She could have chemistry with a toaster,” saysAran Murphy(yes, son of Cillian), who plays her son. “She’s so fizzing with energy.” Rupert Friend puts the emphasis on her agility: “Sharon’s just brilliant at writing. She’s able to do that dance between jokes and pathos in a way that I don’t know anyone else can do.” But it’s Horgan herself who, in an absolutely unboastful way, explains it best: “I’m allergic to sentimentality. I can’t abide anything that is sweet or schmaltzy. But I love genuine emotion. I love to make people feel things. As much as I love the laughs, I’d feel like I’d failed in some way if I wasn’t giving people pain.”Murphy’s Ruari is a gift of a part, the most believably wrecking-ball 18-year-old son you’ve ever seen. Some things he wrecks on purpose (the last day of secondary school), some he wrecks by accident (his first week at university; his life), but the stakes are agonisingly high and the actions all plausible. Horgan has a lot to say about parenting kids this age, “even though I do not have a son, I have daughters” (Sadhbh, 22, and Amer, 18). “Gen Z have that awful feeling of being the last generation. They’re here at a point in time where they’re being told that everything’s fucked and AI’s going to take your jobs. I sometimes don’t know how to get out of bed in the morning, but they’re the ones who care the most and feel things the most.”View image in fullscreen‘Everything just changed when I hit my 50s’ … Sharon Horgan in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBOMurphy is pretty reserved in real life (he speaks to me by Zoom from Italy, where he is on holiday), and the performance he turns in is one of the most thrillingly angry teenagers ever. “We really got lucky with Aran,” says Horgan. “There’s nothing about him that isn’t real. It made life so much easier to be working with someone who you literally can’t see acting.” She wanted Ruari to be “complex but not in a Dawson’s Creek way – a real boy who’s a little bit broken. All Alex wants is for him to normalise. But what’s normal?”Besides, Ruari is probably saying the same about his mother, who he is furious to discover still has gentleman callers. Patrick isn’t Alex’s only love interest; there’s also a sex scene withTim McInnerny(Percy from Blackadder) that I am still laughing at weeks later. None of the relationships, fleeting or otherwise, are at all a classic love story – Rupert Friend says ruefully, “I’m really the best of a bad bunch, which I am happy to take as the quote for my gravestone” – but the men are drawn so truthfully that you can’t help but love them all slightly (apart from the ex-husband, and even he’s not abadguy, more of an emotional no-mark).“When I found myself divorced,” Horgan says, “I genuinely thought I’d be alone for ever. I didn’t even know if I’d ever have sex again. There’s that extreme fear of being alone and being lonely. But at the same time, you think you have a freedom as well. You do suddenly think: ‘My kids have finished school, I’ve got some time to try and get this right.’” Alex’s love life is anything but over, yet this isn’t a “you go, girl” tale where every woman remains perpetually 35 through Botox and force of will. “You put yourself out there in a slightly different way,” says Horgan. “It’s still incredibly difficult, as a woman of that age, to find someone – the men who are left are either institutionally single or they’re divorced or they’re looking for someone much younger.”View image in fullscreenWrecking-ball … Aran Murphy as Ruari in Youth.Photograph: Colin HuttonThe subplot of Alex’s ageing parents, meanwhile, is so honest it’s exhilarating. Dramedy tends to be respectfully saccharine about the elderly, and skate over the inconvenient bits: the stubbornness, the denial, the endless hospital appointments. But (I’m allowed to say this, being an orphan – Horgan’s mother is still alive, her dad died in 2023), those bits are almost the whole of the experience. “There is a huge amount of non-cooperation there,” she says, “and why shouldn’t there be? Ageing is hard. It’s harder when it begins to affect you mentally. When you’ve always been sharp as a tack, or when you begin to lose your mobility and you’ve always been a fucking go-getter. Losing those basic functions is brutal.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut from Alex’s point of view, “all the planning, all the phone calls, it becomes such a huge part of your life. As it goes on, you’ll see how it affects her sibling relationship as well. I wanted to explore that all so much but you run out of time and space. That could have been a whole show.”Alex works in publishing, and there are some fabulous performances by her authors – Anne Reid, as a grande dame of airport fiction, turning her hand to erotica, alongside Harriet Walter as her ice-cold daughter. “I could talk to you about Anne Reid for the entirety of the interview,” Horgan says. “It’s hard to even mention her and not just wax lyrical about being aged 91 and still delivering work on that level and still caring so much.” Damian Lewis, within 30 seconds of arriving on screen, has distilled everything that is bad about publishing, celebrity, London, private members’ clubs and the world. “Everyone who came on to do their bits was influencing the show,” says Horgan. “I was writing it at the same time as making it, which was hell.” On the upside, it meant she was building relationships with her co-stars as she wrote, and incorporating those connections. Friend remembers deep conversations about what love actuallyis. “We talked about how heartbreaking it is to think about things in terms of if they fail. You know, if you meet and immediately think: ‘We could date, but if we date we might break up.’ Why do anything? Everything has a pessimistic possibility, and Alex is always considering it, but it’s no way to live.”Pulling, Sharon Horgan’s 00s comedy, andMotherland, a decade ago, did the same thing – which is to say, if you’d asked: “Do you want to see a show about three single women? How about a school-gate show about neurotic middle-class people and Chardonnay and mini Babybels?” I’d have said: “No, not at all, sounds drab and also too close to home.” But then when they landed, they were all I wanted to watch. Youth is technically about the grinding sandwich years, when everything gets harder at once, and then your joints stop working. But it’s really about the sheer bliss of being alive when so much happens that is funny, stitched together by a fearsomely long to-do list.Youth is on HBO Max from 21 September.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionSharon HorganDramainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Men calling us woke need our show more than most’: punks Piss on finding strength in visceral confrontations of sexual violence | Music | The Guardian
description: The Vancouver band earned a cult fandom for their uncompromising gigs. As they ready their brutal debut album, they discuss subverting audience expectations and the nightly toll of excavating trauma onstage
Author: Emma Garland
Headline: The Vancouver band earned a cult fandom for their uncompromising gigs. As they ready their brutal debut album, they discuss subverting audience expectations and the nightly toll of excavating trauma onstage
Content: Taylor Zantingh of Piss performing at Hit the City festival in Eindhoven, August 2026.Photograph: Kirsten HeskampView image in fullscreenTaylor Zantingh of Piss performing at Hit the City festival in Eindhoven, August 2026.Photograph: Kirsten HeskampMusicInterview‘Men calling us woke need our show more than most’: punks Piss on finding strength in visceral confrontations of sexual violenceEmma GarlandThe Vancouver band earned a cult fandom for their uncompromising gigs. As they ready their brutal debut album, they discuss subverting audience expectations and the nightly toll of excavating trauma onstageFri 4 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’d be hard pressed to find a band with fewer airs and graces than Piss. First, there’s the unavoidable matter of their name, which they style in all caps, no nonsense; a word that scans as vulgar and combative but also somewhat facetious when displayed on their merch in loopy cursive, sometimes decorated with bows. The Vancouver quartet’s music is a merciless cyclone of hardcore, poetry, sound collage and performance art that revolves entirely around singer Taylor Zantingh’s experiences with sexual violence.On stage at Eindhoven’s Hit the City festival in late August, the band greets the stacked crowd with a trigger warning before drummer Garreth Roberts, bassist Gavin Moya and guitarist Tyler Paterson launch into pulverising fits of noise-punk, broken up by audio samples of children laughing and feminist writer Andrea Dworkin talking about pornography. Zantingh hurls herself around, clutching at her stomach and flinging her pigtails before winding down to a nervous, twitching standstill. The intense set is finely tuned to present a narrative of gender-based violence not as entertainment, but as lived experience. They play it exactly the same every night, and have done for the last two years.Piss: Time Loop at Hot Slit – video“I think a lot of people are like, ‘I’m going to see a band called Piss, this is going to be craaaazy!’ And it’s crazy in a different way than they expect,” Zantingh tells me before the show, over chamomile tea. “People come for one thing and then they’re forced to listen to me for half an hour.”The buzz around Piss usually takes bands of their ilk several album cycles to drum up, yet they have released next to no music: a four-track demo on Bandcamp, a few professionally recorded sets and radio appearances on YouTube and some viral fan-filmed clips. Since forming in 2024, their reputation has grown through their live performance, prompting Sub Pop to sign them; their debut album You Made Me / Skin on Linen arrives in October.Recorded over a handful of days in winter 2024, the album was made to mirror the Piss live experience as closely as possible. Throughout, you’ll hear Zantingh gasp for breath or struggle to get words out, lacing traumatic recollections with disturbing imagery of “fingers sewn in the wrong places” and kids “practising blowjobs on glue sticks”. The songs combine Bikini Kill and Fugazi’s DIY approach to “making personal things political” with the uranium-heavy sonics of Chat Pile or Swans. Paterson, who is primarily responsible for shaping the instrumentals, likens his process to scoring a film. “The influences came from a lot of places to uphold the narrative that Tay is weaving,” he says. “The feelings and intention come first, and the sound comes after.”View image in fullscreen‘I have never known how long I’m gonna be able to physically and emotionally do this’ … Piss.Photograph: PRThe way Piss use music, performance art and other voices is fundamental, Zantingh says, because the subject matter is too “monstrous” to be described in words alone. Placing her voice in chorus with a range of others – activists, philosophers, militants, psychoanalysts and transgressive literary figures, including French philosopher Manon Garcia speaking about the trial of Gisèle Pelicot – leaves things open to interpretation. “One reason I feel so strong when I’m on stage is because I’ve found the right way to communicate it, versus trying to confess these things in a literal sense. When I’m telling [the audience] how these events still hurt me today, and they’re watching me hurt myself in real time, they’re watching that injury in a very tangible way.”While Piss try to provide as many access points to their music as possible, it is, at every level, deeply uncomfortable. When I describe their twisted instrumentals as “gross”, drummer Garreth Roberts says, “That’s Ty’s [guitarist Tyler Paterson] favourite word!” Zantingh’s voice jolts unpredictably from soft spoken-word to chainsaw shriek. All lyrics and samples (which they consider a reading list) are also prominently subtitled in their videos, for accessibility and so the subject matter doesn’t take a backseat to the visuals. “I’d like to be able to print them out so people can have them at the shows – almost like a little programme, like when you go to church,” says Zantingh.‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reuniteRead moreIn the queue before the gig, a number of men were sniggering about the name Piss. I wonder whether the band feel their music is always met on its own terms. Zantingh recalls seeing two older men at the front of a festival set. “When I was doing the trigger warning they were like, ‘Woke!’ and then walked off,” she says with a weary smile. “The irony is they probably need that show more than most people there, but I accepted early on that the people I want to play the set for might not be the people I can have the most impact on.”On the precipice of a debut album release through one of the most revered independent labels, Piss find themselves contemplating an uncertain future. “Part of the reason we waited so long to release the record is because I don’t know, and I have never known, how long I’m gonna be able to physically and emotionally do this,” Zantingh states plainly. “I spend my life trying to turn my pain into something beautiful,” she screams on I Wanted to Be a Singer.“The foundation of Piss is built on my suffering,” she continues. “We literally cannot exist the way that we exist if you remove that.” That might be unsustainable in the long run, but for now, she says, “it’s exactly what it’s supposed to be”.You Made Me / Skin on Linen is released via Sub Pop on 30 October. Pissare atBrighton Psych fest on 4 September, End of the Road on 6 September and then tour North America and EuropeInformation and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsMusicPunkRape and sexual assaultPerformance artinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sex symbol in a 70s tank top: how Richard O’Sullivan blazed a trail for funny, frisky, cheeky chappies  | Television | The Guardian
description: The star of Man About the House scored an unprecedented run of hit series during the 70s and 80s, bringing a youthful vitality that audiences – and tabloids – loved
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: The star of Man About the House scored an unprecedented run of hit series during the 70s and 80s, bringing a youthful vitality that audiences – and tabloids – loved
Content: Liberated times … O’Sullivan at the time of Man About the House.Photograph: Fremantle Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLiberated times … O’Sullivan at the time of Man About the House.Photograph: Fremantle Media/ShutterstockTelevisionSex symbol in a 70s tank top: how Richard O’Sullivan blazed a trail for funny, frisky, cheeky chappiesThe star of Man About the House scored an unprecedented run of hit series during the 70s and 80s, bringing a youthful vitality that audiences – and tabloids – lovedRichard O’Sullivan, star of 70s sitcom Man About the House, dies aged 82Dandies, docs and robbers: a life in picturesMark LawsonFri 4 Sep 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHaving started as a child actor – first appearing on screen aged seven – Richard O’Sullivan, who has died aged 82, went on to a major TV career playing still relatively youthful characters, representative of the social and sexual freedoms that grew from the liberations of the 1960s.Between 1972 and 81, he appeared in more than 100 episodes of peak-time ITV comedies as funny, frisky men in their 20s and 30s. The first of these was Dr Lawrence Bingham in the hospital sitcom Doctor in Charge, radiating a cheeky charm that led to his career-defining casting as Robin Tripp in Man About the House, in the mid-70s and its spin-off, Robin’s Nest, a few years later.double quotation markMan About the House spawned a formidable franchise, from Robin’s Nest to George and MildredIn the first, Robin shared a flat with two young single women: Chrissy (Paula Wilcox) and Jo (Sally Thomsett). The living arrangements were platonic, partly to appease the TV regulator – from whom formal approval had been sought to show a “mixed” house – but also to establish a sexual tension unusual in mid-evening shows. In the sequel, Robin had qualified as a chef and, again daringly for the TV times, was living with a woman to whom he was not married.View image in fullscreenDandy highwayman … O’Sullivan in Dick Turpin.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockThe attractiveness of screen actors has become a contentious question amid valid concerns about performers being objectified for looks rather than talent. But O’Sullivan had both – with a role in the Richard Burton-Elizabeth Taylor movie Cleopatra, a Hollywood career at one point seemed possible. But, as remained the case from Poldark in the last millennium to the Poldark remake in this one, casting has often been calculated to make viewers fantasise. In Man About the House, O’Sullivan, Wilcox and Thomsett offered something for every viewer, as long as they were heterosexual.Indeed, a running gag in Man About the House was that Robin was gay, a ruse designed to neutralise the living arrangements in the eyes of their landlords (Brian Murphy and Yootha Joyce as George and Mildred), although the humour depended on Robin projecting randy straightness.View image in fullscreenSexy persona … in Doctor in Charge.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockThe sexiness of O’Sullivan’s onscreen persona – that even the period male fashion for knitted tank tops did little to dampen – was helped by reports of relationships with female co-stars and front page red-top newspaper coverage when Tessa Wyatt, O’Sullivan’s onscreen girlfriend in Robin’s Nest, left her then husband, DJ Tony Blackburn, to replicate the role off-screen.Man About the House spawned probably the most formidable franchise in British TV, with Robin’s Nest running alongside Murphy’s and Joyce’s own spin-off, George and Mildred. Core audiences of tens of millions for O’Sullivan’s two instalments gave him an audience-drawing power on which ITV was keen to continue to capitalise, casting him as another telegenic rebel, a legendary highwayman, in Dick Turpin, which ran from 1979 to 82.Approaching his 40s as that series ended, O’Sullivan faced the challenge of moving on from representing the fun of the young. Although the title of Me and My Girl in the 1980s flirted with offering more of the sitcom same, his character in this was a grey-haired widower and the female lead his teenage daughter, played by Joanne Ridley. The impact of this programme was helped by unusually short gaps between series due to fears that Ridley would age faster than the teenager she was playing.When Me and My Girl ended, O’Sullivan had starred in five successive hit series, with the recognition and wealth that such exposure brings. Sadly, there was to be little more of either. Due to declining health, O’Sullivan’s final screen credit was in 1996 and, after a stroke in 2002, he was cared for at the admirable Brinsworth House entertainers’ retirement home in London.A career ended by ill-health would be a misfortune for any performer but a small consolation in O’Sullivan’s case is that an actor who specialised in projecting youthful vitality and energy remains forever so on rerun channels.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV comedyComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like a tired boxer, battered by applause’: as Andrew Scott’s biopic premieres, Richard Eyre remembers Ian Charleson’s superb, near-death Hamlet | Telluride film festival | The Guardian
description: In 1989, the Chariots of Fire actor took on the incredible task of playing Shakespeare’s prince while terminally ill from Aids. This weekend sees the world premiere of Elsinore, a new film about the episode, itself heavily-tipped for awards
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: In 1989, the Chariots of Fire actor took on the incredible task of playing Shakespeare’s prince while terminally ill from Aids. This weekend sees the world premiere of Elsinore, a new film about the episode, itself heavily-tipped for awards
Content: One of the finest Hamlets seen on stage … Ian Charleson in an earlier version of the play, on tour with the Cambridge Theatre Company in 1974.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyView image in fullscreenOne of the finest Hamlets seen on stage … Ian Charleson in an earlier version of the play, on tour with the Cambridge Theatre Company in 1974.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyTelluride film festival‘Like a tired boxer, battered by applause’: as Andrew Scott’s biopic premieres, Richard Eyre remembers Ian Charleson’s superb, near-death HamletIn 1989, the Chariots of Fire actor took on the incredible task of playing Shakespeare’s prince while terminally ill from Aids. This weekend sees the world premiere of Elsinore, a new film about the episode, itself heavily-tipped for awardsNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentFri 4 Sep 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIan Charleson was one of the finest actors of his generation and an important figure in the fight for gay rights. Yet the extraordinary circumstances of his final performance as Hamlet, just months before his death, are less familiar.Now, a new film is bringing that haunting production back to life. Elsinore, directed by Simon Stone and starring Andrew Scott as the Scottish actor, will premiere at Telluride this weekend beforeopening the London film festival in October.Charleson was 40 and terminally ill with Aids when he was cast as Hamlet in Richard Eyre’s 1989 production at the National Theatre, after Daniel Day-Lewis abruptly left the role. Charleson had first played Hamlet 15 years earlier and persuaded Eyre to let him reprise it, despite the director’s misgivings about his health.“Ian was very bright, very witty, mischievous,” Eyre told the Guardian. “He was beyond good-looking. He was beautiful, and he had a beautiful singing voice.”Eyre remembered sitting with Charleson in the National’s canteen a year earlier, when the actor was starring in Cat on a Hot Tin Roof. “He said, ‘I’m hungry for the big Shakespeare roles’. So when Dan had his breakdown” – Day-Lewis believed he saw the ghost of his father onstage – “I thought, I will approach Ian. We met, and then I realised Ian was was very ill. But I thought I will go with him anyway.”View image in fullscreen‘I realised he was very ill’ … with Lindsay Duncan in Cat on a Hot Tin Roof.Photograph: Alastair Muir/Rex FeaturesThe cast, crew, and audience were told that Charleson’s face was swollen after a sinus operation. In reality, he was suffering from septicaemia, enduring painful acupuncture during rehearsals and, later, chemotherapy.“Ian’s beautiful face was actually deformed by the disease,” Eyre said. “But I just thought, he is determined, and I felt determined, and it was sort of an act of love for a friend. Most people told me I was absolutely insane. The press were characteristically loathsome in their probing. I just stubbornly stuck to my decision. In retrospect, it was the right one. He was heroic, and utterly brilliant in the part.”View image in fullscreen‘He was beyond good-looking’ … Charleson at the Chariots of Fire opening.Photograph: Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection/Getty ImagesThe production ran for six weeks and was widely regarded as one of the finest Hamlets seen on stage. The day after Charleson’s last show, Ian McKellen refused the Evening Standard award for best actor and gave his statuette to Charleson instead.Charleson died on 6 January 1990, eight weeks later, having asked that Aids be recorded as the cause – an unusually public act at a time when the disease was feared and stigmatised.Eyre has written of how fitting it was for Charleson to play Hamlet in the last months of his life. “Do you think I can go on as Hamlet looking like this?” Charleson asked him. “You’ll get better,” Eyre replied. “We have to be positive,” Charleson said.“Hamlet is a poem of death,” Eyre wrote. “It charts one of the great human rites of passage – from immaturity to accommodation with death. Hamlet grows up, in effect, to grow dead.”Born in Edinburgh in 1949, Charleson trained at the Bristol Old Vic. He played Eric Liddell in Chariots of Fire, which won four Oscars including best picture, and also appeared in the following year’s best picture winner, Richard Attenborough’s Gandhi.Charleson seemed to have all the ingredients of a major film career: he was handsome, charismatic and intelligent, with a formidable technical ability. Yet his film career never took off as expected. Instead, he repeatedly returned to the stage, performing Shakespeare, Tennessee Williams, Chekhov, Sam Shepard.Michael Billington, the Guardian’s former chief theatre critic, remembers Charleson as Eddie in Shepard’s Fool for Love at the Cottesloe in 1984. Initially unconvinced by his interpretation, Billington later came to remember the performance for its “mixture of masculinity and sensitivity”. Charleson performed Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, he said, with “the same blend of supposedly contradictory qualities: athleticism and delicacy”.View image in fullscreenBest-known role … as Eric Liddell in Chariots of FirePhotograph: Moviestore/REX/ShutterstockCharleson was gay at a time when being openly so could damage an actor’s career. Diagnosed with HIV in 1986, he took part in Before the Act, McKellen’s 1988 anti-Section 28 gala, alongside Judi Dench, Vanessa Redgrave and Stephen Fry.Scott,who played Hamlet150 times in London in 2017, has found himself returning to the role while portraying the actor who performed it at the end of his life.“The idea that Ian was doing this when he was so sick is still, to my mind, just completely mind-blowing,” Scott told People. “And his decision to do it was just incredibly courageous.”Scott said he was moved by “the opportunity to play a part that Ian and his contemporaries would not have gotten while they were working actors.”He added: “I wanted people to be able to understand that he was trying to live – it’s not about fetishising his death. He was so full of life and fun, and he did this extraordinary thing.”View image in fullscreen‘He looks like Ian, and he touches the heart like Ian’ … Andrew Scott in Elsinore.Photograph: Photo by Anthony Dickenson - © 2026 - Focus FeaturesCritics and industry insiders are heavily tipping Scott for a best actor Oscar nomination following early praise for his performance. Eyre called it “brilliant”. “He looks like Ian, and he touches the heart like Ian,” he said.Charleson’s most celebrated performance was never preserved on film. What remains are recollections, photographs and accounts of an actor performing with extraordinary intensity while his body failed him.Eyre recalled that Charleson had flu and missed two nights, but felt guilty: “If they pay you, you should turn up.” His final, Monday night performance, Eyre wrote, was “like watching a man who had been rehearsing for playing Hamlet all his life. He wasn’t playing the part, he became it.”At the curtain call, Charleson stood “like a tired boxer, battered by applause”.A few weeks before he died, just before Christmas, he wrote to Eyre: “One day when I’m better I’d love to attempt Hamlet again, and all the rest; and together we can revitalise Shakespeare. Anyway I hope this is not a dream and I can’t tell you how much of a kick I got out of doing the part, if only for the short time I could …”Explore more on these topicsTelluride film festivalRichard EyreAndrew ScottnewsShareReuse this content

title: Queer Edward II review – funny, touching time capsule of Derek Jarman at work | Movies | The Guardian
description: Venice film festival: Filmed during the making of his queer royal feature, while the director was living with HIV, the candid footage includes uproarious scenes at a Cliff Richard rehearsal
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Venice film festival: Filmed during the making of his queer royal feature, while the director was living with HIV, the candid footage includes uproarious scenes at a Cliff Richard rehearsal
Content: Beaming patrician authority … Derek Jarman in Queer Edward II.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalView image in fullscreenBeaming patrician authority … Derek Jarman in Queer Edward II.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalMoviesReviewQueer Edward II review – funny, touching time capsule of Derek Jarman at workVenice film festival: Filmed during the making of his queer royal feature, while the director was living with HIV, the candid footage includes uproarious scenes at a Cliff Richard rehearsalPeter Bradshawin VeniceFri 4 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere could hardly be a more vivid time-capsule film about the publicly funded British arts scene in the early 1990s than this engrossing fly-on-the-wall documentary about Derek Jarman and his movie Edward II. Based on the play byChristopher Marlowe, it is about the 14th-century English king and his love affair with his court favourite, Piers Gaveston, with Steven Waddington and Andrew Tiernan as the leads and Tilda Swinton as Queen Isabella.This film uses the tremendously funny and candid making-of footage shot at the time by Seamus McGarvey, who had worked as a camera assistant on earlier Jarman films War Requiem and The Garden, and whose distinguished career as a cinematographer lay ahead. Jarman emerges as an effortless leader with a beaming patrician authority, rather like David Lean or Richard Attenborough, the kind of chief whom subordinates instinctively wish to please while keeping from him the grubby problems that they themselves have to deal with, such as paying quarrelsome extras or handling tabloid press questions. Jarman had had his HIV diagnosis for five years at this stage, managing the situation with meds which McGarvey’s camera notices.Jarman’s tightly budgeted movie was composed in the formalised theatrical setpiece style that Peter Greenaway favoured in the same period; he intended a radically confrontational piece of Brechtian queer cinema, reinventing the Marlowe play as a movie insurgency against homophobia, Section 28, the (declining but still present) indifference to HIV/Aids research, and age-of-consent inequality. Jarman used Peter Tatchell’s OutRage! protesters as extras in the movie studio, effectively making the film and the street protests part and parcel of each other. This was to lead to one of the most bizarre and chaotic footnotes in British movie history, amusingly shown here in all its uproarious craziness: the OutRage! shock troops stormed into the studios next door where Cliff Richard happened to be rehearsing, demanding that he out himself.The “outing” debate now in fact looks very dated and this is the one moment where you can sense that Jarman thinks that the OutRage! protesters got it wrong by harassing and bullying Cliff Richard; we see him assuring his own team later that Tatchell gave them a real telling off for this. (Did Tatchell actually do anything of the kind? Or is that what Jarman felt ought to have happened?) It’s an absorbing and affecting portrait of a dedicated artist at work.Queer Edward II screened at theVenice film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsDerek JarmanChristopher MarlowePeter TatchellLGBTQ+ rightsVenice film festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m used to doing the impossible’: George Lucas unveils new LA museum – what’s its story? | Museums | The Guardian
description: Spaceship-shaped gallery, featuring works from Banksy, Norman Rockwell and Frida Kahlo, is devoted to ‘visual storytelling’ – and is finally ready to open
Author: Matthew Cantor
Headline: Spaceship-shaped gallery, featuring works from Banksy, Norman Rockwell and Frida Kahlo, is devoted to ‘visual storytelling’ – and is finally ready to open
Content: The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art aims to be a testament to visual storytelling across all kinds of media – paintings, comics, murals, photography, sculpture.Photograph: Courtesy Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtView image in fullscreenThe Lucas Museum of Narrative Art aims to be a testament to visual storytelling across all kinds of media – paintings, comics, murals, photography, sculpture.Photograph: Courtesy Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtMuseums‘I’m used to doing the impossible’: George Lucas unveils new LA museum – what’s its story?Spaceship-shaped gallery, featuring works from Banksy, Norman Rockwell and Frida Kahlo, is devoted to ‘visual storytelling’ – and is finally ready to openMatthew Cantorin Los AngelesFri 4 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m used to doing the impossible,”George Lucassaid on Wednesday. But “this one almost broke my will”.The film-maker was describing the decades of work that went into his latest project, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, as it was unveiled to the press inLos Angeleseight years after breaking ground, following attempts to build it in two other cities. Shaped like a spaceship and towering over the nearby University of Southern California – Lucas’s alma mater – the long-awaited institution finally opens on 22 September. It aims to be a testament to visual storytelling across all kinds of media – paintings, comics, murals, photography, sculpture.The result is 100,000 sq ft of gallery space featuring a striking variety of pieces, ranging from works by Judy Baca,Norman Rockwell, Diego Rivera and Banksy to the Wizard of Oz’s Cowardly Lion costume to drawings of Asterix and Garfield. What unites the seemingly disparate works is their function: to tell a story, often in a single frame, as Lucas’s co-founder and wife, Mellody Hobson, told members of the press on Wednesday.Visual storytelling “is the art that surrounds us”, said Ryan Linkof, the museum’s senior curator. “It is the art in the visual history that we assume every day, often without even realizing it. Newspaper photographs, advertisements, book covers, comic books, posters, street art, movies.”View image in fullscreenGeorge Lucas and Mellody Hobson, the founders of the Lucas museum.Photograph: Deanna Templeton/Courtesy of Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtThe couple sees this storytelling as fundamental to the human experience. Narrative art “depicts the myths that anchor us, the stories that we believe in”, Hobson said; pictures, Lucas added, make those myths feel real. All that “creates a group of people with a common belief system, and that common belief system allows them to work together and not kill each other”.The Lucas museum is divided into two sections, one containing most of the galleries and a pair of cinemas, and the other housing its mural collection as well as a research library. With its sleek, flying-saucer-like design, it’s impossible not to think ofStar Wars, though the museum’s architect, Ma Yansong, says he was inspired more by tree canopies and clouds. A plaza between the sections offers shade as well as an oculus: a round opening that allows visitors to “see the sky and the universe”, Yansong told the media.The museum’s construction is a saga of its own. Lucas began collecting art in the 1970s and over the years combined his collection with Hobson’s, Bates said. About 20 years ago, according to Bates, Lucas began working toward the museum’s creation. Plans for it to be built in San Francisco or Chicago fell through. Finally, the project broke ground in Los Angeles in 2018, and eight years later, it is ready to open. LA, Hobson told the media, is “where we believe we were always meant to be”. Bates agreed: “The largest, most popular form of narrative art is cinema. So what better space for it to be than the home of storytelling?”View image in fullscreenThe Robert Flaherty theater in the Lucas museum in Los Angeles.Photograph: Lou Caltabiano/Courtesy Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtThe ground floor features a brief tour through thousands of years of visual storytelling, beginning with an immersive reproduction of cave paintings before moving to paintings, mosaics and sculptures – some original, some reproduced – depicting stories from ancient civilizations and the Bible. The exhibition sets the historical context for the museum’s core collection, mostly from the 20th and 21st centuries, reached via round glass elevators that do nothing to dispel the Star Wars aura.The galleries here are sorted into an odd mix of categories. There are rooms that focus on medium – the comics room contains strips from Krazy Kat, Little Orphan Annie, The Adventures of Tintin and Superman; the children’s stories room contains art from Where the Wild Things Are and fairytale illustrations; the manga room features Astro Boy and a portrait of Pikachu.Other rooms are divided by theme: the “community” area contains neighborhood scenes by Ernie Barnes and aFrida Kahloself-portrait; the “childhood” area hosts a Margaret Keane painting, Children of Paris, and a Picasso drawing titled Little Girl; “civic life” features photography of a 1968 sanitation workers’ strike and a painting by Shepard Fairey and Ernesto Yerena Montejano opposing immigration raids.View image in fullscreenThe Critic’s Corner by renowned African American artist Ernie Barnes.Photograph: Matt Kroening/Courtesy Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtStill other galleries are organized by single artists – NC Wyeth, Jessie Willcox Smith, Maxfield Parrish – and others by genre: science fiction, fantasy, adventure. And while this is very much not a Star Wars museum, it has plenty to offer fans, including an exhibit that focuses on modes of transportation in the films and contains vehicle models, production artwork and costumes. (There are other surprise nods to the films around the museum.)Finally, there is the mural room, with some of the museum’s most memorable pieces. A video traces the length of Judith Baca’s mural of the region’s history along the Los Angeles River; nearby are several Banksy works on walls that have been extracted and hung in the space. There’s also a huge image of the French artist JR’sKikito, an installation that shows a child looking over the US-Mexico border wall.Each work has a small plaque giving its title and year, the artist’s name and the materials used. But there isn’t much else on the walls to tell visitors what they’re viewing – no blurbs or lengthy descriptions. That was deliberate, Linkof said. Lucas and the curators didn’t want a “heavily mediated” experience, telling people “where to look, how to look, what to think, how to understand and interpret something”, he said. “We’re encouraging people to have their own individual encounters with works of art and take away what they feel like speaks to them.” That said, those who are curious about a work’s origins or context can scan the images with their phone to get a brief description of who made the work and why.View image in fullscreenRafael Navarro’s Sonámbulo: Mexican Stand-Off.Photograph: Courtesy Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtMany of the artists here are well-known, but as the museum’s leadership emphasizes, they often don’t receive the same institutional respect their peers do. John Romita Jr’s Spider-Man panels don’t tend to appear in museums that also feature the Sistine Chapel ceiling, re-created here with backlit photography. “Rockwell in his day was not considered an artist, more an advertising illustrator, but actually, the process, the level of depth in those images – he is one of our greatest storytellers,” said Tracey Bates, the museum’s CEO, in an interview. With the museum, Lucas and Hobson – who call the Sistine Chapel “God’s first comic book”, Bates says – hope to elevate the standing of these visual storytellers.“How many of us here in this room have learned to face our fears because of the work of Maurice Sendak, or learn moral lessons while studying EH. Shepard’s drawings of the 100 Acre Wood?” Bates asked. “George calls it the People’sArt, and this museum is its home.”Explore more on these topicsMuseumsLos AngelesArtGeorge LucasStar WarsCaliforniaBanksyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Many of us in Israel live in a state of shock at the savagery’: veteran director Amos Gitai returns to Gaza | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: The writer-director once called Israel’s ‘one-man New Wave’ is in Venice with The Road to Jericho, a new and poetic attempt to highlight the plight of those in the occupied West Bank
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: The writer-director once called Israel’s ‘one-man New Wave’ is in Venice with The Road to Jericho, a new and poetic attempt to highlight the plight of those in the occupied West Bank
Content: ‘Everything has been destabilised and we are now in the hands of people who don’t want peace’ … The Road to JerichoPhotograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalView image in fullscreen‘Everything has been destabilised and we are now in the hands of people who don’t want peace’ … The Road to JerichoPhotograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalVenice film festival‘Many of us in Israel live in a state of shock at the savagery’: veteran director Amos Gitai returns to GazaThe writer-director once called Israel’s ‘one-man New Wave’ is in Venice with The Road to Jericho, a new and poetic attempt to highlight the plight of those in the occupied West BankXan Brooksat the Venice film festivalFri 4 Sep 2026 07.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 08.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Palestinian village of Khan al-Ahmar sits off dust-blown Highway-1, between Jerusalem and Jericho in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. At the village centre is the “school of tires”, a fragile construction of rubber, wood and adobe which is attended by around 300 Bedouin boys and girls. The Israeli authorities denied the villagers an official building permit and ruled that the entire settlement is illegal. For the past eight years the school has been operating under threat of imminent demolition, a symbol of resistance to widespread settler violence.View image in fullscreenAmos Gitai arriving at the Venice film festival, 3 September 2026.Photograph: Laurent Vu/Sipa/ShutterstockIt is only international pressure, says the veteran Israeli writer-director Amos Gitai, that has kept the place upright and still open. “The school has become a litmus paper. It is a test of how far the international community will go [to protect the rights of the people of Khan al-Ahmar]. For once, on this issue, Europe stood up and said no.” As for the future, who can tell?Khan al-Ahmar’s “school of tires” provides an anchor of sorts for Gitai’s The Road to Jericho, a fluid, haunting documentary that elects to frame fraught recent history as a great tidal churn. In tackling the issue of the occupied West Bank, 75-year-old Gitai is also exploring his own role as a ringside observer and frequent commentator, delving back through the bulging back catalogue of a director who the critic Michael Atkinson dubbed “Israel’s one-man New Wave.” His film stirs a documentary portrait of the school with ghostly footage from the past 40 years. So we see a clip of the playwright Arthur Miller from Gitai’s 2001 drama Eden, plus archive interviews with Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Rabin during the golden false dawn of the mid-90s Oslo accords.The future, Gitai admits, looked altogether brighter back then. The wise heads, by and large, have since left the building. “The killing of Rabin [in 1995 by a far-right Israeli law student] decapitated the efforts to create a dialogue,” he explains. “Rabin was very simple, very sober. He wanted an agreement and was prepared to put all the questions on the table and discuss them [because he knew that] you cannot force an agreement. An agreement has to be agreed upon.”And now? “That’s all gone,” he says flatly. “Everything has been destabilised and we are now in the hands of people who don’t want peace, whether it’s extreme-right settlers or Hamas. So this is, absolutely, the worst time I’ve known in my life. Many of us in Israel have been living these last three years in a state of shock at the levels of violence and savagery we are seeing.”View image in fullscreen‘I consider my work as a civic gesture’ … Gitai in 2005.Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianThe Road to Jericho is one of several pictures at this year’s Venice film festival that explicitly focus on the Middle East. NAZA, aco-production with the Guardianthat plays in the main competition, spotlights the Israeli military’s role in the mass killing of Palestinian civilians. Raj’in (We Shall Return), a VR documentary about ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, is a harrowing highlight of the Venice Immersive section. The Road to Jericho, though, is something else again. It’s more akin to a tone poem in that it is elliptical, deeply felt and about as far from polemic as political cinema gets.“I consider my work as a civic gesture,” Gitai says. “I make films when I’m moved or disturbed by something – that’s always the trigger.” He first visited Khan al-Ahmar while shooting another picture, 10 years ago, and was touched by the perseverance and dedication of its Bedouin community. “I wanted to use film-making to defend the school,” he says.He is wary, though, of films that deal in certainties and set out with a clear, laser-focused agenda. “I don’t believe art changes reality,” he says. “That was never the case. What art can do is scratch a memory – and that’s important. Machine guns and money move the world, but so do ideas. And cinema is a great vessel for ideas.”View image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA, a documentary by the Guardian directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianIn Field Diary, his 1982 documentary aboutGazaon the eve of the Lebanon War, the director interviewed Bassam Shakaa, the then-mayor of Nablus. Shakaa was confined to a wheelchair, having lost a leg in an attack by Israeli settlers. Gitai asked him whether he considered himself an optimist or a pessimist. “Pessimism is a luxury we cannot afford,” Shakaa said.More than 40 years on those words resonate more than ever. “I don’t know if I’m an optimist,” Gitai says. “That would be a naive thing to say when we see everything that’s going on. But look at Europe 80 years ago – the stage for the killing of millions and millions of people – and it’s a good historical reference. It shows that people can always still come together and reconstruct, even after the horror of the second world war. So you have to preserve hope. Hope and ideas – these are the great motors for change.”Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalFestivalsGazaPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘If you can’t understand what sex is, it’s irrelevant if you seem to be enjoying it’: how Queen at Sea upended the dementia drama | Movies | The Guardian
description: Lance Hammer’s first film in 18 years is a heart-wrenching masterpiece about family, mental decline and sexual consent. He and supporting actor Juliette Binoche discuss how they brought unabashed realism to a condition rarely seen on screen
Author: David Shariatmadari
Headline: Lance Hammer’s first film in 18 years is a heart-wrenching masterpiece about family, mental decline and sexual consent. He and supporting actor Juliette Binoche discuss how they brought unabashed realism to a condition rarely seen on screen
Content: A bone-deep connection … Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall in Queen at Sea.Photograph: © Seafaring LLCView image in fullscreenA bone-deep connection … Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall in Queen at Sea.Photograph: © Seafaring LLCMovies‘If you can’t understand what sex is, it’s irrelevant if you seem to be enjoying it’: how Queen at Sea upended the dementia dramaLance Hammer’s first film in 18 years is a heart-wrenching masterpiece about family, mental decline and sexual consent. He and supporting actor Juliette Binoche discuss how they brought unabashed realism to a condition rarely seen on screenDavid ShariatmadariFri 4 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first time we see Martin and Leslie, the elderly couple at the centre of Lance Hammer’s wrenching new film, Queen at Sea, they are walking together up a set of stone steps: one of their regular outings, we assume, in days filled with pottering and quiet companionship. They have their backs to us, and we can’t see their destination beyond a bleached sky that fills the top half of the screen. Symbolically, it may be deemed a bit on the nose: two people near the end of their lives, moving gently towards the white light of oblivion. There’s a whiff of sentimentality about it.But any doubts about this story’s willingness to confront difficult truths are blasted away by the next scene. Leslie’s daughter, Amanda, played by Juliette Binoche, pays a visit to the couple’s house in drizzly, middle-class north London, her teenage daughter in tow. Unable to find her mother and stepfather, she arrives at the bedroom door. Opening it, she finds Martin (Tom Courtenay) on top of Leslie (Anna Calder-Marshall), who lies impassively beneath him, the mask of dementia obvious on her face.Mortified and angry – she’s told him before that their sexual relationship should stop – Amanda calls the police, unleashing a series of upheavals that make for often excruciating viewing. No one in their right mind would countenance the possibility of ongoing, nonconsensual sex. But neither would anyone look approvingly on the cold, hard edge of officialdom as it slices through the family’s status quo, leaving Leslie confused and frightened. As we see her disoriented by physical separation from her partner and learn more about their relationship, the audience is forced to hover between two contradictory perspectives.
