It’s a deeply uncomfortable experience.Ambiguity, however painful, is exactly what the film’s director was aiming for. “We weren’t trying to convey a moral position,” says Hammer. “We were trying to say that this is a story with a lot of confusing parts, and we want you to experience it and come to your own conclusions.” Hammer is briefly in London on his way to the Edinburgh International film festival, having landed from LA the night before, and we meet in the mercifully cool Curzon offices on one of the hottest days of the year. The 59-year-old, who trained as an architect and had a career as an art director on big-budget movies, is thoughtful and reserved (“it’s very alien to me”, he says of the process of promoting the film, his first in 18 years), but he’s adamant that the narrative shouldn’t come down clearly on either side. “I just don’t think that’s my role as an artist. My job is to question things, to present something that’s complicated and let the viewer consider it more deeply than they would have.”He does, however, have strong personal feelings about the central dilemma: “I think Amanda’s absolutely right to bring in the institutions. But she doesn’t know what she’s getting into, because how can you?” Has Martin committed a crime, in his view? “Martin loves Leslie, and he’s a human being so maybe he’s living in denial, or he hasn’t been able to see the steps of erosion [of her mental capacity] because he’s so in it. You know, it’s like boiling a frog; he may not fully understand the peril she’s in, and what consent means any more. He’s just operating the way they always have their whole life, and they’ve loved each other deeply.”View image in fullscreenCourtenay and Calder-Marshall jointly accept the Silver Bear for best supporting performance at the Berlinale film festival.Photograph: Ralf Hirschberger/AFP/Getty ImagesThat love is powerfully expressed in Courtenay and Calder-Marshall’s remarkable performances, for which they were jointly awarded a Silver Bear at this year’s Berlinale film festival; Calder-Marshall’s portrayal of the particular bewilderment of dementia will be recognisable to anyone who has seen it in a loved one. Their own bond lends emotional depth to the dynamic – this is the first time they’ve worked with one another since playing Hamlet and Ophelia in 1968. Though they had fallen out of contact for decades, “their souls are entwined in some way”, Hammer says, and it seems real rather than mawkish. “When I was casting Annie, I had a list of people I didn’t know, so I asked Tom because he’s worked with everybody. When he got to Annie’s name, he said: ‘Annie! It has to be Annie. Cast her right now.’” Together, they convey an intimacy borne of a bone-deep understanding, which extends to even minute gestures and changes in expression.The difficulty comes as that understanding begins to crumble, unevenly and unpredictably. “If there’s any chance at all that you could be putting her in danger and she can’t communicate it, then you just have to stop the action,” says Hammer. But as the fallout from Martin’s behaviour and Amanda’s call continues, the characters grapple with a cascade of problems: whether or not to place Leslie in a care home, how to protect her once she’s there, whether to sell houses, change jobs, upend their lives. These are choices many will recognise from first-hand experience, but not, strangely enough, Hammer. Neither of his parents have dementia. “This isn’t from my own life,” hesaid in an interviewearlier this year. “It’s just a moral dilemma that riveted me.”Queen at Sea review – crushingly sad dementia drama offers a startling portrait of intimacyRead moreView image in fullscreenCommunication breakdown … Juliette Binoche and Courtenay.Photograph: © Seafaring LLCThat’s not the case with Binoche. On the phone from Paris, where she’s shooting a film with Turkish director Berkun Oya, she tells me she has a parent with “a sort of dementia, not exactly Alzheimer’s”, and has herself been trapped in the classic pincer movement between the demands of one generation and another. “I remember one time I stood up in the middle of the night thinking: how am I going to deal with this?” she says. “One is going to the tomb, and the other one is [experiencing] all the teenage needs, feelings and emotions. I felt caught in a situation I had no control of.”“I admire people who stop everything and take care of their parents if they can. The thing is, usually we cannot because we’ve got to work, we have kids, we’ve got to run, and so we’re taken aback by the changing needs of older people. Suddenly, you realise you’ve got to submit yourself to a system that is not made for human beings.”Binoche’s view of the sexual question at the heart of the film is also subtly different from Hammer’s. “I mean, Lance answers yes: it was wrong. You know, he’s very clear about that. Me personally, it’s very difficult because you feel they’re a couple, and also because she initiates those needs.” (Later in the film, we discover that Leslie often solicits sexual contact.) “I would say, like Lance, you have to protect somebody who’s not fully himself or herself. At the same time, you wonder [about it]. And that’s what the film is doing.”So what does the law actually say? In England and Wales, the Sexual Offences Act of 2003 makes sexual activity illegal if someone is “unable to refuse because of or for a reason related to a mental disorder” – which includes dementia – and if the healthy partner could be expected to know this. The capacity to choose whether to agree to sex can ebb and flow in someone with dementia – a diagnosis doesn’t by itself mean they cannot consent, and guidance suggests that the consent doesn’t have to be verbal. According toDementia UK: “If the person living with dementia responds positively and with obvious enjoyment when their partner makes sexual advances, there is every reason to believe they are consenting to sex. Alternatively, if their responsiveness, enjoyment or willingness diminishes, this could be an indication that they do not consent to sex, and this should be respected.”All of which is easy enough to put down in writing, but seems impossibly difficult to adjudicate in practice. And whileAlex Ruck Keene, a barrister specialising in mental capacity, agrees that dementia doesn’t automatically mean sex can’t be consensual, “if you simply don’t have the ability to understand what a sexual act is, then it’s completely irrelevant that you appear to be enjoying it”.He continues: “For a long period of time it has been recognised that the law is really not satisfactory, because you’ve got two totally competing policy objectives. One is: consent must mean consent. I mean, we fought for that for years.” The other is to avoid interfering in lawful sexual expression. In the kind of case presented in the film, “if it doesn’t appear to be that the husband is taking advantage of the wife, if it appears to be mutually pleasurable with no power imbalance, it feels weird to then say: ‘Well, the husband’s doing something wrong.’” In practice, where there is a complaint by a family member, the police may find it impossible to gather reliable evidence of an offence, making prosecution difficult. A local authority may, however, determine that safeguards – for example, stopping unsupervised contact – need to be put in place.View image in fullscreenLance Hammer accepts the Silver Bear jury prize at this year’s Berlinale film festival.Photograph: Arturo Holmes/Getty ImagesFor Hammer, getting the procedural stuff right was vital, but the process was thrown into confusion when funding fell through, and a movie originally set in the US had to be reworked for Europe. “I researched it for a US scenario,” he says. “But when we got to the UK, the institutional response is different.” He leaned heavily on experts to help fine-tune the script – so much so that some ended up acting in the film. “They were brought on as consultants for research, and so I talked through the scenes with them. We’d sit down in the workshop space and say: ‘OK, here’s the way the scene’s written. Is this accurate?’ And they’d say: ‘No, it would be like this.’”He was particularly keen to capture the officialese used by police, sexual assault referral centre staff and social workers, and which marks such a stark contrast with the family environment. “I wanted their language,” he says. “It’s a very specific idiom and so I needed that from them, because I can’t write it. I also knew I secretly wanted to cast them if they seemed like they could do it, and so I did.” Marie-Elle Vooijs plays a sexual assault clinician, her real job; likewise social worker Jean Pemberton. “It took a little persuading, but they all wanted to [play these roles] in the end.”View image in fullscreenUpending … Juliette Binoche and Anna Calder-Marshall.Photograph: © Seafaring LLCFor Hammer, making Queen at Sea – for which he won the 2026 Berlinale’s Silver Bear jury prize – has been a long, slow process, but one he felt compelled to see through. This is his first film since 2008, when his debut, Ballast, won the directing award at Sundance. Why has there been such a huge gap between projects? (He tells me he’s supported himself in the meantime by making investments and doing the occasional architectural project.) “It was just hard to find films to make that I cared about, and that I can also make a living doing. I stopped because it was not possible.” Does he have any qualms about returning with such a painful story? “When this subject came up, I realised it was dark and bleak, but there’s meaning in it because a lot of people are experiencing this.”It’s an understatement to say that the end of the film doesn’t offer audiences much in the way of solace. But Hammer is unapologetic. “When you make a choice to pursue a subject, you’re limited by it, and this is the subject. I didn’t want to make it sentimental and heartwarming because that’s not truthful, and with a lot of films about dementia that’s the tactic,” he says. “So then the question is: can I make the most truthful thing that’s possible, and with the most beauty, the beauty [coming from] true loving relationships and compassion for the characters? That’s the goal. If you can manage that, you can make a film that’s maybe worth watching.”Queen at Sea is released in the UK on 18 September, and in the US on 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsDementiaTom CourtenayMental healthHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Latcho Drom director Tony Gatlif dies aged 77 | Movies | The Guardian
description: Film-maker acclaimed for his celebrations of Roma culture had been working on a ‘historical film project’ in Provence
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Film-maker acclaimed for his celebrations of Roma culture had been working on a ‘historical film project’ in Provence
Content: Tony Gatlif in 2025.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTony Gatlif in 2025.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesMoviesLatcho Drom director Tony Gatlif dies aged 77Film-maker acclaimed for his celebrations of Roma culture had been working on a ‘historical film project’ in ProvenceAndrew Pulverand agenciesFri 4 Sep 2026 09.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 09.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTony Gatlif, the French director of more than 20 films that mostly concentrated on celebrating Roma culture across the world, has died aged 77.His family said in a statement to AFP that Gatlif died on Wednesday of “a health issue” while working on a “historical film project” in Arles in Provence,France. “The beauty of his films, his generosity, his joy, his poetry, and his love of music will remain with us forever.”The statement, from his wife, children and grandchildren wished him “Latcho Drom”, a Roma phrase meaning “safe journey”.Latcho Drom is also the title of Gatlif’s breakthrough 1993 film, a celebration of Roma music that moves from India to Spain, and which won the Un Certain Regard award at the Cannes film festival that year.Gatlif had more success in 1997 with Gadjo Dilo, which featured Romain Duris as a Frenchman who is searching for a Roma singer in Romania; it won a Silver Leopard at the Locarno film festival and a César award for best original music.View image in fullscreen‘His joy, his poetry, and his love of music will remain with us forever’ … Latcho Drom.Photograph: Handout/HANDOUTGatlif was born Michel Dahmani in 1948 in Algeria, of part Berber and part Roma heritage. He left Algeria for France in 1960 during the Algerian war of independence and had a tough life as a rootless teenager, telling AFP: “I used to be violent; you didn’t want to mess with me; I was a bad kid … I wouldn’t listen to anyone; to me, adults – everyone – were enemies.” He changed his name to Gatlif, after a park in Algiers, after being stopped by the police as a 12-year-old.Among his later films,Exils, also starring Duris, explored his Algerian heritage, and won the best director award at Cannes in 2004.Catherine Pégard, France’s minister of culture said that Gatlif “had a fondness for the road less travelled, for blurring borders, and for lives that too often go unnoticed”. She added: “He filmed music, movement, exile, and freedom with an energy that was uniquely his own.”Explore more on these topicsFilmFranceRoma, Gypsies and TravellersEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar | Games | The Guardian
description: As one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousands
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousands
Content: Single Pokémon cards for sale, locked in a cabinet.Photograph: Daniella LucasView image in fullscreenSingle Pokémon cards for sale, locked in a cabinet.Photograph: Daniella LucasGamesThieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soarAs one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousandsDaniella LucasFri 4 Sep 2026 05.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePokémon’s success over the last 30 years has seen it grow from a much-loved Game Boy classic, to a world-dominating brand with TV shows, spin-off games, toys and even a theme park. The trading card game is a huge part of that, with more than85bn cardsprinted over its lifetime, and the appetite for them shows no signs of slowing down. Packs get snapped up after release so quickly it’s nowalmost impossible to find them in shops, and a booming resale market is driving the hobby into murky waters.One card recently sold for aneye-watering £12m, and an increasing number of people have gotten into the collecting business on the hunt for huge profits, leading toa rise in thefts targeting card shops. More recently though, some small businesses have reported that their sales have been hit by thieves targeting envelopes within Royal Mail, leading to thousands in lost revenue.Ben Thyer, owner of Bath TCG – a card specialist store in the Bath area, is one of those affected. “We always get the odd parcel going missing, but because it was sporadic, we put that down to unfortunate incidents,” Thyer tells the Guardian. “Then [in late July], we had a message [from a customer] with pictures of a cut-open envelope, and the cards were missing. Then there was a second, and then a third, and then there were seven – all of them from the same batch shipped on the same day. We asked for images from each person, and every envelope had been Sellotaped … we don’t use Sellotape because we have brand new envelopes, and we use our own labels over the seals. It’s clear someone had done it deliberately.”View image in fullscreenBath TCG - an independent shop specialising in trading card games.Photograph: Daniella LucasThe images, seen by the Guardian, show that the mailed envelopes were tampered with in the exact same way. Thyer considers it clear that this was a targeted theft rather than a coincidence. Fortunately, those particular cards weren’t of high value, but he has since had to close down online card sales, considering the risk of theft and damaged reputation to his business to be too high. By stopping those sales he has now lost out on £4,000-6,000 of potential revenue, a huge amount for a small business.Bath TCG is not the only card sales business to be affected, and the issue is not just affecting Pokémon cards. Daniel Stack, director of Mana Rock Games – a specialist in selling Magic: The Gathering cards – has also had issues withRoyal Mailitems going missing. His business is also based in Bath and was affected over similar dates to Bath TCG’s.“I realised it was theft when two customers in different parts of the country sent me pictures of their packages already open with the contents missing, within minutes of each other,” Stack said. “We’d previously had one sent to France turn up the same way a couple of weeks before, but I put it down to the buyer taking a bit of a chance that I’d have no way to hold them to account for pretending there had been an issue. In total we’ve had about £120-worth stolen so far – we had previously sent over 1,200 orders without any issues.”View image in fullscreenSome of BathTCG’s stock.Photograph: Daniella LucasStack also halted online sales for a week, costing him £500 in revenue. Other sellers in the area havementioned similar problemsto him. Unfortunately, as most card businesses in the UK useCardMarketto sell online, it’s the buyer who picks the delivery method, and most often they use Royal Mail services. Cards are often sent in distinctive hard-backed envelopes to protect the contents, often with shop branding on stickers or seals.Royal Mail is investigating the issue and liaising with the affected businesses. A spokesperson told the Guardian: “The safety and security of mail is a top priority and we take any reports of theft very seriously. We investigate concerns thoroughly and take action where necessary, including working with law enforcement.” Investigations are still ongoing; in the meantime, businesses must choose between risking theft and damaged reputation for their stores, or halting online sales and losing revenue.With a new, highly sought-after 30th anniversaryPokémoncard set due to release this month, retailers are already anticipating an increase in scalper and reselling activity, leading to even more potential for thieves to target those selling cards online. We asked the Pokémon Company for comment on how they’re dealing with increased demand and the rise in thefts, but they have yet to respond.Explore more on these topicsGamesPokémonCrimeRoyal MailnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Joe Lycett broadcasts live from an East End pub – what could possibly go wrong? | Television | The Guardian
description: The fully licensed comedian welcomes punters and celebrity guests to his brand new boozer. Plus: a courtroom showdown in The Rainmaker. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: The fully licensed comedian welcomes punters and celebrity guests to his brand new boozer. Plus: a courtroom showdown in The Rainmaker. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Pints of view … Joe Lycett in Live from the Lycett Arms.Photograph: Matt Crockett/Channel 4/PAView image in fullscreenPints of view … Joe Lycett in Live from the Lycett Arms.Photograph: Matt Crockett/Channel 4/PATV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Joe Lycett broadcasts live from an East End pub – what could possibly go wrong?The comedian and aspiring landlord welcomes punters and celebrity guests to his brand new boozer. Plus: a courtroom showdown in The Rainmaker. Here’s what to watch this eveningAli Catterall,Hannah J Davies,Priya Elan,Phil Harrison,Hollie RichardsonandSimon WardellFri 4 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLive From the Lycett Arms10pm, Channel 4In a bid to celebrate and save pubs, Joe Lycett is opening an East End boozer. The goings-on inside the Lycett Arms will be broadcast live for an hour every Friday, as the new landlord welcomes celebrity managers and guests, as well as familiar punters. This could go anywhere – Lycett failed to complete the exam needed to obtain an alcohol licence and issued a plea for help on Instagram. Let the chaos begin!Hollie RichardsonMarin Alsop’s Pick of the Proms7pm, BBC FourThe American maestro – who, infamously, was namechecked in Cate Blanchett’s Tár – talks about being the first female conductor to lead the Last Night of the Proms, in 2013, and discusses her favourite moment of this season: pianist Yunchan Lim’s opening-night performance of Ravel’s Piano Concerto.Priya ElanYou’re Killing Me8pm, U&DramaAnother fun murder mystery to solve with boomer Allie (Brooke Shields) and gen Z Andi (Amalia Williamson). When a car dealer is found dead in his garden, the crime-solving duo recognise similarities to a murder from Allie’s first novel. Will it lead them to the killer?HRThe Marlow Murder Club9pm, BBC TwoThe two-part mystery that began last week concludes. And things are as hair-raising as they ever get in this cosy crime context: there’s clearly going to be another murder unless the team can prevent it, so Tanika takes a gamble and recruits a group of civilian advisers. Will they be too late?Phil HarrisonThe RainmakerView image in fullscreenWrongful death suit … Lana Parrilla and  Milo Callaghan in The Rainmaker.Photograph: FlixPix/Alamy9pm, ITV1Not just a doppelganger for OG Rainmaker Matt Damon, British actor Milo Callaghan also ably leads this highly watchable US legal drama. This week sees Rudy (Callaghan) discover some unlikely evidence for the wrongful death suit, before a courtroom showdown opposite ex-boss Leo (Mad Men’s John Slattery).Hannah J DaviesGrimsburg12.15am, Sky OneWhen useless nepo baby Otis is forced into the, well, force after pressure from the mayor, a horrified Flute (Jon Hamm) concocts a series of ever more extreme schemes to “crush a rich kid’s dreams”. Meanwhile, a cold-ridden Harmony takes too much of Marvin’s “special cough syrup” and conjures up her son’s imaginary skeleton friend, Mr Flesh (Alan Tudyk).Ali CatterallFilm choiceHarvest (Athina Rachel Tsangari, 2024),11.05pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenField of nightmares … Harvest.Photograph: © Jaclyn Martinez/Harvest Film LimitedAthina Rachel Tsangari’s adaptation of Jim Crace’s novel is shot like a homage to 1970s British folk horror films – complete with Wicker Man-style animal masks and rituals. But the horror turns out to be more economic and social than supernatural. In an unnamed rural Scottish village, the diffident Master Kent (Harry Melling) rules benignly over the agricultural workers, including his former servant, the reserved Walter (Caleb Landry Jones). But then Kent’s cousin (Frank Dillane) arrives with plans to enclose the common land and raise sheep. The inequities of power, and the way the dispossessed can blame outsiders for their lot, come to the fore in a brooding, earthy tragedy.Simon WardellLive sportWomen’s Super League Football: London City v Man United,6pm, Sky OneThe season kicks off at Copperjax Community Stadium, with London’s star signings including two-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best recent poetry – review roundup | Books | The Guardian
description: Fetch by Colin Bramwell; Girling by Eve Esfandiari-Denney; The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber by Jay Gao; Belling the Leopard by Clementine Ewokolo Burnley; The Matter by Padraig Regan
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fetch by Colin Bramwell; Girling by Eve Esfandiari-Denney; The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber by Jay Gao; Belling the Leopard by Clementine Ewokolo Burnley; The Matter by Padraig Regan
Content: Jay Gao’s poems embody a tree’s form in The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber.Photograph: Jackyenjoyphotography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJay Gao’s poems embody a tree’s form in The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber.Photograph: Jackyenjoyphotography/Getty ImagesPoetry roundupBooksReviewThe best recent poetry – review roundupFetch by Colin Bramwell;  Girling by Eve Esfandiari-Denney; The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber by Jay Gao; Belling the Leopard by Clementine Ewokolo Burnley; The Matter by Padraig ReganOluwaseun OlayiwolaFri 4 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenFetchby Colin Bramwell(And Other Stories, £14.99)Bramwell’s translation of Fernando Pessoa’s work into Scots won him considerable recognition: it took the Oxford Weidenfeld Translation prize and the Highland Book Prize. Between source and target language, there is always a gap; the translator endeavours within that gap to identify meaning and intention, and that is the difficult work of translation. Fetch, Bramwell’s own debut collection, lyrically thematises this gap in the poet-human’s condition: “I’m an instrument for something else / a digital piano that if you opened it up / you wouldn’t understand the wiring.” Fetch (in Celtic folklore, a doppelganger) is by turns solemnly tender, comically worldly, literarily devout. Here you’ll find deep engagement with Russian poets such as Osip Mandelstam and AnnaAkhmatova, poems that fuse Scots and English, alongside filial memories and premonitions of fatherhood. “Death is certain, but back then I was too young for that shit.” For a debut, Bramwell’s poetics convey an uncanny sense of wisdom, patience and, eventually, peace.View image in fullscreenGirlingby Eve Esfandiari-Denney(Fitzcarraldo, £12.99)Before theme and subject, there is the pure, iridescent beauty of Esfandiari-Denney’s sentences; a singular voice that is alluring and sensuous, pleasurable to follow to whichever subject the poet chooses. The subjects are girlhood-cum-womanhood, the line between debilitating illness and delusional wellness (“thank god / you invested / in lion’s mane”), the flickering concept of free will for a species so programmed by genes: “I have wondered to what extent my cancer diagnosis is my mother’s, or my grandmother’s cell mutation, before my own … I look up from a cigarette mid-sentence…” The collection hybridises recognisable prose forms: the essay, the diary, the text message, the anecdote. These are interspliced with short-lined lyric poems that startle because of the bubbly voice from which they come: “I hope it’s ok to die. I can / become something / like actualised metaphor.” The magic of this collection is that it is never highfalutin, finding a way to make an ending like “DJ are you listening did you read to the end will you blow my voice a kiss” powerfully funny and moving.View image in fullscreenThe Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumberby Jay Gao(Carcanet, £12.99)“This is how the buried live. Poetry”. The title of this collection alone will illuminate what kind of poet Gao is: insistent, sprawling, and conceptually daring. The poems in this collection are notspokenby a tree, but rather embody a tree’s form, each line like a budding leaf, simultaneously discreet, and genetically preordained by the bark from which it sprouts: “Mustering diction in the interest of the non-human”; “On the horizon, a filthy war dog shakes her remaindered vernal atoms free”; or, one of my favourite lines, “You wanted the intimacy of two words who shared a sound to unsecure that wild”. Every couple of pages there are “splinters”, single words with ultra-long dashes that could grammatically and sonically replace a word in the preceding line: “A splinter of duration lodged inside times’ ruche, awaiting salvage …” is followed by a page-long em-dash before the word “selvedge”. Gao joins the ranks of poets such as CD Wright and Lyn Hejinian: not for the faint of heart, but an endless well of brilliance and deep feeling if one can undergo their clause-by-clause compressive inventions.View image in fullscreenBelling the Leopardby Clementine Ewokolo Burnley(Bloodaxe, £14)There’s an imaginative heaviness to Belling the Leopard, so composed of the proper names of people, places and things that each poem feels like a constructed miniature: “Liberated Africans, Jamaicans, and English / missionaries lived side by side in eight / corrugated iron shelters shipped / from Clarence.” The forced migrations and enslavement of colonialism create a latticework of place across the collection, which is Burnley’s primary structuring principle. Between the Caribbean, western Africa and western Europe, Burnley describes the intimate violence and domestic and cultural fallout of their comingling histories: “All the flights from Africa used to transit through a European capital city. Ethiopian Airlines no longer touches down in the nine hours it takes to fly from Turtle Island to Togo. Sometimes the border agencies use commercial flights for deportations.” At times, this debut collection feels overwritten, certain narratives more like onslaughts of information and impression with little effect. It is at its best when memory and lyric fuse, where the line between recounting and reshaping blurs: “We rub each other raw in the same spots / and if you’re starting to lose / arguments, I notice I no longer need to win.” There’s much to admire here.View image in fullscreenThe Matterby Padraig Regan(Carcanet, £12.99)Regan’s sophomore collection echoes the structure of their first: lyric poem sequences with a long(ish) essay splitting up the sections. Here, they intensify their engagements with the material world, “chiefly animals, minerals and vegetables”. Lines from the poem A Venus Flower Basket sum up the stylistic changes Regan has made, from parsed syntactical lines to more high-octane fragmentations: “Drowned Arachne! / except: what it spins / it is. & who wouldn’t / want to wear their bones / on the outside / if they could sparkle”. Elsewhere, the poet addresses Gogotte, a naturally occurring “concretion of very fine, very pure sands”, primarily found in France. Gogotte has a way of looking like finely sculpted ceramic work, allowing the poet to drift from the geological to musings on the body’s evanescence, gay saunas, and language itself: “I am a poet, Gogotte: I spend my life trying to come up with verbal structures commensurate with the unstructurable mess of being-in-the world.” Though the collection can feel unevenly motley in some aspects, Regan has a knack for startling detail and lush description, as in the poem A Belemnite: “An off white seam runs jagged / down its length / like an injury; // its surface is a register / of glances & impacts / against whose grain I read the // long, posthumous biography”. This voice can be spellbinding.Explore more on these topicsBooksPoetry roundupPoetryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Faces of Death review – rework of notorious video nasty turns horror voyeurism into moral panic fable | Movies | The Guardian
description: A retelling of the 1978 ‘video nasty’ follows an online content moderator faced with steadily more appalling footage but reverts to generic bloodletting
Author: Mike McCahill
Headline: A retelling of the 1978 ‘video nasty’ follows an online content moderator faced with steadily more appalling footage but reverts to generic bloodletting
Content: Content warning … Faces of Death.Photograph: Brian Roedel/LegendaryView image in fullscreenContent warning … Faces of Death.Photograph: Brian Roedel/LegendaryMoviesReviewFaces of Death review – rework of notorious video nasty turns horror voyeurism into moral panic fableA retelling of the 1978 ‘video nasty’ follows an online content moderator faced with steadily more appalling footage but reverts to generic bloodlettingMike McCahillFri 4 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmerging amid the original 1970s home-rental boom, John Alan Schwartz’s 1978 film Faces of Death was an ultra-morbid extension of the so-called “mondo” genre. Mashing up gruesome footage – much of it faked, some of it legit enough to provoke ghoulish chatter – it achieved sleepover notoriety and then received a further publicity boost upon making the DPP’s “video nasty” list. What comes now, nearly half a century later, is less a reboot than postmodern rethink. Daniel Goldhaber, who broke through with2022’s tense social-activism thriller How to Blow Up a Pipeline, has patched some of the original’s images into a more conventional digital-age horror narrative that initially resembles an American equivalent of Prano Bailey-Bond’sCensor: a film worrying away at what our ravenous eyes now consume and how good it can really be for us.A thoroughly committed Barbie Ferreira plays Margot, a pill-popping content moderator sequestered within a tech firm’s faceless HQ, attaching appropriate warnings to user-generated footage. Off the clock, she’s dogged by memories (and viral footage) of a horrendous train-track trauma; her workload, meanwhile, gets even more challenging after repurposed Faces of Death clips creep on to her watchlist in pristine HD. Her supervisor (Jermaine Fowler) insists she should wave these through, as DIY horror is doing excellent numbers, but the situation intensifies once it becomes clear that a masked bad guy (Dacre Montgomery) is staging his own remake, involving real victims. More bodies drop, more pills are popped; and the project’s underlying intelligence, alas, begins to turn against itself.The film’s stronger stretches gesture towards rigorous critique: consumers glued to bloodied screens, egging one another on, egged on in turn by conscience-free CEOs. This astute commentary has been packaged, however, within a bog-standard commercial horror format, easier to digest and forget about: straight-ahead kill scenes framed in Scream-like quotation marks, glib supporting characters mouthing dialogue such as “the internet … is fast”. Had he held his nerve, Goldhaber might have updated not just Faces of Death but 1986’sHenry: Portrait of a Serial Killer, that unblinking indictment of video-age voyeurism. Instead – perhaps steered by producers keen to keep the TikTokers on side – he tips us reassuring winks, letting everyone off the hook. Whether real or fake, grim or goofy, everything gets flattened into content.Faces of Death is on digital platforms from 7 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the churning darkness of Barcelona producer Nueen and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Nacho Pezzati’s new album Swerved taps into the moody ambience of the UK north-west underground, ratcheting a tangible and thrilling sense of unease
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Nacho Pezzati’s new album Swerved taps into the moody ambience of the UK north-west underground, ratcheting a tangible and thrilling sense of unease
Content: Tangible unease … Nueen.Photograph: PR IMAGEView image in fullscreenTangible unease … Nueen.Photograph: PR IMAGEAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the churning darkness of Barcelona producer Nueen and the week’s best new tracksNacho Pezzati’s new album Swerved taps into the moody ambience of the UK north-west underground, ratcheting a tangible and thrilling sense of uneaseHugh Morris,Ben Beaumont-ThomasandLaura SnapesFri 4 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromBarcelona, SpainRecommend if you likeSpace Afrika, Shackleton, PurelinkUp nextSwerved out nowSwerved, by Barcelona-based producer Nueen (Nacho Pezzati) is a bassy, moody, darkly ambient album that travels through R&B, drill, cloud rap and dub without any obvious changes in its grey-black weather. But this is slowly churning music, on the brink of rot. By the 10th track, Copicat, the unease is tangible; after a slow, agonising ratcheting build of fanbelt hi-hats, the album’s only drop arrives with the weight and power of a cloudburst. It’s thrilling.Swerved follows Nueen’s 2024 Hyperdub debutYou Said You’d Hold My Hand Through the Firewith rapper Iceboy Violet, and fans of thenorth-west undergroundwill recognise many of its themes. On Atmosphere Is My Style, a drawling Loraine James touches on the dislocation and confusion heard in Rainy Miller’s music. Two tracks featuring Manchester’s RenzNiro hit swaggering and confessional notes, similar to his recent album No Weapon Shall Prosper, and Swerved as a whole feels bathed in the humid ambience of Space Afrika. Nueen synthesises all these approaches, and takes stock, before breaking new ground.The paths he heads down are guided by impressive vocal features. Cloud rapper XzavierStone pulls the sound in an Auto-Tune R&B direction on two tracks, and Baltimore singer Dawuna moans through the hot’n’heavy highlight Shm, which sounds like a lost D’Angelo joint. (Check out the latter’s Bandcamp-onlyAfrican Family Laptop Musickfor more.) Nueen breaks into new territories for an established sound without disrupting an album’s subtle cycles: through heating, simmering, and cooling.Hugh MorrisThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenCandid … Ceebo (right) and Blanco.Photograph: Finn HarneyCeebo x Blanco – Gets Like DatTwo British MCs on rich, riveting form: the flows are as energised as a club track but the beat is mournful, as each of them gets candid about the fear and paranoia of failing in the rap game.BBTKali Malone – Heavy With FruitThe heady Colorado composer jettisoned theory for intuitive emotion on her new album, recorded on the organ at Bach’s resting place. Heavy With Fruit flickers like embers, the dying molten core of something.LSKiko Mizuhara– Feelin’ WeeJohn Carroll Kirby lays down puckish, squelchy keys under the Japanese-American actor-model’s cheeky song about love’s elusiveness, synths pinging to life like daisies bursting at warp-speed through the earth.LSCorto.alto – Noblehill (ft Jacob Alon)Mercury-nominated for his 2024 debut, the Scottish jazz artist closes out his new album Some Small Fortune with this extraordinarily deft ballad, Jacob Alon swooping through a pattering rainshower of strings, piano and breakbeats.BBTDiiv – Kid“Everyone is a little kid,” Zachary Cole Smith whispers on fragile shoegaze that – despite producer AG Cook’s synth toybox puckering away in the background – invites a typically cosy, satisfying kind of wallowing.LSPiss – Time Loop at Hot SlitThe uncompromisingly named Vancouver punk band make good on signing to Sub Pop, singer Taylor Zantingh howling “women don’t come” over thrashing guitar and drums that viscerally stumble under their own weight.LSSilvan Strauss – That’s Who?!? (Fast Barista)Fans of Squarepusher’s electro-skronk opus Music is Rotted One Note will thrill to the Hamburg drummer’s joyous new LP Sprinting, with acid jazz played with the breakneck pace and brittle funk of Chicago footwork.BBTSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Chat Pile: Who Loves the Sun review – sludge metallers resurface with a slightly limiting alt-rock rebrand | Punk | The Guardian
description: The Oklahoma band use hooky vocals to help their lyrics on desensitisation slip down easy, though their third album lacks the distinction of earlier releases
Author: Alastair Shuttleworth
Headline: The Oklahoma band use hooky vocals to help their lyrics on desensitisation slip down easy, though their third album lacks the distinction of earlier releases
Content: Approachable … (from left) Raygun Busch, Cap’n Ron, Luther Manhole and Stin of Chat Pile.Photograph: Ryan LawsonView image in fullscreenApproachable … (from left) Raygun Busch, Cap’n Ron, Luther Manhole and Stin of Chat Pile.Photograph: Ryan LawsonPunkReviewChat Pile: Who Loves the Sun review – sludge metallers resurface with a slightly limiting alt-rock rebrand(The Flenser)The Oklahoma band use hooky vocals to help their lyrics on desensitisation slip down easy, though their third album lacks the distinction of earlier releasesAlastair ShuttleworthFri 4 Sep 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChat Pile’s 2022 debut albumGod’s Countrywas monstrously, miraculously fully formed. The Oklahoma sludge-metal quartet’s oily guitars and grunting mid-tempo percussion conjured their namesake, mining toxic waste mounds, while Raygun Busch’s throat-shredding vocals drew from the city’s real-world violence. But their releases since, from album-offcut tape experiments Blood at Night to In the Earth Again’s team-up with finger-picker Hayden Pedigo have promised another evolutionary stage.View image in fullscreenChat Pile: Who Loves the Sun album coverThe brighter alt-rock of Who Loves the Sun is a partial rebrand, foregrounding a love of XTC teased in the jangly riff of 2024’s Funny Man. Compared to previous albums-proper God’s Country and 2024’s Cool World, the structures are more dynamic, the guitars twangier and the vocals hookier, while Busch’s lyrics zoom out from American violence to the abstract horrors of desensitisation: “Scrolling past the screaming,” he seethes on Influence.Chat Pile smartly tie this concept to the album’s approachability. Intruder’s sprightly groove, melodic chorus and rubbery guitar solo let Busch sneak in his most frightening allegory for systemic violence, a home-intruder cutting someone in their sleep. There’s also a pleasing eclecticism, between the trip-hoppy Same Rules and Shrine’s swingy post-rock leanings.But the overall direction, a straightforward softening of their early ugliness, disappoints. Other roads were open: film score Tenkiller signalled their avant garde potential, sometimes channelling Scott Walker’s Bish Bosch, while In the Earth Again’s melancholic singer-songwriter tracks promised untapped emotional depths. Chat Pile remain stuck between their debut and something equally distinctive, but there’s enough here to renew faith they’ll get there.Explore more on these topicsPunkalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Vista, Saarikoski Songs, Three Preludes album review – Saariaho’s iridescent visions evocatively rendered | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Three works by the idiosyncratic Finnish composer who died in 2023 are recorded for the first time
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Three works by the idiosyncratic Finnish composer who died in 2023 are recorded for the first time
Content: Ear-catching…  Kaija SaariahoPhotograph: Emmi Korhonen/Lehtikuva/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEar-catching…  Kaija SaariahoPhotograph: Emmi Korhonen/Lehtikuva/AFP/Getty ImagesClassical musicReviewVista, Saarikoski Songs, Three Preludes album review – Saariaho’s iridescent visions evocatively renderedKomsi/Nyman/BBC Symphony Orchestra/Oramo(Ondine)Three works by the idiosyncratic Finnish composer who died in 2023 are recorded for the first timeClive PagetFri 4 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKaija Saariaho died in 2023, leaving behind a significant body of unrecorded music. The three works here, all premiere recordings, span 40 years, yet each bears the Finnish composer’s idiosyncratic fingerprints.The most substantial is Vista (2019), a tone poem inspired by a drive along the scenic Interstate 5 highway to San Diego. The first part, Horizons, opens with a lingering oboe duet before brass, winds and gleaming tuned percussion usher in more piquant colours. This is music on cruise control, with otherworldly washes of strings and a deal of ear-catching incident. Targets, which follows, is altogether more dynamic, a turbulent road trip that winds down to a serene conclusion. Fellow Finn Sakari Oramo is a sensitive, sure-footed guide with the BBC Symphony Orchestra commendably precise and texturally detailed throughout.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Kaija Saariaho: Saarikoski Songs, Vista, Three Preludes.The Saarikoski Songs, heard here in the 2021 orchestrated version, are evocative settings of five poems by Pentti Saarikoski chosen in part for their focus on humanity’s impact on the natural world. Anu Komsi, a longtime Saariaho collaborator, is thoroughly idiomatic, her stratospheric soprano soaring over the iridescent orchestral weave. She’s equally authoritative in 1981’s Three Preludes for soprano and organ (Saariaho’s own instrument) where Marzi Nyman handles the angular instrumental lines with aplomb.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: The must-see Bayeux masterpiece, Colombia’s chronicler and a Manchester odyssey – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The Bayeux tapestry arrives, the Americas go mainstream and modern, and Manchester threads its way to Korea and India
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The Bayeux tapestry arrives, the Americas go mainstream and modern, and Manchester threads its way to Korea and India
Content: All human life and more … the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Isogood_patrick/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAll human life and more … the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Isogood_patrick/ShutterstockArt Weekly newsletterArt and designThe must-see Bayeux masterpiece, Colombia’s chronicler and a Manchester odyssey – the week in artThe Bayeux tapestry arrives, the Americas go mainstream and modern, and Manchester threads its way to Korea and India –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 4 Sep 2026 07.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekThe BayeuxtapestryBlood and thunder, friendship and betrayal, marginal monsters and raw sex – all human life and more is depicted in this medieval artistic masterpiece that tells an epic national story with unrivalled punch and power.British Museum, London, from 10 September until 11 July 2027Also showingEmma ReyesA look back at this Colombian painter who brought the subaltern cultures of the Americas into the mainstream of modern art.White Cube Mason’s Yard, London, until 3 OctoberJimmy WrightThere’s an alluring tint of Van Gogh’s Sunflowers to this artist’s recent works.Thomas Dane Gallery, London, until 1 OctoberCatherine MurphyTough no-nonsense realism is taken to the point of surrealism in Murphy’s paintings.Sadie Coles HQ, London, until 7 NovemberEntangled and WovenIf the Bayeux tapestry makes you wonder how textile art is faring, here’s a show threading that theme from India and Korea to Manchester.Whitworth, Manchester, until 3 January 2027Image of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Temi AdegbayibPhotography began as a hobby for Temi Adegbayibi after he started photographing his cousin’s band Ezra Collective. But perseverance, confidence, skill and talent has seen the 26-year-old’s work – which captures the movement, intimacy and joy of performing, particularly in his images of Black musicians – exhibited at the Royal Albert Hall. The photograph above shows Adegbayibi “trying to capture the energy of a drum solo”.Read more hereWhat we learnedAn Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace was stolen in a smash-and-grab raidJackson Pollock’s Blue Poles sparked one of Australia’s most enduring culture warsWilem Frischmann, one of architecture’s most daring engineers, has died aged 95The theft of Renaissance art by Messina from a Sicilian museum baffled investigatorsWoo Jin Joo uses London junk to bring a spirit of playfulness to the art worldThe graffiti artist Helch, who has died, left an indelible mark on high-rise BritainVisitors to Nostell, in West Yorkshire, will be able to watch cutting-edge research on a rare painting of Thomas MoreSculptor Maurizio Cattelan, who had his golden loo stolen and $6m banana eaten, is bringing Hitler and a pope to BerlinMasterpiece of the weekThe Story of David and Goliath by Francesco Pesellino, c 1445-55View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Bruce/© The National Gallery, LondonThis Renaissance painting of conflict was created more than 400 years after the Bayeux tapestry. But for all its greater sophistication and especially its command of the new science of perspective, you can’t really say it is a clearer or more emotionally powerful visual narrative. If anything, Pesellino’s painting is harder to make sense of. Because the Bayeux tapestry tells its tale in a completely linear way, unfolding stage by stage, with no layers of action, it is wonderfully easy to follow. Here, the story’s progress is chaotically clogged with crowd scenes and landscapes in depth. So even though the figures are much more muscled and their faces better drawn, some raw simplicity is lost. At another level, nothing has changed: this is still a medieval artwork from an epoch when horses and battles, castles and armour were the most glamorous themes in art.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It feels like Italy with the volume turned down’: readers’ favourite (smaller) city breaks in Europe | City breaks | The Guardian
description: You share your favourite low-key alternatives to overcrowded hotspots, from an island city in the Med to a Norwegian art nouveau gem
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: You share your favourite low-key alternatives to overcrowded hotspots, from an island city in the Med to a Norwegian art nouveau gem
Content: Piazza Savonarola in Ferrara, Emilia-Romagna.Photograph: Witold Skrypczak/AlamyView image in fullscreenPiazza Savonarola in Ferrara, Emilia-Romagna.Photograph: Witold Skrypczak/AlamyReaders' travel tipsCity breaks‘It feels like Italy with the volume turned down’: readers’ favourite (smaller) city breaks in EuropeYou share your low-key alternatives to overcrowded hotspots, from an island city in the Med to a Norwegian art nouveau gemTell us about your trips in Europe’s mountains– the best wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 4 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRenaissance art without the crowds in ItalyFerrarain Emilia-Romagnawon me over precisely because it feels like Italy with the volume turned down. I stayed in a small family-run hotel nearVia delle Volte, where mornings began with quiet cobbled streets and the smell of fresh pastries. ThePalazzo dei Diamantiwas almost empty when I visited, giving me space to enjoy its Renaissance art without crowds. Evenings meant cycling past terracotta walls to tiny trattorias serving pumpkincappellacci,a traditional pasta dish. It’s a city that lets you slow down, breathe and enjoy its beauty.JohnOne of Germany’s greenest citiesView image in fullscreenThe Great Garden at Herrenhausen.Photograph: DPA/AFP/Getty ImagesNext to flashy Munich or cool Berlin,Hanoverin northern Germany has a reputation of being boring. It is totally undeserved: there are world-class museums, such as the modern art gallerySprengel, one of the best-preserved baroque gardens in Europe – theGreat Garden at Herrenhausen– impressive Victorian era architecture, 640 hectares (1,680 acres) of city forest (the Eilenriede, nearly double the size of New York’s Central Park) and a large artificial lake just south of the centre that you can travel on with a bus ticket (or hire a boat). Explore the city and its surroundings on more than 600 miles of cycle paths, find independent shops in the well-heeled art nouveau district of List or the multiculturalLinden, and relax in a deck chair on Ballhofplatz with tea and cake at theTeestübchen.UlrikeProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The Algarve’s city of craftsView image in fullscreenThe market in Loulé was designed in a neogothic style.Photograph: Cristina Arias/Getty ImagesBursting with Portuguese charm,Louléis 10 miles inland from Faro, capital of the Algarve. The small city has a rich history of preserving traditional crafts, supported byLoulé Criativo, a network of community-driven artisans that keeps alive and celebrates the identity of Loulé and the Algarve. It includes the House of Weaving (Casa da Empreita) and the Watchmakers (Oficina do Relojoeiro) and Stringed Instrument Workshop (Oficina de Cordofones). In these vibrant spaces – where visitors can interact with artisans – the city’s heritage is preserved and passed down through generations.SueUnesco sites in northern FranceView image in fullscreenThe belfry of the Hotel de Ville at Place des Heros in Arras is a Unesco world heritage site.Photograph: Aliaksandr Antanovich/Getty ImagesArras, 35 minutes on the train from Lille, has two Unesco world heritage sites: thebelfry of the Hotel de Villeand theVauban Citadel. Exploring theBoves, a 10th-century network of tunnels which played roles in the first and second world wars, is an amazing experience. Above are two magnificent large squares in the Flemish style with a wide variety of alfresco cafes, restaurants and indie shops. Arras also holds one of the biggest Christmas markets north of Paris, noted for its amazing range of international gourmet foods.Bryan BoeseArtistry and cake in Sweden’s beautiful southView image in fullscreenPoints of View, the 2017 sculptures by Tony Cragg, outside the free Malmö Konsthall arts centre.Photograph: Danita Delimont/AlamyMalmöis easily accessible (being connected by bridge to Copenhagen) and very walkable. We enjoyed the freeMalmö Konsthallarts centre with contemporary exhibitions and also the skateboard artistry in the square outside. TheWestern Harbourcontains architectural gems, such as the twisted skyscraperTurning Turso, restaurants and swimming piers in a former industrial area. The cafeHollandiaoffered classic Swedish cakes and a lovely atmosphere. TheDisgusting Food Museumnext door was an interesting cultural experience showing food considered to be delicacies in some countries, not so much in others. A sign shows the number of people who have thrown up (visit Hollandia first)!ElisabethBrilliant beach and seafood in SardiniaView image in fullscreenThe beautiful sandy beach of Poetto.Photograph: S Parente/Best of Travel/RM/AlamyIf you can tear yourself away from Poetto – surely one of the prettiest city beaches in Europe – you’ll find a lot more to love inCagliari, capital of Sardinia. The huge indoor produce market is a riot of glistening seafood, local pecorino and sweet, nutty Sardinian treats. The town centre strides uphill from the port, with the elegant bulwark ofBastione St Remydelineating the ancientCastello districtand serving up epic rooftop and coastal views. We missed the renowned archaeological museum, but that just gives us the perfect excuse to go back. Cagliari’s affordable seafood was a definite highlight, andTrattoria Lillicu’s chargrilled bream and calamari is another tempting reason to hurry back.Marthaskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStained glass wonder in north-west SpainView image in fullscreenThe windows of the cathedral in the city of León are simply breathtaking.Photograph: Around the Corner Pics/AlamyInLeón, colours grab your attention and take away words.León cathedralcompletely wrongfooted me. This city seems to be under the British tourist radar. I thought I’d already seen stained glass that was worthy of heaven – this was another level. Coupled with this was how visitors were reacting. Everyone was using the free audio guide. No one was just marching round and ticking off the sights. People were learning and savouring the experience. The humble ninth-centurySan Isidoro church, one of the most important romanesque buildings in Spain, is a refreshing contrast.DeborahNorway’s art nouveau gemView image in fullscreenThe art nouveau waterfront of Ålesund.Photograph: Rudi1976/AlamyÅlesundis one of Norway’s most beautiful stops on an already spectacular western coast, despite having been devastated by fire in 1904. We reached the small, rebuilt art nouveau city via the breathtaking winding roads of the Trollstigen (the “Troll’s Path”) and had our first sighting from the top of the panoramicAkslamountain viewpoint. Exactly 418 steps lead down to the historic centre where museums, cafes, restaurants and shops cluster around the Brosundet Canal in renovated warehouses and ornate buildings. Kayaking, a rib boat ride or a trip to the stunningGeirangerfjord? We couldn’t choose so did them all!Teresa StansbyThe French city with a bit of everythingView image in fullscreenSaint-Malo’s tidal bathing pool.Photograph: Sasha Samardzija/Getty ImagesI spent five days inSaint-Malothis August. It has everything: a beautiful walled city with lots of history, a variety of beaches offering shifts in light and character throughout the day, a modernist tidal pool with a high diving platform. The city has so much pride, and the art inspired by its famous landmarks make for great souvenirs. My favourite thing, though? The wonderful cider at La Passage (onInstagram) with my sister. And despite the heat everywhere else, the temperature never got above 25C.Sophie AmosWinning tip: a watery Dutch master of a cityView image in fullscreenLeiden in the Netherlands is full of canals, squares and cafes.Photograph: Peter Conner/AlamyLeidenstarts badly. The walk from the station is grim. Scruffy bars and vape shops. And then, suddenly, this watery Dutch gem reveals itself. Canals shoot off from a boat-filled basin, each one lined with grand brick mansions tapering to elegant finials under the sort of blue lowland skies that typify every good (and bad) Flemish painting. Dig deeper into its narrow traffic-free courtyards and squares with cafes spilling out light and chatter, much as they did when Rembrandt trudged to the school that still stands here, just round the corner from his first tutor’s studio. He’d find it mostly unchanged if he walked back. At Christmas, an ice rink spreads across the main canal, and the smell of warm wine, cloves and crepes hovers over the market stalls.Bill JonesView image in fullscreenThis article was amended on 4 September 2026 to correct a misspelling of the surname of the sculptor Tony Cragg in a caption.Explore more on these topicsCity breaksReaders' travel tipsEurope holidaysShort breaksCultural tripsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Pignut’s hedgerow highball – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: Thoroughly British, a bit rustic, and very much an early-autumn treat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Thoroughly British, a bit rustic, and very much an early-autumn treat
Content: Pignut’s hedgerow highball.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenPignut’s hedgerow highball.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Pignut’s hedgerow highball – recipeThoroughly British, a bit rustic, and very much an early-autumn treatLaurissa HeywoodFri 4 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis easy, food-friendly drink is built around the flavours of the countryside – sharp apple, local honey, garden herbs – rather than imported citrus. A touch of blackberry gives colour and depth without turning it too sweet, and echoes the kind of preserves and foraged fruit that run through our food menu.Hedgerow highballServes140ml London dry gin– any classic dry one will do50ml cloudy apple juice, ideally a tart one1 tsp local honey1 tsp blackberry jam or preserve2 small sprigs fresh thymeSparkling wine, to top1 blackberry, or 1 thin apple slice, to garnishMeasure the gin, apple juice, honey and jam into a cocktail shaker or jam jar filled with ice, then add the thyme and shake hard for about 10 seconds, so the honey and jam dissolve. Fine strain into an ice-filled highball glass, top with sparkling wine (ideally a local one), garnish with a blackberry or slice of apple, and serve.Laurissa Heywood, co-owner,Pignut & The Hare, Scawton, North YorkshireExplore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodFruitAutumn food and drinkBritish food and drinkWinerecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for brown butter apple and blackberry bars | Food | The Guardian
description: A bar for the bountiful season, with a rubbly oat crust, a soft fruit filling and a crisp topping
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: A bar for the bountiful season, with a rubbly oat crust, a soft fruit filling and a crisp topping
Content: Helen Goh’s brown butter apple and blackberry bars.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s brown butter apple and blackberry bars.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotFoodHelen Goh’s recipe for brown butter apple and blackberry barsA bar for the bountiful season, with a rubbly oat crust, a soft fruit filling and a crisp toppingHelen GohFri 4 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeptember is always a wistful time for me. Summer has all but slipped away, the days are noticeably shorter and the children are heading back to school. But there is comfort, too, in settling back into familiar routines. These bars, with their buttery oat crust, soft fruit filling and crisp, golden topping, are just the sort of thing to have waiting for whenever everyone drifts home. I like to use a mixture of apples – some that soften and collapse into the filling, others that hold their shape – to give the bars a little more texture and interest.Brown butter apple and blackberry barsThese will keep for up to three days in an airtight container, and also freeze well, wrapped individually for convenience.Prep10 minCook1 hr 20 minMakes12 barsFor the crumb base and topping250g unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing1 tsp anise seeds(optional)220g plain flour95g rolled oats80g oat flour, or blitz rolled oats until finely ground150g light brown sugar½ tsp fine sea saltFor the fruit filling750g apples(5-6 medium apples), peeled, cored and cut into 1cm dice (about 600g net weight)80g caster sugarFinely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemon3tbsp lemon juiceSeeds from ½ vanilla bean pod, or ½tsp vanilla bean paste1 bay leaf1 cinnamon stick1 pinchfine sea salt1½ tbsp cornflour300g blackberriesGrease and line a 20cm x 30cm baking tin with greaseproof paper, leaving enough overhang to help lift out the bars later. Put the butter in a medium saucepan on a medium heat and cook, swirling the pan occasionally, for about five minutes, until it smells nutty and the milk solids turn a deep golden brown. Take off the heat, stir in the anise seeds, if using, then leave to cool for five minutes.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Meanwhile, mix the plain flour, rolled oats, oat flour, brown sugar and salt in a large bowl. Pour over the browned butter, including all the toasted milk solids, and mix until evenly moistened. The mixture should resemble damp sand and hold together when squeezed.Reserve about 350g of the crumb mix for the topping, then tip the rest into the lined tin, pressing firmly into an even layer ; use the base of a measuring cup or back of a spoon. This will help the bars hold together neatly when slicing. Bake for 18 minutes, until lightly golden around the edges.While the base is in the oven, make the filling. Put the diced apples, sugar, lemon zest and juice, vanilla, bay, cinnamon and salt in a large, deep frying pan on medium-high heat and cook, stirring occasionally, for five minutes, until the apples have softened slightly but still hold their shape.Mix the cornflour with a tablespoon of water to make a smooth slurry, then stir into the apples. Cook for 30 seconds, until the juices thicken, then gently fold in the blackberries, just long enough for some to soften and colour the apples, while leaving plenty still whole. Discard the bay leaf and cinnamon stick.Spread the fruit evenly over the baked base, then squeeze handfuls of the reserved crumb into irregular clusters and scatter over the fruit. A few gaps are nice so the fruit can peek through. Bake for 40-45 minutes, until the topping is deeply golden and the fruit juices are bubbling around the edges. Leave to cool completely in the tin before slicing into bars.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotBakingFruitSnacksBritish food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content
